stories.title: AI stocks are taking a beating amid inflation, interest rate worries
stories.summary: A sell-off for artificial-intelligence stocks is hitting Wall Street again after whipping around the world on worries about how much longer the AI frenzy will last.
stories.author: Chan Ho-him And Matt Ott
stories.content:
A sell-off for artificial-intelligence stocks is hitting Wall Street again after whipping around the world on worries about how much longer the AI frenzy will last.

The S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent early Thursday, and the Nasdaq composite 1.2 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 269 points. Among tech stocks, Nvidia fell 3.2 per cent and Advanced Micro Devices lost 5.4 per cent. South Korea’s Kospi index sank 7.6 per cent.

The losses came as another report signaled inflation has worsened by even more in the United States than economists expected. Wholesale inflation jumped last month, driven by a big increase in energy costs.

Tech stocks appeared to be headed for another sell-off before the bell with inflation anxiety hammering that high-growth sector ahead of the U.S. earnings season.

Artificial intelligence stocks were down again after taking a beating a day earlier.

CoreWeave, which offers AI computing power to customers over the cloud, fell another 3.8 per cent early after tumbling 15.5 per cent a day earlier, its worst day since February. GE Vernova, which is hoping to electrify power-hungry data centres, dropped 3.2 per cent after a 6.2 per cent decline on Wednesday and Oracle sank 1.6 per cent, adding to its nearly nine per cent loss in the previous session.

Chipmaker and AI darling Nvidia fell 1.6 per cent in early trading, as did Broadcom, while Advanced Micro Devices retreated 3.1 per cent.

The yield on 10-year bonds eased to 5.09 per cent from 5.32 per cent, but remains elevated. Higher bond yields that have made borrowing more expensive could make it more difficult for companies to raise cash to build data centres and fill them with AI chips.

The latest inflation figures showed Wednesday that prices remain well above the Federal Reserve’s two per cent target, putting in play another potential interest rate hike before the end of the year, which also puts pressure on the equities market.

The government’s latest report on wholesale prices, the producer price index, arrives Thursday along with another trove of corporate earnings reports.

Canada’s main stock index, the Toronto Stock Exchange, fell 0.2 per cent early Thursday, with shares in Canadian tech giant Celestica falling close to seven per cent.

In Asia, South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index lost 7.6 per cent to 5,554.22. It plummeted more than 16 per cent over the past month and was well below the 9,000 mark that it crossed in June at its all-time high driven by optimism over the global artificial intelligence frenzy.

Samsung Electronics slid 9.5 per cent and South Korean memory chipmaker SK Hynix plunged 11.1 per cent.

Japan’s Nikkei 225 tumbled 4.9 per cent to 64,425.95. OpenAI investor SoftBank Group lost 9.3 per cent. Chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron dropped 7.8 per cent, and memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings lost 12.3 per cent.

Taiwan’s Taiex, which also benefited from the AI boom, fell 3.4 per cent. Its leading chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., or Tsmc, dropped two per cent ahead of its earnings report. Tsmc reported on Thursday another record profit for the latest quarter, which was better than what analysts had expected, and the company said AI demand remains very strong.

“The problem for heavily technology-weighted markets such as Korea and Taiwan, to a lesser extent Japan, is that any risk to perceived AI spending growth May lead to slower demand growth for chips and equipment,” said Lorraine Tan, director of equity research for Asia at Morningstar.

“The key issue is a possible mismatch between the market’s growth expectations for the tech sector and what May eventuate,” she said.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped one per cent to 24,062.72. The Shanghai Composite index slipped 1.6 per cent to 3,707.48.

Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 edged down 0.1 per cent to 8,719.70.

At midday in Europe, Britain’s Ftse 100 rose 0.7 per cent, France’s CAC 40 gave back 0.3 per cent and Germany’s DAX was down 0.4 per cent.

Oil prices fell as tensions and uncertainties surrounding global oil supply and the situation in the Middle East dragged on. Brent crude, the international standard, declined more than one per cent to US$104.91 per barrel. That’s still elevated compared with the approximately $72 per barrel level before the start of the Iran war in late February.

U.S. crude was up 23 cents a barrel to $95.32.

– with a file from Global News’ Ariel Rabinovitch

stories.title: Supreme Court of Canada to hear appeal of First Nation's Nootka Island claim
stories.summary: Ottawa - The Supreme Court of Canada will hear a case about a First Nation's claim to title over a swath of Nootka Island.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Nuchatlaht First Nation brought a claim for Aboriginal title to about 200 square kilometres of the island, which lies off the west coast of Vancouver Island.

The trial judge found the Nuchatlaht had established title over only portions of the claimed area.

Article continues below

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

The First Nation challenged the decision in the British Columbia Court of Appeal.

In April, the Court of Appeal found the trial judge used an “arbitrary boundary” to determine title.

A three-judge panel of the Appeal Court said the Nuchatlaht identified territory it exclusively occupied and used for hunting, fishing and gathering activities, and presented other evidence that established its “strong presence on or over the land claimed.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

stories.title: Supreme Court to rule on Ottawa’s single-use plastics ban
stories.summary: The Federal Court of Appeal overturned a lower court decision in January, allowing the federal government to keep the ban in place
stories.author: Nick Murray
stories.content:
The Supreme Court of Canada said Thursday it will hear an appeal of Ottawa’s ban on single-use plastics.

In 2022, Ottawa phased in a ban on the manufacturing and sale of six single-use plastic items, including straws, stir sticks, cutlery, takeout containers and the six-pack rings used to hold soda and beer cans.

The government said at the time it chose those items because they were commonly found in litter and had known and accessible alternatives.

In order to introduce the ban, the federal government listed “plastic manufactured items” as toxic under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, following a scientific assessment.

In 2023, the Federal Court said that listing was too broad, in part because the federal government had failed to demonstrate that all plastic items harm human health or the environment.

The Federal Court of Appeal overturned the lower court’s decision in January, allowing the federal government to keep the ban in place. The three-judge panel unanimously ruled the decision to list plastic manufactured items as toxic was reasonable.

They argued the lower court had erred by viewing as one step what was actually a two-step process: designating plastics as toxic under the Act and regulating individual plastic items.

The initial decision to list plastics as toxic was challenged by a group representing companies in Canada’s plastics industry, along with three chemical companies which manufacture plastics.

The plastics industry argued, among other things, that a lack of testing to determine which plastics are harmful made Ottawa’s decision unreasonable.

The Court of Appeal dismissed that argument in January.

“To put the matter bluntly … the chemical content of [plastics] is irrelevant to the sea otter choking on a plastic straw. The problem is the plastic item itself, not its chemistry,” the judges wrote.

stories.title: SeatGeek Canada faces two more fines from Ontario over ticket resale violations
stories.summary: Province’s consumer beware website shows the new fines issued to the ticket resale website earlier this month total $22,500 collectively
stories.author: Tara Deschamps
stories.content:
SeatGeek Canada is facing two more fines from the Ontario government for allegedly contravening a recent law capping the sale of event tickets at face value.

The province’s consumer beware website shows the new fines issued to the ticket resale website earlier this month total $22,500 collectively.

The website says the first of the two fines amounts to $15,000 and is for allegedly making a ticket available for sale or facilitating a sale of a seat beyond the resale price limit.

The second fine is for $7,500 and is for allegedly failing to disclose the total price of a ticket when a seat was purchased from a primary seller.

The province and SeatGeek Canada did not immediately respond to questions about what events the fines stem from or whether the reseller will fight the penalties.

The province previously issued $25,000 in fines to the company in August for similar offences.

stories.title: Death toll unknown after intense fire in fatal Highway 401 crash: OPP
stories.summary: Ontario Provincial Police say an intense fire has prevented investigators from determining how many people died in a multi-vehicle crash on Highway 401 Tuesday.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Ontario Provincial Police say an intense fire has prevented investigators from determining how many people died in a multi-vehicle crash on Highway 401 Tuesday.

OPP said officers were called around 4:03 p.m. on Oct. 13 to the eastbound lanes of Highway 401 near Mill Road in the Township of Southwold for reports of a multi-vehicle crash.

Police said traffic had slowed because of an earlier collision in the eastbound lanes of Highway 401 near Colonel Talbot Road in Middlesex County. A second crash then occurred west of the initial scene and involved two transport trucks and a passenger vehicle.

The vehicle and one of the transport trucks caught fire and quickly became engulfed in flames, police said.

Police described the collision as fatal but said investigators had not determined the total number of occupants or deaths because of the intense fire involving the passenger vehicle.

“The driver of the transport truck was able to exit the vehicle and was not injured. The second transport driver was taken to hospital to be treated for minor injuries,” police said in a news release Wednesday.

Highway 401 was closed for approximately 11 hours while emergency crews investigated.

The investigation remains ongoing.

stories.title: Canada aims for India trade deal by year-end, minister says
stories.summary: The two countries exchanged $30.4 billion of goods and services last year, according to Canadian government data.
stories.author: Bloomberg News
stories.content:
Canada

The two countries want to strengthen economic ties and diversify partnerships amid growing global uncertainty

The momentum to reach a trade deal with India is there, says Canadian International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu.Photo by Anindito Mukherjee /Bloomberg

Canada is looking to conclude a trade deal with India by the end of the year as the two countries look to strengthen economic ties and diversify partnerships amid growing global uncertainty.

Negotiators from India and Canada began a fifth round of talks from Oct. 5, building on discussions that concluded last month. Prime Minister Narendra Modi is expected to visit Canada in December and sign a completed trade deal.

“The momentum is there, the energy is there to get it done,” Canadian International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said in an interview with Bloomberg’s Haslinda Amin. “Hopefully we will get it done this year. That is the focus.”

Get a dash of perspective along with the trending news of the day in a very readable format.

A welcome email is on its way. If you don't see it, please check your junk folder.

The push to deepen economic ties with India comes as Canada faces rising trade tensions with the US following the breakdown of negotiations between the two countries. India, meanwhile, is contending with fresh tariff threats from a new law that gives Donald Trump the power to impose levies of as much as 100% on countries that purchase Russian oil and gas.

Canada sees opportunities to deepen ties with India in mining and food security, while also identifying infrastructure investment and nuclear energy as areas for deeper cooperation.

“The business community wants to see this happen,” Sidhu said of the trade deal.

Trade between Canada and India is currently small. The two countries exchanged $30.4 billion of goods and services last year, according to Canadian government data.

“The leaders have set an ambitious target to go from $30 billion to $70 billion,” Sidhu said. “How are we going to get there? Many of the conversations I’ve had in Mumbai with some of the conglomerates is we want to do more on energy. We know we want to do more in critical minerals.”

He signaled Ottawa’s interest in participating in India’s expansion plans.

“As India grows, Canada grows. We want to support India,” Sidhu said. “We can help India build all the supply chains. Negotiations are always tough but we are going to do what is best for our businesses.”

Nuclear energy is another potential area of cooperation. India is opening up its tightly controlled nuclear industry to private companies as it seeks to rapidly expand atomic power generation.

That could create opportunities for Canada, which has some of the world’s largest uranium resources as well as nuclear technology and expertise, to supply fuel and participate in new projects.

—With assistance from Anup Roy and Shruti Srivastava.

stories.title: St. Thomas police reach 20,000 calls for service at earliest point on record
stories.summary: The St. Thomas Police Service says it has reached 20,000 calls for service earlier than ever before, highlighting what officials describe as growing demand for policing in the city.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
The St. Thomas Police Service says it has reached 20,000 calls for service earlier than ever before, highlighting what officials describe as growing demand for policing in the city.

Police announced they recorded their 20,000th call for service on Oct. 13, more than two weeks earlier than last year, when the milestone was reached on Oct. 31.

According to the service, this marks the earliest date on record that officers have surpassed the 20,000-call threshold.

The date has been steadily moving earlier in recent years, reflecting a rise in calls for service. The milestone was reached on Dec. 12 in 2022, Nov. 12 in 2023, Nov. 3 in 2024, Oct. 31 in 2025 and Oct. 13 this year.

Police said the impact of higher call volumes extends well beyond the initial response to incidents.

“Many calls require follow-up investigations, court preparation, disclosure processing and administrative work, creating additional demands across the organization, including communications, frontline patrol, investigative units, court services, information technology and administrative staff,” read a statement from police.

St. Thomas police did not provide a breakdown of the types of calls contributing to the increase.

stories.title: Canada has not interfered in the U.S. midterm elections, former diplomat says
stories.summary: A former Canadian diplomat has dismissed U.S. allegations of Canadian interference in the upcoming midterms elections as “noise.”
stories.author: Devika Desai
stories.content:
A former Canadian diplomat has dismissed U.S. allegations of Canadian interference in the upcoming midterms elections as “noise.”

“I don’t think that it deserves much response,” Colin Robertson, a fellow at the Canadian Global Affairs Institute, told CTV’s Your Morning on Thursday.

Pete Hoekstra, the U.S. ambassador to Canada, suggested in an interview with “The Really Big Show” podcast released earlier this week that the actions of several Canadian politicians could amount to interference in the midterms, which will be held on Nov. 3.

He pointed to an advertising campaign run by Ontario Premier Doug Ford last year that featured a clip of former U.S. president Ronald Raegan talking about the benefits of free trade.

“Did that constitute any kind of interference? No, I think that’s advocacy,” Robertson said.

Hoekstra also criticized Industry Minister Melanie Joly for stating that Canadian counter-tariffs were designed to target certain states.

“Again, that’s quite justified,” Robertson said, as retaliatory action against the U.S. tariffs. “All of which international trade law recognizes.”

Having petitioned U.S. lawmakers in the past to advance Canada’s interests, Robertson said Canadian politicians are now trying to encourage American businesses to advocate against the trade war, ON their behalf.

“We’re seeing this now ... Republican candidates are going out and saying, ‘well we shouldn’t be applying these tariffs.’ So they’re breaking with the president,” the former diplomat said.

“That’s Americans talking to Americans. That’s exactly what we want to see.”

Robertson said he wouldn’t be surprised if Trump blames Canada should Republicans lose the midterms.

“With Donald Trump, you’re never sure of anything,” he said. “And he’s of course made very clear that if he doesn’t win these midterms, it’s not his fault.”

Trump, after losing the 2020 presidential election, accused his opponent Joe Biden of election fraud .

On Wednesday, Trump told a crowd of supporters during a campaign rally in Bullhead City, Ariz., that Canada will “end up being the 51st state.”

U.S. President Donald Trump says Canada will 'be doing something just like Greenland' while speaking at a rally in Bullhead City, Ariz.

He then listed a longstanding number of grievances that the U.S. has with Canada including Canadian tariffs on milk. He also spoke about car companies moving their factories to the U.S. and his renaming of Lake Ontario to “Lake America.”

“They’ll end up being the 51st state, because that’s the only way it works,” he said. “We don’t need them, but they need us.”

stories.title: Canadians split on how much power Ottawa should have in ending labour strikes: poll
stories.summary: Labour groups are opposed to legislation that puts conditions on the use of Section 107 of the Canada Labour Code to end strikes.
stories.author: Bloomberg News
stories.content:
Canada

About a third of respondents support empowering the labour minister to end strikes not in the country's best interest, but slightly believe they need legislation to do so

Author of the article:

Air Canada flight attendants and supporters during a strike at Toronto Pearson International Airport in Mississauga, Ontario, in 2025.Photo by Arlyn McAdorey /Bloomberg

Most Canadians believe the federal government should be able to end a labour strike but are divided over how it should be done, as Prime Minister Mark Carney seeks to entrench a controversial power used by the labour minister to intervene in some disputes.

A poll conducted by Nanos Research Group on behalf of Bloomberg News found 32 per cent of Canadians support giving the federal labour minister the power to end strikes that are believed to be against the national interest, while 36 per cent said the government should have to pass back-to-work legislation to do so. Meanwhile, 25 per cent of respondents said the government should not be allowed to end strikes at all.

Labour groups have pushed back against proposed Carney government legislation that puts conditions on the use of Section 107 of the Canada Labour Code to end strikes. In recent years, labour ministers have invoked the provision to direct a quasi-judicial body to resolve disputes involving flight attendants, postal workers and rail and port employees — without having to go through the politically fraught process of passing back-to-work legislation.

The government has said that the proposed changes will raise the bar for ending strikes using Section 107, while several unions have argued that the government is doubling down on a power it should not have by enshrining it in law.

Business groups have long called on the government to play a more active role in ending labour disputes, arguing that strikes carry significant economic costs and cause uncertainty, both of which could discourage investment.

Nik Nanos, the founder of Nanos Research, said the poll results suggest the government’s solution is not a “slam dunk” politically. That means it will have to put in work to win over Canadians on the issue, he said.

Young people between the ages of 18 and 24 were the least likely to support giving the labour minister the power to end a strike and the most likely to say that the government should not be allowed to play a role.

The poll was conducted between Sept. 27 and 29 with 1,057 respondents, as is considered accurate within three percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

stories.title: Claims that Canada interfered in U.S. midterms are ‘noise,’ former diplomat says
stories.summary: A former Canadian diplomat has dismissed U.S. allegations of Canadian interference in the upcoming midterms elections as “noise.”
stories.author: Devika Desai
stories.content:
A former Canadian diplomat has dismissed U.S. allegations of Canadian interference in the upcoming midterms elections as “noise.”

“I don’t think that it deserves much response,” Colin Robertson, a fellow at the Canadian Global Affairs Institute, told CTV’s Your Morning on Thursday.

Pete Hoekstra, the U.S. ambassador to Canada, suggested in an interview with “The Really Big Show” podcast released earlier this week that the actions of several Canadian politicians could amount to interference in the midterms, which will be held on Nov. 3.

He pointed to an advertising campaign run by Ontario Premier Doug Ford last year that featured a clip of former U.S. president Ronald Raegan talking about the benefits of free trade.

“Did that constitute any kind of interference? No, I think that’s advocacy,” Robertson said.

Hoekstra also criticized Industry Minister Melanie Joly for stating that Canadian counter-tariffs were designed to target certain states.

“Again, that’s quite justified,” Robertson said, as retaliatory action against the U.S. tariffs. “All of which international trade law recognizes.”

Having petitioned U.S. lawmakers in the past to advance Canada’s interests, Robertson said Canadian politicians are now trying to encourage American businesses to advocate against the trade war, ON their behalf.

“We’re seeing this now ... Republican candidates are going out and saying, ‘well we shouldn’t be applying these tariffs.’ So they’re breaking with the president,” the former diplomat said.

“That’s Americans talking to Americans. That’s exactly what we want to see.”

Robertson said he wouldn’t be surprised if Trump blames Canada should Republicans lose the midterms.

“With Donald Trump, you’re never sure of anything,” he said. “And he’s of course made very clear that if he doesn’t win these midterms, it’s not his fault.”

Trump, after losing the 2020 presidential election, accused his opponent Joe Biden of election fraud .

On Wednesday, Trump told a crowd of supporters during a campaign rally in Bullhead City, Ariz., that Canada will “end up being the 51st state.”

He then listed a longstanding number of grievances that the U.S. held with Canada including Canadian tariffs on milk, car companies moving their factories to the U.S. and renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America.”

“They’ll end up being the 51st state, because that’s the only way it works,” he said. “We don’t need them, but they need us.”

stories.title: How these book publishers balance business risk and personal security
stories.summary: It’s important for entrepreneurs to draw lines around their business wealth and their personal wealth
stories.author: Nickie Shobeiry
stories.content:
When it comes to the economics of book publishing, Jack David doesn’t mince words: “It’s a terrible business.”

Mr. David is the co-founder of ECW Press, a Toronto-based independent publisher. The company, now over 50 years old, has published over 3,500 books and hit about $5-million in annual revenue. However, profit margins in publishing can be as narrow as two per cent. After acquiring a book, a publisher May spend 18 months editing, designing and printing, followed by another several months waiting to collect revenue after the book hits the stores.

To help cover expenses, Mr. David has often dipped into his personal finances. When to mingle personal and business assets and when to keep them apart is a common challenge for entrepreneurs. Mr. David says he has been putting his own money into ECW since “day two”, including borrowing against the home he shares with his wife, Sharon, a retired veterinarian.

Because the property is jointly owned, she was required to receive independent legal advice before agreeing to put their home on the line. Her lawyer walked her through what Mr. David jokingly calls the “80 bad things” that could happen: “Is he ever going to be able to pay this off? What if he goes bankrupt?”

Sharon chose to back her husband, but the couple drew some lines around their personal wealth. For example, when they came into an inheritance, they invested the money rather than put it into ECW. They also own Toronto real estate and a cottage, diversifying their assets.

That separation is important for entrepreneurs. “You can’t put all your eggs in one basket,” says Catherine Metzger-Silver, a financial advisor with Edward Jones in Kentville, Nova Scotia. “There’s so much risk management involved.”

Today, ECW is one of Canada’s biggest trade and academic publishers, but getting there has been marked by financial uncertainty. In 2001, both its Canadian and American distributors went bankrupt, leaving the company without money it was owed.

Around that time, Mr. David took a gamble on a manuscript by Neil Peart, drummer for the band Rush, scraping together the money for the advance fee. The band went on tour, which helped promote the book Ghost Rider: Travels on the Healing Road . It has sold roughly 250,000 copies to date.

“You get enough of those hits, you get new books you want to publish,” Mr. David says. “That’s what keeps me involved – apart from the fact that my mortgage is on the line.”

Ms. Metzger-Silver often hears entrepreneurs say, “my business is my retirement”. But if an entrepreneur can’t find a buyer, or the company sells for less than expected, they May have little to fall back on in their later years. She says that makes it especially important to build wealth throughout their career.

David Caron, part of Ecw’s next generation of ownership, is walking the same tightrope between investing in the business and protecting personal finances. He joined the company in 2004 when he was in his mid-30s with two children, aged six and three, and is now co-publisher with Mr. David.

No matter how ECW performed, Mr. Caron and his wife set a minimum amount of household income that needed to be protected, covering their living expenses, mortgage, their children’s post-secondary education and their own retirement contributions. “We’re equal partners in this, that’s my rule of thumb,” he says.

At ECW, Mr. Caron pays himself a salary. “The idea of me taking a dividend – I just keep thinking about the other people at the company,” he says. “You’re constantly reinvesting everything else back into the company.”

Mr. Caron plans to stay in publishing for years to come, but is already planning his eventual exit. His experience buying ECW and, more recently, buying majority ownership of Annick Press has shown him that a well-planned succession can take a decade. “If I want to think about somebody taking things on when I’m in my late 60s, the time is now,” he says.

When selling a business, Ms. Metzger-Silver recommends allowing plenty of runway. “The day you open your business is the day you plan the exit. You never know where life will take you.”

stories.title: Pressure builds on former MP Raj Grewal amid fraud allegations
stories.summary: Father-in-law says 'I am a victim of the fraud' as Peel Regional Police and Ontario legal regulator circle law firm founded by former MP.
stories.author: Tom Blackwell
stories.content:
Former Ontario MP Raj Grewal is facing a dramatic new wave of legal pressure, with police asking for help investigating alleged fraud and other wrongdoing by the lawyer and his colleagues, Ontario’s legal regulator moving to take over the law firm Grewal founded — and even his own father-in-law accusing him of multi-million-dollar fraud and forgery.

The impact of the affair on Grewal’s family is particularly striking.

Father-in-law Kailash Kasal said in an affidavit last month he’s struggling to preserve good relations with his lenders based on “the fact that I have no connection to this fraud perpetrated by Raj Grewal and others and that I am a victim of the fraud.”

The businessman confirmed that his daughter and her husband are estranged, but said he had held off asking Grewal about allegedly tainted funds that appeared in one of his companies’ accounts.

“I did not want to do anything to antagonize Mr. Grewal in a manner that May affect my grandchildren or my daughter,” Kasal said in the affidavit.

The latest developments come after numerous businesses and individuals have filed legal action against Grewal, his associates, the law firm and numbered companies in recent months, charging them with mortgage fraud, misappropriation of funds and handling fake cheques.

Recently filed lawsuits have estimated that $200 million or more is in dispute, based on allegations that are so far unproven but, if validated, would constitute one of the largest-ever cases of financial misconduct by lawyers in Canada.

None of the charges has been proven in court.

Simon Bieber, one of Grewal’s lawyers, said Wednesday that his client denies any wrongdoing, is co-operating with the Law Society of Ontario and “looks forward to continuing his defence.”

As he has indicated before, Bieber said Grewal is involved in many commercial transactions and, especially in uncertain economic times, the parties sometimes have a falling out that leads to litigation. He is the plaintiff in some cases and defendant in others and is “working diligently to resolve all outstanding litigation in a manner that is fair to all involved,” the lawyer said.

Grewal, the former Liberal member for the Brampton East riding west of Toronto, quit Parliament in 2018 after admitting to racking up millions in gambling debts. He later started RSG Law, the name based on his own initials. A paid advertorial in the Toronto Star last July that featured Grewal and was headed by his photograph called it a “thriving legal enterprise” with a 40-person team.

Earlier this year, he voluntarily gave up his licence as the Law Society of Ontario investigates him and others and seeks to have his credentials suspended.

The society went further recently, asking the Ontario Superior Court for permission to take over all accounts, client files and safe-deposit boxes of RSG Law, Grewal and Davinder Khattra, the junior colleague now listed as the firm’s owner. The regulator earlier suspended Khattra’s licence.

The society notes that various plaintiffs name Grewal and Khattra in legal actions related to “the alleged misappropriation of at least $17 million.” Today, $340,303 remains in RSG Law’s accounts, its notice of application says.

The regulator “has a statutory duty to protect the public interest and advance the cause of justice and rule of law,” it said in a notice of application asking to be made a trustee of the firm.

stories.title: Fry and Sim face off in Vancouver, but other mayoral candidates reject spoiler label
stories.summary: Interest in the Vancouver race appears high. The City of Vancouver says more than 103,000 people have voted in advance, up 60 per cent from roughly 65,000 voters in 2022.
stories.author: Marissa Birnie
stories.content:
Vancouver mayoral candidates Ken Sim and Pete Fry view each other as their main rival in the battle for City Hall.

But while recent polling suggests the mayoral race is indeed a faceoff between incumbent Sim and two-term Green Councillor Fry, there are three other big-name candidates who reject the label of spoiler.

Kareem Allam — Sim’s former chief of staff turned litigation adversary — is running with the Vancouver Liberals, which is not affiliated with the federal party.

“The pollsters don’t always get it right. Municipal government is also the hardest level to poll. It’s got its tricks and nuances, especially in an at-large system,” he said in an interview Tuesday.

The Vancouver race culminates Saturday, when municipalities across British Columbia go to the polls.

Interest in the Vancouver race appears high. The City of Vancouver says more than 103,000 people have voted in advance, up 60 per cent from roughly 65,000 voters over five advance days in 2022.

Sim, who is campaigning for a second term as mayor with the right-of-centre ABC Vancouver, said while he would be the first to admit he didn’t get everything right during his tenure, he believes he can lead the city in the right direction.

“We’ve gotten some pretty significant things done, but there’s way more work to do,” he said in an interview Wednesday.

Other candidates include Rebecca Bligh, a two-term councillor who helped get Sim elected with ABC Vancouver in 2022 and is now running with Vote Vancouver, and Team candidate Colleen Hardwick, a former councillor.

Allam, Hardwick and Bligh all rejected the notion their candidacies could split the centre or centre-right vote.

“The question is not left or right. The question is about who we are serving at city hall,” Hardwick said Tuesday.

Bligh said she was running to govern for Vancouver’s ignored middle class, and polling did not change how she campaigned.

“It’s anyone’s race,” she said in an interview Wednesday.

Fry, son of longtime Liberal MP Hedy Fry, has acknowledged benefiting from the narrowing of the progressive field, after the withdrawals of William Azaroff from OneCity Vancouver and Stephanie Allen for Cope Vancouver.

After ending his candidacy, Azaroff appeared at City Hall with Fry, who praised him for running a serious campaign that “raised real issues” such as housing, small business and affordability.

“I think folks are excited to be able to talk up a viable alternative to Ken Sim as the mayor of Vancouver and really reset,” Fry said in an interview Tuesday.

He added that Azaroff’s withdrawal was recognition that he was the person best suited to defeat Sim.

Bligh said she’s a progressive candidate with a centrist platform. Meanwhile, Allam said he believed he was taking votes from Sim and Fry equally.

The candidates’ platforms all emphasize quality-of-life issues, including affordability and public safety. Sim’s promises include a zero per cent property tax increase.

The election ballot also includes two plebiscite questions on public safety.

The non-binding questions ask voters if they’re in favour of the city “strengthening its laws to forbid open-air hard drug use in public spaces,” which is already illegal in B.C. The other asks if the city should ask the province to convert portions of the old St. Paul’s hospital into a “secure medical facility” with 100-plus involuntary care beds.

Hardwick called the questions a “populist election tactic,” while other critics said they aren’t realistic.

Sim said strengthening the city health bylaw — regulating conduct such as smoking in common areas — would allow officers to issue tickets or confiscate drugs without arrests. The involuntary care question, he said, is about asking the province to fulfil its accountability to people who pose a risk to their own safety or others.

Fry said he supports managing drug use in public spaces, but differs from Sim in believing that people should be diverted to supervised consumption sites or shelters.

His platform focuses on housing, transportation and the economy. “Folks should be able to have a good life in this city, he said.

Bligh said Sim’s property tax freezes protect wealthy landowners and undercut critical services. She said she would work with the federal government to leverage city-owned land and provide free transit for youth.

Hardwick said the key to livability in Vancouver is effective city planning. She said she wanted to repeal the city’s official development plan and re-establish neighbourhood planning offices

Allam said he wants to bring youth back to Vancouver by improving affordability through jobs and housing, and investing in parks and community centres.

He said his platform cuts across ideologies, and distanced himself from Sim, who filed a lawsuit in May 2025 alleging Allam falsely accused him of drinking and driving.

Sim faces his own defamation lawsuit from councillor Sean Orr, filed after falsely accusing Orr of distributing illegal drugs in comments to Chinese-speaking reporters.

Trials in both cases are far off.

For now, the focus is on the ballot box.

“I think people will be surprised at the results,” Allam said.

stories.content:
Canadian health ministers meet in Winnipeg today after the federal government announced it would extend funding for mental health, addictions and home care by one year.

Federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel made the announcement on social media late Wednesday, saying the extension represents $1.2-billion in funding.

The existing funding was set to expire next year.

Manitoba Health Minister Uzoma Asagwara is to host provincial and territorial counterparts today, and Michel is to co-chair Friday’s meeting.

Provincial health ministers had said they were worried about “profound and negative” effects on patients and health-care jobs if the federal funding agreements weren’t renewed in this year’s budget.

Provinces and territories also raised concerns about the future of the Canada Health Transfer as the federal budget states the minimum growth rate will drop to three per cent from five per cent in 2028.

Asagwara says they spoke with Michel about the unanimous concerns of health ministers and are keen to hear more on federal health funding.

“I am thrilled to be able to say that I feel Minister Michel has been listening,” Asagwara said Wednesday.

“I look forward to hearing some news from the minister on this, we all do.”

Linda Silas, president of the Canadian Federation of Nurses Unions, said funding commitments should be a priority.

She said the federal government can’t lose sight of the importance of health care as it ramps up spending on defence and other priorities.

“There has to be a just balance, and we have to see our health-care system as an investment, as a human rights issue, and as proud Canadians, it’s the core of our fabric, and we need to hear our prime minister speak more loudly about it.”

The Canadian Medical Association said in a release Wednesday that the meeting is an important opportunity for the federal government to provide certainty on funding to provinces and territories.

The association said strong and reliable federal funding to maintain universal health care is foundational to growing Canada’s economy.

stories.title: Burnaby school district says cyberattack May have leaked student, parent info
stories.summary: The Burnaby School District says in a notice that the ransomware attack it suffered on Sept. 21 affected school websites and portals, internal network services and phone lines.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Public school officials in Burnaby, B.C., say hackers May have obtained student and parental information in a recent cyberattack.

The Burnaby School District says in an online notice that the ransomware attack it suffered on Sept. 21 affected school websites and portals, internal network services and phone lines.

The notice says hackers copied and stole files that May have contained lists of parent, guardian and student names and contact information, as well as birthdates, grades and school names.

It says the hackers May also have obtained registration forms, kindergarten assessment notes and detailed lists of students on specialized learning plans.

The school district says the matter is in the hands of the RCMP and B.C.’s privacy commissioner, adding that its system security is being evaluated to prevent further breaches.

It says staff, students and their families have been offered registration with TransUnion’s fraud alert service and encourages them to be wary of any suspicious communications.

“We understand that incidents of this nature are concerning and we remain committed to keeping the Burnaby Schools community updated throughout this process, as the investigation proceeds and additional information becomes available,” the notice says.

stories.title: ‘Hardly surprising’ many Alberta business leaders staying mum on separation: expert
stories.summary: The silence from many Alberta business leaders on the upcoming provincial referendum comes as no surprise to one corporate leadership expert.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
The silence from many Alberta business leaders on the upcoming provincial referendum comes as no surprise to one corporate leadership expert.

Monday’s vote includes 10 questions: one on whether Alberta should remain in Canada or move toward a binding separation referendum; five on immigration and four on constitutional matters.

Richard Leblanc, a professor of governance, law and ethics at York University, says there’s a tradition in Canada for CEOs to stay in their lanes and not risk alienating shareholders or employees by taking a political stand.

But Leblanc says there May be times a company’s board of directors agrees that a CEO should speak out on a matter that affects the well-being of the business, as Alberta taking steps toward a potential split from Canada arguably would.

A handful of leaders at big, publicly traded companies are among the more than 70 signatories to an open letter from the Calgary Chamber of Commerce warning of the economic fallout of separation, while the top brass at many prominent firms have stayed mum.

A few top executives have made their views known: Imperial Oil’s John Whelan has spoken in favour of Alberta and Canada sticking together while Atco Ltd.’s Nancy Southern has warned of the disruption a split would cause.

“It’s hardly surprising that a majority of CEOs are not speaking up,” Leblanc said. “There’s more to be lost than gained, generally, by speaking up about a political matter.”

Some corporations have former prime ministers, premiers and cabinet ministers as directors on their boards, who can advise on when and how to weigh in on politics, Leblanc noted.

Atco’s board includes former Alberta premier Jason Kenney, who has been a fervent voice in favour of the province staying in Confederation, as well as former federal cabinet minister Rona Ambrose.

Leblanc said customers and employees May have “legitimate expectations” that a CEO take a public stand on something that could affect the business, though getting board sign-off on the message is no easy feat.

“Sometimes the risk of not doing something can be far greater than doing something and dealing with the blowback.”

stories.title: U.S. watching for Canadian ‘interference’ in midterms, Hoekstra says
stories.summary: During an interview on a podcast, Hoekstra said political ads run by the province of Ontario last year could be interpreted as political interference.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra says American officials are “closely watching” Canadian politicians for signs of election interference ahead of pivotal midterm elections next month.

During an interview on “The Really Big Show” podcast that was posted last week, Hoekstra said political ads run by the province of Ontario last year could be interpreted as political interference.

U.S. President Donald Trump ended trade talks with Canada in October 2025 after Ontario aired an ad during the World Series using clips of former U.S. president Ronald Reagan criticizing tariffs and supporting free trade.

Hoekstra also cited recent comments by Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and former prime minister Justin Trudeau and suggested they also could amount to interference.

Hoekstra went on to warn Canadian politicians to keep their “nose out” of American politics in the weeks before the midterm elections.

Trudeau criticized the Trump administration during a discussion at Brown University on Sept. 22.

“There is a pattern here of doing things that are driving up prices for your consumers and not necessarily making anything better for America, by fighting with one of your oldest and best allies,” Trudeau said during the conversation.

In the interview, Hoekstra said Joly made comments about targeting retaliatory tariffs at “politically sensitive states.”

Joly pushed back Wednesday, telling reporters Canada would never engage in election interference and would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada.”

Joly said she has been to the U.S. in recent months and has met with Democrats and Republicans.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says Canada would never interfere in U.S. elections. Her comments came after U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra said Canadians should keep their noses out of American politics during the congressional midterms. (Oct. 14, 2026)

“Fundamentally, what I’ve done in the U.S. is to attract investments,” she said. “I think I’ll be able to have good news of investments by different American companies to Canada. And that’s exactly what I’m doing and that will continue to be my strategy in the U.S. and also around the world.”

Hoekstra said if any actions by Canadians end up amounting to election interference, the United States will respond.

The ambassador declined a request from The Canadian Press for an interview.

Tension between the United States and Canada has increased since Trump won the presidential election in 2024, and began threatening to turn Canada into the 51st state.

That threat, and his attacks on Canada, have become a focal point of his stump speeches as he actively campaigns in battleground states ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which could end Republican control over Congress.

At a rally in Bullhead City, Ariz., ON Wednesday, Trump went after Canada again, listing grievances over dairy sector trade and repeating his claim that Canada treats the United States “very badly.”

He said Canada will end up being the 51st state because “that’s the only way it works.”

“We don’t need them, but they need us,” he said.

The Republicans are under heavy pressure ahead of the midterms, when the entire House of Representatives and one-third of U.S. Senate seats will be contested. While the Republicans currently hold a majority of seats in both chambers, polls suggest the Democrats could win control of both.

Peter Navarro, one of Trump’s trade advisers, warned Ottawa last month against interfering in the midterms and berated Canada over its successful lobbying efforts in the past.

Speaking at the American Growth Summit in Washington, he told the audience that any Canadians in the room intent on lobbying the U.S. government should “get the hell out of our country.”

“The problem you have is you lobby this country, and you’ve been successful in the past and you think you can keep doing that. Memo to Canada: You cannot keep doing that,” Navarro said.

“That game is up and if you interfere in our elections in Maine or Michigan, you will pay even more dearly.”

The Globe and Mail reported recently that Republican political operatives were on the ground in Alberta earlier this year to help the separatist campaign. It also reported that some Alberta separatists went to Washington to lobby for U.S. government support.

In August, Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered the Canadian negotiating team to call off trade talks with the U.S. after accusing the Americans of making unreasonable demands.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre was in Detroit on Tuesday to make a case for tariff-free trade in the auto sector.

Poilievre appeared on CNN, where he continued to pitch the benefits of tariff-free trade.

“We have a 200-year-old relationship, there’s always going to be grievances on both sides of the border,” he said. “We have our grievances with the United States even predating this most recent trade dispute, but I would focus on what we can do together.”

stories.title: Health ministers set to meet in Winnipeg after Ottawa announces funding extension
stories.summary: Winnipeg — Canadian health ministers meet in Winnipeg today after the federal government announced it would extend funding for mental health, addictions and home care by one year.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Federal Health Marjorie Michel speaks during a press conference in the Foyer of the House of Commons on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, ON Thursday, May 28, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Spencer Colby The Canadian Press

By Ian Bickis, The Canadian Press

Posted October 15, 2026 8:06 am.

Last Updated October 15, 2026 9:07 am.

Winnipeg — Canadian health ministers meet in Winnipeg today after the federal government announced it would extend funding for mental health, addictions and home care by one year.

Federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel made the announcement on social media late Wednesday, saying the extension represents $1.2 billion in funding.

The existing funding was set to expire next year.

Manitoba Health Minister Uzoma Asagwara is to host provincial and territorial counterparts today, and Michel is to co-chair Friday’s meeting.

Provincial health ministers had said they were worried about “profound and negative” effects on patients and health-care jobs if the federal funding agreements weren’t renewed in this year’s budget.

Provinces and territories also raised concerns about the future of the Canada Health Transfer as the federal budget states the minimum growth rate will drop to three per cent from five per cent in 2028.

Asagwara says they spoke with Michel about the unanimous concerns of health ministers and are keen to hear more on federal health funding.

“I am thrilled to be able to say that I feel Minister Michel has been listening,” Asagwara said Wednesday.

“I look forward to hearing some news from the minister on this, we all do.”

Linda Silas, president of the Canadian Federation of Nurses Unions, said funding commitments should be a priority.

She said the federal government can’t lose sight of the importance of health care as it ramps up spending on defence and other priorities.

“There has to be a just balance, and we have to see our health-care system as an investment, as a human rights issue, and as proud Canadians, it’s the core of our fabric, and we need to hear our prime minister speak more loudly about it.”

The Canadian Medical Association said in a release Wednesday that the meeting is an important opportunity for the federal government to provide certainty on funding to provinces and territories.

The association said strong and reliable federal funding to maintain universal health care is foundational to growing Canada’s economy.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

paragraphs: Federal Health Marjorie Michel speaks during a press conference in the Foyer of the House of Commons on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, ON Thursday, May 28, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Spencer Colby The Canadian Press
By Ian Bickis, The Canadian Press
Posted October 15, 2026 8:06 am.
Last Updated October 15, 2026 9:07 am.
Winnipeg — Canadian health ministers meet in Winnipeg today after the federal government announced it would extend funding for mental health, addictions and home care by one year.
Federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel made the announcement on social media late Wednesday, saying the extension represents $1.2 billion in funding.
The existing funding was set to expire next year.
Manitoba Health Minister Uzoma Asagwara is to host provincial and territorial counterparts today, and Michel is to co-chair Friday’s meeting.
Provincial health ministers had said they were worried about “profound and negative” effects on patients and health-care jobs if the federal funding agreements weren’t renewed in this year’s budget.

Provinces and territories also raised concerns about the future of the Canada Health Transfer as the federal budget states the minimum growth rate will drop to three per cent from five per cent in 2028.
Asagwara says they spoke with Michel about the unanimous concerns of health ministers and are keen to hear more on federal health funding.
“I am thrilled to be able to say that I feel Minister Michel has been listening,” Asagwara said Wednesday.
“I look forward to hearing some news from the minister on this, we all do.”
Linda Silas, president of the Canadian Federation of Nurses Unions, said funding commitments should be a priority.
She said the federal government can’t lose sight of the importance of health care as it ramps up spending on defence and other priorities.

“There has to be a just balance, and we have to see our health-care system as an investment, as a human rights issue, and as proud Canadians, it’s the core of our fabric, and we need to hear our prime minister speak more loudly about it.”
The Canadian Medical Association said in a release Wednesday that the meeting is an important opportunity for the federal government to provide certainty on funding to provinces and territories.
The association said strong and reliable federal funding to maintain universal health care is foundational to growing Canada’s economy.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

stories.title: All the ways the Alberta referendum could result in an October surprise
stories.summary: Support for remaining in Canada is in the high 60s, while the leave side is in the low 20s. But pollsters have been wrong before.
stories.author: Joseph Brean
stories.content:
With just days to go before Albertans vote on whether to pursue independence, polls suggest residents who want to stay in Canada have a safe lead. Support for remaining is in the high 60s, while the leave sentiment is in the low 20s. But it could go differently. Pollsters have been wrong before, even on separatist votes. The National Post’s Joseph Brean surveys various possibilities for how this referendum on a referendum could turn out to be an October surprise.

This is a question of confidence, both in the polls and in the broader issue. Confidence is a subjective attitude, shifting and hard to measure or predict. If turnout is low, public opinion polling could be a less reliable guide to the actual results.

“Fervent separatists will crawl across broken glass to make their vote count,” said remain campaigner and former Alberta deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk in a recent speech. The danger, he meant, is that a pro-Canada majority will think they have it in the bag and stay home.

In 1980, Quebec’s sovereignty movement under a Parti Québécois government soundly lost a referendum that would have given it a mandate to “negotiate a new constitutional agreement with the rest of Canada, based on the equality of nations.” In 1995, however, the PQ came within a single percentage point of a vote to leave. Turnout of over 90 per cent is thought to have boosted the remain numbers such that projections of a leave victory by a few points turned out to be wrong. Now, another vote seems likely, and is at least promised by the newly elected PQ government.

In Scotland, separatists lost their referendum in 2014 by fully 10 percentage points, with voter turnout at more than 80 per cent.

Alberta’s voter turnout in the last provincial election was 60 per cent, and in the last federal election 67 per cent, but this is obviously a different sort of ballot question.

Curiously, the referendum is not a simple “Yes/No” question. It is a rambling offer of two numbered options. You can almost ignore the setup and get straight to the options, which are clear enough on their own without the wordy question, which reads: “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?”

Still here? Did you drift off a bit at “commence the legal process”? Did you need to be told “the Constitution” is “Canadian”? Did you already assume the “legal process” would be “required”? This referendum has more words than it needs.

Eventually, it gets to the key parts: “Option 1: Alberta should remain a province of Canada. Option 2: The Government of Alberta should commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada.”

It is a referendum, but the ballot reads like a lawyer’s letter. There are also nine other questions, all of which are yes/no, ON things like immigration control, immigrant access to social services, voter identification, judicial appointments and provincial-federal relations. How and even if people read through all that could have measurable impact on the emotionally charged central question among an electorate with a wide spectrum of interests and motivations.

“There’s a lot of people who want to send a message,” said Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on Oct. 7. “There’s a lot of people who think voting for Option 2 will give leverage. If those are your reasons, I would say there is a better way to send a message or to give leverage. And that is to give us a mandate on the other nine questions.”

Scotland was more concise, not troubling voters with too much windup or alternative messages. “Should Scotland be an independent country?” the 2014 referendum asked. The answer was no, according to 55 per cent of Scots.

Another way the true will of Albertans could be misrepresented in referendum results is by invalidation of good faith ballots.

More than 3,000 ballot packages have been invalidated for reasons such as missing declaration forms or problems with identification, though there remains time to fix those problems.

All ballots are to be counted by hand. Question 10, the central one about a referendum on separating, will be counted and reported first, followed by the other nine, with a deadline of 48 hours, according to Elections Alberta.

Quebec sovereigntists have marched farther along the road to separatism, and their history offers cautionary tales for Alberta sovereigntists. But with a new Quebec government seeking the same goal, they also offer inspiration.

The idea that Canada is broken has lately had a run as a political slogan. The idea that it is actually breaking up is a less familiar notion, not exactly new, but surging to unprecedented levels of public interest with two provincial sovereignty movements campaigning simultaneously. So the successes of one could boost the fortunes of the other, even without actual cooperation.

As separatist advocate and leader of the Alberta Prosperity Project Mitch Sylvestre said after a cordial meeting with Paul St-Pierre Plamondon prior to his election as Quebec’s new premier, according to Rick Bell of the Calgary Herald, “You know, we both agreed, and this came out of Paul’s mouth not mine. He said the only level of government neither of us needs is at the federal level.”

The folk wisdom is that bad weather lowers turnout. It has even been measured in the U.S. at one percentage point per inch of rain, and half a point per inch of snow. In Canada, University of Ottawa researchers found that from the 2004 to 2015 federal elections, “each millimeter of precipitation decreases turnout by more than 0.1 percentage points.”

Higher temperatures boost turnout, they found, but only in spring, summer and fall elections. In the winter 2006 election victory for Stephen Harper, warmer temperatures “triggered lower turnout, in particular, when there was also high precipitation.”

This is the October surprise, in which U.S. President Donald Trump could say or do something provocative, or perhaps offer something like the $5,000 payment he has offered American voters if Republicans win the midterm elections. In Alberta’s referendum, he could see some usefulness to his side in the wider trade war.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, therefore, is in a tricky strategic position, needing to both advocate for the Albertan remain side while managing his chaotic conflict with Trump, who is on record as coveting not only Alberta, but all of Canada.

Carney’s play was a Thanksgiving video, posed in a classroom at his Edmonton high school with a world map behind him, ON a long-weekend holiday that was thematically useful.

“It is a chance to give thanks for Canada,” he said. “This year, Thanksgiving is a bit different. A week from today, Albertans will have the opportunity to make an important decision about their future, whether to remain part of Canada, or begin a long and uncertain process through which Alberta could separate from Canada.”

His voice lilted on “could,” a little rhetorical emphasis on the inherent risk of Option 2, in contrast to his pitch for Option 1.

“I’m back home a lot these days, because we are building big things again in Alberta, thousands of new homes, high-speed rail, a new pipeline to the West Coast that will create lasting opportunity and prosperity,” he said. “Canada’s working. Truth is, we can’t achieve any of this if we’re divided. We can’t build big things on fault lines.”

Of all the referendum results that few saw coming, Brexit, Britain’s vote to leave the European Union in 2016, stands out as maybe the most shocking.

It cost Prime Minister David Cameron his leadership, and was a failure of sorts also for Carney, who as Governor of the Bank of England had warned Brexit would cause a recession. He then agreed to extend his term to help avert one.

One immediate political winner was Boris Johnson, the now former prime minister whose appeal was to seem “shambolic,” as the British say, clownish, chaotic, disruptive, but massively likeable, like the earlier Torontonian archetype, the former mayor Rob Ford, who died a few months before Brexit.

A few months after Brexit came the equally momentous surprise first election of Donald Trump, who took that same archetype to new extremes of political power.

Britain still labours under the consequences of that political sea change. So does their Conservative Party’s revolving leadership of less charismatic figures. So, indeed, does the rest of the world, including Alberta.

The tech titan does not have a perfect track record for sage prediction of domestic affairs in other countries, such as Britain where he once said civil war is “inevitable.” But he does take an interest. And, as in Germany, he can speak influentially in support of a populist right-wing movement on its way from the fringe to the mainstream of power, such as the Alternative for Germany.

Often his interest is personal. Musk once posted, then deleted, that “Canada is not a real country” in response to news of a petition to revoke his Canadian citizenship, which is not legally possible.

Musk posted last week on X, the social media platform he owns, in response to news of the Parti Québécois’ election: “Good. Quebec should separate. They would be better off. Alberta and Saskatchewan should separate too.”

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe replied with the word “No.” Alberta Premier Danielle Smith likewise voiced her disagreement.

She said she has already voted for Option 1, “and I hope to be able to convince all of you to vote the same way.”

In 1980, Quebec’s sovereignty movement under a Parti Québécois government soundly lost a referendum that would have given it a mandate to “negotiate a new constitutional agreement with the rest of Canada, based on the equality of nations.” In 1995, however, the PQ came within a single percentage point of a vote to leave. Turnout of over 90 per cent is thought to have boosted the remain numbers such that projections of a leave victory by a few points turned out to be wrong. Now, another vote seems likely, and is at least promised by the newly elected PQ government.
In Scotland, separatists lost their referendum in 2014 by fully 10 percentage points, with voter turnout at more than 80 per cent.
Alberta’s voter turnout in the last provincial election was 60 per cent, and in the last federal election 67 per cent, but this is obviously a different sort of ballot question.
2. An incomprehensible question

Curiously, the referendum is not a simple “Yes/No” question. It is a rambling offer of two numbered options. You can almost ignore the setup and get straight to the options, which are clear enough on their own without the wordy question, which reads: “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?”

Still here? Did you drift off a bit at “commence the legal process”? Did you need to be told “the Constitution” is “Canadian”? Did you already assume the “legal process” would be “required”? This referendum has more words than it needs.

Eventually, it gets to the key parts: “Option 1: Alberta should remain a province of Canada. Option 2: The Government of Alberta should commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada.”

It is a referendum, but the ballot reads like a lawyer’s letter. There are also nine other questions, all of which are yes/no, ON things like immigration control, immigrant access to social services, voter identification, judicial appointments and provincial-federal relations. How and even if people read through all that could have measurable impact on the emotionally charged central question among an electorate with a wide spectrum of interests and motivations.

“There’s a lot of people who want to send a message,” said Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on Oct. 7. “There’s a lot of people who think voting for Option 2 will give leverage. If those are your reasons, I would say there is a better way to send a message or to give leverage. And that is to give us a mandate on the other nine questions.”

Scotland was more concise, not troubling voters with too much windup or alternative messages. “Should Scotland be an independent country?” the 2014 referendum asked. The answer was no, according to 55 per cent of Scots.
3. Invalidated votes
Another way the true will of Albertans could be misrepresented in referendum results is by invalidation of good faith ballots.
More than 3,000 ballot packages have been invalidated for reasons such as missing declaration forms or problems with identification, though there remains time to fix those problems.

All ballots are to be counted by hand. Question 10, the central one about a referendum on separating, will be counted and reported first, followed by the other nine, with a deadline of 48 hours, according to Elections Alberta.
4. Quebec inspiration

Quebec sovereigntists have marched farther along the road to separatism, and their history offers cautionary tales for Alberta sovereigntists. But with a new Quebec government seeking the same goal, they also offer inspiration.

The idea that Canada is broken has lately had a run as a political slogan. The idea that it is actually breaking up is a less familiar notion, not exactly new, but surging to unprecedented levels of public interest with two provincial sovereignty movements campaigning simultaneously. So the successes of one could boost the fortunes of the other, even without actual cooperation.

As separatist advocate and leader of the Alberta Prosperity Project Mitch Sylvestre said after a cordial meeting with Paul St-Pierre Plamondon prior to his election as Quebec’s new premier, according to Rick Bell of the Calgary Herald, “You know, we both agreed, and this came out of Paul’s mouth not mine. He said the only level of government neither of us needs is at the federal level.”
5. Poor weather

The folk wisdom is that bad weather lowers turnout. It has even been measured in the U.S. at one percentage point per inch of rain, and half a point per inch of snow. In Canada, University of Ottawa researchers found that from the 2004 to 2015 federal elections, “each millimeter of precipitation decreases turnout by more than 0.1 percentage points.”

Higher temperatures boost turnout, they found, but only in spring, summer and fall elections. In the winter 2006 election victory for Stephen Harper, warmer temperatures “triggered lower turnout, in particular, when there was also high precipitation.”
6. American meddling

This is the October surprise, in which U.S. President Donald Trump could say or do something provocative, or perhaps offer something like the $5,000 payment he has offered American voters if Republicans win the midterm elections. In Alberta’s referendum, he could see some usefulness to his side in the wider trade war.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, therefore, is in a tricky strategic position, needing to both advocate for the Albertan remain side while managing his chaotic conflict with Trump, who is on record as coveting not only Alberta, but all of Canada.
Carney’s play was a Thanksgiving video, posed in a classroom at his Edmonton high school with a world map behind him, ON a long-weekend holiday that was thematically useful.

“It is a chance to give thanks for Canada,” he said. “This year, Thanksgiving is a bit different. A week from today, Albertans will have the opportunity to make an important decision about their future, whether to remain part of Canada, or begin a long and uncertain process through which Alberta could separate from Canada.”
His voice lilted on “could,” a little rhetorical emphasis on the inherent risk of Option 2, in contrast to his pitch for Option 1.

“I’m back home a lot these days, because we are building big things again in Alberta, thousands of new homes, high-speed rail, a new pipeline to the West Coast that will create lasting opportunity and prosperity,” he said. “Canada’s working. Truth is, we can’t achieve any of this if we’re divided. We can’t build big things on fault lines.”
7. A Brexit-style, surprise generational shift in political attitudes, and the emergence of a new archetype of politician
Of all the referendum results that few saw coming, Brexit, Britain’s vote to leave the European Union in 2016, stands out as maybe the most shocking.

It cost Prime Minister David Cameron his leadership, and was a failure of sorts also for Carney, who as Governor of the Bank of England had warned Brexit would cause a recession. He then agreed to extend his term to help avert one.

One immediate political winner was Boris Johnson, the now former prime minister whose appeal was to seem “shambolic,” as the British say, clownish, chaotic, disruptive, but massively likeable, like the earlier Torontonian archetype, the former mayor Rob Ford, who died a few months before Brexit.
A few months after Brexit came the equally momentous surprise first election of Donald Trump, who took that same archetype to new extremes of political power.

Britain still labours under the consequences of that political sea change. So does their Conservative Party’s revolving leadership of less charismatic figures. So, indeed, does the rest of the world, including Alberta.
8. Elon Musk

The tech titan does not have a perfect track record for sage prediction of domestic affairs in other countries, such as Britain where he once said civil war is “inevitable.” But he does take an interest. And, as in Germany, he can speak influentially in support of a populist right-wing movement on its way from the fringe to the mainstream of power, such as the Alternative for Germany.

Often his interest is personal. Musk once posted, then deleted, that “Canada is not a real country” in response to news of a petition to revoke his Canadian citizenship, which is not legally possible.

Musk posted last week on X, the social media platform he owns, in response to news of the Parti Québécois’ election: “Good. Quebec should separate. They would be better off. Alberta and Saskatchewan should separate too.”
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe replied with the word “No.” Alberta Premier Danielle Smith likewise voiced her disagreement.
She said she has already voted for Option 1, “and I hope to be able to convince all of you to vote the same way.”

stories.title: In Brampton, the house value decline bites hard
stories.summary: The median price of a detached home in Brampton hit $930,000 in September, dropping 37.4 per cent from March, 2022
stories.author: Shane Dingman
stories.content:
In recent years, Brampton, Ont., has played a major role in the Toronto-area housing market as one of the fastest-growing municipalities in the sprawling metro area. It is also among the areas hardest hit by the decline in real estate prices since the 2022 peak.

According to the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board, the median price of a detached home in Brampton hit $930,000 in September, a 37.4 per cent drop from March, 2022, when median prices were $1.486-million.

Brampton’s struggles provide plenty of shocking anecdotes of value destruction. One Reddit thread, entitled “HouseSigma blunders” cited the example of the detached home at 79 Templehill Rd., purchased for $1.875-million in late February, 2022, and sold in late September, 2026, for $1.135-million – a $740,000 change of fortune and a 39.5 per cent loss.

So, what kind of house can you find for prices almost 40 per cent less than four years ago?

Despite its list price, this updated four-bedroom house in the city’s centrally located Peel Village is probably going to sell for less than the city’s median price.

“These guys, they are selling for loss,” said Nav Takkar, a broker with Re/Max President Realty. “They bought this house last year; it looks like it will sell for less than asking price.”

Mr. Takkar is blunt about the reality facing sellers in much of the city. Mortgage costs, falling rents and economic worries are keeping prices depressed, he said. However, for these sellers, there is also opportunity. With good incomes, he said they can afford to take advantage of the situation and are looking to upgrade to a newer, larger home, one with more than 3,500 square feet of living space.

A few years ago, what they are looking for would have cost close to $2.5-million. Today? “The prices in those areas, they are listing for $1.8 to $1.9-million, but actually selling for $1.5 to $1.6-million,” Mr. Takkar said.

Brampton’s larger neighbours – Toronto and Mississauga – also saw median detached prices fall about 25 per cent, but from a higher level and not quite as far: from $1.6-million to $1.2-million. In that price range, inside Brampton, you get a lot more house than you do in Toronto, but it’s also hard to find a buyer for those houses.

Take the example of 22 Oldham, which listing agent Sumit Sharda with Re/Max Realty Services Inc. is selling for the second time this year.

“It sold in July, and the buyer failed to close. So we had to relist it,” he said. Just a few months after that offer for just under $1.2-million fell through, Mr. Sharda is finding the market decidedly slow.

The home has some real assets: A large lot next to a park and an in-ground pool. “The outside of that property is spectacular,” said Mr. Sharda. “Inside it’s kind of dated.” However, he notes the upstairs has 2,200 square feet of living space, with another 2,200 square feet on the lower level that has a walkout at grade. If a buyer could get a basement suite legalized, there might be potential for rental income.

Brampton’s decline has been nearly twice as rapid as the fall of the median detached price across Canada in the same period, according to data from the Canadian Real Estate Association. In March, 2022, the national median price for a detached house was $932,900. It has since fallen 21 per cent to just over $730,000.

There are houses in Brampton at the national median, though at that price there can be demerits caused by curb appeal, according to Bradley Mayer-Harman, with Century 21 Millennium Inc.

“I will be frank, this street is a bit more high-density,” he said, describing the neighbourhood as a solidly middle-class area, one with lots of hard-working people living in it. “There are a lot of townhomes and semis on the street. If your house is one of the largest ones on the street, you’re likely to be on the lower average of similar size homes.”

Mr. Mayer-Harman started working in real estate 16 years ago, and has recently spent a lot of time knocking on doors as he runs for town council in Mono, Ont. According to him, the mood of many homeowners is dark and getting darker.

“People had unbridled confidence that market values were always going to go up. Now it’s interesting to see how vividly that confidence has been shaken,” he said. “I’ve never experienced so many people moving based on fear rather than opportunity. Scared for their kids, scared of AI; it’s unbelievable. There’s a level of anxiety that goes beyond rational.”

stories.title: Pierre Poilievre’s impossible Alberta balancing act
stories.summary: The Big Story discusses how vital a Tory voice could be in the referendum, and whether or not decided-Albertans could be swayed either way.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
Alberta referendum mail-in special ballots are seen in Calgary, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026.THE Canadian Press/Jeff McIntosh THE Canadian Press

By Analysis by The Big Story podcast

Posted October 15, 2026 7:41 am.

In less than a week, Albertans will head to the polls to vote on a series of 10 referendum questions, one of which brings the province’s sovereignty into focus. For the past several months, support for separation has dwindled, as both former and current politicians continue to plead with Albertans to reconsider thoughts of separation.

Among the current names that have stayed out of the spotlight for the most part, however, is Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre. Other than a handful of speaking events, he hasn’t been as loud as other figures in making the case for federalism.

Host Caryn Ceolin speaks to Duane Bratt, a political scientist with Mount Royal University to discuss how vital a Tory voice could be at this point, and whether or not decided-Albertans could be swayed either way.
