stories.title: Cyberattack May have leaked student and parent information, Burnaby school district says
stories.summary: Ransomware attack it suffered on Sept. 21 affected school websites and portals, internal network services and phone lines
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Public school officials in Burnaby, B.C., say hackers May have obtained student and parental information in a recent cyberattack.

The Burnaby School District says in an online notice that the ransomware attack it suffered on Sept. 21 affected school websites and portals, internal network services and phone lines.

The notice says hackers copied and stole files that May have contained lists of parent, guardian and student names and contact information, as well as birthdates, grades and school names.

It says the hackers May also have obtained registration forms, kindergarten assessment notes and detailed lists of students on specialized learning plans.

The school district says the matter is in the hands of the RCMP and B.C.’s privacy commissioner, adding that its system security is being evaluated to prevent further breaches.

It says staff, students and their families have been offered registration with TransUnion’s fraud alert service and encourages them to be wary of any suspicious communications.

“We understand that incidents of this nature are concerning and we remain committed to keeping the Burnaby Schools community updated throughout this process, as the investigation proceeds and additional information becomes available,” the notice says.

stories.title: The right to know about Tumbler Ridge
stories.summary: Canadians are still waiting for answers, and officials in this country seem just fine with that
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
Justice officials recently released some important information about the Tumbler Ridge massacre, including allegations gathered by police about where the killer got their weapons. Unfortunately, this did not come from the officials in Canada.

The shooting left eight Canadians dead, including six children. Canadians should be kept fully up to date about the investigation – by the federal government, or the provincial government, or the RCMP. Instead, these details came from the United States. While it’s good that the information is now public, how it emerged is part of a troubling trend of secrecy in Canada.

This is a problem that goes beyond the police. Too often in Canada, the default assumption among officials is that the public has no right to know. For years The Globe and Mail has been exposing this kneejerk reticence in a project dubbed Secret Canada .

Because of the importance of law enforcement and the justice system – which are crucial both to public safety and to the public’s perception of safety – secrecy from them has a particularly corrosive effect.

In 2020, during the mass shooting that began in Portapique, Nova Scotia, the RCMP did not alert the public for 12 hours that the killer was disguised as a police officer. The Mass Casualty Commission, which examined the incident, found that “the RCMP public communication, sent by Twitter during the evening of April 18, seriously understated the threat presented by the perpetrator and the associated risks to the public.”

More recently, Mounties in Saskatchewan went beyond controlling what they reveal and tried to encourage the media to hold back as well. The police there warned journalists that the act of journalism – specifically, talking to witnesses and publishing what they say – can be dangerous. The police helpfully offered to advise media on how to do their jobs.

This tendency toward secrecy is not unique to the RCMP. In the wake of a synagogue shooting in the eastern Ontario community of Belleville, local police did not reveal that the gunman did not have a firearm licence.

It’s good that a source close to the investigation was willing to share that information with The Globe and Mail. Every extra detail about the shooting helps give Canadians a fuller understanding of what happened. But it’s bad that the information was, officially, deemed secret.

While reasonable people can disagree on which investigative details can be released without jeopardizing an investigation, two aspects of these recent shootings are worth remembering.

First, in both cases the killer is dead. While there could be prosecutions of accomplices, and the U.S. information about Tumbler Ridge was released in relation to a person in that country being charged, the central perpetrator is beyond the reach of justice. Their prosecution cannot be put into danger.

Second, the very fact that the Tumbler Ridge information was released by U.S. officials and not Canadian ones highlights that there are differing views on what must be kept secret. That two different institutions came to two different conclusions shows that the Canadian instinct towards secrecy is not inherently correct – or required.

According to a criminal complaint filed against an accused co-conspirator, Canadians now know a number of allegations related to the Tumbler Ridge shooting. The person charged in the U.S. reported that Jesse Van Rootselaar claimed to have stolen firearms from the family gun safe, convinced someone to buy ammunition for them and possessed a device that U.S. police believed would convert a rifle into a machine gun.

Why does this matter? At the most basic, it May reveal gaps in Canada’s gun-safety regime. But it also helps paint a picture of how an unspeakable tragedy was able to unfold.

There remain many unanswered questions in Tumbler Ridge. Were warning signs missed? Did people deliberately, or inadvertently, help make the crime happen? And beyond this particular tragedy, are there broader vulnerabilities that need to be addressed? Canadians don’t know the answers, and officials in this country seem just fine with that.

The principle of “need to know” is common in security and intelligence jobs. This limits information to those who require it. But officials must remember that the public is not party to any such policy. The public has a default right to know – that’s fundamental to a free and open society.

stories.title: Nan’s House (still) slated for demolition
stories.summary: There will be no last-minute reprieve by London city council for the heritage home at 100 Stanley St. that was unofficially dubbed “Nan’s House” after its last owner Nan Finlayson.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
There will be no last-minute reprieve by London city council for the heritage home at 100 Stanley St. that was unofficially dubbed “Nan’s House” after its last owner Nan Finlayson.

On Wednesday, Council considered the engineering department’s request to demolish the small yellow-brick heritage home to accommodate work to widen Wharncliffe Rd. under the CN Rail tracks just north of Horton Street.

The four-lane arterial road narrows to just three lanes beneath the aging rail overpass.

Finlayson sat and watched council debate the fate of her former home from the public gallery.

Starting in 2016, a public campaign fought to stop the city from taking Finlayson’s home, but she eventually she agreed to sell in 2020.

“I do believe that there is an opportunity to save this building. We don’t need to rush into making decisions right now,” Coun. Anna Hopkins told council colleagues.

A report to the Planning and Environment Committee had stated, “the proposed construction method for the CN Bridge has changed, reducing the original justification for the removal of the heritage house from the protected heritage property at 100 Stanley St.”

“The cost of preservation is going to far exceed the cost of demolition,” Deputy Mayor Shawn Lewis countered, “The city is growing and we need to move a major transportation bottleneck out of the way to keep people going.”

Kelly Scherr, Deputy City Manager of Environment and Infrastructure told council that it is highly unlikely that alternative construction methods could prevent the house from being severely damaged during the replacement of the rail overpass and road widening.

“While we could spend a great deal of money doing so and exploring that, the only way to find out is to go to a tender process, see what is proposed by a contractor, and then make a decision,” Scherr told council. “At that point, we’re going to be substantially down the road with respect to investing costs into a design.”

A motion to refer the matter to a future meeting was defeated, and the demolition request was approved.

No firm date has been set for the demolition to begin.

Citing steep increases in cost estimates, council previously removed the widening project from the 2024-2027 multi-year budget.

Scherr said the demolition would ensure the project is “shovel-ready” in the event funding from senior levels of government is made available.

stories.title: Ken Sim and Pete Fry face off in Vancouver mayoral race
stories.summary: Kareem Allam, Rebecca Bligh and Colleen Hardwick are three other big-name candidates who reject the label of spoiler
stories.author: Marissa Birnie
stories.content:
Vancouver mayoral candidates Ken Sim and Pete Fry view each other as their main rival in the battle for City Hall.

But while recent polling suggests the mayoral race is indeed a faceoff between incumbent Sim and two-term Green Councillor Fry, there are three other big-name candidates who reject the label of spoiler.

Kareem Allam – Sim’s former chief of staff turned litigation adversary – is running with the Vancouver Liberals, which is not affiliated with the federal party.

“The pollsters don’t always get it right. Municipal government is also the hardest level to poll. It’s got its tricks and nuances, especially in an at-large system,” he said in an interview Tuesday.

The Vancouver race culminates Saturday, when municipalities across British Columbia go to the polls.

Interest in the Vancouver race appears high. The City of Vancouver says more than 103,000 people have voted in advance, up 60 per cent from roughly 65,000 voters over five advance days in 2022.

Sim, who is campaigning for a second term as mayor with the right-of-centre ABC Vancouver, said while he would be the first to admit he didn’t get everything right during his tenure, he believes he can lead the city in the right direction.

“We’ve gotten some pretty significant things done, but there’s way more work to do,” he said in an interview Wednesday.

Other candidates include Rebecca Bligh, a two-term councillor who helped get Sim elected with ABC Vancouver in 2022 and is now running with Vote Vancouver, and Team candidate Colleen Hardwick, a former councillor.

Allam, Hardwick and Bligh all rejected the notion their candidacies could split the centre or centre-right vote.

“The question is not left or right. The question is about who we are serving at city hall,” Hardwick said Tuesday.

Bligh said she was running to govern for Vancouver’s ignored middle class, and polling did not change how she campaigned.

“It’s anyone’s race,” she said in an interview Wednesday.

Fry, son of longtime Liberal MP Hedy Fry, has acknowledged benefiting from the narrowing of the progressive field, after the withdrawals of William Azaroff from OneCity Vancouver and Stephanie Allen for Cope Vancouver.

After ending his candidacy, Azaroff appeared at City Hall with Fry, who praised him for running a serious campaign that “raised real issues” such as housing, small business and affordability.

“I think folks are excited to be able to talk up a viable alternative to Ken Sim as the mayor of Vancouver and really reset,” Fry said in an interview Tuesday.

He added that Azaroff’s withdrawal was recognition that he was the person best suited to defeat Sim.

Bligh said she’s a progressive candidate with a centrist platform. Meanwhile, Allam said he believed he was taking votes from Sim and Fry equally.

The candidates’ platforms all emphasize quality-of-life issues, including affordability and public safety. Sim’s promises include a zero per cent property tax increase.

The election ballot also includes two plebiscite questions on public safety.

The non-binding questions ask voters if they’re in favour of the city “strengthening its laws to forbid open-air hard drug use in public spaces,” which is already illegal in B.C. The other asks if the city should ask the province to convert portions of the old St. Paul’s hospital into a “secure medical facility” with 100-plus involuntary care beds.

Hardwick called the questions a “populist election tactic,” while other critics said they aren’t realistic.

Sim said strengthening the city health bylaw – regulating conduct such as smoking in common areas – would allow officers to issue tickets or confiscate drugs without arrests. The involuntary care question, he said, is about asking the province to fulfill its accountability to people who pose a risk to their own safety or others.

Fry said he supports managing drug use in public spaces, but differs from Sim in believing that people should be diverted to supervised consumption sites or shelters.

His platform focuses on housing, transportation and the economy. “Folks should be able to have a good life in this city, he said.

Bligh said Sim’s property tax freezes protect wealthy landowners and undercut critical services. She said she would work with the federal government to leverage city-owned land and provide free transit for youth.

Hardwick said the key to livability in Vancouver is effective city planning. She said she wanted to repeal the city’s official development plan and re-establish neighbourhood planning offices

Allam said he wants to bring youth back to Vancouver by improving affordability through jobs and housing, and investing in parks and community centres.

He said his platform cuts across ideologies, and distanced himself from Sim, who filed a lawsuit in May 2025 alleging Allam falsely accused him of drinking and driving.

Sim faces his own defamation lawsuit from councillor Sean Orr, filed after falsely accusing Orr of distributing illegal drugs in comments to Chinese-speaking reporters.

Trials in both cases are far off.

For now, the focus is on the ballot box.

“I think people will be surprised at the results,” Allam said.

stories.title: ‘Being forced out of business’: Niagara wine industry sees mixed fortunes as harvest begins amid U.S.-Canada trade war
stories.summary: The harvest, one of the most important periods of the year for Ontario's wine sector, comes after months of escalating trade tensions.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By David Zura and Lucas Casaletto

Posted October 15, 2026 6:05 am.

As grape harvest season gets underway across Niagara wine country, growers and wineries are taking stock of a year marked by trade upheaval, shifting consumer habits and sharply different fortunes across the industry.

The harvest, one of the most important periods of the year for Ontario’s wine sector, comes after months of escalating trade tensions between Canada and the United States . The industry has weathered a series of tariffs, retaliatory measures and, most recently, a near-total U.S. import ban on Canadian wine , forcing producers to adapt to a dramatically altered marketplace.

For some, strong domestic demand has more than offset the loss of access to the American market.

“The last couple of years, we have seen demand for our product skyrocket,” said Kevin Watson, chair of the Grape Growers of Ontario and a grower in Niagara-on-the-Lake.

Watson said Canadian consumers have stepped up in a significant way, helping absorb supply that might otherwise have been destined for export markets.

“Three years ago, we had about 5,000 metric tons of grape surplus. In the last couple of years, we have been short on grape. It’s a seller’s market,” he said. “That’s how much the Canadian consumer has helped our industry.”

The shift comes as many Canadian shoppers have increasingly sought out domestic products following months of trade disputes and restrictions affecting wine sales between the two countries.

At Pelham Family Estate Winery, owner Paul Speck said both consumer support and a healthy crop are contributing to optimism about the sector’s future.

“The crop’s coming in nicely, so I’m very, very confident and bullish about the next couple of years,” he said.

Speck added that some international customers are also turning to Canadian wines amid changing global purchasing patterns.

“We’re hearing from our Belgium and Denmark customers that people are, instead of buying American wines, buying Canadian.”

While many growers and wineries are benefiting from the changing market dynamics, others are struggling to adapt.

For John Kocsis, who owns Atlantis Niagara Wines with his wife, the past several years have been marked by one challenge after another.

Kocsis, whose business specializes in tourism-focused experiences and premium products such as ice-wine, said sales had finally begun recovering in 2024 after pandemic-related setbacks. That momentum, he said, was derailed by tariffs and trade restrictions introduced in 2025.

“In early 2025, the tariffs came, and then that was just like another kick,” Kocsis said.

Operating in Niagara since 2018, Kocsis said his business relies heavily on tourists visiting the region and purchasing wine to take home. With uncertainty surrounding cross-border sales and travel-related purchases, he fears the business May not survive.

“We’re basically being forced out of business.”

Kocsis said he sees little opportunity to pivot after years of investing heavily in the operation.

“I’ve got everything that we have tied up in this already. The damage that’s been done is just, for us, so embedded into the business now.”

Watson acknowledged that adapting business models in the wine sector can be difficult, particularly for smaller operators.

“It’s very difficult,” he said.

Despite those challenges, vineyards across Niagara remain focused on bringing in this year’s crop. Growers say harvest conditions have generally been favourable, with grapes continuing to come off the vine through the fall.

The 2026 harvest is expected to continue into November, offering the industry’s strongest performers hope for another successful vintage, even as some wineries face an increasingly uncertain future.

stories.title: Freeland's book reveals Chrétien's power play, crying in cabinet and Trudeau's lecture about using the word 'crazy'
stories.summary: Nearly two years after her shocking resignation that shook the halls of power in Ottawa, Freeland is telling her side of the story.
stories.author: Catherine Lévesque
stories.content:
Ottawa — Nearly two years after her shocking resignation from cabinet that shook the halls of power in Ottawa, Chrystia Freeland is telling her side of the story of how she was about to get dumped by Justin Trudeau as finance minister.

Her new book “Unreliable Boyfriend” is in part a political memoir and in part a reflection of Donald Trump’s America. But it also contains so-far undisclosed details of why she chose to resign from Trudeau’s cabinet the day she was supposed to present the fall economic statement — thus precipitating Trudeau’s own departure weeks later.

Freeland writes that while she thinks history will be kind to Trudeau because he stood up to Trump and implemented social programs such as childcare, she thinks she probably left Trudeau’s cabinet “a year, or maybe two years, too late.”

Here are a few revelations from Freeland’s new book.

Freeland said while many were encouraging her to leave cabinet in her final six months in Trudeau’s cabinet, the pivotal moment was when she was drinking chardonnay with former prime minister Jean Chrétien at his Ottawa home in November 2024.

Chrétien, she writes, started the conservation with a “healthy dose of flattery” — calling her a “very good finance minister” and said she had been “unfailingly loyal” to Trudeau which was “admirable.”

But the tone of the conversation took a turn when Chrétien said Freeland had a responsibility not only to Trudeau, but to the Liberal party and to Canada.

“As long as you support him, he will stay on as PM. And he will lose the next election,” she recalls the former prime minister saying.

He added that Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre would become prime minister, the Liberal Party would be devastated, and she would be partly to blame for that.

“After the gentle caress of Mr. Chrétien’s earlier compliments, those words felt like a slap in the face, or, since we’re Canadian and winter was coming, like stepping out from a warm house into forty-below weather,” she wrote.

Freeland said she did not go back to her hotel room that evening planning to step down from Trudeau’s cabinet, but she did go to bed with “a new and horrible understanding” that she would be partly at fault if Trudeau led the Liberals into the next election.

Despite having served as one of Trudeau’s top ministers for nearly a decade, Freeland said she could count on the fingers of one hand the number of times she met with the prime minister alone. That was about to change in the days prior to her departure.

At the end of a meeting in his office on Dec. 2, 2024, she said that Trudeau called her aside for “a few rare private minutes” to tell her he wanted her to continue serving as his finance minister until the next election, which would happen in less than a year.

Six days later, ON Dec. 8, 2024, Trudeau invited her to his home at Rideau Cottage.

“It was probably the longest time I have spent alone with him,” she wrote.

Freeland said they drank glasses of water and Trudeau mused about his determination to lead the Liberals into the next election. He then made a surprising statement.

“At one point, apropos of nothing, he told me he believed that one day I would become prime minister, and that I would do a good job,” she wrote.

Later that week, Trudeau and his team removed $12 billion in spending cuts she had pushed for in the fall economic statement. The Globe and Mail also reported that Trudeau was again trying to convince Mark Carney to replace her as finance minister.

On Dec. 13, 2024, Trudeau and Freeland had their infamous one-on-one Zoom call.

Trudeau said she would be shuffled out of the finance portfolio the day after presenting the fall economic statement. When she asked who would replace her, Trudeau said with a “half-proud, half-defiant smile” that it would be Carney.

“The Zoom call with Trudeau had taught me that I simply couldn’t trust the PM — and that he had decided not to trust me. I had to leave.”

Trudeau took a lot of heat for correcting a woman who used the word “mankind” instead of “peoplekind” in a town hall meeting in 2018 — but it turns out cabinet ministers also had to mind their language in private, according to Freeland.

In one cabinet meeting, Trudeau apparently took issue with “a very progressive female colleague” casually referring to something as “crazy.”

“That earned her a long, harsh public scolding from Trudeau, who informed her that using ‘crazy’ as a derogatory adjective was insulting to people with mental health issues,” wrote Freeland.

Trudeau suggested they instead use the word “bananas” which was less offensive.

Freeland said that while she has always bristled at accusations of “wokeness” and “political correctness,” she said that “linguistic-purity tests” can also be off-putting to regular people who struggle with which words are okay or not to use.

“And they can give people the sense — and rightly so — that their leaders are more focused on the performance of virtue than on actually improving people’s lives.”

“Crying was routine at cabinet meetings. There were always boxes of Kleenex on hand, and really sad colleagues would sometimes get a hug from the PM,” Freeland wrote.

Yet what troubled her the most about the crying and the lectures “was that it sometimes went along with what seemed like bullying,” she added.

Freeland did not go into detail about the alleged bullying but said one of Trudeau’s “favourite homilies” to cabinet and caucus was talking about the necessity of eating “shit sandwiches” from time to time.

He would also instruct his ministers to stay on message until they “wanted to vomit a little bit in our mouth.”

“By the time he stepped down, PM Trudeau had been so thoroughly caricatured as a woke poser that it was easy to forget that one of the things that had captivated Canadians when he first burst onto the scene was his macho charisma,” she wrote.

Freeland referred to one of his early breakthrough moments as the charity boxing match against Senator Patrick Brazeau, a member of the Algonquin Nation.

In a controversial interview with the Rolling Stone, Trudeau boasted about his wager with Brazeau that the loser of the fight would be required to have his hair cut in the lobby of the House of Commons.

Brazeau apparently resisted as long hair carries deep spiritual significance in many First Nations cultures. Trudeau said that is why he proposed that bet. “When a warrior cuts his hair, it’s a sign of shame, so it’s very apropos,” he told the magazine.

stories.title: Carney needs to completely overhaul the Trudeau-era immigration system, report says
stories.summary: Canada needs to overhaul the Trudeau-era immigration system so that applicants are selected largely on their ability to boost the economy.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa — Canada needs to overhaul the Trudeau-era immigration system so that applicants are selected largely on their ability to boost the economy, a new think tank report suggests, part of a wide-ranging set of policy suggestions for governments at all levels.

The C.D. Howe Institute report, to be released Thursday, argues that Canada should go back to assessing skilled immigrant applicants based on a points system designed to evaluate their likelihood to succeed economically. That system, which was quietly dropped by former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s government in 2023, ran for two decades by rating applicants on key metrics such as education, work experience, language skills and a demonstrated ability to earn a living.

But that changed about three years ago, the report says, when Ottawa started focusing on other metrics, such as preferences for certain professions and applicants who could speak French.

The think tank’s report, a wide-ranging set of policy recommendations to boost Canada’s lagging productivity and economic growth, said the old system worked better because it focused on applicants who were most likely to do well and meant fewer new Canadians doing work that didn’t match their skills.

“The highest scores got in,” the report says.

If adopted, the change would mark another key policy from the Trudeau era to be cancelled or sharply curtailed by Prime Minister Mark Carney. The current Liberal government has already changed direction on such Trudeau-era policies as the consumer carbon tax, a proposed capital gains tax increase and higher immigration levels.

The recommendations on immigration form a key part of the report’s focus on human capital, one of eight policy areas that it addresses. It also calls for governments to do more to verify foreign credentials used in immigration applications, raise admission standards for international students, link immigration levels to economic growth and select more immigrants who are likely to be entrepreneurs.

The report, called The Productivity Blueprint: An Agenda for Higher Living Standards in Canada, calls for more than 100 policy changes that would help close the gap between the country’s lagging productivity and that of other industrialized countries. Between 2014 and 2024, real gross domestic product per capita, one of the most common measures of living standards, grew just 3.5 per cent in Canada, the worst performance among nine peer countries. In the U.S., by comparison, the economy grew 20.2 percent during that same period based on the same metric.

Successful immigration depends on 'shared values,' not ancestry, Trudeau tells Finns

Canadians' immigration views are changing. How will that affect the economy?

Productivity, which measures how much is produced per hour worked, is considered the primary lever behind rising incomes and living standards.

Jeremy Kronick, the institute’s chief executive officer, was quoted in a release saluting some of the Carney government’s steps to boost the economy, such as its new Major Projects Office and the accounting changes for business investment, but said long-term improvement will take a commitment to change. “There’s no quick fix for productivity,” he said. “If Canadians want stronger wages and living standards over the long term, raising productivity needs to be Canada’s number one priority.”

The Carney government is also trying to inoculate the Canadian economy as much as possible from the trade war started by U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariff policies.

The federal government’s initial response was to offer short-term support payments for companies and workers hit by the disruption from the south, but has in recent months been focusing more on structural factors such as pipelines, transportation infrastructure, faster approval times for major projects and making Canada a more competitive place to invest.

The C.D. Howe report also calls for sweeping changes to the country’s tax policy regime, including a reduction in the general corporate income tax rate to 10 per cent from 15. Ottawa has already cut corporate income taxes almost in half since 2000-01, when the rate stood at 28 per cent. Yet during that time, the federal government’s revenue from that stream has climbed in the last fiscal year to $97.1 billion from $28.3 billion.

The report, which draws on decades of research, also calls on Ottawa to reduce the number of personal income tax brackets to three from five and to replace most existing tax credits with a $10,000 basic allowance. To help spur business, the report also calls on the federal government to rein in business subsidies, which have grown 125 per cent since 2015, consuming $37.4 billion of taxpayer dollars.

It also calls on governments to improve the country’s transportation networks, boost competition, make regulations smarter, and cut spending to reduce debt.

While many of the proposed changes carry hefty price tags, a more productive, competitive economy means higher wages and profits that lead to healthier government coffers. The C.D. Howe report says the suggested changes would unlock $140 billion in new business investment and would add 2.5 per cent to the overall economy.

stories.title: Rain expected overnight ahead of chilly weekend in London
stories.summary: Cloudy skies are expected across London on Thursday, with rain moving into the area overnight ahead of a chilly weekend.
stories.content:
Cloudy skies are expected across London on Thursday, with rain moving into the area overnight ahead of a chilly weekend.

CTV News London meteorologist Julie Atchison says the city should remain mostly dry through the day, with some sunny breaks and a forecast high of 16 C.

Showers are expected to arrive after 8 p.m., followed by steady rain and gusty winds Friday morning. Between 10 and 15 millimetres of rain could fall before conditions ease to showers Friday afternoon.

A cold front is expected to move through the area Friday evening, bringing a sharp drop in temperatures for the weekend.

Daytime highs are forecast to range from 10 to 15 C, with overnight lows falling to between 1 and 2 C.

Atchison says the colder air will bring some of the coolest temperatures of the season so far, but conditions are expected to clear, bringing sunshine back to the region.

A mix of sun and cloud is forecast for Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, with temperatures gradually recovering to a high of about 18 C by midweek.

stories.title: Kawhi Leonard’s return to the Toronto Raptors is a sequel worth waiting for
stories.summary: The team spent most of its history searching for the superstar who would choose Toronto as much as Toronto chose him
stories.author: Alex Wong
stories.content:
Alex Wong is co-host of the Hello and Welcome podcast. His most recent book is Prehistoric: The Audacious and Improbable Origin Story of the Toronto Raptors .

Earlier this summer, the Toronto Raptors held a press conference to officially announce Kyle Lowry’s retirement. A celebratory mood permeated the team’s practice facility where the event was held. The locker room was decorated with photographs, game-worn jerseys and a treasure trove of memorabilia celebrating the star point guard’s greatest moments with the team. As the greatest Raptor of all time prepared to address the media, friends, family and former colleagues on hand, Lowry’s former teammate Kawhi Leonard casually strolled in to take a seat. A few days earlier, the Raptors had agreed to – but not yet completed – a trade with the Los Angeles Clippers to bring Leonard back to the city he delivered a championship to seven years ago.

The parallels are almost too on-the-nose for this second go round. Once again, the Raptors have fallen short in the postseason, without any available path for a significant roster upgrade. And once again, Leonard became available at a reasonable price, making the acquisition a no-brainer. But that’s where the parallels end.

Back in 2018, when Leonard was traded to the Raptors – before the championship and unforgettable parade through downtown Toronto, before he had an entire country rooting for a basketball team, before the shot and all the other on-court memories he created during the magical playoff run – Leonard had come to Toronto reluctantly, as it is believed he wanted to be traded from the San Antonio Spurs to Los Angeles instead.

He kept the entire city at arms length during his one year in Toronto, remained non-committal about re-signing with the team when his contract expired at the end of the season, and rarely gave us a glimpse into his personal life, leaving fans to spend the year desperately searching for clues that might indicate his intentions. When Leonard decided to return home and join the Clippers just weeks after he gave a proverbial last laugh at the parade, the guarded superstar had accomplished everything he could with the team, yet somehow left without ever connecting with the city and the fanbase.

If you asked me to describe Toronto as a sports city, I would say we are a bit – okay, a lot – insecure. We’re always looking for validation, for ourselves and for our city, through the pro athletes we root for. Since the beginning, Raptors fans have reckoned with the fact that players have always viewed Toronto as a layover, not a landing spot. Our first superstar, Damon Stoudamire, requested a trade after two and a half seasons and was sent home to Portland. Vince Carter sank an entire era of the franchise when his trade demands were met. Chris Bosh was a perennial All-Star who took less money to win championships in Miami. Even Leonard won the title in Toronto and still decided to leave a perfect basketball situation to return home.

Kawhi Leonard spoke to reporters at the Toronto Raptors’ season-opening media day and says he just wants to focus on basketball after he and the Los Angeles Clippers were investigated for salary cap circumvention.

The Canadian Press

It’s why we fall for players like Lowry, and DeMar DeRozan – the rare ones who loudly pledge their allegiance to the city, and allow us to experience the ups and downs of the season in a way that feels more than just watching a bunch of guys hoop for 48 minutes a night. It’s why Blue Jays first baseman Vladimir Guerrero Jr. is still beloved even after a disastrous season and some ill-timed comments to the media. He has always made the “Toronto” on the front of his jersey matter. Here in Toronto, we don’t simply anoint players because they helped raise their franchises to new heights. We embrace them because they acknowledge the city in return. They understand the implied agreement between themselves and the fans as part of being a star in Toronto.

Even as Leonard was showered with love – in the form of plants , New Balance T-shirt sales, and offers of free meals across the city – he left everyone feeling a little bit empty. Sure, it’s a bit hard to ask for more from a guy who delivered the franchise’s only championship, but it was the most glaring missing piece of the Kawhi experience the first time around.

It looks like he might be filling in those blanks in his return. He has already expressed more about his desire to be part of the city and the franchise’s future than when he first arrived eight years ago, has been more engaged with coaches and teammates, and on media day on the eve of training camp, he was more open with journalists than ever before.

Leonard joked about being the “fun guy.” He shared an anecdote about his kid – who was born in Canada – being excited to see the Maple Leaf flag again. He talked about the importance of helping the next generation of hoopers in the country through his involvement with local basketball gyms and camps. He praised the team’s roster and expressed his desire, after signing a contract extension after the trade finally became official , to have a much longer stay with the franchise, and potentially retire as a Raptor.

Listen, you can be cynical about this reunion. Leonard needed a place to land after he was part of a league-mandated investigation into salary cap circumvention, and according to reports, received millions of dollars in a number of questionable sponsorship deals. After burning his relationships in both San Antonio and Los Angeles, Toronto was the perfect spot for him to rebuild both his reputation and give him a chance to complete a legacy with a single NBA team. Perhaps this is, once again, a marriage of convenience. But we don’t need to be on pins and needles. Leonard is starring in an improbable sequel, but, this time, it feels like he actually wants the role.

The Raptors have spent most of their history searching for the superstar who would choose Toronto as much as Toronto chose him. That history is part of why this reunion feels so significant. For once, the superstar who left is the one who came back. We don’t know what the next few years will look like, and expecting another 2019 would be asking for something close to a miracle. But maybe the point is that we’re getting something different this time: We’re getting Kawhi Leonard in Toronto – on his own terms.

There’s always a danger in reunions. They may just remind you that you’re chasing something that doesn’t exist anymore, like high-school friends you shared the most wonderful memories with who are now all at different stages in their lives. But in this particular case, Kawhi Leonard’s reunion with the Raptors doesn’t need to surpass the original. And maybe the best part of his return to Toronto isn’t what he does on the court at all. It’s that, after everything that happened the first time, he finally seems to understand that being a Raptor is about more than what he accomplished in a single postseason.

He already gave this city its greatest basketball memory. Now, seven years later, he’s ready to try to add a few more chapters to what we thought was a finished story. That’s a sequel worth waiting for.

stories.title: How a contested B.C. supportive housing project won over its neighbours
stories.summary: For years, acrimony dominated the conversation in this Fraser Valley community – but residents’ worst fears never materialized
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
About this series

The Globe is reporting from cities and towns in Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia to hear from residents about the issues affecting their communities and their votes in the municipal elections.

Julia Clissold and her husband had just settled into their new Maple Ridge, B.C., condo in the summer of 2022 when they learned that the residential development planned for next door would be supportive housing.

They had concerns: The 52-unit building, which would come to be known as Rivers Reach, would replace a nearby temporary modular housing project where drug use, fires and noise disturbances were common. Police were “constantly” at that site, as were people who loitered and camped out at the property, Ms. Clissold recalled.

“We’re like, ‘It’s just going to move over here,’” she said in an interview. “We wouldn’t walk our dogs down there, we wouldn’t drive by, because there were always people on the road in various states of what have you. So we were very scared at that point.”

Many others in their new-construction condominium, located on a quiet residential street, were similarly apprehensive, said Ms. Clissold, who is president of the building’s strata council. Some felt deceived by the realtors and developers who sold them their homes along with the idea that a complex similar to theirs was planned for next door.

But a year and a half later, Ms. Clissold has become an unlikely champion of the supportive housing project. The fears she and others had never materialized; Ms. Clissold attributes its success to careful planning, attentive management and the operator’s responsiveness to community feedback.

The tensions that once gripped this community are hardly unique. Across B.C., disputes over homeless encampments and supportive housing have dragged on for months or years, in big cities, sleepy suburbs and northern communities. This year alone, proposed supportive housing projects in Abbotsford, Burnaby and the District of North Vancouver have been cancelled amid backlash.

The issue has also become a flashpoint in municipal election debates leading up to Saturday’s general vote.

In Richmond, fierce opposition to supportive housing has put mayoral candidates under pressure to make their positions clear, prompting some to explicitly declare their opposition . In Surrey, one candidate has taken the opposite approach, pledging to build 1,000 new units annually for four years and blaming the past council’s resistance to such projects for worsening street homelessness. Candidates in Vancouver’s contest have been grilled on whether they would reverse the incumbent administration’s freeze on net-new supportive housing.

The experience in Maple Ridge offers a case study in how local leadership can help overcome entrenched opposition to supportive housing projects – particularly as an incumbent provincial government that is seeking re-election signals it would rather direct limited funding to communities willing to embrace them.

In an interview with The Globe and Mail last week, NDP Leader David Eby said ahead of the Oct. 24 provincial vote that his government is done with overriding municipalities that oppose supportive housing. “If they’re happier with an encampment in their community, if they’re willing to live with that rather than to have the hard conversation with their community about the supportive housing that’s needed, I struggle to know why I wouldn’t dedicate that money to a local government that actually wants to close the encampment and open housing,” he said.

Efforts to address homelessness in Maple Ridge have stretched back more than a decade, marked by encampments, temporary shelters and contentious housing proposals that have galvanized residents, shaped elections and pitted local leaders against the province.

Former Maple Ridge mayor Nicole Read, who advocated for unhoused people and supported low-barrier options during her term from 2014 to 2018, was the subject of online harassment that became so heated she was forced to curtail public appearances as the RCMP investigated threats to her personal safety.

In May, 2017, people began erecting tents and makeshift shelters at a vacant downtown site slated for a neighbourhood park, creating an encampment that would become a highly visible indictment of the city’s shortage of affordable housing. The site, which came to be called Anita Place, persisted for more than two years. At its peak, nearly 200 people sheltered there, with many saying it offered more security than being alone.

But the encampment drew the ire of other community members and local officials who raised crime and safety concerns. People staying at the camp used portable heaters, propane tanks and electrical connections to stay warm, sparking numerous fires and creating significant safety risks, firefighters said. Police said they received dozens of calls about weapons and stolen items.

In response, B.C.’s NDP government announced a plan to move about 50 people from the camp into temporary modular housing on province-owned land nearby while permanent housing was being built. Coast Mental Health, a non-profit that operates housing and other social support services, would manage the site.

The move went against the wishes of the local council and was met with such fierce community opposition that the provincial government and BC Housing, the Crown corporation in charge of subsidized housing, had to seek a court injunction to clear community members who camped at the modular site in protest.

The work-camp-style housing opened in October, 2018. Minutes from community advisory committee meetings around that time detailed neighbourhood complaints, including reports of people congregating at the site and visitors yelling to get the attention of tenants. Residents of a nearby seniors’ home said they didn’t like seeing people under the influence and were upset by their use of foul language.

The controversy over the new housing coincided with a municipal election. Just two days after the modular site opened, voters in Maple Ridge ushered in a new mayor, Mike Morden, and four new councillors. Mr. Morden, a two-term city councillor who campaigned on a tougher response to the homelessness and addiction issues that he said were driving crime in the city, won a decisive victory.

The new mayor and council feuded with the province over the site throughout their term, arguing that the B.C. government’s efforts to build supportive housing in the city undermined their local authority. They were also at odds about what that housing should look like; Mr. Morden said anything short of complex care with intensive health and social supports would be inadequate.

It was hard to deny that more support was needed. From 2019 to 2025, the temporary housing site was associated with 17 deaths – 15 from drug toxicity and two that were natural deaths, the BC Coroners Service said in response to a request from The Globe.

Some residents were living with significant mental health and addiction issues, the report said, and the repurposed modular building was already “at the end of its useful life” when people moved in.

As the province forged ahead with a permanent housing site, which would also be operated by Coast Mental Health, some residents said they felt their concerns about safety and the capacity of emergency services were being ignored. The tension in the city became such that drivers began to pelt unhoused people with objects as they sped by. Coast Mental Health and local health authority employees who worked with the homeless population were advised not to wear identifying badges or clothing out of fear they could be targeted.

In November, 2021, the province announced that it would use its authority under B.C.’s Interpretation Act, also called statutory immunity, to bypass Maple Ridge’s usual bylaws and processes to fast-track construction of permanent supportive housing.

It cited the urgent need to replace the aging modular site, and its inability to find a “mutually agreeable site” with the city – a move that led to further acrimony between the two governments.

In an interview, Mr. Morden said the city had scrambled to put forth an alternate proposal that included a different site, operator and location, but received no response from the province before its announcement.

The following year, Keir Macdonald was named CEO of Coast Mental Health. Mr. Macdonald, who had most recently led the Phoenix Society, a Surrey-based not-for-profit social welfare organization, recalled being onboarded as the housing project faced “complete and almost universal opposition.”

It was the first time Coast Mental Health planned for a new housing project with no involvement from the local council, Mr. Macdonald said in an interview. The provincial government’s use of statutory immunity also meant there would be no conventional public process through which it could formally engage with residents and respond to misinformation.

The non-profit made its case for integrated health supports at the new building, laying bare to the Fraser Health Authority and the provincial government the significant health challenges its clients faced. It presented them with internal incident reports describing overdose deaths and concerning mental health episodes at the modular housing site.

The effort would eventually lead to Fraser Health funding the equivalent of four full-time positions in-house – a rarity in supportive housing, where nonclinical staff typically connect residents to off-site services.

In October, 2022, a municipal election again remade council. Dan Ruimy, a former MP for Pitt Meadows-Maple Ridge, unseated Mr. Morden as mayor and won control of city hall alongside four councillors from his A Better Maple Ridge team. Mr. Macdonald invited the new council to tour Coast Mental Health’s other Maple Ridge sites, finding a receptive audience and a “fresh opportunity to engage.”

In an interview, Mr. Ruimy said his administration was keen on helping to move Rivers Reach forward, knowing its completion would allow the troubled temporary modular site to close. Rather than fighting the province, he said his team engaged with it and Coast Mental Health, seeking assurances around security, staffing and building access, drawing on lessons from the earlier project.

In late 2024, with construction under way, Coast Mental Health struck a community advisory committee to solicit feedback and address concerns. Staff went door to door to distribute notices introducing their organization and the supportive housing project, inviting neighbours to join the committee.

By now, Ms. Clissold and her husband had lived at their new condo for about a year. They watched the construction of the building next door from their ground-floor unit – probably one of those that would be at the highest risk for break-ins, Ms. Clissold thought at the time. Her anxiety grew with every completed storey.

As Ms. Clissold wondered whether they would have to move again, an invitation to join the building’s community advisory committee landed in her mailbox.

“At that point,” she said, “I’m like, ‘Oh, hell, yeah.’”

Ms. Clissold, unsure of what to expect, recalled being ushered through a “beautiful” facility and into a meeting room where she was met by representatives from the city, Fraser Health, BC Housing, the fire department and police, among others.

Illicit drug use would be permitted only at a designated outdoor tent at the back of the property, or in an indoor supervised consumption room where staff could monitor for adverse reactions.

Rules were laid out to prospective tenants during an initial interview and again during intake, according to the operator. Those who couldn’t adhere to them were directed to other housing.

When it was Ms. Clissold’s turn to speak, she told the group that she and others were worried that the chaos of the modular site would follow residents to the new building.

But she left the meeting feeling hopeful.

“The amount of thought that went into how they were going to operate this building, like from that first meeting, I remember it was very evident that they wanted this to be a success,” she said.

Over the next several months, Ms. Clissold continued to bring feedback from her building to the advisory committee, which met regularly.

In response to a complaint about garbage on the street, the building created a “clean team” that offered tenants an honorarium equivalent to minimum wage to don a Coast Mental Health reflective vest and collect litter. A gripe about the building’s unsightly dumpsters resulted in the construction of a wooden pergola to conceal them. Over several months, the initial chill began to thaw.

Ms. Clissold began to exchange pleasantries with her new neighbours, her dogs serving as an easy icebreaker. One resident from up north told her he used to have an Alaskan malamute that resembled her mini husky. Another had a little dog just like her miniature pinscher.

“It no longer felt like it was the building next door filled with people who have addiction challenges, or have experienced homelessness,” Ms. Clissold said. “It’s a building of neighbours.”

The designers of Rivers Reach hoped community gardening would give residents a project to be proud of, and a source of food for the building’s cooks. Jennifer Gauthier/The Globe and Mail

Sylvie Hiekel, 61, moved into Rivers Reach from a nearby shelter, where she had stayed for nine months after fleeing an abusive relationship.

The former bakery manager and construction foreman, who receives provincial disability assistance, had her own reservations about supportive housing after hearing horror stories about other sites.

But despite her initial apprehensions, Ms. Hiekel said she’s found the building to be supportive and safe, crediting attentive staff. She has also embraced the cooking and crafting classes offered on-site, and enjoys aquatic exercise at a nearby recreation centre where tenants receive a discount.

As someone who does not use illicit drugs, Ms. Hiekel has mixed feelings about drug use being permitted on-site. Allowing it can potentially enable use, she said, though she also acknowledged that using at the building can be a life-saving alternative to using alone on the streets.

Tenants who do use drugs have been respectful, she said, and their use has not intruded on her daily life.

“We all look out for each other,” Ms. Hiekel said. “Everybody needs a family, and a lot of these people that live here don’t have a family. We’re family.”

In an interview, Ms. McKenna, the program manager, said building a community required intentional efforts to foster trust and communication among neighbours, tenants and staff.

They also sought to create a home that tenants would take pride in, she said, a goal reflected in the building’s colourful artwork, towering sunflowers and railing planters full of pansies. In the community garden, residents tend to zucchini, spinach, corn and other vegetables that the building’s two cooks prepare for meals.

Ms. McKenna said there are often preconceived notions about the people Coast Mental Health serves, and assumptions that its role as a recovery-oriented organization means most of its clients are recovering from addiction.

“It could be profound social isolation, struggling with mental health issues, finding a safe place to be, people who were injured at work,” she said, adding that tenants at Rivers Reach range in age from 25 to their early 70s.

The building hasn’t won everyone over. Mr. Morden, the former mayor, said he knows people at the building and believes that some are breaking the rules by using drugs in their rooms. He also continues to argue that anything short of 24-hour medical and social supports, along with addiction treatment on demand, is insufficient.

“People don’t get better; people don’t move along,” said Mr. Morden, who is seeking to return to city hall with a seat on council in this Saturday’s election.

Mr. Macdonald, the Coast Mental Health CEO, agreed that it remains difficult for many people to access timely substance use and recovery services. But he disagreed with the idea that everyone should follow the same trajectory, with independent living as the end goal. Instead, his organization seeks to provide stability through permanent housing and connect people to health and social services when they are needed, he said.

“I don’t think it’s a failure if someone requires that ongoing support and structure that a supportive environment brings.”

Mr. Ruimy, who is seeking re-election as Maple Ridge mayor, said the experience has shown how stigma can impede progress, and how important it is for local governments that are facing similar challenges to remain open to dialogue.

“I think we’ve shown what happens when you have a municipality that collaborates with other levels of government,” he said. “You end up with a better solution.”

Meanwhile, Ms. Clissold said negative perceptions of supportive housing persist, with some neighbours continuing to make snarky remarks about the project. Its most vocal critics, whose worst fears did not materialize, now seem more inclined to ignore its success than acknowledge it, she said.

The community advisory committee, left with few pressing issues to address, has shifted to meeting as needed.

Invited back to Rivers Reach over the summer to celebrate its one-year anniversary, Ms. Clissold later reflected on the journey in a social-media post. Despite the initial doubts of many, she wrote, operators showed that such projects can succeed by listening to the community, meeting tenants where they are and learning from past challenges.

“And the tenants have shown that, when given a chance, they form their own supportive community that beautifully integrates into the neighbourhood.”

Despite the initial doubts of many, she wrote, operators showed that such projects can succeed by listening to the community, meeting tenants where they are and learning from past challenges.
“And the tenants have shown that, when given a chance, they form their own supportive community that beautifully integrates into the neighbourhood.”

content_blocks.text: Julia Clissold and her husband had just settled into their new Maple Ridge, B.C., condo in the summer of 2022 when they learned that the residential development planned for next door would be supportive housing.

content_blocks.text: The tensions that once gripped this community are hardly unique. Across B.C., disputes over homeless encampments and supportive housing have dragged on for months or years, in big cities, sleepy suburbs and northern communities. This year alone, proposed supportive housing projects in Abbotsford, Burnaby and the District of North Vancouver have been cancelled amid backlash.

content_blocks.text: In Richmond, fierce opposition to supportive housing has put mayoral candidates under pressure to make their positions clear, prompting some to explicitly declare their opposition . In Surrey, one candidate has taken the opposite approach, pledging to build 1,000 new units annually for four years and blaming the past council’s resistance to such projects for worsening street homelessness. Candidates in Vancouver’s contest have been grilled on whether they would reverse the incumbent administration’s freeze on net-new supportive housing.

content_blocks.text: The experience in Maple Ridge offers a case study in how local leadership can help overcome entrenched opposition to supportive housing projects – particularly as an incumbent provincial government that is seeking re-election signals it would rather direct limited funding to communities willing to embrace them.

content_blocks.text: In an interview with The Globe and Mail last week, NDP Leader David Eby said ahead of the Oct. 24 provincial vote that his government is done with overriding municipalities that oppose supportive housing. “If they’re happier with an encampment in their community, if they’re willing to live with that rather than to have the hard conversation with their community about the supportive housing that’s needed, I struggle to know why I wouldn’t dedicate that money to a local government that actually wants to close the encampment and open housing,” he said.

content_blocks.text: Efforts to address homelessness in Maple Ridge have stretched back more than a decade, marked by encampments, temporary shelters and contentious housing proposals that have galvanized residents, shaped elections and pitted local leaders against the province.

content_blocks.text: Former Maple Ridge mayor Nicole Read, who advocated for unhoused people and supported low-barrier options during her term from 2014 to 2018, was the subject of online harassment that became so heated she was forced to curtail public appearances as the RCMP investigated threats to her personal safety.

content_blocks.text: In May, 2017, people began erecting tents and makeshift shelters at a vacant downtown site slated for a neighbourhood park, creating an encampment that would become a highly visible indictment of the city’s shortage of affordable housing. The site, which came to be called Anita Place, persisted for more than two years. At its peak, nearly 200 people sheltered there, with many saying it offered more security than being alone.

content_blocks.text: But the encampment drew the ire of other community members and local officials who raised crime and safety concerns. People staying at the camp used portable heaters, propane tanks and electrical connections to stay warm, sparking numerous fires and creating significant safety risks, firefighters said. Police said they received dozens of calls about weapons and stolen items.

content_blocks.text: In response, B.C.’s NDP government announced a plan to move about 50 people from the camp into temporary modular housing on province-owned land nearby while permanent housing was being built. content_blocks.text: The move went against the wishes of the local council and was met with such fierce community opposition that the provincial government and BC Housing, the Crown corporation in charge of subsidized housing, had to seek a court injunction to clear community members who camped at the modular site in protest.

content_blocks.text: The work-camp-style housing opened in October, 2018. Minutes from community advisory committee meetings around that time detailed neighbourhood complaints, including reports of people congregating at the site and visitors yelling to get the attention of tenants. Residents of a nearby seniors’ home said they didn’t like seeing people under the influence and were upset by their use of foul language.

content_blocks.text: The controversy over the new housing coincided with a municipal election. Just two days after the modular site opened, voters in Maple Ridge ushered in a new mayor, Mike Morden, and four new councillors. Mr. Morden, a two-term city councillor who campaigned on a tougher response to the homelessness and addiction issues that he said were driving crime in the city, won a decisive victory.

content_blocks.text: The new mayor and council feuded with the province over the site throughout their term, arguing that the B.C. government’s efforts to build supportive housing in the city undermined their local authority. They were also at odds about what that housing should look like; Mr. Morden said anything short of complex care with intensive health and social supports would be inadequate.

stories.title: Ontario power bills likely to rise after OPG reaches settlement on rates
stories.summary: Increases reflect the cost of large capital projects at nuclear plants
stories.author: Matthew McClearn
stories.content:
Ontario Power Generation has reached a settlement with ratepayer and industry groups concerning its proposed rates for the next five years, setting the stage for rising electricity bills in the province.

The agreement , published earlier this month on the Ontario Energy Board’s website, would see the province’s Crown utility earn significantly more for power generated by its nuclear plants between 2027 and 2031, although less than what OPG sought in its initial application filed in December.

The typical Ontarian’s monthly power bill, currently around $142, would increase by a total of nearly $13 during the five-year period as a result of the settlement, according to Opg’s estimate. (OPG had originally sought a total increase of $17.)

These higher rates reflect a series of large capital projects under way at Opg’s nuclear plants. Its application revealed that the newly refurbished Darlington nuclear station requires extensive additional maintenance in the next few years, expected to cost nearly $3-billion.

OPG is also building a small modular reactor at the same station that’s expected to enter service in 2030 – the first of four units with a combined price tag estimated at $20.9-billion. And in late September, OPG shut down four reactors at its Pickering station for a $26.8-billion overhaul.

Payments to OPG for power from its hydro dams would also rise under the settlement, albeit by far less than it wanted in its application. At roughly $47 a megawatt hour next year, its price would be less than one-quarter the cost of nuclear power. OPG is also refurbishing many of its hydro dams.

The proposed settlement must be approved by the Ontario Energy Board. Last week, the OEB scheduled an Oct. 30 meeting to hear presentations from the parties and said it plans to issue a written decision.

Power bills across the continent are rising rapidly after a prolonged period of relative stability. According to an analysis by The Globe and Mail of provincial electricity price indexes from Statistics Canada, so far this decade electricity costs have increased most rapidly in Alberta, where the cumulative increase has been nearly 39 per cent.

New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland have also experienced increases significantly above the national average, which was just over 20 per cent. Ontario’s increase during the period was only slightly above the national average.

Ontarian’s bills reflect the cost of generating and delivering the electricity they use. Opg’s nuclear and hydroelectric plants comprise a significant portion of total generating costs, but bills are also influenced by the cost of power from the Bruce nuclear station (operated by Bruce Power) and natural gas-fired plants, which generate a large and rising portion of the province’s electricity.

The negotiations concerning Opg’s power payments began early this summer. Participants included the Association of Major Power Consumers in Ontario, which represents large industrial users including auto plants and steel mills, the Building Owners and Managers Association Toronto, the Consumers Council of Canada, and the Vulnerable Energy Consumers Coalition, which represents residential customers it says “experience greater hardship” than most due to age, income or other factors.

Ampco president Brad Duguid welcomed the agreement and said it would save his members money.

“However, we cannot lose sight of the bigger challenge ahead,” he said in a statement. “The unprecedented investments required to maintain and expand Ontario’s electricity infrastructure, while essential to ensuring a reliable supply of power, will place enormous additional pressure on electricity bills in the years ahead.”

Tom Ladanyi, a consultant who represented the non-governmental organization Energy Probe in the negotiations, said that while Ontario’s government promotes electrification, the coming rate increases will make it more difficult.

The government “currently subsidizes the cost of electricity by about $8-billion a year,” he added. “It May have to increase that subsidy to keep electricity costs from increasing faster than the cost of natural gas.”

The settlement, which runs more than 300 pages, includes a proposal to blunt impacts on ratepayers next year by deferring collection of $350-million of nuclear revenue for the utility to 2028. OPG also agreed to reduce its proposed nuclear revenue requirements by $1.8-billion over the period.

The parties adopted an all-or-nothing approach with the settlement, asking the regulator to accept or reject it outright rather than consider its many aspects individually.

One issue remained unresolved among the parties: Opg’s proposal to recover $170-million from ratepayers relating to the early return to service of refurbished units at the Darlington station. The parties requested a separate hearing to address that issue.

stories.title: Ottawa to announce $100 million toward offshore wind projects in Nova Scotia
stories.summary: Ottawa - The federal government is set to announce a $100-million commitment toward developing offshore wind energy in Nova Scotia in the hope of attracting private investment to projects like the province's Wind West plan.
stories.author: Nick Murray The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - The federal government is set to announce a $100-million commitment toward developing offshore wind energy in Nova Scotia in the hope of attracting private investment to projects like the province’s Wind West plan.

Federal Energy Minister Tim Hodgson is expected to deliver the announcement in Halifax on Thursday morning. A media advisory says he is to be joined by Justice Minister Sean Fraser — whose riding brushes up against Halifax and who last month attended the world’s largest wind industry trade show in Germany.

stories.title: AI, resources and water bombers: Draft document maps Canada, EU path to closer ties
stories.summary: Montreal — Canada and the European Union are laying out concrete steps to strengthen ties around digital security, critical resources and a would-be fleet of Canadian water bombers, according to a draft joint statement ahead of a major summit at month’s end.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Montreal — Canada and the European Union are laying out concrete steps to strengthen ties around digital security and defence as well as critical resources and a would-be fleet of Canadian-made water bombers, according to a draft joint statement ahead of a summit at month’s end.

The document, seen by The Canadian Press, states that Ottawa and Brussels aim to let Canadian companies bid on cloud and artificial intelligence infrastructure contracts typically reserved for European companies in another push away from dependence on the United States.

Dubbed an “alliance for the future,” the renewed partnership also launches plans for Canada to join in Europe’s Galileo satellite navigation system and wraps up a deal to facilitate European investment in Canadian critical minerals, according to the leaked statement.

It also heralds the joint purchase of 50 Canadian-made De Havilland water bombers it claims will be ready for use in fighting wildfires in 2030.

More broadly, the statement showcases Prime Minister Mark Carney’s ongoing effort to shore up Continental links in areas ranging from trade to education and the military, as Canada and the European Union try to guard against a less reliable America and take up the flag of the rules-based international order.

The challenge lies in fending off backlash from the White House and continuing to bolster cross-Atlantic bonds beyond the next election cycle, said Patrick Leblond, an associate professor of public and international affairs at the University of Ottawa.

“The Americans, they’re playing a power game. For them, if Canada and other countries band together in a way to reduce their dependence on the U.S., the current U.S. administration — and potentially others in the future — will try to prevent that from happening,” Leblond said.

“Divide and conquer, that’s the power approach.”

The draft statement, dated Sept. 22, pledges to “strengthen digital sovereignty” and align emerging regulatory frameworks “through associated country status for Canada” under the European Commission’s proposed Cloud and AI Development Act.

That means Canada would be treated as a member country when it comes to bidding on contracts for critical digital infrastructure.

“Whether it’s Google, Amazon, Microsoft, we’re very dependent on these platforms. And as we know, it could be weaponized against our economy, against our governments,” said Leblond.

“The message here is, let’s work together. We trust each other.”

The provision comes after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed last month that Canada become the first associate member of the European Union.

Where possible, European contractors are already inclined to work with Canadian firms over American ones because of the export controls the United States tends to impose on sales to a third-country market, said Wendy Gilmour, vice-chair of the Conference of Defence Associations Institute.

However, persuading U.S.-oriented tech firms in Canada to cast their eyes toward Europe could pose a hurdle.

“There’s been a slow take-up by Canadian business because Canadian business has just been so used to working with the American market,” Gilmour said.

“It’s easy. It’s English-speaking. It’s just a simpler prospect than to work in a European regulatory environment with 27 different countries.”

The push for greater distance from Canada’s next-door neighbour extends to space, with the draft document kicking off talks for Canadian participation in the EU’s Galileo satellite navigation system. The move carries military implications.

Canadian Forces currently rely on America’s Global Positioning System for an encrypted U.S. military signal designed to resist jamming and spoofing. Galileo has its own encrypted signal, but access for any non-EU country requires a formal agreement.

The joint statement, which May undergo revisions before the summit kicks off in two weeks, further says the two sides have hammered out a deal that makes it easier for investment in Canada’s critical resources — “in particular, critical minerals” — by the European Investment Bank, and for their export to Europe.

The measure responds to Canada’s need for greater diversity of both buyers and sources of capital for its natural resources, Gilmour said. Specifically, it marks an attempt to reduce dependence on the U.S. market and Chinese supply chains and to spur more mining and processing at home.

“We rely too heavily on offshore processing,” she said, noting that China enjoys a near-stranglehold on critical minerals refining.

On disaster preparedness, the joint purchase of water bombers from De Havilland marks a win for the Calgary-based plane maker. But it remains unclear whether the 50 planes would be in addition to the 38 already ordered by six EU countries and three Canadian provinces since 2024.

A De Havilland spokesperson said in an email the company was “not engaged in these discussions.”

The summit statement lays out other commitments ranging from the specific — new talks for participation in Erasmus, the popular EU student-exchange program — to the aspirational: “We will fight to protect and promote human rights everywhere, for everyone.”

While stressing “unprecedented geopolitical challenges,” the document doubles down on middle-power co-operation. “Our partnership May become a model for other countries seeking friendship in a challenging world,” it reads.

The Canada-EU summit, set for Oct. 29 and 30 in Montreal, will see Carney host von der Leyen as well as European Council president António Costa and other EU leaders.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

Christopher Reynolds, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Warm welcome for Carney in Calgary, stumping for unity as Alberta hurtles toward vote
stories.summary: Calgary — Prime Minister Mark Carney started Thursday with selfies and flowers in Calgary, as he began his last-ditch tour stumping for Canadian unity days away from Alberta's separation referendum.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney announces a new federal heat pump rebate program while visiting Dettson, a manufacturer of residential and commercial Hvac systems in Sherbrooke, Que., ON Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Christinne Muschi

By Bill Graveland, The Canadian Press

Posted October 15, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated October 15, 2026 2:02 pm.

Calgary — Prime Minister Mark Carney started Thursday with selfies and flowers in Calgary, as he began his last-ditch tour stumping for Canadian unity days away from Alberta’s separation referendum.

In the morning, Carney was met by supporters at a restaurant in the city’s northeast. He was later given a bouquet of flowers by staff and posed for photos.

Many wore small red and white Canadian flags in their shirt pockets.

“I like the red,” Carney said as he shook hands.

One woman said: “It’s for you.”

“It’s for us. It’s all for Canada,” replied Carney.

Premier Danielle Smith has put 10 questions on Monday’s referendum, with the key one asking if Alberta should stay in Canada or hold a second, binding vote on quitting the country.

The other nine questions deal with proposals Smith has put forward for immigration and constitutional reform.

On Thursday night, Carney is set to join former Alberta deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk at a rally for his Forever Canadian group, which has been campaigning to keep the province in Confederation.

At the same time, Smith is scheduled to headline a $500-a-plate United Conservative Party fundraiser also in Calgary.

Smith released a video Wednesday saying she voted at an advance poll and checked the box to keep the country together.

She said she knows many Albertans are frustrated with the federal government but that the province is starting to see headway with major projects, including a proposed new oil pipeline to the West Coast.

Monday is the official polling day but advance polls are open this week.

Carney, asked Thursday about his message for Albertans, said if people are decided that they need to get out and vote.

“Polls don’t vote. People do,” Carney said.

“For those who are undecided, it’s hard to think of a worse time for a referendum or a better time for the province. The world is dangerously divided,” he said.

He added that Canada is working, pointing to infrastructure investment, including in energy.

Tonight’s rally isn’t the first time Carney and Lukaszuk have teamed up to spread a pro-Canada message.

Last month, the prime minister invited Lukaszuk’s group to attend a cabinet retreat in Banff, Alta., and Carney signed the Maple Leaf-wrapped motorhome Lukaszuk has been touring the province in.

The prime minister is also scheduled to attend a rally with Lukaszuk in Edmonton on Friday.

Also Friday, Smith and federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre are scheduled to speak at a conservative conference in Calgary.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

Bill Graveland, The Canadian Press
