stories.title: Major projects CEO faces B.C. First Nations frustrated over lack of consultation
stories.summary: Ottawa - Major Projects CEO Dawn Farrell told First Nations in B.C. today that the frustrations expressed over a lack of consultation made her feel like Canada is "never going to work," but her office is determined to try.
stories.author: Nick Murray and Alessia Passafiume The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Major Projects CEO Dawn Farrell told First Nations in B.C. on Wednesday that the frustrations expressed over a lack of consultation on the Pacific Link pipeline made her feel like Canada is “never going to work,” but her office is determined to try to be better.

Farrell was addressing the B.C. Assembly of First Nations at its annual general meeting in Vancouver. Media were asked to leave the room before Farrell’s appearance, but the meeting continued to be publicly streamed on the B.C. Assembly of First Nations YouTube channel.

First Nations in B.C. are calling on Ottawa to set national standards for Indigenous consultations on major projects. They say they were given just 11 working days to review and engage on whether the proposed Pacific Link pipeline should be designated as a project of national interest.

The standard, they say, should include “minimum procedural protections,” including protected timelines for consultations before decisions are made.

The proposed pipeline from Alberta to B.C. was named a project in the national interest on Oct. 1 by Prime Minister Mark Carney alongside Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.

The designation does not eliminate the requirement for the government to consult with First Nations on the impact of the project itself. Rather, the goal is to complete the required reviews and consultations over the next year so construction can begin next September.

Tkʼemlúps te Secwépemc Chief Rosanne Casimir, who presented the call for a national consultation standard, said the current process expects First Nations to review thousands of documents under tight timelines and with limited funding.

“Even in your presentation initially starting off, you shared that there was excessive amounts of papers and documents. Well, we’re receiving that after the fact,” Casimir said, referring to an anecdote Farrell shared about having two binders of 1,200 pages on her coffee table.

“Meaningful consultation is difficult when nations, communities, are still trying to understand the project while decisions are continuing to move forward. For the (Pacific Link) oil pipeline, we raised process concerns, and Canada took nearly a month to respond and only 11 working days remained for the review and engagement.”

Farrell said she agrees with the concept of national consultation standards but she wondered how such standards would work alongside the government’s accelerated timelines for project approvals.

“I hear your pleas and I hear your discussions and I hear, you know, sort of a disbelief that it’s ever going to change, and a cynicism. And I feel like, ‘Oh my God, we can never get this country to work. Like it’s never going to work. We’ll never make it,’” Farrell said.

She added that staff in her office have “very, very big scars” from working on projects like the Trans Mountain pipeline that didn’t have the depth of Indigenous consultation the Pacific Link pipeline “has after two months.”

“Because we’re all committed in our office to try to do it better. Now, what does doing it better look like? It’s really hard to sit here and actually lay out what a day looks like and what the work looks like, and really, you’re not going to believe us at all,” Farrell said.

“No amount of presentation that I’m going to give … is going to give you a sense of what we’re trying to accomplish. The only thing that will give you that sense of it is if we actually do, in action, get to a different place.

“The best I can do is the best I can do. Our office is working hard to try to accommodate all the concerns you brought here today. And I totally get that you will not believe us until we deliver. And so we’ll mostly spend all of our time delivering, and maybe next year when we come back we’ll have some examples of how we try to deliver.”

The federal government initially planned to hold consultations for one month on whether to designate the pipeline as a project in the national interest under the Building Canada Act. That was extended to two months after Indigenous leaders raised concerns about the tight timeline.

A summary of those consultations posted online by the federal government says Indigenous groups decried a lack of information about the project, which they said prevented them from fully assessing its impact.

On Wednesday, Farrell acknowledged adequate consultation was key for seeing a project be successful.

“The projects that we have to deliver out of our office have to achieve your rights. We have to make sure that we go through your processes,” Farrell said.

“We can’t just make stuff up. The courts will just come and overturn the projects and we’ll be like Canada’s always been, 10, 15 years, dragging stuff around in the ditch and not getting it done and wasting time and money and resources, and your time and your people’s resources. We can’t keep doing that.”

Farrell faced criticism at the meeting over the federal government’s push to move quickly on approving major projects.

“Our concern is not efficiency itself. It’s whether the speed and certainty for proponents are being advanced equivalent protection for Aboriginal title and rights, our governance and the lands and waters that sustain our people,” said Shana Thomas, hereditary chief of the Lyackson First Nation.

“Consultation is something you do. We are a partner at this table and we need to be part of the decision-making process. What we have to say is not something that you can then evaluate and make your own decision based on what you think about what we said. We have to be at the table as equal partners.”

Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak has said staff in the Major Projects Office do not understand how to work with First Nations communities and that “junior staffers” aren’t helping to build relationships.

She also said Farrell has been unavailable to meet with leadership, including at Assembly of First Nations gatherings.

Farrell said in the closed-door meeting Wednesday the only way she knows how to do her work is “to not talk very much.”

“They can’t get me on planes to go anywhere because I feel a huge responsibility to make sure that these projects that we’re working on hit the standards that you’re talking about today,” she said.

In an emailed statement last week, the Privy Council Office said the Major Projects Office works closely with Indigenous communities and that senior officials make themselves available to meet with communities when asked.

First Nations in B.C. also passed a resolution at Wednesday’s meeting calling on Prime Minister Mark Carney to halt the advance of the Building Canada Act and to repeal Bill C-39 if it passes through Parliament.

The legislation would fast-track approvals for major projects, cut their review times and create zones of “national interest” to pre-approve certain types of projects.

First Nations chiefs have warned the government it risks ending up in court if it approves and builds projects without their free, prior and informed consent, as outlined in the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.

Chiefs are set to meet with Carney and the country’s premiers in Ottawa later this month, and major projects are expected to be a major topic of debate.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Joly says 'everything is on the table' but still no court filing against Stelco layoffs
stories.summary: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said "everything is on the table" when it comes to her government's response to layoffs at Stelco.
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa – Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said “everything is on the table” when it comes to her government’s response to layoffs at Stelco but stopped short of announcing any legal action against the steelmaker.

“We expect Stelco to follow the undertakings that they’ve committed to…the Government of Canada,” Joly told reporters in Ottawa on Wednesday.

“And right now, a business decision or even a change in market conditions cannot be used to not follow the commitment,” she added.

Joly was referring to the commitments made by American-based Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. when it acquired Stelco in 2024.

Joly’s predecessor approved the purchase, following a review under the Investment Canada Act (ICA), which included a commitment to maintain the same amount of unionized employees for a period of five years.

The union representing steelworkers at the Stelco plant in Hamilton has confirmed layoffs are now underway. Layoffs are also expected to take place at Stelco’s Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke, Ont. Stelco has cited U.S. tariffs as the main reason for the “temporary” job cuts.

Last week, the industry minister threatened the “full force of the law” if Cleveland-Cliffs failed to comply with its undertakings that it agreed to when it purchased the steelmaker.

On Wednesday, Joly said she is “always open to sit down with a company and find a solution, but we’re looking at everything that is possible to keep jobs in Canada.”

On Oct. 5, Joly sent a letter to Stelco’s president, and a legal team is reviewing the response from the company, which was received on Friday.

Joly said she has been in contact with the unions and called the layoffs “unacceptable.”

On Tuesday, NDP Leader Avi Lewis and Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles called for Stelco to be nationalized.

The Conservative opposition has urged Joly to sue Stelco over the layoffs and noted the minister should have already taken action.

“The hundreds of workers being laid off don’t have 10 months to wait,” said Conservative MP Ned Kuruc, who represents the riding of Hamilton East—Stoney Creek, in a statement Wednesday.

“Their mortgage payment is at the end of the month, their grocery trip is this weekend, and Christmas planning is happening right now,” he added.

Joly cited Section 40 of the ICA which could lead to a few possible outcomes from a court process, including financial penalties towards the company, forcing them to abide by the commitment, and forced divestiture.

On Sunday, Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves disputed the government’s claims and told CBC News he was prepared to fight Canada in court.

Notably, this is not the first time Stelco plants have idled due to bad market conditions. U.S. Steel, which acquired Stelco in 2007, began layoffs at the company following the 2008 financial crisis.

The federal government filed a lawsuit against U.S. Steel in 2009 for failing to meet their job commitments when they made the Stelco purchase. The lawsuit resulted in an out-of-court settlement in 2011, with commitments to keep production going by U.S. Steel.

However, U.S. Steel filed for creditor protection and severed ties with its Canadian operations, before those pledges could be followed through on.

stories.title: Foreign student enrolment at Atlantic Canada universities fell by nearly 50% since 2024, data show
stories.summary: East Coast schools that used to rely on tuition paid by international students continue to struggle, survey shows
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
The number of foreign students studying at universities in Atlantic Canada has dropped by nearly 48 per cent since 2024, a steeper decline than the federal government intended and a reflection of the body blow Canada’s reputation has suffered on the international education market.

There were 13,775 full-time visa students enrolled in undergraduate and graduate programs at universities in the four Atlantic provinces as of Oct. 1, an 18-per-cent reduction from 16,795 at the same time last year, according to new data released Wednesday.

The Association of Atlantic Universities’ annual enrolment survey offers one of the first looks at postsecondary education trends in Canada for the 2026-27 academic year. This fall’s survey – much like last year’s – shows that East Coast schools that used to rely on high tuition paid by foreign students continue to struggle.

“Atlantic Canada is the most severe example of a huge challenge we see across the country, which is our universities are fighting to make Canada competitive again in the race for international talent,” said Gabriel Miller, president and chief executive officer of Universities Canada, which represents postsecondary institutions nationwide.

“That’s taking an enormous amount of work and a lot of time because of the damage that was done by radical changes made by the previous federal government.”

In January of 2024, the Liberal government of Justin Trudeau began capping the number of international study permits it would grant annually.

The policy change was one of several Ottawa made in the ensuing months and years to curb an international student program that had grown so large it sparked a public backlash over temporary residents competing for housing, jobs and health care.

Canada’s international student cap helped lower rents. But will it bring colleges and universities down as well?

But many in Canada’s higher-education sector say the pendulum has swung too far in the opposite direction, in part because the changes have created uncertainty for applicants who once would have considered the country’s postsecondary system to be straightforward to access.

The federal government’s target is to receive 155,000 new international students this calendar year. As of the end of July, only 28,200 had arrived .

“I will go as far as to say that if we don’t have population growth in the Atlantic region, it could jeopardize some of the big programs that the prime minister has announced in national defence [and] in energy,” said David Dingwall, the president of Cape Breton University and a former Liberal cabinet minister. “You need people. You need intelligent people, and without that, we are in a very difficult situation in the Atlantic.”

Cape Breton University has seen the most precipitous decline in foreign students of any university in the Atlantic region, according to the preliminary enrolment survey.

In 2023-24, when international enrolment was at its peak, nearly 7,000 full-time visa students studied at the institution in Sydney, N.S. This year, 1,388 full-time visa students are enrolled at Cape Breton University.

International student enrolment has also declined at some of the largest universities in Eastern Canada, including Dalhousie University in Halifax, the University of New Brunswick and Memorial University of Newfoundland.

Ava Czapalay, chief executive officer of the Association of Atlantic Universities, said fewer overseas students are applying because of Canada’s tarnished reputation and because they fear visa requirements might change again. The unpredictability is turning international students off Canada, she added.

“In speaking with the federal government, we have tried to emphasize the hit that Canada’s reputation has taken globally by having opaque rules,” Mr. Czapalay said. When foreign students realize they could invest significant time and money applying to a Canadian university or college only to be denied a study permit, “they’re going to go to a country where they feel like they’re going to be more welcome.”

On top of that, Ms. Czapalay said federal visa officers are rejecting international students bound for Atlantic universities at rates higher than for universities in larger provinces.

“We don’t know why that is,” Ms. Czapalay said, “since our universities offer a great program, great experience, great value for money.”

In a March report on international student program reforms, federal Auditor-General Karen Hogan noted that smaller provinces were “disproportionately impacted” by lower study permit approvals, although colleges were hit harder than universities.

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, the department that processes visa applications, told The Globe and Mail by e-mail Wednesday that it recently provided a list of best practices to designated colleges and universities about what they can do to improve the quality of study permit applications.

“Designated learning institutions are responsible for their own recruitment and enrolment practices, which affect study permit approval rates,” spokesperson Jeffrey MacDonald said.

He also said policy changes designed to raise the share of international students in higher-level programs “have shown promising initial results,” with university students accounting for 40 per cent of new study permit holders in 2025, up from 30 per cent the year before.

Despite the decline in numbers of international students at Atlantic Canadian universities, there was some encouraging news for those institutions in the new data. Overall enrolment among full-time, first-year students was up by 3.4 per cent across the 16 universities in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland and Labrador.

“We think that is a positive sign because our universities offer an exceptional first-year experience for undergraduate students,” Ms. Czapalay said.

stories.title: Veteran bookseller Ben McNally wins Toronto International Festival of Authors Ivy Award
stories.summary: McNally is the first bookseller to win the prize, which has typically been awarded to executives at major publishing companies
stories.author: Josh O’Kane
stories.content:
Long-time bookseller Ben McNally has won the Toronto International Festival of Authors Ivy Award, given each year to a major contributor to the Canadian publishing sector.

McNally, 77, has been selling books across the festival’s home city since 1970 – at his namesake downtown shops since 2007, but also at Nicholas Hoare Books, Book City, Coles and more.

He’s the 15th winner of the award, which is administered by the writing fest’s International Visitors Programme. The program helps members of the Canadian book sector build relationships with international partners and expand the global reach of the country’s books.

McNally is also the first bookseller to win the prize, which has typically been awarded to publishing executives such as HarperCollins Canada’s Iris Tupholme, Simon & Schuster Canada’s Nicole Winstanley and Kegedonce Press’s Kateri Akiwenzie-Damm.

“It’s nice, as a bookseller, to be representing all the booksellers in the country for all that we do,” McNally said in an interview. After all, he said, the business of getting Canadian stories into the world is not strictly a top-down affair. “We really need authors, like authors need us, and we really need publishers, and publishers need us. And the general public needs us more than anybody else.”

This has been a particularly strong year for the publishing industry’s recognition of the entrepreneurs who get books in front of Canadian readers, he added. The Giller Prize, which has undergone significant changes after a boycott earlier this decade over past sponsors’ ties to Israel’s war in Gaza, appointed an all-indie-bookseller jury this year. The jurists include Rupert McNally and Danielle McNally, his children who now run his shop’s day-to-day operations.

Festival director Roland Gulliver said that the Ivy Award has always celebrated the people who champion Canadian publishing, and that booksellers are a key part of the sector. “Ben has been such a stalwart of the literary community,” Gulliver said. “This felt like the point to honour his work for many, many decades.”

Bookselling has undergone numerous transformations since McNally began slinging hardcovers and paperbacks fresh out of school at the turn of the seventies. Independent bookstores have struggled to survive the sector’s consolidation of power, including the amalgamation of book chains that resulted in today’s physical-store domination by Indigo Books and Music, and the subsequent encroachment of Amazon on all booksellers. Today, he says, real-estate costs only add to the difficulties for independents in Canada.

But, McNally said, “If we were not optimists, we wouldn’t be in this business in the first place.” He and other booksellers have found new ways to get voracious readers in their doors, especially with author speaking events. “In the old days, nobody thought about doing that.”

The Professional Association of Canadian Literary Agents, in conjunction with the festival, also announced that McClelland & Stewart executive editor Anita Chong would be named its Person of the Year. Chong acquires and edits fiction and memoir with a focus on under-represented voices, and has worked on award-winning titles such as Souvankham Thammavongsa’s How to Pronounce Knife , Michael Christie’s Greenwood and Eleanor Catton’s Birnam Wood .

The Toronto International Festival of Authors, recently separated from its long-time home at the city’s Harbourfront Centre, will run from Oct. 28 to Nov. 1 at the University of Toronto’s Victoria University. Dave Eggers, Ann-Marie MacDonald, Patrick deWitt, Vivek Shraya, Canisia Lubrin and Téa Mutonji are among this year’s participating authors.

The festival’s International Visitors Programme helps Canadian authors, publishers and agents to find buyers for books’ international rights and has run since 2008. It routinely appoints global publishing leaders as fellows to attend the festival to deepen connections with Canada’s literary scene.

The Ivy Award will be officially awarded on Oct. 28 alongside a keynote conversation between Barnes & Noble chief executive officer James Daunt and Craig Swinwood, CEO of Harlequin & HarperCollins Canada.

stories.title: Canada's economic ambitions face skilled workforce challenges, Liberal MPs warn
stories.summary: Two Liberal MPs responsible for supporting Ottawa's labour and industry agendas say Canada's plan to fast-track major projects is putting mounting pressure on a workforce already struggling to meet demand.
stories.author: Brett Bundale The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canada’s plan to fast-track major projects is putting mounting pressure on a workforce already struggling to meet demand, two Liberal MPs responsible for supporting Ottawa’s labour and industry agendas said Wednesday.

Leslie Church, parliamentary secretary to the minister of jobs, said the federal government’s push to develop key nation-building projects is making long-standing weaknesses in Canada’s labour force harder to ignore.

“We are out there trying to build — build quickly,” Church said during a panel discussion at a conference hosted by the Future Skills Centre in Toronto.

“We’re trying to energize an economy that is under threat, diversify to new markets, open up supply chains, invest in transportation (and) build the housing that is at the core of a strong economy,” she said. “All of this creates this incredible pressure and strain on the workforce.”

Church added: “Who does the building?”

She said the issue is not new to Canada but rather one that has been compounding for years amid growing industrial and technological transformation and is becoming increasingly urgent.

“This is a crucial challenge for us right now,” Church said.

She said there is also a disconnect between workers looking for jobs and the industries struggling to find workers, including a mismatch of skills, training barriers and other challenges.

“We are ships in the night in Canada,” Church said. “We have a lot of people looking for work, or with a certain set of skills, but we have all these industries that are also looking for labour, and it’s almost like the two never meet.”

Church said the government is aiming to close that gap through investments in apprenticeships and training to accelerate workforce development, while employers and schools also need to work together to ensure training and labour needs are aligned.

The federal government has made developing major infrastructure and industrial projects a centrepiece of its economic agenda.

The push is aimed at boosting economic growth, attracting investment and reducing Canada’s reliance on the United States.

Yet Canada has an enduring shortage of skilled trades, gaps in worker training and a mismatch between the skills jobseekers have and those employers need.

It’s those labour force issues that could intensify as Ottawa looks to accelerate construction of major projects.

Karim Bardeesy, parliamentary secretary to the industry minister, said one of the issues is that Canadian employers have lagged on workforce skills development.

“There’s historic underinvestment in training by employers in Canada ... compared to other Oecd countries,” he said during the panel talk.

Bardeesy said federal apprenticeship incentives are aimed at helping develop a more skilled workforce but that employers still have a role to play in on-the-job training.

He said employers are also grappling with gaps in workers’ interpersonal skills, which he called a lingering effect of the pandemic.

“The COVID hangover as it relates to soft skills is real,” Bardeesy said.

Meanwhile, he said universities and colleges need to move beyond small, incremental improvements in order to keep pace with rapid technology advancements and the changing circumstances of students.

“The innovations on the margins are not going to be enough,” Bardeesy said.

“It doesn’t mean rushing to the latest labour market or industrial fad. It just means attending to the fundamentals of very quickly changing technology and very quickly changing student needs.”

stories.title: Quebec Court of Appeal hears case on granting tenants the right to have pets
stories.summary: MONTRÉAL - The Quebec Court of Appeal is hearing arguments on whether the right to have pets should be protected by law.
stories.author: Pierre Saint-Arnaud The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - The Quebec Court of Appeal is deliberating after hearing arguments on Wednesday on whether the right to have pets should be protected by law.

Last March, housing tribunal Judge Suzanne Guèvremont ruled that lease clauses banning pets violate Charter rights to liberty and privacy.

Guèvremont also argued in her decision that the evolution of animal protection laws, which recognize the bond between humans and their pets, required case law to evolve as well.

Amilis, the company that owns the building in which the complainant lives, appealed the decision.

The case was brought to court after a tenant, identified as M Desjardins, had taken over a lease that included a clause banning pets. However, it had been established at the time that Desjardins’ pets — a dog and a cat — were not causing any problems and that other pets in the building were tolerated.

But a new company, Amilis, purchased the building and enforced the no-pet clause.

The company’s lawyer, Damarys Pineda, argued that the judge had gone beyond her authority by acting as a substitute for the legislature, which is responsible for no-pet clauses.

The lawyer also argued that the no-pet clause is intended to protect the well-being of all tenants in a building and that it would be unreasonable to force landlords to allow pets in their buildings if they do not want them.

While landlord-tenant agreements are possible, she argued that any tenant can now contest a no-pet clause by invoking the Charter.

Desjardin’s lawyer, Kimmyanne Brown, stressed that Guèvremont’s decision only applied to Desjardins.

Court documents indicate Desjardins needed pets for animal-assisted therapy due to anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress. She added that the court cannot rule on issues not raised in the initial case, such as the protection of others who May be allergic or afraid of animals.

The Spca also intervened in the case.

Marie-Claude St-Amant, the lawyer representing the Spca, argued that the legislature now allows pets to be considered members of the family and that as a result Desjardins’s rights had been violated.

She also said she asked the office of the Attorney General of Quebec if it wished to intervene in the case, which it declined. St-Amant argued the response is proof that Guèvremont did not overstep her authority.

After the hearing, Spca spokesperson Julie Gaillard said she expected a series of appeals in this case, which could eventually reach the Supreme Court.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Hoekstra tells Canada ‘keep your nose out of American politics’ ahead of midterms
stories.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra warned Canadian politicians to "keep your nose out of American politics" in a podcast appearance.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra has warned Canadian politicians to “keep your nose out of American politics” in a podcast appearance ahead of the U.S. midterms.

“We are closely watching Canadian activities because it appears that some of this, from our perspective, and the way that we view our elections, could be inferred to be election interference,” he said in an appearance on The Really Big Show , a Canadian news podcast.

“Keep your nose out of American politics,” he added, warning that “America will respond to it,” if the behaviour of Canadian politicians is deemed to be election interference.

Joly has previously been open about the fact that Canadian counter-tariffs were in part designed to “target states” and “put political pressure” on the Trump administration after 50 per cent tariffs were imposed on $28 billion worth of Canadian goods.

When asked about the breakdown in trade negotiations between Canada and the U.S., Hoekstra said: “We thought we had a deal in August … it’s the best deal that any country in the world has received.”

He added that U.S. negotiators thought they had the deal “ironed out,” until Prime Minister Mark Carney called his negotiating team back to Ottawa and suspended talks.

Hoekstra’s warning comes as Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre made a trip to Detroit, Michigan, to pitch a tariff-free auto pact between Canada and the U.S.

Michigan has become a crucial battleground in the upcoming U.S. midterm elections and is currently considered a toss-up for the Senate race by The Cook Political Report . It’s one of the states hit hardest by the trade war between the two countries, due to its automakers ​relying on integrated cross-border supply chains.

Meanwhile, Hoekstra isn’t the only U.S. politician who is accusing Canada of interference in America. Last month, President Donald Trump’s trade adviser Peter Navarro told Canadian lobbyists to “get the hell out of our country” and warned that “if you interfere in our elections in Maine and Michigan, you will pay even more dearly.”

Neither Navarro nor Hoekstra offered any evidence that Canadian lobbying or retaliatory tariffs amounted to election interference.

The Democrats need to gain four more seats to win back the Senate majority in the upcoming mid-term elections on Nov. 3.

stories.title: Expert insight: How Nasa’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will open a window into the Milky Way
stories.summary: Western University PhD candidate Samantha Lambier explains what makes Nasa’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope so unique.
stories.author: Jacquelyn Mitchell
stories.content:
Look up at the night sky with your naked eye and it May seem like it rarely changes. Yet the universe is in constant flux. Stars drift through space, orbiting the centre of the Milky Way as planets orbit them. They rotate, showing off spots on their surfaces and sometimes producing violent outbursts that affect planetary atmospheres much like solar storms produce auroras on the Earth.

As stars age, they can die dramatically as supernovae, releasing material that will form the next generation of stars and planets.

A new Nasa telescope – named after Nasa’s first chief of astronomy and first female executive, Nancy Grace Roman – will let us observe these changes to the night sky, almost as if we are watching a cosmic high-definition movie.

This is thanks to three capabilities working together: sharp images, a huge field of view and repeated observations.

The Nancy Grace Roman Telescope is often described as the successor to the Hubble Space Telescope. It has the same size mirror as Hubble and also observes visible and infrared light. But it is capable of observing a much larger patch of the sky – up to 200 times larger.

Nasa’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope transits the sun on board a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket during launch on Aug. 30, 2026, at Nasa’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. (Nasa/John Kraus)

Usually, seeing a bigger patch of sky means sacrificing spatial resolution. Both the Kepler and the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite planet-hunting telescopes have watched enormous numbers of stars, but their lower spatial resolution means nearby stars can blend together.

On the other hand, the James Webb Space Telescope can see more sharply, but its much smaller field of view makes it impractical for monitoring millions of objects at once. The Roman telescope is notable for combining high resolution with a wide field of view.

A comparison of the Hubble Space Telescope, Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and James Webb Space Telescope. Roman has a much larger field of view than Hubble and Webb. (Nasa, A. James (STScI))

The final key to Roman’s power is time: by repeatedly observing the same patches of sky, Roman will reveal changes that a single image could never capture.

Those changes unfold on timescales ranging from hours to years, revealing different physical processes. By simply tracking how the light of objects changes over time, Roman is able to distinguish different patterns and use them to uncover what is happening throughout the universe.

Two of Roman’s core surveys are designed to watch different parts of the sky for different kinds of change. The High-Latitude Time-Domain Survey will capture distant phenomena such as supernovae, while the Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey will monitor the packed centre of the Milky Way.

In the galactic bulge, thousands of stars (along with gas and dust) obscure our view of the centre of the galaxy. These same stars appear to our eyes as almost a solid white, smeary “Milky Way.”

Roman, however, can see the individual stars to use them as a backdrop for interesting science.

One of the primary focuses of the Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey is finding objects through microlensing. This is a process through which gravity from a passing object can warp and magnify light from a distant star behind it, allowing us to have a better view of that distant star.

These passing foreground objects can include stars, Mars-sized planets and even black holes hundreds of times the mass of the Sun.

During its first five years, the Roman telescope is expected to observe more than a billion galaxies. (Nasa’s Goddard Space Flight Center)

Roman will also find planets using the transit method, when planets dim starlight by passing in front of their star, revealing their presence. The sheer number of stars in the galactic bulge means astronomers predict they will find around 100,000 transiting planets.

Staring at stars can also reveal how stars themselves rotate and change over time. This change is particularly interesting for the very smallest and coolest stars.

Along with magnetic spots, clouds are also expected on the surface of stars cooler than roughly 2,500 C. As the stars rotate, these features come in and out of view, allowing astronomers to measure their rotation periods.

Comparing rotation across many targets can reveal patterns in how these stars change over broad timescales. Yet these stars are quite faint and red, making studying large numbers incredibly difficult with current surveys.

As stars rotate, features like clouds and magnetic spots come in and out of view, allowing astronomers to measure their rotation periods. (Samantha Lambier)

The Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite telescope, which has observed almost the entire sky over the past eight years, has revealed rotation periods for hundreds of these tiny stars. But this telescope observes in visible light, where these stars appear relatively faint, and its low spatial resolution makes crowded fields challenging.

Roman’s wide-field, high-resolution and near-infrared observations can significantly increase this sample, allowing astronomers to study rotation and activity across a much larger population of these smallest stars. A larger and more diverse sample could reveal how these stars’ environments vary, helping us understand worlds found around them.

From supernovae in distant galaxies to the smallest stars in our own, Roman will capture a cosmos that is constantly changing. Look closely, and the seemingly static sky is anything but.Image 4: The Conversation

Samantha Lambier, PhD Candidate in Astronomy, Western University

The Nancy Grace Roman Telescope is often described as the successor to the Hubble Space Telescope. It has the same size mirror as Hubble and also observes visible and infrared light. But it is capable of observing a much larger patch of the sky – up to 200 times larger.
Nasa’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope transits the sun on board a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket during launch on Aug. 30, 2026, at Nasa’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. (Nasa/John Kraus)

Usually, seeing a bigger patch of sky means sacrificing spatial resolution. Both the Kepler and the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite planet-hunting telescopes have watched enormous numbers of stars, but their lower spatial resolution means nearby stars can blend together.

On the other hand, the James Webb Space Telescope can see more sharply, but its much smaller field of view makes it impractical for monitoring millions of objects at once. The Roman telescope is notable for combining high resolution with a wide field of view.

content_blocks.alt: A complex visual comparing wavelength, mirror size and field of view of the three telescopes
content_blocks.caption: A comparison of the Hubble Space Telescope, Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and James Webb Space Telescope. Roman has a much larger field of view than Hubble and Webb. (NASA, A. James (STScI))

content_blocks.text: A comparison of the Hubble Space Telescope, Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and James Webb Space Telescope. Roman has a much larger field of view than Hubble and Webb. (Nasa, A. James (STScI))
The final key to Roman’s power is time: by repeatedly observing the same patches of sky, Roman will reveal changes that a single image could never capture.

Those changes unfold on timescales ranging from hours to years, revealing different physical processes. By simply tracking how the light of objects changes over time, Roman is able to distinguish different patterns and use them to uncover what is happening throughout the universe.

Two of Roman’s core surveys are designed to watch different parts of the sky for different kinds of change. The High-Latitude Time-Domain Survey will capture distant phenomena such as supernovae, while the Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey will monitor the packed centre of the Milky Way.
In the galactic bulge, thousands of stars (along with gas and dust) obscure our view of the centre of the galaxy. These same stars appear to our eyes as almost a solid white, smeary “Milky Way.”
Roman, however, can see the individual stars to use them as a backdrop for interesting science.

One of the primary focuses of the Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey is finding objects through microlensing. This is a process through which gravity from a passing object can warp and magnify light from a distant star behind it, allowing us to have a better view of that distant star.
These passing foreground objects can include stars, Mars-sized planets and even black holes hundreds of times the mass of the Sun.
During its first five years, the Roman telescope is expected to observe more than a billion galaxies. (Nasa’s Goddard Space Flight Center)

Roman will also find planets using the transit method, when planets dim starlight by passing in front of their star, revealing their presence. The sheer number of stars in the galactic bulge means astronomers predict they will find around 100,000 transiting planets.
What changing starlight reveals
Staring at stars can also reveal how stars themselves rotate and change over time. This change is particularly interesting for the very smallest and coolest stars.

Along with magnetic spots, clouds are also expected on the surface of stars cooler than roughly 2,500 C. As the stars rotate, these features come in and out of view, allowing astronomers to measure their rotation periods.

Comparing rotation across many targets can reveal patterns in how these stars change over broad timescales. Yet these stars are quite faint and red, making studying large numbers incredibly difficult with current surveys.

content_blocks.alt: A scatter graph with 'star brightness' on the vertical axis, 'time' on the horizontal axis, and yellow orbs shown as rotating underneath
content_blocks.caption: As stars rotate, features like clouds and magnetic spots come in and out of view, allowing astronomers to measure their rotation periods. (Samantha Lambier)

content_blocks.text: As stars rotate, features like clouds and magnetic spots come in and out of view, allowing astronomers to measure their rotation periods. (Samantha Lambier)

The Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite telescope, which has observed almost the entire sky over the past eight years, has revealed rotation periods for hundreds of these tiny stars. But this telescope observes in visible light, where these stars appear relatively faint, and its low spatial resolution makes crowded fields challenging.

Roman’s wide-field, high-resolution and near-infrared observations can significantly increase this sample, allowing astronomers to study rotation and activity across a much larger population of these smallest stars. A larger and more diverse sample could reveal how these stars’ environments vary, helping us understand worlds found around them.

From supernovae in distant galaxies to the smallest stars in our own, Roman will capture a cosmos that is constantly changing. Look closely, and the seemingly static sky is anything but.Image 4: The Conversation

stories.title: Farm Boy cheeses, 2 other brands recalled for listeria risk across Canada
stories.summary: Health Canada issued a recall notice for various cheese products sold in stores across Canada for a risk of listeria contamination, which it says could cause illness if ingested
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (Cfia) issued a recall notice on Wednesday for various cheese products sold in stores across Canada, including Farm Boy brand products, for a risk of listeria contamination.

In severe case, listeria can lead to death.

The recall comes after testing was done by the Cfia, and although no illnesses associated with consumption of the products have been reported, the recall notice says the Cfia is continuing to investigate and other products May be recalled.

The Cfia says food contaminated with listeria, also known as Listeria monocytogenes, can make you sick — even if the food doesn’t look or smell spoiled.

If someone is ill from ingesting the bacteria, symptoms May include vomiting, nausea, persistent fever, muscle aches, severe headache and neck stiffness. The notice adds that there is a greater risk for pregnant women, the elderly and people with weakened immune systems.

For pregnant women in particular, the recall notice says if they become infected, they May only experience mild, flu-like symptoms, but there could still be a serious risk of premature delivery, infection of the newborn or even stillbirth.

If someone thinks they have become sick from consuming these or any recalled products, the Cfia says they should contact their healthcare provider.

Recalled products are currently being removed from the marketplace, but consumers are being urged to be aware of the products in case they are still in circulation.

Consumers are being asked to check if they have the recalled products, and not to consume, serve, use, sell or distribute them. Those products should then either be returned to the location where they were purchased or thrown out.

Those products confirmed by the Cfia so far include:

stories.title: Stelco owner could be forced to divest assets if layoffs proceed, Joly warns
stories.summary: Industry Minister says layoffs are breach of commitments Cleveland-Cliffs made when it acquired steelmaker
stories.author: Steven Chase, Niall McGee
stories.content:
U.S. steelmaker Cleveland-Cliffs, owner of Stelco Inc., could face financial penalties or be forced to divest its Canadian operations if it proceeds with hundreds of layoffs in Ontario, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said Wednesday.

Stelco announced on Sept. 28 that it was laying off up to 500 workers in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont., saying it couldn’t compete in the galvanized steel market as a result of the trade war with the United States. Ottawa considers these layoffs a breach of commitments that the steelmaker made when it acquired Stelco.

The Industry Minister told reporters that she’s not backing down and that she expects Stelco to uphold its commitments.

Ms. Joly spoke after a fireside chat at The Globe and Mail’s defence summit in Ottawa. “Right now, a business decision or even a change in market conditions cannot be used to not follow the commitment,” Ms. Joly said.

Earlier this month, Ms. Joly warned that she would invoke the “full force of the law” to enforce those obligations.

When the federal government approved Cliffs’s $3.4-billion acquisition of Stelco in 2024, it imposed legally binding conditions, including that it maintain at least the same number of unionized employees in Canada for five years, as well as the vast majority of non-unionized workers.

Cliffs did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Stelco informed Ottawa in a letter sent Friday that it is not in violation of its Investment Canada Act (ICA) job commitments, and it is proceeding as planned with hundreds of layoffs in Canada.

Ms. Joly said Ottawa is reviewing the letter.

“But let me be clear: Under Section 40 of the Investment Canada Act, a few possible outcomes of a court process can lead to financial penalties towards the company, forcing them to abide by the commitment, and also a forced divestiture, so forcing them to sell their Canadian assets,” Ms. Joly said.

“Everything is on the table, and so therefore I’m always open to sit down with the company and find a solution, but we’re looking at everything that is possible to keep jobs in Canada.”

On Oct. 5, Ms. Joly had issued the Ohio-based steelmaker an ultimatum to map out a plan within five business days for complying with its employment guarantees under the Investment Canada Act or possibly face legal action.

In the company’s response letter, obtained by The Globe and Mail, Stelco president and general counsel Paul Simon said the company wasn’t in violation of its ICA commitments, citing a legal provision around the promises and the government’s own guidelines under the act.

He said the undertakings did not stipulate a commitment to avoid layoffs at Stelco. In addition, the promise around maintaining job levels did not apply to every single day of the five-year period, he said.

Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves said he is prepared to immediately call back laid-off workers at Stelco if Ottawa can reach a “Fortress North America” trade pact with the U.S.

The 50-per-cent U.S. tariff imposed on Canadian steel last year means Cliffs can no longer profitably sell galvanized steel into that market, Mr. Goncalves said.

Last year, Ottawa cracked down on the dumping of foreign steel into Canada below normal prices through the imposition of tariff-rate quotas, and it has mandated that publicly funded projects use Canadian steel wherever possible.

However, Mr. Goncalves maintains that the Canadian government hasn’t done enough to reduce foreign dumping of galvanized steel in the country, which he says is hurting Stelco’s ability to compete in the domestic market.

Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, said he was open to the idea of Cliffs selling Stelco and hopes Ottawa nationalizes the company.

“If divestment is one of the options, so be it. It would probably be better for Canada if we have a nationalized steel company,” he said.

“Steel is essential to the supply chain and for national security. We wouldn’t be dependent on a multinational foreign corporation controlling our steel destiny.”

The Conservative opposition in Ottawa said Ms. Joly should already have taken action by suing Stelco, procuring court orders against Cleveland-Cliffs including penalties and, where warranted, pursuing a court-ordered sale with the goal of securing a Canadian buyer.

“The hundreds of workers being laid off don’t have 10 months to wait,” Ned Kuruc, Conservative member of Parliament for Hamilton East—Stoney Creek, said in a statement Wednesday.

“Their mortgage payment is at the end of the month, their grocery trip is this weekend, and Christmas planning is happening right now.”

The MP said Ottawa needs to uphold the deal it signed.

“The Liberals approved the Stelco takeover on the strength of their job guarantees. Now they must enforce them,” Mr. Kuruc said.

There is precedent for Ottawa to sue, and it revolves around an earlier iteration of the same Canadian steelmaker. After U.S. Steel Corp. acquired Stelco in 2007, it made commitments under the Investment Canada Act around jobs and production levels. After the financial crisis hit in 2008, U.S. Steel laid off workers in Canada.

The federal government then sued the company for allegedly reneging on its legally binding commitments. A settlement was reached in 2011, with U.S. Steel agreeing to a new set of commitments , including around production levels and investment in Canada.

stories.title: Heated Rivalry author Rachel Reid reflects on Nova Scotia, pressure of overnight fame at Massey Hall
stories.summary: Reid appeared on stage in a Q&A with Mattea Roach to discuss Heated Rivalry’s new collector’s edition
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
On Tuesday evening, fans of Heated Rivalry – the book by Rachel Reid and the hit TV adaptation by Jacob Tierney – swarmed Massey Hall in Toronto. They wore jerseys inspired by their favourite fictional hockey players; they clutched new special editions of Reid’s bestselling novel, the edges of their pages sprayed with gold glitter.

In the lead-up to Reid’s Q&A with CBC’s Mattea Roach, the 2,534-person crowd was positively buzzing. And who could blame them? Now’s a great time to be a fan of Heated Rivalry : Filming of the show’s second season is well under way , and Reid’s next book in her Game Changers series, Unrivaled , is set to be published in June.

Reid started the night by underlining that she couldn’t share anything about the next book or the show’s second season. Roach, best known as the most successful Canadian to appear on Jeopardy! , pivoted quickly to HarperCollins’s new collector’s edition of Heated Rivalry , printed in hardcover with full-colour character art and a stamped foil cover – a far cry from Heated Rivalry ’s earlier paperback editions.

“I certainly never expected to have a hardcover of this book when I first submitted it to publishers,” said Reid. “I never thought of the move beyond e-books, so I was quite thrilled the first time I got an audiobook, then the mass market paperback and the trade paperback. . .I just think it’s nice that people are so into tangible books again.”

Reid published Game Changer , the first book in the eponymous series, in 2018, at a time when there was “some stigma” around reading romance books in public. “Romance was very much an e-book genre when I started publishing, and I thought it would just stay there,” she said. But during the pandemic, romance readership exploded, and Reid’s work experienced a sizable bump in popularity – though nothing could have prepared her for the success of Tierney’s TV adaptation, which made Heated Rivalry all but a household name.

“It would be tough to convince myself back then that any of this is real,” Reid said, adding that in the early stages of her career she had to learn how to talk about her books outside the “safe bubble” of the romance world. “I didn’t like explaining what I wrote or why to people who didn’t want to understand.” That’s changed in the last year, she said, thanks to the show’s extraordinarily positive reception.

Much of Tuesday’s conversation focused squarely on hockey – and Nova Scotia, the shared home province of Reid and Roach. “I feel like all of my characters are secretly Nova Scotian,” said Reid, laughing. One of her quirks as a writer, she said, is her highly regional sense of grammar and idioms: When writing Heated Rivalry , for instance, she had to explain to her American editor what Canadian hockey star Shane Hollander meant when discussing “going to the cottage.”

“My mushy, terrible Nova Scotia grammar leaks in at times,” she said.

To that end, Reid has no plans of leaving her home in Halifax, even as work obligations increasingly pull her to Ontario and the U.S. – earlier this month she appeared in New York to support the Irina Foundation , a new fund launched by Heated Rivalry production company Accent Aigu Entertainment to promote mental well-being and inclusivity through organized sports and arts programs.

“I’ve never lived anywhere else, so it’s a comfort thing,” said Reid of Nova Scotia. “After I do things like this, it’s quiet, and life feels very normal there. People are so proud, and they’re really excited for me, which is really nice. I think the pace of life there suits me. I do feel sometimes that I’m missing out on things by not living in Toronto. . .maybe I’ll split my time some day. But I can’t imagine ever not having my home base in Nova Scotia.”

After some prodding, Reid revealed herself to be a fan of the Montreal Canadiens, and dug into the occasionally ugly complexities of Canadian hockey culture, encouraging fans to read Rick Westhead’s We Breed Lions: Confronting Canada’s Troubled Hockey Culture .

“If you read that book, you’ll see I go very easy on hockey culture in my books,” she said. (A number of her characters are forced to contend with leaguewide homophobia over the course of the Game Changers series.) “That was kind of why I wanted to write hockey romance at all. It was to explore the more toxic elements of hockey culture, and I thought a romance would be a good way to do that.”

In a slight teaser for Heated Rivalry ’s second season – and Unrivaled – Reid revealed that the last year has shown her firsthand how it feels to be famous. That learning curve, she said, has informed the arcs of Shane and Russian hockey star Ilya Rozanov as they navigate life in the public eye.

“These are characters who are famous, who are being watched, who people have opinions about, and whose lives change very suddenly,” she explained. “I can relate to that.” Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams, who play Ilya and Shane on the show, have experienced a similarly fast rise to prominence.

“Last year, they were two unknown actors playing very famous hockey players,” she said. “They’re now way more famous than those hockey players.”

stories.title: Newfoundland and Labrador expecting windfall from soaring oil prices
stories.summary: ST. John's - Newfoundland and Labrador's finance minister says skyrocketing oil prices are expected to deliver a windfall for the province.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
ST. John’s - Newfoundland and Labrador’s government is expecting a boost to the province’s revenues this year after the war in Iran sent oil prices skyrocketing across the globe.

Finance Minister Craig Pardy has previously said he anticipated additional revenues of more than $500 million, as oil prices soared. On Wednesday, the minister said that figure is even higher, though he said it was too soon to provide specific details.

However, Pardy said he agreed with Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham, who promised during a state-of-the-province speech that his government would not centre its financial planning around windfalls from wars.

“Those same elevated oil prices are hitting Newfoundlanders and Labradorians at the pump around their home heating bills,” Wakeham said to a crowd of more than 100 at a St. John’s Board of Trade event. “We cannot, and should not, and will not be counting on artificially high oil prices in perpetuity.”

Wakeham’s address marked one year since his Progressive Conservative Party ended 10 years of Liberal governments in Canada’s easternmost province. He promised a plan to expand the province’s offshore oil and gas industry and use its proceeds to build “something that lasts.”

He spoke of the opportunity in the oil and gas industry, and of promised returns from a sweeping new energy agreement with Quebec to develop wind and hydroelectric projects along the Churchill River in Labrador. He also took several opportunities to rail against the previous Liberal government.

Though the province expects more revenue from oil prices, it is also facing towering financial burdens. Pardy’s most recent budget forecast a net debt of nearly $21 billion by the end of the current fiscal year in March. By contrast, the province’s entire budget for the year is roughly $11.5 billion.

The budget also estimated an end-of-year deficit of about $688.5 million.

Pardy promised to deliver a debt management plan for the province later in the fall, though again, he was hesitant to reveal many details.

“We want to arrest our borrowing, and then we certainly want to make sure that we minimize it, and then get that net debt paid off,” he said after Wakeham’s speech. That will be accomplished by generating more revenue and controlling expenses, he said.

In the meantime, Wakeham said his government is still considering buying a piece of Equinor’s proposed Bay du Nord offshore oil project, which would be the first deepwater oil development in the country.

The Newfoundland and Labrador government holds shares in three of four oil projects currently operating off the east coast of St. John’s.

Bay du Nord would be the fifth, if Equinor decides to proceed. The Norwegian energy company is expected to make that call early next year.

Officials said earlier this year that the Newfoundland and Labrador government was considering buying up to 10 per cent of Bay du Nord. In that case, the provincial government would make an estimated $6.4 billion from the development through royalties, taxes and the equity stake.

Wakeham said he was waiting for recommendations from his government’s Department of Energy Mines and OilCo, the province’s oil and gas corporation.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

In the meantime, Wakeham said his government is still considering buying a piece of Equinor’s proposed Bay du Nord offshore oil project, which would be the first deepwater oil development in the country.
The Newfoundland and Labrador government holds shares in three of four oil projects currently operating off the east coast of St. John’s.
Bay du Nord would be the fifth, if Equinor decides to proceed. The Norwegian energy company is expected to make that call early next year.

Officials said earlier this year that the Newfoundland and Labrador government was considering buying up to 10 per cent of Bay du Nord. In that case, the provincial government would make an estimated $6.4 billion from the development through royalties, taxes and the equity stake.
Wakeham said he was waiting for recommendations from his government’s Department of Energy Mines and OilCo, the province’s oil and gas corporation.

stories.title: Irene Mathyssen has died at 75
stories.summary: Irene Mathyssen, a long-time Member of Parliament for London Fanshawe has died. She was 75. As an NDP politici...
stories.author: Owen Schuller
stories.content:
Irene Mathyssen, a long-time Member of Parliament for London Fanshawe has died. She was 75.

As an NDP politician, Mathyssen was known as a fierce advocate for human rights. She represented London for nearly three decades at the provincial and federal level.

Mathyssen was elected as the MPP for Middlesex in 1990 and served in provincial politics until 1995. She then moved to federal politics in 2006, winning the riding of London-Fanshawe. She was re-elected three times before retiring from federal politics in 2019 .

A spokesperson for Mathyssen’s family confirmed she died Monday at her home after a battle with cancer, surrounded by family.

stories.title: B.C. teacher receives two-week suspension for posting sexual photos of himself on Reddit
stories.summary: Two students who found Ho’s Reddit account reported feeling shocked and told other teachers at the school, the regulator states.
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
A B.C. high school teacher has been suspended after his students discovered nude and sexual photos he posted on his personal Reddit account, according to the profession’s provincial regulator.

According to the agreement, two Grade 11 students at Ho’s school in Richmond, B.C., found his Reddit account after doing an internet search. One of the search results showed Ho clothed with a link to his Reddit account.

“The students (then) viewed Ho’s Reddit profile page which displayed posts and comments Ho had made on various sub-communities of the platform over time. These included nude photographs of Ho, photographs of Ho engaged in sexual acts, and posts of a sexual nature,” Donaree Nygard, the commissioner, wrote in the agreement.

The agreement also notes that the profile contained clothed photos of Ho “in connection with school activities.” One shot was taken at the school.

The agreement goes on to report that news of Ho’s account spread quickly through the school community.

“The two students who found Ho’s Reddit account reported feeling shocked and reported what they had found to other teachers at the school, as they felt that the posts were inappropriate,” the agreement states.

Ho has been on leave from the Richmond School District since mid-September 2023, after the posts were found.

“By having sexual images of himself available on a public website, where he was identified as being a teacher, Ho failed to maintain the integrity, credibility and reputation of the teaching profession,” Nygard wrote.

Ho admitted to the facts and conduct described in the agreement, and agreed to the suspension.

stories.title: High protein pancake bowls dominate social media
stories.summary: Protein pancake bowls are the latest health and wellness trend dominating social media.
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
Protein pancake bowls are the latest health and wellness trend dominating social media. “If you like the taste and enjoy a pancake with protein in it then it’s for you,” said Hailey Belaire-De Oliveira, a registered dietitian.

“If that feels best for an individual in their life then I’m all for it.” The six-ingredient recipe packs 30 to 45 grams of protein into one meal. “We estimate that everybody every day should have about 10 to 35 per cent of their intake coming from protein, but that amount of protein will vary between individuals,” said Belaire-De Oliveira.

“A good rule of thumb that we go by as dietitians is about 20 to 30 grams of protein per meal.” Belaire-De Oliveira said protein is important for a variety of reasons. “One of which being body repair and maintenance,” she said.

“It’s also one of the key ingredients in hair, skin, and nails and also it can be important if folks are looking to build muscle.” Recipe: One egg ¼ cup plain Greek yogurt ¼ cup milk One teaspoon maple syrup ⅓ cup whole wheat flour Two tablespoons protein powder ¼ teaspoon cinnamon ½ teaspoon baking powder ¼ cup of toppings of choice

stories.title: Toronto soldiers charged in kidnapping were looking for cryptocurrency, police say
stories.summary: "No one is above the law," Toronto Police Service Chief Myron Demkiw told reporters Wednesday.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
A violent Toronto kidnapping involving three Canadian soldiers was an attempt to force the victim into handing over access to cryptocurrency, police said Wednesday, revealing the alleged motive for the bizarre plot.

The July 25 kidnapping took place in a residential Toronto neighbourhood at Finch Avenue East and Bayview Avenue. The target: the owner of a cryptocurrency exchange.

The kidnappers grabbed their victim as he approached his vehicle and abducted him at gunpoint, Toronto Police Service Chief Myron Demkiw told reporters at a press conference.

“He was handcuffed and assaulted. The suspects allegedly attempted to gain access to his cryptocurrency assets” and business-related security systems.

The victim was later released and threatened not to contact police, said Chief Supt. Joe Matthews of Detective Operations.

But he did just that.

Police wouldn’t say Wednesday whether the kidnappers were successful in getting cryptocurrency from their victim, who suffered minor injuries. His name is banned from publication.

“What started as a kidnapping investigation became much larger,” said Demkiw. “In total, seven suspects have been arrested and 82 criminal charges have been laid.”

Within 24 hours, police had identified a vehicle used by the kidnappers, and two suspects were arrested, Matthews said.

“By Sept. 24, all seven accused had been arrested and charged,” Matthews said.

Police — who conducted searches of vehicles and residences across the Greater Toronto Area — seized four firearms during their probe, two of which were 3D printed, two silencers, 10 overcapacity magazines, more than 2,700 rounds of ammunition, half of which were blanks, cell phones, a replica firearm and “a large quantity of methamphetamine, cocaine and other controlled substances,” Matthews said.

“Investigators later determined that approximately 2,500 rounds of the ammunition and five over-capacity magazines had been stolen from the Canadian Armed Forces.”

The investigation “highlights an evolving trend that we are seeing in serious criminal activity,” Matthews said.

The victim was targeted because the kidnappers thought he had access to cryptocurrency assets, he said. “Criminals continue to adapt their methods and identify new opportunities for financial gain.”

Police haven’t connected the kidnapping to other Toronto abductions “at this point,” Matthews said, though police are still going through cell phones seized during the investigation.

The three soldiers charged are Talarambage Sachintha Fernando, James Moreau and Jack Miley. All three men are members of the 7th Toronto Regiment, a reserve artillery unit based at Moss Park Armoury in Toronto.

stories.title: Nationwide recall issued for various brands of cheese
stories.summary: The Canadian Food Inspection Agency has issued a nation-wide recall for various brands of cheese due to the presence of Listeria monocytogenes.
stories.author: Aarjavee Raaj
stories.content:
A nationwide recall for various brands of cheese has been issued due to the presence of Listeria monocytogenes.

According to a food recall warning posted to Health Canada Wednesday, the following products from Farm Boy, L’Ancêtre and Life Smart have been recalled from the marketplace:

Farm Boy Organic Swiss Cheese – 190 g

Farm Boy Organic Medium Cheddar Cheese – 200 g

Farm Boy Organic Old Cheddar Cheese – 200 g

Farm Boy Organic Extra Sharp Cheddar Cheese – 200 g

Farm Boy Organic 3-Year-Old Cheddar Cheese – 195 g

L’Ancêtre Organic Swiss Cheese – 200 g

L’Ancêtre Organic Cheddar Cheese - Shredded Old – 2 kg

L’Ancêtre Organic Mozza - Cheddar Shredded Cheese Blend – 200 g

L’Ancêtre Organic Mozzarella Cheese - Shredded Partially Skimmed – 1 kg

L’Ancêtre Organic Swiss Cheese - Shredded – 1 kg

Life Smart Organic Part Skim Mozzarella Cheese - 200 g

“There have been no reported illnesses associated with the consumption of these products,” the recall said.

The federal agency advised customers to check if they are in possession of the recalled products and not consume, serve, use, sell or distribute them. Instead, customers are being asked to discard or return the recalled products to the location of purchase.

“Food contaminated with listeria monocytogenes May not look or smell spoiled but can still make you sick,” the recall notice said. “Symptoms can include vomiting, nausea, persistent fever, muscle aches, severe headache and neck stiffness.”

The notice also warned that pregnant women, the elderly and people with weakened immune systems are “particularly at risk.”

“Although infected pregnant women May experience only mild, flu-like symptoms, the infection can lead to premature delivery, infection of the newborn or even stillbirth,” the recall read. “In severe cases of illness, people May die.”

The recall was triggered due to test results by the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (Cfia) and a food safety investigation is underway which could lead to more recalls, the notice said. The Cfia is also verifying that all recalled products are being removed from the marketplace.

stories.title: Ottawa's international student cap hurting Atlantic universities: association
stories.summary: Halifax - The Association of Atlantic Universities says the region's schools have been disproportionately hurt by the Canadian government's restrictions on international student enrolment.
stories.author: Lyndsay Armstrong The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Halifax - The Association of Atlantic Universities says the region’s schools have been disproportionately hurt by the Canadian government’s restrictions on international student enrolment.

The number of international students enrolled in its universities has dropped by nearly 48 per cent since the federal government imposed new restrictions in 2024, the association said.

The association said it has 3,000 fewer international students enrolled in Atlantic universities than it did last year, and universities and communities in the region are suffering as a result.

“There’s a financial impact, and there’s the impact of having fewer people in our communities to volunteer, to contribute, to buy goods and services, everything,” association CEO Ava Czapalay said in an interview Wednesday.

She said the reductions are affecting small businesses and community organizations since many international students work and volunteer where they study.

Atlantic Canada is dealing with an aging workforce, and last year the Atlantic provinces recorded the population had declined for the first time since 2020.

Czapalay said to address these issues the region needs to support talented newcomers who want to study and live in Atlantic Canada.

“The universities work very, very hard to recruit well-qualified international students who will contribute to our universities and our communities here, and many who will, when they graduate, contribute to our workforce,” she said.

“It’s a vital part of the labour market pipeline for this region, and we really hope that the federal government listens to us and works with us towards a solution,” Czapalay added.

The federal Immigration Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

When former federal immigration minister, Marc Miller, announced the restrictions in 2024, he said the measures were aimed at protecting a system “that has become so lucrative that it has opened a path for its abuse.”

“Enough is enough. Through the decisive measures announced today, we are striking the right balance for Canada and ensuring the integrity of our immigration system while setting students up for the success they hope for,” he said in a statement Jan. 22, 2024

Czapalay said the federal government’s “one-size-fits-all” strategy to reduce international student numbers has resulted in fewer visa application approvals out of Atlantic Canada compared to the rest of the country.

“So our question to the federal government would be, why is that? Our universities are credible. They offer the same quality experience, sometimes we would say a better quality experience, for students. So why would our universities not have the same approval rate?” she said.

Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham said Wednesday the province’s university needs more international students.

“The federal government, right now, has restrictions on the number of foreign students who can come and be educated in our province,” Wakeham said after delivering a state of the province address at a St. John’s hotel. “That needs to change.”

He vowed to appeal to the federal government to allow more students from outside of the country to study at Memorial University.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

— With files from Sarah Smellie in St. John’s.

stories.title: Forest City Film Festival draws out-of-towners
stories.summary: Nearly half of the tickets sold for this year's Forest City Film Festival (Ffcf) were bought outside of London...
stories.author: Ben McFadden
stories.content:
Nearly half of the tickets sold for this year’s Forest City Film Festival (Ffcf) were bought outside of London, organizers say.

The annual festival is getting ready to starts it’s four-day run on Thursday, showing up to 140 films that give local creatives a chance in the spotlight.

“About 40% of our ticket sales are from outside of London… which is huge!” said Ethan Hickey, a Western graduate with international acclaim from 4 films and executive director of the festival.

This year marks the 11th annual Forest City Film Festival, which has been growing every year since 2016 and with this one featuring big names such as hometown hero Jay Baruchel.

Baruchel will play the main character in The Stunt Driver, directed by London’s Michael Dowse, which is featured at the festival this Thursday.

As the Ffcf becomes a bigger name the events in the city are thrilled to see an influx of not only locals but people from all over coming to see what the creative minds in London have to offer.

“Everything is bigger this year, and it’s really showing great growth,” Hickey said.

The festival runs between Oct. 15-25 with most major events happening within the first four days, to open up the excitement a gala will be hosted at Goodwill Industries and sponsored by London Hydro.

Tourism is expected to see a boom as London continues to show its leaves.
