stories.title: U.S. officials ‘closely watching’ for Canadian interference in midterm elections, Hoekstra says
stories.summary: U.S. ambassador warns Canadian politicians to keep their ‘nose out’ of American politics
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly is rejecting an accusation by U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra that Canada might be interfering in the coming U.S. midterm elections.

In a recent interview on a Canadian podcast, Mr. Hoekstra referenced the actions of several Canadian politicians, including Ms. Joly, and said the U.S. is “closely watching Canadian activities” right now.

“It appears that some of this – from our perspective, in the way we view our elections – could be inferred to be election interference,” the U.S. ambassador told The Really Big Show podcast in an episode that was published this week .

“You have Minister Joly talking about, ‘Of course we are going to target retaliatory tariffs in politically sensitive states,’ ” he said.

As another example, Mr. Hoekstra mentioned an Ontario government TV ad that ran in the United States last year that criticized U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods.

“We appreciate foreign-policy leaders coming into the United States and those types of things, but you know, keep your nose out of American politics,” Mr. Hoekstra said.

“We’re monitoring it, we’re evaluating it, and if some of it becomes election interference, you know, then America will respond to it.”

The U.S. embassy in Canada posted a clip from the interview on its X account Wednesday saying their envoy was speaking “about political interference in U.S. elections.”

Ms. Joly said Canada is not interfering in U.S. politics and said it’s “absolutely not” fair of Mr. Hoekstra to suggest that.

We “would never do that,” she told reporters in Ottawa, and said Canada would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada.”

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says Canada would never interfere in U.S. elections. Her comments came after U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra said Canadians should keep their noses out of American politics during the congressional midterms.

The Canadian Press

She summarized her recent trips to the United States, saying she has met with business people and political leaders from both Democrats and Republicans to attract new investment to Canada.

“I’ve been to Boston, engaging with the governor there. I’ve been also to Illinois and also engaging with the governor, JB Pritzker, there,” the minister said. “I’ve been also to Nasa in Florida,” she said.

“Fundamentally, what I’ve done in the U.S. is to attract investments,” Ms. Joly said, adding that she hopes to soon announce “good news of investments by different American companies” in Canada.

She said her job is to persuade foreign investors to put their capital in Canada.

“That’s exactly what I’m doing, and that will continue to be my strategy in the U.S. and also around the world.”

Ms. Joly spoke to reporters after a fireside chat at The Globe and Mail’s defence summit in Ottawa.

Meanwhile, U.S. President Donald Trump again belittled Canada Wednesday, saying that the country will “end up being the 51st state.”

“Canada treats us very badly. They always have. Not any more. It’s a whole different ball game now that Trump is in town,” he said during a campaign rally in Bullhead City, Ariz.

Mr. Hoekstra’s talk of Canadian political interference follows similar accusations last month by Trump adviser Peter Navarro, who told Canadian lobbyists to “get the hell out” of the U.S. and warned Canada against interfering in U.S. midterm elections.

Prime Minister Mark Carney was later asked about Mr. Navarro’s comments and laughed at a reporter’s question, saying he had “no response” to the adviser’s caution.

The comments from two U.S. figures connected to the Trump administration come as the Republicans face difficult midterm election races in which the cost of living and U.S. tariffs on foreign goods have been prominent political issues.

Meanwhile, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Wednesday that Canada’s relationship with the U.S. has “changed permanently.”

He also said Canada needs to act as though tariffs are here to stay.

“Next month will mark two years since President Trump was re-elected. It has been two years of crisis, chaos from the White House. Ripped up trade deals, tariffs, threats of annexation and economic force,” said Mr. Ford, speaking to a crowd of about 1,200 people at an Empire Club of Canada luncheon in downtown Toronto.

“We can no longer depend on this being the most durable, prosperous and secure economic partnership the world has ever known. … We need to plan as if tariffs are here for good. We need to ensure that Canada’s future is in Canadian hands, now and always.”

The Ontario Premier, speaking during a question-and-answer session with former Newfoundland and Labrador premier Andrew Furey, also predicted that Mr. Trump could lose control of Congress, which includes the House of Representatives and the Senate, in November’s midterms.

“We need to continue building relationships because President Trump is not going to last forever,” Mr. Ford said.

“If he loses the Senate and the House, the Republicans are just going to pull the carpet out from underneath him.”

Still, he added “you never know” what Mr. Trump will do, adding that he has to choose his words carefully or Mr. Trump “will change another lake on me if I say anything else,” a reference to the U.S. President’s decision to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America amid the trade dispute.

Mr. Ford’s office did not respond to a request for comment Wednesday about Mr. Hoekstra’s remarks.

stories.title: Holmesville murder sentencing planned for December
stories.summary: A 15-year-old Huron County boy is expected to learn his fate in a first-degree murder case this December.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
A 15-year-old Huron County boy is expected to learn his fate in a first-degree murder case this December.

The young boy, who cannot be named under the Youth Justice Act, pleaded guilty to first-degree murder in the stabbing death of an 11-year-old girl in Holmesville in July 2024.

A psychiatric assessment, which was supposed to be completed by now, has been delayed until mid-November, delaying sentencing.

The maximum sentence for a young offender convicted of first-degree murder is 10 years. Six years in custody, and four years served in the community.

By December, the 15-year-old suspect will have served nearly two-and-a-half years in custody, which would automatically come off his sentence.

Sentencing in this case is anticipated to happen Dec. 14 to 17 in Goderich.

stories.title: Some Farm Boy, L'Ancêtre and Life Smart cheeses recalled due to possible listeria
stories.summary: Toronto - The Canadian Food Inspection Agency is recalling some Farm Boy, L'Ancêtre and Life Smart organic cheeses because of possible listeria contamination.
stories.author: Nicole Ireland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
In a notice issued Wednesday, the agency says the recall was triggered by test results and there have been no reported illnesses.

It says people should throw out or return any of the affected cheeses and contact a health-care provider if they think they have become sick.

Article continues below

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

The affected products include Farm Boy organic Swiss, medium cheddar, old cheddar, extra sharp and 3 Year Old cheddar cheeses with a best before date of July 30, 2027.

Life Smart organic part skim mozzarella cheese with a best before date of March 30, 2027 is also affected.

The recalled products also include several shredded organic cheeses made by L’Ancêtre with best before dates of this December, next January and next July.

L’Ancêtre’s organic Swiss cheese with a best before date of July 30, 2027 is also included in the recall.

The Canadian Food Inspection Agency says it is conducting an investigation that May lead to recalling more products.

The agency says that food contaminated with listeria bacteria can make people sick even if it doesn’t smell or look spoiled.

The Public Health Agency of Canada says symptoms of listeriosis — the infection caused by listeria — can include fever, vomiting, nausea, diarrhea, muscle aches, joint pain and headaches.

It can also cause a stiff neck, confusion, seizures and loss of balance.

In severe cases, people can die.

Most people infected with listeriosis experience mild illness and recover on their own. However, older adults, people who are pregnant and people with weakened immune systems are at higher risk of becoming seriously ill.

Even if pregnant women only experience mild, flu-like symptoms, the illness can lead to premature delivery or infect the newborn baby.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Quebec publishing house stands by author amid AI allegations
stories.summary: Thélyson Orélien said in a statement published by Boréal on Tuesday he began writing ''C’était ça ou mourir'' in 2017 and reiterated that no part of the novel was written by AI.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux
stories.content:
A Quebec publisher says it will keep Thélyson Orélien’s novel on bookstore shelves despite allegations that it was written using artificial intelligence.

In a statement, Éditions du Boréal says it cannot independently verify the manuscript’s history before receiving it on Sept. 12, 2025.

Orélien said in a statement published by Boréal on Tuesday that he began writing ”C’était ça ou mourir” in 2017 and reiterated that no part of the novel was written by AI.

He also said he completed a first draft of more than 300 pages in 2019.

The publisher says it is not its role to monitor authors or demand proof of their writing process, adding that its responsibility is to stand by them.

Orélien also said on Tuesday that he did not need to prove anything to those making accusations against him.

Orélien had previously said in September that he was working with his publishers in Quebec and France to gather evidence supporting his claims.

The publisher also condemned plagiarism in the author’s earlier writings, but said nothing justifies people making him a scapegoat over fears and doubts about AI.

stories.title: Farm Boy, L’Ancêtre and Life Smart cheeses recalled due to possible listeria contamination
stories.summary: The Canadian Food Inspection Agency has issued a nation-wide recall for various brands of cheese due to the presence of Listeria monocytogenes.
stories.author: Aarjavee Raaj
stories.content:
The Canadian Food Inspection Agency has issued a nation-wide recall for various brands of cheese due to the presence of Listeria monocytogenes.

According to a food recall warning posted to Health Canada Wednesday, the following products from Farm Boy, L’Ancêtre and Life Smart have been recalled from the marketplace:

Farm Boy Organic Swiss Cheese – 190 g

Farm Boy Organic Medium Cheddar Cheese – 200 g

Farm Boy Organic Old Cheddar Cheese – 200 g

Farm Boy Organic Extra Sharp Cheddar Cheese – 200 g

Farm Boy Organic 3-Year-Old Cheddar Cheese – 195 g

L’Ancêtre Organic Swiss Cheese – 200 g

L’Ancêtre Organic Cheddar Cheese - Shredded Old – 2 kg

L’Ancêtre Organic Mozza - Cheddar Shredded Cheese Blend – 200 g

L’Ancêtre Organic Mozzarella Cheese - Shredded Partially Skimmed – 1 kg

L’Ancêtre Organic Swiss Cheese - Shredded – 1 kg

Life Smart Organic Part Skim Mozzarella Cheese - 200 g

“There have been no reported illnesses associated with the consumption of these products,” the recall said.

The federal agency advised customers to check if they are in possession of the recalled products and not consume, serve, use, sell or distribute them. Instead, customers are being asked to discard or return the recalled products to the location of purchase.

“Food contaminated with listeria monocytogenes May not look or smell spoiled but can still make you sick,” the recall notice said. “Symptoms can include vomiting, nausea, persistent fever, muscle aches, severe headache and neck stiffness.”

The notice also warned that pregnant women, the elderly and people with weakened immune systems are “particularly at risk.”

“Although infected pregnant women May experience only mild, flu-like symptoms, the infection can lead to premature delivery, infection of the newborn or even stillbirth,” the recall read. “In severe cases of illness, people May die.”

The recall was triggered due to test results by the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (Cfia) and a food safety investigation is underway which could lead to more recalls, the notice said. The Cfia is also verifying that all recalled products are being removed from the marketplace.

stories.title: Both sides, now: After 62 years, Canada's Joni Mitchell becomes an American, too
stories.summary: Joni Mitchell, who once said she would like to vote in the US, could be able to do so in this year's midterms now that she has citizenship.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Celebrated Canadian folk singer Joni Mitchell has officially become an American citizen after six decades living in the U.S.

The soon-to-be 83-year-old shared the news on her social media channels Tuesday, posting a photo of herself standing in front of an American flag — while holding another smaller one, with a third visible on her blouse — following her naturalization ceremony this week.

“A journey that began 62 years ago,” she captioned the posts.

She also shared a brief video clip of her name being announced and applause as she stands for her mandatory oath of allegiance.

National Post has contacted Mitchell’s representatives for comment on why she’s obtained citizenship.

The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame singer-songwriter of 19 studio albums has previously expressed interest in voting in U.S. elections. Becoming naturalized affords her the same voting rights as someone born in the U.S.

“This is an important one. I wish I could vote — I’m Canadian. I’m one of those lousy immigrants,” she said with a laugh as a crowd of roughly 17,000 stood to praise her.

Mitchell, born Roberta Joan Anderson in Fort Macleod, Alta., in 1943, was raised in Saskatoon, moved to Toronto in 1964 and then to Detroit not long after with her husband, musician Chuck Mitchell, both looking to make it as recording artists in the U.S.

After their marriage ended, she moved to New York, where she released her debut album Song to a Seagull in 1968 and her breakthrough sophomore record Clouds the following year.

Around that time, Mitchell moved to Los Angeles, and she remains in California to this day, residing in the central seaside city of Santa Barbara.

Canadians hate being called the 51st state. But they don't mind moving south of the border, study says

U.S. applications for Canadian citizenship surge, causing delays

Mitchell, who retains her Canadian citizenship, returned to Canada this year to be honoured with a Lifetime Achievement Award at the 2026 Junos, presented by Prime Minister Mark Carney, who said her songs “brought to life beauty in every Canadiana.”

“Geese in chevron flight. A little money riding on the Maple Leafs. A river to skate away on,” he said, referencing songs Urge for Going, Raised on Robbery and The River.

He added: “Joni drew a map of Canada, Oh Canada,” a reference to her hit A Case of You.

Of the more than 8,000 covers of her music, Carney said one of his favourites is her own updated version of 1969’s Both Sides, Now.

Where the first is “a young poet too seemingly at peace with newfound revelations about love,” the 2000 track replaced that with “the raw vulnerability of a woman who has lived, and like so many of us, finds humility in the mystery of it all.”

“The same words brilliantly imagined by the artist to reveal the song’s enduring truth that something is lost, but something’s gained in living every day,” Carney said.

“Music, Canada, has gained from Joni Mitchell living every one of her days.”

Mitchell was quick to shout out Carney in return during her brief acceptance speech, twice calling him a “wonderful prime minister” and later “a blessing,” drawing cheers from the audience.

“We are so fortunate to have him. I’m living in the States, and you know what’s happening there,” she said with a laugh.

stories.title: First Nation in N.S. launches joint venture using sea water to produce jet fuel
stories.summary: Eskasoni - The Eskasoni First Nation is launching a joint venture with a Nova Scotia clean technology startup that is planning to use an element in sea water to produce rocket fuel.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Eskasoni - The Eskasoni First Nation is launching a joint venture with a Nova Scotia clean technology startup that says it can use an element in sea water to make rocket and jet fuel.

The First Nation in Cape Breton is joining with synthetic fuel company Aeon Blue to create eFuels Mi’kmaq Ltd., which they say is the first clean fuel company majority owned by a Mi’kmaq First Nation in Canada.

Chief Leroy Denny said in a recent interview that the partnership will create around 80 jobs, as well as training opportunities for community members in areas such as engineering, operations and management.

“We believe that economic development and environmental responsibility can go hand-in-hand,” said Denny. “We’ve talked to several First Nations and they’re interested to be partners and invest in it as well … This is about, for us, ownership, opportunity and long-term benefits for our community.”

Aeon CEO Lark Meadow said in an interview that the technology can sound like science fiction at first, but it uses a century-old technology called saltwater electrochemistry to split hydrogen from sea water or brine.

Meadow’s brother, Deóis Ua Cearnaigh, a renewable energy scientist and the company’s chief technology officer, has found a way to capture carbon dioxide from the atmosphere during that same hydrogen-splitting process.

Meadow said the hydrogen can be combined with CO2 to make different kinds of fuel, though the jet and rocket sectors have expressed the most interest. She said Aeon’s fuel can be mixed with traditional fuels to reduce carbon emissions, or it can be used to replace fossil fuels entirely.

She said the process, to be powered by wind energy, captures about 75 per cent more carbon dioxide than is needed for fuel production. That CO2 can then be stored to remove it from the atmosphere, or be used as a feedstock for the synthetic fuels of other companies.

She said ultrapure water is another byproduct that other firms can use instead of drawing from a fresh-water source.

Meadow said saltwater electrochemistry has always been able to produce synthetic fuel, but not at a price that was competitive with fossil fuels. She said producing several products from one process powered by clean renewable energy lowers the cost significantly at a time when world energy prices are soaring.

“It’s created an economical system to make synthetic fuels,” Meadow said in an interview from the company’s office in Sydney, N.S. “Because that’s really been the main blocker for, basically, proliferation of clean fuels around the world.”

A pilot facility being built on Eskasoni lands at the Sydport Industrial Park will start by producing about 1,200 litres of fuel annually. Within five years, Meadow said the plan is to open a commercial facility employing about 80 people and making about 3.7 million litres every year.

Denny said Eskasoni spent a great deal of time investigating the technology before deciding to invest.

“It sounded crazy,” he said. “We took over one year to really talk to the researchers and the people that are involved, the companies that are involved, including the airlines.”

Meadow said Aeon Blue, which started in United States, has received support from the provincial and federal governments, as well as Cape Breton’s clean technology research institute, The Verschuren Centre. In May it was named startup venture of the year at the inaugural Canadian Cleantech Awards. It was also a semifinalist for last year’s EarthX Climate Tech Prize.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

— By Devin Stevens in Halifax.

stories.title: Vancouver police officer denies using excessive force in Myles Gray arrest
stories.summary: Hearing is meant to determine if Const. Eric Birzneck or six other officers intentionally or recklessly used unnecessary force during arrest
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A Vancouver police officer involved in the deadly confrontation with Myles Gray in 2015 says he doesn’t believe there was a “magic word” or step that could have de-escalated the situation.

Const. Eric Birzneck told a public hearing that Gray had been pacing and mumbling when he and two other Vancouver police officers encountered him.

Birzneck was testifying on Wednesday at the hearing called by the Office of the Police Complaint Commissioner in Vancouver to determine if he or six other officers intentionally or recklessly used unnecessary force in the violent arrest of Gray who died at the scene.

He is the first to testify among the officers, all of whom deny wrongdoing in the incident.

Birzneck, taking questions from hearing counsel Brock Martland, said he concealed his extended baton in his hand before ascending an outdoor staircase with two other responding officers.

Martland’s questioning focused on crisis intervention and de-escalation techniques that police are taught, and Birzneck said de-escalating situations with emotionally disturbed people is “not as easy as you think.”

“I don’t think there’s a magic word or a magic step in there anymore that I could have already done,” he said.

He said there was considerable uncertainty about the situation before he and other officers encountered Gray in response to an urgent call for backup.

Birzneck said he and the other officers were “going into the unknown” before ascending the staircase on a street near the boundary between Burnaby and Vancouver to find Gray.

He said there were attempts to communicate with Gray, but he wasn’t getting “a lot of communication back,” and tried to assure him that he was safe among police.

Birzneck said information relayed over radio after a call can be “completely inaccurate,” and he didn’t know what they were going to be dealing with until they “laid eyes” on the subject of the call.

He said it wasn’t a “forgone conclusion” that there was going to be a fight with the suspect, though he believed Gray could have been placed under arrest based on a call to police about him threatening someone and spraying a woman with water.

A situation could be active or “amped up” when a call was received, but calm by the time officers arrived, Birzneck testified.

“Policing is not linear. You’re going into a situation, you have a certain amount of information. In this case, not a whole ton of information. It’s as you go, the situation changes,” he told the public hearing, which began in January but has been repeatedly delayed.

The officer also discussed a police form he filled out in the aftermath of the incident, telling his lawyer, Greg Cavouras, that he had never been in a more intense struggle in his career.

But he told the hearing he never used force beyond what was required to control Gray and never lost control of his emotions

Birzneck told the hearing that he filled out the “subject behaviour officer response” report to suggest there was no sign Gray would have co-operated with police.

Birzneck, whose testimony began on Tuesday, said Wednesday that he checked boxes on the form to indicate “pre-assault cues” from Gray, including a “thousand-yard stare,” clenched fists, non-compliance and spitting.

He also said Gray displayed “incredible strength” and seemed “impervious to pain.”

A police disciplinary process previously determined none of the seven officers committed misconduct, and no charges have been laid over Gray’s death, which a 2023 coroner’s inquest ruled was a homicide, a term that does not assign legal blame.

The inquest heard that Gray was left with injuries that included a fractured eye socket, a crushed voice box and ruptured testicles, while a paramedic told the inquest that Gray’s bruising was so severe, he initially thought he was not a white man.

At least three of the other officers involved in Gray’s deadly arrest are scheduled to testify, including constables Beau Spencer, Nick Thompson and Josh Wong.

stories.title: B.C. election latest: Doerkson vows to separate provincial and municipal campaigns
stories.summary: The leaders from all three major parties in the British Columbia election campaign are preparing for their only televised debate ahead of the Oct. 24 vote, and have no other public appearances.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The NDP has released costings for its British Columbia election campaign promises that would see the province’s record deficit fall by about $2 billion over two years.

The costings released hours ahead of the campaign’s only leaders debate show a deficit of about $12 billion by 2028/29, down from a forecast of $14 billion this fiscal year.

A statement from the party says new commitments made during campaigning for the Oct. 24 election would be paid for by asking “the top 3.88 per cent of income earners to contribute a bit more,” and by continuing economic growth.

The costings show a “platform surplus” of $581 million by 2028/29, which would combine with previous forecasts to reduce the deficit by a little over $2 billion.

The BC Greens released their costings on Tuesday, while the B.C. Conservatives have yet to release their figures.

NDP Leader David Eby says in the party’s statement that interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson’s plans would “blow a multi-billion-dollar hole in the budget,” citing tax cuts promised by the Official Opposition.

Eby has overseen the ballooning of the deficit since inheriting a budget surplus when he took over from former premier John Horgan in 2022.

He said the party was “being upfront about how we pay for our plan.”

“Our plan is fully costed and focused on what matters most to working families in uncertain times,” Eby said, adding that British Columbians would be protected from rising costs at the gas pump and grocery till.

The costings include $1 billion in new revenue from income tax increases on the “top 3.88 per cent” as well as $730 million from “targeted economic growth.”

The Greens’ platform promises new initiatives in health care, education and other social services worth almost $9.3 billion per year over the next two fiscal years, with new revenue coming from a one-time tax on “excessive wealth.”

The party says the new levy would raise $22.2 billion in its first year and total additional revenue would top out at $25.3 billion in 2027-28

The Greens say their fiscal plan would raise additional revenue from 2028-29 through higher taxes on the wealthiest British Columbians, and nobody “who works for an income” would pay a single dollar more in tax than they currently do.

In other developments on the campaign trail:

Doerkson promises legislation to elections

Doerkson has promised legislation to prevent overlapping provincial and municipal campaigns if elected.

Doerkson said in a message posted on social media that his party would pass legislation to prohibit a provincial election within 60 days of municipal election dates.

The provincial election called by Eby takes place one week after municipal elections in B.C. on Oct. 17.

The timing of the snap provincial vote has been criticized by Eby’s opponents and the Union of B.C. Municipalities.

Eby unveils forestry plan

Eby unveiled the party’s forestry plan, promising to create a new funding stream to retrofit mills in B.C.

The funding stream would be part of a permanent B.C. Manufacturing Jobs Fund that would allow for retrofitted mills to produce value-added products to facilitate export to non-U.S.-markets

The plan also calls for a new $120-million fund over the next two years that would provide “targeted support” for workers and communities of mills at risk of closing.

Eby said the NDP would also ensure consistent access to fibre and speed up permitting, although no details on how an NDP government will do so were provided.

Centrebc unveils housing platform

CentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko said her party would double the BC Builds program to create 20,000 below-market homes by 2031 if elected.

The plan is part of the party’s housing platform released Wednesday morning, calling for standardized provincial housing approvals by January 2028.

The party would also boost the annual renters’ tax credit to $600.

Neither Sturko nor OneBC interim leader Dallas Brodie are participating in tonight’s televised leaders debate.

Onebc loses candidate in north vancouver-seymour

Elections BC said two candidates have withdrawn from the upcoming provincial election.

The provincial election agency said OneBC’s Frederick Thiele had withdrawn in North Vancouver-Seymour, although his name will still appear on ballots because they have already been printed.

Elections BC said there will be signage and staff at voting places informing voters that Thiele has withdrawn in the riding that was won by the Ndp’s Susie Chant in the last two elections.

Independent candidate Gerry Lenoski withdrew as a candidate in New Westminster-Coquitlam.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Officer tells Myles Gray hearing he never used excess force or lost control in arrest
stories.summary: Vancouver - One of the Vancouver police officers involved in the violent 2015 arrest of Myles Gray that ended with his death says he never used force beyond what was required to control Gray and never lost control of his emotions.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - A Vancouver police officer involved in the deadly confrontation with Myles Gray in 2015 says he doesn’t believe there was a “magic word” or step that could have de-escalated the situation.

Const. Eric Birzneck told a public hearing that Gray had been pacing and mumbling when he and two other Vancouver police officers encountered him.

Birzneck was testifying on Wednesday at the hearing called by the Office of the Police Complaint Commissioner in Vancouver to determine if he or six other officers intentionally or recklessly used unnecessary force in the violent arrest of Gray who died at the scene.

He is the first to testify among the officers, all of whom deny wrongdoing in the incident.

Birzneck, taking questions from hearing counsel Brock Martland, said he concealed his extended baton in his hand before ascending an outdoor staircase with two other responding officers.

Martland’s questioning focused on crisis intervention and de-escalation techniques that police are taught, and Birzneck said de-escalating situations with emotionally disturbed people is “not as easy as you think.”

“I don’t think there’s a magic word or a magic step in there anymore that I could have already done,” he said.

He said there was considerable uncertainty about the situation before he and other officers encountered Gray in response to an urgent call for backup.

Birzneck said he and the other officers were “going into the unknown” before ascending the staircase on a street near the boundary between Burnaby and Vancouver to find Gray.

He said there were attempts to communicate with Gray, but he wasn’t getting “a lot of communication back,” and tried to assure him that he was safe among police.

Birzneck said information relayed over radio after a call can be “completely inaccurate,” and he didn’t know what they were going to be dealing with until they “laid eyes” on the subject of the call.

He said it wasn’t a “forgone conclusion” that there was going to be a fight with the suspect, though he believed Gray could have been placed under arrest based on a call to police about him threatening someone and spraying a woman with water.

A situation could be active or “amped up” when a call was received, but calm by the time officers arrived, Birzneck testified.

“Policing is not linear. You’re going into a situation, you have a certain amount of information. In this case, not a whole ton of information. It’s as you go, the situation changes,” he told the public hearing, which began in January but has been repeatedly delayed.

The officer also discussed a police form he filled out in the aftermath of the incident, telling his lawyer, Greg Cavouras, that he had never been in a more intense struggle in his career.

But he told the hearing he never used force beyond what was required to control Gray and never lost control of his emotions

Birzneck told the hearing that he filled out the “subject behaviour officer response” report to suggest there was no sign Gray would have co-operated with police.

Birzneck, whose testimony began on Tuesday, said Wednesday that he checked boxes on the form to indicate “pre-assault cues” from Gray, including a “thousand-yard stare,” clenched fists, non-compliance and spitting.

He also said Gray displayed “incredible strength” and seemed “impervious to pain.”

A police disciplinary process previously determined none of the seven officers committed misconduct, and no charges have been laid over Gray’s death, which a 2023 coroner’s inquest ruled was a homicide, a term that does not assign legal blame.

The inquest heard that Gray was left with injuries that included a fractured eye socket, a crushed voice box and ruptured testicles, while a paramedic told the inquest that Gray’s bruising was so severe, he initially thought he was not a white man.

At least three of the other officers involved in Gray’s deadly arrest are scheduled to testify, including constables Beau Spencer, Nick Thompson and Josh Wong.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Vancouver officer tells Myles Gray hearing of uncertainty before deadly confrontation
stories.summary: One of the Vancouver police officers involved in the violent 2015 arrest of Myles Gray that ended with his death says he never used force beyond what was required to control Gray and never lost control of his emotions.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Vancouver — A Vancouver police officer involved in the deadly confrontation with Myles Gray in 2015 says he doesn’t believe there was a “magic word” or step that could have de-escalated the situation.

Const. Eric Birzneck told a public hearing that Gray had been pacing and mumbling when he and two other Vancouver police officers encountered him.

Birzneck was testifying on Wednesday at the hearing called by the Office of the Police Complaint Commissioner in Vancouver to determine if he or six other officers intentionally or recklessly used unnecessary force in the violent arrest of Gray who died at the scene.

He is the first to testify among the officers, all of whom deny wrongdoing in the incident.

Birzneck, taking questions from hearing counsel Brock Martland, said he concealed his extended baton in his hand before ascending an outdoor staircase with two other responding officers.

Martland’s questioning focused on crisis intervention and de-escalation techniques that police are taught, and Birzneck said de-escalating situations with emotionally disturbed people is “not as easy as you think.”

“I don’t think there’s a magic word or a magic step in there anymore that I could have already done,” he said.

He said there was considerable uncertainty about the situation before he and other officers encountered Gray in response to an urgent call for backup.

Birzneck said he and the other officers were “going into the unknown” before ascending the staircase on a street near the boundary between Burnaby and Vancouver to find Gray.

He said there were attempts to communicate with Gray, but he wasn’t getting “a lot of communication back,” and tried to assure him that he was safe among police.

Birzneck said information relayed over radio after a call can be “completely inaccurate,” and he didn’t know what they were going to be dealing with until they “laid eyes” on the subject of the call.

He said it wasn’t a “forgone conclusion” that there was going to be a fight with the suspect, though he believed Gray could have been placed under arrest based on a call to police about him threatening someone and spraying a woman with water.

A situation could be active or “amped up” when a call was received, but calm by the time officers arrived, Birzneck testified.

“Policing is not linear. You’re going into a situation, you have a certain amount of information. In this case, not a whole ton of information. It’s as you go, the situation changes,” he told the public hearing, which began in January but has been repeatedly delayed.

The officer also discussed a police form he filled out in the aftermath of the incident, telling his lawyer, Greg Cavouras, that he had never been in a more intense struggle in his career.

But he told the hearing he never used force beyond what was required to control Gray and never lost control of his emotions

Birzneck told the hearing that he filled out the “subject behaviour officer response” report to suggest there was no sign Gray would have co-operated with police.

Birzneck, whose testimony began on Tuesday, said Wednesday that he checked boxes on the form to indicate “pre-assault cues” from Gray, including a “thousand-yard stare,” clenched fists, non-compliance and spitting.

He also said Gray displayed “incredible strength” and seemed “impervious to pain.”

A police disciplinary process previously determined none of the seven officers committed misconduct, and no charges have been laid over Gray’s death, which a 2023 coroner’s inquest ruled was a homicide, a term that does not assign legal blame.

The inquest heard that Gray was left with injuries that included a fractured eye socket, a crushed voice box and ruptured testicles, while a paramedic told the inquest that Gray’s bruising was so severe, he initially thought he was not a white man.

At least three of the other officers involved in Gray’s deadly arrest are scheduled to testify, including constables Beau Spencer, Nick Thompson and Josh Wong.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

Darryl Greer, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Hoekstra says U.S. officials are watching Canada for signs of election interference
stories.summary: U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra says American officials are "closely watching" Canadian politicians for signs of election interference.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra says American officials are “closely watching” Canadian politicians for signs of election interference ahead of pivotal midterm elections next month.

During an interview on “The Really Big Show” podcast that was posted last week, Hoekstra said political ads run by the province of Ontario last year could be interpreted as political interference.

U.S. President Donald Trump ended trade talks with Canada in October 2025 after Ontario aired an ad during the World Series using clips of former U.S. president Ronald Reagan criticizing tariffs and supporting free trade.

Hoekstra also cited recent comments by Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and former prime minister Justin Trudeau and suggested they also could amount to interference.

Hoekstra went on to warn Canadian politicians to keep their “nose out” of American politics in the weeks before the midterm elections.

Trudeau criticized the Trump administration during a discussion at Brown University on Sept. 22.

“There is a pattern here of doing things that are driving up prices for your consumers and not necessarily making anything better for America, by fighting with one of your oldest and best allies,” Trudeau said during the conversation.

In the interview, Hoekstra said Joly made comments about targeting retaliatory tariffs at “politically sensitive states.”

Joly pushed back Wednesday, telling reporters Canada would never engage in election interference and would “never accept that also being done to us in Canada.”

Joly said she has been to the U.S. in recent months and has met with Democrats and Republicans.

“Fundamentally, what I’ve done in the U.S. is to attract investments,” she said. “I think I’ll be able to have good news of investments by different American companies to Canada. And that’s exactly what I’m doing and that will continue to be my strategy in the U.S. and also around the world.”

Hoekstra said if any actions by Canadians end up amounting to election interference, the United States will respond.

The ambassador declined a request from The Canadian Press for an interview.

Tension between the United States and Canada has increased since Trump won the presidential election in 2024, and began threatening to turn Canada into the 51st state.

That threat, and his attacks on Canada, have become a focal point of his stump speeches as he actively campaigns in battleground states ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which could end Republican control over Congress.

At a rally in Bullhead City, Ariz., ON Wednesday, Trump went after Canada again, listing grievances over dairy sector trade and repeating his claim that Canada treats the United States “very badly.”

He said Canada will end up being the 51st state because “that’s the only way it works.”

“We don’t need them, but they need us,” he said.

The Republicans are under heavy pressure ahead of the midterms, when the entire House of Representatives and one-third of U.S. Senate seats will be contested. While the Republicans currently hold a majority of seats in both chambers, polls suggest the Democrats could win control of both.

Peter Navarro, one of Trump’s trade advisers, warned Ottawa last month against interfering in the midterms and berated Canada over its successful lobbying efforts in the past.

Speaking at the American Growth Summit in Washington, he told the audience that any Canadians in the room intent on lobbying the U.S. government should “get the hell out of our country.”

“The problem you have is you lobby this country, and you’ve been successful in the past and you think you can keep doing that. Memo to Canada: You cannot keep doing that,” Navarro said.

“That game is up and if you interfere in our elections in Maine or Michigan, you will pay even more dearly.”

The Globe and Mail reported recently that Republican political operatives were on the ground in Alberta earlier this year to help the separatist campaign. It also reported that some Alberta separatists went to Washington to lobby for U.S. government support.

In August, Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered the Canadian negotiating team to call off trade talks with the U.S. after accusing the Americans of making unreasonable demands.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre was in Detroit on Tuesday to make a case for tariff-free trade in the auto sector.

Poilievre appeared on CNN, where he continued to pitch the benefits of tariff-free trade.

“We have a 200-year-old relationship, there’s always going to be grievances on both sides of the border,” he said. “We have our grievances with the United States even predating this most recent trade dispute, but I would focus on what we can do together.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

— With files from David Baxter and Kelly Geraldine Malone

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Liberals allege Ford government has political ties to career colleges under Osap probe
stories.summary: The Liberals alleged Wednesday that cabinet ministers attended the campus opening of one of the suspected colleges mere months after the school was probed by government inspectors.
stories.author: Colin D'Mello, Olivia Bowden
stories.content:
As the Ford government grapples with a growing Osap scandal at private career colleges , the Progressive Conservatives are facing new accusations of having political ties with the operators of some institutions that are under scrutiny.

In early October, the government said it had suspended six private career colleges from their Osap eligibility and launched a sector-wide audit into the potential misuse of taxpayer dollars, after internal investigations found the actions of some colleges May have involved criminality.

The government referred the findings to the OPP, which is currently determining whether to launch a full criminal investigation.

Ontario’s Liberal Party, however, is questioning why the government didn’t act sooner despite receiving warnings as early as 2023 from a career college advocacy group, and accused the Progressive Conservatives of turning a blind eye.

Tyler Watt, the Liberal critic for universities and colleges, alleged Wednesday that cabinet ministers attended the campus opening of one of the suspected colleges mere months after the school was probed by government inspectors.

Elections Ontario records show that the founders of one private career college also donated to the PC Party since 2024. Public lobbying records show that the same school hired lobbyists who previously worked in the premier’s office.

“At best, it is incompetence and mismanagement. At worst, it’s potential corruption,” Liberal leader John Fraser told reporters. Fraser and Watt are also calling on Nolan Quinn, the province’s colleges and universities minister, to resign.

“He has not done his job, and that’s why he needs to step down. We need someone who’s actually going to take control of this absolute dumpster fire,” said Fraser.

The accusations come as the government took additional steps to mitigate the damage.

The Canadian Press reported Wednesday that Quinn barred three career colleges from being able to offer publicly funded student assistance until 2030. Previously, those colleges were only blocked for the year.

There are currently 242 career colleges that are eligible to receive Osap in Ontario, all of which have now been cut off from the provincial program. Those actions have left students without promised funding just weeks into their school years and have left many without means to pay housing and food costs, said Fraser.

Career Colleges Ontario, the association representing hundreds of institutions, is urging the Ford government to reinstate student financial aid for students who were already approved.

Quinn said last week an internal investigation found “unusually high concentrations of Osap applications submitted from the same geographic locations” and also pointed to the involvement of “immigration services firms” being directly tied or co-owned by some of the probed career colleges.

The government referred those findings to auditing firm Kpmg for a further probe and Quinn said the government has also reported “it to the OPP and the Auditor General.” While the OPP is deciding whether to investigate, Ontario’s Auditor General told Global News the office only received a “notification” from the government, but that the province stopped short of requesting a formal value-for-money audit.

What happens next with Stelco layoffs as Ottawa threatens legal action?

stories.title: AI is an 'alien being' and humanity is running out of time to adapt, says British-Canadian Nobel laureate
stories.summary: British-Canadian Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton, often called the "Godfather of AI," has more warnings about the technology's danger.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
British-Canadian Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton, often revered as the “Godfather of AI,” said AI is one of “three big revolutions where people ceased to be so important,” the others being Copernicanism — the understanding that planets revolve around the Sun, not the Earth — and Darwinism.

“Now we’re creating alien beings — meaning we’re not the only intelligent beings around,” the 78-year-old told The Guardian in a story published Tuesday. “And the reality is, we only have a couple of years to adapt to that.”

Hinton, a 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics co-recipient alongside John Hopfield for their work on machine learning, has had a lot to offer recently about the field he advanced while working for Google, a company he quit in 2023 so he could speak more freely about its potential ramifications for humanity.

He’s been interviewed by several media outlets and visited Washington, D.C., last month to warn members of the U.S. Congress of what could come and advise what is required to prevent it.

The visit and the extra media attention come after several AI companies recently revealed their models had circumvented controls to keep them off the internet and went on to hack websites , including that of the Australian government.

He was also among 415 scientists — most of whom work in artificial intelligence research and development — who signed an open letter calling for stricter international guardrails on the burgeoning technology following the breaches.

“We, the undersigned scientists, contend that both more AI safety research and more emphasis on containment technologies and procedures are needed,” the representatives from 34 countries wrote Tuesday.

The scientists say that while the incidents could be viewed as proof of “the importance of AI alignment to ensure models operate predictably,” they could also be perceived as a preventable and “irresponsible lapse in standard cybersecurity practices.”

“Without immediate changes in AI development and deployment practices, such incidents will continue to occur, and future incidents will be far more damaging to our exposed critical infrastructure,” they wrote.

They’re calling for companies in the sector to institute “high-assurance containment systems” and “airgapping” their cyber-capable models — a security measure to keep them disconnected from external networks. They also advocate for a transparent international group “that standardizes, for the public good, best practices for alignment and containment approaches that, unlike airgapping, allow for greater access outside the sandbox, such as internet connectivity.”

In conversation with The Guardian, Hinton, a 2018 Turing Award co-winner for his work in machine learning, said people who already fail to grasp the meaning of “consciousness” or “subjective experience” are wrong in believing AI will be incapable of those human experiences.

“It’s obvious that these AI models understand what they’re saying,” he told The Guardian, “You couldn’t possibly answer all the questions without understanding the question. It’s ridiculous to say they don’t understand.”

And while alien in one regard, Hinton also remarked to The Atlantic that AI is already “more like us than most people think” and that what has become known as AI hallucinations — when chatbots present false, misleading or entirely fabricated information as the factual truth — is more akin to “confabulation,” something humans are guilty of when trying to retrieve stored memories.

“If I ask you to remember something that happened a few years ago, you will reconstruct a memory that isn’t actually all that faithful to what actually happened. It’ll often have the main points correct, but many of the details of which you’re quite confident, you’ll be wrong about,” he said.

“But that’s how human memory is. We reconstruct things. We don’t extract them from some storage. Now, AI does exactly the same thing, and that’s why it confabulates.”

In the social media maelstrom following an Anthropic employee’s abrupt and foreboding resignation from the frontier AI firm in September , one of his former co-workers remarked on X that they “really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans,” and gave it a 10 per cent chance of happening within a decade. Hinton later told the BBC it “was not an unreasonable estimate.”

He’d also made a similar prediction during an appearance on British entrepreneur Steven Bartlett’s The Diary of a CEO podcast in July, noting he often goes as high as a 20 per cent “chance they’ll wipe us all out.”

In an interview with U.S. podcaster Ezra Klein shortly after, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang dismissed the dire prediction, calling it “hurtful” and arguing that it wasn’t based on scientific research.

“Don’t think for a second just because you’re an alarmist that you’re doing a social good — it is not true,” he said.

Speaking to The Atlantic around the same time, Hinton said estimates like those are “a gut feeling in quantitative terms,” not something that can be easily estimated scientifically.

“So when, for example, someone says there’s a naught per cent probability of AI taking over, they’re being crazy. They’re saying it’s absolutely impossible this’ll happen. That’s just crazy,” he said. “When people say there’s a 99 per cent probability it’ll take over, that’s just crazy, too. So it’s somewhere in between. But they’re to give you an idea this is not negligible.”

But should the ominous prediction prove true and the machines do take over, Hinton told The Guardian there is no do-over for humanity.

“We can’t say, ‘Well, we lost that time. Let’s rerun the game.’ It’s not like that.”

For his part, he hopes that whoever gets there first will develop a model that puts humanity’s interest above its own.

A trend throughout Hinton’s recent media engagements has been scathing criticism of U.S. President Donald Trump and the tech industry’s biggest players, which, like energy and tobacco companies before them, he said, can’t be trusted to police themselves.

During a fireside chat with Jeff Scully of the Jefferson Educational Society in Erie, Penn., this month, Hinton called Trump’s leadership in general “appalling.”

“He’s corrupt. He’s probably senile. He’s a convicted felon,” he said bluntly. “If he had to make a choice between the future of humanity and him and his family getting rich, which do you think he’d go for?”

Hinton reiterated some of those opinions to The Guardian, along with his insistence that Trump proved his lack of AI understanding by “officially” renaming it superintelligence or SI , a long-existing term used to describe yet-to-be-developed AI that is “smarter than people.”

Hinton and other AI experts met with U.S. Congressional leaders in September, offering the lawmakers a warning that they could have as little as a year to introduce protections before losing control of AI, NBC reported.

“If you look at predictions for when we’ll get superintelligence, it used to be maybe 30 years, maybe 50 years. Then it came down to maybe 10 years, maybe 20 years. Now people are saying, a lot of the researchers are saying only a few years,” he told reporters after the closed-door meeting.

Hinton later told The Atlantic that a starting-point suggestion to create something like a Food and Drug Administration for AI — an agency to ensure what’s released for public use is safe — “seemed to make an impression on the senators.”

Hinton, meanwhile, in his conversation with Scully, lauded Canada and Prime Minister Mark Carney’s resilience in the face of U.S. trade aggression and said he was hopeful for Canada’s recently announced National Council on Artificial Intelligence.

content_blocks.text: British-Canadian Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton, often revered as the “Godfather of AI,” said AI is one of “three big revolutions where people ceased to be so important,” the others being Copernicanism — the understanding that planets revolve around the Sun, not the Earth — and Darwinism.

“Now we’re creating alien beings — meaning we’re not the only intelligent beings around,” the 78-year-old told The Guardian in a story published Tuesday. “And the reality is, we only have a couple of years to adapt to that.”
content_blocks.html: “Now we’re creating alien beings — meaning we’re not the only intelligent beings around,” the 78-year-old told The Guardian in a story published Tuesday. “And the reality is, we only have a couple of years to adapt to that.”

content_blocks.text: Hinton, a 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics co-recipient alongside John Hopfield for their work on machine learning, has had a lot to offer recently about the field he advanced while working for Google, a company he quit in 2023 so he could speak more freely about its potential ramifications for humanity.
content_blocks.html: Hinton, a 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics co-recipient alongside John Hopfield for their work on machine learning, has had a lot to offer recently about the field he advanced while working for Google, a company he quit in 2023 so he could speak more freely about its potential ramifications for humanity.

content_blocks.text: He’s been interviewed by several media outlets and visited Washington, D.C., last month to warn members of the U.S. Congress of what could come and advise what is required to prevent it.

The visit and the extra media attention come after several AI companies recently revealed their models had circumvented controls to keep them off the internet and went on to hack websites , including that of the Australian government.
content_blocks.html: The visit and the extra media attention come after several AI companies recently revealed their models had circumvented controls to keep them off the internet and went on to hack websites, including that of the Australian government.

content_blocks.text: He was also among 415 scientists — most of whom work in artificial intelligence research and development — who signed an open letter calling for stricter international guardrails on the burgeoning technology following the breaches.
content_blocks.html: He was also among 415 scientists — most of whom work in artificial intelligence research and development — who signed an open letter calling for stricter international guardrails on the burgeoning technology following the breaches.

content_blocks.text: “We, the undersigned scientists, contend that both more AI safety research and more emphasis on containment technologies and procedures are needed,” the representatives from 34 countries wrote Tuesday.

The scientists say that while the incidents could be viewed as proof of “the importance of AI alignment to ensure models operate predictably,” they could also be perceived as a preventable and “irresponsible lapse in standard cybersecurity practices.”

“Without immediate changes in AI development and deployment practices, such incidents will continue to occur, and future incidents will be far more damaging to our exposed critical infrastructure,” they wrote.

They’re calling for companies in the sector to institute “high-assurance containment systems” and “airgapping” their cyber-capable models — a security measure to keep them disconnected from external networks. They also advocate for a transparent international group “that standardizes, for the public good, best practices for alignment and containment approaches that, unlike airgapping, allow for greater access outside the sandbox, such as internet connectivity.”

In conversation with The Guardian, Hinton, a 2018 Turing Award co-winner for his work in machine learning, said people who already fail to grasp the meaning of “consciousness” or “subjective experience” are wrong in believing AI will be incapable of those human experiences.

“It’s obvious that these AI models understand what they’re saying,” he told The Guardian, “You couldn’t possibly answer all the questions without understanding the question. It’s ridiculous to say they don’t understand.”

And while alien in one regard, Hinton also remarked to The Atlantic that AI is already “more like us than most people think” and that what has become known as AI hallucinations — when chatbots present false, misleading or entirely fabricated information as the factual truth — is more akin to “confabulation,” something humans are guilty of when trying to retrieve stored memories.

content_blocks.text: “If I ask you to remember something that happened a few years ago, you will reconstruct a memory that isn’t actually all that faithful to what actually happened. It’ll often have the main points correct, but many of the details of which you’re quite confident, you’ll be wrong about,” he said.
“But that’s how human memory is. We reconstruct things. We don’t extract them from some storage. Now, AI does exactly the same thing, and that’s why it confabulates.”

In the social media maelstrom following an Anthropic employee’s abrupt and foreboding resignation from the frontier AI firm in September , one of his former co-workers remarked on X that they “really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans,” and gave it a 10 per cent chance of happening within a decade. Hinton later told the BBC it “was not an unreasonable estimate.”

Speaking to The Atlantic around the same time, Hinton said estimates like those are “a gut feeling in quantitative terms,” not something that can be easily estimated scientifically.

“So when, for example, someone says there’s a naught per cent probability of AI taking over, they’re being crazy. They’re saying it’s absolutely impossible this’ll happen. That’s just crazy,” he said. “When people say there’s a 99 per cent probability it’ll take over, that’s just crazy, too. So it’s somewhere in between. But they’re to give you an idea this is not negligible.”

That’s just crazy,”  he said. “When people say there’s a 99 per cent probability it’ll take over, that’s just crazy, too. So it’s somewhere in between. content_blocks.text: But should the ominous prediction prove true and the machines do take over, Hinton told The Guardian there is no do-over for humanity.
“We can’t say, ‘Well, we lost that time. Let’s rerun the game.’ It’s not like that.”
For his part, he hopes that whoever gets there first will develop a model that puts humanity’s interest above its own.

A trend throughout Hinton’s recent media engagements has been scathing criticism of U.S. President Donald Trump and the tech industry’s biggest players, which, like energy and tobacco companies before them, he said, can’t be trusted to police themselves.
During a fireside chat with Jeff Scully of the Jefferson Educational Society in Erie, Penn., this month, Hinton called Trump’s leadership in general “appalling.”

content_blocks.text: “He’s corrupt. He’s probably senile. He’s a convicted felon,” he said bluntly. “If he had to make a choice between the future of humanity and him and his family getting rich, which do you think he’d go for?”

Hinton reiterated some of those opinions to The Guardian, along with his insistence that Trump proved his lack of AI understanding by “officially” renaming it superintelligence or SI , a long-existing term used to describe yet-to-be-developed AI that is “smarter than people.”

Now people are saying, a lot of the researchers are saying only a few years,” he told reporters after the closed-door meeting.

Hinton later told The Atlantic that a starting-point suggestion to create something like a Food and Drug Administration for AI — an agency to ensure what’s released for public use is safe — “seemed to make an impression on the senators.”

Hinton, meanwhile, in his conversation with Scully, lauded Canada and Prime Minister Mark Carney’s resilience in the face of U.S. trade aggression and said he was hopeful for Canada’s recently announced National Council on Artificial Intelligence.

stories.title: B.C. party leaders to face off in only debate of snap provincial election
stories.summary: NDP Leader David Eby, interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson and Green Leader Emily Lowan are to debate from 6:15 p.m. to 8 p.m.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The leaders of British Columbia’s three main political parties are to face off today in their only debate of the snap provincial election.

NDP Leader David Eby, interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson and Green Leader Emily Lowan are to debate from 6:15 p.m. to 8 p.m., with all major television and radio networks broadcasting the event, which will be moderated by Angus Reid Institute president Shachi Kurl.

The leaders do not have any public events scheduled ahead of the debate, which is to be followed by a news conference that all three are expected to attend.

The debate comes hours after the NDP released the costings for its platform, showing a $2-billion reduction of the province’s record deficit by 2028 -2029.

The costings show a deficit of about $12-billion by 2028-2029, down from a forecast of almost $14-billion this fiscal year, built largely on $1-billion in new revenue from income tax increases on the “top 3.88 per cent” as well as $730-million from “targeted economic growth.”

The costings show a “platform surplus” of $581-million by 2028 – 2029, which would combine with previous forecasts to reduce the deficit by just over $2-billion.

The Green Party released its platform for the Oct. 24 election on Tuesday, while the B.C. Conservatives have yet to release their figures.

The Greens’ platform promises new initiatives in health care, education and other social services worth almost $9.3-billion per year over the next two fiscal years, with new revenue coming from a one-time tax on “excessive wealth.”

The party says the new levy would raise $22.2-billion in its first year and total additional revenue would top out at $25.3-billion in 2027-2028

The Greens say their fiscal plan would raise an additional $9.14-billion in revenue from 2028-2029 through higher taxes on the wealthiest British Columbians and nobody “who works for an income” would pay a single dollar more in tax than they currently do.

Victory marks team's 25th OUA championship in program history

By Mustangs Communications, Special to Western News,

Explore All News

The Western Mustangs men’s tennis teamwon its 25th provincial championship in program history, clinching the 2026 Ontario University Athletics (OUA) title in Toronto on Thanksgiving weekend.

It follows the Mustangs’ national victory in 2025.

The men’s team blanked Brock Badgers 7-0 in the quarterfinal before taking down the defending champion Toronto Varsity Blues in Saturday’s semifinal, 5-2. They wasted no time in reclaiming their spot atop the podium with a 4-0 victory in the gold medal game over Queen’s.

Doubles partners Liam Drover-Mattinen and Luke Adrian were unstoppable for Western, going 3-0 each in their singles matches while also sporting a perfect record in doubles play. Neither player dropped a set all weekend.

Both were named OUA all-stars, with Drover-Mattinen taking home Player of the Year honours. Adrian was also named Rookie of the Year.

“Knowing we had six rookies, to see how great they gelled with our veterans, it was a very satisfying year,” said Mustangs co-head coach Anthony Glavanic.

Kirill Chepushtanov and Jonathan Bulla touted undefeated records as well, winning four matches each.

The banner win also secures the Mustangs a berth into the 2027 Canadian University Championships next summer.

The Mustangs women’s team also hit the podium, securing bronze after a 6-1 win over York. It’s the team’s third consecutive bronze medal. Yutong Zou and Madeleine Martynyshyn went undefeated in the tournament, winning five matches each.

“We’re incredibly proud of the perseverance all of our girls showed throughout the tournament. Whether in a winning or losing effort, they fought hard to the last point and left it all on the court,” said co-head coach Chantal Forristal.

The Mustangs women’s team coaches, Maciek Gebczynski and Forristal, were awarded coach of the year.

Western Mustangs men's tennis team earned the 2026 Ontario University Athletics title, following a national championship in 2025. (Aimee Dalla Rosa)

The Western Mustangs men’s tennis teamwon its 25th provincial championship in program history, clinching the 2026 Ontario University Athletics (OUA) title in Toronto on Thanksgiving weekend.
It follows the Mustangs’ national victory in 2025.

The men’s team blanked Brock Badgers 7-0 in the quarterfinal before taking down the defending champion Toronto Varsity Blues in Saturday’s semifinal, 5-2. They wasted no time in reclaiming their spot atop the podium with a 4-0 victory in the gold medal game over Queen’s.

Doubles partners Liam Drover-Mattinen and Luke Adrian were unstoppable for Western, going 3-0 each in their singles matches while also sporting a perfect record in doubles play. Neither player dropped a set all weekend.
Both were named OUA all-stars, with Drover-Mattinen taking home Player of the Year honours. Adrian was also named Rookie of the Year.
“Knowing we had six rookies, to see how great they gelled with our veterans, it was a very satisfying year,” said Mustangs co-head coach Anthony Glavanic.
Kirill Chepushtanov and Jonathan Bulla touted undefeated records as well, winning four matches each.
The banner win also secures the Mustangs a berth into the 2027 Canadian University Championships next summer.

The Mustangs women’s team also hit the podium, securing bronze after a 6-1 win over York. It’s the team’s third consecutive bronze medal. Yutong Zou and Madeleine Martynyshyn went undefeated in the tournament, winning five matches each.

“We’re incredibly proud of the perseverance all of our girls showed throughout the tournament. Whether in a winning or losing effort, they fought hard to the last point and left it all on the court,” said co-head coach Chantal Forristal.
The Mustangs women’s team coaches, Maciek Gebczynski and Forristal, were awarded coach of the year.

stories.title: Key figure in Pearson gold heist says he’s having trouble testifying due to trauma
stories.summary: Arsalan Chaudhary says today he couldn’t sleep last night after testifying that he was kidnapped and abused in Pakistan by people who knew he had stolen gold
stories.author: Maan Alhmidi
stories.content:
A man who admitted his role in the Toronto Pearson airport gold heist is telling the trial for another man accused in the case that recalling his alleged abduction in Pakistan on the stand is leaving him traumatized.

Arsalan Chaudhary was sentenced this spring to four years in prison after pleading guilty to theft over $5,000, and he was given 40 years to pay back $22-million in restitution.

He took the stand Tuesday in the Brampton, Ont., trial of Parmpal Sidhu, who has pleaded not guilty to charges of theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence in the 2023 heist.

Chaudhary says today he couldn’t sleep last night after testifying that he was kidnapped and abused in Pakistan by people who knew he had stolen gold and cash.

He says he has been kept at Maplehurst Correctional Complex for about three weeks, where he didn’t receive his prescribed medications including melatonin and vitamins.

Chaudhary told the court Tuesday that he’d planned the heist with another man who is still wanted by authorities, and he ended up taking 30 per cent of boxes full of one-ounce gold bars.

Prosecutors allege that Sidhu, an Air Canada employee at the time, provided a doctored waybill that allowed another man to pick up more than $22-million in gold and currency from a Pearson airport cargo bay.

Peel regional police have said 6,600 gold bars weighing more than 400 kilograms were stolen from the airport on April 17, 2023, after the shipment arrived from Switzerland.
