stories.title: Former CP health reporter Helen Branswell remembered as excellent journalist and loving person
stories.summary: Toronto - Helen Branswell, the former Canadian Press health reporter known for her award-winning infectious disease coverage, died Tuesday from complications from cancer. She was 69 years old.
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Helen Branswell, the former Canadian Press health reporter known for her award-winning infectious disease coverage, died Tuesday from complications from cancer. She was 69 years old.

Branswell spent nearly 30 years at The Canadian Press, beginning as a general assignment reporter before eventually landing on the health and medical beat, where she established herself as an essential source of information through her dogged reporting, including of the 2003 Sars outbreak.

Later, while working at the Boston-based health news outlet Stat, her exhaustive coverage of the COVID-19 pandemic proved prescient and garnered her acclaim as she emerged as an authoritative voice on the virus.

“She leaves behind a very significant record as a journalist, an excellent journalist,” said Jack Branswell, her younger brother. “But we just also knew her as our sister and somebody who really cared and loved people.”

Branswell joined the wire in 1986, first working as a reporter-editor out of the Halifax bureau. In the following years, she spent time in Calgary, Ottawa and London, England. She covered a range of stories and topics, including politics, foreign affairs and sports.

In 2000, Branswell moved to the Toronto bureau, and it was there that she discovered her passion for health and medical reporting.

She spearheaded coverage of the 2003 Toronto Sars outbreak. Branswell became a fixture at daily news briefings, never shying away from asking probing questions that helped readers better understand the emerging medical threat.

“Her work was absolutely stellar,” said former CP health reporter Sheryl Ubelacker. “She developed all kinds of sources and she was really on top of the story and probably led everybody on that particular epidemic. She did wonderful work.”

At CP, Branswell also covered bird flu, polio and Ebola and demonstrated a relentless dedication to the demands of the health beat. She wrote science-backed stories with precision and accuracy, Ubelacker said, but did so in a way that the average reader or listener could comprehend.

“After she realized how much she loved medical reporting, it became a calling,” Ubelacker said. “And she was going to do the very best job she could ever do.”

Following her time at CP, Branswell joined Stat when it launched in 2015. There, she continued to report on infectious diseases and global health until the time of her death.

In January 2020, she published a detailed report on an emerging outbreak believed to be caused by a coronavirus when there wasn’t much reliable information in the U.S. about what would later become known as COVID-19. According to a 2021 news release from Stat, the veteran reporter, citing experience covering Sars, recognized the dangerous potential of the virus early when she saw an alert about four unexplained pneumonia cases in China in December 2019.

Branswell became an authority on the pandemic and COVID-19 through her continued coverage, leading to multiple accolades including winning the George Polk Award for Public Service in 2021. That same year, Branswell and her colleagues were finalists for the Pulitzer Prize for pandemic reporting.

“She was already on her way to becoming a legend and that story made her a legend in my estimation,” said Gerry Arnold, the former executive editor of The Canadian Press and longtime friend of Branswell. “The Canadian Press has turned out many, many, many great journalists over the years and Helen would be near the very, very top of that list of the greats.”

Branswell was born in Sherbrooke, Que., as one of six children. Her brother said she would say “she fell into” her career as a reporter. After graduating with a bachelor’s degree in English literature from St. Thomas University in Fredericton, she freelanced for the local newspaper, The Daily Gleaner, before working there full time.

Arnold first met Branswell in Halifax while she worked for the wire and he reported for a local newspaper. Later, when Arnold joined the wire service, they worked together on Parliament Hill during the early 1990s.

Then, Arnold said, he and Branswell were part of a tight-knit friend group who held dinner parties for those who didn’t have family close by. Arnold described Branswell as the person who “made every dinner party she attended better,” making sure the music was playing and the wine was cold. She was always quick to laugh, too, he said.

“She was a fabulous friend to so many people and the life of the party,” Arnold said. “I’ll never forget those Ottawa dinner parties.”

Her brother said she often would check in on people, especially if they were experiencing difficult things in their lives, but never wanted to take credit for her kindness.

“She did a lot of things quietly and in the background and she was a wonderful, wonderful human being,” Jack said.

As for her reporting, Arnold said what made Branswell stand out was her fearlessness.

“She was never intimidated by power or the pretension of power,” he said. “It didn’t bother her to stand up in a crowded news conference and ask an awkward question of somebody in a position of power that she knew might make waves or might make them feel uncomfortable. She didn’t care about that. She was there to get the story.”

Jack said his sister approached her work as a public service to keep people informed.

“A lot of people have reached out and said, ‘Your sister was kind of a light and a beacon at the start of the pandemic when we all had no information,’” he said.

Following news of her death, the director-general of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said in a statement posted to X that Branswell was a journalist with “integrity and professionalism”

“Throughout her career, Helen demonstrated an unwavering commitment to evidence, science and truth, helping the public understand some of the most complex and consequential health challenges of our time. At a moment when misinformation competes with facts, her reporting was a trusted source of clarity, honesty and insight,” the statement read.

During her career, Branswell earned numerous awards and honours, including the Victor Cohn Prize for Excellence in Medical Science Reporting and an honorary degree from Ottawa’s Carleton University in recognition of her outstanding career.

She also received several fellowships, including the Southam Fellowship at the University of Toronto and the Nieman Global Health Fellowship at Harvard University, focusing on polio eradication. As a CDC Knight Fellow in 2004, she embedded at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for three months.

Her brother said he looked up to Branswell, and followed in her footsteps to pursue journalism along with their sister, Brenda. He said he hoped people remember Helen always sought to bring truth out into the world as a reporter and that “aside from being a fantastic journalist, that she was just such a loving and caring person.”

stories.title: Halifax’s beloved 104-year-old tortoise is recovering after a successful surgery
stories.summary: Believed the be the oldest living gopher tortoise, Gus underwent a procedure to remove a bladder stone on Tuesday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Halifax’s beloved 104-year-old gopher tortoise, Gus, is recovering after a successful surgery.

Believed the be the oldest living gopher tortoise, Gus underwent a procedure to remove a bladder stone on Tuesday.

The Nova Scotia Museum of Natural History, where Gus lives, says he is now resting comfortably in private and will remain with a veterinary care team for 48 hours.

Gus’s many fans will have to wait up to 10 weeks before they can see him in public.

The museum says it will continue to share updates on his recovery.

In the two weeks since the museum first shared news of Gus’s surgery, he has received hundreds of letters, get-well cards and pieces of art.

Meanwhile, the museum’s social media accounts have received thousands of messages from around the world.

stories.title: Father receives life sentence in New York for murder of Montreal girl
stories.summary: A Montreal man has been sentenced to life in prison for killing his nine-year-old daughter and leaving her in a marsh in rural New York.
stories.author: Joseph Ryan
stories.content:
A Montreal man has been sentenced to life in prison for killing his nine-year-old daughter and leaving her in a marsh in rural New York.

The sentence comes two months after a jury in Essex County Court convicted Luciano Frattolin of second degree murder and concealment of a human corpse in the death of Melina Frattolin.

Judge Tatiana Coffinger delivered the sentence after rejecting a motion to set aside the guilty verdict.

Frattolin would not be eligible for parole before 25 years.

The defence issued a notice of appeal following the sentence.

The girl had been living in Montreal with her mother and had gone on a road trip to the U.S. with her father in July 2025.

On the night they were scheduled to return home, Luciano Frattolin called police, reporting she had been kidnapped after he had stopped the car he was driving on the side of the road.

During the three-week-long trial, the defence tried to argue that local police had not adequately investigated Frattolin’s claims that his daughter was kidnapped.

The prosecution called several police officers and experts over the trial who used car location data, cellphone data and surveillance camera footage to recreate Frattolin’s movements on the day his daughter died and prove his story was false.

The jury spent an hour deliberating on Aug. 10 at the end of the trial, before concluding that Frattolin was guilty.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

stories.title: A tough housing market could revive multigenerational homes, poll suggests
stories.summary: More than half (53 per cent) of respondents looking to buy a home within the next two years said they would consider living in a multi-generational home, a new poll said.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Canadians shopping for a home say they are willing to live with mom and dad just to be able to afford a home, a new poll by the Royal Bank of Canada has found.

More than half (53 per cent) of respondents looking to buy their next or first home within the next two years said they would consider living in a multi-generational home, the RBC Home Ownership Poll found.

However, the enthusiasm for multi-generational living is not necessarily matched by mom and dad. In contrast to prospective homebuyers, 35 per cent of current homeowners say they would sell their home and buy one with their children to help them get into the market.

Driving this trend is the high cost of housing, the poll found. Among prospective buyers, 34 per cent said multi-generational living is becoming more common because of housing affordability, while 32 per cent said it was a “smart way” for families to manage housing costs.

However, it is still not the preferred choice for many as more than a quarter (26 per cent) said they would only consider a multi-generational home out of necessity, not choice.

Conventional homebuying wisdom says a new entrant should buy a starter home before moving on to a bigger house. But many homebuyers today are skipping the starter home altogether.

The average prospective buyer feels they will be 41 when they buy their first home, while current homeowners said they were 29 when they first bought theirs.

Instead of a starter home, nearly three-quarters (74 per cent) said they would rather purchase a home within the next two years that they can stay in longer, rather than one they will outgrow.

“We look at what a larger purchase does to the monthly payment against what moving up in five years would cost. For some, the bigger first home is the better decision. For others it isn’t, and it’s worth knowing which of those two scenarios fits your situation before you start looking,” said Brad Evjen, senior mortgage specialist at RBC.

The average prospective buyer feels they will be 41 when they buy their first home, while current homeowners said they were 29 when they first bought theirs.
Instead of a starter home, nearly three-quarters (74 per cent) said they would rather purchase a home within the next two years that they can stay in longer, rather than one they will outgrow.

“We look at what a larger purchase does to the monthly payment against what moving up in five years would cost. For some, the bigger first home is the better decision. For others it isn’t, and it’s worth knowing which of those two scenarios fits your situation before you start looking,” said Brad Evjen, senior mortgage specialist at RBC.

stories.title: Lotto Max hits $90M, biggest lottery prize in Canadian history
stories.summary: There were a number of winners of Maxmillions, Maxplus and Encore in Tuesday's draw, but no one has yet to snag the big Lotto Max jackpot.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
The upcoming Friday Lotto Max jackpot has hit $90 million, the largest lottery prize ever offered in Canada.

The latest prize pot comes after the previous prizes of $80 million last Friday and $85 million Tuesday saw no winning ticket.

It’s not just the $90 million prize up for grabs this Friday either, with 18 Maxmillions worth an estimated $1 million each and 90 Maxplus prizes worth $100,000 also available.

In total, the value of top prizes in Friday’s draw total $117 million.

According to the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation, though the Lotto Max jackpot wasn’t won, there were still some very lucky Ontarians celebrating a win.

Two Maxmillions worth $1 million were sold in Whitby and Hamilton, with two people from Toronto and Mississauga sharing a third Maxmillion to receive a total of $500,000 each.

Some Ontarians also walked away with $100,000 each with 12 Maxplus winning tickets sold. Three other people shared a $50,000 Maxplus prize, with one sharing their winning numbers with someone from British Columbia.

A person in York Region and another in Willowdale also were winners of the Lotto Max second prize, each receiving $81,541.10.

Encore saw a few winners in Ontario as well, with people in Stouffville and Ajax and a third who bought their ticket online set to receive $100,000.

Lottery players are reminded to check their tickets to see if they won and visit OLG.CA to claim their prize. If you purchased online, you can visit your account and visit the lottery ticket history where you’ll be prompted to complete a claim declaration form.

Winners who received under $1,000 will either be automatically added to your OLG cash balance if you purchased online, or you can claim your prize at a lottery retailer.

stories.title: 3 people suffer life-threatening injuries in Kincardine crash
stories.summary: Police, along with Kincardine Fire and Emergency Services, were called to the scene shortly after 3 p.m. on Tuesday.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Three people suffered life-threatening injuries, following a crash near Kincardine.

The collision happened shortly after 3 p.m. on Tuesday, ON Highway 21, in front of Kincardine Township-Tiverton Public School, just north of Kincardine.

Police say four vehicles were involved.

A section of Highway 21 was closed for several hours, as police investigated the cause of the crash.

Anyone with information regarding this incident is asked to contact the Ontario Provincial Police at 1-888-310-1122. Should you wish to remain anonymous, you May call Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477 where you May be eligible to receive a cash reward of up to $2000.

stories.title: London Knights draft picks helping St. Thomas Stars to best start in decades
stories.summary: With a red-hot goaltender and four London Knights draft picks on the roster, the St. Thomas Stars are off to an 8-1 start.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
With a red-hot goaltender and four London Knights draft picks on the roster, the St. Thomas Stars are off to an 8-1 start. Goaltender Dylan Durno said he cannot remember a stretch in which he has played as well as he is now.

The reigning Gohl goalie of the month is 8-0 this season with a 1.48 goals-against average. “I think it’s just starts in practice and then competing with these boys out here, it just makes you better than it transitions to the game,” said Durno a London, Ont. native in his second season with the Stars.

It’s been so long since they’ve had a start like this, the league’s website doesn’t even go back that far. Practices at the Joe Thornton Community Centre in St. Thomas look a little different these days. The second-place Stars are young, fast and full of confidence.

“They bring a lot of talent, they bring some jump and they bring some pep,” said head coach Jason Williams. This season, the club has expanded its partnership with the London Knights. London rookies Ryan Beaulieu, Ryker Kesler and Graham Littlejohn are all playing for the Stars and injured goalie Charlie Weiss will also play.

“They’re also with us for practice and video and all the extra development off ice, but it’s shown it to be a really good blend between both leagues, and to be able to have that relationship with St. Thomas is a great thing.

“There’s lots of guys like Jarred Woolley, Easton Cowan and my dad [Josh Beaulieu] just bunch of great hockey players who just developed here [in the Gohl] going into their draft year and it’s just a great spot to be,” said Beaulieu.

“The main goal is next year being in our draft year, obviously I want to get drafted to NHL. So just to come here to develop and Graham and I were together last year too, so it’s just unreal.” Williams is thrilled to have these young talented players and understands his job is to get them back to the Ontario Hockey League “Sometimes this isn’t the spot where they want to necessarily be,” said Williams.

“Actually being here, getting the minutes and getting the puck touches is so crucial for their development. [Knights owners] Mark [Hunter] and Dale [Hunter] have done this for years and have had a lot of success with moving players on to the NHL.

I’m not going to question what they’re what they’re thinking but the fact that we get these guys, I’m excited.” The early season success is starting to create a buzz around the city, both for the fans and the players. “The guys are starting to get really close in the room and we’re starting to be with the fans more in the city and going out to events,” said Durno.

“It’s been really good and super happy for this group of guys.” Simpson, who scouts many Gohl games understands that having high profile draft picks in the league can translate to more fans in the stands. “Their fans can come watch a first rounder, a second rounder, and Weiss was a pick a couple of years ago and Littlejohn this year,” said Simpson.

“It’s always exciting when you can see players early and then you’ll see how they translate into the OHL.”

stories.title: Citytv launches Canadian edition of Dateline, Diana Swain to host
stories.summary: The inaugural episode will revisit the disappearance of Elizabeth Bain, a University of Toronto student who vanished in Scarborough in 1990
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
Citytv is bringing the internationally known Dateline franchise to Canada for the first time with a new investigative news special focused on one of the country’s most enduring unsolved cases.

Dateline Canada will premiere Nov. 26 at 8 p.m. ET/PT, marking the first international expansion of Nbc’s long-running Dateline newsmagazine franchise. The two-hour special will air on Citytv and Citytv+ and will be led by award-winning journalist Diana Swain.

The inaugural episode will revisit the disappearance of Elizabeth Bain, a University of Toronto (U of T) student who vanished in Scarborough in 1990. More than three decades later, the case remains one of Canada’s most high-profile unsolved mysteries.

“I’m proud to bring this story to Canadian audiences,” Swain said in a statement. “With Dateline Canada, we have an opportunity to re-examine a complex story through a fresh lens, connect pieces that May have been overlooked, and bring viewers a deeper understanding of the events that shaped this case and investigation.”

The two-hour special will air on Citytv and Citytv+ and will be led by award-winning journalist Diana Swain. Photo: Diana Swain Strategies/website.

The program will explore several aspects of the Bain case, including the wrongful conviction of Robert Baltovich, subsequent reviews of the evidence and newly uncovered information identified through extensive examination of police records.

Baltovich, Bain’s former boyfriend, was convicted of second-degree murder in 2000. However, the conviction was later overturned, and prosecutors ultimately chose not to proceed with a retrial. Bain’s disappearance remains unsolved.

“For more than three decades, Dateline has been telling stories that resonate with audiences,” longtime NBC correspondent Keith Morrison said in a statement. “To see the franchise expand with Diana Swain leading the new Canadian edition is an exciting evolution for the broadcast.”

stories.title: How a Bay Street legend taught Ryan Bushell to make clients his priority
stories.summary: The CEO of New Haven Asset Management walks us through his investment strategy
stories.author: Unknown
stories.content:
On his first day at an investment firm, Ryan Bushell expected career advice from his then-boss. Instead, he got a lesson about fancy and ordinary office chairs that still shapes how he manages money.

Today, Ryan is chief executive officer and portfolio manager at New Haven Asset Management in Toronto, where he continues to put his distinctive investing philosophy into practice. He and Brenda discuss the mentor who changed his approach to wealth management, the challenges of starting over in his thirties and why he steers clear of investing in technology stocks.

stories.title: Toronto police to give update on 2 Canadian soldiers facing 49 charges
stories.summary: Sachintha Fernando, 22, and James Moreau, 29, were arrested on Aug. 11 and face a total of 49 charges, including kidnapping for ransom and forcible confinement.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Toronto police will hold an update Wednesday regarding an investigation centred around two Canadian Armed Forces members facing dozens of charges.

Chief Myron Demkiw and Supt. Joe Matthews are set to speak to reporters at 11 a.m. ET, just over a week after the arrests of Bombardiers Sachintha Fernando and James Moreau were announced.

Fernando, 22, and Moreau, 29, were arrested on Aug. 11 and face a total of 49 charges, including kidnapping for ransom, forcible confinement and use of a firearm during the commission of an indictable offence.

Fernando was also charged with multiple firearms-related offences, including unauthorized possession of a prohibited device, possession of property obtained by crime and careless storage of ammunition, a police spokesperson told Global News on Oct. 6.

Fernando and Moreau are members of the 7th Toronto Regiment, a spokesperson for the Department of National Defence told Global News last week.

Moreau enrolled in the Canadian Army as a reservist in March 2018 and Fernando enrolled in the Canadian Army as a reservist in January 2020, the spokesperson said.

Fernando has not been deployed on a CAF operation, whereas Moreau served on Operation Laser in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Both soldiers were removed from military duties after their arrests, and their access to military equipment, facilities and bases was restricted, the defence spokesperson said.

They remain members of the military pending the outcome of an administrative review, a formal process used to assess matters that May affect a member’s continued service while providing procedural fairness.

Fernando was also charged with multiple firearms-related offences, including unauthorized possession of a prohibited device, possession of property obtained by crime and careless storage of ammunition, a police spokesperson told Global News on Oct. 6.
Fernando and Moreau are members of the 7th Toronto Regiment, a spokesperson for the Department of National Defence told Global News last week.
Moreau enrolled in the Canadian Army as a reservist in March 2018 and Fernando enrolled in the Canadian Army as a reservist in January 2020, the spokesperson said.
Fernando has not been deployed on a CAF operation, whereas Moreau served on Operation Laser in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Both soldiers were removed from military duties after their arrests, and their access to military equipment, facilities and bases was restricted, the defence spokesperson said.

They remain members of the military pending the outcome of an administrative review, a formal process used to assess matters that May affect a member’s continued service while providing procedural fairness.

stories.title: Cross-border visits by Canadian and U.S. residents up from last year: StatCan
stories.summary: Statistics Canada says more Canadians and Americans have travelled across the border between the two countries over the last six months compared to last year.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Statistics Canada says more Canadians and Americans have travelled across the border between the two countries over the last six months compared to last year.

The agency says Canadian residents made 1.9 million return trips from the United States last month by automobile and by air, up 6.8 per cent compared to September 2025.

Statistics Canada says the spike marks the sixth consecutive month of year-over-year growth of visits to the U.S. by Canadian residents.

StatCan says trips by Canadian residents to the U.S. last month remain 31.1 per cent lower than in September 2024 despite the rise compared to the same month last year.

It says U.S. residents’ visits to Canada also increased by 17.2 per cent last month compared to the same month last year totaling 1.8 million trips.

The agency says the spike is the eighth consecutive month of year-over-year increase of travel of U.S. residents to Canada.

The rise in cross-border travel comes amidst an ongoing trade war between the two countries that saw U.S. President Donald Trump introduce outright bans on imports of certain Canadian goods last month including most Canadian-made booze, dairy byproducts and some motorcycles.

The bans marked the latest escalation of the trade war as the Trump administration seeks to pressure Canada into trade concessions after Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended trade talks in August.

Both countries accused each other of adding eleventh-hour changes to the agreement. U.S. tariffs hit $28 billion in Canadian goods the next day, followed by Canadian retaliatory tariffs on Sept. 8.

MIDDLESEX COUNTY(October 14,2026):Middlesex County was pleased to welcome three high school students from across the County as “Warden for a Day” on October 13, 2026. The initiative offered an engaging, hands-on opportunity for local students to experience municipal government in action and learn about the important role County Council plays in supporting Middlesex communities.

As part of the experience, students Katherine Legg, Kaevan Cormier, and Iver Clark joined Warden Sue Clarke for a full day of leadership and learning at the County Administration Building.

The day’s agenda will included a mock swearing-in ceremony, meetings with County staff, and a guided tour of the building, including the historic Middlesex County Gaol. Students also participated in job shadowing sessions with various departments including Forestry and Natural Heritage, Library Services, and the Middlesex-London Paramedic Service.

Later in the day, students sat down with Warden Clarke and County Councillors to discuss the challenges and rewards of municipal leadership and watched an official Middlesex County Council meeting. This provided students with a behind-the-scenes look at how decisions are made that shape services and support residents across the County.

The County of Middlesex extends its thanks to the participating students for their enthusiasm, thoughtful engagement, and interest in local government throughout the day.

“Spending time with young people always leaves me optimistic about the future of our communities,” said Warden Sue Clarke. “Programs like Warden for a Day help students connect with local government and recognize the important role they can play in shaping Middlesex County’s future.

Middlesex Countyis an innovative,well-run organization offering high-value programs and services to the best community in which to live, visit, and do business in Southwestern Ontario.The County serves a vibrant, growing community of 81,700 people and offers a great place to call home,offering exceptional lifestyle,a wide variety of local attractions,and wonderful sense of community.

MEDIA CONTACT: Middlesex County Media Relations Legislative Services Division mediarelations@middlesex.ca

Middlesex County is a great place to call home. Our modern telecommunications infrastructure, excellent health and social services, retail shopping, recreation facilities, beautiful landscapes and great people, make Middlesex the place to be!

stories.title: Statistics Canada reports building permits up $1.1B in August at $13.6B
stories.summary: Ottawa — Statistics Canada says the total value of building permits issued in Canada in August rose $1.1 billion month-over-month to $13.6 billion, boosted by strength in the residential sector.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Statistics Canada says the total value of building permits issued in Canada in August rose $1.1 billion month-over-month to $13.6 billion, boosted by strength in the residential sector.

The agency says construction intentions for the homebuilding sector rose $1.1 billion to $8.5 billion in August.

The increase came as permits for multi-unit buildings rose to $5.8 billion, while the total value of permits for single-family homes edged down to $2.6 billion.

The value of non-residential building permits edged lower by $29.8 million to $5.1 billion in August.

The move came as plans for commercial construction fell $380 million to $2.2 billion, offset in part by a $317.3-million gain in the industrial sector which totalled $1.1 billion.

The institutional building component rose $32.9 million to $1.8 billion.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Why Canada’s caregivers say their retirement plans are being ‘decimated’
stories.summary: Canada’s caregivers are feeling the squeeze financially, a new report by financial firm Edward Jones has found, with many stopping or pausing savings.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
When Tracy Slaney imagined her life after retirement, she says she pictured travelling the world with her husband. But like many caregivers in Canada, the cost of looking after her loved ones means she had to put her plans on hold.

“Those retirement plans that I once had are gone. They are decimated,” she said.

In 2014, she became a caregiver for her father after he was diagnosed with terminal cancer. Within days of his passing, her mother received a dementia diagnosis. Slaney then stepped into a caregiver role for her until she died in 2019.

On Valentine’s Day 2020, she found her husband had been diagnosed with stage four colorectal cancer. She spent most of her time, energy and finances caring for him, until he passed away in April this year.

“I’ve been caregiving for 12 years, back-to-back,” she said.

Canada’s caregivers are feeling the squeeze financially, a new report by financial firm Edward Jones has found. More than seven in 10 of Canadians who care for loved over the age of 65 are also financial caregivers, spending thousands of dollars on the care.

These caregivers say they “May reduce or stop their savings or tap into their non-retirement savings,” the report says.

“They May also reduce retirement contributions, and some even borrow from or draw on their retirement accounts,” it adds.

More than nine in 10 said they’re spending their own money, out of pocket, to care for their loved ones, said Tracey McLennan, a director and financial planner at Edward Jones and a caregiver.

“Even more compelling is about 83 per cent of them are telling us that they have at least one impact on their lifestyle. They’re either moving, they’re relocating those that they’re caring for, they are changing their own expenses, they’re impacting their lifestyle,” she said.

More than half (54 per cent) of caregivers surveyed said are “sandwiched” between two generations, meaning they have children they are supporting in addition to caring for another loved one.

Most often (63 per cent of the time), the recipient of the care is a parent. But they can also be grandparents (10 per cent), spouses (nine per cent), parents-in-law (nine per cent) or a friend, sibling or other relative (nine per cent).

In cases when the recipient of the care cannot reimburse the caregiver, they end up spending an average of $10,190 a year.

Even with health insurance, the costs add up, Slaney said.

“There were drugs that were not covered, even with an insurance plan. There were medical supplies that were not covered. There’s travel cost. We had to have a care support worker at times when I couldn’t be there. That is expensive,” she said.

Slaney was 38 when her father was diagnosed with cancer and the decade that followed saw her pass up promotions, miss time at work and spend time with her loved ones who needed care.

“I was in the prime of my career at that point,” she said.

“We’ve lost basically everything. We had two cars, we had the savings, we had everything. Unfortunately, no one is prepared for that type of scenario – to go down to one income, as well as take time off work myself,” Slaney added.

Canadians who take time off work to care for loved ones “get punished twice” for it, said Liv Mendelsohn, CEO of the Canadian Centre for Caregiving Excellence.

“You get punished for leaving the workforce, you miss out on advancement, but you get punish come time to collect your CPP (Canada Pension Plan) because you haven’t paid in at the full capacity that you would have,” she said.

Slaney has felt the cascading effects of the financial loss.

“Over the course of the last six years, we have lost over $100,000 in earnings, savings, RRSPs. Everything is gone in the caregiving journey,” she said.

Those who are caring for younger family members between the ages of 18 to 64 have to be caregivers for much longer, McLennan said.

“They are more likely to put in their own financial resources and it is much more likely, to impact their health physically,” she said.

Caregivers are also ageing as they spend money, time and energy caring for someone else. The average age of the caregiver is 49, with the average caregiving tenure lasting seven years, the Edward Jones report said.

This is typically the age when many Canadians hit their peak earning years, and when financial experts say when you should be saving aggressively. For many, this is also when they have to ramp up spending on sending their kids to college.

According to the Canadian Centre for Caregiving Excellence, one in five caregivers is already over the age of 65.

“We’re seeing more and more caregivers who themselves are one fall or one hospital visit away from needing care,” Mendelsohn said.

“If mom is looking after dad and mom has a fall, then their children, if they have children, are immediately thrust into a double caregiving role.”

The “sandwich generation” is turning into a “club sandwich” in Canada, said Laura Tamblyn Watts, CEO of the nonprofit advocacy group CanAge.

“We don’t just have a sandwich generation anymore. We’ve got a club sandwich,” she said.

“Someone who is 90 might be receiving care from someone who’s 68 and still working full-time. While the 68-year-old next door is receiving care from younger family members,” Watts added.

Nearly half (49 per cent) of caregivers surveyed for Edward Jones found that their own health was being negatively affected as they cut back on expenses for their own medical care.

Money is a hard subject to talk about when a loved one is dealing with a debilitating illness, Mendelsohn said.

“People feel terrible guilt when they’re making those choices between putting food on the table for their family and caring for dad in the way that they want to,” she said.

But getting past the initial awkwardness can help in the long term, McLennan said.

“There’s certain taboo topics that we were told don’t talk about around the dinner table. We don’t about death. We don’t talk about money,” she said.

Asking your parents about how they want to age and making sure you speak with your siblings about responsibilities ahead of time can help, she said.

“We have to have a conversation about roles. We know from this study that typically, caregiving falls on one individual, and quite frequently it falls on a female in the family,” McLennan said.

Having a caregiving role thrust on you doesn’t have to mean your plans have to be abandoned entirely, McLennan said.

“It doesn’t mean giving up all your plans, but it May mean amending them,” she said, adding that this could include working with a financial planner to figure out what your trade-offs could be and how can keep squirreling money away into your Rrsp.

Once Slaney retires from her government job in five years, she won’t have her husband by her side. But she hopes to still travel with her two children.

When asked what her top three bucket list destinations are, she doesn’t miss a beat when she says, “Hawaii. Hawaii. Hawaii.”

“That was on my husband’s bucket list, and we are going to fulfill that wish,” she says.

stories.title: Dessert Club is an ode to artist Diane Borsato’s favourite global sweets
stories.summary: The artist’s new book is part taxonomy of desserts and their origin stories and part memoir
stories.author: Dakshana Bascaramurty
stories.content:
Diane Borsato’s eyes dance as she surveys the colourful palette of offerings at Booza Emessa, a Syrian ice cream shop on Halifax’s Bedford Highway, contemplating how the three scoops she’ll select will complement one another. For the Toronto-based visual artist and art professor, looks are as important as taste.

Borsato ultimately chooses a darker-than-charcoal black vanilla, a pastel-toned blood orange and creamy white mastic, adorned with chopped pistachios. Traditional booza is stretchier and melts more slowly than North American ice cream, thanks to the mastic, or tree resin, used in its preparation and a style of churning that involves pounding with a wooden pestle.

On the ice cream shop’s patio, she admires the medley before scooping up some of the mastic (which, in the context of booza , is the basic, classic flavour), with her spoon.

“You know, these are aesthetic experiences, too. They’re like edible sculptures,” she says.

Borsato brings that artistic lens to her new book, Dessert Club , a genre-defying ode to her favourite global sweets. It’s part taxonomy of desserts and their origin stories – complete with whimsical illustrations by artist Kelsey Oseid – and part memoir, highlighting her notable first experiences with the dishes in question.

On a visit to Nova Scotia this past summer, she joined me for a dessert crawl through Bedford, a suburb of Halifax, where we savoured some of the treats she pays tribute to in her book.

We chose Bedford for a reason: It’s a part of Halifax that has grown rapidly in recent years and an influx of immigrants have opened up dozens of eateries in the area, making it one of the most exciting places in the city to eat. Within the radius of a few kilometres, one can sample Singaporean, Syrian, Lebanese, Korean, Japanese, Filipino, Indian, Vietnamese and Turkish cuisine.

Borsato credits her own adventurous palate in part to growing up in Mississauga, where many of her classmates were newcomers or the children of newcomers. She’s found the suburbs a reliable place to start when in search of new desserts to try.

“Regions rich in immigrants are rich in delicious, interesting flavours and food traditions,” she says. And she’s observed that when immigrant groups butt up against each other, their cuisines naturally hybridize, giving way to things like tiramisu mochi doughnuts or ube lamingtons.

We find the latter at Tinàpe, a Filipino bakery on the ground floor of an apartment complex in West Bedford, and Borsato is in awe. She’s never before seen this riff on lamingtons, the Australian butter cakes typically coated in chocolate and shredded coconut.

Here, the coating of the cakes is tinted violet from ube, the purple yam used in many Filipino desserts. We pick up a package of those, as well as slices of ube mamon , layers of chiffon cake with just a few millimetres of buttercream holding them together. The cake’s crumb is an airy cloud and the cream tastes like whipped salted butter, only lightly sweetened.

“These are so delicious,” she gushes approvingly after a few bites.

It was in the homes of her childhood friends from the Philippines that Borsato first sampled ube-flavoured desserts. From then on, she’s approached the unfamiliar things on dessert menus or behind pastry cases with curiosity.

In her early 20s, she tried Taiwanese bubble tea for the first time, which was “a revelation.” A stint living in Japan not only influenced her art, but also her palate, introducing her to delights such as matcha parfaits and kakigori , a shaved-ice dessert. Borsato now makes itineraries for travels to international cities based around desserts she’d like to try. And in the past several years, she’s created a bond with her son, Felix, based largely on their shared sweet tooth.

Early on during pandemic lockdown, both mother and son were frustrated by online school. At one point, Borsato said, “We don’t have to do all that. We can just bake all day.” And so they did, conquering all manner of pastries. Her son now looks back on lockdown with nostalgia, she says.

“He was making beautiful things, and we were having nice moments, and we weren’t rattled with tension.”

Once restrictions lifted, the two started going on dates all over the Greater Toronto Area to sample desserts: from Palestinian kunafa made with stretchy Nabulsi cheese imported from the West Bank to the crispy rolled Mexican crepes filled with caramel and condensed milk called marquesita . Their lockdown kitchen experiments helped them develop a deeper appreciation for what they were eating: the technical skill, the time and the care that had gone into making these confections.

Their dessert excursions have given them a chance to taste the world but also experience molecular gastronomy and sample rare ingredients in a relatively affordable way.

“You can have an exquisite thing and it’s still cheaper than a cocktail in Toronto or eating dinner out,” Borsato says. “It’s like a nice little sample of something extraordinary, something that might be the best in the world. But it’s still under $20.”

Now a teenager, Felix often communicates with his mother through Instagram DMs – he’ll send a post about a strawberry tart with “impossibly perfect slices of strawberries in a geometric spiral,” or a new neighbourhood café making the Hong Kong-style fruit soups filled with pearls of sago and coconut milk he knows his mother adores.

It was through Instagram that I learned that an Indian grocer on Bedford Highway called Brampton Cash and Carry served one of the desserts Borsato was interested in sampling on our crawl: royal falooda . Tucked at the back, past all the aisles stocked with prepackaged masalas, stainless steel cookware and hefty sacks of basmati rice, there was a massive display of mithai (Indian sweets) and a wall-mounted digital menu advertising snacks and drinks.

When presented with the royal falooda , Borsato eyed it with disappointment. The versions she’d had in the past were as much a feast for the eyes as the tongue: a tall sundae glass filled with a rainbow of colours from sweet syrups, creamy ice cream, chopped nuts and chewy jellies, basil seeds and vermicelli. This one was less of a showstopper, served in a beige takeout bowl with muted colours and a small amount of toppings.

Ever the art professor, she headed back to the counter and asked if they could add more garnish, make it look more pleasing to the eye. After a minute, the falooda was returned to her, now with more crimson rose syrup, chopped nuts and shimmering edible silver leaf. The ratios still seemed off, but this was an improvement.

Borsato picked up a fork, winding the syrup-slicked vermicelli around it like one would with strands of spaghetti. With great optimism, she took a few bites and then set her fork down. “I want to save space to taste other things,” she said diplomatically. As she’s learned through a lifetime of dessert exploration, not every dish is a winner, and that’s okay.

We get back in the car and start driving to our next stop, an infinite number of delicious possibilities on the road ahead.
paragraphs: Diane Borsato’s eyes dance as she surveys the colourful palette of offerings at Booza Emessa, a Syrian ice cream shop on Halifax’s Bedford Highway, contemplating how the three scoops she’ll select will complement one another. For the Toronto-based visual artist and art professor, looks are as important as taste.

Borsato ultimately chooses a darker-than-charcoal black vanilla, a pastel-toned blood orange and creamy white mastic, adorned with chopped pistachios. Traditional booza is stretchier and melts more slowly than North American ice cream, thanks to the mastic, or tree resin, used in its preparation and a style of churning that involves pounding with a wooden pestle.
On the ice cream shop’s patio, she admires the medley before scooping up some of the mastic (which, in the context of booza , is the basic, classic flavour), with her spoon.
“You know, these are aesthetic experiences, too. They’re like edible sculptures,” she says.

Borsato brings that artistic lens to her new book, Dessert Club , a genre-defying ode to her favourite global sweets. It’s part taxonomy of desserts and their origin stories – complete with whimsical illustrations by artist Kelsey Oseid – and part memoir, highlighting her notable first experiences with the dishes in question.
On a visit to Nova Scotia this past summer, she joined me for a dessert crawl through Bedford, a suburb of Halifax, where we savoured some of the treats she pays tribute to in her book.

We chose Bedford for a reason: It’s a part of Halifax that has grown rapidly in recent years and an influx of immigrants have opened up dozens of eateries in the area, making it one of the most exciting places in the city to eat. Within the radius of a few kilometres, one can sample Singaporean, Syrian, Lebanese, Korean, Japanese, Filipino, Indian, Vietnamese and Turkish cuisine.

Borsato credits her own adventurous palate in part to growing up in Mississauga, where many of her classmates were newcomers or the children of newcomers. She’s found the suburbs a reliable place to start when in search of new desserts to try.

“Regions rich in immigrants are rich in delicious, interesting flavours and food traditions,” she says. And she’s observed that when immigrant groups butt up against each other, their cuisines naturally hybridize, giving way to things like tiramisu mochi doughnuts or ube lamingtons.

We find the latter at Tinàpe, a Filipino bakery on the ground floor of an apartment complex in West Bedford, and Borsato is in awe. She’s never before seen this riff on lamingtons, the Australian butter cakes typically coated in chocolate and shredded coconut.

Here, the coating of the cakes is tinted violet from ube, the purple yam used in many Filipino desserts. We pick up a package of those, as well as slices of ube mamon , layers of chiffon cake with just a few millimetres of buttercream holding them together. The cake’s crumb is an airy cloud and the cream tastes like whipped salted butter, only lightly sweetened.
“These are so delicious,” she gushes approvingly after a few bites.

It was in the homes of her childhood friends from the Philippines that Borsato first sampled ube-flavoured desserts. From then on, she’s approached the unfamiliar things on dessert menus or behind pastry cases with curiosity.

In her early 20s, she tried Taiwanese bubble tea for the first time, which was “a revelation.” A stint living in Japan not only influenced her art, but also her palate, introducing her to delights such as matcha parfaits and kakigori , a shaved-ice dessert. Borsato now makes itineraries for travels to international cities based around desserts she’d like to try. And in the past several years, she’s created a bond with her son, Felix, based largely on their shared sweet tooth.

Early on during pandemic lockdown, both mother and son were frustrated by online school. At one point, Borsato said, “We don’t have to do all that. We can just bake all day.” And so they did, conquering all manner of pastries. Her son now looks back on lockdown with nostalgia, she says.
“He was making beautiful things, and we were having nice moments, and we weren’t rattled with tension.”

Once restrictions lifted, the two started going on dates all over the Greater Toronto Area to sample desserts: from Palestinian kunafa made with stretchy Nabulsi cheese imported from the West Bank to the crispy rolled Mexican crepes filled with caramel and condensed milk called marquesita . Their lockdown kitchen experiments helped them develop a deeper appreciation for what they were eating: the technical skill, the time and the care that had gone into making these confections.
Their dessert excursions have given them a chance to taste the world but also experience molecular gastronomy and sample rare ingredients in a relatively affordable way.

“You can have an exquisite thing and it’s still cheaper than a cocktail in Toronto or eating dinner out,” Borsato says. “It’s like a nice little sample of something extraordinary, something that might be the best in the world. But it’s still under $20.”

Now a teenager, Felix often communicates with his mother through Instagram DMs – he’ll send a post about a strawberry tart with “impossibly perfect slices of strawberries in a geometric spiral,” or a new neighbourhood café making the Hong Kong-style fruit soups filled with pearls of sago and coconut milk he knows his mother adores.

stories.title: In the aftermath of the Okanagan wildfire, winemakers are harvesting grapes with caution
stories.summary: Wineries are working with local labs to measure the various chemical markers of smoke taint in their grapes
stories.author: Christopher Waters
stories.content:
Richard Charnock, the winemaker at JoieFarm in the Okanagan, relies on laboratory analysis to determine the sugar, acidity and pH levels of the grapes he uses to produce wine. After the Bald Range wildfire in August, this is the first time he is also consulting data to identify potential risks to the fruit from smoke exposure.

Exposure to smoke is a significant issue for vineyards, especially fresh smoke, as it contains high concentrations of volatile compounds that grapes absorb quickly through their skin. Vineyards located farther away from the burn are seen to have reduced risk, however.

Charnock explains that severe risk of smoke taint, which can give wine an undesirable smoky or ashy taste, begins when concentrations of smoke-derived compounds exceed 20 parts per billion (ppb). One of their chardonnay samples from a vineyard in northern Oliver measured 189 ppb.

“We are going to make wine from the grapes we grow. We’ve already spent the money so we will use this as an opportunity to benchmark smoke exposure and see how it shows up in the bottle,” Charnock says. JoieFarm will be sharing its data with other British Columbia wineries as the industry works toward creating a predictive system for the future.

Wineries in the Okanagan are working with local labs to measure the various chemical markers of smoke taint in their grapes. Charnock says JoieFarm sent between 15 and 20 samples to Frind Lab Services at a cost of $170 a sample. In the past, the winery relied on ETS Laboratories in California for smoke taint monitoring, but their samples cannot be sent to the United States for testing because of the current trade war.

“They were denied at the border and sent back,” he says.

Meanwhile, JoieFarm and many other wineries working with grapes grown near Summerland, B.C., have adjusted their winemaking practices as a precaution. White and rosé wines are at less risk than red wine because smoke-derived phenols are more concentrated in the skin of the grapes. Reducing or eliminating contact between the pressed juice and the grape skins minimizes the risk of smoke taint in the finished wine.

Charnock explains that the majority of JoieFarm’s production is centred on its popular rosé and an aromatic white wine called a Noble Blend. The 2026 vintage will also see an increase in pinot gris production, from 200 to 1,300 cases. He intends to bottle these 2026 white wines in January and release them quickly. Smoke taint can take time to emerge in the bottle. Ideally, JoieFarm’s 2026 inventory will be sold for immediate consumption.

“The good thing so far is that all of our ferments smell amazing,” he says. “We are obsessively looking for off aromatics, and there’s nothing right now.”

Some wineries have rejected grapes or decided not to produce certain varieties or styles of wine this year. The bumper wine harvest of 2025 will help wineries to meet demand, particularly for red wines, until next year’s harvest.

According to Gavin Miller, owner of Upper Bench Estate Winery in Naramata, who has been making wine in the Okanagan since 2004, the overall effect of the smoke will vary case by case, vineyard by vineyard. He wonders if having the lab results has made some winemakers too risk averse.

“We have tasted a lot of the grapes. We have done trial ferments and we’re not finding anything,” he says. “We have been through this so many times and have never had to dump grapes before.”

Miller worries that mixed messages can cause confusion for consumers who are left with questions when some wineries announce they won’t make wine because of a wildfire, while others will. “There are different motives and different reasoning at work for each winery,” he says. “Smoke shouldn’t define this year.”

Researchers around the world are working to improve their understanding of smoke taint, including how different factors affect its presence and perception, and how growers and wineries can reduce its impact.

Unfortunately, there’s not always a remedy available.

At Ruby Blues Winery, one of the few British Columbia wineries that doesn’t charge a tasting fee, owner Prudence Mahrer says most of their harvest has been deemed unsuitable for winemaking because of prolonged exposure to smoke and ash. The decision to drop the fruit means that winemaker Graham Pierce will harvest less than 10 per cent of the anticipated crop from the property. “It’s not a nice story, but it’s our choice,” explains Mahrer, who founded Ruby Blues in 2007 after selling Red Rooster, which was one of the first Naramata-based wineries to open in 1997.

Harvest continues in many regions in the Okanagan with many red wine varieties still hanging in southern vineyards. A complete assessment of the 2026 harvest will become clearer in the weeks ahead.

According to Gavin Miller, owner of Upper Bench Estate Winery in Naramata, who has been making wine in the Okanagan since 2004, the overall effect of the smoke will vary case by case, vineyard by vineyard. He wonders if having the lab results has made some winemakers too risk averse.
“We have tasted a lot of the grapes. We have done trial ferments and we’re not finding anything,” he says. “We have been through this so many times and have never had to dump grapes before.”

Miller worries that mixed messages can cause confusion for consumers who are left with questions when some wineries announce they won’t make wine because of a wildfire, while others will. “There are different motives and different reasoning at work for each winery,” he says. “Smoke shouldn’t define this year.”

Researchers around the world are working to improve their understanding of smoke taint, including how different factors affect its presence and perception, and how growers and wineries can reduce its impact.
Unfortunately, there’s not always a remedy available.

At Ruby Blues Winery, one of the few British Columbia wineries that doesn’t charge a tasting fee, owner Prudence Mahrer says most of their harvest has been deemed unsuitable for winemaking because of prolonged exposure to smoke and ash. The decision to drop the fruit means that winemaker Graham Pierce will harvest less than 10 per cent of the anticipated crop from the property. “It’s not a nice story, but it’s our choice,” explains Mahrer, who founded Ruby Blues in 2007 after selling Red Rooster, which was one of the first Naramata-based wineries to open in 1997.

stories.title: Neurologist to continue testifying at inquest into Toronto woman’s fatal balcony fall
stories.summary: A neurologist who examined Regis Korchinski-Paquet's records after her death is set to continue testifying Wednesday at a coroner's inquest.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A neurologist who examined Regis Korchinski-Paquet’s records after her death is set to continue testifying Wednesday at a coroner’s inquest.

Dr. Julien Hébert is the first witness to be called at the inquest, which comes more than six years after Korchinski-Paquet fell to her death from a Toronto balcony while police were in her home.

Hébert said Tuesday that in the years preceding her death, Korchinski-Paquet on several occasions showed symptoms in keeping with postictal delirium or postictal psychosis, both mental states that can occur after seizures.

The inquest heard Korchinski-Paquet had a long history of seizures from epilepsy, often followed by confusion, aggressive behaviour and temporary amnesia.

She had two seizures the morning of the day she died.

The inquest was announced earlier this year and is slated to last 14 days, with 13 witnesses expected to take the stand.

Korchinski-Paquet’s mother, father and brother have been named as potential witnesses, as have five of the six police officers who attended the scene.

stories.title: Ottawa investing $50 million in high-tech forestry centre in New Brunswick
stories.summary: Fredericton - The federal government says it plans to invest $50 million in a proposed digital forestry centre in New Brunswick.
stories.author: Eli Ridder The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Fredericton - The federal government says it plans to spend $50 million on a proposed digital platform that will help New Brunswick’s forestry industry cut costs and increase its wood supply.

Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson made the announcement Wednesday, saying the proposed Strategic Innovation Centre in Digital Forestry will, among other things, produce a digital replica of the province’s forests.

By creating a virtual model of forest ecosystems, foresters will be able to experiment with ideas before taking action in the physical world, Hodgson told a news conference in Fredericton.

For example,he said it could be used to simulate harvesting regimes and reforestation plans, as well as testing wildfire management plans.

“Being able to do those all in a digital world first saves an immense amount of money and actually teaches you how to manage the forest better,” Hodgson said.

The centre is also expected to offer centralized dispatching to streamline log transportation and reduce empty truck miles.

Provincial Natural Resources Minister John Herron said it would function like an “Uber in the forest” to improve logistics.

The proposed $86-million centre is a collaboration between the Northern Hardwood Research Institute and Research New Brunswick, which asked for federal funding earlier this year.

Ottawa’s contribution is conditional on project approval, the Natural Resources Department said. The rest of the money will largely come from the provincial government, according to Herron.

Gaetan Pelletier, executive director of the Northern Hardwood Research Institute, said the centre could help the industry reduce costs by about $25 million annually in New Brunswick.

Pelletier said that using more technology in the forestry sector won’t result in layoffs. Instead, he said it will create more jobs as the sector diversifies.

“I’m honestly a firm believer that this will create the most interesting jobs in the forest sector,” he said.

The forestry industry is a mainstay in New Brunswick.

It contributes about $1.5 billion annually to the province’s economy, according to provincial government figures. It supports about 9,700 direct jobs and another 14,100 spinoff jobs.

Last month, however, the owners of an aging pulp mill in Nackawic, N.B., announced it would temporarily shut down on Nov. 4, resulting in hundreds of layoffs.

Later the same day, that bad news was somewhat offset by an announcement from Crown-owned electric utility NB Power, which confirmed it had signed agreements with domestic suppliers to buy forestry byproducts to feed a power plant that will eventually stop burning coal.

Meanwhile, Canada’s $22-billion forestry industry, which supports about 200,000 jobs, has been pummeled by tightening supply, increased operational costs, low pulp prices and ongoing tariffs placed on Canadian wood products exported to the United States.

Hodgson confirmed Wednesday the federal Liberal government will announce its planned national forestry sector strategy when it tables a new budget next month.

“The strategy will acknowledge that the future of our forestry sector will not be defined simply by our resources — it will be defined how intelligently we use them,” he said.

A spokesperson for Natural Resources Canada confirmed the plan will include billions of dollars in funding, but didn’t provide specifics.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Canadian Armed Forces race to expand drone capabilities
stories.summary: As drone-fuelled warfare rages on half a world away in Ukraine, the Canadian Army’s program for rapidly acquiring basic drones is just ramping up.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — As drone-fuelled warfare rages on half a world away in Ukraine, the Canadian Army’s program for rapidly acquiring basic drones is just ramping up.

And the pressure is on for the Canadian Armed Forces to speed up its adoption of drones as the technology changes the nature of modern warfare.

Lt.-Col. Jonathan Penney is a reservist who previously worked in defence manufacturing and now co-ordinates the forces’ Minerva drone program. He said that while the army feels pressure to pick up the pace, it’s focused both on finding the right mix of tech for its current needs and on building up the domestic drone industry.

“The army is really good at adapting and evolving,” he said in an interview with The Canadian Press.

The Minerva program launched a batch of tenders in recent months for a range of new drones — everything from low-cost Arctic surveillance drones for the Canadian Rangers to ground and aerial drones that can conduct cargo supply runs.

“We are figuring out what ‘right’ looks like,” Penney said. “Instead of just jumping in, buying a whole bunch of things that we don’t need, we buy things that can use today and then let the system evolve so that it’s integrated in how we conduct operations.”

The Minerva program operates unlike a typical procurement, which sees the military draft a list of requirements.

Instead, Minerva launches what it calls “industry challenges” — ongoing projects which task companies with creating prototypes for specific uses. Army personnel will be testing those prototypes until roughly next summer or fall.

Another item the army is currently searching for is a low-cost targeting drone — an aerial spotter that allows artillery crews to hit targets they can’t see.

As Russia tests Nato allies in Europe with repeated drone incursions, Canada’s military is looking for ways to counter the emerging threat.

stories.title: Record $90M Lotto Max jackpot up for grabs Friday, largest lottery prize in Canadian history
stories.summary: The jackpot rolled over after Tuesday night's Lotto Max draw went unclaimed, allowing the prize pool to continue growing ahead of Friday.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
Canadians will have a chance to play for the largest lottery prize ever offered in the country this week, with a record-breaking $90 million Lotto Max jackpot available in Friday night’s draw.

The historic jackpot surpasses the previous Canadian lottery record of $85 million and could result in the biggest lottery win in the country’s history if a single ticket matches all winning numbers.

In addition to the $90 million jackpot, an OLG spokesperson says lottery players will also be competing for an estimated 18 Maxmillions prizes worth $1 million each and 90 Maxplus prizes valued at $100,000 each. Combined, the top prizes available in Friday’s draw are expected to total $117 million.

The jackpot rolled over after Tuesday night’s Lotto Max draw went unclaimed, allowing the prize pool to continue growing ahead of Friday’s draw.

While no one claimed the grand prize Tuesday, several winning tickets were sold across Ontario.

Two Maxmillions tickets worth $1 million each were sold in Whitby and Hamilton, the OLG says, while a pair of shared Maxmillions prizes worth $500,000 each were also sold in Toronto and Mississauga.

Twelve Maxplus prizes valued at $100,000 each were sold across the province, including winning tickets in Middlesex County, Kitchener, the Kenora-Rainy River region, Kingston, Whitby, Oakville, Thornhill, North York, Willowdale, two locations in Toronto and one sold through OLG.CA.

Ontario also produced two second-prize Lotto Max tickets worth $81,541.10 each, with winning tickets sold in York Region and Willowdale.

Three Encore prizes worth $100,000 each were sold in Stouffville, Ajax and through OLG.CA.

stories.title: Buildings with impact hit the screen at Toronto’s Architecture and Design Film Festival
stories.summary: This year’s festival, which takes place from Nov. 4 to Nov. 7 at the Tiff Lightbox, will screen 11 films, including one about the CN Tower
stories.author: Dave LeBlanc
stories.content:
Love it or hate it, RuPaul’s Drag Race has become a major cultural touchstone, elevating the once-underground art form of drag to heights filmmaker John Waters or the minds behind The Rocky Horror Picture Show never dreamed possible. And that riot of colour, over-the-top costumes, sass and silliness was, during the pandemic (and still is), exactly the right dose of dopamine many of us needed to carry on.

Googie is the drag of the architecture world. It’s colourful, it wears a costume that amplifies and exaggerates Modernism, there is sass aplenty, and the pleasure it generates is addictive. And, like drag, everyone with an open mind is invited to the party.

“Googie is a chapter in the story of modern architecture as important as any other,” confirms California-based architecture critic Alan Hess just before the credits roll to close Jake Gorst’s new film, Googie . “Good architecture is good architecture. . . Googie architecture is a democratic architecture; it is meant to improve the lives of the average person going about their daily life.”

The film is one of 11 being screened at this year’s Architecture and Design Film Festival (Adff), which takes place from Nov. 4 to Nov. 7 at the Tiff Lightbox in Toronto.

“Do not ignore Googie,” adds humorist/historian Charles Phoenix. “Googie is important, Googie has a place in the scheme of all architectural styles.”

They’re right. But what place? Well, as the film suggests, it’s not downtown, although the Los Angeles restaurant that gave the style its name, Googie’s (John Lautner, 1949), was located on a rather dense patch of Sunset Boulevard about a block away from the Chateau Marmont. It’s some time after neon signs decamped from shop windows to become flashing beacons that could be spotted from the freeway. It’s when the buildings themselves, using unorthodox shapes, became lantern-like flycatchers (well, people-catchers) as prominent as the signage, perhaps more so. And it could not have been born anywhere but California in the 1950s and 60s – although it did spread. It died by the time of the moon landing and Richard Nixon.

To set the stage, the 58-minute film discusses the postwar suburban expansion and how plentiful jobs meant the explosion of automobile ownership. But, since international travel was still a luxury, most folks took pleasure drives in their own regions . . . and they needed to stop and eat. Or bowl. Or get the car washed.

Googie’s predecessors, says the film, were the circular drive-ins and diners of the 1930s, the programmatic architecture of the 1940s, such as the hotdog-shaped Tail o’ the Pup, or the early-1950s experiments with novelty signage, such as Randy’s Donuts giant rooftop doughnut. These, says Mr. Hess, created the “perfect storm of elements to create Googie.”

By the time Googie-masters Louis Armét and Eldon Davis brought the style to its zenith, flamboyant and buoyant roofs became floating sculpture with no apparent support, expanses of glass were so large potential customers could see inside long before entering, and materials were so futuristic (Formica, vinyl, plastic, steel) a feeling of optimism was transmitted instantly (although, with the use of fieldstone in many, there was a Flintstones meets The Jetsons element).

It was, says Mr. Hess, “a whole new type of building.”

“It’s like an event you don’t forget,” says Mr. Phoenix. “You go to a Googie restaurant, and it created an impression.”

The Canadian National Tower, as it was rising in the early-1970s, created a deep impression on Torontonians. How could it not? Opening Mark Myer’s 90-minute film, The Tower That Built a City , architect John Andrews says that while it was built “primarily . . . as a communications device,” it quickly took on a “much more significant role” that “could be likened to the Sydney Opera House in that it’s serving not only the function for which it was built but it’s become a very definite symbol of the city.”

Tracking backward from Toronto’s snatching of Montreal’s crown to become Canada’s largest city – right around the same time the CN Tower opened in 1976 – to the 1960s and the city’s proposal for “Metro Centre,” which had an early, three-antennaed version of the tower as part of a large development of office towers (81 hectares), the film asks a very important question: “Who exactly designed the tower?”

The answer, however, has more than three prongs. There was the Australian, John Andrews, of course, and then there was Webb Zerafa Menkes Housden (Wzmh), but there were also architects Roger Du Toit and Ned Baldwin, and engineers such as Nicolet Carrier Dressel, Jamir Mardukhi and Dr. Franz Knoll. Dr. Knoll, the film posits, is to be credited with the joining of the three independent legs into one sculptural, graceful shape.

After describing the construction of the landmark – “Olga” the helicopter is a highlight – the film zooms forward to spend the next 45 minutes considering the city’s coming-of-age vis-a-vis sports (the Blue Jays arrived a year after the tower opened), theatre, television (Moses Znaimer says it’s “up there with the Eiffel Tower and the other great erections of the world”), multiculturalism and music (specifically, the pioneering work of Cfny, Q107 and MuchMusic).

While the CN Tower itself didn’t bring about those attitudes, it did act as an enormous, concrete push-pin: We are here. We are doing great things. We May be a little bit shy, but come and have a look.

And a half-century later, the city’s inferiority complex has finally evaporated: “It’s an interesting place to be,” finishes music video director Director X (Julien Christian Lutz). “It is a kid that didn’t think they were cool but then realized maybe they’re cool.”

Adff: Toronto runs from Nov. 4 to 7 at the Tiff Lightbox (350 King St. W.). Tickets available through the website: adfilmfest.com/adff-toronto My drag persona, Irma Girdle, will be on hand to discuss Googie after the screening on Saturday, Nov. 7. along with the Toronto Society of Architects.

content_blocks.text: They’re right. But what place? Well, as the film suggests, it’s not downtown, although the Los Angeles restaurant that gave the style its name, Googie’s (John Lautner, 1949), was located on a rather dense patch of Sunset Boulevard about a block away from the Chateau Marmont. It’s some time after neon signs decamped from shop windows to become flashing beacons that could be spotted from the freeway. It’s when the buildings themselves, using unorthodox shapes, became lantern-like flycatchers (well, people-catchers) as prominent as the signage, perhaps more so. And it could not have been born anywhere but California in the 1950s and 60s – although it did spread. It died by the time of the moon landing and Richard Nixon.

content_blocks.text: The Canadian National Tower, as it was rising in the early-1970s, created a deep impression on Torontonians. How could it not? Opening Mark Myer’s 90-minute film, The Tower That Built a City , architect John Andrews says that while it was built “primarily . . . as a communications device,” it quickly took on a “much more significant role” that “could be likened to the Sydney Opera House in that it’s serving not only the function for which it was built but it’s become a very definite symbol of the city.”

content_blocks.text: The answer, however, has more than three prongs. Dr. Knoll, the film posits, is to be credited with the joining of the three independent legs into one sculptural, graceful shape.

stories.title: Price set below $500,000 accelerates Etobicoke condo sale
stories.summary: The 485-square-foot condo faced plenty of competition from other one-bedroom units on the market
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
30 Shore Breeze Dr., No. 2019, Toronto

Asking price: $499,900 (August, 2026)

Selling price: $450,000 (August, 2026)

Previous selling price: $302,997 (June, 2020)

Taxes: $2,417 (2026)

Days on the market: 15

Listing agent: Luke Dalinda, Royal LePage Real Estate Services Ltd.

This summer, this 485-square-foot condo faced plenty of competition from other one-bedroom units for sale in the same two-tower complex known as Eau du Soleil, and in adjacent buildings overlooking Humber Bay Shores Park. The best strategy, according to agent Luke Dalinda, was setting an asking price below $500,000.

“Inventory was really high with about 50 one-bedroom units in the area,” said Mr. Dalinda.

“At the time, there were a lot in the $500,000 to $550,000 range.”

The alluring price, coupled with unobstructed views southwest, brought 16 visitors over two weeks in August. One buyer presented an offer, which the seller accepted, of $450,000.

“This property, while small at only 485 square feet, had really nice water views,” Mr. Dalinda said.

“When units are priced to today’s reality, buyers will show up.”

This roughly six-year-old unit has one bedroom and a living room, both with sliding doors to a southwest-facing balcony.

There is a dining area and an L-shaped kitchen with quartz countertops, plus a three-piece bathroom and a closet for stacked laundry machines.

The unit has a storage locker and one parking spot. Monthly fees of $515 cover heating and concierge. There are guest suites, a gym, a saltwater pool, a hot tub, a theatre and terraces on the seventh floor.

“It’s definitely one of the popular buildings with a lot of amenities,” Mr. Dalinda said.

“There’s a very large gym complex, outdoor barbecues, indoor party rooms and meeting rooms.”
