Toronto star illustration using photos from X and Dreamstime[](http://www.thestar.com/news/morning-digest/a-policing-dynasty-meets-project-south/article_1de09df2-6027-4d6b-9419-1b378aca3c2f.html)

ByPaige Oldfield Digital producer

Good morning. This is the Wednesday, Oct. 14 edition of First Up, the Star’s daily morning digest. Sign up to get it earlier each day, in your inbox.

With less than two weeks to election day, a new poll shows an already tight mayoral race could hinge on voter turnout in all corners of the city. Edward Keenan is off till Thursday but joins us briefly today to write about the matter of the two very different Chows listed on the ballot in the race for mayor of Toronto. More on that below.

Three generations of the Madeley family have worked for the Toronto Police Service: grandfather, father and son, each named John Madeley. But a shadow was cast on that policing legacy after two of them were charged in Project South, a sprawling investigation into allegations of police corruption. The middle John, a retired officer, was arrested for allegedly improperly using a police database and was accused of working with an alleged loan shark. Weeks later, his constable son Madeley Jr. was arrested and charged with unlawful computer searches and breach of trust. Lawyers for the pair declined to comment.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

How a former actress turned private eye ended up in the crosshairs of the Project South police corruption probe.

She hasn’t been charged. But the Project South allegations have branded her with a “scarlet letter.”

Watch: We untangle the web of alleged connections between accused crime figures and Toronto police officers.

“All options are on the table”: Ottawa could sue Stelco at any time over the up to 500 layoffs it has planned in Hamilton.

Shareholders for Roots, the decades-old Canadian brand best known for its comfy sweatpants, have approved a deal to take it private under U.S. ownership, with a Canadian operating partner.

This nail salon chain owes more than $50,000 in unpaid wages to nine workers. Immigration and work reporter Ghada Alsharif spoke with the employees and the salon owners.

Cycling advocates want to take the fight to save key downtown bike lanesto the Supreme Court of Canada. The Ford government began removing them on Bloor Street Tuesday and were temporarily thwarted by protests.

A record 222,550 Torontonians cast early ballots, marking the highest advance voting turnout in more than 10 years.

David Miller: Brad Bradford is promising to fix a water problem that doesn’t exist. His “solution” is bad news for all Torontonians.

Six years after Regis Korchinski-Paquet fell to her death during a police call, a coroner’s inquest examines whether her history of epilepsy and seizures played a role.

Toronto police have arrested and charged a 29-year-old man with arson after Israeli flags were burned near a North York church on Oct. 7.

With just days left before Albertans decide on whether to set the path for provincial secession, separatist campaign groups are not preparing to quit.

ICYMI: In his Thanksgiving video Monday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada is “worth fighting for.”

When Mayor Olivia Chow came out of the voting booth last week, she made a startling admission: she almost voted for someone else. “I just noticed there is two ‘Chow’ on the ballot, and there is one before me,” she said.

That’s when many people would have learned for the first time that a man named Braeden Chow is also running for mayor. Alongside dozens of other people, which is part of what might make this a problem: the ballot is very long and formed into a grid crowded with names. Scanning the names, it is very easy to see how the boldface Chow listed eighth, the Chow listed ninth and the Choy listed tenth could lead to some confusion. You have to squint a bit at the fainter first names listed way over on the opposite side of the column to be sure who is who.

Olivia Chow’s campaign is now engaged in a public message push to alert people to the possible confusion. With polls tightening, there’s some fear miscast ballots could wind up being decisive. It would certainly seem like a travesty if that wound up being the case.

The Star’s Elissa Mendes spoke with Braeden Chow about his previously under-the-radar campaign. He denied that he was encouraged to run by the current mayor’s opponents. “I did this for a love of the game,” he said. “I have real plans, and I think it’s time for a change in the city.”

As a reader named Chris said in the comments, “The guy’s allowed to use his own name. It’s up to voters to show due diligence and double-check before voting.” Certainly, most of us would agree. But Chris points at another problem some would think is evident on that ballot: “I’m more concerned about these dozens of candidates for the same job in some elections. The elections people need to put a reasonable upper limit and have criteria to weed out nuisance candidates.”

This is a sentiment you hear — that perhaps the required monetary deposit or minimum number of signatures needed to register should be higher, to discourage fringe candidates (including any whose motive for running might be mischievous). But that strategy limits access to running for office to those with more resources. I’ve heard plenty of objections to that over the years.

I wonder if there isn’t a way the ballot could be designed to be less confusing. Something as simple as putting the first and last names closer together. Or changing the spacing between the names.

What do you think? Do you have a suggestion to make the long ballot less confusing? Do you think it’s a problem that so many people are able to run no-hope campaigns? Or do you think all’s fair in love and elections, and it’s up to voters to avoid confusion themselves? Let us know in the comments section here.

— Edward Keenan, host of First Up

SUSAN DELACOURT:Chrystia Freeland’s book is a plea to all those dealing with Donald Trump to be the bad cop.

ADAM RADWANSKI:Mark Carney says he might ramp up immigration again. We need to see his plan first.

MARTIN REGG COHN:Doug Ford is at the middle of an actual scandal, but this isn’t it.

Pigeon racing involves champion birds fetching high prices. As Mark Colley reports, the sport is “dying.” Can these Ontarians save it from extinction?

John Green talks with us about his first adult novel, “Hollywood, Ending,” centered on two young actors navigating sudden fame after starring in an Andy Warhol biopic.

Basketball: Kawhi Leonard took to an NBA court in a Toronto uniform again Tuesday night and it was nothing but good.

Hockey: The Maple Leafs couldn’t outscore their many flaws on display in a 5-4 loss to the Utah Mammoth on Tuesday.

In the Star’s recent profile on Toronto-Centre, city hall bureau chief Ben Spurr spoke with residents about how homelessness and public safety concerns are shaping up the race to become councillor there. There was a lot of discussion on what harm reduction actually does:

“The very term ‘harm reduction’ says it all, if the only way we can help these people is to stop them from killing themselves, I would argue we’re not doing a good enough job.” — Peter

Others pointed out the need to do more to solve the housing issue:

“We need to look at why they lost their housing in the first place to find out the best way to help them be successfully housed now.” — Susan

stories.title: Janice Kennedy: It’s tricky being a patriotic Canadian right now — no matter where in Canada you’re from
stories.summary: Quebec’s recent election rings alarm bells, and the whole country is watching Alberta.
stories.author: Janice Kennedy
stories.content:
With all the raised voices and slamming doors, our family seems pretty troubled these days, doesn’t it? It’s tough to be an impassioned Canadian in this best-of-times/worst-of-times moment.

On the one hand, Canadian pride has never been fiercer. Collectively, there’s an energizing determination to fight the trade war every way possible, from buying Canadian (or at least not American) to vacationing here or anyplace except you-know-where. Across the country, the maple leaf is ubiquitous.

On the global stage, we get to bask in the spotlight as Prime Minister Mark Carney earns standing ovations, Anne Carson wins the Nobel Prize in Literature and half the American population apologizes to us for the bozo eruptions of their idiot-in-chief.

Furthermore, like most of the rest of the world, we appreciate knowing what we’re not: a nation in love with guns, the death penalty and live-streamed executions by firing squad.

Being Canadian feels good — until you start hearing those raised voices and slamming doors inside the house.

There’s the unity worry. Quebec’s recent election, returning the separatist Parti Québécois to power , rings alarm bells. And next Monday, the whole country will be watching Alberta .

Eight days remain in the campaign in which Albertans will decide whether to set their province on the path to secession.

As if that weren’t enough, news reports lately are peppered with stories of Canadian far-right extremists, white nationalists, antisemites and Islamophobes, the whole vile bunch of them spreading their gospel of hatred as far and wide as they can. A new anti-immigration group based in Ottawa wants to enforce mass deportations to “reclaim our homeland.”

It’s all disgusting, of course, and cause for concern — but it’s no reason for a nervous breakdown. Hatemongers have always been with us, carbuncles that need to be treated with each eruption. But they’re nasty, not terminal.

A dose of perspective also goes down well for national-unity anguish. Take Quebec, where PQ leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has already deferred his promised separation referendum until after the U.S. president is gone. Polls show an overwhelming lack of enthusiasm for a referendum generally, reflected in the fact that the PQ’s minority government is built on an unprecedentedly low 28 per cent of the vote. Current polls on Quebec separation itself hover around the same number, hardly a ringing endorsement.

There are, of course, pundits who just won’t let go of the scary breakup scenario, hanging on to it like a dog with a juicy bone. But the less dramatic reality is far more comforting.

It’s more comforting with Alberta, too. Polls there suggest an overwhelming number of “No” votes next Monday to holding a separation referendum, because there are clearly as many proud Canadians in Alberta as anywhere else in this country. But the malcontents — a branch plant of Maga Inc., which has thrown them its support — will keep at it. Like the Quebec minority, they’ll try to wear everybody out with their relentless complaining. Instead of suggesting solutions to perceived irritants, separatists seem to prefer sloganeering and kvetching.

They won’t win, but they do threaten the hopes of the rest of the country for nation-building, strengthening our defences and reaching out to other nations for new alliances and investment. Divisive chatter from within only plants seeds of doubt in potential allies and investors. What would be welcome right now from the loudmouths? A little silence.

But let’s cheer up. Most Canadians — including in Alberta and Quebec — are not whiners, racists, malcontents, or tiresome troublemakers. Our glass is a lot more than half-full.

Apart from having a prime minister with smarts and more energy than a Duracell warehouse, we have a large resilient economy, a highly educated population, vast natural resources and an enviable international reputation. We are, by any measure, blessed.

No, we’re not perfect, but as Governor General Louise Arbour noted, “We have a remarkable capacity to pause, to examine our failures and to learn from them.” Examining our past, we’re continually moving forward to correct mistakes, right wrongs, heal injustices.

In short, we have reason to take heart. Despite headwinds, we’re still strong and free. We’re still the same diverse, boisterous, decent jumble of people we’ve always been, squabbling and celebrating. We’re still one big family.

Our noisy old house always seems to need fixing. But we’ll see to it, because it’s where we live. This is our family home.

Polls show an overwhelming lack of enthusiasm for a referendum generally, reflected in the fact that the PQ’s minority government is built on an unprecedentedly low 28 per cent of the vote. Current polls on Quebec separation itself hover around the same number, hardly a ringing endorsement.

Instead of suggesting solutions to perceived irritants, separatists seem to prefer sloganeering and kvetching.

stories.title: Farm Boy, Smart Life and L’Ancêtre organic cheeses recalled due to listeria risk
stories.summary: The Canadian Food Inspection Agency said test results prompted a national recall for a dozen cheeses. No illnesses have been reported.
stories.author: Megan Mills Devoe
stories.content:
Twelve types of organic cheeses with the Farm Boy, Smart Life and L’Ancêtre brands are being recalled across Canada due to possible listeria contamination.

The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (Cifa) issued the recall Thursday , warning that the cheeses May be contaminated with Listeria monocytogenes, a bacteria which can cause illness, and in some cases, death.

stories.title: Knights survive comeback, defeat Rangers in shootout

stories.content:
The London Knights ended their first losing streak of the season with a 4-3 win over the Kitchener Rangers Tuesday night.

The Knights were perfect in the shootout though, with Marcus Nordmark and Thomas Zocco finding the back of the net on their two attempts. Both of the Rangers’ shooters failed to score on Knights goaltender, Aleksei Medvedev, who made 25 saves in the win.

stories.title: Steven Galloway accuses UBC of making up excuses to fire him to protect it’s reputation
stories.summary: Author says university gave him list of reasons for his dismissal, but apart from extramarital affair, those reasons remain secret
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
Bestselling author Steven Galloway accused the administration of the University of British Columbia of making up excuses to fire him in order to protect the school’s reputation after a former student accused him of sexual assault and harassment.

Mr. Galloway told the B.C. Supreme Court Tuesday that the university’s administration provided him with a “laundry list” of reasons for his dismissal in 2016, but apart from the extramarital affair with the student in his creative-writing program, those reasons remain secret.

His lawyers won a pre-trial motion this summer to keep the majority of his termination letter confidential, but Justice Neena Sharma is expected to weigh in Wednesday on a new motion by the counsel for the defendants to gain access to the redacted rationale for his firing.

During the second week of the defamation trial Mr. Galloway has been pursuing for eight years, the former chair of Ubc’s creative-writing program testified under cross-examination that the allegations, levelled by the woman in November, 2015, were false and asserted his June, 2016, termination was under the auspices of the post-secondary institution trumping up other instances of his misconduct.

“You’re living in a world where UBC is an honourable, respectful, rule-following organization and you’re attempting to get me to engage with you as though that’s the case,” Mr. Galloway told Arden Beddoes, lead counsel for the woman known as A.B. due to a publication ban.

“I believe they’re about as corrupt an institution as you’re likely to find and whatever rules that exist, they’re likely to make them up as they go.”

Thandi Fletcher, a spokesperson for UBC, issued a statement Tuesday evening saying the school has “well-established, mature policies” to deal with allegations of sexual misconduct, but noted it could not comment on Mr. Galloway’s testimony because of privacy obligations and the fact that it is not a party in the trial.

A B.C. Supreme Court judge began hearing Mr. Galloway’s defamation trial last week against A.B. and three others. More than a dozen people originally named in his lawsuit have settled, including two UBC professors.

Mr. Galloway acknowledged in court that a former judge hired by UBC to investigate A.B.’s claims found he had sexually harassed her and found other instances of misconduct leading to his firing. The court has heard the former judge did not find that he sexually assaulted the woman.

Ubc’s announcement of a formal investigation of “serious allegations” involving Mr. Galloway in 2015 led to an online firestorm over Mr. Galloway’s right to due process versus the rights of his alleged victim.

UBC fired Mr. Galloway in 2016 without severance, but two years later, an arbitrator awarded him more than $220,000 in two separate awards for violating his privacy during the process of suspending and dismissing him.

He was never charged with a crime and in 2018 he launched his defamation suit, arguing the defendants repeated claims online that he had sexually assaulted a student.

On Tuesday, Mr. Beddoes showed the court a copy of Mr. Galloway’s termination letter and noted that the second, third, fourth and fifth pages were entirely redacted after Mr. Galloway’s lawyers secured an order this summer to keep the letter secret. Mr. Galloway’s lawyers argued the letter was unrelated to the core allegations of sexual assault levelled by A.B.

Mr. Galloway conceded that he violated school policy and some of his conduct was “unprofessional, unethical,” and did not meet his standards or that of a UBC faculty member. But, he testified, he shouldn’t have been fired for his actions.

“Insofar as I was made aware at this time, there had been two tenured faculty members terminated in the recent decade: myself and the guy who stole millions of dollars from a First Nations dental clinic,” he testified.

Lawyers for the defendants have argued Justice Sharma should allow Mr. Galloway’s termination letter to be made public so he can be cross-examined about his actions.

Justice Sharma reserved her decision. She is also expected to rule this week on a Globe and Mail application to get access to an exhibit detailing A.B.’s draft negligence lawsuit against UBC for up to $3-million , which was brought up in court last week.

On Friday, Mr. Galloway testified there was no official prohibition on sexual relationships between students and faculty, and that he knows of “numerous instances” of similar relationships in the university’s faculty of arts.

He testified that “absent A.B.’s sex assault allegations nobody had any reason to think negatively” about him.

Mr. Beddoes and counsel for two of the other three defendants argued Tuesday that’s not the case.

stories.title: Former Alberta premiers argue against separation as referendum vote approaches
stories.summary: Rachel Notley shared a stage with her long-time political foe, Jason Kenney, to form a unified front on Tuesday
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Four of Alberta ’s former premiers are setting aside their partisan differences in the final week leading up to next Monday’s high-stakes provincial referendum.

Former Alberta NDP premier Rachel Notley on Tuesday shared a stage with her long-time political foe, former United Conservative premier Jason Kenney, to form a unified front against the threat of separatism.

“Whatever frustrations we May have, whatever imperfections our country May have, we still have one of the greatest countries in the world,” Mr. Kenney, seated next to Ms. Notley, said at a Canadian Chamber of Commerce event in Edmonton.

Ms. Notley also joined former Progressive Conservative premiers Ed Stelmach and Alison Redford in writing an op-ed, expected to be published this week, imploring Albertans to reject Premier Danielle Smith ’s five referendum proposals centred on immigration, which could strip some newcomers of access to public health care and education. The op-ed does not explicitly address the question of separation but calls on Albertans to “choose Canada.”

“When you’re in a position of power – when you’ve been elected to lead a province – you learn that your job is to govern in the best interests of the majority of Albertans,” Ms. Notley said in an interview with The Globe and Mail.

“We know that new Canadians have always contributed to our province. That is part of the formula of our province’s success.”

Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi is encouraging Albertans to head to the polls as 311 polling stations opened Tuesday for the first of five days of advanced voting for the Oct. 19 referendum.

The Canadian Press

Lines of people snaked out of schools and churches on Tuesday as advance voting began in Alberta’s referendum, with residents weighing in on 10 questions centred on provincial separation, immigration and constitutional issues.

The tenth of those questions, which asks voters to pick between remaining in Canada or working toward a second, binding separation referendum, is what’s drawing the country’s political brass to Alberta this week.

Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed on Tuesday that he’ll appear at pro-Canada rallies in Calgary and Edmonton on Thursday and Friday, while Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre plans to give a speech in the province and appear at a gathering of conservatives later this week in Calgary.

Separatist factions, meanwhile, are organizing a Saturday rally at the Alberta legislature while trying to activate hundreds of thousands of supporters they’ve identified at town halls and online over the past several years.

It joins two active threats to Canadian sovereignty: one to the east, with the recent election of a minority separatist government in Quebec, and the other to the south, with U.S. President Donald Trump’s continuing tariff war and musings about annexation.

“Compassion, I don’t think, is measured by which political party you belong to,” he told The Globe in a phone interview.

“If our message is that we are xenophobic internal finger-pointers, then people are going to say, ‘Yeah, no thanks. That’s not where I’m raising my family,’ ” she said.

Ms. Notley said she disagrees with the premise that Alberta needs leverage to deal with Ottawa.

“This idea that you have to do this simplistic saber-rattling thing as a means of practicing federal-provincial advocacy is incorrect and, quite frankly, I don’t think that our case has been helped particularly by it.”

“This is just the beginning of the independence movement gaining more attention,” Mr. Stelmach said.

stories.title: Seniors not allowed home following apartment fire
stories.summary: As many as 67 seniors still are allowed home, following a fire at a Bruce County run housing complex in Kincardine.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
As many as 67 seniors still are allowed home, following a fire at a Bruce County run housing complex in Kincardine.

No one was injured during Friday’s fire at the Cedar Grove Apartments at 915 Huron Terrace in Kincardine, but everyone living in the 68 unit senior’s complex had to be evacuated.

Bruce County says they’ve found temporary housing for all the tenants, while restoration work is completed.

There is no reported timetable for the seniors to return home.

Several restoration companies, and contractors were at the housing complex on Tuesday working on getting the building ready for occupancy.

stories.title: London tech company gets federal funding for AI diagnostics software
stories.summary: From use in ambulances and hospitals, to use in the field by military personnel. New AI software developed in London, Ont. is helping make medical diagnoses easier and quicker.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
From use in ambulances and hospitals, to use in the field by military personnel. New AI software developed in London, Ont. is helping make medical diagnoses easier and quicker.

“Do I have a life-threatening condition, do I have a cough, or do I have pneumonia? These kinds of questions come up every day for people,” explained Dr. Rob Arntfield, CEO of London based medical software company, Deep Breathe.

The company is on the receiving end of $1 million from the federal government’s Regional Artificial Intelligence Initiative. Deep Breathe has developed AI assisted diagnostic ultrasound technology.

“Our software now sits in this medical hardware that turns it into something user-friendly that an almost novice can use, whether you’re someone in the military, somebody in an ambulance, somebody in a hospital, when you need answers quickly, ultrasound that’s fast, that’s portable. And now you don’t need to know how to use it quite as much because the software enables it,” said Arntfield.

The way it works is, an ultrasound probe used on a person is attached to a smart phone, providing answers to its user. London MPs Arielle Kayabaga and Peter Fragiskatos had a chance to try their hand at the new tech at a funding announcement Tuesday.

“Think of men and women of the armed forces serving on the frontlines. If they’re injured, is it a collapsed lung, or is it something else? This technology can help. Think about a senior, who, a chest x-ray would not pick up some abnormalities in the lung. The technology here, which is an ultrasound technology, that picks up things that wouldn’t be evident to the naked eye,” said Fragiskatos.

The funding is part of a $700 million federal initiative to strengthen AI capabilities and sovereignty.

“It’s especially encouraging to see companies like Deep Breathe continue to grow and advance its work, demonstrating what can happen when innovative ideas can match with determination and expertise,” said Kayabaga.

The new tech is in the advanced prototype stage. Arntfield says the funding will be used for Health Canada regulatory approvals, and to attract new talent.

The federal government says it is making an additional $500 million available over five years to help Canadian businesses adopt artificial intelligence technologies and bring Canadian-developed AI products to market.

Federal officials said support will be focused primarily on sectors where Canada has established expertise and growth potential, including health and life sciences, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, manufacturing and robotics. Regional agencies will also have flexibility to support other local economic priorities.

The government said the expanded program will also help Canadian AI companies attract investment, secure customers and commercialize homegrown technologies. Funding will also be available to organizations that provide businesses with specialized expertise and support related to AI adoption and commercialization.

The federal government also said the investment is intended to encourage broader AI adoption across Canada, help domestic AI firms grow while remaining based in Canada, and support economic growth and productivity.

Funding will also be available to organizations that provide businesses with specialized expertise and support related to AI adoption and commercialization.

The federal government also said the investment is intended to encourage broader AI adoption across Canada, help domestic AI firms grow while remaining based in Canada, and support economic growth and productivity.

stories.title: Cycling advocates rally, petition Supreme Court to rule on Toronto bike-lane removal
stories.summary: Cyclists gather along Bloor Street West to hold night-long protest against removal of bike lanes
stories.author: Patrick White
stories.content:
On a normal Wednesday afternoon, Adam Rodgers loads his five-year-old daughter onto the rear seat of his Tern cargo bike, and together they rattle along Toronto’s pockmarked bike lanes to her swimming lessons.

This Wednesday, they’re bracing for a far bumpier ride – one section of those bike lanes along Bloor Street West could be gone.

“I don’t even know how we’re getting there,” he said. “It’s frustrating.”

The barrier is bigger than any pothole. A small strip of their 15-minute journey has become so mired in legal and political wrangling that, ON Tuesday, the province vowed to start removing it by day’s end and cycling advocates asked the country’s highest court to intervene. All this lands just two weeks before a mayoral election in Toronto between two front-runners who’ve staked out opposing bike-lane positions.

The formal motion to the Supreme Court of Canada – a request for leave to appeal – was made public at a press conference organized by Cycle Toronto, one of the applicants in the case, ON Tuesday morning. It asks the court to overturn an Ontario Court of Appeal decision that allowed Premier Doug Ford’s government to proceed with a 2024 law ordering the removal of bike lanes along Bloor Street, University Avenue and Yonge Street.

The Ford government is adamant that converting bike lanes back to car lanes will help reduce traffic, which it says costs the provincial economy $56-billion a year.

A lower-court judge had ruled that the removal posed a safety risk to cyclists, constituting a serious violation of Section 7 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms guaranteeing security of the person and right to life.

The appellate court declared that reasoning erroneous, stating that legislatures are free to regulate road use without implicating the Charter.

Cycling advocates want the Supreme Court to clarify the scope of Section 7 and whether it applies in this case. “The consequences of this case reach far beyond bike lanes,” Bronwyn Roe, a lawyer with Ecojustice, an environmental law charity representing the applicants, said at the press conference.

The Supreme Court generally takes several months to decide if it will hear an appeal – far too late to influence the Ford government’s immediate plans for the Bloor bike lane. It aimed to start removing a 1.2-kilometre section between Clissold Road and Royal York Road on Tuesday night.

“Following the ruling by the Ontario Court of Appeal, the province announced in September that it would immediately begin restoring motor vehicle lanes on Bloor Street West. That work begins Tuesday,” Dakota Brasier, spokesman for Ontario Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria, said in an e-mail.

By Tuesday afternoon, bike lane advocates were already massing to hold a night-long protest against the measures.

The push to build bike lanes on Bloor goes back to the 1970s, but only materialized in the 2010s. Road engineers and cycling advocates viewed it as an ideal east-west biking thoroughfare for its flatness and proximity to the Bloor subway. “It has always been seen as the holy grail of bike lanes,” said Albert Koehl, co-founder of Toronto Community Bikeways Coalition, who has been championing cycling infrastructure for nearly 20 years.

Throughout that time, he has encountered resistance from local businesses, who predict bike lanes will snarl traffic, reduce parking and lessen foot traffic. The Kingsway neighbourhood in Etobicoke showed that resistance when the city placed bike lanes there in 2023 and 2024, he said.

A group of Kingsway businesspeople have proved to be organized and influential in their opposition. Last year, 40 area businesses filed a lawsuit against the city over the bikes lanes, claiming $10-million in damages.

But few residents walking the Kingsway section of Bloor – where coffee shops, fruit stores and restaurants abound – felt strongly about the issue on Tuesday.

“I really don’t think the bike lanes makes a difference in the traffic levels,” said Pat Phillips, a 13-year resident of the neighbourhood. “I think they are fantastic.”

The resistance around Kingsway, she said, comes from the suburban nature of the neighbourhood. Most homes have driveways and two-car garages. They expect speedy drive times. Plus, she said, Mr. Ford is part of an Etobicoke political dynasty that has long fought against what he and his late brother, former mayor Rob Ford, called “the war on the car.”

John Rydzanicz, who’s lived in the area for 35 years, said he had mixed feelings. “I think we should make it safe for bikes, but the lanes have definitely slowed down traffic,” he said. “I don’t even bother leaving the house if it’s after 4 p.m.”

The City estimates that removing all the bike lanes covered by the provincial law will cost $48-million. Once the Kingsway work is done, the rest of the removals are slated to start in the spring.

The removal work is scheduled to take place in the middle of an intense mayoral campaign, where bike lanes have become a political bone of contention.

Under Mayor Olivia Chow, the city has tried to work with the province on plans to restore vehicle lanes while preserving bike lanes – to no avail.

Ms. Chow’s main challenger, Brad Bradford, has said he would take out the contested bike lanes in Etobicoke if elected.

Mr. Rodgers and his daughter just want a safe ride to swimming lessons. He’s contacted the province several times to ask how the route might change. So far, nobody has responded.

stories.title: Guilty plea in connection with Kelowna teen’s death
stories.summary: Brandon Kazakoff’s defence lawyer, Glenn Verdurmen, described the incident in court on Tuesday as “one horrendous, horrible mistake.”
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
A painful day in court for the family and friends of Tristan Seeger , a Kelowna teen who was fatally run down by a vehicle three years ago.

They packed a Kelowna courtroom Tuesday as the man responsible for the 15-year-old’s death, Brandon Kazakoff, pleaded guilty to dangerous driving causing death and assault.

The guilty pleas stem from an incident on Oct. 21, 2023.

“I’m glad he admitted what he did to my son, whether or not it’s remorseful or not, only he knows,” Tristan’s father, Jason Seeger, said.

Tristan’s mother, Paule Moore, said she wanted Kazakoff to face the family.

“He killed my son with a car. He didn’t even have the guts to look him in the eye, and he needed to look us in the eye,” she said.

Court heard that shortly before the fatal collision, Tristan was part of a group of teenagers involved in an incident in which Kazakoff’s father was bear-sprayed.

After learning about the incident, Kazakoff went looking for the group.

He eventually found the teenagers and assaulted one of them, according to the court proceedings.

Kazakoff then got back into his vehicle. While stopped at an intersection, Tristan deployed bear spray toward the passenger side of the car. Kazakoff turned the vehicle around and drove into the teenager.

He fled the scene. In the days that followed, Kazakoff changed his licence plates and set his vehicle on fire along a forest service road.

Kazakoff’s defence lawyer, Glenn Verdurmen, described the incident as “one horrendous, horrible mistake.”

Verdurmen said his client feels remorse for his actions and understands the impact the case has had on the community.

“It’s ripped up a lot of people in the Rutland and Kelowna area, and the hurt has gone deep, and that’s not lost on my client,” Verdurmen said. “He tells me that this is what he thinks about every day.”

For Tristan’s family, the guilty plea means they will not have to relive the painful details of the case through a trial. But they say no outcome in court can undo their loss.

Asked what justice would look like, Jason Seeger said for him, there isn’t any.

“Bring my son back, but we know that’s not going to happen,” he said, choking back tears.

Instead, the family is left holding on to memories of a teenager they remember for his laughter, charisma and adventurous spirit.

“His cheeky grin and his devil-May-care attitude and his willingness to just do anything,” Moore said. “I miss that stuff about him. You know, we miss him every day.”

Kazakoff is expected to be sentenced at a later date, likely in early 2027.

content_blocks.text: They packed a Kelowna courtroom Tuesday as the man responsible for the 15-year-old’s death, Brandon Kazakoff, pleaded guilty to dangerous driving causing death and assault.
content_blocks.html: They packed a Kelowna courtroom Tuesday as the man responsible for the 15-year-old’s death, Brandon Kazakoff, pleaded guilty to dangerous driving causing death and assault.

content_blocks.text: The guilty pleas stem from an incident on Oct. 21, 2023.
“I’m glad he admitted what he did to my son, whether or not it’s remorseful or not, only he knows,” Tristan’s father, Jason Seeger, said.
Tristan’s mother, Paule Moore, said she wanted Kazakoff to face the family.
“He killed my son with a car. He didn’t even have the guts to look him in the eye, and he needed to look us in the eye,” she said.
Court heard that shortly before the fatal collision, Tristan was part of a group of teenagers involved in an incident in which Kazakoff’s father was bear-sprayed.
After learning about the incident, Kazakoff went looking for the group.
He eventually found the teenagers and assaulted one of them, according to the court proceedings.

Kazakoff then got back into his vehicle. While stopped at an intersection, Tristan deployed bear spray toward the passenger side of the car. Kazakoff turned the vehicle around and drove into the teenager.
He fled the scene. In the days that followed, Kazakoff changed his licence plates and set his vehicle on fire along a forest service road.
Kazakoff’s defence lawyer, Glenn Verdurmen, described the incident as “one horrendous, horrible mistake.”
Verdurmen said his client feels remorse for his actions and understands the impact the case has had on the community.

“It’s ripped up a lot of people in the Rutland and Kelowna area, and the hurt has gone deep, and that’s not lost on my client,” Verdurmen said. “He tells me that this is what he thinks about every day.”

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Plasma drive in memory of Kelowna teen'

content_blocks.text: For Tristan’s family, the guilty plea means they will not have to relive the painful details of the case through a trial. But they say no outcome in court can undo their loss.
Asked what justice would look like, Jason Seeger said for him, there isn’t any.
“Bring my son back, but we know that’s not going to happen,” he said, choking back tears.
Instead, the family is left holding on to memories of a teenager they remember for his laughter, charisma and adventurous spirit.
“His cheeky grin and his devil-May-care attitude and his willingness to just do anything,” Moore said. “I miss that stuff about him. You know, we miss him every day.”
Kazakoff is expected to be sentenced at a later date, likely in early 2027.

stories.title: B.C. party leaders make economic pitch to business community ahead of election
stories.summary: Eby touted major projects and supports for job creation as opposition leaders took aim at NDP government’s economic record
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
British Columbia’s opposition party leaders took aim at the NDP government’s economic record on Tuesday, accusing it of failing to deliver prosperity despite years of spending, while NDP Leader David Eby pointed to a pipeline of major projects worth billions and unveiled new supports for job creation.

Mr. Eby, Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson and Green Leader Emily Lowan were speaking at an event hosted by the Greater Vancouver Board of Trade ahead of the Oct. 24 provincial election.

Each pitched their visions on how to spur economic growth: the Ndp’s public investment and government-led partnerships to advance major projects, the Conservatives’ emphasis on cutting taxes and red tape, and the Greens’ call to rethink B.C.’s reliance on natural resources as a driver of economic growth.

They spoke to a room of business leaders deeply concerned by the economic trajectory of the province. In her opening remarks, board president and chief executive officer Bridgitte Anderson cited a new member survey showing that 77 per cent believe the economy is on the wrong track, 95 per cent are concerned with the province’s fiscal outlook and 80 per cent lack confidence in the government’s economic strategy.

“At times like these, leadership and economic literacy matters,” Ms. Anderson said during her speech.

Acknowledging the economic challenges facing the province, Mr. Eby said his government has attracted major investments by speeding up permitting processes and working with the business sector and Indigenous communities. He pointed to $130-billion in major projects reaching final investment decisions in the next two years – half of which have already done so – and the province’s target of $200-billion in investment for major projects by 2035.

To encourage further investment, Mr. Eby pledged to make permanent B.C.’s Manufacturing Jobs Fund, which will support manufacturing companies with $60-million in annual funding for capital projects, expand food-processing opportunities across the Agricultural Land Reserve and build a new shipyard in the province in partnership with the federal government.

“The path forward for us as a province is to build,” Mr. Eby said. “British Columbia is in an unparalleled opportunity right now.”

After Mr. Eby’s remarks, Mr. Doerkson accused the NDP leader of spending heavily without delivering results, pointing to job losses, mill closures, delays in major liquified natural gas projects, the province’s projected $13.8-billion deficit and repeated credit downgrades.

He promised that a Conservative government would permanently repeal the planned provincial sales tax expansion on professional services that Mr. Eby said his government would pause “for the duration of the trade war.” A Conservative government would also establish a 120-day approval framework for major capital projects over $250-million, and cut red tape by passing a law requiring government to eliminate two existing regulations for every new one introduced, Mr. Doerkson said.

“If elected, we are going to move aggressively to put these measures in place and unleash the potential of B.C.,” he said. “We want to be the catalyst for this growth. But you will be the engine.”

Ms. Lowan accused successive governments of “pouring more money into the gaping pit of resource extraction” without ensuring such projects translate into prosperity for average British Columbians.

A Green government envisions resource communities being rebuilt with thousands of union jobs developing the green industry, while keeping more of the resulting wealth in the hands of the workers and communities that generate it, Ms. Lowan said. A tax on the ultra-wealthy would help fund public services, including universal child care, she added.

“It’s time to have a new debate, to ask who owns our economy, who’s profiting and who’s left carrying the bag,” Ms. Lowan said.

The board’s survey, released Tuesday, drew 351 responses from members, Ms. Anderson said.

The top issues were economic vision; attracting capital and major projects; affordability; crime and public safety; B.C.’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act; permitting, licensing and red tape; and debt and deficits.

Among other key findings, 76 per cent said B.C.’s housing situation is affecting their business, 85 per cent believe traffic and congestion patterns in the Lower Mainland have worsened in the past four years, and 66 per cent said they feel less safe in Greater Vancouver than they did five years ago.

On LNG, 87 per cent support expanding exports to global markets and 83 per cent support a new oil pipeline to B.C.’s southern coast.

stories.title: Transit troubles a key issue for Winnipeg voters as civic election looms
stories.summary: Since Winnipeg Transit's new routes, many Winnipeggers are feeling mixed about the new changes with some wanting to go back to how it was One Winnipegger plans to buy a car.
stories.author: Toni De Guzman
stories.content:
Fatima Bashir’s main way of getting around was the bus, but since the new changes, she plans to buy a car.

“Buying a car wasn’t even in my plan…but now they’re (buses) late and I’m walking more now,” said Bashir, at a bus shelter on Osborne Street.

The City of Winnipeg unveiled the largest change to its transit system on June 29, 2025. The system features a spine-and-feeder model, which is composed of rapid and express lines as the central Primary Transit Network that forms the spine.

Community and connector routes links riders to a main line, which is called a feeder route. The new system has around 4,000 bus stops from 5,200 before the changes.

Many Winnipeggers feel mixed about the city’s transit, with some saying they want to go back to the old transit system.

Bashir said she wants the old transit system back.

“It’s not nice…So many people are complaining about this new system. No one is happy about it,” she said.

Feasibility to switch to old transit

Mike Vogiatzakis, a mayoral candidate, pitched to change transit back within 30 days in office, at a news conference in August. Don Woodstock also pledged to “immediately cancel” the transit plan upon taking office but doesn’t mention how it will impact the current routes, according to his campaign website.

The city has spent around $20.4 million towards the implementation of the new network.

It would take “millions and millions of dollars to convert back to the old system,” said Janice Lukes, Public Works chair.

Lukes said the new grid-like transit routes are built to grow with Winnipeg’s growing population and size.

James Van Gerwen, president of the Amalgamated Transit Union Local 1505, said he doesn’t see any logic behind going back to a system that was broken.

Van Gerwen is calling for more buses and funding to support bus drivers to make transit better.

He and other advocates are also pushing for a different funding model which requires the province to step up funding for transit.

50-50 funding agreement

The 50-50 funding agreement is an operational bill for transit to be split between the province and the city. This model was scrapped 10 years ago, and provincial funding for transit has remained stagnant, according to the Climate Action Team Manitoba.

“We continue to increase support for municipalities year after year,” said a provincial spokesperson on behalf of Glen Simard, minister of Municipal and Northern Relations. The province did not address specific questions about the 50-50 funding model.

Functional Transit Winnipeg is advocating for more financial support from the province.

Kyle Owens, president of Functional Transit Winnipeg, said re-adopting the funding model means transit will be more reliable with frequent service and expansion of routes.

“Nostalgia is always popular in Winnipeg. It’s an easy way to get attention and get people engaged in transit to talk about the old system and the old routes, but Winnipeg Transit isn’t going back,” said Owens.

Lukes said next year the city plans on having the supporting infrastructure: benches and shelters installed to the new stops.

Around 40 new bus shelters will be installed by the end of 2026, and there are 84 shelters with polycarbonate glass panels throughout the city, according to a city spokesperson.

An Abacus Data poll (formerly Probe Research) shows around a quarter of Winnipeggers want safety and security needs to be addressed on buses.

Election day is October 28.

stories.title: Longtime London politician Irene Mathyssen dies at 75
stories.summary: Mathyssen was a former teacher who was first elected to Queen’s Park in 1990 as a member of Bob Rae’s New Democrats Party government.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Irene Mathyssen has died at the age of 75.

Irene was a former teacher who was first elected to Queen’s Park in 1990 as a member of Bob Rae’s New Democrats Party.

She later moved to federal politics, representing London-Fanshawe in the House of Commons.

Irene was elected as an MP in 2006 and re-elected in the next three federal elections.

Irene’s daughter, Lindsay Mathyssen said in a Facebook post , “To Londoners and Canadians, she was known for her public service, her dedication to her community, and her commitment to the people and causes she believed in.”

“Her legacy is not only in what she accomplished, but in the lives she touched and the strength she gave to those fortunate enough to know her,” said Lindsay.

“Your legacy of making this world a better place will live on.”

stories.title: ‘This little bit of perfection’: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk on seeing Earth from space
stories.summary: Kutryk says living in microgravity is like being a child again, as he relearns how to eat, move and sleep in space.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Mike Armstrong
stories.content:
Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk says his first two weeks aboard the International Space Station have been unforgettable as he adjusts to life in microgravity and begins research into the effects of long-term space travel on the human body.

“It’s one of the most amazing things I’ve ever seen,” Kutryk said of looking back at Earth from the station.

Growing up in northern Alberta, Kutryk was familiar with the northern lights, but he said seeing them from above offered an entirely different perspective.

“To see the whole Earth, the curvature of the Earth, just embraced by this blanket of dancing fluorescent oranges and yellows and pinks — magical,” he said.

Kutryk, 44, launched Oct. 1 as part of Nasa’s four-person Crew 13, arriving at the space station in just under eight hours.

The former CF-18 fighter pilot is serving as a mission specialist during the six-month mission, which will include scientific experiments, research and critical maintenance work.

“It is important for Canada to be here,” Kutryk said Tuesday while answering questions from Canadian journalists in Longueuil, Que.

“We take a lot of benefits from these missions and it’s something that we hope we can continue.”

Kutryk said the launch itself was exhilarating and spectacular, adding that no amount of training could fully prepare him for the experience.

“Everything about being here for the first couple weeks is very special,” he said.

“You just feel so lucky and fortunate to be living this experience.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "You just feel so lucky and fortunate to be living this experience."

But living in space also requires an adjustment. Kutryk said even routine tasks such as eating, sleeping and moving around can take practice in microgravity.

“You have to sort of learn to do everything again, almost like you’re a child,” he said. “How you eat, how you move around, how you sleep, how you fall asleep, what do you do with your neck when you’re sleeping, what do you do with your hands.”

Kutryk has already begun experiments, several of which are related to the physical challenges astronauts experience during extended periods in space. He said he has lost five pounds since arriving at the station.

“Humans on a six-month mission lose a lot of bone, a lot of muscle and come back to Earth, frankly, a lot older physiologically and not very healthy,” Kutryk said. “So it’s a big concern of ours.”

The mission includes Canadian-led studies examining how space travel and microgravity affect human health. During Tuesday’s orbital press conference, Kutryk was wearing equipment for the AstroFit research project, which monitors his health and is aimed at finding ways to allow humans to spend longer periods in space.

The space station is a long way from the Alberta cattle farm where Kutryk grew up, but a small piece of his family’s history is there with him.

A pocket watch his relatives brought with them when they immigrated to Canada from Ukraine four generations ago had been sent to the station ahead of him.

Kutryk said the watch sits near where he sleeps. Holding it makes him think about how much technology has changed over the past century and how his ancestors could never have imagined the journey he is now taking.

His own journey to space was a lifelong goal, and Kutryk said it was difficult to describe the first time he saw Earth from orbit.

“It’s just one world. It’s one thing hanging in the blackness of space and you don’t see all the countries and the problems and all the challenges,” he said.

“You just see this little bit of perfection that we should really, really be trying to protect.”

Kutryk’s mission comes in the same year Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen travelled aboard the Artemis II mission in April. The 10-day lunar fly-around marked humanity’s first journey to the moon in more than 50 years.

Kutryk said Canada’s presence aboard the space station demonstrates what the country can accomplish when it pursues ambitious goals and takes risks, while encouraging Canadian industry, academia and commercial interests to take part in space exploration.

“That’s how we innovate, that’s how we develop new technologies, that’s what we want to be doing,” he said.

–with files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canada’s Wonderland, La Ronde close roller-coasters after fatal accident at Six Flags in Georgia
stories.summary: Both Canada’s Wonderland and La Raonde has temporarily closed some of its roller-coasters after a man died and several others were injured in an incident at a Six Flags park near Atlanta.
stories.author: Heather Wright
stories.content:
Toronto – Canada’s Wonderland has temporarily closed two of its roller-coasters – the Behemoth and the Leviathan – after a man died and several others were injured in an incident at a Six Flags park near Atlanta.

La Ronde in Montreal has also temporarily closed its Goliath roller-coaster.

Officials have not yet said how the man died or how the others were injured, but witnesses say he came out of his seat during the ride.

“He turned sideways and he’s flipping in the air,” one woman told ABC News. “He comes down and slams into our cart. People reached out trying to grab him … and we couldn’t.”

While the investigation is in its early stages, experts say a focus will likely be on the lap bar. The Goliath uses a single “clamshell” restraint and does not have a secondary belt.

“When I think back to years gone by, a lot of coasters did have sort of a double-safety system,” said Doug Perovic, a forensic engineer and professor at the University of Toronto. “A lot of those have disappeared for the ride or excitement side of things, but also for the speed at which you can load and unload the passengers.”

Both the Leviathan and the Behemoth have backup lap belts, which were added to the rides after they were installed.

La Ronde marketing director Carole Bricault said its “Goliath” ride will also be closed indefinitely while crews “conduct a thorough safety review in collaboration with the ride’s manufacturer.”

“It will not reopen until this review is complete and we are fully satisfied that it can be operated safely,” Bricault said.

The Canadian Association of Amusement Operators (Caao) said accidents of this kind are rare in Canada, pointing to Ontario as having some of the highest safety standards in the world.

“If you can meet … the standard to operate safely here in Ontario, then you can meet the standard anywhere in the world,” said Andrew Gidaro, a director with the Caao.

In a statement to CTV News, the Technical Standards and Safety Authority (Tssa), Ontario’s public safety regulator, said amusement park rides must follow strict safety checks.

“In addition to obtaining the required design approvals, licenses and annual permits from Tssa, owners and operators must ensure that trained employees and certified mechanics conduct daily, weekly and monthly safety checks specific to each ride,” said Tssa spokesperson Gray Chan.

Perovic said officials will be reviewing the inspection logs at Six Flags Over Georgia as part of their investigation.

“The amusement ride world has very stringent, well-developed guidelines for inspection, maintenance,” he said. “And so … they’ll be checking into that because those inspections are all logged and recorded.”

Neither Canada’s Wonderland nor La Ronde have given a timeframe in terms of how long their rollercoasters will be closed.

stories.title: ‘Catastrophic’ brake failure led to Columbia Icefield rollover that killed 3 people
stories.summary: The Ice Explorer bus lost control on a road leading to the Athabasca Glacier in July 2020, tumbling about 50 metres down an embankment before coming to rest on its roof.
stories.author: Bill Graveland
stories.content:
A fatality inquiry report into a deadly tour bus rollover in Jasper National Park says it was the result of a “catastrophic” brake failure and neglected repairs.

The Ice Explorer bus lost control on a road leading to the Athabasca Glacier at the Columbia Icefield in July 2020, tumbling about 50 metres down an embankment before coming to rest on its roof.

Three people died and 14 others were seriously injured.

“In short the brakes suffered a catastrophic failure because they were worn, improperly inspected and concerns with respect to the brakes functioning were not attended to,” Justice Vaughn Myers wrote in his 13-page report.

The inquiry held a year ago, heard the driver of the bus complained the vehicle, which had air brakes, was not stopping quickly enough.

The report from the Alberta Court of Justice judge said the bus was in neutral when it stopped at the top of the hill and then reached speeds of nearly 50 kilometres an hour when it raced down.

The top speed for the Ice Explorer in 4th gear is limited to 14 kilometres an hour.

“There are two primary contributing factors. The first is the driver, for reasons unknown, negotiating the lateral moraine in neutral and without the six-wheel drive engaged,” he wrote.

“Unable to use engine power to slow the bus, the driver would have to rely on conventional braking. We know that the driver attempted to brake as a result of the sounds of the airbrakes. We can safely assume she applied the brakes because she said she did and it would be the natural human reaction to do so.”

Myers also noted that there is no requirement on the bus to have seatbelts and those who died were thrown out of the vehicles as it rolled down the embankment.

A fatality inquiry cannot assign blame but makes recommendations to prevent similar deaths.

Dionne Durocher, 24, of North Battleford, Sask., as well as Kamleshbai Patel, 58, and Griva Patel, 28, of Edmonton, died in the crash.

Myers made a number of recommendations, including that future inspection reports should be dated, as well as identify and detail what work was done during the inspections.

His report listed other contributing factors in the deaths due to the lack of seatbelts and the slope of the hill, which at 40 per cent is above the maximum grade specifications of 36 per cent set out by the manufacturer.

Brewster, also known as Pursuit, conducted its own internal investigation of the crash. The company added seatbelts to its buses and made changes to training for its drivers.

content_blocks.html: The Ice Explorer bus lost control on a road leading to the Athabasca Glacier at the Columbia Icefield in July 2020, tumbling about 50 metres down an embankment before coming to rest on its roof.

content_blocks.text: Three people died and 14 others were seriously injured.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Columbia Icefield bus crash survivor believes seatbelts could have saved girlfriend’s life'

content_blocks.text: “In short the brakes suffered a catastrophic failure because they were worn, improperly inspected and concerns with respect to the brakes functioning were not attended to,” Justice Vaughn Myers wrote in his 13-page report.
The inquiry held a year ago, heard the driver of the bus complained the vehicle, which had air brakes, was not stopping quickly enough.

content_blocks.alt: Left: Passengers inside the tour bus, and right, showing where it rolled-over on the Columbia Icefield near Jasper, Alta., Sunday, July 19, 2020.
content_blocks.caption: Left: Passengers inside the tour bus, and right, showing where it rolled-over on the Columbia Icefield near Jasper, Alta., Sunday, July 19, 2020. Courtesy: Vinay Patel and eff McIntosh, The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: The report from the Alberta Court of Justice judge said the bus was in neutral when it stopped at the top of the hill and then reached speeds of nearly 50 kilometres an hour when it raced down.
The top speed for the Ice Explorer in 4th gear is limited to 14 kilometres an hour.
“There are two primary contributing factors. The first is the driver, for reasons unknown, negotiating the lateral moraine in neutral and without the six-wheel drive engaged,” he wrote.

“Unable to use engine power to slow the bus, the driver would have to rely on conventional braking. We know that the driver attempted to brake as a result of the sounds of the airbrakes. We can safely assume she applied the brakes because she said she did and it would be the natural human reaction to do so.”

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Former drivers say Columbia Icefield tour buses frought with safety issues, poor maintenance'

content_blocks.text: Myers also noted that there is no requirement on the bus to have seatbelts and those who died were thrown out of the vehicles as it rolled down the embankment.
A fatality inquiry cannot assign blame but makes recommendations to prevent similar deaths.
Dionne Durocher, 24, of North Battleford, Sask., as well as Kamleshbai Patel, 58, and Griva Patel, 28, of Edmonton, died in the crash.
Myers made a number of recommendations, including that future inspection reports should be dated, as well as identify and detail what work was done during the inspections.

His report listed other contributing factors in the deaths due to the lack of seatbelts and the slope of the hill, which at 40 per cent is above the maximum grade specifications of 36 per cent set out by the manufacturer.
Brewster, also known as Pursuit, conducted its own internal investigation of the crash. The company added seatbelts to its buses and made changes to training for its drivers.

stories.title: Montreal announces new metro security measures, 5% service increase
stories.summary: Montreal is investing in more metro security, social workers and surveillance while planning a five-per-cent increase in service starting in 2027.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Phil Carpenter
stories.content:
The City of Montreal and its public transit agency are rolling out a series of measures aimed at improving safety in the metro network, including hiring more special constables, increasing surveillance and adding social workers.

The plan comes as transit advocates say many passengers continue to feel unsafe using the metro.

“We know that one rider on two doesn’t feel safe in the metro,” said Brian Nash of Trajectoire Québec.

Six measures are being introduced, including a $6.5-million investment to hire more special constables and $3 million to improve electronic surveillance. The city also plans to increase collaboration with Montreal police and add more social workers in the metro system.

Dimitrios Jim Beis, a member of Montreal’s executive committee, said more than 50 constables will be added by the end of 2027.

“We are clearly responding to the insecurity that folks are feeling,” Beis said.

Starting this fall, St. John Ambulance will help provide social workers, with two teams operating seven days a week during the winter and one team during the summer months.

Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada said the approach is intended to ensure different situations receive different responses.

“If you have a person that is in a homelessness situation, with a personal situation or a crisis, that doesn’t need to have the Spvm to come,” she said. “Maybe it’s the St. John Ambulance, the intervention of a social team that will come.”

Alongside the safety measures, city officials and the STM plan to increase metro service by five per cent as of 2027, with most of the additional service coming in the evenings.

“We see a lot more people having schedules outside of rush hour, so it is good news for them,” Nash said.

The service increase is expected to cost $8 million.

“The cost of not doing it is bigger than the cost of doing it,” Martinez Ferrada said.

Transit advocates welcomed the new measures but said more investment is still needed, particularly for bus service.

stories.title: Gus, the world's oldest tortoise, wished a speedy recovery from surgery by N.S. politicians
stories.summary: Gus, 104, who has been a fixture at Halifax’s Museum of Natural History for decades, went into surgery Tuesday to remove a bladder stone.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
A lowly 104-year-old tortoise that underwent surgery Tuesday to remove a bladder stone is getting encouragement from high places in his Nova Scotia home.

“Premier Tim Houston shared his well-wishes for Gus when it was announced that he would be undergoing surgery,” Houston’s press secretary, Catherine Klimek, said Tuesday in an email.

“It’s been very sweet seeing all the love Gus has received the last few weeks.”

Gus has been a fixture at Halifax’s Museum of Natural History for decades. He is believed to be the oldest gopher tortoise in the world, celebrating his 104th birthday on Aug. 10.

Halifax Mayor Andy Fillmore also had words of encouragement for the slow-moving museum attraction.

“For decades, Gus has welcomed countless visitors from all around the world,” Fillmore said in a written statement.

“Over these past few weeks, we’ve seen a remarkable display of appreciation and affection for him. I join the many residents who are wishing him well as he heads into surgery, and look forward to visiting him again very soon.”

Gus went into surgery early Tuesday to remove a bladder stone, said Rob Maguire, who speaks for Nova Scotia’s Department of Communities, Culture, Tourism and Heritage.

“The last I checked, he was still in surgery,” Maguire said mid-afternoon.

By 5 p.m., Gus was awake and doing well, according to Jeff Gray, the museum’s manager.

“They were able to remove the entire bladder stone,” Gray said. “It was a complete success … According to the vets, he’s doing great.”

Gus will stay at the animal hospital for 48 hours.

“When he does get back, we expect it will be eight to 10 weeks before he goes back on public view here at the museum,” Gray said.

Gus was initially diagnosed with the bladder stone in 2009. Bladder stones are common in reptiles and tortoises like Gus, Maguire said.

It wasn’t causing him any problems, and the veterinarian recommended leaving it alone.

“The alternative of removing it was a fairly invasive surgery,” Maguire said.

Fast forward to his most recent scans from this year. “It had grown, so the decision was made to go in and remove it now because if it grew any further, it might start to pose a problem for him,” Maguire said.

“Also, since 2009, there have been advances in veterinary care that have made this surgery a lot less invasive than it would have been back then.”

In 2009, surgeons would have had to cut through Gus’s shell to access his abdomen, Maguire said.

“Now they’re able to do it by creating a small incision in his leg and to access his bladder through his abdominal cavity through that leg,” he said.

“It’s much less invasive, it decreases the risk of surgery, and it makes recovery a lot easier and shorter.”

Generations of children have visited Gus for decades to feed him lettuce and bananas.

“My father (age 71) who was born and raised here — he remembers seeing Gus when he was a kid,” Maguire said.

“Now I’ve got a seven-year-old niece who also loves him, too.”

Gus is a Gopher Tortoise, otherwise know as gopherus polyphemus, which are native to the U.S. South and one of the oldest living species on the planet.

“But for Haligonians, we call him Gopher Gus the Lettuce King. Or just Gus, for short.” reads a history of Gus prepared by Halifax Public Libraries

One of the museum’s former curators acquired Gus in 1942 from a reptile institute in Silver Springs, Fla. He is believed to have been about 20 years old when he was purchased, according to the library’s Gus primer.

When he first took up residence in Halifax, he was given free rein of the museum. “He used to walk around the halls, in between the library stacks. Wherever you went, you were apt to fall over Gus.”

stories.title: Washington resident charged with conspiracy in Canada shool shooting is ordered detained
stories.summary: Seattle (AP) — A Washington state resident charged with conspiracy in one of the worst school shootings in Canada’s history has been ordered detained pending further hearings in the case.
stories.author: Gene Johnson The Associated Press
stories.content:
Seattle (AP) — A Washington state resident charged with conspiracy in one of the worst school shootings in Canada’s history has been ordered detained pending further hearings in the case.

Melody Bryant, also known as James Cody Bryant, of Bellingham, Washington, was charged this month with conspiring to murder people in a foreign country. Investigators said she provided assistance to Jesse Van Rootselaar , who killed eight people and wounded 27 in the mountain community of Tumbler Ridge in February.

stories.title: Mark Carney to attend ‘Forever Canadian’ rallies ahead of Alberta referendum
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney, who grew up in Alberta, focused his Thanksgiving Day message on the province's upcoming separation referendum, saying Canada is 'worth fighting for.'
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to attend two Forever Canadian rallies in Alberta this week, just ahead of the province’s referendum .

On Oct. 19, Albertans will vote on the whether to stay in Canada or hold a future separation referendum. There are also nine other questions involving constitutional and immigration issues.

The “Forever Canadian” campaign, launched by Alberta’s former deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk, seeks to encourage Albertans to vote to stay in Canada.

The organization’s website says Carney was invited to one rally in Calgary on Oct. 15 and another in Edmonton on Oct. 16. The Prime Minister’s Office confirmed Carney will attend both.

“We want the country’s leader to see what we see every day: Albertans from every walk of life standing up for a united Canada,” says the Forever Canadian website.

Carney, who grew up in Alberta, focused his Thanksgiving Day message on Alberta’s upcoming separation referendum , saying Canada is “worth fighting for.”

“This year, Thanksgiving is a bit different,” he said in a video message posted Monday and filmed at his old high school in Edmonton.

“A week from today, Albertans will have the opportunity to make an important decision about their future: whether to remain part of Canada or begin a long and uncertain process through which Alberta could separate from Canada.”

Carney said the federal government is building “big things” in Alberta — including a planned new pipeline to the West Coast — but Canada can’t achieve those goals if the country is divided.

“You can’t build big things on fault lines,” he said.

Carney also said Canadians are “stronger together” as they face down threats to their economy, security and culture.

“Generations of Albertans helped build this country. It’s yours, it’s ours, and it’s worth fighting for,” he said.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is expected to deliver his own speech supporting Canadian unity in Calgary on Friday.

Poilievre is set to speak during the Canada Strong and Free Network conference on Oct. 16 in Calgary. His speech is expected to be followed by an address from Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.

— With files from David Baxter and Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

Carney said the federal government is building “big things” in Alberta — including a planned new pipeline to the West Coast — but Canada can’t achieve those goals if the country is divided.
“You can’t build big things on fault lines,” he said.
Carney also said Canadians are “stronger together” as they face down threats to their economy, security and culture.
“Generations of Albertans helped build this country. It’s yours, it’s ours, and it’s worth fighting for,” he said.

stories.title: Saskatchewan politician says paid nearly $30K for private jets; NDP wants answers
stories.summary: Regina - A Saskatchewan Party backbencher says he paid close to $30,000 out of his own pocket for two trips on a private jet and that one of those flights was for government business.
stories.author: Jeremy Simes The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Regina - A Saskatchewan Party backbencher says he paid close to $30,000 out of his own pocket for two trips on a private jet and that one of those flights was for government business.

Kevin Weedmark released a letter Tuesday from Maurice Herauf, the province’s conflict of interest commissioner, who provided his opinion on the airfare expenses.

Herauf wrote in the Sept. 18 letter that Weedmark’s invoices indicate he paid for the flights with his own money and therefore did not violate a section of Conflict of Interest Act.

“Since you paid for the flights from your personal funds there is absolutely no financial benefit that can be attributed to your decision to fly to functions on either date,” Herauf wrote.

The letter says Weedmark had asked Herauf to provide an opinion on his flights after the Opposition NDP had flagged it as a concern.

The trips took place over the course of a year.

On Aug. 21, 2025, Weedmark spent $8,271 on a private jet to fly the owners of the Moosomin Dairy Queen and two of their family members to the Jim Pattison Children’s Hospital in Saskatoon for a tour. The Dairy Queen had raised $42,000 for the hospital and Weedmark was one of their volunteers. Herauf wrote the trip was private in nature.

On Aug. 27 of this year, Weedmark spent $20,106 on another jet for two government functions in the province before making a stop in Regina and then flying back to Moosomin. One of the functions was an official opening of an addictions treatment facility in Lloydminster on the Alberta boundary, and the other was to celebrate the anniversary of a seniors complex in Saskatoon.

The letter says the health minister’s office had requested Weedmark attend both events, as Weedmark is also the minister’s legislative secretary. Weedmark has also said it would have been difficult for him to drive to Lloydminster in time, so he chose to fly.

However, the Opposition NDP says Weedmark still needs to show the receipts to prove he didn’t improperly benefit from his role as a legislature member.

Earlier Tuesday, the NDP sent a letter to Herauf asking for an opinion on whether Weedmark breached conflict of interest rules.

Meara Conway, the Ndp’s health critic, said she wants to know if Weedmark had paid commercial value for the flights. She said the NDP got a private jet quote for a similar aircraft. That quote came in above $20,000.

“If the flight was below commercial value, it was a prohibited gift or personal benefit under (the act),” she said. “The rules exist to make sure that decisions are being made in the public interest.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.
