stories.title: Man arrested in connection with Israeli flags set alight in Toronto: police
stories.summary: Police have arrested a Toronto man in connection with an arson investigation after several Israeli flags were set on fire outside a church.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
Police have arrested a Toronto man in connection with an arson investigation after several Israeli flags were set on fire outside a church on Wednesday.

Toronto Police said in a news release on Tuesday that Syed Raza, 29, was arrested and charged with arson, mischief under $5,000, mischief interfering with the lawful enjoyment of property, and disobeying a lawful order of court.

It added that on Oct. 7, at approximately 1:02 a.m., Raza attended the area of Sunrise Avenue and O’Connor Drive and removed Israeli flags that were placed in front of the Word of Faith International Christian Centre and set them alight.

On Saturday, the accused was identified by investigators while at a demonstration in the area of Dundas Street East and Yonge Street at approximately 4:06 p.m.

He was scheduled to appear in court at the Toronto Regional Bail Centre on Oct. 11.

The incident came on the third anniversary of the October 7 Hamas-led attack on Israel, which killed 1,200 people and saw 251 taken hostage.

A police spokesperson previously confirmed to National Post that the incident was being investigated by the TPS Hate Crime Unit.

The Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs (Cija) and UJA Federation of Greater Toronto issued a joint statement on the day of the incident, calling it “disturbing.”

“Faith International Christian Centre has stood with the Jewish community and with Israel. To see that solidarity answered with fire is a disturbing reminder that hatred does not stop with Jews. Increasingly, those who stand beside us are being targeted too,” the statement read.

It went on to say that Cija and UJA are “deeply grateful” for the “friendship and solidarity” from the Faith International Christian Centre, and called on leaders at every level of government to condemn the attack and “confront the extremism that is making intimidation and violence increasingly commonplace.”

Israeli flags set on fire in Toronto, police investigating as suspected hate-motivated attack

Terry Newman: Accused in Israeli flag burning wears Hamas shirt to court in Montreal

“When simply standing with the Jewish community carries a cost — when allies are intimidated, threatened, or attacked because they refuse to turn away — this is no longer only a Jewish problem,” the two organizations said. “It is a threat to the kind of country we all want Canada to be.”

“I’m thinking today of Jewish families across Toronto who have spent 3 years watching this kind of thing move closer to their homes, their schools and their synagogues, and who are tired of being told it’s being taken seriously while it keeps happening,” he wrote.

stories.title: Astronaut says it's important there's a Canadian at the International Space Station
stories.summary: Longueuil - Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk says his presence on the International Space Station shows Canada can contribute to the leading edge of space exploration.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Longueuil - Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk says he is having a blast on the International Space Station and is showing the world how Canada can contribute to the leading edge of space exploration.

“It is important for Canada to be here,” Kutryk said Tuesday as he floated in the space station while taking questions from Canadian journalists in Longueuil, Que.

“We take a lot of benefits from these missions and it’s something that we hope we can continue.”

The 44-year-old is two weeks into a six-month mission which will see him conduct experiments and research and take part in critical maintenance work.

He launched on Oct. 1 as part of Nasa Crew 13 in the fastest flight ever to the space station — just under eight hours.

Kutryk, who served as a CF-18 fighter pilot, said the launch was exhilarating and spectacular. He said no amount of training can prepare you for the experience.

Kutryk is a mission specialist on the four-person crew, which also includes commander Jessica Watkins and pilot Luke Delaney — both of Nasa — and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov, another mission specialist.

Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk says he's having a blast on the International Space Station but the mission also shows how Canada can contribute to the leading edge of space flight. Kutryk is on a six-month mission to the ISS. (Oct. 13, 2026)

“Everything about being here for the first couple weeks is very special,” Kutryk said. “You just feel so lucky and fortunate to be living this experience.”

This adventure has been a lifelong goal for Kutryk. He said it’s hard to describe the first time he saw Earth from the station.

“It’s just one world. It’s one thing hanging in the blackness of space and you don’t see all the countries and the problems and all the challenges,” he said, noting the space station was crossing over Canada while he was answering questions.

“You just see this little bit of perfection that we should really, really be trying to protect.”

The space station is a long way from the Alberta cattle farm where Kutryk grew up.

He brought a small piece of his family’s history with him to the station — a pocket watch his relatives brought from Ukraine to Canada four generations ago.

Kutryk said the watch sits beside the area where he sleeps. He said he holds it and thinks about how much has changed over the past century, and what that means for the future.

The astronaut has been busy since he arrived at the station. The mission includes Canadian-led studies on how space travel and microgravity can affect human health.

During his orbital press conference, Kutryk was wearing gear for an AstroFit research project monitoring his health. The project is meant to find ways to allow humans to stay in space for longer periods of time.

Life in space does come with challenges, Kutryk said.

It’s difficult at first to eat, move around, sleep or use tools in microgravity, he said, adding he had to learn some basic tasks again like a “child.”

Kutryk’s mission to Earth’s orbit adds to a memorable year for Canadian space exploration and research.

Canadian Jeremy Hansen was one of four astronauts aboard the Artemis II mission in April — humanity’s first trip to the moon in more than 50 years. The 10-day lunar fly-around saw Hansen and his crewmates travel farther from the surface of the Earth than anyone before them.

Kutryk said his time on the space station is a testament to what Canada can do when it seizes on a bold vision and takes risks.

And having a Canadian on the space station also encourages Canada’s industry, academia and commercial interests to get on board, he said.

“That’s how we innovate, that’s how we develop new technologies, that’s what we want to be doing,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

— By Kelly Geraldine Malone in Washington

“It is important for Canada to be here,” Kutryk said Tuesday as he floated in the space station while taking questions from Canadian journalists in Longueuil, Que.
“We take a lot of benefits from these missions and it’s something that we hope we can continue.”
The 44-year-old is two weeks into a six-month mission which will see him conduct experiments and research and take part in critical maintenance work.
He launched on Oct. 1 as part of Nasa Crew 13 in the fastest flight ever to the space station — just under eight hours.

Kutryk is a mission specialist on the four-person crew, which also includes commander Jessica Watkins and pilot Luke Delaney — both of Nasa — and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov, another mission specialist.

The city says 222,550 Torontonians went to advance polls over six days ahead of election day on Oct. 26.

That’s a big jump from the nearly 130,000 advance votes cast in the 2023 mayoral byelection, and nearly 116,000 votes cast in the 2022 municipal election.

stories.title: Federal government expands expands AI program with $500M boost
stories.summary: The federal government says it is making an additional $500 million available over five years to help Canadian businesses adopt artificial intelligence technologies and bring Canadian-developed AI products to market.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
The federal government says it is making an additional $500 million available over five years to help Canadian businesses adopt artificial intelligence technologies and bring Canadian-developed AI products to market.

The announcement was made in London on Tuesday by Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation Minister Evan Solomon, who said the funding will expand the Regional Artificial Intelligence Initiative, bringing total federal support for the program to $700 million.

The initiative is part of the federal government’s AI for All strategy, unveiled in June 2026, which is aimed at increasing the use of artificial intelligence across Canada while strengthening the country’s AI sector and technological sovereignty.

Federal officials said support will be focused primarily on sectors where Canada has established expertise and growth potential, including health and life sciences, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, manufacturing and robotics. Regional agencies will also have flexibility to support other local economic priorities.

The government said the expanded program will also help Canadian AI companies attract investment, secure customers and commercialize homegrown technologies. Funding will also be available to organizations that provide businesses with specialized expertise and support related to AI adoption and commercialization.

The federal government also said the investment is intended to encourage broader AI adoption across Canada, help domestic AI firms grow while remaining based in Canada, and support economic growth and productivity.

stories.title: 'I did everything for nothing': Pearson Airport gold heist ringleader says fortune lost
stories.summary: Star witness at the trial of a former Air Canada employee takes the stand and says kidnappers took the gold and cash.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
The mastermind of the spectacular Toronto airport gold heist lost his share of the loot after fleeing to Pakistan, where he said he was kidnapped by police, blindfolded and tortured until he told them where he hid his gold and cash.

” Arsalan Chaudhary, 43, of Mississauga, Ont., testified Tuesday as a reluctant witness in court in Brampton, Ont.

Chaudhary said he was the man behind the gold heist, along with an inside man who worked with Air Canada, but after they split the stolen gold and cash, worth more than $22 million, he left Canada for Pakistan, where he was grabbed by men in police uniforms.

While he was in captivity and suffering torture and threatened with death, he was connected by FaceTime video calls to his kidnappers’ colleagues in Canada; he told them where to go to get his stash of gold hidden in a Toronto-area condo, and then to his family’s home to collect his cash.

“Before they could do anything further, I pretty much told them, ‘I’ll give you everything. You don’t need to do anything. You have me. My life is worth more than any money.’ They had their people go where the gold was, and they got the cash and the gold, everything.”

Once they had his loot, a hood was pulled over his head and driven from the small room where he had been held. When the car stopped, he said he was told to stay down and count to 30 before looking up or they would shoot him.

Chaudhary was asked by Crown prosecutor Jelena Vlacic how he felt at that point.

“I was just thankful to be alive,” he said, “and I wanted to get the F out of Pakistan Asap.

“All of this was not even worth it. I destroyed people’s lives. I did everything for nothing.”

Chaudhary is the star witness at the trial for an alleged co-accused in the gold heist, Parmpal Sidhu, a former Air Canada employee in the cargo warehouse where the crate of gold and cash was stolen in 2023 shortly after arriving on a flight from Zurich, Switzerland.

Although the trial is for Sidhu, who has pleaded not guilty to theft over $5,000 and conspiracy, Chaudhary said the Air Canada employee who was the key inside man at the cargo warehouse who he planned the heist with was Simran Preet Panesar, who is a wanted fugitive in the case, and believed to be living in India.

Chaudhary said that Panesar was in charge of getting the crate of gold and cash out of the cargo warehouse, and Chaudhary was in charge of handling it once it got out.

Chaudhary said he followed the truck that had collected the crate after Air Canada insiders redirected the cargo, as it headed north from the airport.

At a farm, which he said he couldn’t remember where, he, Panesar and the driver divided the loot with Chaudhary taking 30 per cent of the gold.

Chaudhary is in custody, serving his sentence at Maplehurst Correctional Complex, and was escorted into court by a police officer. He walked with casual confidence, almost a swagger.

His testimony was jagged, peppered frequently with him saying he didn’t recall key elements, such as most names and places, times and dates. He said he had post-traumatic stress disorder from his ordeal.

He said he was not testifying willingly, only after being served a subpoena by the Crown.

He pleaded guilty to theft over $5,000 in March and in April was sentenced to four years.

Chaudhary’s testimony continues today, and Sidhu’s trial continues for several days.

stories.title: Ontario father runs nearly 8,000 kilometres across Canada to raise awareness about mental health
stories.summary: By the time Myles Dininio reached the Pacific coast, he had raised more than $50,000 for Camh on his journey.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Silvia Pontecorvi, Omni News

Posted October 13, 2026 1:45 pm.

Last Updated October 13, 2026 1:52 pm.

For 148 days, Myles Dininio ran across Canada, covering nearly 8,000 kilometres from Newfoundland to British Columbia. But for the 40-year-old Ontario father of two, reaching the finish line wasn’t necessarily the accomplishment he had imagined.

“It never felt like a sense of accomplishment or a great achievement,” Dininio said. “I’ve been trying to process the end of it all, and understand what it is I am feeling.”

Dininio, from Zephyr, Ont., set out from Newfoundland on April 1 and reached Vancouver on Aug. 22, completing a cross-country journey aimed at raising awareness about mental health and funds for Toronto’s Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (Camh).

The challenge was deeply personal.

“Mental health has affected me my whole life,” he said. “From a very young age, I had little issues that I didn’t realize were known as mental health issues.”

Running thousands of kilometres across the country meant facing physical exhaustion, isolation and a daily mental battle.

“I quit this run probably 50 times in my head, ON the side of the road, but never actually followed it through,” Dininio recalled.

But what began as a test of endurance gradually became something much bigger.

Along the way, strangers joined him for stretches of the journey, offering encouragement and companionship. Others stopped to share their own experiences with mental health, sometimes opening up about deeply personal and painful struggles.

Dininio said listening to those stories was both moving and emotionally overwhelming. At first, he struggled with the weight of what people were sharing with him.

Those encounters eventually changed how he viewed the purpose of his run.

By the time Dininio reached the Pacific coast, his journey had raised more than $50,000 for Camh, one of Canada’s leading mental health research and treatment institutions.

But he says the impact of the conversations he had along the way became more meaningful than the money raised.

“I lost interest in the actual fundraising part, not lost interest, but the fundraising didn’t matter once I realized how many people I was actually reaching,” he said. “And that was worth more than any dollar amount.”

For Dininio, the experience reinforced the importance of talking openly about mental health and creating spaces where people feel comfortable sharing their struggles.

Now back home in Ontario, Dininio is adjusting to everyday life after nearly five months on the road.

While he continues to process the experience, he hopes the message behind his journey will resonate long after the running has stopped.

“One of the primary things when we deal with mental health issues is that we feel so alone,” he said. “And I think we all need to know we are not alone. There is always someone willing to listen.”

For Dininio, the nearly 8,000 kilometres were never just about reaching the other side of Canada. They were about reminding people that, even in their most difficult moments, they don’t have to face their struggles alone.

stories.title: 'Did you do your job?': Poilievre says Liberal government should have protected Stelco workers
stories.summary: N/A
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa — Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is calling in to question whether the Liberal government did enough to secure job protections for steel workers at Stelco, after it approved its sale to American-based Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. in 2024.

“It was up to the Liberal government to negotiate job protections when it approved the takeover of Stelco a few years back,” said Poilievre, during a press conference in Windsor, Ont., ON Tuesday.

“So, the question really goes to the Liberals: Did you do your job and protect the steelworkers when the foreign takeover happened?” asked Poilievre.

Poilievre’s comments come after Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and Prime Minister Mark Carney have threatened legal action against Stelco’s Ohio-based parent company Cleveland Cliffs Inc., for laying off 500 workers at its plants in Hamilton and Lake Erie.

Stelco was acquired by Cleveland Cliffs in 2024, with the sale approved by Joly’s predecessor François-Philippe Champagne under the Investment Canada Act (ICA).

The approval was contingent on several binding commitments, including maintaining the same number of unionized employees and most non-unionized employees for a period of five years.

Stelco has cited the ongoing U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel, which remain at 50 per cent, as one of the main reasons for the cutbacks.

Earlier this month, Carney called the layoffs a “betrayal” to workers and said there was still federal money on the table for Stelco to retain its employees.

On Oct. 5, Joly sent a letter to Stelco president Paul Simon, in which she listed the remedies available to the government should the investor fail to comply under the ICA.

Those remedies include “an application to the superior court for orders that May include directing compliance, divestiture, or monetary penalties.”

On Sunday, in an interview with CBC News’ Rosemary Barton Live, Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves disputed the government’s claims.

“There is no provision in the contract that I have to keep employment at a certain level every single day of the five years,” he said. “If that was an imposition of the Canadian government, I would not have accepted.”

Goncalves has called the layoffs “temporary” until Canada and the U.S. have reached a trade agreement. Goncalves is a supporter of U.S. President Donald Trump’s Section 232 tariffs and said he’s prepared to fight the Canadian government in court.

Joly has received a response to her letter from Stelco. On Saturday, she said a legal team is reviewing it and “all options are on the table.”

On Tuesday, NDP Leader Avi Lewis called on the federal government to nationalize Stelco.

“It’s a positive sign that the federal government is preparing to take legal action, but a court process will take years to resolve,” said Lewis, in a statement.

“If we’re serious about saving these jobs and the Canadian steel industry, we need immediate action,” he added. “That action must include nationalizing the plant.”

Poilevre said Conservatives are calling on the federal government to pursue legal action, but more importantly get back to the negotiating table with the U.S., to secure a tariff-free trade deal.

“It’s a positive sign that the federal government is preparing to take legal action, but a court process will take years to resolve,” said Lewis, in a statement.
“If we’re serious about saving these jobs and the Canadian steel industry, we need immediate action,” he added. “That action must include nationalizing the plant.”
Poilevre said Conservatives are calling on the federal government to pursue legal action, but more importantly get back to the negotiating table with the U.S., to secure a tariff-free trade deal.

stories.title: Roots shareholders approve deal for retailer to be taken private
stories.summary: New York-based Marquee Brands will acquire the company and pay shareholders $4.10 a share
stories.author: Tara Deschamps
stories.content:
Roots Corp. Root-T shareholders have voted in favour of the retailer going private through a transaction led by a New York brand management firm.

The apparel company says the shareholder vote passed but did not immediately disclose how much support the deal garnered.

The transaction is subject to other court and regulatory approvals but is expected to close in the fourth quarter of the year.

Under the deal with Marquee Brands announced in August, Roots shareholders will receive $4.10 per share.

Marquee will then use Club Monaco founder Joe Mimran’s company JM&A Design and Development Inc. to develop, manufacture and distribute Roots clothing for Canadian and U.S. stores.

Marquee Brands also manages the Martha Stewart, Laura Ashley and Roberto Cavalli labels and intends to expand Roots to other markets like Korea, India and Mexico.

stories.title: Canada's Wonderland closes Leviathan and Behemoth after roller coaster death in Georgia
stories.summary: One man was killed and four others injured on a ride at Six Flags Over Georgia, a theme park outside Atlanta run by the same company.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
Canada’s Wonderland has closed two of its roller coasters after one man was killed and four others injured on a similar ride at Six Flags Over Georgia, a theme park outside Atlanta.

Both parks are owned and operated by U.S.-based Six Flags, which has 34 properties in North America and two in Saudi Arabia. Canada’s Wonderland is its only Canadian location, after Montreal’s La Ronde was sold to EPR Properties of Missouri in May.

“I can confirm our coasters Leviathan and Behemoth were closed yesterday,” a Canada’s Wonderland spokesperson told National Post. “We do not have a timeline for reopening.”

The spokesperson added: “Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily closed similar attractions across our parks. The safety of our guests and team members is our highest priority.”

The park remains open Thursdays through Sundays (its regular fall hours) this month.

The death at Six Flags Over Georgia happened on Monday, according to local news reports. A man reportedly fell from Goliath , which the park refers to as a “hypercoaster,” meaning it has a height of least 61 metres. The ride, introduced in 2006, reaches speeds of 112 km/h.

The man, who has been identified by police as 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem of Atlanta, was reportedly thrown from his seat, fell and hit the ride multiple times. The park was evacuated after the incident.

CNN reported that what caused Kariem to fall off the roller coaster remains unclear, and that the cause of death has not been disclosed, nor have details of other injuries in the incident.

The accident left a number of riders in the next train of cars stuck on a steep incline when the ride was halted. News footage showed park workers rescuing those riders and leading them down the steep, open-air stairwell to the ground.

One person sent to hospital after reportedly falling 30 to 40 feet from Canada's Wonderland ride

A Canadian man is selling a 900-foot water slide on Facebook Marketplace for $150K

Six Flags temporarily closed nine roller coasters across six amusement parks on Monday, including the two at Canada’s Wonderland. Behemoth and Leviathan were both manufactured by Bolliger and Mabillard, the same company that made Goliath.

Canada’s Wonderland opened in 1981 in Vaughan, Ont., just north of Toronto. It was acquired by Paramount and became Paramount Canada’s Wonderland in 1993, but reverted to its original name after it was purchased by U.S.-based Cedar Fair Entertainment Co. in 2006. Cedar Fair and Six Flags merged in 2024.

The park boasts 18 roller coasters. The Behemoth opened in 2008 and features a climb to a height of 70 metres, followed by a 75-degree drop with speeds reaching 125 km/h, and a track length of over 1.6 km. The Leviathan , which opened four years later, has a climb 97.7 metres and an 80-degree drop, reaching speeds of 148 km/h.

stories.title: Canadians with children more likely to rely on charities, non-profits: survey
stories.summary: Two out of five Canadians said they relied on the service of a charity or a non-profit in the last 12 months, an Ipsos survey conducted for the RBC found on Tuesday.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Two out of five Canadians said they relied on the service of a charity or a non-profit in the last 12 months, an Ipsos survey conducted for the Royal Bank of Canada found on Tuesday.

However, the proportion of Canadians needing support is much higher among those who have children.

Canadians with children were far more likely (49 per cent) to seek support compared to those without kids (36 per cent), the RBC survey said.

Charities and non-profits working in the healthcare space found their services were most utilized (68 per cent) followed by food charities in second place (26 per cent) and education services (15 per cent) in third place.

Canadians also sought help from charities and non-profits working in sectors such as housing (12 per cent), social programming (12 per cent), employment (nine per cent), professional/skill development (six per cent) and cultural or recreational programming (six per cent).

Among those who used these services in the last 12 months, nearly four in five (79 per cent) said their use is “occasional” while more than one in five (21 per cent) said they “regularly” use help from charities or non-profit organizations.

The kind of service Canadians use depends on their age, with younger Canadians relying more on education and employment services while older Canadians rely mor heavily on healthcare supports.

Gen Z had the highest use of charities among all generations, with nearly half (44 per cent) having used these services in the last 12 months.

stories.title: Canadian ransomware negotiator arrested amid FBI hacker crackdown
stories.summary: A Canadian ransomware negotiator was arrested Thursday and faces unspecified extortion charges, according to court documents, prison records and a person familiar with the matter, as the FBI cracks down on a hacking group that stole information about its employees.
stories.author: Reuters Staff
stories.content:
Washington - A Canadian ransomware negotiator was arrested Thursday and faces unspecified extortion charges, according to court documents, prison records and a person familiar with the matter, as the FBI cracks down on a hacking group that stole information about its employees.

Edward Dubrovsky faces charges of conspiracy to “threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with intent to extort money” and “interference with commerce,” according to court documents filed with the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, which covers Philadelphia.

The records, which are partially sealed, provide conflicting spellings of his last name — “Dobrovsky” or “Dobrosky” — and do not identify his age, profession, or employer. A person briefed on the matter said the person was Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky.

Federal prosecutors in Philadelphia did not return repeated messages seeking comment about the discrepancies. Attempts to reach Dubrovsky and his attorneys were unsuccessful. Repeated attempts to reach the company displayed on Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile, CyberSteward, were similarly unsuccessful.

CyberSteward advertises itself online as specializing in “threat actor engagement, cyber-extortions, complex negotiations, and settlement facilitation.” On LinkedIn, Dubrovsky presents himself as a specialist in the process of negotiating with cybercriminals over ransom payments.

Electronic wallet records leaked in 2010 and preserved by dark-web intelligence firm District 4 Labs identify Dubrovsky as a resident of Richmond Hill, north of Toronto, and put his current age at 54. Federal prison records show that a 54-year-old named Edward Dubrovsky is currently being detained at a federal detention centre in Philadelphia.

News of Dubrovsky’s arrest was earlier reported by Politico and independent journalist Brian Krebs .

The arrest comes as the Federal Bureau of Investigation is leading a global crackdown on the hacking group ShinyHunters, which rattled the bureau last month by stealing information on what it said was nearly every FBI employee.

When Reuters asked the FBI about Dubrovsky’s arrest, it referred the news agency to FBI Director Kash Patel’s statement on Friday revealing that the bureau had arrested a “suspected co-conspirator of the ShinyHunters group” and declined further comment.

🚨 Our agents in the field have arrested another suspected co-conspirator of the ShinyHunters group – the group believed to be responsible for the recent https://t.co/RG0D4I5KFS incident, which occurred on a platform managed by a third-party vendor. This is the latest arrest… — FBI Director Kash Patel (@FBIDirectorKash) October 9, 2026

Raphael Satter and AJ Vicens, Editing by Jamie Freed, Reuters

stories.title: Czech defence company CSG buys 9.5 per cent stake in MDA Space
stories.summary: has bought a 9.5 per cent stake in MDA Space Ltd., making it the Canadian company’s largest shareholder.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal — Czech defence company CSG has bought a 9.5 per cent stake in MDA Space Ltd ., making it the Canadian company’s largest shareholder.

CSG says it views MDA Space as a strategic investment and sees opportunities to explore potential co-operation between the two companies over time.

Latest updates on company news here

CSG chair Michal Strnad says MDA Space is a highly respected, well led, profitable and growing space company with exceptional technological capabilities.

He pointed to the possibility of co-investing with MDA in manufacturing or assembly facilities in Europe and partnering on strategic acquisitions.

MDA Space CEO Mike Greenley welcomed the investment and said CSG is a leading European industrial group with a proven track record in building high-quality defence businesses.

MDA Space shares were down 23 cents at $39.95 in early-afternoon trading on the Toronto Stock Exchange.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: New Brunswick gets $219 million loan from Ottawa for hydroelectric dam repair work
stories.summary: The bulk of the money is a $219-million loan from the Canada Infrastructure Bank to extend the life of the province's largest hydroelectric dam.
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
The federal government is spending nearly $270 million to help New Brunswick modernize a pair of energy facilities that officials say are key to Ottawa’s plan to double the capacity of Canada’s electrical grid by 2050.

The bulk of the money is a $219-million loan from the Canada Infrastructure Bank to extend the life of the province’s largest hydroelectric dam, located west of Fredericton on the Saint John River.

The province will also receive a $50-million grant to upgrade its Salisbury Terminal near Moncton, which officials say is key to managing the flow of electricity across the provincial grid.

Federal Energy Minister Tim Hodgson made the announcements Tuesday during a news conference in front of the massive Mactaquac Dam.

“New Brunswick is critical to this plan and so are today’s investments,” he said. “Together, these two projects will strengthen New Brunswick’s electricity system while creating jobs, attracting investment, supporting affordability, and lowering emissions.”

New Brunswick’s Crown-owned electric utility is preparing the 672-megawatt Mactaquac Generation Station for a multibillion-dollar overhaul aimed at extending its operational life to 2068.

The new funding will pay for technical studies, regulatory reviews, First Nations engagement and planning for the Mactaquac Life Achievement Project, according to Natural Resources Canada.

In 2016, NB Power agreed to a plan in 2016 to spend up to $3.6 billion to prolong the life of the dam, which would have otherwise been decommissioned by 2030 due to concrete swelling.

The new funding will support technical studies, regulatory reviews, First Nations engagement and planning for the Mactaquac Life Achievement Project, according to Natural Resources Canada.

On Tuesday, NB Power CEO Lori Clark said the total cost for the project is now expected to be close to $9 billion.

Hodgson would not commit the federal Liberal government to spending more on the dam, noting that electricity generation is within provincial jurisdiction.

However, he said the federal government will need to help provinces and territories keep costs low as they work to meet federal clean energy regulations that call for a net-zero electricity grid by 2050.

“In the budget coming up, you will see a number of initiatives we are working on to work … with provinces and territories to help them realize the growth that they need in an affordable way,” the minister told reporters.

“This is clearly an indication that we understand how important it is for our prosperity to grow our electricity generating capabilities and we understand that the federal government needs to do its part in helping to make that affordable.”

New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt said the Mactaquac Generating Station is important to the entire Maritime region.

In the event of a system-wide blackout, the dam can start generating electricity without relying on an external power supply, making the largest so-called “black-start” facility in the region.

“We often call it the battery of the Maritimes,” said Holt. “Having this kind of renewable energy that we can turn on and off is critical, not only to our province, but to our neighbours in Prince Edward Island and in Nova Scotia and beyond.” The dam supplies 30 per cent of the province’s renewable energy requirements and 20 per cent of its overall electricity demand, officials said.

The investments come as NB Power is looking for ways to fix ageing infrastructure without imposing massive rate hikes on its customers.

Since the 1980s, concrete portions of the the dam have been affected by a chemical process called alkali-aggregate reaction. The reaction causes concrete to swell and crack, requiring substantial repairs and maintenance.

Just last week, NB Power applied to the provincial regulator to raise rates by 17.4 per cent over the next three years as it plans to spend $4 billion on maintaining the provincial grid.

Some of that money will be used to transition the province’s only remaining coal-fired generating plant to a facility that burns wood pellets to generate electricity.

stories.title: Canada joins allies in expressing regret over postponed Palestinian elections
stories.summary: Ottawa — Canada has joined allies France, the U.K. and Australia in expressing deep "regret" over the postponement of Palestinian presidential and legislative elections.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Canada, France, the United Kingdom and Australia expressed deep “regret” Tuesday over the postponement of Palestinian presidential and legislative elections.

The votes were set to happen next month. Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas has delayed them until September 2027.

In a media statement, Canada and its allies said the delay deprives Palestinians of the chance to vote and noted that elections are an important element of the Palestinian Authority’s commitment to reform.

“We call on the Palestinian Authority to reconsider the decision to postpone elections and to take the necessary steps to hold legislative and presidential elections, without further delay,” the statement said.

Abbas has been president since 2005.

The last Palestinian legislative election was held in 2006 and Hamas took over Gaza in a brief civil war the following year. Hamas has been in control of the territory since, while the Palestinian Authority is in power in the West Bank.

The executive committee of the Palestine Liberation Organization said in a statement over the weekend that conditions in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip are not conducive to holding elections and that Israel hasn’t allowed election materials and international observers to enter Gaza.

Israel’s foreign minister Gideon Saar called that “another ridiculous lie” in a post on X.

Prime Minister Mark Carney announced Canada’s intention to, along with several other countries, formally recognize a Palestinian state in July 2025.

Carney said that recognition would be “predicated on the Palestinian Authority’s commitment to much-needed reforms.” In a September 2025 press release, the government said those reforms would include demilitarization and holding elections in 2026 “in which Hamas can play no part.”

Canadian government officials said at the time that Abbas had committed to those reforms — but the Palestinian Authority cautioned last fall that an election would not be possible until a year after the end of the conflict in Gaza.

Carney said his government’s recognition of Palestinian statehood was meant to preserve the possibility of a two-state solution, with Israel and a Palestinian country coexisting in peace. Ottawa says the two-state solution has been undermined by the Israeli government and Palestinian militants such as Hamas.

A ceasefire deal has been in effect in Gaza for a year but Human Rights Watch reports the region is still experiencing ongoing violence and serious problems with obtaining food, water and other aid. Hamas remains in control in Gaza.

The UN also has warned of an uptick in extremist Israeli settler violence in the West Bank.

The statement released by Canada and its allies on Tuesday acknowledged “significant challenges and impediments” to the ability to conduct elections in a manner consistent with international standards.

It noted the Central Elections Commission had advanced practical preparations to address those challenges and allow people to vote, and it called on Israel to refrain from actions that could impede elections.

“Strengthening Palestinian governance is essential to continue building the institutional foundations of a viable two-state solution, which is the only path to lasting peace and security for both Israel and Palestine,” the statement said.

The statement added that Hamas — which Canada has designated as a terrorist group — can have no role in future Palestinian governance.

Carney’s office and Global Affairs Canada did not immediately respond to questions about what the postponement will mean for Canada’s recognition of Palestinian statehood.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said Canada “should not be giving aid to a government that’s breaking its promise” to hold elections.

“I don’t know why we would be sending Canadian tax dollars from people who can’t afford to pay their bills to a dictatorial, terrorist regime like that,” he said at a press conference in Windsor, Ont. on Tuesday.

The Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs said in a statement on Tuesday that Canada and its allies are implying the Palestinian Authority has broken one of its commitments underlying the recognition of statehood, “yet the Canadian government offers no indication of what consequences the PA will face, while suggesting that Israel is somehow to blame.”

The Israeli government has been critical of Canada’s recognition of Palestine. Israeli Ambassador to Canada Iddo Moed said last month the Palestinian Authority is corrupt and not serious about living in peace alongside Israel.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

— With files from The Associated Press

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Dominion Dynamics to jointly produce Ukrainian drones in Canada
stories.summary: Ottawa — The Ottawa-based defence company Dominion Dynamics is partnering with Ukrainian robotics company Tencore to start building its ground-based drone vehicles in Canada as early as next year.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Ottawa-based defence company Dominion Dynamics is partnering with Ukrainian robotics company Tencore to start building its ground-based drone vehicles in Canada as early as next year.

The two companies signed a memorandum of understanding at a defence conference in Washington, D.C., today which outlines their plans to manufacture Tencore’s Termit drone in Canada and install Dominion’s software in the vehicles.

The Termit drone, which runs on treads and looks almost like a miniature tank, has been deployed to Ukraine’s front lines for operations that would be hazardous for humans, such as resupply missions and mine-laying.

The federal government has been pushing for joint production of drones by Canadian companies and Ukraine’s battle-tested defence industry.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met in Calgary last month and signed a joint declaration on defence production.

Dominion is also independently developing its own autonomous collaborative platform: drones guided by humans that fly alongside fighter jets, such as F-35s or Gripen fighters.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Backstreet Boys' larger-than-life Toronto residency adds 12th show
stories.summary: Toronto - The Backstreet Boys apparently refuse to quit playing games with our calendars.
stories.author: Alex Nino Gheciu The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The architects of late ‘90s teen-pop just tacked on another show at Rogers Centre, extending their blockbuster 2027 residency at the Toronto stadium to a staggering 12 shows.

The boy band announced on social media today that they are adding “one more show” to the run on Sunday, March 7.

Article continues below

Jeremy Renner says he is ‘not in’ Avengers: Doomsday

Dubbed “Into the Millennium - Homecoming: Live in Canada,” the residency was originally announced as a four-night night run, kicking off Feb.12, before the group added more shows last week, citing “overwhelming demand.”

The 12-show run eclipses Taylor Swift’s historic six-night stand at the Rogers Centre in November 2024, when fans from around the world swarmed Toronto for the Eras Tour.

In a post on X, the Backstreet Boys expressed surprise at the demand for their shows: “We never thought you guys would be this excited,” they wrote.

The residency will be the band’s only North American stadium shows of 2027.

Canada was actually the launch pad for the Backstreet Boys in North America. Their 1995 track “We’ve Got It Goin’ On” became a massive hit there well before they hit it big in the U.S.

Their music seemingly strikes a nostalgic chord with Canadian millennials — including Drake, who joined the band onstage during their last Toronto show in 2022 to sing their 1999 hit “I Want It That Way.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Bike lane advocates to challenge Ford government’s removal plans at Supreme Court
stories.summary: Ahead of the lane removal, CycleTO and EcoJustice, two groups that launched the charter challenge, revealed they are appealing the case to Canada's highest court.
stories.author: Colin D'Mello, Olivia Bowden
stories.content:
Cycling advocates are looking to escalate the legal battle over bike lanes on three major Toronto streets, asking the Supreme Court of Canada to take on the Ford government’s years-long effort to tear them out.

In a mid-August ruling, the Ontario Court of Appeal overturned a lower court’s decision that removing bike lanes violated the Canadian Charter, allowing the government to proceed with its plan.

The decision reactivated a policy that the Ford government first put in place at the end of 2024 to restore space for vehicles — and remove bike lanes — from portions of Bloor Street West, Yonge Street and University Avenue.

On Tuesday, the government said it would begin that work by reverting a 600-metre section of Bloor to vehicle-only lanes.

Ahead of the removal, CycleTO and EcoJustice, two groups that launched the charter challenge, revealed they are appealing the case to Canada’s highest court asking it to strike down the policy as unconstitutional and weigh in on the government’s ability to implement potentially life-threatening legislation.

“The consequences of this case reach far beyond bike lanes and beyond Ontario,” said Bronwyn Roe with Ecojustice.

“We are asking the Supreme Court to hear this case in order to provide clarity about the scope of the rights to life and security of the person protected by Section 7 of the Charter.”

In the August ruling that paved the way for the lanes’ removal, Justice Grant Huscroft took issue with the lower court allegedly meddling in the business of the legislature.

Huscroft wrote “it is illegitimate for courts to involve themselves in matters of legislative policy.”

While Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria said the ruling underscored the government’s “clear and direct mandate” to fight gridlock, advocates argue their substantive arguments still apply.

“The Ontario Court of Appeal found that, as a matter of law, removing protected bike lanes could not infringe the Charter if there was no positive right to the bike lanes in the first place. The court did not consider, let alone overturn, the superior court’s factual findings,” Roe said.

Michael Longfield, the executive director of Cycle Toronto said their principal arguments will be reintroduced in front of the supreme court, if the case is heard.

“Bike lanes do not cause traffic congestion, ripping them out will put people’s lives at risk, there’s no network of side streets that can replace the bike lanes that are here,” Longfield said.

The Supreme Court of Canada will only hear an appeal if the case “raises a question of public importance,” the court states on its website.

According to the Court, a case that meets that bar for appeal could include one that involves the interpretation of constitutional rights, or if it raises a new issue of law or if it requires the Court to resolve conflicting decisions from courts of appeal.

stories.title: Coroner’s inquest begins examining death of Toronto woman who fell from balcony
stories.summary: A coroner’s inquest has begun to examine the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet, a Toronto woman who fell from a highrise balcony while police were in her home more than six years ago.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto -- A coroner’s inquest has begun to examine the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet, a Toronto woman who fell from a highrise balcony while police were in her home more than six years ago.

Korchinski-Paquet, a woman of Ukrainian, Black and Indigenous ancestry, died on May 27, 2020 after police responded to calls about a family dispute at the apartment. She was 29.

Inquest counsel say Korchinski-Paquet had been diagnosed with epilepsy and experienced seizures earlier that day.

Roger Shallow says the inquest’s scope includes how police and first responders are informed about epilepsy and how to ensure safety when a person’s behaviour May be influenced by postictal delirium, a condition that May occur in the period after a seizure.

He says the inquest will not look into general mental health challenges or psychiatric care, however, or the investigations by various police watchdogs into the case.

Shallow says Korchinski-Paquet’s death was “sudden and profoundly tragic” and no matter what the jury concludes, her family has been left to grapple with a loss no one should experience.

Korchinski-Paquet’s death came on the heels of the police killing of George Floyd, a Black man from Minneapolis, spurring further protests amid growing calls to defund the police.

It also cast a spotlight on how police interact with people experiencing mental health crises.

Ontario’s police watchdog investigated the case and eventually cleared Toronto police of wrongdoing in Korchinski-Paquet’s death. The Special Investigations Unit found it happened as she was trying to move from her apartment balcony to an adjacent one.

The inquest was announced earlier this year and is slated to last 14 days, with 13 witnesses expected to take the stand. Korchinski-Paquet’s mother, father and brother have been named as potential witnesses, as have five of the six police officers who attended the scene.

The inquest jury does not assign criminal responsibility but May make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths in the future. The chief coroner’s office does not have the authority to impose the recommendations, however.

On the anniversary of her death this year, Korchinski-Paquet’s parents joined advocates in calling for the recommendations issued in coroner’s inquests to be binding and implemented within a reasonable timeframe.

Her mother, Claudette Beals, also said there should be a different system in place to investigate allegations of wrongdoing against police officers, adding she has no faith in “police investigating police.”

“My daughter’s been gone for six years and no one’s held responsible for that,” she said in a news conference at the provincial legislature.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

Paola Loriggio, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Cyclists ask Supreme Court to weigh in on Toronto bike lane removal plan
stories.summary: Cyclists said they will seek leave to appeal to the top court, the same day as Ontario said it would start taking out more bike lanes along parts of Bloor Street West
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Cyclists challenging Ontario’s plan to tear up Toronto bike lanes will ask the Supreme Court of Canada to weigh in, the groups backing the case said Tuesday, as more removal work was slated to begin.

The groups say a recent Appeal Court decision in their case goes beyond bike lanes and raises the question of under what circumstances a government can pursue life-risking policies.

“The facts are clear: bike lanes do not cause traffic congestion, ripping them out will put people’s lives at risk, and no network of side streets can replace the 19 (kilometres) of protected bike lanes on Bloor, Yonge, and University,” said Michael Longfield, executive director of Cycle Toronto, an advocacy group that brought the case.

Work was scheduled to begin Tuesday to start removing bike lanes along a stretch of Bloor Street West, the province said. A spokesperson for Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria did not immediately respond to e-mailed questions about where the work was taking place, how long it would last, or at what cost.

“The people of Ontario gave our government a clear mandate to tackle the traffic that is costing our economy over $56 billion a year by removing the bike lanes on some of Toronto’s busiest streets,” Dakota Brasier wrote.

The request for Canada’s top court to weigh in is the latest chapter in a legal case over a 2024 law empowering the province to take out bikes lanes on those three major Toronto roads, a move framed by the province as a bid to cut down on traffic congestion. The legislation also required municipalities to seek approval to install new bike lanes that cut into traffic.

A spokesperson for Mayor Olivia Chow said the city repeatedly shared with the province designs that keep both vehicle and bike lanes intact. Work has already been completed to restore a car lane and keep the bike lane on a short stretch of Bloor Street between Kipling and Islington subway stations.

The Toronto bike lane removal plan was initially blocked by a lower court judge who found it to be an unconstitutional risk to cyclist safety. The judge ruled the government pursued the plan despite its own advisers finding it would not accomplish its stated goal to reduce traffic congestion, and could possibly make it worse. Even accepting that goal at face value, the judge found it to be way of step with the law’s intent.

But that decision was overturned by the Ontario Court of Appeal in August.

In a strongly worded ruling, a panel of three judges said the lower court had effectively created a right to bike lanes where none existed. The trial judge, they found, had not only misapplied the law, but improperly strayed into the legislature’s domain of policy-making and political considerations.

Anyone who receives a judgment from a top provincial or territorial court can seek leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. The Supreme Court only hears a fraction of those cases, which typically must involve a key constitutional question, conflicting lower court decisions or a new issue of law.

“This case is about the scope of the protections provided by Section 7 of the Charter to everyone’s rights to life and security of the person. We’re asking the Supreme Court to hear this appeal to bring clarity to this broader legal question,” said Bronwyn Roe of Ecojustice, an environmental law charity backing the case.

Work was scheduled to begin Tuesday to start removing bike lanes along a stretch of Bloor Street West, the province said. A spokesperson for Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria did not immediately respond to e-mailed questions about where the work was taking place, how long it would last, or at what cost.

“The people of Ontario gave our government a clear mandate to tackle the traffic that is costing our economy over $56 billion a year by removing the bike lanes on some of Toronto’s busiest streets,” Dakota Brasier wrote.

The request for Canada’s top court to weigh in is the latest chapter in a legal case over a 2024 law empowering the province to take out bikes lanes on those three major Toronto roads, a move framed by the province as a bid to cut down on traffic congestion. The legislation also required municipalities to seek approval to install new bike lanes that cut into traffic.

A spokesperson for Mayor Olivia Chow said the city repeatedly shared with the province designs that keep both vehicle and bike lanes intact. Work has already been completed to restore a car lane and keep the bike lane on a short stretch of Bloor Street between Kipling and Islington subway stations.

The Toronto bike lane removal plan was initially blocked by a lower court judge who found it to be an unconstitutional risk to cyclist safety. The judge ruled the government pursued the plan despite its own advisers finding it would not accomplish its stated goal to reduce traffic congestion, and could possibly make it worse. Even accepting that goal at face value, the judge found it to be way of step with the law’s intent.
But that decision was overturned by the Ontario Court of Appeal in August.

In a strongly worded ruling, a panel of three judges said the lower court had effectively created a right to bike lanes where none existed. The trial judge, they found, had not only misapplied the law, but improperly strayed into the legislature’s domain of policy-making and political considerations.

Anyone who receives a judgment from a top provincial or territorial court can seek leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. The Supreme Court only hears a fraction of those cases, which typically must involve a key constitutional question, conflicting lower court decisions or a new issue of law.

“This case is about the scope of the protections provided by Section 7 of the Charter to everyone’s rights to life and security of the person. We’re asking the Supreme Court to hear this appeal to bring clarity to this broader legal question,” said Bronwyn Roe of Ecojustice, an environmental law charity backing the case.

stories.title: Ontario’s northwest region to end time changes to align with Manitoba
stories.summary: Indigenous Affairs Minister says there is overwhelming consensus among municipalities, First Nations and businesses to make the time change permanent
stories.author: Liam Casey
stories.content:
Ontario is set to move parts of the province’s northwest region to permanent daylight time in order to align with Manitoba, Indigenous Affairs Minister Greg Rickford told The Canadian Press.

Rickford said there is overwhelming consensus among municipalities, First Nations and businesses to make the time change permanent.

The province intends to make a regulatory change in the Time Act on Nov. 1 to allow regions west of the 90th meridian to align with Manitoba, he said.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew announced last month the province would stop twice-annual clock changes and stay on daylight time year-round in the central time zone, leaving it one hour ahead of the other Prairie provinces rather than aligned with them.

“That put northwestern Ontario, who sits in the central standard time zone, in a bit of a spot, to say the least,” Rickford said.

The province had three options, he said.

One, the northwestern region could shift to eastern time to align with the rest of the province. Two, they could continue on with time changes, but then they’d be out of step with the rest of Ontario and Manitoba.

“The other option … we took by unanimous consensus, was to not change our clocks and go to what I’m calling Wab Kinew time,” Rickford said.

Much of the province’s northwest jumped into action after Kinew’s announcement to figure out a way forward. Rickford said the province reached out to municipalities, businesses and First Nations to get their thoughts.

“What ended up coming back was overwhelmingly unanimous, 90 to 94 per cent from every survey,” he said.

New Democrat Sol Mamakwa, who represents the riding of Kiiwetinoong that is home to the majority of Ontario’s remote, fly-in First Nations, also helped figure out a way forward.

“After having brought the voices of our communities across the northwest to the table, we are happy the advocacy to observe daylight savings will be implemented permanently,“ Mamakwa said in a statement.

”We are proud of our collaborative efforts to deliver what works for the North. We thank everyone who reached out and shared their thoughts on this important decision.”

British Columbia said in March that it was moving to permanent Pacific daylight time.

Alberta also switched to permanent daylight time this year in what it calls Alberta time, which means it now has the same time as Saskatchewan year round.

stories.title: Trans Canada Trail urges Ottawa to continue funding world’s longest trail system
stories.summary: With federal funding set to expire in 2027, the sprawling Trans Canada Trail is calling on Ottawa to continue supporting what has become the longest multi-use trail system in the world.
stories.author: Daniel Otis
stories.content:
With federal funding set to expire in 2027, the sprawling Trans Canada Trail is calling on Ottawa to continue supporting what has become the longest multi-use trail system in the world.

Spanning more than 30,000 km, the expansive trail network stretches across every province and territory and connects Canada’s Atlantic, Pacific and Arctic coasts. Used by an estimated 29 million Canadians every year, the trail system winds through wilderness regions, rural communities, small towns and even major cities like Montreal, Toronto, Calgary and Vancouver.

“What we’re saying to government is at a time when you’re investing in important things – like resource development, new export opportunities, Canadian defence – don’t forget about something that has been built by successive generations of Canadians over 35 years that now is part and parcel and central to Canadian identity,” Trans Canada Trail government affairs director Matt DeCourcey told CTV’s Your Morning on Tuesday.

While each section of the trail is managed by one of more than 650 local groups, the overall network is supported by the Trans Canada Trail registered charity , which receives funding from donors, provincial and municipal governments, as well as the federal government.

In the 2022 federal budget, Ottawa committed $55 million over five years to maintain, enhance and expand the trail network. That funding, which came via Parks Canada, is set to expire on March 31, 2027.

The Trans Canada Trail is now seeking another $55-million, five-year commitment in the next federal budget, which is expected to be tabled in November. Ottawa has so far invested $145 million in the trail since 1992, when the trail network was founded. The network achieved coast-to-coast-to-coast connection in 2017 to mark the 150th anniversary of Canadian Confederation.

“The federal government has been a key investor in the building and sustaining and building the quality of this trail over almost 35 years,” DeCourcey said.

“We see it as vitally important that they continue to be a seed investor at the table so that our organization can continue to go out and work with the many Canadians who have provided private donations over the years, as well as corporate partners and philanthropic organizations, to ensure that this trail stays connected, stays sustainable and accessible for future generations.”

Without renewed government funding, a recent report from the Trans Canada Trail estimates that 11,000 km of the trail could fall into disrepair and become impassible by 2045, which could result in a projected 78 million fewer trail visits and $2 billion in lost tourism spending per year.

“Largely that’s in small centres, remote and wilderness communities that don’t have the local resources there to ensure that this trail is kept up and sustainable and accessible for future generations,” DeCourcey said.

While DeCourcey describes the group’s conversations with Ottawa as “constructive,” the network is still awaiting a final funding decision from Parks Canada, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“This is something that can keep us connected,” DeCourcey added. “This is something that adds economic vitality to communities right across the country, and this is something that connects us to the thing that is central to our identity as Canadians, that being nature.”

stories.title: Canada trade ties run deep in Republican strongholds. But will it matter to Trump?
stories.summary: Republican candidates are speaking out against Trump’s tariffs in places like Michigan and Maine, but deep-red states could also be hurting.
stories.author: Tracy Moran
stories.content:
Washington, D.C. — It makes sense that states along the Canada-U.S. border are feeling the pinch of the trade war, whether it’s Michigan’s heavily integrated automotive manufacturing or Maine’s lumber trade. But a new analysis by Advancing American Freedom (AAF) shows that Canada also plays an important economic role in deeply red Republican states like Montana and North Dakota.

Canada accounts for 62 and 55 per cent of Maine and Vermont’s international goods trade, according to AAF, and a whopping 77 per cent in North Dakota and Montana, states President Donald Trump carried by 36 and 20 percentage points, respectively, in 2024.

The nature of the exposure is different for Montana and North Dakota, says AAF policy analyst Kat Miller. “Canada buys about … 82 per cent of everything North Dakota sells abroad,” she said, while “88 per cent of everything Montana buys from abroad comes from Canada.” But dependence is not the same as tariff exposure: mineral fuels account for 80 per cent of North Dakota’s exports to Canada, according to Miller, and are exempt from Canadian countertariffs.

Either way, with the U.S. midterm elections looming, the tariff impact in deep-red states raises the question of whether it makes them pressure points for the White House — or whether Republican loyalty makes that trade exposure easier for Trump to ignore.

In recent days, Republicans seeking midterm votes have publicly spoken out against the tariffs.

“Canada is not China. It is our neighbour, our friend, our closest ally, and our biggest trading partner,” said Maine’s Sen. Susan Collins during a Senate debate on Oct. 6.

“I have been strongly voting against the tariffs with Canada, but I’ve also been working behind the scenes,” she added.

In Michigan, U.S. Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers has also spoken out. Having originally defended Trump’s tariffs, Rogers launched a campaign ad against them on Oct. 7.

“Here in Michigan, we know Canada is not our enemy,” he said. “We need to end this tariff war now.”

Those appeals come from competitive Senate contests, and it is less clear whether dependence on Canada is generating similar pressure from safer Republican areas.

But Richard Stern, vice president of the Plymouth Institute for Free Enterprise at Advancing American Freedom, says a lot more is happening behind the scenes.

“A lot of the private conversation is trying to push to stop this war with Canada,” he said. “A lot of them privately are putting pressure on this … and are going to the Commerce Department, Treasury, White House and saying, ‘Look, you’re really hurting Americans here. Knock it off.’”

So will these efforts and the impact on even redder states have some leverage over Trump?

“I think it does matter,” said Christopher Hernandez-Roy, acting director and senior fellow at the Americas Program of Csis in Washington, referring to currently Republican states with exposed economies to Canada. “In fact, this has always been part of Canada’s playbook, which is to lobby with state and local governments that are Republican that are trade dependent with Canada.”

“Whether it’s sufficient to … nudge the president is another matter altogether,” he added, noting that it “doesn’t necessarily mean that the president is gonna change his tune.”

Christopher Sands, director of the Center for Canadian Studies at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies in Washington, also noted that such red-state dependence would normally be a channel to the president through their senators.

“In a normal presidency, yes, because it means there’s somebody who the president knows who can pick up the phone and have a conversation … and say, ‘We really need to do this for my voters who are your voters, too,’” he said.

The caveat: this is not a normal presidency. Sands pointed to how much Trump has ignored Congress over the past two years.

“This president hasn’t worked Capitol Hill that much … (Trump) seems to write off the whole institution as irrelevant,” Sands said.

The tariffs themselves help reflect how Trump is imposing policy without Congress, so trade watchers are skeptical that Republican senators and representatives will have much pull with Trump.

“In terms of trade policy, it’s very executive-driven these days,” said Alfredo Carrillo Obregon, a trade policy analyst at the Cato Institute in Washington.

“Even if Congress did (push back), it probably wouldn’t have made a difference,” he said.

Even AAF, a conservative think tank and policy advocacy organization, doubts that Republican candidate pushback and the potential damage to deep-red states by the trade war will sway Trump.

“It does not seem like Trump seems to care … whether tariffs are popular or not or whether people are being harmed or not,” Stern acknowledged.

Sands also expressed dismay at the president’s apparent indifference to the electoral costs his tariffs and spat with Canada May bring.

“His indifference to the fate of his party in Congress is … pretty unusual,” he said.

While many believe Trump will stick with his tariff agenda, whatever the cost to the GOP, election polling shows that a majority of Americans — amid today’s affordability crisis — oppose the tariffs.

“You don’t get very far in American politics by telling people, ‘I’ve got your vote in the bag, and I don’t care about you,’” Stern said.

The question for Nov. 3 is whether that opposition will translate into votes. As for what he hopes voters know heading into election day, Stern said he and his colleagues have been trying to educate Americans about tariffs.

“What I would like voters … to pull out of all this at the end of the day is to understand that tariffs are taxes,” he said.

“They’re not taxes on foreigners; they’re taxes on your own people, your own industries, your own businesses, and that this is not the solution.”

stories.title: Winter heating bills are about to soar for these homeowners
stories.summary: Trump’s war with Iran is sending heating costs for some Canadian homeowners surging.
stories.author: Garrett Barry
stories.content:
ST. John’s - With higher heating bills expected this winter, retiree Donna Lawlor is cutting back on travel, groceries and entertainment to keep her budget on track.

Lawlor is one of several thousand Newfoundlanders and Labradorians who heat their home with furnace oil. That group is facing a huge jump in bills this winter, with war in the middle east spiking fuel costs across Canada.

“My biggest fear is keeping the oil in the house, you know, keeping up with the price of the oil and the gas.”

On Oct. 3, furnace oil in St. John’s cost $2.16 per litre, almost a whole dollar more than it did on that same day in 2025.

For Lawlor, that means increasing her monthly budget for heat from $300 to $400 and trying her best to save elsewhere.

“I got to cut where I’m going,” she said. “I can’t go out and go run around like I used to, gas is so expensive.”

“I got to say, I’m pretty good with money. Because if I wasn’t, I wouldn’t be able to stay here and run this house.”

The U.S. war with Iran that started in February brought a disruption in the global oil market, sending prices to a three-year high.

Prices peaked in May, and following a short slide in June, are once again elevated just in time for Canadians to start turning their household furnaces back on for the winter.

Oil heat is disproportionately popular in Quebec and Atlantic Canada, but remains highest on P.E.I. where more than half of homes relied on oil furnaces in 2020, according to Natural Resources Canada.

A standard 900-litre oil tank is set to cost $1950 to fill, following Oct. 3 prices in St. John’s. Taxes will push that bill to about $2240.

Those high bills and high tax shares have renewed calls for federal and provincial governments to remove more taxes from home heating products.

“The Carney government did move a little bit on the federal excise tax, the effect of that was only to drop diesel prices four cents per litre,” said Dan MacTeague, head of the Canadians for Affordable Energy lobby group.

“We’re flirting with three dollars a litre, not four cents.”

A Home Heating Supplement program in Newfoundland and Labrador will give $500 back to Lawlor and other families — provided their income was less than $150,000 in 2025 — who use oil heat for their homes.

The provincial government is also promising a 15 per cent break on electrical bills if the renegotiation of the controversial Churchill Falls hydroelectric deal reaches the finish line.

“Our government continues to look at all options when it comes to affordability measures and will have more to share in the near future,” a spokesperson for the Newfoundland and Labrador Department of Finance said in a statement.

“I got to cut where I’m going,” she said. “I can’t go out and go run around like I used to, gas is so expensive.”
“I got to say, I’m pretty good with money. Because if I wasn’t, I wouldn’t be able to stay here and run this house.”

content_blocks.caption: As a retiree, Donna Lawlor lacks one vital tool that could really help bring her budget back in line this winter: The ability to head back to the job market. (Garrett Barry/CTV News)

content_blocks.text: The U.S. war with Iran that started in February brought a disruption in the global oil market, sending prices to a three-year high.
Prices peaked in May, and following a short slide in June, are once again elevated just in time for Canadians to start turning their household furnaces back on for the winter.

Oil heat is disproportionately popular in Quebec and Atlantic Canada, but remains highest on P.E.I. where more than half of homes relied on oil furnaces in 2020, according to Natural Resources Canada.
A standard 900-litre oil tank is set to cost $1950 to fill, following Oct. 3 prices in St. John’s. Taxes will push that bill to about $2240.
Those high bills and high tax shares have renewed calls for federal and provincial governments to remove more taxes from home heating products.

“The Carney government did move a little bit on the federal excise tax, the effect of that was only to drop diesel prices four cents per litre,” said Dan MacTeague, head of the Canadians for Affordable Energy lobby group.
“We’re flirting with three dollars a litre, not four cents.”

A Home Heating Supplement program in Newfoundland and Labrador will give $500 back to Lawlor and other families — provided their income was less than $150,000 in 2025 — who use oil heat for their homes.
The provincial government is also promising a 15 per cent break on electrical bills if the renegotiation of the controversial Churchill Falls hydroelectric deal reaches the finish line.

“Our government continues to look at all options when it comes to affordability measures and will have more to share in the near future,” a spokesperson for the Newfoundland and Labrador Department of Finance said in a statement.

stories.title: Quebec author admits to plagiarism in earlier work, denies AI use
stories.summary: In a statement released by his publisher, Éditions du Boréal, Orélien apologized for making what he described as unacceptable mistakes in his youth.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Quebec author Thélyson Orélien is admitting he plagiarized other writers in his earlier work, but maintains he didn’t use artificial intelligence to write his acclaimed novel.

In a statement released by his publisher, Éditions du Boréal, Orélien apologized for making what he described as unacceptable mistakes in his youth.

He also rejected allegations that his novel, C’était ça ou mourir, was written using AI.

Orélien says he began writing the novel in 2017 and finished writing the first draft in 2019.

He says no sentence in the book was generated by a machine.

The statement comes after allegations surfaced in October about the novel’s possible use of AI and plagiarism in Orélien’s earlier writings.

The prestigious French literature prize, the Académie Goncourt, subsequently removed the novel from its selection while Boréal suspended promotional activities surrounding the book.

stories.title: Toronto cyclists ask Canada's top court to weigh in on Ford's bike lane removal plan
stories.summary: Toronto - Cyclists challenging Ontario's plan to remove major Toronto bike lanes are asking Canada's top court to hear their appeal.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Cyclists challenging Ontario’s plan to tear up Toronto bike lanes will ask the Supreme Court of Canada to weigh in, the groups backing the case said Tuesday, as more removal work was slated to begin.

The groups say a recent Appeal Court decision in their case goes beyond bike lanes and raises the question of under what circumstances a government can pursue life-risking policies.

“The facts are clear: bike lanes do not cause traffic congestion, ripping them out will put people’s lives at risk, and no network of side streets can replace the 19 (kilometres) of protected bike lanes on Bloor, Yonge, and University,” said Michael Longfield, executive director of Cycle Toronto, an advocacy group that brought the case.

Work was scheduled to begin Tuesday to start removing bike lanes along a stretch of Bloor Street West, the province said. A spokesperson for Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria did not immediately respond to emailed questions about where the work was taking place, how long it would last, or at what cost.

“The people of Ontario gave our government a clear mandate to tackle the traffic that is costing our economy over $56 billion a year by removing the bike lanes on some of Toronto’s busiest streets,” Dakota Brasier wrote.

The request for Canada’s top court to weigh in is the latest chapter in a legal case over a 2024 law empowering the province to take out bikes lanes on those three major Toronto roads, a move framed by the province as a bid to cut down on traffic congestion. The legislation also required municipalities to seek approval to install new bike lanes that cut into traffic.

A spokesperson for Mayor Olivia Chow said the city repeatedly shared with the province designs that keep both vehicle and bike lanes intact. Work has already been completed to restore a car lane and keep the bike lane on a short stretch of Bloor Street between Kipling and Islington subway stations.

The Toronto bike lane removal plan was initially blocked by a lower court judge who found it to be an unconstitutional risk to cyclist safety. The judge ruled the government pursued the plan despite its own advisers finding it would not accomplish its stated goal to reduce traffic congestion, and could possibly make it worse. Even accepting that goal at face value, the judge found it to be way of step with the law’s intent.

But that decision was overturned by the Ontario Court of Appeal in August.

In a strongly worded ruling, a panel of three judges said the lower court had effectively created a right to bike lanes where none existed. The trial judge, they found, had not only misapplied the law, but improperly strayed into the legislature’s domain of policy-making and political considerations.

Anyone who receives a judgment from a top provincial or territorial court can seek leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. The Supreme Court only hears a fraction of those cases, which typically must involve a key constitutional question, conflicting lower court decisions or a new issue of law.

“This case is about the scope of the protections provided by Section 7 of the Charter to everyone’s rights to life and security of the person. We’re asking the Supreme Court to hear this appeal to bring clarity to this broader legal question,” said Bronwyn Roe of Ecojustice, an environmental law charity backing the case.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.
