stories.title: Ontario to move northwest regions to permanent daylight time
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario is set to move parts of the province's northwest region to permanent daylight time in order to align with Manitoba, Indigenous Affairs Minister Greg Rickford told The Canadian Press.
stories.author: Liam Casey The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Ontario is set to move parts of the province’s northwest region to permanent daylight time in order to align with Manitoba, Indigenous Affairs Minister Greg Rickford told The Canadian Press.

Rickford said there is overwhelming consensus among municipalities, First Nations and businesses to make the time change permanent.

The province intends to make a regulatory change in the Time Act on Nov. 1 to allow regions west of the 90th meridian to align with Manitoba, he said.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew announced last month the province would stop twice-annual clock changes and stay on daylight time year-round in the central time zone, leaving it one hour ahead of the other Prairie provinces rather than aligned with them.

“That put northwestern Ontario, who sits in the central standard time zone, in a bit of a spot, to say the least,” Rickford said.

The province had three options, he said.

One, the northwestern region could shift to eastern time to align with the rest of the province. Two, they could continue on with time changes, but then they’d be out of step with the rest of Ontario and Manitoba.

“The other option ... we took by unanimous consensus, was to not change our clocks and go to what I’m calling Wab Kinew time,” Rickford said.

Much of the province’s northwest jumped into action after Kinew’s announcement to figure out a way forward. Rickford said the province reached out to municipalities, businesses and First Nations to get their thoughts.

“What ended up coming back was overwhelmingly unanimous, 90 to 94 per cent from every survey,” he said.

New Democrat Sol Mamakwa, who represents the riding of Kiiwetinoong that is home to the majority of Ontario’s remote, fly-in First Nations, also helped figure out a way forward.

“After having brought the voices of our communities across the northwest to the table, we are happy the advocacy to observe daylight savings will be implemented permanently,” Mamakwa said in a statement.

“We are proud of our collaborative efforts to deliver what works for the North. We thank everyone who reached out and shared their thoughts on this important decision.”

British Columbia said in March that it was moving to permanent Pacific daylight time.

Alberta also switched to permanent daylight time this year in what it calls Alberta time, which means it now has the same time as Saskatchewan year round.

stories.title: Quebec author admits past plagiarism, denies AI use in novel
stories.summary: Quebec author Thélyson Orélien maintains he didn't use artificial intelligence to write his novel, which was nominated for a prestigious French literature prize.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - The Quebec author of an acclaimed novel has admitted there was plagiarism in some of his earlier work, but denies allegations that he used artificial intelligence to write his latest book.

The novel by Thélyson Orélien, “C’était ça ou mourir,” which translates to “It was either that or dying,” came under scrutiny last month over allegations of AI use. This was followed by other news reports that raised questions about passages in the author’s previous work.

In a statement released Tuesday by his publisher, Éditions du Boréal, Orélien apologized for making what he described as unacceptable mistakes in his youth.

He said that after leaving Haiti following the 2010 earthquake, he became fascinated by the work of numerous authors, but acknowledged that he had crossed a line.

“Admiration does not give you the right to take, to claim as your own texts that are not yours,” he wrote.

However, he rejected allegations that his novel was written using AI, saying no sentence was generated by a machine. He acknowledged using tools for research, for example, to look up foreign-language expressions.

“I wrote this novel myself,” he said, adding that the story was inspired by his experiences and those of other migrants.

Orélien also said journalists have the right to investigate his work and readers are free to criticize it, but condemned what he described as weeks of threats, racist harassment and public attacks.

“What I am going through is cruel,” he wrote. “By attributing a text, one that is mine (...) to a machine, they have not only called into question my status as a writer but also my humanity.”

He said his past mistakes May raise legitimate questions but should not be treated as proof that his novel was generated by AI.

“I did not write this book to win prizes or become famous,” he wrote. “I have nothing to prove to those who accuse me.”

The allegations first surfaced last month when a social media account using the name “Balance ton Claude” shared an analysis of Orélien’s novel using AI-detection software Pangram. The account alleged that much of it May have been AI-generated.

Samuel Fitoussi, a columnist for the French newspaper Le Figaro and one of the people behind the project, said the group tested several other books, and none received similarly high AI-detection scores.

Fitoussi defended publishing the findings, arguing readers should know whether they are reading human-written or AI-generated work.

The controversy expanded when La Presse reported that articles attributed to Orélien and published between 2012 and 2014 contained passages also found in previously published work by other authors.

The newspaper said it used Pangram to identify paragraphs that appeared to have been plagiarized.

When CP put an excerpt of the novel through Pangram on Friday, a message on the platform stated the text was “a mix of AI and human-written content.”

The novel by Thélyson Orélien, “C’était ça ou mourir,” which translates to “It was either that or dying,” came under scrutiny last month over allegations of AI use. This was followed by other news reports that raised questions about passages in the author’s previous work.
In a statement released Tuesday by his publisher, Éditions du Boréal, Orélien apologized for making what he described as unacceptable mistakes in his youth.
He said that after leaving Haiti following the 2010 earthquake, he became fascinated by the work of numerous authors, but acknowledged that he had crossed a line.
“Admiration does not give you the right to take, to claim as your own texts that are not yours,” he wrote.

However, he rejected allegations that his novel was written using AI, saying no sentence was generated by a machine. He acknowledged using tools for research, for example, to look up foreign-language expressions.
“I wrote this novel myself,” he said, adding that the story was inspired by his experiences and those of other migrants.
Orélien also said journalists have the right to investigate his work and readers are free to criticize it, but condemned what he described as weeks of threats, racist harassment and public attacks.
“What I am going through is cruel,” he wrote. “By attributing a text, one that is mine (...) to a machine, they have not only called into question my status as a writer but also my humanity.”

stories.title: Key figure in Pearson airport gold heist testifying at trial of another accused man
stories.summary: A man who admitted his role in the massive gold heist at Toronto's Pearson airport is testifying today at the trial of another man accused in the case.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
A man who admitted his role in the massive gold heist at Toronto’s Pearson airport told a Brampton, Ont., court that he melted and sold some of the gold before travelling to Pakistan, where he claims he was kidnapped and abused to give up the loot.

Arsalan Chaudhary started testifying Tuesday in the trial of Parmpal Sidhu, a former Air Canada employee who has pleaded not guilty to charges of theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence in the April 2023 heist.

Prosecutors allege that Sidhu provided a doctored waybill that allowed another man to pick up more than $22 million in gold and currency from a Pearson airport cargo bay in what investigators have called one of the largest gold heists in Canadian history.

Chaudhary, who was sentenced this spring to four years in prison after pleading guilty to theft over $5,000, told Sidhu’s trial that he planned the heist with Simran Preet Panesar, who is wanted by authorities.

He said they divided boxes full of one-ounce gold bars and he took 30 per cent of the boxes while Panesar took 70 per cent.

“That’s the deal we made,” he said. “I didn’t know at first it was going to happen. So, I was like ‘OK, and if it does happen, 30 per cent of that, I’m pretty happy with it.'”

Chaudhary said he didn’t really know Sidhu and that he only called or texted him when he couldn’t get a hold of Panesar.

He said the gold bars had TD Bank markings and he took his share to a condo in the Greater Toronto Area, adding that he doesn’t remember its address. Chaudhary said he started melting the gold for sale, acquiring $200,000 to $300,000 in cash.

“Whatever gold I had, I started melting it … I had a machine, a gold melting machine,” he said. “It’s not brain surgery. It’s pretty simple: Turn it on, heat it up, put it in there, it melts.”

He said he doesn’t recall how much gold he melted each time nor how much of his share he melted, but said he was doing it so the gold could not be traced.

Chaudhary said he travelled to Mexico and Portugal before he ended up in Pakistan to “invest the money and buy a business or something.”

He testified that a group of people in police uniforms abducted him in Pakistan and abused him, so he was forced to let people they worked with take the remaining gold and cash from his condo in Canada, as well as the cash he left at his cousin’s house in Pakistan.

“They took me to (an) area. I was blindfolded so I couldn’t tell. When I got there they abused me,” he testified. “Before they could do anything further, I … told them, ‘I will give you everything. You don’t need to do anything. You have me. My life is worth more than any money.'”

Chaudhary said he believed the kidnappers learned he had money from a man he met in Pakistan, who had helped him procure his gold-melting machine and transfer cash from Canada to Pakistan.

He said the kidnappers let him go and he went to Dubai, where he stayed at his cousin’s house looking for work until he came back to Canada on Jan. 12, 2026.

As part of his sentencing, Chaudhary was given 40 years to pay back $22 million in restitution.

“All of this was not even worth it. I destroyed people’s lives. I did everything for nothing,” he said on the witness stand. “Now, I’m here.”

The Crown asked Chaudhary about text and group chat messages related to the heist, but he repeatedly said he did not remember or recall the content of these conversations, nor who was involved in them.

The stolen gold and foreign currency were ordered from Zurich, Switzerland, and transported in the hull of an Air Canada flight to Toronto, police said when they released details of the investigation dubbed Project 24K. The shipment was then brought to an Air Canada cargo facility at the airport, police said.

Later that day, a suspect presented a fraudulent airway bill to warehouse employees, who loaded the shipment onto his five-tonne truck, police alleged.

Chaudhary is expected to continue his testimony on Wednesday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

Maan Alhmidi, The Canadian Press

stories.summary: In some cases, the activities can result in violent and/or criminal behaviour, Durham Regional Police said in a social media post.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Police in Durham Region are warning parents, caregivers and the community about an increase in online threats involving coordinated groups they call “The Com.”

“The Com,” or the Community as it’s also known as, is a network of online predators who use a variety of tactics to exploit young people. The network uses manipulation, coercion , grooming and intimidation to build trust and create secrecy through fear or shame to then pressure victims into harmful or unsafe activities.

In some cases, the activities can result in violent and/or criminal behaviour, Durham Regional Police said in a social media post.

This has included coercing victims to participate in crimes such as making hoax 911 calls, online attacks, or sharing harmful content that police say they don’t realize the seriousness of doing so.

Children and youth aged eight to 17 are the primary target of “The Com,” and are communicated with through online platforms such as Discord, Telegram, Snapchat, Roblox, Minecraft, Twitch and Steam.

Police say they have recently responded to a number of incidents in the community they believe are linked to the predatory group.

Among the tactics used are building trust through friendship or romance, manipulating youth with fear, guilt or intimidation and forcing compliance through threats such as exposing private information, doxing, or swatting.

Victims are also coerced into harmful or unsafe activities including creating or sharing inappropriate and exploitative images or victims, engaging in self-harm or harm towards others or animals or displaying concerning usernames, symbols or messages.

Parents, caregivers and members of the community are encouraged to watch for behaviour patterns in children and youth.

This can include using encrypted apps like Discord or Telegram without parental knowledge, showing an increased or secretive use of phones or electronic devices, a change in mood or declining performance in school, or an interest in extreme or harmful online ideologies.

Authorities caution one of these signs May not be a problem, but “multiple indicators” could prompt action. Police are urging parents to talk with their children about the risks of sharing personal information or images online, and to ask direct, non-judgmental questions about the platforms they use and people they interact with.

If people notice any concerning online activity or people on online platforms they believe could pose a safety risk, they should report it to police at 1-888-579-1520.

stories.title: ‘New norm’: election signs missing and vandalized across Manitoba
stories.summary: More campaign signs are being vandalized and going missing in Winnipeg and Portage la Prairie for this year's election, council candidates say.
stories.author: Toni De Guzman
stories.content:
More campaign signs are being vandalized and going missing in Winnipeg and Portage la Prairie ahead of this year’s municipal elections , council candidates say.

Throughout the campaign, Chris Sweryda says his signs have disappeared and more voters in the ward are afraid of putting signs up because it could attract vandalism and damage.

A slew of his orange and teal signs along Hespeler Avenue were vandalized, Sweryda says.

“It’s quite upsetting. It certainly is a drain in the campaign and takes time from dealing with the actual issues in this ward,” he said, noting he has spent around $9,000 dollars on signage with each sign costing around $22.50 depending on size.

Council candidates Nafiya Naso and Jasmine Brar in the Waverley West ward also had their signs spray-painted with hurtful messages and ripped apart in August and September.

“It’s not just in Winnipeg. It’s everywhere, and sadly I think it’s just become the new norm,” said Naso in a telephone interview on Monday.

A Portage la Prairie councillor seeking re-election said more than half of his signs are gone and a few other candidates in the area are also losing theirs.

“It has been a pretty big issue this year,” said Colin Doyle, a councillor candidate in Portage la Prairie. “It took them some time to actually do this amount of damage to the signs, and they’re not easy things to destroy either.”

His signs were ripped, mangled, and soiled, images reviewed by Global News show.

Watch the video above for the full story.

stories.title: Carney addresses Alberta separation referendum in Thanksgiving message
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney focused his Thanksgiving Day message on Alberta’s upcoming separation referendum, saying Canada is "worth fighting for."
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija and Lisa Johnson
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney focused his Thanksgiving Day message on Alberta’s upcoming separation referendum , saying Canada is “worth fighting for.”

“This year, Thanksgiving is a bit different,” he said in the video message. “A week from today, Albertans will have the opportunity to make an important decision about their future: whether to remain part of Canada or begin a long and uncertain process through which Alberta could separate from Canada.”

Albertans will vote on Oct. 19 on whether the province should stay in Canada or hold a second, binding separation referendum.

In the video posted Monday and filmed in his old high school in Edmonton, Carney noted he grew up in Alberta.

Carney said the federal government is building “big things” in Alberta, including a new pipeline to the West Coast, but that Canada can’t achieve those goals if the country is divided. “You can’t build big things on fault lines,” he said.

Carney also said the country must be strong as it faces threats to its economy, security and culture, and that we are “stronger together.”

“Generations of Albertans helped build this country. It’s yours, it’s ours, and it’s worth fighting for,” he said.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is scheduled to speak in Calgary on Friday, urging the province to stay within Canada.

In his own Thanksgiving message, BC NDP Leader David Eby, who is in the middle of a provincial election campaign, encouraged Albertans to vote for unity with Canada. He said the two provinces have bonds of family, friendship and business and are “stronger together.”

stories.title: Rides closed at Canadian theme parks after deadly U.S. fall from Six Flags coaster
stories.summary: Rides at two Canadian theme parks have been closed after a man in the United States reportedly fell to this death from a Six Flags roller-coaster in Georgia.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Rides at two Canadian theme parks were closed after a man in the United States fell to this death from a Six Flags roller-coaster in Georgia.

Two rides at Canada’s Wonderland in Toronto and another at La Ronde in Montreal were temporarily shuttered “out of an abundance of caution,” the parks said. Six Flags owns Wonderland and recently sold La Ronde.

stories.title: Canada joins other nations denouncing Iran’s air base attack plot in the UK
stories.summary: Canada has joined more than two dozen other countries in denouncing Iran’s apparent involvement in a planned attack on an air base in England.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
Canada has joined more than two dozen other countries in denouncing Iran’s apparent involvement in a planned attack on an air base in England.

The countries said in a joint statement Monday they “condemn in the strongest terms Iran’s use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners.”

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday that a suspected terror plot at a U.S.-run military air base last month was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Revolutionary Guard.

“We recognise the United Kingdom’s attribution of Iran’s involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford on 27 September,” the statement says.

“The UK has also confirmed this event demonstrates the Irgc’s continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks and proxy actors.”

The statement also notes a “recent campaign of attacks across Europe targeting Jewish communities, Iranian journalists and U.S. interests, claimed by Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya,” a pro-Iran group.

The signatories include the United States, France, Germany and Australia, among others. They say any attempt by Iran to threaten individuals on their territory through proxies is unacceptable.

“Anyone who conducts hostile activities on behalf of Iran, or any other state, should know that we will take action to identify, investigate, disrupt and prosecute these acts,” the statement says.

Police have arrested seven men in the investigation into the alleged plot at RAF Fairford, but all suspects have been released on bail and no one has been charged so far.

The RAF Fairford air base has been used by American bombers to strike Iran in the ongoing war.

Iran has denied involvement, although it has previously said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.

stories.title: Storm to bring up to 60 millimetres of rain to parts of Ontario, Quebec
stories.summary: A weather system moving into Ontario and Quebec could bring heavy rainfall through much of Tuesday with thunderstorms also possible.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Some Ontarians and Quebecers will need to grab those umbrellas Tuesday as parts of both provinces could see up to 60 millimetres of rain depending on where people live.

In Ontario, eastern parts of the province are under special weather statements with Environment Canada forecasting a low pressure system will move eastward bringing showers and thunderstorms.

The agency warns local rainfall amounts could range from 40 to 60 mm, with Kingston, Peterborough, Picton, Parry Sound and Haliburton among those affected.

There is also the possibility of severe thunderstorms forming, along with heavy rainfall, this afternoon.

The stormy weather is expected to clear from west to east this afternoon or early this evening, Environment Canada said.

Next door in Quebec, special weather statements and yellow rainfall warnings are in effect for southern parts of the province due to a “nearly stationary” warm front that’s associated with a low pressure system moving south of the border.

According to Environment Canada, the Bois-Francs and Eastern Townships areas could see 30 to 50 mm between Tuesday morning and late Wednesday night or early Thursday morning.

Yellow warnings are also in place in the Montreal, Vaudreauil and Monteregie areas from Tuesday morning until the evening.

In those areas, the rainfall could reach 40 to 60 mm, with the agency warning water will likely pool on roads and in low-lying areas. Visibility could also be suddenly reduced at times.

stories.title: AI hacking will be more common if changes aren’t made, scientists warn
stories.summary: Dozens of Canadian academics are among an international group of scientists calling for better containment measures for AI models.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
Dozens of Canadian academics are among an international group of scientists calling for better containment measures for AI models.

“Multiple organizations have disclosed high-profile security failures: their AI models bypassed insufficiently sandboxed environments to compromise the systems of external organizations,” they say in an open letter.

The letter, released Tuesday, says that unless immediate changes are made to how AI is developed and deployed, “such incidents will continue to occur, and future incidents will be far more damaging to our exposed critical infrastructure.”

They say there is a need for more research on AI safety as well as emphasis on containment technologies and procedures. The scientists also want to see an international body that standardizes best practices.

“In the short term, strong sandboxing mechanisms including airgapping (disconnecting from the internet) should be used to provide high-assurance containment of cyber-capable AI models,” the letter says.

The Canadian signatories to the letter include AI pioneers Yoshua Bengio and Geoffrey Hinton, as well as Nicolas Papernot and Catherine Régis, who co-lead the research program at the Canadian AI Safety Institute. Johns Hopkins University professor Gillian Hadfield, who was recently named to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s new AI advisory council, is also on the list.

stories.title: More than 220K cast advance votes in 2026 Toronto election, city says
stories.summary: More than 220,000 people cast ballots during advanced voting in the upcoming Toronto municipal election – a new record.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
More than 220,000 people cast ballots during advance voting in the upcoming Toronto municipal election – a new record.

The City of Toronto said Tuesday that 222,550 eligible voters went to the polls during the six days of advance voting, which began on Oct. 6 and ended on Oct. 11.

The city said 36,743 voters cast ballots on Oct. 6, 31,018 voters did on Oct. 7 and 28,666 voters turned out on Oct. 8.

On Oct. 9, 33,579 voters headed to the polls, and 39,181 voters followed suit on Oct. 10. Oct. 11 saw the highest turnout of all the advance voting days with 53,363 voters casting ballots.

The advance turnout for the 2026 election surpasses figures seen in previous advanced votes.

The city said 129,745 advance votes were cast in the 2023 mayoral by-election, compared to 115,911 advanced votes in the 2022 election, 124,299 advanced votes in the 2018 election, 161,147 advanced votes in 2014 and 77,365 advance votes in 2010.

The next time Torontonians can vote is between 10 a.m. and 8 p.m. on Oct. 26 – election day.

stories.title: Cineplex posts record $45.1M box office revenue for September
stories.summary: Cineplex says Spider-Man: Brand New Day and the Odyssey helped drive the results as both movies generated exceptional attendance across its premium offerings.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Cineplex Inc. says its box office revenue totalled $45.1 million in September to set a record for the month, up from $37.7 million a year earlier.

The movie theatre company says the result brought its third-quarter box office revenue to a record $215.7 million, up from $159.5 million in the same quarter last year.

The increase came as third quarter box office revenue per patron topped $14 for the first time as moviegoers increasingly chose premium formats.

Cineplex says Spider-Man: Brand New Day and the Odyssey helped drive the results as both movies generated exceptional attendance across its premium offerings.

It says September also benefited from the performance of Resident Evil.

Cineplex CEO Bill Walker says the consistency over the past several quarters, including a record-setting third quarter, reflect the appeal of the theatrical experience.

stories.title: B.C. party leaders make campaign stop at Vancouver trade board ahead of election
stories.summary: The leaders of B.C.'s three major political parties will pitch their plans to business leaders in Vancouver with less than two weeks to go before the provincial election.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The leaders of British Columbia’s three major political parties will pitch their plans to business leaders in Vancouver with less than two weeks to go before the provincial election.

NDP Leader David Eby, Conservative interim leader Lorne Doerkson and Green Party Leader Emily Lowan are slated to speak at an event this afternoon hosted by the Greater Vancouver Board of Trade.

The leaders won’t debate each other, though each will address attendees.

That will be followed by a question-and-answer session with board president Bridgitte Anderson.

The board says the event is designed to allow people to hear directly from the leaders as they present their vision for the province and discuss their priorities for B.C.’s future.

A televised leaders’ debate is set for Wednesday ahead of election day on Oct. 24.

stories.title: Former political rivals Notley, Kenney to unite at event ahead of separation vote
stories.summary: Two former premiers who were on the opposite ends of the political spectrum in Alberta will unite Tuesday to keep the province from quitting Canada.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Two former premiers who were on the opposite ends of the political spectrum in Alberta will unite Tuesday to keep the province from quitting Canada.

Jason Kenney and Rachel Notley are set to speak at an event in the province’s capital.

The Edmonton Chamber of Commerce is hosting them.

Kenney was premier under the United Conservative Party, defeating Notley’s NDP government in 2019.

The event comes days before Albertans vote on 10 questions in a referendum on Monday.

The most contested one will ask whether the province should stay in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

stories.title: Two-bedroom Victorian home in Toronto’s Riverdale locks in one offer at full price
stories.summary: About 100 potential buyers toured the 141-year-old home, but only one returned with an offer
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
231 Boulton Ave., Toronto

Asking price: $899,000 (September, 2026)

Selling price: $899,000 (September, 2026)

Previous selling price: Not available

Taxes: $5,002 (2025)

Days on the market: Seven

Listing agents: Shane Little and Jenny Simon, Sage Real Estate Ltd.

This 141-year-old Victorian needed extensive updating, a deficit that could have turned off buyers around Gerrard Street and Broadview Avenue. The owner tackled some jobs, such as replacing the flooring and repainting the interiors, before listing the home for $899,000 in September.

“There was definitely some work to be done,” agent Shane Little said. “We wanted to present it in a way buyers could connect with it. We priced it where we did to get people through the door.”

About 100 potential buyers toured the home, including 75 guests at three open houses. Only one returned with an offer on the presentation date, but it matched the full asking price.

“In the east end, there were 11 homes that came out on the same day we listed,” Mr. Little said.

“Some of them didn’t sell on their offer nights and ended up relisting. Buyers at that price point are really discerning.”

The brick row home has 998 square feet of living space, including two full bathrooms, and two bedrooms on the second floor.

There is a living room with an original, wood-burning fireplace and a recreation area in the basement.

The dining area is next to a kitchen with sliding doors to a deck and yard. A back gate opens to a parking spot and a laneway behind the 14- by 90-foot lot.

“It’s only a two-bedroom home, but the primary bedroom has vaulted ceilings, a semi-ensuite bathroom and a walk-in closet, which people really loved,” Mr. Little said.

“People also connect with its heritage as a Victorian, and its location in Riverside. Having parking out back was a huge bonus.”

stories.title: A timeline of key events in the Regis Korchinski-Paquet case
stories.summary: A coroner's inquest is scheduled to start in the case of Regis Korchinski-Paquet who fell from a Toronto highrise balcony while police were in her home in 2020.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A coroner’s inquest is scheduled to start Tuesday in the case of Regis Korchinski-Paquet , a 29-year-old Afro-Indigenous woman who fell from a Toronto highrise balcony while police were in her home in 2020.

Here is a timeline of key events in the case:

May 27, 2020: The Special Investigations Unit says it is investigating the death of a woman who fell from a 24th-floor balcony while police were in the apartment. Korchinski-Paquet’s death sparks questions from her family, local politicians, and on social media about the role of police officers in the incident. In the days that follow, Korchinski-Paquet’s mother says she called police that day hoping they would take her daughter to the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health but instead the woman ended up dead.

May 30, 2020: Thousands of people take to the streets in Toronto to protest against racism and demand answers in Korchinski-Paquet’s case. Several smaller marches follow over the next few weeks.

June 3, 2020: The SIU urges police to stop speaking on the case after Korchinski-Paquet’s family postpones meeting the watchdog, citing concerns about possible police leaks.

June 8, 2020: Two Toronto city councillors put forward a motion to defund the city’s police force by 10 per cent and use the money for community resources.

June 10, 2020: Korchinski-Paquet’s family says it will talk to the SIU.

June 11, 2020: The family holds a small funeral for her.

June 29, 2020: Toronto city council votes against defunding the police budget but approves numerous reforms to the service, including anti-racism measures and the implementation of body-worn cameras.

July 25, 2020: Family, friends and community members gather for a memorial and walk to honour Korchinski-Paquet.

Aug. 26, 2020: The SIU clears police of wrongdoing in her death, finding the officers tried to de-escalate the situation and “though their efforts were unsuccessful,” none of them broke the law. Korchinski-Paquet’s family rejects the findings.

Feb. 3, 2021: Toronto announces a pilot project to send crisis-support workers instead of police to certain 911 calls in the city. The pilot, set to begin the following year, comes after widespread calls for police reform, including improvements to how police deal with those experiencing mental-health crises.

May 26, 2021: A lawyer for Korchinski-Paquet’s family says they recently filed a complaint with the Office of the Independent Police Review Director because they believe the report by the SIU doesn’t make sense. The Oiprd confirms it is investigating but declines to comment further, citing confidentiality.

June 19, 2021: Korchinski-Paquet’s relatives speak at Juneteenth event in Ottawa aimed at demanding accountability and changes to the justice system. Several Black and Indigenous families whose loved ones were harmed or killed by police also attend the event organized by Black Lives Matter Toronto.

June 2022: Korchinski-Paquet’s family files a $10-million lawsuit against several police officers and the head of Ontario’s police watchdog, as well as Ontario’s attorney general, the City of Toronto and the Toronto Community Housing Corporation. Here is a timeline of key events in the case:

May 27, 2020: The Special Investigations Unit says it is investigating the death of a woman who fell from a 24th-floor balcony while police were in the apartment. Korchinski-Paquet’s death sparks questions from her family, local politicians, and on social media about the role of police officers in the incident. In the days that follow, Korchinski-Paquet’s mother says she called police that day hoping they would take her daughter to the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health but instead the woman ended up dead.
May 30, 2020: Thousands of people take to the streets in Toronto to protest against racism and demand answers in Korchinski-Paquet’s case. Several smaller marches follow over the next few weeks.
June 3, 2020: The SIU urges police to stop speaking on the case after Korchinski-Paquet’s family postpones meeting the watchdog, citing concerns about possible police leaks.
June 8, 2020: Two Toronto city councillors put forward a motion to defund the city’s police force by 10 per cent and use the money for community resources.
June 10, 2020: Korchinski-Paquet’s family says it will talk to the SIU.
June 11, 2020: The family holds a small funeral for her.
June 29, 2020: Toronto city council votes against defunding the police budget but approves numerous reforms to the service, including anti-racism measures and the implementation of body-worn cameras.
July 25, 2020: Family, friends and community members gather for a memorial and walk to honour Korchinski-Paquet.

Aug. 26, 2020: The SIU clears police of wrongdoing in her death, finding the officers tried to de-escalate the situation and “though their efforts were unsuccessful,” none of them broke the law. Korchinski-Paquet’s family rejects the findings.

Feb. 3, 2021: Toronto announces a pilot project to send crisis-support workers instead of police to certain 911 calls in the city. The pilot, set to begin the following year, comes after widespread calls for police reform, including improvements to how police deal with those experiencing mental-health crises.

May 26, 2021: A lawyer for Korchinski-Paquet’s family says they recently filed a complaint with the Office of the Independent Police Review Director because they believe the report by the SIU doesn’t make sense. The Oiprd confirms it is investigating but declines to comment further, citing confidentiality.

June 19, 2021: Korchinski-Paquet’s relatives speak at Juneteenth event in Ottawa aimed at demanding accountability and changes to the justice system. Several Black and Indigenous families whose loved ones were harmed or killed by police also attend the event organized by Black Lives Matter Toronto.

June 2022: Korchinski-Paquet’s family files a $10-million lawsuit against several police officers and the head of Ontario’s police watchdog, as well as Ontario’s attorney general, the City of Toronto and the Toronto Community Housing Corporation. The lawsuit alleges her relatives suffered severe emotional distress after they were provided with “misleading information” at the time of her death.
April 2, 2026: Coroner Dr. Richard Wells announces that an inquest into Korchinski-Paquet’s death will be held.

May 27, 2026: Korchinski-Paquet’s parents join advocates at the provincial legislature to call for reforms, including that the recommendations issued by coroner’s inquests be binding and implemented in a reasonable time frame.
Sept. 15, 2026: The date of the coroner’s inquest is announced.
Oct. 13, 2026: The coroner’s inquest begins.

stories.title: Cineplex reports record September box office revenue at $45.1 million
stories.summary: Toronto — Cineplex Inc. says its box office revenue totalled $45.1 million in September to set a record for the month, up from $37.7 million a year earlier.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Toronto — Cineplex Inc. says its box office revenue totalled $45.1 million in September to set a record for the month, up from $37.7 million a year earlier.

The movie theatre company says the result brought its third-quarter box office revenue to a record $215.7 million, up from $159.5 million in the same quarter last year.

The increase came as third quarter box office revenue per patron topped $14 for the first time as moviegoers increasingly chose premium formats.

Cineplex says Spider-Man: Brand New Day and the Odyssey helped drive the results as both movies generated exceptional attendance across its premium offerings.

It says September also benefited from the performance of Resident Evil.

Cineplex CEO Bill Walker says the consistency over the past several quarters, including a record-setting third quarter, reflect the appeal of the theatrical experience.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

Companies in this story: (TSX:CGX)

stories.title: Poilievre heads to Detroit to push for tariff-free trade
stories.summary: Ottawa — Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is scheduled to be in Detroit today where he says he will advocate for tariff-free trade, with a focus on the auto sector.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre was in Detroit on Tuesday to make a case for tariff-free trade in the auto sector.

Poilievre appeared on CNN, where he continued his pitch on the benefits of tariff-free trade.

“We have a 200-year-old relationship, there’s always going to be grievances on both sides of the border,” he said. “We have our grievances with the United States even predating this most recent trade dispute, but I would focus on what we can do together.”

At a news conference in Windsor, Ont. before crossing into the United States, Poilievre said he planned to meet with representatives of a General Motors plant in Detroit and officials from a Ford plant in nearby Dearborn, Mich.

He was also scheduled to meet with members of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers while in Michigan.

Poilievre said he would be joined by members of the Conservative caucus from the Windsor area.

The Conservative leader blamed the trade war for declining auto production on both sides of the border.

“The story is not rosy there either and that is because of this ridiculous trade war that is only helping China and other overseas competitors. We should not be fighting with each other while our risks and rivals abroad get stronger,” Poilievre said.

The trade war has emerged as a major factor in the U.S. midterm election race in Michigan, the heart the of the U.S. auto industry.

Despite having previously supported U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs, Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers released a video last week saying “Canada is not our enemy” and calling for an end to the trade war.

In a debate last week with his Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed, Rogers said he wants a deal with Canada and the current tariffs are too high.

The U.S. currently has a 25 per cent tariff on Canadian autos. President Trump has threatened to increase that tariff to 50 per cent on Jan. 1 in response to Canada’s counter-tariffs.

When asked about Trump’s adviser Peter Navarro recently warning that Canada would pay a price for any interference in the midterm elections, Poilievre said he doesn’t see his visit ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm vote as meddling.

“I think we’re going there to fight for tariff-free trade on both sides of the border and Americans want lower prices and more jobs and we’re offering a plan for them to have both,” Poilievre said.

Trump ended trade talks with Canada last year after Ontario aired an ad during the World Series using clips of former president Ronald Reagan criticizing tariffs and supporting free trade.

In August, Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered the Canadian negotiating team to call off trade talks with the U.S. after accusing the Americans of making unreasonable demands.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Coroner’s inquest set to begin examining death of Toronto woman who fell from balcony
stories.summary: An inquest is set to begin to examine the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet, a Toronto woman who fell from a highrise balcony while police were in her home more than six years ago.
stories.author: Paola Loriggio
stories.content:
A coroner’s inquest is set to begin Monday to examine the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet, a Toronto woman who fell from a highrise balcony while police were in her home more than six years ago.

Korchinski-Paquet, a woman of Ukrainian, Black and Indigenous ancestry, died on May 27, 2020 after police responded to calls about a family dispute at the apartment. She was 29.

Her death came on the heels of the police killing of George Floyd, a Black man from Minneapolis, spurring further protests amid growing calls to defund the police.

It also cast a spotlight on how police interact with people experiencing mental health crises.

Ontario’s police watchdog investigated the case and eventually cleared Toronto police of wrongdoing in Korchinski-Paquet’s death.

The Special Investigations Unit found it happened as she was trying to move from her apartment balcony to an adjacent one.

The inquest was announced earlier this year and is slated to last 14 days, with 15 witnesses expected to take the stand.

The inquest jury does not assign criminal responsibility but May make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths in the future. The chief coroner’s office does not have the authority to impose the recommendations, however.

On the anniversary of her death this year, Korchinski-Paquet’s parents joined advocates in calling for the recommendations issued in coroner’s inquests to be binding and implemented within a reasonable timeframe.

Her mother, Claudette Beals, also said there should be a different system in place to investigate allegations of wrongdoing against police officers, adding she has no faith in “police investigating police.”

“My daughter’s been gone for six years and no one’s held responsible for that,” she said in a news conference at the provincial legislature.

stories.title: Indigenous groups invest $65.3 million in Coastal GasLink pipeline in B.C.
stories.summary: Calgary - A group representing five First Nations says it has invested $65.3 million for an interest in the Coastal GasLink pipeline, which brings natural gas from northeastern B.C. to the LNG Canada plant in Kitimat — and is set for a big expansion.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary - A group representing five First Nations says it has invested $65.3 million for an interest in the Coastal GasLink pipeline, which brings natural gas from northeastern B.C. to the LNG Canada plant in Kitimat — and is set for a big expansion.

FN CGL Pipeline Ltd. Partnership said in a news release Tuesday that members are putting up their own funds.

“Our Nations are making this investment with their own capital. No government loan guarantees, no borrowed money,” said Chief Harley Chingee of McLeod Lake Indian Band.

“It was a deliberate choice, the best way to secure maximum benefits from what we believe to be a sound commercial investment. The returns will now belong entirely to the communities, as will decisions as to how they are used.”

Other members of the group are the Haisla Nation, Halfway River First Nation, Saulteau First Nations and West Moberly First Nations.

“This investment framework recognizes the importance of partnership, financial certainty and shared prosperity, while supporting our communities’ ability to make decisions about our own economic future,” Chief Roland Willson of West Moberly First Nations said.

TC Energy chief executive François Poirier congratulated the First Nations on completing the deal.

“This transaction reflects years of collaboration, leadership and determination by the Nations involved to create a long-term economic opportunity for their communities.”

Coastal GasLink runs 670 kilometres from northeastern B.C. to Kitimat, B.C., with a capacity of 2.1 billion cubic feet per day. It is operated by TC Energy Corp.

Under the deal, FN CGL and TC Energy collectively now hold an indirect 35 per cent interest in the pipeline through a TC subsidiary. The remaining 65 per cent is held by KKR Co. and Alberta Investment Management Corp. on behalf of certain clients.

“The structure provides stable cash flows without typical equity volatility, helping support long-term planning and managing of community priorities,” a spokesperson for TC Energy said in an emailed statement.

“It provides long-term predictable distributions, providing stable investment income while reducing risks associated with direct ownership.”

Tuesday’s deal is the first of two planned Indigenous investment transactions related to Coastal GasLink. TC Energy says a second transaction with another First Nations entity is expected to close in the fourth quarter of this year.

In 2022, TC Energy announced the signing of option agreements to sell a 10 per cent equity interest in the pipeline to Indigenous communities across the project corridor.

The company recently announced plans to double the existing capacity of the Coastal GasLink pipeline by adding new compressor stations and upgrading facilities.

For the second phase of the pipeline, LNG Canada — owned by Shell Canada and four Asian partners — is leading construction, limiting the Coastal GasLink owners’ spending and cost and schedule risk. The Coastal GasLink partners remain owners.

Construction is to begin in early 2027 and the expansion is set to come into service in the early 2030s.

The decision came after LNG Canada announced a final greenlight for the Phase 2 expansion of its facility, which enables natural gas chilled into a liquid state to be shipped across the Pacific. The first phase started up in the summer of 2025.

stories.title: Toronto condo owners reject low offers, sell $100,000 below what they paid
stories.summary: The one-bedroom unit’s west-facing, walkout terrace was an attractive feature for buyers
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
150 Sudbury St., No. 104, Toronto

Asking price: $619,900 (July, 2026)

Previous asking price: $619,900 (May, 2026)

Selling price: $595,000 (August, 2026)

Previous selling prices: $695,000 (November, 2021); $521,000 (October, 2017); $248,547 (August, 2012)

Taxes: $2,548 (2025)

Days on the market: 12

Property days on market: 96

Listing agent: Christopher Bibby, Re/Max Hallmark Bibby Group Realty

The owners bought this one-bedroom unit with a den at Westside Gallery Lofts, near Queen and Dufferin streets in 2021, at the height of the market, for $695,000. This year, needing more space, they decided to sell. Agent Christopher Bibby warned them that the ground-floor unit would likely sell far below what they paid, but that spring was a good season to show off its best asset: a west-facing terrace.

“There were some units on higher floors that had no exterior space or maybe a smaller 20-foot balcony,” Mr. Bibby said.

“This unit has a big walkout terrace that almost felt like you had a backyard. The condo corporation also allowed these owners to put up an enclosure for a lot more privacy.”

For three months, the unit’s asking price stayed at $619,900, during which time the sellers rejected two offers. After negotiations, they signed off on a third and closed the deal at $595,000.

“In the last few years, if your unit is unique, you’re going to do better than most,” Mr. Bibby said.

“We sold for $595,000 for a 670-square-foot unit. Around the same time, there was a sale for a 640-square-foot unit that went for $500,000.”

This roughly 15-year-old unit has a loftlike design with exposed concrete finishes and floor-to-ceiling windows in the den and living room.

The kitchen is across from a dining area and next to a bedroom with a semi ensuite bathroom.

The unit has a storage locker and one parking spot. Monthly fees of $539 cover water, heating and use of a gym.

“Years ago, Vogue magazine rated Queen West one of the top neighbourhoods in the world,” Mr. Bibby said.

“The Ossington strip, maybe two-and-a-half blocks away, has a handful of highly acclaimed and ranked restaurants.”

stories.title: Anthony Scaramucci on Trump, Carney, and the trade war
stories.summary: The Big Story discusses the relationship between Canada and the U.S. and how Americans view the trade war.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
It’s hard to think of a time in the modern age when relations between the U.S. and Canada were at a lower point. Since U.S. President Donald Trump started the trade war, tensions have risen, while Canadians’ opinion of our neighbour to the south have fallen. While some politicians and commentators south of the border have taken aim at Canada and Prime Minister Mark Carney’s handling of the relationship, others are glad someone is finally standing up to Trump.

Host Caryn Ceolin is speaking with Anthony Scaramucci, host of The Rest is Politics: US , former White House communications director, and managing partner at Skybridge Capital, about the relationship between Canada and the U.S., how Americans view the trade war, and why he believes Carney now “leads the west.”

stories.title: Warm temperatures gives way to cooler, unsettled stretch in London forecast
stories.summary: Londoners can expect one more taste of summer-like weather Tuesday before a cooler and wetter pattern settles into the region for the rest of the week.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Londoners can expect one more taste of summer-like weather Tuesday before a cooler and wetter pattern settles into the region for the rest of the week.

Environment Canada is calling for a mix of sun and cloud Tuesday, with temperatures climbing to a high of 26 C and a humidex value of 33. There’s a 40 per cent chance of showers early in the day and a 30 per cent chance of showers late in the afternoon, along with the risk of a thunderstorm.

The chance of showers and thunderstorms will linger into the evening before skies become partly cloudy overnight. The temperature is forecast to fall to 13 C.

A cooler air mass will arrive Wednesday, bringing mainly cloudy skies and a 30 per cent chance of morning showers. The daytime high is expected to reach 16 C before dipping to 7 C overnight.

The unsettled weather pattern is expected to continue through the remainder of the week.

Thursday’s forecast calls for cloudy conditions and a 30 per cent chance of showers, with a high of 14 C. Shower chances increase to 70 per cent Thursday night.

Friday is expected to remain cloudy with a 70 per cent chance of showers and windy conditions. The temperature is forecast to top out at 14 C before dropping to about 4 C overnight.

By Saturday, temperatures will cool further, with cloudy skies and a forecast high of just 9 C.

stories.title: Roller-coasters at Canada’s Wonderland, La Ronde closed after deadly fall at Georgia park
stories.summary: Several people were injured and one man died on Monday after witnesses described watching him come out of his seat on a ride at Six Flags Over Georgia
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Rides at two Canadian theme parks were closed after a man in the United States fell to this death from a Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia.

Two rides at Canada’s Wonderland in Toronto and another at La Ronde in Montreal were temporarily shuttered “out of an abundance of caution,” the parks said. Six Flags owns Wonderland and recently sold La Ronde.

A 42-year-old man was killed while riding a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday, prompting the theme park operator to close nine similar rides across Canada and the U.S. The man was thrown from his seat and struck other patrons before landing below the ride, police said Tuesday.

The Leviathan and Behemoth roller coasters at Canada’s Wonderland were closed, a spokesperson for the park said. There was no timeline for their reopening.

“The safety of our guests and team members remains on our highest priorities,” the spokesperson said in a written statement.

stories.title: In B.C., a dose of judge-made drug policy
stories.summary: A B.C. Supreme Court ruling overreaches by striking down the federal law of possession for the purpose of trafficking
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
The death toll from toxic street drugs in British Columbia and much of the rest of the country is both astonishing and horrifying. But even in the context of a public health emergency, a judge’s ruling striking down the federal law of possession for the purpose of trafficking in hopes of reducing the death toll is misbegotten – the latest example of judges dressing up political decisions as legal or constitutional ones.

The case before Justice Catherine Murray of the B.C. Supreme Court focused on two people who bought street drugs such as methamphetamines, cocaine and heroin from the dark web, tested them for fentanyl and other impurities at university labs and sold them at cost to drug users.

In essence, Justice Murray found that drug users have a constitutional right, under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, to be exempted from federal possession and trafficking laws in B.C., so they May receive a “safer supply.”

It’s worth elaborating on what Justice Murray is asking Ottawa to do. People who use drugs must be permitted a source of drugs not overseen by the medical profession. Such is their need to avoid withdrawal, they need near-instant access, and medical supervision doesn’t work for them. They cannot be denied what she frames as a non-medicalized supplier.

This is an extreme ruling, by any measure. To Justice Murray, it is justified by the extreme times in which drug users find themselves – 2,585 deaths in British Columbia in 2025, or seven a day. She has given Ottawa six months to make legislative reforms, which would necessarily apply across Canada. For what, exactly? Is she demanding Ottawa also allow exemptions for people who promise to test drugs purchased from organized crime? If the federal government proves unwilling to accept the cartels’ involvement, should it instead create a public-private partnership of some kind that would provide pharmaceutical-quality drugs to so-called compassion clubs for distribution? Would the simplest answer be to decriminalize possession? Make methamphetamines available without regulation?

It’s not hard to see that each of these solutions would also bring serious problems. And that is what happens when judges take it upon themselves, as Justice Murray did, to make policy decisions better left to government – though to be fair, governments and health regulators have not done a good job on the drugs crisis. For instance, the widespread distribution of hydromorphone, a safer alternative to street drugs, led to large-scale diversion, with the cash used to buy even more fentanyl. It was a well-intentioned disaster.

In reaching her conclusions, Justice Murray held a mini-inquiry of the street drug-using environment, assessed facts and came to certain judgments. It is challenging terrain, and some of her factual assessments are shaky. For instance, more than half of users who purchased the drugs went on to divert them to others. Did they use any resulting cash to buy other drugs, perhaps because they sought the fentanyl high? To what extent did this program simply add to the street drug supply? The judge’s answer, that any diversion May have actually enhanced public safety, seems speculative at best.

And what of the fact that drug-testing kits, which allow anyone to test drugs within five minutes, are widely available for free? Justice Murray accepted the view that drug users don’t like showing up at medical-related institutions (not even the downtown pharmacies where the kits are placed conveniently on the counter) because of “stigma,” which she says federal law has helped create. Yet thousands of these kits are in circulation each year in Vancouver.

We’ve seen other rulings in which various groups accuse government of putting their lives at risk. In Toronto last year, a judge effectively declared a constitutional right to bike lanes – a right mercifully tossed aside by an appeal court. Three years ago, the then Chief Justice of the B.C. Supreme Court, Christopher Hinkson, blocked B.C.’s law keeping drug users away from playgrounds and child-care spaces, during a period when normally illegal use was exempted from federal drug laws; his thought was that using drugs in public could save lives. These are extreme rulings that turn judges into policy-makers, and ignore legislators’ role in addressing social problems. (More on that later in the week.)

Fentanyl and other impurities have made street drugs more potent and deadly. But inventing a constitutional right to the non-medicalized provision of dangerous drugs has its own dire risks.

stories.title: Lions fans gather for watch party in London, Ont. as Detroit blows out Arizona
stories.summary: In what has been a roller coaster season so far for Detroit Lions fans, they couldn’t have picked a better game to have a watch party with a few hundred supporters.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
In what has been a roller coaster season so far for Detroit Lions fans, they couldn’t have picked a better game to have a watch party with a few hundred supporters.

Members of the ‘One Pride’ community packed the Canadian Brewhouse in north London, Ont. for the third annual stop on the Detroit Lions’ Raise the Roar Canadian Bar tour.

“As a Lions fan I love this,” said Aaron Bayer from London.

“Pulling up and seeing all the blue and white all that Honolulu Blue, it’s as close to being at a tailgate in Detroit as we get here right now.”

The past two years, the party was held on Dundas Place and the watch party inside Canada Life Place. This time, the Lions switched to a bar tour.

“I’m from Windsor, and me and my dad were season ticket holders back home, so it is awesome to see stuff like this,” said Lions fan Ryan Walker.

“It still seems like a decent enough crowd here. Obviously when it was downtown they had a bigger venue, different experience and they were able to put more stuff on. But I mean, I think they’ve done a good job here with what they’ve had.”

Outside in the parking lot, they had games and photo opportunities with a giant helmet and signs. Inside they had a DJ, the Lions cheerleaders, more games and a photo booth.

After an up and down 2-2 start to the year, this date couldn’t have been better to watch a game. Detroit blew out Arizona 45-17.

The Lions were granted marketing rights in Canada in April 2024 and hosted its first Canadian watch party later that year. There are two more area stops to come in Kitchener on Nov. 15 for the US Thanksgiving game, and in Windsor on Nov. 26.

“It’s nice seeing that Canada is getting stuff like this now,” added Walker.

“It’s nice that they finally saw that there’s a lot of fans in Ontario and to put something like this together is awesome, especially for the city.”

stories.title: Inquest begins in death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet who fell from balcony while police were in her home
stories.summary: Toronto woman died in 2020 after police responded to calls about a family dispute at the apartment
stories.author: Paola Loriggio
stories.content:
A Toronto woman who fell from a highrise balcony while police were in her home more than six years ago had a long history of seizures due to epilepsy, often followed by confusion and aggressive behaviour, a coroner’s inquest into her death heard Tuesday.

Regis Korchinski-Paquet had experienced two seizures the morning of May 27, 2020, hours before police were called in the late afternoon over a “rapidly developing and violent family disturbance that involved knives,” coroner’s counsel said.

Korchinski-Paquet herself had made three of the five calls to police, and a neurologist who heard the recordings told the inquest she sounded distressed and repetitive, as though she couldn’t remember her previous calls.

Less than half an hour later, Korchinski-Paquet, a woman of Ukrainian, Black and Indigenous ancestry, was dead, having fallen from the 24th-floor. She was 29.

“Today, we begin this inquest hoping to get answers, understand what happened and help ensure that people experiencing a crisis receive a safe and compassionate response from first responders,” her family said in a statement read to jurors.

“Regis brought people together across our city. Let’s take this opportunity to work towards meaningful change for the years to come.”

Police and paramedics were called on multiple occasions in the years preceding Korchinski-Paquet’s death, some of them related to her seizures and others including mentions of her seizures, according to an agreed narrative read at the inquest.

Medical records showed her seizures were often followed by symptoms such as “confusion, irritability, physically and verbally abusive behaviour and episodic amnesia,” the inquest heard.

Dr. Julien Hbert, a neurologist specializing in epilepsy who reviewed Korchinski-Paquet’s records for the inquest, testified that on several of those occasions, she showed patterns of behaviour in keeping with postictal delirium or psychosis, both mental states that can occur after seizures.

Postictal psychosis is marked by a disconnect from reality, while postictal delirium — the more common of the two — involves an altered state of awareness and confusion, though it can also include a disconnect from reality, he said.

In one incident in October 2017, an ambulance was called for Korchinski-Paquet after she appeared confused on a public transit bus, he said. She ended up walking out of the ambulance and into oncoming traffic, “suggesting that she had impairment in her appreciation of her environment and her awareness as well as her judgment,” the neurologist said.

Another incident in September 2019 “had several echoes of the situation that occurred on the day that Regis passed away,” Hbert said, including reports that she was being aggressive with her family and that a knife was involved. She had missed her anti-seizure medication that day, and even missing one dose can be enough to trigger a seizure, he said.

Hbert suggested several possible recommendations jurors could make, including increasing awareness of epilepsy and its potential effects.

“The knowledge that seizures and epilepsy can lead to a state of postictal delirium or postictal psychosis has not permeated all sort of strata in the society,” he said.

“So I think ... a first step would be to recognize that patients with epilepsy can have a phase after their seizure during which they will exhibit confusion, disorientation, behavioural changes and cognitive changes.”

The inquest’s scope includes how police and first responders are informed about epilepsy and how to ensure safety when a person’s behaviour May be influenced by postictal delirium, inquest counsel Roger Shallow said.

The inquest will not look into general mental health challenges or psychiatric care, however, or the investigations by various police watchdogs into the case, he said.

Korchinski-Paquet’s death was “sudden and profoundly tragic” and no matter what the jury concludes, her family has been left to grapple with a loss no one should experience, Shallow said.

”Regis Paquet was not an incident. She was not a file number. She was not simply the subject of an (Special Investigations Unit) investigation or coroner’s inquest,“ he said in his opening remarks.

”She was a daughter, a sister, an auntie, a member of a family, and a young woman whose life ended in circumstances that have had a profound impact on many people.“

Korchinski-Paquet’s death came on the heels of the police killing of George Floyd, a Black man from Minneapolis, spurring further protests amid growing calls to defund the police.

It also cast a spotlight on how police interact with people experiencing mental health crises.

Ontario’s police watchdog investigated the case and eventually cleared Toronto police of wrongdoing in Korchinski-Paquet’s death. The Special Investigations Unit found it happened as she was trying to move from her apartment balcony to an adjacent one.

The inquest was announced earlier this year and is slated to last 14 days, with 13 witnesses expected to take the stand. Korchinski-Paquet’s mother, father and brother have been named as potential witnesses, as have five of the six police officers who attended the scene.

The inquest jury does not assign criminal responsibility but May make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths in the future. The chief coroner’s office does not have the authority to impose the recommendations, however.

Korchinski-Paquet herself had made three of the five calls to police, and a neurologist who heard the recordings told the inquest she sounded distressed and repetitive, as though she couldn’t remember her previous calls.
Less than half an hour later, Korchinski-Paquet, a woman of Ukrainian, Black and Indigenous ancestry, was dead, having fallen from the 24th-floor. She was 29.

“Today, we begin this inquest hoping to get answers, understand what happened and help ensure that people experiencing a crisis receive a safe and compassionate response from first responders,” her family said in a statement read to jurors.
“Regis brought people together across our city. Let’s take this opportunity to work towards meaningful change for the years to come.”

Police and paramedics were called on multiple occasions in the years preceding Korchinski-Paquet’s death, some of them related to her seizures and others including mentions of her seizures, according to an agreed narrative read at the inquest.

Postictal psychosis is marked by a disconnect from reality, while postictal delirium — the more common of the two — involves an altered state of awareness and confusion, though it can also include a disconnect from reality, he said.

stories.title: Senior theatre company prepares for the Matchmaker at the Grand Theatre
stories.summary: Silver Spotlight Theatre Inc. (Ssti) is rehearsing for its first production as its own charitable non-profit.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Silver Spotlight Theatre Inc. (Ssti) is rehearsing for its first production as its own charitable non-profit.

The group of senior actors is rehearing three times per week in preparation for a five-day run of The Matchmaker production later this month.

“If you know the story for Hello Dolly!, the Matchmaker is what it’s based on,” said Rick Smith, director of the Matchmaker for Ssti.

“Dolly Levi is hired by Horace van der Gelder to find himself a new wife. Little does he know, her plan is to marry him herself. Along the way, she’s brought in other members of his of his crew and people he knows to mess things up a little bit so that she has a better chance of winning the prize at the end.”

In 2025 Ssti separated from the umbrella of Musical Theatre Productions which got them started in 2023. After doing musicals including Babes in Arms, Grease, Into the Woods and Showtune this will be the first non-musical production.

“I’ve wanted to work with this group for quite some time,” said Sam Sabathy, who plays Dolly and is doing her first Ssti production.

“I’ve seen all their shows and when I found out that they were doing a play, that’s their inaugural production for Ssti, I thought, I’ve got to audition and Rick picked me, so here we are.”

Sabathy has a degree in drama from Western University and studied in New York. She moved back to Canada and got into local theatre around Southwestern Ontario.

Over the past four years, the senior actors have not only made great shows but great friends.

“We have people that we’ve known through every production, but then also we meet new people,” said Mitchell Zimmer, who plays Rudolph in the play.

“We meet behind the scenes at restaurants, breakfasts, get togethers. It’s become bigger than just theatre, it’s family.”

Sabathy describes the cast and crew as having an “absolute blast”.

“We’re laughing every single night, and it’s just so much fun and encourage everyone to try and do it,” she said.

For this production, half of the cast is new to Ssti and others have experience with the company.

“You can see the development over the past five productions,” said Smith.

“They continue getting that support from our other experienced cast members. So, it really is that community and they’re all supportive of each other as we’ve gone through the process.”

The five-day run on the Auburn Stage at the Grand Theatre takes place Oct. 28-Nov. 1, 2026.

stories.title: A military underfunded, undermanned and underprepared
stories.summary: Benchmark Canada: “The armed forces of Canada have basically been left to rot,” says ex-navy chief Mark Norman. “I’m not overstating it.”
stories.author: National Post
stories.content:
Countries don’t typically get report cards, but there are hard facts that can be collated, assessed and compared. Enter Benchmark Canada , a new project from the Macdonald-Laurier Institute that brings together more than 40 different metrics that measure this nation’s performance . This fall, the National Post is examining many of those findings.

The radars watching over Canada’s Arctic region were designed when the Soviet Union was a country. The Royal Canadian Navy’s frigates and the Royal Canadian Air Force’s fighter jets are nearing the end of their useful lives. As Canada looks to reinvigorate its defence sector with billions of dollars in new spending, years of neglect May have left Canadian Forces short of the equipment they need to fight alongside their allies.

Canada is expected to put 25 per cent of its 2026 defence budget toward major equipment, according to Nato data compiled by Benchmark Canada, a Macdonald-Laurier Institute project that ranks the country against its allies. That would exceed Nato’s 20 per cent guideline for a second consecutive year, but leave Canada ranked 28 among the 31 allies measured.

“It’s somewhat troubling but not surprising,” said retired vice-admiral Mark Norman, a former commander of the Royal Canadian Navy and vice-chief of the defence staff.

Canada’s spending pales in comparison to figures for its European allies such as Poland at 55.9 per cent, Lithuania at 46 per cent and Hungary at 45 per cent. Only Italy, at 24.5 per cent, Croatia and Norway rank below Canada.

Meanwhile, a recent report by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce puts the average equipment share for the United States, Britain, France, Germany and Italy at 31.2 per cent, 6.2 percentage points above Canada’s estimate. France has about 202,000 military personnel, Germany 182,000 and Britain 126,000, compared with Canada’s 71,000.

Canada devoted just 11 per cent of its defence budget to equipment in 2015. Norman said military training, maintenance, spare parts and equipment purchases are often cut when budgets tighten because spending on salaries and bases is harder to reduce.

“The Armed Forces of Canada have basically been left to rot,” Norman said. “I’m not overstating it.”

An attitude shift is happening, spurred on by the Trump administration’s demand that its Nato allies increase defence spending to five per cent of GDP to alleviate the burden on the U.S. shouldering much of the alliance’s military capabilities.

Canada’s defence budget grew by 138 per cent between 2014 and 2025, compared with 125 per cent in Germany and less than 30 per cent in France and Britain, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce report found. Canadian spending reached about $64 billion, or two per cent of GDP, in 2025, and the Carney government has pledged to reach the target of five per cent of GDP by 2035.

Retired lieutenant-general Christopher Coates, a former deputy commander of Norad and director of the Macdonald-Laurier Institute’s foreign policy, national defence and national security program, said the increase reflects how low Canada’s spending had been.

“We were digging a hole,” he said. “That two per cent (of GDP) starts to slow down the digging of the hole. But it doesn’t fill it up.”

Coates said much of the new defence spending had gone toward increasing pay for its existing soldiers rather than an increase in troop size. Canada ranks 29 among 30 Nato countries measured for military personnel as a share of population, ahead of only Luxembourg, which notably devotes more than half its defence budget to equipment, he said.

The Canadian Chamber of Commerce estimates that meeting Nato’s target of 3.5 per cent of GDP for core defence capabilities by 2035 would require about $160 billion in annual spending, roughly 2.5 times the 2025 level. Including a further 1.5 per cent of GDP for security-related spending would bring the total to at least $228 billion. Defence would account for nearly 30 per cent of federal spending, up from about 11 per cent, according to the report.

Poland has doubled defence spending as a share of GDP between 2021 and 2025, to 4.5 per cent, as it relies heavily on foreign suppliers, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce’s report said. In Canada, Canadian-controlled private firms account for just 18 per cent of the defence industry’s $17.3 billion in annual sales.

The Parliamentary Budget Officer has flagged years of unspent defence capital funds as equipment nears its end-of-life date. Fixing old equipment to return it to operations becomes an ongoing challenge as parts for 30-year-old jet planes “are not sitting on a shelf somewhere waiting to be purchased,” Norman said.

Meanwhile, Coates said Canada keeps too few fighter jets on alert and lacks airborne early-warning aircraft. “We’re just being lazy about it,” he said.

“I think Canadians might assume their military can operate shoulder-to-shoulder alongside our allies, and I think that’s questionable,” Coates added. He said Canada still has gaps in deploying long-range strike weapons, anti-armour and air-defence systems, and the ability to fly drones in large numbers.

“The people are trained and motivated and committed,” he said. “I just don’t think they’re equipped and resourced.”

Norman said Canada’s procurement system was built to “pace, regulate and control” spending and is not well suited to handling a rapid increase, while also criticizing how the Canadian Forces has sometimes over-engineered its equipment. The Canadian Navy’s River-class destroyer, which he described as a concept more than 20 years old whose design has still not been finalized, is “arguably the wrong platform for the wrong time,” he said.

Both Coates and Norman pointed to Poland, Germany and the Baltic states as examples Canada could follow to improve their civil defence, procurement and ties to their domestic defence industry.

Coates also wants Ottawa to be more transparent about what its defence spending delivers and explain which threats it is preparing to confront. “You don’t ever hear a discussion of the threats,” he said.

At a time when public support for defence spending is stronger than Norman has ever seen, further delays could cost Canada military capabilities, lives and the confidence of its allies, he said.

“You cannot surge trust,” he said. “You either have it, or you don’t.”
