stories.title: Exercise treats depression as effectively as medication, but Canadian doctors rarely prescribe it
stories.summary: Camh project in Toronto is offering structured 10-week exercise classes, but doctors May need to change their thinking.
stories.author: Kerry Gillespie
stories.content:
Odile Vander Zaag’s first experience with the mental health system was “scary and overwhelming.” In the seven years since, she has tried therapy, group programs and medication.

But this year, after she raised concerns with her doctor about a medication’s side effects, she was offered something new: a structured exercise program designed to treat depression.

Vander Zaag, who’s in her mid-30s, was part of an exercise pilot program at Toronto’s Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (Camh). Knowing that everyone in the twice-weekly class was facing struggles of their own helped her show up. “We all got better together,” she said. “If you ever deal with depression, the feeling of loneliness and isolation is such a big part of it.”

Vander Zaag left the 10-week program feeling better and returned to the boxing classes she used to enjoy before work stress and depression got in the way. Months later, those benefits have persisted: “I feel a bit more confident that I can do hard things.”

Her experience is rare in Canada. But experts say it shouldn’t be.

Canadian clinical guidelines have listed supervised exercise as a recommended therapy for mild to moderate depression since 2016, based on substantial research showing it can reduce symptoms as effectively as medication or talk therapy. And yet a decade after exercise was added to the guidelines from the Canadian Network for Mood and Anxiety Treatments (Canmat), it’s prescribed so rarely that the British Journal of Sports Medicine published an editorial last year asking: Could not prescribing exercise for depression be psychiatric malpractice?

Toronto studies see some success in treating pain, depression. But ketamine’s potential is still poorly understood.

Dr. Nicholas Fabiano, a psychiatry resident and researcher at the University of Ottawa, was the Canadian co-author. Treating exercise as real medicine, he said, requires changes to how physicians are trained, links between health-care providers and community programs, and funding to make it accessible and affordable.

“If we don’t hesitate to prescribe a pill, why do we hesitate with exercise?” he said.

Doctors leave medical school and residency with little to no formal training on how to discuss or prescribe exercise as a treatment for depression, Fabiano said. Research shows whether a patient is even told about it as an option depends largely on their own doctor’s physical activity and confidence in talking about it, he said.

“It wouldn’t be acceptable for your psychiatrist to say, ‘I don’t know how to prescribe this medication, sorry, ask someone else.’” Fabiano said. “But for some reason, it’s acceptable when we have a measure like exercise — that has shown equivalent effects in mild and moderate cases — to not be prescribed.”

The Camh pilot offers what experts say is needed: a supervised program, led by clinicians, at no cost to patients. It’s run by Dr. Johny Bozdarov, a Camh staff psychiatrist and assistant professor of psychiatry at the University of Toronto, and it’s the first program of this kind to be offered at a mental health hospital in Canada.

The hour-long sessions, led by Bozdarov and a personal trainer, wouldn’t look out of place in most gyms: a warm-up, strength training, aerobic circuits and a cool-down. But the environment is extra-supportive for people who May not have exercised in years or are experiencing medication side effects, and the end goal is different.

“It’s not about fitness, gaining muscles, or losing weight,” said Bozdarov, who has a background in boxing. “The goal is to be here for yourself and for your mental health.”

In the first week, Vander Zaag was lifting five to 10 pounds, focusing on form. By the end, she was lifting 30 to 35. “It felt good to progress,” she said. Others did, too: some who began the program working out from a chair were standing by the end, and people who were uncomfortable doing lunges were “going as low as they can,” she said.

The key is a supervised program, said Bozdarov. “Everyone knows we should exercise. It’s good for you. Now imagine being depressed, imagine having a medical history with pains and body aches, and now you’re on medications that maybe cause you to move less. It’s just a lot harder.”

The first group started in January. Despite winter weather and rush-hour traffic, attendance at the Queen Street West facility held at 88 per cent — the average participant missed just over two of 20 sessions. That’s a rate unlikely to be matched by the general population, Bozdarov said, “and they were experiencing depression in the dead of winter.”

“I was surprised ... Maybe that showcases that we’re on to something here,” he said.

The exercise pilot, which has funding for two years, starts sessions for its third group this fall. Bozdarov is evaluating the program throughout and intends to publish his findings, focusing on the feasibility and barriers of running this kind of exercise program and how patients accept and adhere to it.

Dr. Johny Bozdarov, a Camh staff psychiatrist and assistant professor of psychiatry at U of T, leads the hour-long sessions with a personal trainer. He’s pictured with Odile Vander Zaag, who joined the pilot program.

Scaling it up so more people can benefit the way Vander Zaag did will take better links between the health system and community gyms, and trainers equipped to lead sessions for people with depression.

Bozdarov said the editorial’s “psychiatric malpractice” question was “a good sound bite to alert others that we need to start integrating exercise.”

“The time is now to get the government involved, to implement resources within our mental health facilities, (medical) school programming, and have essentially free supervised exercise.”

When asked about public funding for supervised exercise to treat depression, Lily Barnes, a spokesperson for Ontario Health Minister Sylvia Jones, pointed to the government’s commitment of $3.8 billion over 10 years for mental health and addictions services but did not directly address the question.

The gap between what guidelines recommend and what the health system funds is familiar to Guy Faulkner. He helped develop the 2016 Canmat guidelines, which recommended exercise as a first-line treatment for mild to moderate depression. A 2023 update maintained exercise as a first-line treatment for mild depression and made it a second-line treatment for moderate depression.

He leads the Population Physical Activity Lab at Ubc’s School of Kinesiology and is one of Canada’s leading researchers on the link between physical activity and mental health.

“Unless there is active integration into the curriculum for clinical psychologists or psychiatrists, and funding for implementation to provide subsidized exercise programming for people, then they probably will fall flat.”

Faulkner co-developed a program to train qualified exercise professionals to work with clients who have depression, hoping trainers and gym owners would be more entrepreneurial about partnering with health professionals. Now, he’s planning a study with an economist hoping to bolster exercise as a treatment by making the case that funding exercise to treat depression would save the health system money.

Vander Zaag wishes that more people had the opportunity she did.

“The fastest thing to give people is a prescription and send them on their way,” she said. But with exercise, “you feel better and you’re feeling optimistic, instead of just this crazy pill I’m supposed to take that doesn’t totally make me feel good.

“If the system doesn’t offer anything outside of medication, it’s hard for people to feel optimistic and committed and trusting that this is helpful.”

stories.title: Union says Stelco layoffs have begun, setting up possible court battle with Ottawa
stories.summary: Union official says about 90 employees are out and 80 more are expected this week, as Ottawa demands a plan within five days
stories.author: Omar Mosleh
stories.content:
Stelco has moved ahead with layoffs at its Hamilton facility, according to a union official, setting the stage for a potential court battle with the federal government.

The company, owned by U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs, announced last week it would lay off up to 500 steelworkers at its Hamilton and Lake Erie operations because of U.S. tariffs and market conditions.

Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, said notices were handed out last week and about 90 employees have already been laid off. He added they’re expecting roughly 80 more workers to lose their jobs at the end of this week, with more to come.

The office of Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said in a statement it expects Stelco to meet legally binding commitments to employees that were stipulated when the government of Canada approved the takeover of Stelco by U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs.

“These commitments were agreed upon as undertakings under the Investment Canada Act and do not cease to apply because of changing business strategy or market conditions,” Joly’s office said.

In a letter sent by Joly to Stelco president Paul Simon , Joly demanded that the company provide a plan within five days for how it will maintain jobs in Canada as promised. The minister said the approval stipulated the company would “continue to employ at least the same number of unionized employees and the vast majority of non-unionized employees as were employed when the transaction was announced.”

She noted the Investment Canada Act provides options for dealing with any breaches, and that includes resorting to a lawsuit in court “for orders that May include directing compliance, divestiture, or monetary penalties.”

“As our legal team reviews the Stelco letter, all options are on the table,” Joly’s office said in a statement.

Wells said he listened to Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves defend the layoffs in a CBC interview, disputing that the company is breaching its commitments because of the tariff war and market conditions. Wells called the argument a “stretch.”

“I think they’re really playing with the wording to make an argument, because I don’t think they have an argument,” he said.

Officials from Stelco and Cleveland-Cliffs did not respond to a request for comment.

Business lawyer Nassira El Hadri said it’s unclear if Stelco has breached the agreement because it’s possible there was an exclusion in the agreement that hasn’t been made public.

She added she expects the matter to end up in court.

“The federal government has pressure, because this is not only a matter of law, it’s a matter of politics and it’s domestic politics and international politics,” said El Hadri, founder of Hadri Law in Toronto.

“They are pressured to take this further because they cannot just let it go. It’s impacting our economy, and it’s a very key industry, specifically in the areas of Hamilton and Nanticoke,” she added.

However, it’s possible the dispute could be resolved through negotiations, El Hadri said.

The actual text of the agreement between Cleveland-Cliffs and the Liberal government is not public, but a ministerial statement at the time summarized what then-minister François-Philippe Champagne said was the basis for the approved foreign takeover.

Those included what Ottawa then called a “significant package of binding, five-year-long undertakings.”

Wells said the federal government and Cleveland-Cliffs “assured us, the steelworkers, that the employment was basically guaranteed for five years.”

He said they want to see the government get a trade deal that protects Canadian steelmakers, for Stelco to maintain their commitments and for Ottawa to enforce those commitments.

With files from Tonda MacCharles.

stories.title: Eby asks interim B.C. Conservative leader to remove campaign chief over anti-Islam post
stories.summary: Call for Katy Merrifield’s removal comes after Lorne Doerkson fired Conservative candidate Joachim Agou for comments about Muslims earlier this week
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner
stories.content:
Whether an unelected campaign official should be held accountable for comments has become an issue in British Columbia’s election, with NDP Leader David Eby calling on interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson to fire his party’s campaign director.

Eby, speaking Saturday at an unrelated campaign announcement on Vancouver Island, said Doerkson must remove Katy Merrifield for her social media comments related to the release of a report from the leader of the anti-immigration Restore Britain party.

The privately-funded report called “Rape Gang Inquiry” was published by Rupert Lowe in June.

Merrifield’s post, first published on June 17, placed an expletive in front of the word Islam and she called on her audience to defend “Western civilization.”

She called Islam an “abhorrent ideology,” which needs to be expelled.

Eby’s call for Merrifield’s removal came after Doerkson fired Conservative candidate Joachim Agou for comments about Muslims, for which Agou has since apologized.

Merrifield has since said on social media that she took down her original post within hours. Her anger, she added, was directed “at the extremism used to justify these horrific crimes, not at Muslims or their faith.”

She said that as a woman and rape survivor, she was brought to tears reading the report, which she said details sexual abuse of young girls and failure by authorities at multiple levels to protect them.

“I was heartbroken, horrified, and angry,” she says in a post. “I abhor the people who perpetuated that violence justified by their extreme ideology.”

When Eby was asked why he is calling for the removal of a person who is not on the ballot, he said that Doerkson has a chance to show where he stands.

“Either he removes her, or he very clearly would only remove a candidate where they didn’t stand a snowball’s chance in hell of winning,” he said.

Victoria-Beacon Hill, where Agou was running for the Conservatives, is considered a safe NDP seat.

Conservative candidate Zeeshan Wahla said in a statement that Doerkson took swift and decisive action to remove Agou who made abhorrent comments toward the Muslim community.

One of Agou’s posts showed video of a car driving into a group of pro-Palestinian protesters in Switzerland. Agou said in a comment that the driver should have reversed too.

Wahla said there is a clear distinction. The fired candidate was inciting violence, while Merrifield was reacting to violence.

“I want to be clear that the language used in Ms. Merrifield’s original post from several months ago was unacceptable,” he said. “She also swiftly acknowledged that and made it clear that her reaction was informed by her past sexual trauma.”

Wahla said that Eby’s call for Merrifield’s resignation is a ploy. Wahla also described Eby’s call for a snap election while the Conservative party was in the middle of a leadership change as cynical.

“Now,” Wahla said, “he’s trying to remove our campaign manager because we are winning and he is losing.”

stories.title: Toronto headmaster asks students, ‘What kind of man will you be?’ in wake of Cornell sexual-assault allegations
stories.summary: Stephen Beatty, headmaster at an independent all-boys school, urged his students last week to not be silent bystanders
stories.author: Unknown
stories.content:
An investigation into the alleged sexual assault of a Cornell University student has sparked much public outcry and conversations among students, parents and educators.

One Toronto principal at an independent all-boys school urged his students last week “to speak up and act” when they know “something isn’t right.”

Stephen Beatty, headmaster at Royal St. George’s College, spoke at an assembly for Grades 9 through Grade 12 students, about not being silent bystanders.

New York State prosecutors have reopened an investigation into the alleged 2024 sexual assault after the woman filed a civil lawsuit last month saying she was drugged and sexually assaulted by several members of a campus fraternity.

The woman’s complaint accuses the university of not preventing the alleged assaults and failing to properly address sexual violence on campus. It includes a photo that it says shows a group chat between frat members discussing the night’s events and inviting other men to assault the woman.

The following is an excerpt of Beatty’s address to students on Oct. 5:

This is a big conversation and it will begin and end with a big question. A simple question but one that we need, right now, to ask: What kind of man do you want to be? What kind of man will you be?

In this space a few years ago, the first time I had this conversation with Senior School boys, I spoke about the Steubenville rape case in Ohio in which two high school students, big-shot football players, sexually assaulted a girl who was passed out drunk at a party. She only knew what had happened to her when the photos started appearing on social media. She had the courage to press charges and speak up. The boys were found guilty of the crime and spent time in prison. All three of their young lives changed. As the boys said in court, “Our lives are ruined.” I suspect he’s right.

School is about learning and, perhaps the most important thing you are learning is about yourself. I’ll ask again. What kind of man do you want to be? What kind of man will you be? Because let’s agree that simply not being the instigator of an assault or not being an active or even passive participant is not even close to enough. I know I don’t need to say that.

We need to be better than that. I think what we need to reflect on is the silence. The silence that at least 50 Cornell students reportedly left hanging in the air while a young woman was allegedly raped. The silence that meant a young woman in Steubenville only came to understand what happened to her when she saw pictures on other people’s social media. The silence that is, I think, the one thing I want you to remember from this morning and our commitment to not remain silent.

What do we do when someone makes a degrading joke about a girl or woman and the whole group laughs?

What do you do if someone shows you a private photograph that was never meant for you?

What would you do when a group chat turns cruel, or a friend starts talking about someone as though she is a prize to be won or a possession to be had?

Do you join in? Do you stay quiet because you don’t want to make things awkward? Do you tell yourself that your friend doesn’t really mean it? That he’s a good guy after all just doing something stupid.

Do you choose voice or do you choose silence?

I’ve been here a long time. I’ve worked with a lot of kids. I was also a young man once too. I know that silence is safe. I know that silence allows us to keep being one of the boys. I know why silence is the safer path.

But silence is the opposite of safe to the girls and women we care about. Our silence is their risk. Our silence can be their harm. Our silence allows the men who do harm women to continue to do so. And our silence makes us complicit in that harm.

And, this is the thing from an old man that cares for you. That silence is insidious. Our silence doesn’t just allow harm to others, to women. It eats away at us, as men. Knowing something is wrong, and knowing that we know others around know it’s wrong, and none of us saying so is corrosive in men. It’s the silence that numbs young men’s souls. It’s the same silence that keeps men, that keeps us, feeling alone when we need to not be alone. It’s what stops men from asking for help.

Silence can be framed as some manly quality. “The strong silent type.” Don’t believe that. It is not strong. Please believe me. What is truly masculine and strong is breaking silence. We need to be brave. Not silent. Decide that the man you are and the man you will be will not be silent.

Decide now, decide today, that you are going to be that man who does not stand by in silence.

The words are easy enough. The courage to say them is the strength of the person you are:

To the joke or gesture: “That’s enough.”

To the person sharing the image: “Don’t send me that.”

To the person showing you the image: “Delete it.”

You might need to tell a friend: “This is wrong. Don’t do it.”

Silence is the weak part. That’s what will really leave anyone feeling shame. The real strength is in not being silent.

The “why” is because we can’t be silent. For the women in our lives, for anyone who is alone and vulnerable and, ultimately, for ourselves. We can’t be silent because we just can’t live with the harmful impact of silence.

And when breaking the silence is about something more serious and more injurious, when the breaking of the silence makes sure someone gets home safely or stops an attack like what happened in Steubenville requires a remarkable amount of courage. It May be the most courageous thing you ever do.

We practice fire drills and lockdown drills to make sure we are ready to act in the case of an actual situation. I’d like to suggest how you might manage a situation like the ones I’ve been describing. Let’s talk about it now, in this safe space, and maybe in the actual situation you can remember this training.

First, do what you can to not let it get anywhere near this situation. If you see someone, male or female, who has had too much to drink or is otherwise unable to take care of themselves, whether you know them or not, you need to help keep them safe. If it is your friend, get an Uber, get in with them and take them home. Or call their parents and introduce yourself and tell them to come pick up their kid. Do not leave someone who can’t take care of themself alone. Ever. They need to get home safely.

If it is a girl, I recognize that there can be added difficulty. Find her friends. Tell them they Need to take her home. Or they Need to call her parents to come and get her. If they won’t or don’t, then you need to call her parents yourself to come and get her. Or you need to stay with her until she can do that for herself. Keep a friend with you. Do not leave her alone.

And yes. I recognize I am asking you, instructing you to do something that is incredibly courageous. As I said before and I’ll say again, this might be the most important thing you ever do.

If you sense a situation where someone else is at risk or vulnerable to be assaulted or is being assaulted and isn’t able to say no, or isn’t being listened to when she does say no, well there’s only one option. You need to do whatever you can to stop it. No silence. You need to speak up and act. You are loud instead of silent.

This is an enormous act of courage. To be the person to say, “No. This is not happening” in a situation like this May be risky, and will certainly be lonely. The high road is not well travelled.

You don’t need to do this alone. You should not do this alone. Again, find her friends and get them involved. Find the other person who will stand with you and say, “That’s not right. That does not happen!” At the party, in the park, by the lake or wherever you are, find those people who will stand with you. I promise they are there and they are waiting for someone to say something first. I think you’ll find a lot of them in this room right now. If there’s one person ready to be the first in, there are always a lot willing to follow.

Somewhere in all of this, it’s time to call your parents. Especially if speaking up or acting May put you at risk. And even if that’s not the case. I promise you, as a father of three kids who’ve been out in the real world, I promise you your parents or the trusted adult in your life will not be upset with you. They won’t be mad that you’re somewhere where drinking or drugs are going on and you need help. They will be ready to help. They will be glad to help. They will be proud of you for getting help. Tell them where you are and what’s going on. Tell them you need them to help you stop this. Tell them you cannot and will not be silent.

If saying no doesn’t stop it, then you do what you do when there’s an emergency to get help. You make something big happen. Pull a fire alarm. Break a window. Push the yellow strip on the subway. Someone being assaulted is an emergency and it requires a big, loud response.

If you need to call an adult in this room, you can do that. If you need to call me, you call me. At the end of this talk I’m going to give you permission to pull out your phone and take my number. Hundreds of Rsgc kids have my cell number and I’ve never, ever regretted sharing it. I have taken more than one call from a Georgian, at university who found himself a little out of his league and needed help. And I know I’m not the only adult in this room who has done so. I love you. I will do it again.

Today, you should go home and tell your parents that we talked about this in Chapel. “Mr. Beatty talked to us about the Cornell story. I will not be silent. But I might need your help.” Tell them you want to be able to call them, without questions or consequences, to help you do the right thing in a situation like this. You can tell them Mr. Beatty said so.

This is a tough conversation. I wish we didn’t have to have it. But we do because we live in the real world and we simply can’t be silent. I know you. I know that’s the kind of man you want to be and the kind of man you will be.

The full text can be read here .

content_blocks.text: This is a big conversation and it will begin and end with a big question. A simple question but one that we need, right now, to ask: What kind of man do you want to be? What kind of man will you be?

content_blocks.text: In this space a few years ago, the first time I had this conversation with Senior School boys, I spoke about the Steubenville rape case in Ohio in which two high school students, big-shot football players, sexually assaulted a girl who was passed out drunk at a party. She only knew what had happened to her when the photos started appearing on social media. She had the courage to press charges and speak up. The boys were found guilty of the crime and spent time in prison. All three of their young lives changed. As the boys said in court, “Our lives are ruined.” I suspect he’s right.

content_blocks.text: School is about learning and, perhaps the most important thing you are learning is about yourself. I’ll ask again. What kind of man do you want to be? What kind of man will you be? Because let’s agree that simply not being the instigator of an assault or not being an active or even passive participant is not even close to enough. I know I don’t need to say that.

content_blocks.text: We need to be better than that. I think what we need to reflect on is the silence. The silence that at least 50 Cornell students reportedly left hanging in the air while a young woman was allegedly raped. The silence that meant a young woman in Steubenville only came to understand what happened to her when she saw pictures on other people’s social media. The silence that is, I think, the one thing I want you to remember from this morning and our commitment to not remain silent.

stories.title: The scaffolding will be removed from the facade of Notre-Dame Basilica in Montreal
stories.summary: While the restoration of the facade is complete, the basilica still has several years of work ahead of it.
stories.author: Alexis Drapeau-Bordage
stories.content:
After close to ten years behind scaffolding, the Notre-Dame Basilica in Montreal is preparing for the grand unveiling of its facade, scheduled for October 25.

While the restoration of the facade is complete, the basilica still has several years of work ahead of it. About 20 per cent of the necessary work has been completed, said Michel Issa, executive director of the Fabrique de la paroisse Notre-Dame de Montréal.

He estimates that work on the exterior of the church will take four years, but said this figure May be optimistic. The interior restoration of the basilica might take another five to ten years, he said.

The total cost of the restoration will add up to $100 million, said Issa. To fund this work, the basilica organizes benefit concerts, generates revenue from its coffee shop, Le Firmament, and holds fundraisers.

The latest fundraising campaign is based on a new idea: leaving a virtual mark on the church’s stones.

Donors have the option to “sponsor a stone” and inscribe a digital message on the building’s facade.

“We would have liked to engrave the stones themselves, but unfortunately, that’s a logistical nightmare that’s impossible to pull off,” said Issa, adding that the process would reduce the stones’ durability.

The messages will be viewable using a cellphone directly on the church’s facade via augmented reality, or elsewhere by projecting a model of the facade onto a flat surface. Issa compared this augmented reality process to the one used by the viral app Pokemon Go.

People can already sponsor a stone, but the messages will not be viewable until early 2027.

The renovations come with this steep price tag because they involve the entire structure of the basilica.

“All the masonry in the building needs to be reinforced and restored,” said Mathieu Verreault, director of tourism and operations for the basilica.

“After years of freezing and thawing, the stone has cracked in several places.”

The stones used to build the basilica came from an old quarry in the Mile End neighbourhood of Montreal. Those placed higher up were salvaged from the bottom of the quarry and were of lower quality, said Verreault.

On top of that, some were placed “the wrong way.”

“It’s sedimentary stone, so there are layers, and they have to be laid horizontally. If you lay them vertically, the stones are more permeable to rain,” he said.

Some of the mortar that held the stones in place was also replaced with epoxy, which put greater pressure on the stones.

“People were doing the best they could with the knowledge they had at the time, and, of course, in the long run, all these choices — which have proven questionable over time — have led to the situation we see today,” said Verreault.

These exterior weaknesses also affect the interior, with water infiltration and moisture problems leading, for example, to the deterioration of painted decorations.

These are not being repainted. Instead, the parish is attempting to reattach each flake of paint.

“(It’s) very labour-intensive, very time-consuming, but it’s best practice in heritage conservation,” said Verreault.

The basilica’s star-studded blue vault is among the sections that will need to be restored.

“We’re talking about scaffolding about ten storeys high, which means our concerts and tours will most likely be interrupted,” which will cut off the church’s revenue, said Issa.

If all this work is not done, the deterioration threatens to progress exponentially, causing even more problems in the future.

stories.title: B.C.'s Eby asks Doerkson to remove campaign chief over social media slamming Islam
stories.summary: Victoria - British Columbia NDP Leader David Eby is calling on Conservative interim leader Lorne Doerkson to fire his party's campaign director for comments that called Islam an "abhorrent ideology" which needs to be expelled.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - Whether an unelected campaign official should be held accountable for comments has become an issue in British Columbia’s election, with NDP Leader David Eby calling on interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson to fire his party’s campaign director.

Eby, speaking Saturday at an unrelated campaign announcement on Vancouver Island, said Doerkson must remove Katy Merrifield for her social media comments related to the release of a report from the leader of the anti-immigration Restore Britain party.

stories.title: Two youths charged after disturbance at Kincardine business results in charges
stories.summary: The South Bruce Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) has charged two youths after a report of a disturbance at a business in Kincardine.
stories.author: Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
The South Bruce Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) has charged two youths after a report of a disturbance at a business in Kincardine.

On Wednesday, Sept. 30 shortly after 12:15 p.m., South Bruce OPP officers received reports of a group of youths engaged in a physical confrontation at a business on Queen Street.

As a result of investigation, ON Friday Oct. 9, investigators arrested and charged two 17-year-old youths from Kincardine with three counts of assault, with one of the youths also being charged with one count of mischief.

The names of the youths are not being released as per the Youth Criminal Justice Act.

Both accused are scheduled to appear at Ontario Court of Justice - Walkerton at a later date.

The investigation is ongoing. Anyone with information surrounding this incident is asked to call the South Bruce OPP at 1-888-310-1122 or Crime Stoppers anonymously at 1-800-222-8477 or visit ontariocrimestoppers.CA.

stories.title: Flu season is starting early. Here’s what Canadians need to know
stories.summary: Flu activity is starting earlier than in recent years, prompting an infectious disease specialist to urge Canadians to get vaccinated as soon as they can. Dr. Isaac Bogoch explains how to recognize warning signs, when to seek medical care and how to reduce the risk of respiratory infections.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
Flu season is getting an early start in Canada, and an infectious disease specialist says people should not wait for cases to surge before taking steps to protect themselves.

Dr. Isaac Bogoch, an infectious disease specialist, told CTV News Channel on Saturday that flu activity is appearing earlier than in recent years, while COVID-19 levels are in line with expectations and respiratory syncytial virus ( RSV ) activity remains low for now.

With respiratory viruses expected to circulate more widely through the fall, he says vaccination and simple preventive measures can help reduce the risk of illness.

Why getting a flu shot now matters

The timing of vaccination is important because protection does not develop immediately after receiving a shot.

“We know once people get the vaccine, it’s going to take about 10 days to 2 weeks for an individual to achieve that level of immunity that we would like them to against the flu,” Bogoch said.

With the flu circulating in many parts of the country, he said getting vaccinated now is a good idea for those who have access to the vaccine.

However, access remains a challenge because vaccine programs are rolling out at different speeds across Canada, and some people May have to pay for a flu shot in certain regions.

Bogoch said more flexible programs that “lower barriers” to vaccination could help ensure people receive protection when they need it.

Can you tell flu, COVID-19 and RSV apart?

Although the three respiratory infections can cause different levels of illness, their symptoms can overlap considerably, making it difficult for people to identify which virus they have based on how they feel.

“You absolutely can’t tell these infections apart. I think it would be extremely challenging,” Bogoch said.

He said people should pay attention to the severity of their symptoms rather than trying to determine the virus on their own.

“When we’re talking about the youngest, infants and little children, look for the number of wet diapers, look for feeding behaviour, look for change in behaviour,” he said.

Difficulty breathing, dehydration or being too ill to manage at home are warning signs that medical attention May be needed. People who are concerned about their symptoms should seek advice from a health-care professional.

How to reduce your risk

Vaccination is one way to lower the risk of respiratory infections and, if infection occurs, potentially reduce the severity of illness.

Bogoch also emphasized the importance of staying home when sick, including keeping children home from school when they are unwell.

He said masks can help reduce the risk of infection, while improving indoor air quality can limit the spread of respiratory viruses.

Hand hygiene remains important , because some respiratory infections can spread through contact.

As the season progresses, Bogoch said, taking these precautions can help protect individuals and those around them.

stories.title: Two dead in small plane crash near Fergus, Ont.
stories.summary: Police say they responded to the scene of a fiery plane crash on Friday morning
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ontario Provincial Police have revealed that two people died in a fiery plane crash near Fergus, Ont., ON Friday.

Police say they responded to the scene Friday morning near the intersection of Beatty Line and Wellington Road 17, north of Guelph, where the plane had crashed into a field.

The aircraft was on fire, police say, but was successfully extinguished.

At the time, police said the extent of the injuries from the crash was unknown.

But in an update on Saturday, they say the plane was occupied by two people when it crashed and they were both pronounced dead at the scene.

Police say the investigation into the crash continues.

stories.title: ‘I’ve been in Canada for 10 days’; Newcomer Day helps connect Londoners with services and organizations
stories.summary: New Canadians making new connections.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
New Canadians making new connections.

Abdaallah Siidi has just arrived in London, Ont. from Morocco last week.

“I’m just a tens day in Canada,” said Siidi.

He is here looking for a new life and hoping to land a job using his background in carpentry and urban planning.

“I am looking for I am the new opportunities, and I am looking for my integration in Canada,” added Siidi.

“I think this day is very good for me for a newcomer like me.”

The City of London has rolled out the welcome mat with a one-stop shop to discover everything they have to offer from jobs, to transit and services.

“Today is a great opportunity for somebody who’s new to the city, whether you be from somewhere else in Ontario or from around the world, to come and discover what London has to offer,” said Robert Collins, co-chair of the London Newcomer Strategy Advisory Body

“What are those services that can help you feel really welcome? Whether it be in employment, whether it be in recreation, whether it be the school boards, they’re all here. It’s really important for us to make sure that we are making sure that people do understand how things work, and then to be able to actually make that difference for themselves and their families.”

Newcomers at the event were able to connect with more than 50 service clubs and organizations.

“We’ve already had some great conversations with people who have been here anywhere from one year to ten days,” said Mike Sherlock, president of Knighthunter.com

“We’re helping employers promote the opportunities that they have and then we’re also hoping that candidates are going to go to our site and apply directly to the employment opportunities that we have there.”

As families settle in London, the event is intended to help them connect, thrive and seek employment.

“I got some emails and business cards,” said Mohammed Rajah, who came to London from Syria in the past year.

“I will contact them later when I go back home. I’m looking for new opportunities for me and my wife and making connections here.”

stories.title: 2 dead after plane crash, fire near Fergus, Ont.
stories.summary: Two people are dead after a small plane crashed into a field and caught fire near Fergus, Ont., Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) said.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Two people are dead after a small plane crashed into a field and caught fire near Fergus, Ont., Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) said.

First responders were called to the scene near Beatty Line and Wellington Road 17 around 10:15 a.m. on Friday after receiving reports of the crash.

A spokesperson for the Transportation Safety Board (TSB) told Global News in an email that an amateur-built sporting biplane took off from the Fergus airport around 10 a.m. for an aerobatic training flight.

OPP said the aircraft crashed into the field and subsequently caught fire. The fire was successfully extinguished by first responders.

In an update Saturday, OPP said there were two people in the plane at the time of the crash. Both were pronounced dead at the scene.

The TSB said both occupants were experienced pilots.

OPP cleared the scene around noon Saturday.

TSB said it will continue to gather information in the coming days.

content_blocks.text: Two people are dead after a small plane crashed into a field and caught fire near Fergus, Ont., Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) said.
content_blocks.html: Two people are dead after a small plane crashed into a field and caught fire near Fergus, Ont., Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) said.

content_blocks.text: First responders were called to the scene near Beatty Line and Wellington Road 17 around 10:15 a.m. on Friday after receiving reports of the crash.

A spokesperson for the Transportation Safety Board (TSB) told Global News in an email that an amateur-built sporting biplane took off from the Fergus airport around 10 a.m. for an aerobatic training flight.
OPP said the aircraft crashed into the field and subsequently caught fire. The fire was successfully extinguished by first responders.
In an update Saturday, OPP said there were two people in the plane at the time of the crash. Both were pronounced dead at the scene.
The TSB said both occupants were experienced pilots.
OPP cleared the scene around noon Saturday.
TSB said it will continue to gather information in the coming days.

stories.title: Lotto Max jackpot jumps to record-breaking $85M prize
stories.summary: Another Lotto Max draw ended without a jackpot winner on Friday night, sending the top prize soaring to a record-breaking $85 million.
stories.author: Denio Lourenco
stories.content:
Another Lotto Max draw ended without a jackpot winner on Friday night, sending the top prize soaring to a record-breaking $85 million.

No ticket for Friday’s draw matched the winning combination: 06, 10, 19, 25, 29, 39, 50 and bonus 30. The jackpot was set for $80 million and will now roll over to the next draw.

Anyone who buys a Lotto Max ticket for the draw on Tues. Oct. 13, will have a chance at winning the $85 million jackpot, which is the largest lottery prize in Canada’s history.

The previous record was $80 million, which was claimed in December 2025 and split between two lucky friends in London, Ont.

When OLG announced that it was raising the price of a Lotto Max ticket from $5 to $6 in April, officials said the changes could bring a potential jackpot of $90 million, but so far, every draw has been claimed before approaching the new cap.

In addition to Tuesday’s jackpot, ticket buyers will also have the chance to win 16 maxmillions prizes worth an estimated $1 million each and 85 maxplus prizes worth $100,000 each.

stories.title: Jewish group calls on Carney government to hold Palestinian Authority to account for failure to hold elections
stories.summary: Cija points out that Carney recognized Palestinian statehood based on commitment by Palestinian Authority to hold general elections in 2026.
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
On Saturday, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas announced the postponement of legislative elections scheduled for next month until Sept. 11, 2027, Reuters is reporting. Abbas blamed Israel and the security concerns in the Palestinian territories for the delay, says the news agency.

This followed a report on Thursday from the Associated Press that Palestinian factions were discussing postponement. A top official with the Hamas-allied Islamic Jihad group told AP that the factions had reached an agreement to delay the vote.

Cija has released a statement in response, pointing out that the prime minister recognized Palestinian statehood based on commitments made by the Palestinian Authority, including a promise to hold general elections in 2026, as well as undertake reforms.

David Cooper, Cija’s vice president of government relations, said in a statement emailed to National Post that the “recognition of Palestinian statehood was predicated on several commitments, including holding general elections in 2026 in which Hamas would have no role.”

He said the reports that the Palestinian Authority has postponed elections amid cooperation with Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad, “raises serious questions whether the Palestinians will hold true to their word.”

Cooper noted that Cija has raised these concerns directly with the government “including the imbalance between rewards to the Palestinians and punitive measures against Israel. We expect the government to hold the Palestinian Authority accountable for failing to meet its commitments.”

In July 2025, Carney announced his government’s commitment to recognize a Palestinian state in a statement, saying: “Canada intends to recognize the State of Palestine at the 80th Session of the United Nations General Assembly in September 2025. This intention is predicated on the Palestinian Authority’s commitment to much-needed reforms, including the commitments by Palestinian Authority President Abbas to fundamentally reform its governance, to hold general elections in 2026 in which Hamas can play no part, and to demilitarize the Palestinian state.”

However, Cija says that if “recognizing Palestinian statehood has not secured even the commitments on which that recognition was predicated, Canadians deserve to know what Canada’s approach is achieving.”

Canada promises trade ban on goods from 'illegal' Israeli settlements in new joint statement

Raymond J. de Souza: The growing problem of settler violence in the West Bank

The PA has also failed to enact reforms, notes Cija, pointing in particular to ending payments to terrorists and the families of those who murdered innocent civilians.

“While Israel faces punitive measures from the Canadian government, the Palestinian Authority has yet to face accountability for failing to deliver on its commitments. This is a dangerous double standard that has implications for both the region and here in Canada where security experts warn that criticism of Israel has been exploited to fuel antisemitism, violence and even acts of terror.”

The Palestinians have not held legislative or presidential elections since 2005-06, states Reuters. After that, Islamist group Hamas seized control of Gaza, ousting Abbas’ loyalists. He has ruled by decree since his presidential mandate expired in 2009.

National Post has reached out to Global Affairs Canada for comment. There was no immediate comment from Israel about Abbas’ announcement, said Reuters.

stories.title: London police cracking down on risky driving behaviours over long weekend
stories.summary: The London Police Service is joining services across the country for Operation Impact 2026 over the Thanksgiving long weekend.
stories.author: Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
The London Police Service is joining services across the country for Operation Impact 2026 over the Thanksgiving long weekend.

It’s a national public awareness and traffic enforcement campaign focused on reducing preventable collisions, injuries and deaths on Canada’s roads.

Through education and enforcement, LPS officers aim to do their part to help ensure everyone reaches their destination safely.

“Every serious collision leaves a lasting impact on families and our community. This long weekend, our officers will be watching for the driving behaviours that put people at risk. Slow down, stay focused, drive sober, and buckle up. Your choices can save a life,” said Staff Sgt. Anderson of the London Police Service’s Road Safety Section.

Taking place from Oct. 9 to 12, Operation Impact encourages all road users to make safe, responsible choices behind the wheel. This year’s campaign theme, “Safety is in your hands,” highlights the important role every driver plays in helping keep Canada’s roads safe.

Whether travelling across the country or just across town, drivers are encouraged to plan ahead, drive sober, avoid distractions, obey posted speed limits, remain alert and well-rested, and ensure everyone in the vehicle is properly buckled up.

Police say recent police-reported data demonstrates the continued need for education, awareness and enforcement.

In 2025, police services across Canada reported more than 123,000 Criminal Code traffic offences, including nearly 67,400 alcohol- and drug-impaired driving offences, while hundreds of collisions causing bodily harm involved alcohol or drug impairment (Statistics Canada). Dangerous driving contributed to 139 fatal collisions and 556 collisions causing bodily harm .

stories.title: Lotto Max jackpot set for $85M, largest prize in history of Canadian lotto
stories.summary: With no ticket matching all seven numbers on Friday night’s Lotto Max draw, players now have the chance to win $85 million, the largest jackpot in the history of Canadian lotto.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Lotto Spot street teams will be out across the prairies next week asking people one thing: “What would you do with $85 million?”

With no ticket matching all seven numbers on Friday night’s Lotto Max draw, players now have the chance to win $85 million, the largest jackpot in the history of Canadian lotto.

“This is a first for Lotto MAX, and we want to celebrate it with players right here in the Prairies,” Kevin van Egdom, a spokesperson for Lotto Spot said in a news release. “It’s been exciting to watch the conversation grow across the Prairies as this jackpot has climbed.”

The last major Lotto Max win came in December 2024, when a player from Hamiota, Man. shared the jackpot with a winning ticket sold in Quebec.

Earlier this year, Lotto Max upgraded its jackpot cap to $90 million and added new $100,000 prizes on every draw.

The $85 million draw will take place on Tuesday, Oct. 13.

Alongside the $85 million jackpot, the draw will offer 16 prizes of $1 million and 85 additional prizes of $100,000 each.

stories.title: Stelco says it is proceeding with Ontario layoffs after Ottawa issues ultimatum
stories.summary: Company says in letter it is not violating Investment Canada Act commitments
stories.author: Niall McGee
stories.content:
Stelco Inc. has informed Ottawa it is not in violation of its Investment Canada Act job commitments, and it is proceeding as planned with hundreds of layoffs in Canada.

Stelco, which is owned by U.S. steelmaker Cleveland-Cliffs Inc., said on Sept. 28 that it was laying off up to 500 workers in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont., saying it couldn’t compete in galvanized steel as a result of the trade war.

When the federal government approved Cliffs’ $3.4-billion acquisition of Stelco in 2024, it imposed legally binding conditions, including maintaining at least the same number of unionized employees in Canada for five years, as well as the vast majority of non-unionized workers.

On Monday Industry Minister Mélanie Joly issued the Cleveland-based steelmaker an ultimatum to map out a plan within five business days for complying with its employment guarantees under the Investment Canada Act or possibly face legal action .

In the company’s response letter obtained by The Globe and Mail, Stelco president and general counsel Paul Simon on Friday told Ms. Joly the steelmaker is in fact not in violation of its commitments, citing a legal provision around the promises, and the government’s own ICA guidelines.

“Your representation that Stelco’s planned layoffs cause it to breach its undertakings is false,” Mr. Simon wrote. “As the undertakings do not stipulate a commitment to avoid layoffs, nor do they include a requirement that employment levels be above a certain amount on each day of the five years of the undertakings.”

He added that the spirit of ICA gives the government plenty of flexibility to allow layoffs in unforeseen circumstances. The company argues that the imposition last year of a 50-per-cent tariff on Canadian steel exports to the U.S. was an event that was out of its control.

“Throughout the history of the Investment Canada Act and its predecessor foreign investment acts, it has consistently been understood that changes in circumstances May necessitate the non-enforcement or renegotiation of undertakings,” he wrote. “This decades-old principle is set out in the Government of Canada’s Investment Canada Act Guidelines – Administrative Procedures: Monitoring of Investments.”

Mathis Denis, director of communications for Ms. Joly, refuted Stelco’s argument in an e-mail, and said the government expects the company to honour its legally binding commitments to employees.

“These commitments were agreed upon as undertakings under the Investment Canada Act and do not cease to apply because of changing business strategy or market conditions,” he said.

“As our legal team reviews the Stelco letter, all options are on the table.”

Owing to Stelco’s inability to profitably make galvanized steel anymore, Mr. Simon said it is proceeding with the idling of its Hamilton Works operation. Laid off workers will have the opportunity to apply for job openings at Lake Erie Works, he added. The local union has said that only 46 positions were available at Lake Erie Works.

Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, said he is severely disappointed that Cliffs is proceeding with the layoffs, but it wasn’t unexpected.

“It’s not shocking that they are trying to weasel out of the agreement,” he said.

Mr. Wells says he now wants Ottawa to follow through on its threats and sue Cliffs.

“I’m sure if it went to court, and hopefully it does, the federal government would prevail,” he said.

There is precedent for the government to sue and it revolves around the same Canadian steel maker. After U.S. Steel acquired Stelco in 2007, it made commitments under the Investment Canada Act around jobs and production levels. After the financial crisis hit in 2008, U.S. Steel laid off workers in Canada. The federal government later sued the company for allegedly reneging on its legally-binding commitments. A settlement was reached in 2011 with U.S. Steel agreeing to a new set of commitments , including around production levels and investment in Canada.

Cliffs has said it is prepared to immediately call back laid off workers in Canada if Ottawa can reach a “Fortress North America,” trade pact with the U.S. but it has also been clear it believes the government has not done enough to reduce foreign dumping of galvanized steel in the country, which is hurting Cliffs’ ability to compete in the domestic market.

Ottawa has already aggressively cracked down on the dumping of foreign steel into Canada through the imposition of tariff-rate quotas and mandated that publicly funded projects use Canadian steel wherever possible.

“The most important step the government could take,” Mr. Simon wrote, “would be to impose further restrictions on imports of cold-rolled and coated steel products into Canada, limit import substitution, and eliminate remissions for steel products that Canadian producers, including Stelco, can supply.”

He also took issue with the government’s contention that it was blindsided by Cliffs’ announcements to lay off workers in Canada.

Cliffs, he said, had been clear, both in its direct communications with Ottawa dating back to July, and in its public comments to investors, that its galvanized business was in trouble and that layoffs in Canada were imminent.

Furthermore, he said that Ottawa had suggested a meeting to discuss “proposed revisions to the undertakings” owing to the expected idling of the affected Stelco operations.

“Your suggestion that you only recently learned of Stelco’s intentions to indefinitely idle its Hamilton Works finishing lines is therefore inaccurate and misleading to the Canadian public,” Mr. Simon wrote.

“By failing to mention or acknowledge these regular communications, your letter created the false impression that we have not been cooperative and transparent. This is profoundly regrettable at a time when we hope to lower public tensions and engage in a dialogue with you.”
paragraphs: Stelco Inc. has informed Ottawa it is not in violation of its Investment Canada Act job commitments, and it is proceeding as planned with hundreds of layoffs in Canada.

Stelco, which is owned by U.S. steelmaker Cleveland-Cliffs Inc., said on Sept. 28 that it was laying off up to 500 workers in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont., saying it couldn’t compete in galvanized steel as a result of the trade war.

When the federal government approved Cliffs’ $3.4-billion acquisition of Stelco in 2024, it imposed legally binding conditions, including maintaining at least the same number of unionized employees in Canada for five years, as well as the vast majority of non-unionized workers.

On Monday Industry Minister Mélanie Joly issued the Cleveland-based steelmaker an ultimatum to map out a plan within five business days for complying with its employment guarantees under the Investment Canada Act or possibly face legal action .

In the company’s response letter obtained by The Globe and Mail, Stelco president and general counsel Paul Simon on Friday told Ms. Joly the steelmaker is in fact not in violation of its commitments, citing a legal provision around the promises, and the government’s own ICA guidelines.

“Your representation that Stelco’s planned layoffs cause it to breach its undertakings is false,” Mr. Simon wrote. “As the undertakings do not stipulate a commitment to avoid layoffs, nor do they include a requirement that employment levels be above a certain amount on each day of the five years of the undertakings.”

He added that the spirit of ICA gives the government plenty of flexibility to allow layoffs in unforeseen circumstances. The company argues that the imposition last year of a 50-per-cent tariff on Canadian steel exports to the U.S. was an event that was out of its control.

“Throughout the history of the Investment Canada Act and its predecessor foreign investment acts, it has consistently been understood that changes in circumstances May necessitate the non-enforcement or renegotiation of undertakings,” he wrote. “This decades-old principle is set out in the Government of Canada’s Investment Canada Act Guidelines – Administrative Procedures: Monitoring of Investments.”
Mathis Denis, director of communications for Ms. Joly, refuted Stelco’s argument in an e-mail, and said the government expects the company to honour its legally binding commitments to employees.
“These commitments were agreed upon as undertakings under the Investment Canada Act and do not cease to apply because of changing business strategy or market conditions,” he said.
“As our legal team reviews the Stelco letter, all options are on the table.”

Owing to Stelco’s inability to profitably make galvanized steel anymore, Mr. Simon said it is proceeding with the idling of its Hamilton Works operation. Laid off workers will have the opportunity to apply for job openings at Lake Erie Works, he added. The local union has said that only 46 positions were available at Lake Erie Works.
Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, said he is severely disappointed that Cliffs is proceeding with the layoffs, but it wasn’t unexpected.
“It’s not shocking that they are trying to weasel out of the agreement,” he said.
Mr. Wells says he now wants Ottawa to follow through on its threats and sue Cliffs.
“I’m sure if it went to court, and hopefully it does, the federal government would prevail,” he said.

There is precedent for the government to sue and it revolves around the same Canadian steel maker. After U.S. Steel acquired Stelco in 2007, it made commitments under the Investment Canada Act around jobs and production levels. After the financial crisis hit in 2008, U.S. Steel laid off workers in Canada. The federal government later sued the company for allegedly reneging on its legally-binding commitments. A settlement was reached in 2011 with U.S. Steel agreeing to a new set of commitments , including around production levels and investment in Canada.

Cliffs has said it is prepared to immediately call back laid off workers in Canada if Ottawa can reach a “Fortress North America,” trade pact with the U.S. but it has also been clear it believes the government has not done enough to reduce foreign dumping of galvanized steel in the country, which is hurting Cliffs’ ability to compete in the domestic market.

Ottawa has already aggressively cracked down on the dumping of foreign steel into Canada through the imposition of tariff-rate quotas and mandated that publicly funded projects use Canadian steel wherever possible.

“The most important step the government could take,” Mr. Simon wrote, “would be to impose further restrictions on imports of cold-rolled and coated steel products into Canada, limit import substitution, and eliminate remissions for steel products that Canadian producers, including Stelco, can supply.”
He also took issue with the government’s contention that it was blindsided by Cliffs’ announcements to lay off workers in Canada.

Cliffs, he said, had been clear, both in its direct communications with Ottawa dating back to July, and in its public comments to investors, that its galvanized business was in trouble and that layoffs in Canada were imminent.
Furthermore, he said that Ottawa had suggested a meeting to discuss “proposed revisions to the undertakings” owing to the expected idling of the affected Stelco operations.

“Your suggestion that you only recently learned of Stelco’s intentions to indefinitely idle its Hamilton Works finishing lines is therefore inaccurate and misleading to the Canadian public,” Mr. Simon wrote.

“By failing to mention or acknowledge these regular communications, your letter created the false impression that we have not been cooperative and transparent. This is profoundly regrettable at a time when we hope to lower public tensions and engage in a dialogue with you.”

stories.title: Rain expected in London area Thanksgiving weekend forecast
stories.summary: Get ready for a bit of everything this week if you’re in the London, Ont. area.
stories.author: Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
Get ready for a bit of everything this week if you’re in the London, Ont. area.

Environment Canada says Saturday starts off mainly cloudy with a 30 per cent chance of showers early in the morning, but it is expected to clear up in the afternoon.

Southeast winds will pick up to 20 km/h gusting to 40 km/h Saturday morning, and the high temperature is forecast to reach 21C, with a moderate UV index of 5.

Saturday night will be clear, becoming partly cloudy near midnight. Winds will remain from the southeast at 20 km/h gusting to 40 km/h, with a low temperature of 14C.

Sunday is expected to bring periods of rain. Southeast winds will continue at 20 km/h gusting to 40 km/h, with a high temperature of 17C and a low UV index of 1. Sunday night will be cloudy with a 60 percent chance of showers and a low of 12C.

Monday, will be cloudy with a high of 22C. Monday night will remain cloudy with a 40 per cent chance of showers and a low of 11C.

Here’s the extended forecast:

On Tuesday, expect cloudy skies with a 40 per cent chance of showers and a high of 18C. Tuesday night will feature cloudy periods with a 30 per cent chance of showers and a low of 7C.

Wednesday is set to be sunny with a high of 15C. Wednesday night will have cloudy periods with a low of 6C.

Thursday will be cloudy with a 40 per cent chance of showers and a high of 17C. Thursday night will also be cloudy with a 40 percent chance of showers and a low of 9C.

Friday will be cloudy with a high of 14C.

stories.title: World Medical Association adopts policy combatting false health information
stories.summary: First-of-its-kind policy comes at a time when doctors must compete with misleading online content
stories.author: Alanna Smith, Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
The World Medical Association, which represents physicians worldwide, has adopted its first-ever policy focused specifically on combatting false health information, following work led by the national associations of Canada and France.

On Saturday, delegates from medical associations across the globe voted in favour of the policy at the annual general assembly, held this year in the Netherlands. It provides recommendations for governments, technology companies and medical professionals to address the growing and critical issue of health misinformation.

The policy has been adopted at a crucial time as doctors must compete with a barrage of false and misleading online content about health that’s easily accessible on social media platforms. Making the matter worse, artificial intelligence is helping to produce and legitimize this content, directly threatening public health.

Patients can be misdiagnosed because of false health information or suffer side effects from treatments they’ve opted to follow. This type of information online is also undermining scientific research by adding to the erosion of public trust of medical professionals and the health system at large.

Alika Lafontaine, who is representing Canada on the World Medical Association Council and is past president of the Canadian Medical Association, said the issue can feel too big to solve, but he doesn’t believe that’s the case. He hopes this policy will spark the needed action to combat it.

“There’s a lot of work to do, but this is this is where it starts,” he said in an interview from Rotterdam. “There’s a real responsibility for everyone to step up and confront this when it has very real consequences on peoples’ livelihoods and their long-term health.”

Among the recommendations are that medical associations develop awareness campaigns on the risks of false health information, that regulatory measures are introduced to “minimise profiteering” from disinformation campaigns and ensuring licensing boards take appropriate disciplinary action when health professionals spread inaccurate information.

In Canada, for example, doctors have been disciplined for spreading misleading or false information about vaccines, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Additionally, the policy suggests that medical authorities engage with social media companies to ensure there are rapid reporting mechanisms to remove harmful content and that AI-generated content is clearly labelled.

Once a policy is adopted by the World Medical Association, it stands as the ethical standards for physicians worldwide, but is not legally binding.

The CMA and the Conseil national de l’Ordre des Médecins, or French Medical Council, developed the policy in collaboration. Dr. Lafontaine said France is dealing with many of the same challenges as Canada.

Earlier this year, the CMA and research firm Abacus Data released the results of a survey that found nearly all Canadian doctors who participated said they had to intervene to prevent harm or to address consequences after patients accessed false or misleading health information online.

In total, 97 per cent of the 645 practicing physicians who were surveyed said they faced these challenges, including because of advice patients accessed through AI.

Also, in the Cma’s Health and Media Tracking Survey from February, it found that 27 per cent of Canadians trust AI to provide accurate health and health care system information. People who follow AI health advice are five times more likely to experience harms than those who did not, according to the association.

As well, Canadian gynecologists have sounded the alarm about the impact of social media videos. They say that content, which is often misleading and created by individuals with large followings and no medical credentials, are reshaping conversations in their clinics, largely among twentysomethings.

Philippe Cathala, delegate for the French Medical Council, said in a statement that the policy highlights the need for a co-ordinated international response.

“It calls on all involved in producing, publishing and disseminating health-related information to develop a greater sense of responsibility and ensure that information provided to the public is evidence-based.”

The newly adopted global policy is a call to action for health policymakers, medical professionals and their governing bodies to develop strategies to reduce harms associated with the spread of false information.

It underscores that marginalized groups, such as those with limited access to health care services, are disproportionately impacted by the swell of inaccurate health claims.

However, the policy makes clear that scientific debate is distinct from false information, underscoring that medical knowledge is advanced through the careful testing of new hypotheses.

“Physicians May express evidence-based positions that diverge from prevailing professional consensus when they do so in good faith and are transparent about the state of the evidence, the degree of uncertainty, and whether the position reflects established guidance, emerging evidence, clinical judgment, or hypothesis,” reads the policy.

stories.title: Suspect sought in early morning break-in, sexual assault: Toronto police
stories.summary: Through the investigation, police determined the victim was asleep in their residence when they were awoken by an unknown suspect.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Toronto police are searching for a suspect following a break and enter and sexual assault in the city’s Old Town neighbourhood.

Police said they received the call for help Friday around 5 a.m.

Officers were dispatched to the area of Richmond Street East and Sherbourne Street.

Through the investigation, police determined the victim was asleep in their residence when they were awoken by an unknown suspect.

The suspect then allegedly assaulted and sexually assaulted the victim.

The victim was able to escape their apartment and call for help, police said.

Officers said the suspect exited the apartment and left the scene in an unknown direction.

The suspect is described as a white male with a skinny build and scruffy facial hair, according to a police news release.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Toronto police.

stories.title: Friendship Inn seeing increase in demand ahead of Thanksgiving Weekend
stories.summary: The Friendship Inn has seen an increase in numbers in the past few months, they say this Thanksgiving Turkey Dinner is expected to be their most attended.
stories.author: Ashley Beherns
stories.content:
It’s been a busy few months for Saskatoon’s Friendship Inn, serving 55,000 meals in September, marking the third consecutive month they plated over 50,000 meals.

With a growing demand, CEO Sandra Kary says it won’t slow down for Thanksgiving weekend.

“Thanksgiving is always our favorite event of the year. I mean, Christmas is fantastic, but Thanksgiving has its own really special charm,” Kary said.

“It’s our biggest meal of the entire year. And there’s just a really great vibe in the community to come together and offer that wonderful traditional turkey dinner on that day.”

The team works to prepare the food about a week in advance, so they are ready to go on the day.

Kary said they are anticipating serving many meals this year.

“This is probably our highest one. Last year, we did do I think, close to 2,500 meals, and we might go over that this time,” she said.

“But every year grows, and every year we’re just amazed at how it all comes together.”

As to why the numbers are increasing, Kary said the cost of living and the growth of the city play a role.

“When those costs increase and people are struggling to make ends meet or they’re on a fixed income, like say someone who has a pension that is a fixed income. Food is the first thing that gets pushed to the side, and I think we see that directly.”

The friendship Inn is all set for volunteers and food for the holiday, but they will always take more donations.

“We are always excited when the community still supports us with turkeys or whatever else is on our wish list for donations. We’re always looking for things like coffee and peanut butter and jam. And of course, finances is the best way you can help us right now. It takes five dollars per plate to make a meal,” said Kary.

Watch the video above for more on the demand for food

stories.title: 'Extra stress': Tension peaking among Albertans as separation vote nears
stories.summary: Edmonton - Some families and friends across Alberta are set to gather for a Thanksgiving meal this weekend with the hope that the only thing that gets roasted is the turkey.
stories.author: Fakiha Baig The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - Some families and friends across Alberta are set to gather for a Thanksgiving meal this weekend with the hope that the only thing that gets roasted is the turkey.

Sarah Batchelor says politics will be off the dinner table at her home in Airdrie, a city north of Calgary, so her loved ones don’t end up arguing with one another over the Oct. 19 vote on separation.

“At the end of the day, when we sit down, we’re not that far apart on a lot of the concerns,” says Batchelor, a music teacher who plans to vote to stay in Canada.

“We’re just very divided on where the blame should be placed.”

In a central Alberta town, Kathy Bradshaw says she plans to be more careful with her words as the vote nears.

“It’s a little tense,” says Bradshaw, a 64-year-old resident of Sylvan Lake who has already voted to remain in Canada.

Albertans are set to vote in person in nine days on 10 questions. The 10th and most debated question will ask whether they want to stay in Canada or have a second, binding referendum on leaving Confederation.

The debate has become personal, and ugly, in some workplaces and among some families and friends.

Bradshaw says there has been more tension lately in her office.

“I love my work and I love my colleagues, so I sense their discomfort when it comes up,” she says.

Some of her co-workers, who she has been working with for decades, plan to vote to leave.

“People say to me, and this I find the most ridiculous, ‘I don’t want to separate, but I want to send Ottawa a message,’” she says.

“And I keep saying to them, ‘If they know the gun is fake, why do you think the teller is going to hand over the money.’”

In Edmonton, Sheree Zielke, 71, says she has been feeling similar tension, but with her neighbour.

Zielke says she wants to see an independent Alberta, unlike the family she has lived next to for decades.

”(We) don’t talk as much, let’s put it that way. There’s no arguments.”

Batchelor says the debates have been overwhelming.

“I’m feeling more dysregulated just because of the extra stress and having to navigate those conversations carefully at (my work) and even within my home.”

Since Alberta Premier Danielle Smith ordered the vote in May, disputes have also erupted across small towns.

A rodeo parade in the town of Sundre, northwest of Calgary, was cancelled in June amid threats and abuse after parade organizers rejected a float festooned with Alberta flags they feared would be viewed as a political statement.

A pro-separation billboard in the southern town of Taber also garnered attention that same month.

Separatist Cory Morgan, who paid for the billboard, refused to take it down despite an order from the town claiming it was a public nuisance.

Smith has said she supports Alberta staying a part of Canada and plans to vote that way in the referendum. She has also said that hundreds of thousands have signed petitions for and against separation, and it’s time to put the issue to rest.

Critics, pointing to long-standing opinion polls indicating massive support for Alberta staying in Canada, have accused Smith of calling the vote to appease separatists hardliners in her party.

Lara Descartes, a family studies professor at Ontario’s Western University, has some advice for Albertans nervous about tension over the separation debate with loved ones peaking in the coming days.

“Lower your expectations,” she says. “Don’t expect it to be perfect.”

She says differences are normal.

“People are their own individuals with their own histories and beliefs. Some of them May never mesh with our own, but it’s part of life,” she says.

“Accepting this can let us take responsibility for our own emotional state.”

Archbishop of Edmonton Stephen Hero is one of five Catholic bishops in the province who recently penned a letter to parishioners calling on them to cast a vote, and think carefully about the potential impact of it on vulnerable people.

The Oct. 1 letter alluded to the questions on immigration, including whether the government should have more authority to impose limitations and financial guardrails around some newcomers.

The letter said Catholics May reach different conclusions about what is in the interest of the common good, but “whatever the outcome, our responsibilities to one another will endure.”

In a recent interview, Hero acknowledged that the referendum has been polarizing, within families, workplaces or even in churches.

So, he said the call is to be respectful of each other’s decisions and to listen to each other carefully.

He said: ”(To) love one another, and not let it divide us, whatever happens.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 10, 2026.

— With files from Lisa Johnson
