stories.title: Changing tastes help Poplar Grove expand its view of the Okanagan
stories.summary: Working with grapes grown in 160 acres of vineyards, B.C. winery has built on a solid reputation for its red wines
stories.author: Christopher Waters
stories.content:
During last Saturday’s busy lunch service at Poplar Grove Winery, owner Tony Holler kept an eye on what the restaurant’s guests were drinking. On this sunny October afternoon with a slight nip in the air, staff served glasses of pinot gris, chardonnay and merlot to the various tables, while Holler discussed the continuing evolution of the Okanagan wine industry.

“You can’t ignore consumer preferences,” says Holler, who bought the winery overlooking Okanagan Lake in Penticton, B.C., from founders Ian Sutherland and Valerie Tait in 2007. He explains the quality of Poplar Grove’s red wines, specifically its ripe and complex cabernet franc, was the reason he and his wife Barb purchased the winery.

“That cabernet franc was proof that the Okanagan could grow great grapes and make great wine,” he says.

Working with grapes grown in 160 acres of vineyards, mostly around Naramata with an additional 40 acres located further south in Osoyoos, Poplar Grove has built on a solid reputation for its red wines. Its syrah, cabernet and merlot wines, including its flagship red blend, Legacy, continue to attract critical and commercial acclaim.

To demonstrate the aging potential of these expressive wines, they started re-releasing bottles after 10 years. Next month, a new release of Library Collection wines from 2016 will be offered to wine club members, with a wider release planned for next year.

Meanwhile, the growing popularity of white wines has driven growth in other areas of the portfolio. Pinot gris now accounts for one-third of Poplar Grove’s total production, and according to Holler, it sells out every year.

To meet the demand, the winemaking team is working two shifts per day, around the clock, to process the 2026 harvest. After receiving all the pinot gris grapes, they will move on to chardonnay and viognier grapes, while the red varieties continue to ripen.

Rosé and sparkling wine are recent additions, introduced at the request of wine club members, Holler explains. “We now produce 5,000 cases of rosé.”

After seven years of working with a partner, Holler took over management of the restaurant in October, 2019. While many tourist-based businesses in the Okanagan only operate from April to October, Holler sees an opportunity to cater to guests during the so-called “shoulder season.” The restaurant closes in early December and reopens in March.

“You’re not going to build a business working seasonally,” he says. “I think we’re a good example of what happens when you stay open.”

stories.title: Supreme Court split over sentencing when the offender and the victim are both Indigenous
stories.summary: The split decision reflects divergent views on how best to protect Indigenous victims while ensuring rehabilitation for Indigenous offenders
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
The Supreme Court of Canada has tried to resolve competing judicial imperatives of addressing Indigenous overincarceration and high rates of violence against Indigenous women in cases when a male offender and a female victim are both Indigenous.

The complexity and importance of this tension was highlighted by 22 groups being granted intervenor status to offer input in the case, including the attorneys general of three provinces, First Nations and Indigenous organizations, law groups, and numerous human rights, civil liberties and constitutional advocacy organizations.

The fact the nine Supreme Court justices were split five to four in their decision, released Friday, reflects divergent views on how best to protect Indigenous victims while ensuring rehabilitation for Indigenous offenders.

In a bid to reconcile what the court called Canada’s “twin crises,” the majority opinion laid out a framework for sentencing judges to follow when confronted by situations like the case of a vicious beating in Halifax.

In 2021, Harry Arthur Cope, a Nova Scotia man, attacked a woman who was his common-law partner on a sidewalk in Halifax. The victim was repeatedly punched and thrown to the ground. When police found her, her face was swollen and covered in blood. Doctors said she suffered severe injuries to her face and upper torso.

It wasn’t the brutality of the intimate partner violence that pushed the case to Canada’s highest court, it was the demographic complications arising in Canada’s courts when the offender is an Indigenous man and the victim is an Indigenous woman.

The personal narratives of the offender and the victim require balancing of two special judicial imperatives.

“Indigenous people find themselves disproportionately and excessively imprisoned, while Indigenous women and girls suffer from unacceptably high levels of violence and abuse,” the Supreme Court says in its decision.

Why Indigenous offenders get shorter sentences

Who is Glenn Joyal, Canada's most recent appointee to the Supreme Court?

“Both of these pressing issues have been shaped by the experiences of colonization and addressing them together is central to the ongoing process of reconciliation. Parliament has sought to address both concerns through the criminal sentencing process.”

The tension between the issues arose at Cope’s 2023 sentencing after his guilty plea to aggravated assault. At his original trial, court heard that Cope had severe mental health challenges and stopped taking his medications and began consuming illicit drugs a year before the attack. He had a significant criminal record.

For his sentencing, Provincial Court of Nova Scotia Judge Christine Driscoll ordered an Indigenous Background Report. A First Nations’ sentencing circle said community members did not feel more incarceration would help Cope and recommended in-patient treatment.

Driscoll considered Cope’s background, as Canadian courts must do when sentencing an Indigenous offender, known as Gladue factors. She also weighed special factors from the perspective of the victim — that the assault was violence against a vulnerable Indigenous woman.

Driscoll rejected the proposal for a conditional sentence by the sentencing circle and sentenced Cope to five years’ imprisonment. Nova Scotia’s Court of Appeal then reduced his sentence to three years.

It was the Crown’s appeal of that appeal that took Cope’s case to the Supreme Court, where its contentiousness remained over two days of hearings last December, after which the justices reserved their decision.

A slim majority of Supreme Court judges — Andromache Karakatsanis, Nicholas Kasirer, Michelle O’Bonsawin, Mary T. Moreau, and the now-retired Sheilah Martin — upheld the appeal decision of a reduced sentence for Cope. Dissenting justices Chief Justice Richard Wagner, Suzanne Côté, Malcolm Rowe and Mahmud Jamal would have restored the trial judge’s five-year sentence.

In the Supreme Court, majority rules.

The majority presented a workflow for judges to keep paying special attention to Indigenous offenders in the Gladue process while incorporating newer provisions to account for vulnerable victims and Indigenous females that followed recommendations by the Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls inquiry.

“In cases where an Indigenous offender commits an offence against his intimate partner who is an Indigenous woman, a sentencing judge must apply the principles related to both Indigenous offenders and victims of crime, and do so harmoniously to arrive at a just and proportionate sentence,” the majority opinion says.

The court understands the importance of protecting victims, but there is disagreement on the best ways to achieve protection

The court found the sentencing judge should have more keenly linked mental-health factors to the offender’s moral blameworthiness and more meaningfully engaged with the sentencing circle’s input.

“The lessons of the sentencing circle are more than just a source of factual information relevant to a fit sentence, but are key to understanding the Indigenous perspective on sentencing…. What is required is that a sentencing judge reasonably engage with the perspectives expressed in the sentencing circle in crafting a fit and appropriate sentence.”

The majority opinion said the sentencing circle process “will be relevant both to understand the availability of alternative sentencing options that May exist in the community, as well as the community perspective on the sentence that will best achieve the relevant sentencing objectives.”

The minority of justices said the original five-year sentence should be restored, writing that the sentencing judge appropriately considered the nature of the crime and the victim’s particular vulnerabilities. She also properly considered the circumstances of the offender, the Gladue factors, and his mental illness.

“The majority’s proposed sentencing framework fails to reflect Parliament’s direction to sentencing judges… to prioritize denunciation and deterrence, and to generally impose harsher sentences for the abuse of vulnerable victims, including Indigenous women and girls,” the minority opinion says.

Philippe Boucher, a PhD student in Legal Studies at Carleton University and criminology lecturer at Université de Montréal, has been studying the Cope case and said the division on the court shows an evolution in opinion.

When the court ruled on the original Gladue process in 1999, the decision was unanimous, he said.

“We can see how the issues at stake were more sensitive and controversial this time. Especially, 10 years after the launch of the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls, the court understands the importance of protecting victims, but there is disagreement on the best ways to achieve protection.”

After watching the hearings on the case, he said he was not surprised by how tight the split was.

“This shows how complex it is for judges to establish a sentence when both the accused and the victim are Indigenous,” Boucher said.

She also properly considered the circumstances of the offender, the Gladue factors, and his mental illness.

“The majority’s proposed sentencing framework fails to reflect Parliament’s direction to sentencing judges… to prioritize denunciation and deterrence, and to generally impose harsher sentences for the abuse of vulnerable victims, including Indigenous women and girls,” the minority opinion says.

Philippe Boucher, a PhD student in Legal Studies at Carleton University and criminology lecturer at Université de Montréal, has been studying the Cope case and said the division on the court shows an evolution in opinion.
When the court ruled on the original Gladue process in 1999, the decision was unanimous, he said.

“We can see how the issues at stake were more sensitive and controversial this time. Especially, 10 years after the launch of the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls, the court understands the importance of protecting victims, but there is disagreement on the best ways to achieve protection.”
After watching the hearings on the case, he said he was not surprised by how tight the split was.
“This shows how complex it is for judges to establish a sentence when both the accused and the victim are Indigenous,” Boucher said.

stories.title: How to talk to a stranger and make friends
stories.summary: Talking to strangers is good for us, and a growing number of places have started campaigns, events and programs to kickstart those conversations
stories.author: Erin Anderssen
stories.content:
Robert Young arrived early on a Tuesday morning to meet his stranger at a cafe in Cumberland, B.C. “Find a seat,” he told his guide dog, Curly.

Mr. Young is blind, which, he says, makes it tricky enough to find someone you actually know in a restaurant; locating someone you’ve never met is even harder.

So he was already waiting at Curly’s chosen table, when Emily Osborne walked in and spotted an older man with a black Labrador retriever settled at his feet.

The pair had been matched on a website called Comox Valley Coffee and Conservation that connects people who would otherwise likely never have a one-hour, face-to-face chat.

Ms. Osborne, a 34-year-old travel adviser and Mr. Young, a 70-year-old retiree who lost his eyesight to glaucoma, fit the description of an unlikely coffee-talk duo.

Yet within minutes, Ms. Osborne was describing her trail run the previous July weekend, and Mr. Young was regaling her with stories from his years coaching long-distance runners. They discovered a shared love of dogs. Both relative newcomers to the small village on the east coast of Vancouver Island, they realized they actually lived on the same street.

Ms. Osborne left for work, buzzing, as she described it, with a sense of connection. Over the summer, she met seven strangers for early morning coffee. Each time, she says, “it feels like it kicks off my day on a high note.”

It’s a telling indicator of these disconnected, increasingly lonely times, that we’re now booking coffee with random strangers the way we’d schedule a yoga class.

And yet, if we wanted to chat more with the friendly woman in the grocery line, study after study suggest, we’d only have to ask. In real life, strangers are far less dangerous, significantly more honest and much happier to chat with us than we believe – and than crime TV and social media suggest.

Instead, we pass each other by, eyes averted, heads crooked toward screens, missing out on the everyday greetings and more meaningful interactions that boost well-being and create safer, more caring communities.

Talking to strangers is so healthy for humanity that a growing number of places have started campaigns, events and programs to kickstart those conversations. Next month, for instance, national Talk To a Stranger Week will challenge Canadians to get more chatty on the bus, at the dog park, in passing on the street – a public awareness campaign started four years ago by Genwell, a Toronto-based, non-profit group working to reduce loneliness by fostering human connection. Medicine Hat, Alta., proclaimed its first Good Neighbour Day on Oct. 2. And this past summer, two residents in Montreal’s Nôtre-Dame-de-Grâce area took the challenge on themselves, playing host to weekly Neighbour Nights on their street.

Around the world, there’s a sense that humanity generally needs a neighbourly tune-up. In Sweden, the northern city of Lulea created Sag hej! to prompt citizens to say hello. Australia now has Say G’day Day. In November, Fédération Française pour les lien sociaux (the French Federation for Social Connections) launches the first national “Semaine des liens” – a week of connection partly inspired by the Canadian example, says the federation’s co-founder and executive director Arnaud Goulliart.

The Comox Valley Coffee and Conversations were started by tech entrepreneur Maxine Cunningham, CEO and founder of Pick My Brain, a global online marketplace where people connect to buy, sell or gift their knowledge.

After moving to area in 2021, Ms. Cunningham wanted to find a way to connect in person with interesting people. In June, with her partner Marie-Clo, a singer-songwriter who’d also relocated to Comox, she launched a local, in-person version of her company’s virtual model. For $100 – a cost that covers creating and operating the platform, and, Ms. Cunningham says, ideally incentivizes people to follow-through – participants are matched to ten strangers for in-person coffee chats, much like a dating app. On their profiles, they can choose to list the type of people they want to meet, the topic they’d like to discuss, and the cafes where they’d prefer to meet.

So far, 133 people in Comox Valley have had 425 conversations, Ms. Cunningham says, with another 312 names on a waiting list. This month, with the help of local co-ordinators, Ms. Cunningham’s company will launch similar websites in Nova Scotia and Nanaimo, and another one Australia, that is both in-person and virtual. Ms. Cunningham hopes to keep expanding her business model to get people talking all around the world. “Conversation is the new currency,” she says.

Ms. Osborne, who moved to Comox Valley two years ago, signed up because a one-hour coffee with a stranger felt like low stakes with potentially high rewards. “I figured it would probably attract some interesting characters,” she says, “and I’d be excited to hear their stories.” She’s met entrepreneurs, artists and retired people, meeting mostly in the morning before starting work – and left each one, she says, inspired and upbeat.

Vivian Vaillant, 50, who works remotely, saw the coffee matches as motivation to step away from her desk. “It’s a chance to ask another human being, ‘what’s life like for you right now?’” she says. Not because you want something from them. Just because you’re curious.

One stranger started the discussion by praising a local politician that Ms. Vaillant dislikes. “My choices are to tune out, walk away or lean in,” she says. “I signed up to have coffee. I don’t get to scroll to the next thing that I’d rather read.” She decided to listen without debating, to use the experience to reflect on her own biases. In the end, she says, her opinion didn’t change, but it was softened hearing someone else’s enthusiastic perspective.

For Phillippe Duprey, a 41-year-old father of three, the conversations have ranged from a two-hour debate about the risks of AI to sharing parenting challenges with another dad. “The trick is to stay open and let the discussion blossom,” he says. “Then it’s just like wandering down a lovely path with a friend.”

Ms. Cunningham emphasizes, however, that the coffee conversations are meant to be no-strings-attached moment of connection, not friendships. She doesn’t track what happens after the first meeting, she knows half a dozen people who have met up a second time. One woman has invited all her coffee matches to dinner.

Ms. Osborne and Mr. Young have not had coffee since they met this summer. But now when Ms. Osborne runs past Mr. Young on their street, he recognizes her greeting. They’ve met up by chance and walked their dogs together.

“It opens up this whole new perspective on your neighbourhood when you get to know the person down the street,” Ms. Osborne says.

And not just your neighbourhood, says Gillian Sandstrom, a Canadian researcher and professor of psychology at the University of Sussex in Brighton, who conducts experiments to test how to make people more comfortable talking to people they don’t know.

As she recounts in her recent book, Once Upon a Stranger, Dr. Sandstrom was once so shy, she found it painful to draw any attention to herself. As part of her own research, she started asking a lot of random people “Whatcha doing?” She learned that asparagus can grow 25 centimetres in 24 hours from an English pub owner and once finagled herself an invitation to a book club.

Talking to strangers, she says, is a free and easy way to build social skills, to learn to how to start a conservation and actively listen, to see beyond first impressions, and live with the uncertainty that comes from not knowing how a story ends. When you’ll probably never see someone again, it’s easier to hear their opinion minus the emotion of a political debate with your dad. We also tend to be more receptive to a stranger’s advice, Dr. Sandstrom says; they’ll never know whether we followed it.

In her early studies, however, participants were hard to convince that strangers really did like talking to them; they believed positive encounters were outlier, were reluctant to try again. So for a follow-up experiment, she designed a week-long scavenger hunt and sent people out each day to talk to a someone wearing a hat, for example, or a stranger drinking coffee.

“Day by day, a little bit at a time, people were less worried about being rejected and felt more confident in their own conversational skills,” she says. Her published conclusion – that seven-days of practise was enough foster a habit – led to Canada’s week-long stranger-engagement campaign, says Pete Bombaci, the Founder of CEO of Genwell.

For those who still feel nervous, Dr. Sandstrom has analyzed three successful openers from her tracking her own interactions: ask a question, find something in common, or open with kindness. Other helpful props, according to studies, include puppies and statement t-shirts.

Don’t overthink it, says Mr. Young. “I’ve never really had any problem talking to people,” he says. “I got even better when I couldn’t see.” He can’t judge somebody’s appearance or overreact to an expression, and he’s learned to actively listen for a shift in tone that signals he’s perhaps been talking too much.

Most interactions with strangers will end where they begin. But not always. In 2015, at the end of a breastfeeding class in Saskatoon, Karla Combres stopped at the door, turned to the two dozen new moms not talking to each other, and asked: “Does anyone want to go for a walk?” Only one, Claire Miller, said, “Yes. I’ll join you.” That first walk led to playdates, dinners and girl’s trips, and supporting each other through trials and loss. Ms. Combres and Ms. Miller have been close friends for a more than a decade – because one stranger asked, and another answered.

Most of the conversations we have with strangers, Dr. Sandstrom says, are not “dazzling, life-changing moments” that lead to epiphanies or friendship. But maybe it’s relief to have everyday encounters that don’t beg to be posted to social media, that are just warm and easy enough to create that positive buzz Ms. Osborne describes.

“We’re all kind of faking it through life, making it up as we go,” says Ms. Combres. We May as well say hello.

stories.title: B.C. universities and colleges in limbo as they await release of independent review
stories.summary: Schools have been forced to make tough budgetary choices ever since Ottawa began curtailing international enrolment
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
Carissa Wilson felt blindsided when she learned that the cabinetmaking certificate program she was supposed to start at North Island College this fall had been suspended.

Ms. Wilson, 46, was a mature student seeking a fresh start as her youngest son headed off to college. She was already looking for places to live in Port Alberni, the Vancouver Island city that was home to North Island’s 10-month furniture design and joinery program until the college’s board voted to pause it and 14 other programs last February.

“I was gutted,” she said.

The news landed like a blade to the abdomen for Ms. Wilson because she figured skilled trades programs – currently the darlings of Canadian politicians everywhere – would be spared as North Island worked to balance its books without millions in international student revenue.

But not even trades courses were safe from the financial reckoning for postsecondary institutions in British Columbia, the province that relied more on foreign student fees than any jurisdiction except Ontario.

Colleges and universities across B.C. have been forced to make tough budgetary choices ever since the federal government began curtailing the international student program in early 2024.

The abrupt loss of revenue prompted Premier David Eby’s NDP government to order an independent review of the sector late last year. Reviewer Don Avison, a former board chair of Emily Carr University of Art + Design, submitted his findings to the government last spring, but his report has yet to be released. The snap election call further delayed it.

B.C.’s universities and colleges are now stuck in limbo. Most continue to make or contemplate cuts while hoping their woes will attract the attention of political leaders before the Oct. 24 provincial vote.

“There are a number of postsecondary institutions right now in the province who are very close to the edge of sustainability, and that is of deep concern,” said Joy Johnson, the president and vice-chancellor of Simon Fraser University, which lost nearly $80-million in revenue when the international student boom went bust.

The Burnaby research university, like most of its counterparts, has already sliced away the fat and muscle in its budget. “The question I have for SFU is, ‘how close to the bone are we right now?’” Dr. Johnson said. “I think we’re pretty close.”

If the next B.C. government doesn’t lift a long-standing 2-per-cent annual cap on domestic tuition fee increases or provide more public funding to the sector, Dr. Johnson foresees more pain ahead. “Hard choices are going to have to be made,” she said.

Mr. Eby told The Globe and Mail’s editorial board on Friday that a re-elected NDP government would keep the tuition limit in place. He promised to release the Avison report in full. He touted his government’s investments in new postsecondary spaces for trades and health workers.

He also emphasized that postsecondary institutions have an obligation to control costs and to “ensure that they are living within the budgets that they have.”

That’s no surprise, considering the province is grappling with a monster deficit and the terms of reference for Mr. Avison’s review stipulated that “a large injection of permanent, net new funding for the sector is not expected given the fiscal reality.”

B.C. Conservative MLA Peter Milobar told The Globe in an interview that his party would release the Avison report and examine its conclusions before making any promises. The Green Party didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Where does that leave B.C.’s colleges and universities? Matt Milovick, the vice-president of administration and finance at Thompson Rivers University in Kamloops, is blunt in his assessment.

“I don’t think for a moment we should assume there’s any new resources that that are going to be recommended through the Avison report to help us with the current situation,” he said. “This is our problem to solve.”

Prior to the federal about-face in 2024, fees from international students accounted for about 18 per cent of total revenues for B.C.’s public colleges and universities. At some schools, the share was as high as 40 per cent.

By the time Mr. Eby’s government appointed Mr. Avison last November, 19 of B.C.’s 25 publicly funded postsecondary institutions were forecasting at least one annual deficit in the next three years , and nine were in an accumulated operating deficit position. That was despite many having already slashed faculty, staff and programs to save money.

The B.C. Federation of Students, which has been tracking the provincewide cuts through board documents and union communications, says more than 200 programs have been cut or paused, and nearly 1,400 faculty and staff laid off in recent years.

“Students are experiencing these cuts through fewer course sections, long wait lists and reduced services like counselling, academic advising [and] library hours – these have real consequences,” said Debi Herrera Lira, chairperson of the federation.

To take one example of a school hit hard by the loss of international student revenue, consider Kwantlen Polytechnic University, whose main campus is in Surrey in Metro Vancouver.

In 2023-2024, international tuition and fees accounted for $129-million, or 41 per cent, of Kwantlen’s $312-million budget. There were 7,398 foreign students enrolled at the university that year.

By 2025-2026, the number of international students had dropped to 2,976. This year, international student revenue is projected to account for $46-million, or 18 per cent, of its $250-million budget.

To balance its budget, Kwantlen has had to cut 175 full-time equivalent roles since 2024, cease operations at its Civic Plaza campus in Surrey and suspend six programs, including a Bachelor of Arts major in policy studies and a diploma of technology in environmental protection.

“It’s had a devastating effect on the institution,” Diane Purvey, president and vice-chancellor of Kwantlen, said.

Dr. Purvey believes the institution will be able to retrench and thrive by leaning into its status as a polytechnic – a degree-granting institution with a heavy emphasis on practical job training. Kwantlen also has the advantage of operating campuses in Surrey, Richmond and Langley, some of B.C.’s largest cities.

Colleges and universities in more remote parts of B.C. don’t have the same pool of potential local applicants to draw upon.

Small rural campuses are generally expensive to operate because they can’t achieve the economies of scale available to their big-city peers. Yet they are essential guarantors of access to higher education, especially in a province where the next nearest campus might be hours and a mountain pass away.

Thompson Rivers University, whose main campus is in Kamloops, about four hours northeast of Vancouver, caused a minor stir earlier this year when it floated the possibility of closing a satellite campus in Williams Lake by 2028.

Surinderpal Rathor, the mayor of Williams Lake, a city of about 12,000 in the Cariboo Chilcotin region of interior B.C., told local media he was shocked at the prospect of losing the educational lifeline. He and city council vowed to fight it.

In May, Thompson Rivers and the city of Williams Lake signed a letter of understanding binding them to maintain postsecondary education access in the region, while publicly consulting and “reimagining” where courses might be offered.

Currently, the university runs the satellite campus in an old high school that is too big for its needs, Mr. Milovick said – especially now that the student head count at Williams Lake has dropped to 256, down from 391 in 2024-2025.

“We are committed through and through to postsecondary education in Williams Lake, and the region,” said Dr. Airini, the president and vice-chancellor of TRU, who goes by one name. “The question now really is how our university can best deliver education sustainably into the future.”

The same question applies at other colleges and universities around B.C.

To Jasmine Nicholsfigueiredo, president of the Federation of Post-Secondary Educators of British Columbia, the answer is obvious: more public funding.

The federation was among the groups that sponsored a report from the think tank B.C. Policy Solutions that recommended a substantial increase in government operating funding, while maintaining the 2-per-cent tuition increase cap that has been in place since 2005.

“If you want to increase your economy, grow your communities, build your businesses, you have to invest in the infrastructure,” Dr. Nicholsfigueiredo said. “And sorry – that’s postsecondary education. It’s not the pipeline. It’s not the LNG. It’s the people.”

Dr. Nicholsfigueiredo and her faculty and student association colleagues are frustrated that the government instructed Mr. Avison not to consider new public funding.

Mr. Avison is the second former deputy minister and university leader named Don tasked with reviewing B.C.’s higher education sector in less than five years.

In 2022, then-premier John Horgan appointed Don Wright, a former president of the British Columbia Institute of Technology, to examine the provincial funding formula for colleges and universities.

While Mr. Wright was collecting feedback, Mr. Horgan stepped down, Mr. Eby took over and the review was shelved before Mr. Wright could complete his work.

The B.C. Federation of Students obtained through a freedom-of-information request a draft slide deck that Mr. Wright submitted in January of 2023.

A slide titled “Current Formula” opened with the bullet point, “Punchline: ‘there is no funding formula.’” It went on to explain that most public funding was distributed as block grants with no rewards for schools that hit their enrolment targets or consequences for those that didn’t.

“20 years of this zero-consequence funding approach has resulted in a management culture within many [postsecondary institutions] of ‘don’t manage, rather complain about inadequate funding,’” the presentation deck said.

However, it also mentioned that if the government was open to a material increase in postsecondary funding, it would require about $200-million more a year, over and above increases for collective bargaining compensation.

In an interview with The Globe this week, Mr. Wright said nobody in government told him explicitly why his review was paused. He figures Mr. Eby had other priorities.

Mr. Wright said he hopes that at some point soon, a B.C. government takes a serious look at putting in the right formulas and incentives to make colleges and universities financially stable.

One option could be lifting B.C.’s tuition-increase cap, he added, as long as it’s done carefully and grandfathers in existing students. B.C. has the fifth-lowest average undergraduate tuition fees in Canada, after Newfoundland and Labrador, Quebec, Manitoba and Yukon.

“I’ll get in trouble with the students’ associations here, but low tuition is such an ineffective way to improve access to postsecondary education,” Mr. Wright said. “You get much better value for money if you target it and you have needs-based financial aid.”

For now, postsecondary institutions in B.C. have little choice but to keep scouring their operations for savings, as North Island College did last February when it suspended 15 programs, including the furniture design and joinery program Ms. Wilson hoped to take.

Enrolment in the program had declined to single-digit students in the last three years, according to an analysis of the program presented to the North Island board of governors. Cabinet-making wasn’t as aligned with local labour-market needs as other trades; as a result, the program tended to attract “hobbyists and retirement learners.”

While Ms. Wilson bemoans the suspensions and service cuts she has witnessed as executive director of the North Island Students’ Union – including the closing of campus bookstores – she found another path to her fresh start.

She switched to North Island’s Campbell River campus, where she is happily studying to be a welder.

Enrolment in the program had declined to single-digit students in the last three years, according to an analysis of the program presented to the North Island board of governors. Cabinet-making wasn’t as aligned with local labour-market needs as other trades; as a result, the program tended to attract “hobbyists and retirement learners.”

While Ms. Wilson bemoans the suspensions and service cuts she has witnessed as executive director of the North Island Students’ Union – including the closing of campus bookstores – she found another path to her fresh start.
She switched to North Island’s Campbell River campus, where she is happily studying to be a welder.

stories.title: Ontario township of Centre Wellington grapples with controversial AI data centre proposal
stories.summary: Policy-makers wrestle with technological challenges as AI data-centre proposals collide with resident concerns
stories.author: Jill Mahoney, Photography by Cole Burston
stories.content:
About this series

The Globe is reporting from cities and towns in Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia to hear from residents about the issues affecting their communities and their votes in the municipal elections.

On a recent early fall evening, the mayor and six councillors of the southwestern Ontario township of Centre Wellington took their seats around a wooden horseshoe table in council chambers overlooking the picturesque village of Elora.

The elected officials settled in for what was, in many ways, a typical small-town council meeting. They presented certificates to local teenage athletes and smiled for photos. They debated parking charges, approved a plan from the fire chief and passed a heritage designation for a 174-year-old limestone cottage.

They also grappled with a big challenge: How should they handle a controversial proposal for an AI data centre in the neighbouring town of Fergus?

Before them was a motion for a one-year moratorium on data centre projects in the area, which would allow staff to study possible issues with such facilities and develop guardrails. One councillor said a freeze was particularly important because of province-wide municipal elections later this month.

“I really hope that this gives the new council the opportunity to understand what this is all about and make sure we’re doing the right thing for our community,” said Councillor Bronwynne Wilton, who proposed the motion.

Policy-makers in towns and cities across the country are wrestling with complex and rapidly evolving technological challenges as an influx of AI data-centre proposals collide with residents’ concerns about energy demands, water use and noise. In the Greater Toronto Area, councillors in Mississauga and Oakville recently imposed one-year moratoriums on new data centre developments.

In Centre Wellington, a largely agricultural area of 35,000 people that includes the twin communities of Fergus and Elora about 100 kilometres northwest of Toronto, some residents are concerned about plans for an AI data centre. Spur Innovation, a Waterloo-based tech venture studio and AI infrastructure operator, is proposing to retrofit an old copper tubing plant into a data centre.

The former Wolverine Tube site in Fergus currently stands vacant; Spur calls it a “contaminated brownfield.” Video surveillance and no trespassing signs hang on a chain-link fence around the 25-acre property as a flock of Canada geese wander in a grassy field. Across the street is a neighbourhood with tidy homes and a nearby elementary school.

After reading local media coverage of Spur’s data centre plan in the summer, Carolyn Sharp, an artist who lives in Elora, started a petition calling for a moratorium. It received more than 2,300 signatures. “The community definitely does not want it,” she said. “It just feels like it’s being forced upon us, and I think there should be a lot more strict regulations in place.”

In a presentation during the Sept. 28 council meeting, Ms. Sharp urged the township to “take a measured approach to a development that could fundamentally change the footprint of this community” by taking time to develop stronger standards for noise, energy, water, air quality and environmental protection.

Sharif Virani, chief executive officer of Spur Innovation, also addressed councillors and argued that the project would support the area’s agricultural focus.

Mr. Virani said the first phase of the plan is for an air-cooled data centre under 10 megawatts. The rest of the property would be “a test space for agricultural robotics, food innovation in a county where farming actually happens,” he said.

“These computers are not the building; they are the utility in the corner,” he said.

Spur hasn’t yet submitted an application to the municipality, however. Asked about timing, Mr. Virani said “it’s a longer-tailed question” involving financing and supply issues. He later said in an e-mail to The Globe that “we are still in consultation and planning.” The company has other AI data centres, including in the former BlackBerry RIM headquarters in Waterloo.

Before council debated the motion, Brett Salmon, the township’s managing director of planning and development, told councillors they could prohibit data centre developments for a year and could later extend the freeze by an additional year under Ontario’s Planning Act.

Councillor Jennifer Adams called on the Ontario government to provide “real legislation with real regulations” to help guide municipalities, noting that AI is advancing rapidly. “They definitely have more resources than we do,” she said.

Other towns and cities have also urged Queen’s Park to act. In a submission last month, the Association of Municipalities of Ontario asked for “clear and consistent provincial guidance” for communities and a “collaborative process” for reviewing proposed facilities that involves the government, municipalities and Indigenous communities.

The provincial government did not provide specific responses to questions from The Globe about Centre Wellington councillors’ call for stronger standards governing AI data centres. Premier Doug Ford has been critical of moratoriums.

Evan Robinson, a spokesperson for Vic Fedeli, Minister of Economic Development, Job Creation and Trade, said the province “will continue to work” with municipalities and companies on digital infrastructure projects.

Mr. Robinson noted that the government launched its data centre “playbook” in the summer “to ensure Ontario is well positioned to benefit from the tremendous economic opportunities AI adoption will bring, while protecting critical data, safeguarding people’s information and ensuring Canadians’ data stays in Canada.” The framework requires data centres to pay their full electricity costs and invest in communities.

In Centre Wellington’s council chambers, as the view through tall windows turned from daylight to sunset to inky black night, the mayor and councillors voted unanimously to pass a one-year moratorium on data centres. Light applause rippled from the crowd.

In the Greater Toronto Area, councillors in Mississauga and Oakville recently imposed one-year moratoriums on new data centre developments.

In Centre Wellington, a largely agricultural area of 35,000 people that includes the twin communities of Fergus and Elora about 100 kilometres northwest of Toronto, some residents are concerned about plans for an AI data centre. Spur Innovation, a Waterloo-based tech venture studio and AI infrastructure operator, is proposing to retrofit an old copper tubing plant into a data centre.

The former Wolverine Tube site in Fergus currently stands vacant; Spur calls it a “contaminated brownfield.” Video surveillance and no trespassing signs hang on a chain-link fence around the 25-acre property as a flock of Canada geese wander in a grassy field. Across the street is a neighbourhood with tidy homes and a nearby elementary school.

After reading local media coverage of Spur’s data centre plan in the summer, Carolyn Sharp, an artist who lives in Elora, started a petition calling for a moratorium. It received more than 2,300 signatures. “The community definitely does not want it,” she said. “It just feels like it’s being forced upon us, and I think there should be a lot more strict regulations in place.”

In a presentation during the Sept. 28 council meeting, Ms. Sharp urged the township to “take a measured approach to a development that could fundamentally change the footprint of this community” by taking time to develop stronger standards for noise, energy, water, air quality and environmental protection.
Sharif Virani, chief executive officer of Spur Innovation, also addressed councillors and argued that the project would support the area’s agricultural focus.

Mr. Virani said the first phase of the plan is for an air-cooled data centre under 10 megawatts. The rest of the property would be “a test space for agricultural robotics, food innovation in a county where farming actually happens,” he said.
“These computers are not the building; they are the utility in the corner,” he said.

Spur hasn’t yet submitted an application to the municipality, however. Asked about timing, Mr. Virani said “it’s a longer-tailed question” involving financing and supply issues. He later said in an e-mail to The Globe that “we are still in consultation and planning.” The company has other AI data centres, including in the former BlackBerry RIM headquarters in Waterloo.

Before council debated the motion, Brett Salmon, the township’s managing director of planning and development, told councillors they could prohibit data centre developments for a year and could later extend the freeze by an additional year under Ontario’s Planning Act.

Councillor Jennifer Adams called on the Ontario government to provide “real legislation with real regulations” to help guide municipalities, noting that AI is advancing rapidly. “They definitely have more resources than we do,” she said.

Other towns and cities have also urged Queen’s Park to act. In a submission last month, the Association of Municipalities of Ontario asked for “clear and consistent provincial guidance” for communities and a “collaborative process” for reviewing proposed facilities that involves the government, municipalities and Indigenous communities.

The provincial government did not provide specific responses to questions from The Globe about Centre Wellington councillors’ call for stronger standards governing AI data centres. Premier Doug Ford has been critical of moratoriums.

Evan Robinson, a spokesperson for Vic Fedeli, Minister of Economic Development, Job Creation and Trade, said the province “will continue to work” with municipalities and companies on digital infrastructure projects.

Mr. Robinson noted that the government launched its data centre “playbook” in the summer “to ensure Ontario is well positioned to benefit from the tremendous economic opportunities AI adoption will bring, while protecting critical data, safeguarding people’s information and ensuring Canadians’ data stays in Canada.” The framework requires data centres to pay their full electricity costs and invest in communities.

In Centre Wellington’s council chambers, as the view through tall windows turned from daylight to sunset to inky black night, the mayor and councillors voted unanimously to pass a one-year moratorium on data centres. Light applause rippled from the crowd.

stories.title: Power Ball, Le Bal du MAC celebrate Canadian contemporary art
stories.summary: Power Ball returns following a seven-year hiatus and raises more than $525,000, Le Bal du MAC raises $1.4-million
stories.author: Nolan Bryant
stories.content:
Power Ball, September 17, Toronto

Power Ball, founded in 1999 to support Toronto’s The Power Plant Contemporary Art Gallery, returned on the evening of Sept. 17 following a seven-year hiatus. To mark the occasion, as has been the case in years past, a series of one-night-only installations took over the gallery. A party for key sponsors kicked things off, and as guests jockeyed for a spot in line at the bar, the first works emerged. A group called Imaginary Percussion Ensemble , and later, singer, poet, vocal coach and improviser Shaghayegh Bagheri and composer and pianist Kasra Faridi, contributed to a sound installation. Carolyn Vesely , the executive director of The Power Plant, as well as the evening’s co-chairs, Victoria Webster and David Palumbo, the latter of whom also serves as vice president of the Board of Directors, delivered remarks. Corrie Jackson , RBC senior curator, spoke on behalf of the bank, which was one of the night’s sponsors. Later, several hundred more contemporary art enthusiasts flooded the gallery for the main party. An installation of Ella Gonzales’s painted fabric panels were installed in the gallery’s soaring hall leading to the sprawling terrace, where guests packed the dance floor. Back inside, artists Rah Eleh and Sami Tsang, under the creative direction of Adelina Vlas, The Power Plant’s artistic director, took over the gallery’s two main spaces. Among those in attendance were artist and key supporter Ray Mantella; fashion designer Kirk Pickersgill; artists Oluseye , Derek Liddington and Kendra Yee ; Alica Hall, executive director of Nia Centre for the Arts; and committee members Derreck Martin, Kulin Matchhar and Jennen Phelan. The evening raised more than $525,000.

Le Bal du MAC, September 25, Montreal

The Fondation du Musée d’art contemporain de Montréal held its most important annual fundraiser – a highlight on the city’s cultural calendar – in late September. The ball raised funds of $1.4-million to support the Mac’s collection. Titled “L’éclat d’un soir” (“the brilliance of an evening”), this year’s event was inspired by the radiance and intensity of contemporary art, as well as the essential role it plays in our lives. The theme came to life with a selection of works assembled by curator Erika Del Vecchio , including those by artists Arta Ajeti, Geneviève Cadieux, Wanda Koop and Suzy Lake (the pieces were also up for auction). In the middle of the dance floor, an audio-reactive visual installation titled Avec la langue , by artist Rafael Lozano-Hemmer , emerged, each sound triggering a kiss on a giant screen. There was also a surprise gospel performance. Marc Barbeau, executive vice president, chief legal officer and corporate secretary at Air Canada; Guy Côté, senior wealth advisor and portfolio manager at National Bank Financial; and Roger T. Duguay, managing partner at Boyden and leader of the Canadian practice of CEO and board recruitment, served as the evenings co-presidents. Also in attendance: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly ; Montreal mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada; Philippe and Nanette de Gaspé Beaubien; artist Pascale Bourbeau; Claridge inc. executive chairman Stephen Bronfman and his wife, Claudine Blondin Bronfman; and MAC director Stéphan La Roche. The MAC, currently in the midst of a major renovation, is scheduled to reopen at its main Place des Arts location in 2028. It’s currently operating in a temporary space at Place Ville Marie.

stories.title: Share what you love about author Robert Munsch ahead of a live chat on Oct. 16
stories.summary: Did reading his stories leave a lasting impression on you? Did you ever see Munsch tell stories live?
stories.author: Globe Staff
stories.content:
The memory of famed Canadian children’s author Robert Munsch is faltering. But Canadians everywhere keep the memories of him and his books close to their hearts.

The author of classics such a s Love You Forever and The Paper Bag Princess was known to pop into schools and libraries for improvised storytelling sessions for children – especially in his chosen city of Guelph, Ont., where nearly everyone has a story of meeting Munsch somewhere in the community.

Last fall, Munsch made headlines for disclosing to the New York Times that he has chosen Maid, or medical assistance in dying, a decision spurred by a 2021 Parkinson’s and dementia diagnosis.

Deputy arts & books editor Rebecca Tucker, who was born and lives in Guelph, spoke to locals about their enduring impressions of Munsch, and the impact he had on their lives .

Now, we want to hear about your memories of Robert Munsch . Did reading his stories – either as a child or for your own children – leave a lasting impression on you? Did you ever see Munsch tell stories live? Are you a Guelph local yourself?

Share your memories in the live chat below, and take the chance to interact with other readers. On Friday, Oct. 16 at 11 a.m. ET, Tucker will join the chat and share her insights from her article.

The author of classics such a s Love You Forever and The Paper Bag Princess was known to pop into schools and libraries for improvised storytelling sessions for children – especially in his chosen city of Guelph, Ont., where nearly everyone has a story of meeting Munsch somewhere in the community.
Last fall, Munsch made headlines for disclosing to the New York Times that he has chosen Maid, or medical assistance in dying, a decision spurred by a 2021 Parkinson’s and dementia diagnosis.
Deputy arts & books editor Rebecca Tucker, who was born and lives in Guelph, spoke to locals about their enduring impressions of Munsch, and the impact he had on their lives .

Now, we want to hear about your memories of Robert Munsch . Did reading his stories – either as a child or for your own children – leave a lasting impression on you? Did you ever see Munsch tell stories live? Are you a Guelph local yourself?

stories.title: What ‘made-in-Canada’ means to five heritage footwear brands
stories.summary: These longstanding brands offer a picture of a Canadian footwear industry rooted in heritage, function and craftsmanship
stories.author: Christopher Danforth
stories.content:
Canadian footwear has long been shaped by the country’s climate, landscape and industrial heritage, from the logging camps and factories that helped establish its bootmaking tradition to the Indigenous footwear designs that are older than Canada itself.

Quebec, in particular, developed a robust shoemaking trade, with manufacturers producing rugged footwear for labourers and the military that continues to thrive today. Alongside these utilitarian innovations are Indigenous styles such as moccasins, made with techniques that have been carried forward across generations.

Together, these longstanding brands offer a picture of a Canadian footwear industry rooted in heritage, function and craftsmanship.

Viberg traces its roots back nearly 100 years to Shellbrook, Sask., where Edwin and Gladys Viberg established their eponymous brand in 1931.

Specializing in hardy, robust leather work boots, Viberg was a pioneer with styles such as a five-inch ankle boot made for industrial workers. Today, 100 per cent of the company’s footwear is manufactured at its workshop in Victoria, B.C.

“Manufacturing in Canada is simply part of who we are and how the company has developed over generations,” said third-generation shoemaker Brett Viberg. “Our focus is on making the best footwear we can, and our workshop in Victoria is where we have the people, knowledge and experience to do that.”

The brand has admirers around the globe, but it is particularly beloved in Japan, a country with a strong appreciation for craftsmanship. Viberg expressed concern that Canadian craft and manufacturing is fading, suggesting that Canada look to countries such as Italy, France, England or Japan as examples of places that have supported and encouraged a heritage of domestic making.

Still, he said, “I think consumers generally have a positive perception of made-in-Canada and associate it with quality, integrity and supporting domestic industry.”

Dayton Boots was founded in East Vancouver in 1946, initially producing ski boots before shifting to hard-wearing logging and work boots. The brand’s first logging boots were named the Dayton 64, after the address of the Lumberman’s Social Club (64 East Hastings).

In 2023, Dayton Boots rebranded as Wohlford & Company after the shop’s original founder. According to current owner and self-described “steward,” Hall Risk, the brand’s best-known style is the Black Beauty, a Western-style ranch boot designed by co-founder Wayne Wohlford for his ranch hands. The shoe has since become a signature for the brand.

Wohlford makes its boots using Goodyear welt construction – a method that reinforces the shoe – as part of the 230-step process to make each pair. The process allows the boots to be resoled and maintained for decades.

For Risk, durability is “what happens when you build a boot for a job it was originally designed to do.”

Today, the brand operates three workshops in Vancouver, Winnipeg and León, Mexico. All custom and made-to-order boots are produced in Vancouver. Before a fire destroyed its factory there, in April, 2025, approximately 90 per cent of Wohlford’s stock was made in Canada. (As the company rebuilds, that figure is now closer to 60 per cent).

For Risk, Canadian manufacturing is inseparable from the people who make Wohlford’s boots.

“The people who make them are the reason the boots are what they are,” he said.

Founded in 1878 in Wendake, Quebec, home of the Wendat Nation, Bastien has been producing traditional moccasins and handcrafted leather goods for nearly 150 years. Today, the Indigenous-owned company’s flagship products remain its genuine leather and moose hide moccasins, which are manufactured at its Wendake factory.

For the brand, maintaining production in Canada is closely tied to preserving the skills and cultural legacy behind its wares. The brand sources a majority of its materials, such as moose hide and cowhide, from Canadian suppliers.

Producing in Canada allows the brand to preserve the specialized skills passed down through generations, said president Jason Picard-Binet, adding that it also provides employment within the community.

The cost of Canadian manufacturing remains a challenge, Picard-Binet said, particularly when competing with mass-produced footwear made overseas. But Bastien sees local production as essential.

Founded in the late 1890s in Montreal, Kamik has been making footwear in the province for more than 125 years.

Today, the company specializes in what it calls “bad weather boots”: models built for winter and the outdoors. Kamik’s all-purpose Tundra style has been part of its catalog for decades, tracing its roots back to Canada’s logging camps. Its ultra-tough Work Horse – one of the brand’s most iconic designs – has a waterproof shell and slip-resistant sole, making it a go-to for demanding industries. Both are suitable for minus 40 C temperatures and made in Canada (other select styles and parts are manufactured abroad, including in the United States).

According to the brand, a commitment to local production allows the company to stay connected to its roots while supporting nearby communities.

Founded by local businessman Georges-Alidor Boulet in 1933 in Saint-Tite, Que., Boulet Boots started out as a manufacturer of men’s dress shoes. During the Second World War, the company became a major supplier of footwear, including work boots, to the Canadian Armed Forces, producing up to 300 pairs per day with roughly 75 per cent destined for the feet of Canadian soldiers.

In the 1960s, Boulet’s sons, Robert, Roger and Reynald, branched out into Western-style boots, with the brand becoming the first Canadian company to specialize in manufacturing them. Western and cowboy boots remain at the core of the business today.

Now run by a fourth generation of the family, Boulet continues to operate at its original factory in Saint-Tite, where around 200 employees produce up to 200,000 pairs of boots annually.

stories.title: Legal group seeks to force Quebec MNAs to swear oath to King
stories.summary: Lawyers seeking to temporarily suspend the Quebec law are facing a tight timeline, with the national assembly's 44th legislature slated to begin Nov. 17.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Timothy Sargeant
stories.content:
A constitutional battle is brewing in Quebec as a non-profit legal organization seeks to suspend a provincial law that no longer requires members of the national assembly to swear allegiance to the monarch.

The legal challenge comes as premier-elect Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and the Parti Québécois prepare to take office following the party’s election victory Monday night.

St-Pierre Plamondon, who has previously refused to swear allegiance to the King , has no plans to take the oath.

Lawyer Lawrence David, founder of the Public Interest Litigation Institute, is challenging the Quebec law and seeking an interim injunction to suspend it.

“Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon is well aware, as a lawyer, that we live in a democracy governed by a constitution, laws and that one cannot simply freely flout the rules that one does not agree with,” David told Global News on Friday.

David argues the Quebec law is unconstitutional and cites Section 128 of the Constitution Act, 1867, which refers to the oath of allegiance.

He also points to Section 41 of the Constitution Act, 1982, which he says requires unanimous consent from the House of Commons and all provinces for changes.

“Quebec’s law is unconstitutional. We’re challenging it and now we’re seeking this interim injunction to freeze it as soon as possible,” David said.

The legal fight comes four years after St-Pierre Plamondon refused to swear allegiance to the King and was initially denied entry to the national assembly’s Blue Room.

“There’s nothing that obliges a consequence just because we didn’t swear an oath to the King of England,” St-Pierre Plamondon said back in 2022.

The premier-elect said Tuesday that a legal opinion is needed on whether the Lieutenant-Governor, Quebec’s representative of the monarch, must be present during the swearing-in ceremony.

St-Pierre Plamondon met with his newly elected MNAs this week for the first caucus meeting of all 59 members following the PQ’s victory.

Lawyers seeking to temporarily suspend the Quebec law are facing a tight timeline, with the national assembly’s 44th legislature slated to begin Nov. 17.

“The politicians who are refusing to take the oath are saying they’re standing up for the people but their manoeuvres are literally leading to violations,” David told Global.

Lawyers for both sides are expected back in court later this month to make their arguments before a judge.

If the court grants the injunction sought by the non-profit organization, St-Pierre Plamondon could be required to swear allegiance to the King before assuming office.

stories.title: Nickelback Plans Massive 2027 World Tour With Seven Canadian Concert Stops.
stories.summary: Toronto - Canadian rock band Nickelback has announced a massive 2027 world tour on its official Instagram page.
stories.author: David Augustine The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Canadian rock band Nickelback has announced a massive 2027 world tour on its official Instagram page.

The tour kicks off Feb. 6 in Pittsburgh, with nearly 70 concerts planned across North America, Europe and Australia.

Chad Kroeger, front, of Nickelback, performs during a concert Sunday, Aug. 3, 2025, at the Pro Football Hall of Fame in Canton, Ohio. (AP Photo/David Dermer)

Seven Canadian stops are scheduled, including Toronto, Hamilton, Montreal, Saskatoon, Edmonton, Calgary, and Vancouver.

The tour supports the band’s upcoming 11th studio album, “Everything Under the Sun,” set for release on Oct. 30.

British rock band Don Broco will join Nickelback as the opening act throughout the tour.

Presale tickets go on sale Tuesday, Oct. 13, with general ticket sales beginning Friday, Oct. 16.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 10, 2026.

stories.title: Complaint filed to medical regulator over MP saying fentanyl 'readily available' in Maid report
stories.summary: Toronto - Remarks made by a member of Parliament, who is also a doctor, suggesting illicit drugs such as fentanyl are a “painless” and “readily available” option to end one’s life are now the subject of a complaint filed to the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario.
stories.author: Hannah Alberga The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Remarks made by a member of Parliament, who is also a doctor, suggesting illicit drugs such as fentanyl are a “painless” and “readily available” option to end one’s life are now the subject of a complaint filed to the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario.

The complainant, Claire Brosseau, a 49-year-old woman who has been trying to get access to medical assistance in dying for persistent mental disorders that began when she was a child, said she was triggered by Dr. Marcus Powlowski’s “irresponsible, thoughtless and dangerous” words.

She takes issue with his supplementary opinion, attached to a special joint committee report published in June on medical assistance in dying and mental disorders as a sole underlying medical condition. In it, he wrote:

“The option to end one’s life remains, irrespective of MAID, readily available in Canada. Furthermore, there are painless options readily available. One example being illicit narcotics like fentanyl. To my dismay it is arguably easier for my teenage sons to access fentanyl in my hometown of Thunder Bay than it is for me (a doctor) to renew my Lipitor prescription (a cholesterol medication).”

The quote is included in Powlowski’s written argument against expanding access to MAID for mental illness until fundamental concerns are addressed. He outlines his reasons, saying it is impossible to determine that a person’s mental illness is irremediable, as required by law. He also raises the issue of access to mental health services and social supports, and says testimony from practitioners suggests there is no consensus on how to distinguish suicidality from rational decision-making.

In a section titled “Why do we try to prevent suicide?,” Powlowski analyzes the role of authorities in intervening in suicide attempts in order to prevent harm, versus personal autonomy. It’s there that the lines Brosseau takes issue with are written.

From Brosseau’s perspective, “He gave us information on how to kill ourselves,” she said in an interview from bed in Toronto, where she says she spends most of her days, hair bundled in a bandana.

Her written complaint has been reviewed by The Canadian Press, along with her emails with an investigator from the regulatory college, who said in the correspondence that Powlowski has until Oct. 22 to file a response before it goes to a committee for review.

However, Powlowski’s chief of staff said that the Liberal MP for Thunder Bay-Rainy River, who was an emergency room doctor before he was elected in 2019, had not received notification of the complaint and did not want to answer questions about it.

“He prepared something, but in the end, he decided he doesn’t want to comment on it,” William Fassett, his chief of staff, said over a phone call.

The college said it could not confirm whether an investigation was underway because the complaints process is confidential.

On Wednesday, the federal government said it will introduce legislation this fall that would bar people suffering solely from a mental illness to access medical assistance in dying.

THE COMPLAINT

Brosseau acknowledges in the complaint that a member of Parliament is entitled to freedom of speech. And though she was personally pained by the findings of the parliamentary committee — which Powlowski was the co-chair of and which recommended the federal government “indefinitely pause” an expansion of MAID to people with mental disorders — she says her complaint is separate from all of that.

“In a public document dealing directly with suicide, mental illness and medical practice, he stated that ending one’s life is ‘readily available,’ characterized illicit fentanyl as a ‘painless’ option, and added that fentanyl is arguably easier for his teenage sons to obtain than it is for him to renew a prescription,” Brosseau wrote.

“Those statements identify and normalize a lethal means, present a medically misleading account of opioid poisoning, and create a foreseeable risk of harm to vulnerable readers.”

Brosseau argues that Powlowski positions suicide in an attractive manner, contrary to the college’s standards, which characterize unprofessional behaviour as “words, actions or inactions by a physician that interfere with (or may interfere with) the delivery of quality care, public trust in the profession, the safety or perceived safety of others.”

“It is therefore reasonable for the college to examine whether the statement was misleading and whether Dr. Powlowski adequately considered its foreseeable impact,” Brosseau states in the complaint.

“It triggered me and I’m not the only one,” she said.

Avery Teplitsky, who says he’s spent most of his life in the mental health system, said he was also outraged by the level of disregard coming from someone who is both a doctor and an elected official. “It’s just completely missing the entire point,” Teplitsky, 53, said of Powlowski’s remarks.

In a blog post for Dying with Dignity, Justin Dickie also wrote about the fentanyl comments from his perspective as someone who lives with depression. “Does this sound like an unbiased party to you?” he wrote in August.

Less than a week before Brosseau filed the complaint, a Toronto judge denied her motion for a constitutional exemption from a law that currently prevents people from applying for MAID on the basis of mental illness alone.

She is also the plaintiff in a constitutional challenge, arguing that excluding Canadians whose sole underlying condition is a mental illness from accessing MAID is a breach of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

“I’m clinging to life by my fingernails,” she said.

Brosseau said she does not care if the timing of her complaint looks strategic with her court battle – she just wants Powlowski to acknowledge the danger of his remarks.

The regulatory college says complaints can result in issuing advice to a doctor on how to improve their practice or conduct; requiring remedial self-study; ordering the doctor to take specific courses; issuing a verbal caution; or, where appropriate, referring the matter to the Ontario Physicians and Surgeons Discipline Tribunal.

Brosseau said she wants Powlowski to make a public statement taking back what he said, and informing people of what happens when you overdose on fentanyl, including how awful it is.

“But what I want and what’s going to happen are two very different things.”

If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, support is available 24-7 by calling or texting 988, Canada’s national suicide prevention helpline.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 10, 2026.

stories.title: Overlapping local, provincial elections in B.C. causing confusion: candidates
stories.summary: Cori Ramsay, a candidate for city council in Prince George, B.C., says a voter told her they can't wait to cast a ballot for her on Oct. 24. The voter would surely be disappointed, as Ramsay's election is a week earlier, ON Oct. 17.
stories.author: Marissa Birnie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Cori Ramsay, a candidate for city council in Prince George, B.C., says a voter told her they can’t wait to cast a ballot for her on Oct. 24. The voter would surely be disappointed, as Ramsay’s election is a week earlier, ON Oct. 17.

As British Columbians contend with local and provincial elections in October, some candidates say the overlap is confusing and overwhelming voters.

The local elections on Oct. 17 will see voters elect mayors, councillors, school board trustees and other local officials, while a provincial vote will be held Oct. 24 to elect 93 members of the legislature, which will determine B.C.‘s next premier.

NDP Leader David Eby’s decision to call a snap election came as the local election campaign period had already begun, and earned swift condemnation from the Union of BC Municipalities, which represents local governments in the province.

Ramsay, the union’s former president, said she thinks the decision has put an unfair strain on the electorate.

“I’m hearing candidates going door-to-door for the municipal election being told that ‘I can’t vote for you because I’m voting for our MLA,’” she said.

The union’s current president, Jenna Stoner, who is running for mayor in Squamish, B.C., said she’s seen voters confused about where and when to vote.

While the election dates are separate, the local election day overlaps with provincial advance voting.

“There’s just so much confusion in the community right now that we’re having to navigate, and it’s just so frustrating,” Ramsay said.

She said the dual elections are hurting voters’ ability to assess candidates in a crowded field, and that one frustrated and overwhelmed voter said she would base her vote on a “vibe check.”

Tanya Webking, who is running with the BC Green Party for Vancouver-Strathcona in the provincial election, said she’s had voters mistake her as running for the Green Party of Vancouver. A few said they forgot about the double elections.

She said she’s heard from multiple voters who are angry about the provincial election call and view it as costly and unnecessary.

Paul Thompson, a Vancouver voter, said it’s been difficult to get a handle on the multiple candidates running in the city’s municipal elections, where there are more than 100 people on the ballot.

“It’s pretty much impossible to sit down and read every single person’s point of view and what they’re campaigning for,” he said.

It was also hard to understand how the city and its various bodies, such as the park board, differ, he said.

Thompson has since cast his votes early in both elections, but said the provincial election call was a poor choice.

“They had the majority in the government and they still went ahead and wasted taxpayers’ money on something that nobody that I’ve spoken to actually wanted,” he said.

When asked about the overlapping elections at a campaign event on Wednesday, Eby said he had confidence in electors’ ability to vote in two elections.

“The local candidate elections, as far as I can tell, are running just fine,” he said, adding that a future report from Elections BC May address the issue.

Elections BC said it hasn’t weighed the outcomes or impacts of the dual elections because the provincial election campaign is not finished.

The independent agency, which administers the provincial election, added that it has received a “large number” of applications for election officials and other staff, more than the last provincial election. It previously said 17,000 election officials were needed for the 2026 election.

“However, in rural and remote communities, we are still hiring election officials and office staff up to final voting day,” Elections BC said in an email on Thursday.

Stoner, Ramsay and Webking each expressed concerns about the dual elections’ effect on campaign volunteers and election staffing.

Stoner said she’s seen volunteer burnout, and there is the potential of volunteers or polling staff being pulled to provincial campaigns at the expense of local efforts.

“There’s limited capacity in the system and we’ve doubled the requirement of that system without necessarily doubling the resources,” she said.

Ramsay said the local election has lost some campaign workers who went to work on the provincial election instead, since it offers a few extra days of employment at more pay.

Michael MacKenzie, a professor of political studies and the Jarislowsky chair in trust and political leadership at Vancouver Island University, said the overlapping campaigns are bad for democracy.

“We tend to think that our municipal governments are somehow less important. This is not true. They make important decisions that affect our lives,” he said.

He noted that both local and provincial candidates often rely on the same volunteer base to run their campaigns, and resources are stretched thin. Some of his own students are volunteering in multiple elections or have switched campaigns entirely.

He said he doesn’t think voter fatigue will be an issue because British Columbians are already used to having elections every four years.

“The problem really is just the work that needs to be done to cast an informed vote,” he said.

Municipal elections tend to have abysmal voter turnouts, and competing with the more visible provincial election could siphon the attention of voters, MacKenzie said.

In Prince George, where Ramsay is pursuing a third term on city council, voter turnout in the local elections has been among the lowest in the province in recent years.

“I’m hoping that we see some activity at the polls, but I do think that voters will favour one election over the other at the end of the day,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 10, 2026.
