stories.title: Alberta Court of Appeal says Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional
stories.summary: The Court found that, among other things, the act still grants the power to stop a project in provincial jurisdiction if it has even the smallest impact on federal jurisdiction.
stories.author: Nick Murray
stories.content:
The Alberta Court of Appeal has ruled the federal government’s Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional, following a second court challenge of the federal legislation.

The act, otherwise known as Bill C-69 , was first passed by the Liberals under former prime minister Justin Trudeau to set out a process to review the environmental, economic, health and social effects of proposed projects like ports, mines and pipelines.

In a 4-1 decision issued Friday, the court said even though Ottawa modified the law after the Supreme Court struck down much of it in 2023, the new version still infringes on provincial jurisdiction.

The Court of Appeal found that, among other things, the act still gives Ottawa the power to stop a project in provincial jurisdiction if it has even the smallest impact on federal jurisdiction.

“While Parliament May have the power to create an impact assessment scheme that complements existing regulation in environmental matters, the (Impact Assessment Act) creates great uncertainty due to the potential for previously unpronounced standards to apply to designated projects,” the court wrote.

“This merely exacerbates the concern that a federal assessment scheme might enable the federal government, ON the pretext of some narrow ground of federal jurisdiction, to conduct a far-ranging inquiry into matters that are exclusively within provincial jurisdiction.”

The court said while some of the changes Ottawa made to the previous version of the act weren’t constitutionally problematic, the law still gave Ottawa overly broad powers in areas of provincial jurisdiction.

“The decision maker May regulate the project causing the impacts through imposition of conditions and followup programs, or indefinite prohibitions on entire projects and matters within provincial jurisdiction rather than confining oversight to federal effects caused by the project,” the court wrote.

Ontario and Saskatchewan both backed Alberta’s legal challenge.

The Impact Assessment Act has been staunchly opposed by oil and gas industry players and critics such as federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre.

Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney dubbed it the “no more pipelines act.”

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said on social media Friday that the ruling was “yet another big win for Alberta.”

“I’m calling on the federal government to accept this ruling, refrain from yet another appeal, and immediately work with Alberta and the other provinces to clean up this flawed Trudeau-era legislation once and for all so it no longer inhibits economic development in our country,” she said.

Friday’s ruling comes as Ottawa and Alberta are partnering on a new oil pipeline to the West Coast.

Earlier this month, the Pacific Link pipeline project became the first to receive a national interest designation under Ottawa’s new Building Canada Act.

And while the Building Canada Act gives Ottawa the power to skirt a dozen federal laws to help move hand-picked projects forward, critics like Poilievre have long called for the Impact Assessment Act to be repealed.

Through the newly tabled Bill C-39, Ottawa is trying to transfer the assessment process for pipeline and energy transmission projects from the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada to the Canada Energy Regulator.

The federal government has said it has been told by industry that the level of expertise on energy projects that existed at the Canada Energy Regulator couldn’t be found at the Impact Assessment Agency.

Ottawa has said the Canada Energy Regulator will still be bound by the provisions of the Impact Assessment Act — which the Alberta Court of Appeal now says is unconstitutional — when carrying out its reviews.

In a statement, the office of federal Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said the government is reviewing the decision and considering next steps.

”To position Canada for long-term prosperity in a rapidly changing global economy, the Government of Canada is moving forward to build at a pace not seen in decades. The (Impact Assessment Act) is fundamental to the advancement of this work,” wrote press secretary Amy Falkner.

”The (Court of Appeal) opinion does not change our commitment to engage all provinces in the spirit of co-operative federalism.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 9, 2026.

— With files from Lauren Krugel in Calgary.

stories.title: Encampment removal in Saskatoon ‘very sad,’ but necessary, advocate says
stories.summary: Thursday's removal of a Saskatoon encampment at 20th Street and Avenue K South has left many residents seeking resources from Saskatoon outreach groups, they say.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
The removal of a Saskatoon encampment earlier this week was upsetting, but necessary, a local outreach advocate said.

The reaction comes following the City of Saskatoon’s decision to remove the encampment on city-owned private property at 20th Street and Avenue K South on Thursday. In a news release that evening, the city said 120 people left the site.

Eighty tents were removed from the encampment, the City of Saskatoon added.

“It was very sad for us to see the encampments go down, but to be honest, they needed to. There has been a lot of violence,” Shirley Isbister, president of the Central Urban Métis Federation Inc. (Cumfi), told Global News.

“There was alcohol, drugs being moved in and that’s not a good environment for safety for the people in the encampments or for the people in the community.”

Following the cleanup of the encampment, Cumfi’s president said a large number of its residents arrived at the Saskatoon nonprofit and set up in its area.

Many of them set up close to the nearby railroad tracks, she said, adding two previous encampment residents sought shelter in the group’s Mobile Housing and Community Resource Centre Bus. The bus has Wi-Fi, as well as contact information for people to get housing.

“We have a lot of encampments here. And we have the bathrooms, and we have the showers but it’s also getting cold,” Isbister said, noting that those facilities are expected to close at the end of this month in anticipation of winter weather.

“That tells me that there’s a lot of people who aren’t ready to be housed yet,” she continued.

“People gather and they stay in the encampments because that’s where they’re happy.”

Isibister said the charity will continue providing support and resources, such as clothing and blankets, to people who reach out, including those who have established encampments around Cumfi.

Melissa Zimmer, president and founder of Bridge City Warmth, a volunteer group who distributes supplies to people who are homeless in Saskatoon said her group was visiting the encampment on 20th Street multiple times a day in recent weeks to hand out business cards.

She said Thursday’s takedown led to the group assisting in finding housing for five people.

“Since the encampment’s been taken down, we’ve had all kinds of calls, text messages, emails just looking for assistance with housing, and just we’re finding that there’s just so many barriers for those looking for housing,” Zimmer said.

On Thursday night, the nonprofit had a street patrol which observed many residents from the encampment who needed a hot meal or new supplies, she continued. Those living at the now-removed site are scattered across the city – including some who found spots in shelters before they filled.

“When we showed up last night at our street patrol, we left with nothing. People need stuff. They’re cold, they’re hungry, they’re tired,” Zimmer said.

Ahead of the winter, the group has put out a call for highly requested items, such as blankets and jackets.

The reaction comes following the City of Saskatoon’s decision to remove the encampment on city-owned private property at 20th Street and Avenue K South on Thursday. In a news release that evening, the city said 120 people left the site.
Eighty tents were removed from the encampment, the City of Saskatoon added.

“There was alcohol, drugs being moved in and that’s not a good environment for safety for the people in the encampments or for the people in the community.”

stories.title: Canadians’ mental health is at a decade low: Western prof explains why, and what May help
stories.summary: Western University professor Eric Collins reflects on mental health worsening in Canada, and what could be done to tackle the problem.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
In Canada, almost a third of the population rated their mental health fair or poorlast year, an increase from five years earlier. By the age of 40, one in two Canadians will have had, or be living with, a mental illness.

Mental health has only worsened since the COVID-19 pandemic, and reflects a pattern of declining rates across the globe. We’re in the midst of a systemic mental health crisis that has evolved over the past several decades, explained Western University’s Eric Collins.

A professor of health studies within the Faculty of Health Sciences, Collins specializes in teaching and researching mental illness. Today’s crisis is the culmination of an ever-shifting notion of mental health, he said, and the policies that have sprung forth from those views.

In the ancient world, mental illness was often framed as a supernatural curse or moral failure, laying the groundwork for centuries of stigma and cruelty to those affected. With the discovery of brain networks and neurochemistry, the 20 th century brought a modern understanding of mental health, rooted in science. Advancements in technology have further unearthed its complexity.

We still haven’t got it figured out, Collins stressed.

An over-emphasis on the biological mechanisms of the brain has turned mental health into a checklist, he says, where “people are labelled as mentally ill or having a diagnosis because of how they check off a number of boxes in a diagnostic manual. It is a mistake to think of our mental health in isolation from our physical environment, from our social relationships, our workplace, and all these factors,” he added.

Mental health is a collection of our emotional, psychological and social capacity – which, together, allow us to deal with adversity and tough times, Collins said.

But external factors are weighing on us more than ever. Collins considers the current affordability crisis one of the greatest contributors to our worsening mental state.

“It’s impossible to ignore because of the implications it has on an everyday basis. We need bread, we need vegetables, we need somewhere to live,” he said. “If those things are out of reach or putting us into debt, that affects us every single day.”

Even more pervasive, and just as influential, is social media. Collins points to the slew of mixed content that floods feeds, often filled with violent and graphic imagery, as taking a significant toll on our well-being. And while this negative content stirs up immediate feelings of angst, aspirational content from influencers showcasing their fitness or wealth lifestyle can be equally as disheartening.

“It’s become, for many people, the benchmark they’re trying to reach. And if they’re not there, they feel at a deficit through this comparison,” Collins said.

While extending our ability to connect with people online, Collins also recognizes how internet culture has re-shaped our social lives, an irreplaceable ingredient to happiness.

“We’re not machines or robots. We’re designed to connect with one another in-person, in real life,” he stressed. “If our existence is not structured to facilitate that, we pay a price.”

The price is an all-encompassing weight on our well-being, extending to our physical health as well.

Our bodies are always responding in a way to try to help us survive, and in many cases, thrive, he said. “When our mental health is poor, it can be difficult to get off the couch, get out of bed, find the energy to do the things we know would help.”

This is why reframing mental health holistically – as an experience deeply responsive to the web of our surroundings – is an important starting point for understanding and effectively addressing this crisis, Collins said. Not only does it take pressure off the individual, “it exposes many societal problems contributing to our well-being.”

As long as these pressures – soaring affordability costs, constant exposure to harmful social media content and the absence of meaningful in-person social connection – continue to dominate daily life, solving the mental health crisis will be difficult, Collins believes. But he remains hopeful. On a systemic level, he sees expanding access to high-quality, community-based mental health support as an essential, timely strategy that can provide immediate relief to those most in need while broader social reforms are implemented.

Because specialized mental health care is largely privatized and out of reach, many Canadians are left navigating years-long public waitlists. In the absence of timely professional care, some people use harmful coping strategies, such as substance misuse, chronic gambling or other high-risk behaviours for temporary relief, Collins said.

Encouraging young adults to choose a career in the mental health care field, amid a shortage in the industry, and ensure there is available services for those who need them, is a possible solution to democratizing care, Collins said.

“You need to have the bricks and mortar, the hospitals, the clinics, the institutions available to house people or patients, but also the trained experts to work. All this lowers barriers to access.”

On a personal level, he encourages people to center the fundamentals, and take it step by step.

“If you’re fortunate enough to have a home that has a roof over it and has a refrigerator and shower, try your best to take care of yourself that way,” he said.

Collins’ Tips:

Get good quality sleep.

Limit your exposure to social media.

Try to eat nutritious food.

Take care of your hygiene.

Try to exercise.

Connect with others in-person.

“I am optimistic that we’re figuring it out, painfully, but in a way that’s moving us in a positive direction,” Collins said.

Reflecting on his childhood and adolescence, Collins experienced his own mental health struggles. He credits the support of people around him, access to quality mental health care and a relentless determination, with leading him to recovery. This triumph gave him invaluable insight into what mental health means, and how we can all navigate it.

“I’ve learned that there is a pathway to recovery. I’ve lived it, and it’s possible for others as well,” he said.

“It’s inevitable that we’ll experience adversity in our personal lives, we’re all recovering from something – but in that, we can find deep meaning and establish connections that really make it all worth it.”

stories.title: All evidence heard in trial of former babysitter charged in toddler’s death
stories.summary: Following 49 days of testimony, lengthy legal arguments and numerous adjournments all of the evidence is now in at the trial of a former Strathroy area babysitter charged in the death of a toddler.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
Following 49 days of testimony, lengthy legal arguments and numerous adjournments all of the evidence is now in at the trial of a former Strathroy area babysitter charged in the death of a toddler.

Meggin Van Hoof, 47, has plead not guilty to one charge of manslaughter in connection to the death of Nathaniel McLellan.

The 15-month-old boy had been in the care of Van Hoof on the day he was rushed to hospital by his mother 11 years ago.

He died in October 2015 after suffering blunt force trauma to the head.

Van Hoof would not be charged until six years later.

After the Crown closed its case on Friday, the defence said it was not calling any evidence and that the accused herself would not be testifying.

Justice Michael Carnegie then told the court, “It is the Crown that bears the burden of proving the offence beyond a reasonable doubt.”

The matter has now been put over until Oct. 28 to set a date for closing submissions which May not be heard until February of next year.

stories.title: 7 Alberta referendum signs vandalized in Fort McMurray
stories.summary: More than half of the signs encouraging Albertans to vote to have a second, binding referendum to leave Canada were vandalized in Fort McMurray over the past week.
stories.author: Karen Bartko
stories.content:
Treason. No to the nine. Not your land.

Those are just some of the words spray-painted this week on several Alberta referendum political signs placed throughout Fort McMurray.

Wood Buffalo RCMP were alerted Thursday about the damage to more than half of the signs promoting Alberta separatism in the northern Alberta community.

RCMP said they received a report that seven signs relating to the upcoming Oct. 19 referendum had been damaged with spray paint, sometime between Sept. 29 and Oct. 4.

Elections Alberta granted permission for 11 signs from third-party campaign group Let Alberta Decide to be placed around the community.

The signs were all spray painted with various graffiti, bearing messages like “No Treason Gtfo!!!” and one said “Go 2 America!”

It’s a criminal offence to destroy, damage or steal election signs, which RCMP has pointed out several times over the years when signs in other elections have been vandalized or gone missing.

The vandalism happened to two signs along Thickwood Boulevard, two along Confederation Drive, and one each on Hospital Street, MacKenzie Boulevard and along Highway 63 across from the dump station.

The Let Alberta Decide campaign is promoting Albertans selecting option two on the tenth question being asked in the Oct. 19 referendum.

It states: “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?”

The RCMP said the signs have since been repaired and are now asking for the public’s assistance in identifying those responsible for damaging them.

Anyone who witnessed suspicious activity near any of the above-mentioned locations, has relevant surveillance or dash camera footage, or has information that could help the investigation is asked to call Wood Buffalo RCMP at 780-788-4040.

content_blocks.text: RCMP said they received a report that seven signs relating to the upcoming Oct. 19 referendum had been damaged with spray paint, sometime between Sept. 29 and Oct. 4.
Elections Alberta granted permission for 11 signs from third-party campaign group Let Alberta Decide to be placed around the community.
The signs were all spray painted with various graffiti, bearing messages like “No Treason Gtfo!!!” and one said “Go 2 America!”
It’s a criminal offence to destroy, damage or steal election signs, which RCMP has pointed out several times over the years when signs in other elections have been vandalized or gone missing.
The vandalism happened to two signs along Thickwood Boulevard, two along Confederation Drive, and one each on Hospital Street, MacKenzie Boulevard and along Highway 63 across from the dump station.
The Let Alberta Decide campaign is promoting Albertans selecting option two on the tenth question being asked in the Oct. 19 referendum.

It states: “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?”
The RCMP said the signs have since been repaired and are now asking for the public’s assistance in identifying those responsible for damaging them.

Anyone who witnessed suspicious activity near any of the above-mentioned locations, has relevant surveillance or dash camera footage, or has information that could help the investigation is asked to call Wood Buffalo RCMP at 780-788-4040.

stories.title: Family of Walkerton crash victim pushing for school transportation and grief counselling reform
stories.summary: It’s been more than a year since four Walkerton high school softball players and their coach were taken in a tragic crash near London.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
It’s been more than a year since four Walkerton high school softball players and their coach were taken in a tragic crash near London.

Coach and teacher Mat Eckert was driving the SUV carrying Olivia Rourke, Rowan McLeod, Danica Baker, and Kaydance Ford when it collided with a transport truck on May 23, 2025.

While she holds no blame towards Coach Eckert, Kaydance Ford’s mother believes the practice of teachers or coaches driving students to off-site sports, or school sanctioned activities should no longer be happening.

“A lot of the time there’s teachers and coaches who are driving students and that should not be the norm. It shouldn’t be common. I don’t know why it was ever made a thing because it’s not in their job description. They should not be responsible to transfer students to a school sanctioned event. That never should have been a thing,” said Jessica Ford, Kaydance Ford’s mother.

Jessica has submitted a 14 point Student Grief and Traumatic Loss Reform Proposal to the Bluewater District School Board. At it’s core, she’s calling for a school sanctioned school bus or coach bus to be the main source of transportation for students to off-site activities.

“I want to see not necessarily a bus for every single school sanctioned event, but for most of them, if it makes sense to fund a bus then fund a bus. If there’s no funding then ask parents if they can pay for the bus. We used to do that all the time when I was young, so there’s really no reason why we can’t do it again,” she said.

Jessica is also calling for a more standardized framework for death and traumatic loss through the school board, including long term student grief counselling, and a bereaved family liaison to help families navigate help and support during their darkest days.

“Yes, the initial tragedy needs fast support, but not just after that first week or first month. It needs to be ongoing. And it can’t be that the student has to be responsible for reaching out to ask for that. We shouldn’t have to ask for grief support when we’re grieving,” she said.

She wants better communication for the next family that faces a tragedy like theirs. As an example, she says her family wasn’t informed the school was making “memorial tables” for the crash victims until they were already in place.

“Because we didn’t learn about the memorial tables until later, we very well could have been the only family that their daughter’s table didn’t have personal things. And that hurt us, but it also would have ended up hurting her friends, and other students and staff,” she said.

The Bluewater District School Board says they are looking over Jessica’s reforms. While they are proud of their response in the wake of the crash tragedy, they acknowledge more could possibly be done in the future.

As far as student transportation to off-site activities goes, the school board says they too want school bus transportation for all students but that’s not always possible.

“Efforts are made to secure bus transportation for trips and excursions where possible. However, there are limitations and unique circumstances that must be considered and applying this approach consistently to all trips across more than 40 school locations presents some challenges. We will continue to review all options available to us while prioritizing the safety of our students and staff,” said a Bluewater District School Board statement.

Jessica has met with school board officials regarding her proposed changes to trauma response, and off-site school transportation.

“I really hoped that we would learn from our tragedy. We can’t change what happened to our family, but we can advocate for changes to happen before something else happens to another family because we don’t live in a perfect world.

This wasn’t the first tragedy, and it won’t be the last. So we need to learn from it. And we really need to look at how we transport our children. I don’t want to see another family go through the added trauma or the added stress that we have.

And I in a perfect world, it wouldn’t happen again. But in reality, we live in an imperfect world. So I want to see something in place that can prevent as much of this as possible,” said Jessica.

To learn more about Jessica’s Student Grief and Traumatic Loss Reform Proposal, you can visit the Kaydance Ford Athletic and Trades Foundation website .

The full response to Ford’s proposal, from the Bluewater District School Board.

“Bluewater District School Board has received the proposal and is reviewing its recommendations with staff in the applicable portfolios.

When it comes to critical incidents affecting our schools, we are continually learning, refining our practices, and looking for meaningful ways to strengthen our existing supports and communication practices. The tragedy impacting Walkerton District Community School in May 2025 was significant.

Our school and system-level staff closely followed our established tragedy response and crisis communications processes that have guided us through many previous school-based incidents. This included consulting and working closely with other experts outside of our organization, such as the Center for Trauma Informed Practices (Ctip) and Victim Services.

These are living documents that will continue to be refined through our direct experiences in managing situations involving tragedy. While our primary focus has been to support the students and staff of a school when they experience a traumatic event, we are exploring ways to better support directly impacted families in our approach, which is one of the key areas outlined in the proposal.

Regarding student transportation for trips and events, we follow board policy BP 5602-D Field Trips and Excursions and its accompanying procedure AP 5602-D Field Trips and Excursions – Approval Process . As outlined in the procedure, it is currently a requirement that any volunteer drivers who are transporting students must first obtain appropriate formal authorization.

Our broader transportation policy, BP 6501-D Transportation , indicates the intent to provide transportation (i.e., busing) for school-sponsored educational, sports, and general-interest programs, within the limits established by the annual budget.

In accordance with the policy, efforts are made to secure bus transportation for trips and excursions, where possible. However, there are limitations and unique circumstances that must be considered and applying this approach consistently to all trips across more than 40 school locations presents some challenges.

We will continue to review all options available to us while prioritizing the safety of our students and staff.”

stories.title: Canadian arrested in FBI hack that exposed employees’ personal data
stories.summary: Arrest was the latest targeting ShinyHunters, the group that claimed responsibility for the hack on the bureau’s jobs portal
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The RCMP says a Canadian has been arrested by the FBI in connection with an attack from a criminal hacking group which breached the bureau’s jobs portal and obtained sensitive and personal data on nearly all the Fbi’s employees.

FBI Director Kash Patel confirmed on Friday the arrest of another co-conspirator in the ShinyHunters attack. He said the arrest had taken place earlier this week, related to a hack of FBIjobs.gov.

“This is the latest arrest this FBI has made in a matter of days involving this network, as we work non-stop to dismantle the group, pursue new leads and evidence, and act quickly,” Patel said. “This arrest demonstrates the strength and reach of our efforts to protect Americans from cybercrime. We will continue to work closely with our partners to disrupt what’s left of the ShinyHunters group and their associates, no matter where they operate.”

The arrest was the latest targeting ShinyHunters, the group that claimed responsibility for the hack, as the FBI continues a global investigation into the breach of its network, which Patel said “occurred on a platform managed by a third-party vendor.”

The identity of the person arrested was not immediately clear, nor what charges they might face. The FBI would provide no more details of the arrest.

RCMP spokesperson Ian Lordon said Friday “the RCMP is aware of the arrest of a Canadian in the U.S. in connection with the ShinyHunters hack,” but directed all further questions to the FBI.

“The RCMP does not comment on investigations being conducted by other countries,” Lordon said.

In a message taking responsibility for the hack and announcing the collection of sensitive information, ShinyHunters said it had taken action over false allegations contained in an FBI public advisory from May that described the organization as a “cyber criminal group specializing in large-scale data breaches and extortion.”

That advisory characterized ShinyHunters as “threat actors” who often “use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims,” commonly harass or threaten people and “May falsely claim to have sensitive or compromising information, including embarrassing photographs or videos of victims, which frequently do not exist.”

Experts said that although the data that appeared to be compromised was the type of personal information that is routinely accessed during a breach, the hack nonetheless had alarming national security implications given that it could expose agents and their families to extortion, swatting and other harassment and because the identities of spouses were also said to have been obtained.

With reports from the Associated Press

stories.title: Why Canada’s fertility rate remains at a record low
stories.summary: Canada’s fertility rate remained at a record low in 2025, while the average age of mothers at childbirth continued to climb, according to the latest figures from Statistics Canada.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
Canada’s fertility rate remained at a record low in 2025, while the average age of mothers at childbirth continued to climb, according to new data.

The latest figures from Statistics Canada found women had an average of 1.26 children, unchanged from the all-time low reached in 2024, while most provinces and territories recorded what the national agency called “all-time low” fertility rates.

The longer-term decline has been underway for years, raising questions about the changing circumstances in which Canadians are deciding whether and when to have children.

How the trend started

Maria Porcellato, CEO of the Alberta-based EndoDiagnosis, said in an interview with CTVNews.CA the trend reflects changes that have been building for decades, including working conditions, the cost of living, lifestyle choices and delays in childbearing.

“These fertility rates have been declining for decades, and there are things that have changed over that time,” she said.

Canada’s fertility rate began its general decline in 2009, according to Statistics Canada. The decrease became sharper between 2017 and 2023, with data showing an average annual decline of four per cent, excluding 2021, when an increase was recorded.

The rate slightly fell by 0.8 per cent in 2024 before it remained unchanged last year.

The total fertility rate estimates the number of children a woman would have over her lifetime if the age-specific birth rates observed in a given year remained constant. It is a statistical measure, rather than a prediction of how many children women today will ultimately have.

The long-term decline is not unique to Canada. Among 20 selected high-income countries, Canada had the seventh-lowest fertility rate in 2025.

The United States had the highest rate at 1.57 children per woman, followed by Iceland and France, both at 1.56. South Korea had the lowest, at 0.80.

Canada’s rate was closer to the middle of the group for many years, but began shifting toward countries with the lowest rates in 2018.

More women are having children later

The average age of mothers at childbirth reached 31.9 years in 2025, another record high. In 1976, the average was 26.7.

Porcellato said delaying childbearing can make conception more difficult, while conditions such as endometriosis and polycystic ovary syndrome (Pcos) can further complicate reproductive health.

“Many women carry these,” she said, referring to gynecological conditions, adding that endometriosis, a chronic condition in which tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows elsewhere in the body, affects as many as one in four women.

Endometriosis can cause pain and, in some cases, fertility problems. Meanwhile, Pcos is a hormonal and metabolic condition that can interfere with ovulation.

Porcellato argued that earlier recognition and management of these conditions could help women make more informed decisions about their reproductive health.

“If we are not, as a medical system, practising preventative health, and detecting these diseases early in a woman’s life, and we’re letting them progress,” she said, “these diseases go from simple to complex.”

Lifestyle and stress under scrutiny

Porcellato also pointed out that lifestyle choices can affect reproductive health. “Dietary choices, exercise, sleep habits, and a sedentary lifestyle ... can have a huge impact on our fertility,” she said, adding chronic stress May influence cortisol levels and metabolic processes, including insulin resistance.

She said that women juggling work, family responsibilities and caregiving can face sustained pressures that affect their health.

stories.title: Former Isis bride pleads guilty to terror-related charge in B.C. court
stories.summary: Vancouver - A British Columbia woman who married an Islamic State fighter has pleaded guilty to terrorist-related charges in a Vancouver court.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Public Prosecution Service of Canada confirms that Kimberly Polman pleaded guilty on Thursday to leaving Canada to participate in activities of a terrorist group, namely the Islamic State.

Polman had been held in a Syrian detention camp for several years before being returned to Canada in 2022.

Article continues below

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

She was in poor health, suffering from hepatitis, and her sister said in an interview before she returned that Polman had post-traumatic stress and other challenges.

Her sister, who spoke to The Canadian Press on condition of anonymity, said in an interview in 2021 that Polman met an Islamic State fighter online and married him, but they soon separated and she later denounced the group.

Polman’s trial on two charges was to begin on Nov. 9, and a sentencing hearing hasn’t yet been set.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 9, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Alberta’s referendum on a separation vote is approaching. Ask us your questions
stories.summary: Our Alberta-based reporters and editors will be answering questions on how both sides have been campaigning and what the result could mean for the province – and Canada as a whole
stories.author: Globe Staff
stories.content:
Alberta’s Oct. 19 referendum could be the province’s most consequential vote yet, as Albertans decide whether to remain in Canada or move toward a binding referendum on independence, among a number of questions on the ballot .

The looming referendum and fierce campaigns for and against leaving have highlighted deep fractures in Confederation as Canada faces separatist threats on two fronts.

In the lead-up to the pivotal vote, The Globe has covered how some Alberta separatists have received tactical assistance from U.S. political operatives and offered the province’s natural resources in exchange , the federalist side’s cash-strapped efforts to keep the province within Canada , and much more .

On Thursday, Oct. 15, at 11 a.m. MT, Alberta-based reporters Carrie Tait and Matthew Scace and opinion editor Tyler Dawson will be answering reader questions on the referendum, how both sides have been campaigning and what the result could mean for the province – and Canada as a whole.

Submit your questions in the box below, or send us an email at audience@globeandmail.com .

stories.title: Canada backs International Criminal Court after U.S. imposes sanctions
stories.summary: Ottawa - Canada signed a joint statement in support of the International Criminal Court after the United States moved to sanction the organization today.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Canada signed a joint statement in support of the International Criminal Court after the United States moved to sanction the organization Friday.

Canada joined Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom in issuing the statement, which says they strongly disagree with the sanctions.

The statement says the signatories reaffirm their “continued and unwavering support for the independence, impartiality, and integrity of the ICC.”

It says if the sanctions take effect, they will “have a significant impact on the Court’s work, its dedicated staff and their families. They work every day to bring those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice and to support their victims.”

The sanctions cut the court off from U.S.-based financial services, technology companies and U.S. currency. They are part of a U.S. campaign to dismantle the tribunal in response to investigations into the United States and its allies, including Israel.

The Trump administration has imposed sweeping new sanctions on the International Criminal Court as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal that the U.S. believes has become politicized and attempted to unfairly and illegally prosecute Americans and Israelis on war crimes charges. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the sanctions Friday, after the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to South African prosecutor Navi Pillay, a former judge at the ICC and other international courts. Trump has coveted that prize for himself. The move, however, long predated the Nobel Prize announcement. (Oct. 9, 2026)

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the sanctions Friday, calling the court “fake.”

“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling their ability to operate against us,” he said in a video statement.

“Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC.”

He said he expects U.S. allies to “rein in this rogue court” — and if they don’t, “the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC piece by piece until Americans are threatened no longer.”

The sanctions were announced after the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to South African jurist Navi Pillay.

Pillay chaired a commission that last year concluded Israel was responsible for a genocide with a specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza.

The Trump administration has previously sanctioned ICC officials, including Canadian judge Kimberly Prost. Prost was sanctioned last year for authorizing an ICC investigation of the actions of U.S. personnel in Afghanistan.

The State Department also took action against ICC officials from France, Fiji and Senegal over the tribunal’s investigation of Israel’s actions in Gaza and the West Bank.

Rubio said at the time the U.S. would “hold accountable those responsible for the Icc’s morally bankrupt and legally baseless actions against Americans and Israelis.”

With files from The Associated Press and Kelly Geraldine Malone

stories.title: FBI arrests Canadian in ShinyHunters hack of the bureau’s jobs portal
stories.summary: Ottawa — The RCMP says a Canadian has been arrested by the FBI in connection with an attack from a criminal hacking group which breached the bureau's jobs portal and obtained sensitive and personal data on nearly all the Fbi's employees.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The RCMP says a Canadian has been arrested by the FBI in connection with an attack from a criminal hacking group which breached the bureau’s jobs portal and obtained sensitive and personal data on nearly all the Fbi’s employees.

FBI Director Kash Patel confirmed on Friday the arrest of another co-conspirator in the ShinyHunters attack. He said the arrest had taken place earlier this week, related to a hack of FBIjobs.gov.

“This is the latest arrest this FBI has made in a matter of days involving this network, as we work non-stop to dismantle the group, pursue new leads and evidence, and act quickly,” Patel said. “This arrest demonstrates the strength and reach of our efforts to protect Americans from cybercrime. We will continue to work closely with our partners to disrupt what’s left of the ShinyHunters group and their associates, no matter where they operate.”

The arrest was the latest targeting ShinyHunters, the group that claimed responsibility for the hack, as the FBI continues a global investigation into the breach of its network, which Patel said “occurred on a platform managed by a third-party vendor.”

The identity of the person arrested was not immediately clear, nor what charges they might face. The FBI would provide no more details of the arrest.

RCMP spokesperson Ian Lordon said Friday “the RCMP is aware of the arrest of a Canadian in the U.S. in connection with the ShinyHunters hack,” but directed all further questions to the FBI.

“The RCMP does not comment on investigations being conducted by other countries,” Lordon said.

stories.title: Poilievre to campaign for Canadian unity in Alberta next week ahead of referendum
stories.summary: Pierre Poilievre is scheduled to deliver his speech during the Canada Strong and Free Network conference in Calgary on Oct. 16, followed by an address from Premier Danielle Smith.
stories.author: David Baxter
stories.content:
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said Friday he will be in Alberta just days before the province’s referendum to deliver a speech on Canadian unity.

The House of Commons will be on a break next week after MPs head back to their ridings for the Thanksgiving weekend.

Poilievre is scheduled to deliver his speech during the Canada Strong and Free Network (formerly the Manning Centre) conference in Calgary on Oct. 16.

The schedule lists the title of Poilievre’s speech keynote: “The Canadian Drift: Reclaiming Confidence, Abundance and Freedom for Alberta.”

His speech is expected to be followed by an address from Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who will also take part in a fireside with columnist Rick Bell.

Jason Kenney will also be speaking at the gathering of movers and shakers in conservative politics.

The former premier, who has been fiercely vocal about staying in Canada, is set to participate in a debate and fireside chat titled ” The Sovereignty Vote and the Path Forward” alongside Calgary Confederation CPC hopeful Elan Harper , Fraser Institute fellow and law professor Bruce Pardy and former MLA-turned-publisher of the Western Standard Derek Fildebrandt.

Poilievre told a press conference in Burlington, Ont., ON Friday he will also be doing “additional campaigning on the ground” in Alberta.

“We encourage all Canadians of all parties to join in uniting all Canadians to make ourselves safe, affordable, and fully independent here at home,” Poilievre said.

When asked about tech industrialist Elon Musk saying recently that Alberta, Saskatchewan and Quebec should separate , Poilievre said “Canadians control their own destiny.”

“Frankly, people can tweet whatever they want, but tweets and memes do not affect Canada. What affects Canada is the decisions made by the Canadian people,” he added.

The premiers of Alberta and Saskatchewan brushed off Musk’s comments, while Quebec’s new premier has said he won’t trigger a separation vote while U.S. President Donald Trump is in office.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said the future of Canada will be decided by Canadians when asked Thursday about Musk’s comments at a press conference in Sherbrooke, Que.

While born in South Africa, Musk holds Canadian citizenship and has lived in several parts of the country.

His mother was born and raised in Saskatchewan, where the tech titan spent time living and working on a family farm as a teenager.

He moved on to Vancouver before attending Queen’s University in Ontario, where he met his first wife .

Alberta Conservative MP Dane Lloyd has been tasked with leading the federal Conservatives’ unity campaign in the province.

Responding to reports in The Globe and Mail about Alberta separatists allegedly seeking the help of the U.S. government in exchange for potential water rights and oil royalties, Lloyd said Monday “no one has the right to promise away Alberta’s birthright.”

Lloyd stopped short of describing that activity as foreign interference, saying more information needs to be gathered.

Mitch Sylvestre of the separatist Alberta Prosperity Project denied offering oil and water rights to the U.S. in his group’s three conversations with U.S. State Department officials in Washington. He also said he only attended one of those meetings.

Albertans will vote on the prospect of a future separation referendum, along with nine other questions involving constitutional and immigration issues, ON Oct. 19.

— With files from Karen Barto, Global News and The Canadian Press reporter Jack Farrell in Edmonton

stories.title: Expert insight: How prediction markets could affect public health, democracy
stories.summary: Western University expert Noah Vanderhoeven examines how prediction markets could affect public health and democratic elections.
stories.author: Jacquelyn Mitchell
stories.content:
Polymarket, a U.S.-based prediction-market website, is taking wagers on who will be London, Ont.’s next mayor. There are also markets for Toronto, Windsor and even Stratford.

The past two years have seen commercial prediction markets move from a niche forecasting tool into mainstream finance, allowing users to buy and sell contracts tied to the outcomes of real-world events ranging from elections to economic indicators.

A 2024 U.S. federal court ruling allowing regulated prediction markets to offer contracts on political outcomes helped accelerate the growth of platforms such as Kalshi and Polymarket.

As these markets become more visible and their election forecasts reach wider audiences, questions are emerging about what their growth could mean for public health and democratic life.

Because prediction markets package real-time wagering in the language of trading rather than betting, researchers have argued that they function as an emerging and largely unregulated form of gambling.

Their structural features – rapid feedback, round-the-clock access and engagement-optimized design – May carry the same addiction and financial-harm risks long associated with sports betting and other high-frequency wagering products.

A well-established body of addiction research on legalized gambling raises public health concerns as online gambling becomes easier to access across digital technologies. Similar concerns have emerged following the expansion of online sports gambling.

Since the 2018 U.S. Supreme Court decision allowing states to legalize sports betting, studies have documented a rise in gambling-related harms, including increases in internet searches and helpline calls for gambling addiction. Canada followed by legalizing online sports gambling in 2021.

Research has found gambling companies can disproportionately affect young people and individuals with addictive personalities, who are at greater risk of gambling addiction and the antisocial behaviours associated with it.

Furthermore, public health reviews have linked commercial gambling expansion to worsening mental health outcomes, including depression, anxiety, substance use and self-harm. These links predate the current prediction-market boom but reflect some of the same underlying mechanisms as online sports betting.

Research consistently frames gambling harms as shaped by individual behaviour, expanding access, low-friction digital platforms and industry designs aimed at continuous engagement.

Beyond participation in these markets, prediction markets are becoming part of the information voters May access when making voting choices, alongside traditional avenues such as news coverage, campaign events, candidate debates and polls.

They are a source of new information that voters have not previously had in this form, offering continuously changing odds that can appear to provide a real-time assessment of an election.

In their earlier years, prediction markets were often accurate at forecasting election outcomes. However, research supporting their accuracy was conducted when these markets were relatively niche, attracting people who were highly engaged with specific electoral contests.

Today’s platforms operate on a much larger scale, are hosted on widely used financial platforms and May reach participants with less political knowledge or expertise.

Nonetheless, their purported forecasting ability is part of what gives prediction markets their appeal, but it also raises questions about how they are interpreted. Prices can be swayed by individual traders with large stakes or insider information, and prediction markets lack some of the transparency associated with election polls.

In Canada, companies are not currently permitted to offer political prediction markets domestically, but Canadians can still encounter markets operated in other countries.

This means prediction markets are becoming part of Canadians’ political information environment, even when Canadians are not participating directly in those markets.

We do not yet know how much these odds influence voters, or whether exposure to them changes how people understand an election. As prediction markets become more prominent, those questions will become harder to ignore.

Like debates over AI governance and misinformation regulation, attitudes toward online gambling and prediction markets ultimately turn on how societies navigate the trade-off between market freedom and protective regulation.

Understanding these attitudes therefore offers a case study in public reasoning about emerging technology governance more broadly, not just a narrow inquiry into gambling policy.

It is not yet clear whether the public supports broad access to online gambling technologies or regulatory restrictions on different types of prediction markets, including political, financial or sports markets.

There are also various regulatory approaches, including stake or wager limits, online identification requirements and advertising rules. Prediction market companies have strong incentives to expand access to jurisdictions like Canada, but that carries public health risks based on existing research.

Given the consistent public health concerns surrounding digital gambling platforms, and growing discussions about how prediction markets May affect democracy, public opinion on their legalization and regulation remains understudied. It will be important to start by getting a clearer picture of what people think about these digital technologies and how they use them.

Prediction markets are arriving in politics before we know how people feel about them. The odds May start speaking before the public does.Image 1: The Conversation

Noah Eliot Vanderhoeven, PhD, Political Science, Western University

They are a source of new information that voters have not previously had in this form, offering continuously changing odds that can appear to provide a real-time assessment of an election.

In their earlier years, prediction markets were often accurate at forecasting election outcomes. However, research supporting their accuracy was conducted when these markets were relatively niche, attracting people who were highly engaged with specific electoral contests.
Today’s platforms operate on a much larger scale, are hosted on widely used financial platforms and May reach participants with less political knowledge or expertise.

Nonetheless, their purported forecasting ability is part of what gives prediction markets their appeal, but it also raises questions about how they are interpreted. Prices can be swayed by individual traders with large stakes or insider information, and prediction markets lack some of the transparency associated with election polls.
In Canada, companies are not currently permitted to offer political prediction markets domestically, but Canadians can still encounter markets operated in other countries.
This means prediction markets are becoming part of Canadians’ political information environment, even when Canadians are not participating directly in those markets.

We do not yet know how much these odds influence voters, or whether exposure to them changes how people understand an election. As prediction markets become more prominent, those questions will become harder to ignore.
What can be done?

Like debates over AI governance and misinformation regulation, attitudes toward online gambling and prediction markets ultimately turn on how societies navigate the trade-off between market freedom and protective regulation.
Understanding these attitudes therefore offers a case study in public reasoning about emerging technology governance more broadly, not just a narrow inquiry into gambling policy.

It is not yet clear whether the public supports broad access to online gambling technologies or regulatory restrictions on different types of prediction markets, including political, financial or sports markets.

There are also various regulatory approaches, including stake or wager limits, online identification requirements and advertising rules. Prediction market companies have strong incentives to expand access to jurisdictions like Canada, but that carries public health risks based on existing research.

Given the consistent public health concerns surrounding digital gambling platforms, and growing discussions about how prediction markets May affect democracy, public opinion on their legalization and regulation remains understudied. It will be important to start by getting a clearer picture of what people think about these digital technologies and how they use them.
Prediction markets are arriving in politics before we know how people feel about them. The odds May start speaking before the public does.Image 1: The Conversation

stories.title: Galloway testifies of ‘numerous’ faculty-student relationships in UBC arts program
stories.summary: Vancouver - Author and former University of B.C. creative writing chair Steven Galloway says there was no prohibition on sexual relationships between students and faculty, and he knows of “numerous instances” of similar relationships in the university’s faculty of arts.
stories.author: Darryl Greer The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - Author and former UBC creative writing chair Steven Galloway has told a court that he is ashamed of having had an affair with a student, but there was no prohibition on sexual relationships between faculty and students.

Galloway — who is now suing the woman and others for defamation after she made unproven accusations of sexual assault against him — said he knew of “numerous instances” of similar relationships in the University of B.C.‘s faculty of arts.

The defamation trial entered its fifth day in B.C. Supreme Court with the lawyer for the woman, known as A.B., telling Galloway his cross-examination would not be a “tea party.”

Arden Beddoes questioned Galloway about a voice mail he left A.B. in November 2015, apologizing, saying he was ashamed and working to be a better person, and that he had “turned over a new leaf.”

Galloway told the court he didn’t think he would be fired for violating the university’s conflict-of-interest policy. But he was suspended, then fired, and now sells boats for a living, telling the trial on Thursday he can no longer write.

He said on Friday that no other faculty members had ever been terminated for similar conduct, though he should not have cheated on his wife, let alone with a student.

“I know of numerous instances in the faculty of arts where there have been relationships similar to this. And I’m unaware of anyone getting anywhere close to being, at this point, terminated for it,” Galloway said.

Beddoes asked Galloway if he kept having sexual relationships with students, bringing up his current wife and fellow writer Katie Wagner, but Galloway said Wagner had not been a student for “well over a year” when they got together.

“I remain ashamed of having had an affair period, let alone an affair with a student at the university I was at,” he said. “I should not have been cheating on my wife, and I should have not been doing it with a student.”

Galloway, the award-winning author of “The Cellist of Sarajevo,” alleges his career was destroyed by allegations of rape and sexual assault, which he denies and were found unsubstantiated in a report by a former B.C. Supreme Court judge.

His lawsuit against A.B. and others was originally filed in 2018.

Several people originally named as defendants have settled with Galloway and offered public apologies, while A.B., whose name is under a publication ban, is not testifying in the case due to mental health struggles related to the lawsuit.

The court heard this week that her defence no longer includes an assertion she was assaulted, but rather that she reported the alleged assaults.

The court heard on Friday that Galloway repeatedly called both A.B. and fellow faculty member Keith Maillard in November 2015, after receiving an email in which the woman, who was several years older than Galloway, described feeling at risk and “unsafe.”

Beddoes suggested the numerous calls were him “panicking,” but Galloway said he wanted to tell Maillard, a mentor and “father figure,” about the affair himself, knowing his longtime friend would be disappointed.

Galloway said it was “concerning” that someone he cared about felt that way about their relationship, which ended in the spring of 2013.

He said his repeated calls to both A.B. and Maillard were not an attempt to “get ahead of” anything as Beddoes suggested, and he was trying to tell Maillard himself about the affair.

“I don’t know if he would have continued to be my friend,” he said. “I wanted to be the one to tell him for that reason, not to diminish anything (A.B.) might say to him, but because I had done a bad thing and I owed it to him to tell him the bad thing.”

Beddoes told the court Maillard expressed disapproval about “fraternizing” with students in the UBC-sanctioned investigation conducted by retired judge Mary Ellen Boyd.

The court heard that Maillard told Boyd that students’ personal lives weren’t his business, but “only their writing.”

Galloway was cross-examined about staff and student social interactions, which he said included them attending an on-campus pub.

“If you were to go to Koerner’s Pub today after class, you would see students and professors. So, it’s not like people are doing shots. It’s been going on since forever. Perhaps it shouldn’t, but I was not unique, nor do I think it was inappropriate,” he said.

The court heard that A.B. alleged she woke up on the floor of Galloway’s office in May 2011 after one of three alleged assaults, and he had been watching a hockey game on his computer.

But Galloway denied that occurred, saying he didn’t have cable to watch games in his office, nor were games streamed online in 2011.

“I can also say that I have no memory of, at that point, ever watching any hockey game, let alone that one in my office. It just wasn’t a thing,” he said.

Galloway also said students and faculty went to a weekly “standing gathering” of writers at a legion on Main Street in Vancouver.

Maillard had told Boyd he “felt very uncomfortable with Stephen’s regular Thursday night gatherings with students to drink at the legion.”

But Galloway said other faculty members attended, it wasn’t confined to students and it wasn’t his event, only one he was “part of.”

Beddoes later turned to specifics of Galloway’s book sales, taking the court through royalty statements and challenging the author on his claims that the ordeal tanked his career.

Beddoes showed the court royalty statements for “The Cellist of Sarajevo,” both before and after the allegations surfaced in November 2015.

There is no discernible difference, Beddoes said.

Galloway said selling around 2,500 books in a six-month period is “exponentially more” than most Canadian books sell, and to see sales drop to around 600 in another period was, in his view, a “crater.”

The court has heard that Galloway had been working on a three-book comedy series about a ventriloquist detective, for which he’d received a $100,000 advance.

Beddoes suggested the advance was less than he’d received in the past and reflected waning confidence by his publisher, which Galloway said wasn’t an accurate assessment.

“In fact, most writers, if they pitched a book about a ventriloquist detective, would be told. ‘hey, stick to what you’ve done, author of serious war novel,’” Galloway said. “I think, if anything, them letting you do this shows a confidence in me, or at least a willingness to continue to take risks on me.”

The trial is set to resume on Tuesday with Galloway’s cross-examination continuing.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 9, 2026.

stories.title: ‘The explosion would have been a huge ball of flame!’: Suspected chainsaw hydro pole cutter risked all for little return
stories.summary: Police and London Hydro officials continue their search for information after a high-voltage utility pole was allegedly cut down by a chainsaw, sparking an explosion and widespread power outage.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
Police and London Hydro officials continue their search for information after a high-voltage utility pole was allegedly cut down by a chainsaw, sparking an explosion and widespread power outage. Hydro officials concede the blast could have seriously harmed or killed the perpetrators.

The incident took place shortly after 5 p.m. Tuesday on Exeter Road near Sholto Drive when lines touched, sparking a 27,000-volt blast. “The explosion would have been a huge ball of flame! It was so intense, and the heat was so, so high,” said Allan Van Damme, VP of engineering and construction at London Hydro.

As fire and line crews contained the blaze, Van Damme said officials worked to assess the damage. “It became evident very quickly that this was not a normal failure of a component on our grid.” Hydro later confirmed a chainsaw was used to take the pole down.

Grainy video surveillance images released by police show a suspect, wearing a black hoodie with writing on it and grey sweatpants. Police want the public to help identify him and their assistance in tracking this 2019 Honda CRV.

Meanwhile, Van Damme conceded that the suspect or suspects are fortunate to be uninjured. “They are extremely lucky because they would have been standing right in the line of fire as that explosion came down to the ground.

So, it appears that they left the site through the surveillance footage and that they made it out alive. But that could have ended very differently.” The motivation for the act is being investigated by police. It comes as London Hydro continues to be hit by copper thieves who risk their lives for what Van Damme says is very little return.

The incident took place shortly after 5 p.m. Tuesday on Exeter Road near Sholto Drive when lines touched, sparking a 27,000-volt blast. “The explosion would have been a huge ball of flame! It was so intense, and the heat was so, so high,” said Allan Van Damme, VP of engineering and construction at London Hydro.

As fire and line crews contained the blaze, Van Damme said officials worked to assess the damage. “It became evident very quickly that this was not a normal failure of a component on our grid.” Hydro later confirmed a chainsaw was used to take the pole down.

stories.title: Province interfering in Edmonton housing sets disturbing precedent: Calgary mayor
stories.summary: After ordering Edmonton to overturn its bylaws to scale back infill, Jeromy Farkas said there's nothing stopping the province from imposing its will on Calgary over other matters.
stories.author: Dayne Patterson
stories.content:
Calgary’s mayor says the province’s decision to overturn some Edmonton infill housing rules is disturbing attack on local democracy.

On Friday, Jeromy Farkas said while the order from Premier Danielle Smith’s government is not asking Calgary to do the same on this issue, there’s nothing stopping the province from imposing its will on his city on another matter.

He said it’s important to respect the mandate given to municipal leaders to make decisions deemed best for their citizens.

Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack retweeted a video posted by Farkas on Friday in which he expressed his concerns.

A day earlier, Smith directed the City of Edmonton to abandon rules allowing for multi-unit complexes in older, established neighbourhoods on the grounds the units may not be a good fit and don’t make proper room for parking.

Calgary has already rolled back similar rules due to public outcry, and on Thursday Smith directed Calgary keep those rules in place.

Smith said her government does not want to intervene in municipal affairs, but the impact of the multi-units and the concern her government is hearing from Edmonton residents forced the province to step in.

— More to come…

stories.title: Pitching in: Fundraising for Princess Margaret Hospital one goal at a time
stories.summary: John Brezina started out playing in road hockey tournaments that benefit the hospital as a hobby, but it is now his passion
stories.author: Paul Waldie
stories.content:
The organizer: John Brezina

The pitch: Raising $330,000 and climbing

The cause: Toronto’s Princess Margaret Hospital

Like a lot of Canadian kids, John Brezina grew up playing hockey on the street outside his home. He loved the game so much he organized a road hockey league while studying at the University of Toronto and started a lunchtime game after joining Toronto-based technology company Vertafore Canada where he still works.

In 2010, Mr. Brezina was driving down the Don Valley Parkway when he noticed a billboard advertising a day-long, three-on-three ball hockey tournament to raise money for the Princess Margaret Hospital. Mr. Brezina wasn’t familiar with the hospital but he loved the idea of entering a big tournament. “I was sold from that day forward,” he said.

He quickly organized a team from work and they raised around $27,000. He’s been playing in the tournament ever since.

In 2018, Mr. Brezina began having breathing problems. He couldn’t run very hard and tired easily during games. After playing in the tournament, he went to see his doctor who referred him to Princess Margaret. He was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia, a rare form of cancer that affects the blood and bone marrow.

Mr. Brezina underwent months of chemotherapy at the hospital and had a stem cell transplant to rebuild his immune system. He was still able to participate in the 2019 road hockey tournament and returned to work in 2020.

Mr. Brezina, 59, has fully recovered and his last cancer treatment was more than seven years ago. “I’m considered cured,” he said. “I have about as much chance of dying of leukemia as the general population.”

He played in this year’s tournament last weekend. The team’s composition has varied over the years, but Mr. Brezina has remained a constant. In total, he has raised $330,000 for the hospital.

“This has gone from a hobby to a passion of supporting this incredible hospital,” he said. If it wasn’t for road hockey, he added, it might have taken much longer his cancer to be diagnosed. “I used to say ‘I live for road hockey.’ Now I say ‘I live because road hockey.’”

stories.title: Alberta's employment rate increases despite national decline
stories.summary: While national employment rates are on the decline, Alberta saw an uptick in employment in September, according Statistics Canada.
stories.author: Devon Dekuyper
stories.content:
As Canada’s labour market flopped under the weight of expanding tariffs last month, Alberta reinforced its claim as the country’s leading job creator with the addition of 23,000 positions.

The strong September gains mean Alberta has now created 76,000 jobs in the past year; the province’s employment rate rising to 64.5 per cent, from 64 per cent a month earlier.

“It’s a story of both Alberta doing well, but also a story of the rest of the country not doing well because of the tariffs,” said Charles St‑Arnaud, chief economist at Servus Credit Union.

Across Canada, employment saw a September drop of 68,000 jobs, resulting in a decrease in the national employment rate by 0.2 percentage points, and an increase in unemployment by 0.1 percentage points, according to Statistics Canada.

September marks the second consecutive month that national employment has fallen amid the ongoing trade war with the United States. A further 42,000 jobs were lost nationally in August.

St‑Arnaud said Alberta, despite making up only 13 per cent of Canada’s labour market, has created about 80 per cent of new jobs across the country over the past year.

He attributes the relative strength of Alberta’s labour market to two factors: its strong population growth, and a lesser impact from the U.S. tariffs.

Alberta’s effective tariff rate is around one per cent, he said, compared to Quebec’s 12 per cent and Ontario’s 10 per cent.

“It’s clear that Alberta is a bit more insulated from all the negative impacts of the tariffs,” he said. The province’s population growth has also “outperformed” that of the rest of the country, he said, with a growth rate of 1.5 per cent compared to the national average of around 0.5 per cent.

Optimism in the oil and gas industry, with higher oil prices and pipeline conversations underway, has yet to generate any direct impact on employment.

“We can expect that, in the medium term, we’re going to start seeing that, but so far, higher oil prices have not translated into higher jobs in that sector,” he said.

Uncertainty around the upcoming referendum has also had minimal impacts on the job market so far.

“There might have been a marginal slowing since the start of the discussions . . . but I would say it’s pretty mild, if anything,” he said.

But if Albertans vote on Oct. 19 to hold a second referendum, “that’s going to be really different because then the level of uncertainty is going to jump up very quickly.”

Brad Parry, president and CEO of Calgary Economic Development (CED), said Calgary’s labour market “remains highly resilient” amid global uncertainty.

“This is the first full month of labour market data following the latest round of U.S. tariffs, and Calgary’s economy continues to compare favourably with major Canadian cities,” he said.

“Our diverse economy, lower direct exposure to tariff-affected industries, and continued population growth are providing a structural buffer.”

About 2,100 people entered Calgary’s labour force in September, and the city’s employment rate of 66.8 per cent remains the highest of Canada’s major cities, CED said in a Friday report.

The city’s unemployment rate fell by 0.4 percentage points to 6.3 per cent — lower than Toronto, Edmonton and Ottawa-Gatineau, and 0.2 percentage points lower than the national average.

Year-over-year, Calgary’s public administration, construction and health care and social assistance sectors saw the highest employment gains.

Some industries did see declines, however, including professional, scientific and technical services; finance, insurance, real estate, rental and leasing; and accommodation and food services.

Alberta’s unemployment rate fell to 6.4, its lowest rate since February and below the national average for the first time in six months following a summer slowdown, according to ATB.

Employment was 2.9 per cent higher in September than the same time last year — the third highest year-over-year increase among provinces behind only P.E.I. and Nova Scotia.

“In short, the labour market is rebalancing, as jobs are now keeping pace with population growth and entry into the labour force,” it said.

Joseph Schow, Alberta’s Minister of Jobs, Economy, Trade and Immigration, said in a Friday statement that the increase shows “the Alberta Advantage in action.”

“These are not accidental statistics — they are the result of deliberate, business-friendly policies brought in by this government that welcome investment and facilitate growth,” he said.

stories.title: ‘Sometimes I didn’t really have much food to eat at all’: Volunteer reflects on past need as Thanksgiving Food Drive enters final phase
stories.summary: A wave of economic pressure – and government relief – has resulted in a significant swing in the number of people using the London Food Bank (LFB).
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
A wave of economic pressure – and government relief – has resulted in a significant swing in the number of people using the London Food Bank (LFB). But officials contend the need remains as the Thanksgiving Food Drive enters its final stretch at grocery stores and drop-off sites across the city.

Some volunteers sorting through donations at LFB headquarters on Leathorne Street truly understand the need. Michelle Seah is among them. Today, she is a new volunteer, but a decade ago she was a client. “Sometimes I didn’t really have much food to eat at all, but the LFB would come with the essential food, so I never had to worry about going hungry if I didn’t have the money to go and buy groceries,” she said.

Running out of money for food is a reality for 5,700 London families that use the LFB every month. One in six are parents who work full-time jobs, said co-executive director Jane Roy. “And those folks might only come in once or twice a year.

They don’t come in all the time, but they’ve just had a bad patch, and here they are.” 2026 has been a rollercoaster of need. Roy said the year began with peak demand, then eased as summer approached. “There was the new grocery benefit, and then the increase in the grocery benefit by 25 per cent,” said Roy.

“So, we actually saw our numbers drop, which was great. Now, we are starting to see our number incline once again.” Which highlights the need for a big weekend of donations as many families prepare to celebrate. “Just pick up a few extra items, pop in the bin at the grocery store, and know that it makes a huge difference to the people that are coming to us for help,” said Roy.

The Thanksgiving Food Drive coincides with a milestone anniversary. “40 years ago, October 1986 was their first month of statistics, and we helped 360 families a month,” recalled Roy. They were the first of thousands who would benefit from the efforts of a community that always seems to find a way to give back.

Seah concedes she wouldn’t have it any other way. “Yes, definitely, because I’ve been through that. I wanted to get back later because I knew how much it meant to me when I needed help,” she said.

stories.title: Ontario's top court paves way to reopen challenge of Hamilton's anti-encampment law
stories.summary: Ontario’s top court has revived a constitutional challenge brought by a group of homeless people in Hamilton against the city’s anti-encampment bylaw.
stories.author: Jordan Omstead The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A challenge to Hamilton’s anti-encampment bylaw was revived on Friday by Ontario’s top court, after a panel of appeal judges found the lower court relied on stereotypes to discount the testimony of some homeless residents.

The Ontario Court of Appeal left the constitutionality of the bylaw and the city’s enforcement practices for a new trial judge to decide.

The challenge was brought by 14 encampment residents who argued their evictions and the city’s bylaw that blocks sleeping in parks were unconstitutional. It’s among a number of court cases in Canada to grapple with whether a city can clear an encampment when there’s no viable alternative place to shelter and city-run sites are filled up.

The Appeal Court’s unanimous ruling found the trial judge’s rejection leaned heavily on his finding that none of those evictions had taken place overnight, contrary to the testimony of several residents.

The trial judge treated the residents’ testimony as unreliable because all but one of the residents suffered from mental health and addictions issues, which he suggested impacted their memory or perception, the Appeal Court ruling said.

“The application judge’s apparent blanket assumption that the appellants’ evidence was unreliable because of those considerations perpetuates myths and stereotypes about some of the most vulnerable people in our society,” read Friday’s decision.

“It was incumbent on the application judge to analyze their evidence individually and, if he rejected it based on this individual assessment, to articulate why, without resorting to myths and stereotypes.”

The errors extended to other parts of the initial decision, the Appeal Court said. The panel found the trial judge improperly excluded evidence, including data about Hamilton’s homeless population, and failed to engage with the proper legal tests to determine whether a breach of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms had been made.

On key legal issues, the trial judge’s reasons “lacked the depth of analysis that is required” when dealing with homeless encampments, an issue of “great public importance”.

“The errors I identify in each ground of appeal can be traced back to the lack of analysis and the conclusory nature of the decision,” read the decision penned by Justice Lise Favreau.

The Appeal Court sent the case back to Superior Court to be decided by a different judge.

The City of Hamilton said it’s reviewing the implications of the Appeal Court decision, which does not affect enforcement of its bylaw.

“The city remains committed to supporting individuals experiencing homelessness with compassion and care while ensuring all residents can safely access and enjoy parks and other public spaces,” the city said in a statement, adding that it has invested more than $130 million in housing and homelessness supports this year.

Friday’s ruling follows a court decision earlier this year to block Waterloo Region from clearing an encampment after a judge found the region lacked adequate alternative shelter spaces for those residents. The ruling drew the ire of Premier Doug Ford who later called the decision “cockamamie” and mused about using the notwithstanding clause.
