stories.title: B.C. NDP talks health care on the campaign, promises tuition discounts for rural work
stories.summary: Victoria - British Columbia NDP Leader David Eby is pledging a new training program for international medical graduates and discounted tuition or loan forgiveness for health-care workers willing to work in rural communities.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
British Columbia NDP Leader David Eby is making election campaign pledges of a new training program for international medical graduates and discounted tuition or loan forgiveness for health-care workers willing to move to rural communities.

Eby spent Friday in Surrey, at a campaign stop at the site for a new medical school, while B.C. Conservative interim leader Lorne Doerkson was in Coquitlam laying out his promises for seniors, which include giving those waiting for long-term care beds “portable public funding” so they can pick where they want to be, including in non-government facilities.

Eby said if the New Democrats are elected on Oct. 24, the new medical school at Simon Fraser University will offer a first-of-its-kind “bridging to practice” training for qualified foreign graduates already living in the province but who are unable to practice family medicine because of a lack of residency spots.

”(It is) for international medical graduates and people with international medical experience, so they can get the practical training they need to get off the sidelines, whatever they’re doing right now, and get into our hospitals and into our communities delivering the care that people need,” Eby said.

Other promises laid out in the NDP health platform include discounted tuition, loan forgiveness, and moving expenses for workers heading to underserved rural areas.

“Recruiting new physicians to move to rural communities helps them deepen roots there and commit for the long-term to serve rural communities — an urgent issue that we know needs more attention,” Eby said.

Many emergency rooms in B.C., most of them rural, have experienced years of temporary closures caused by a lack of staff. The Conservatives say emergency rooms closed 2,400 times in two years.

Doctors of B.C., which represents about 20,000 physicians and medical students in the province, called on party leaders in the campaign to address specialist wait-lists and shortages, to ensure more access to family doctors, to improve access to emergency care and to strengthen rural health care.

In the lead-up to calling the election last month, Eby’s government celebrated what it said was one million people being connected to primary care in B.C. since 2018, but about a million more B.C. residents are still without a family doctor.

The Conservatives have argued that the Ndp’s proposal to increase taxes on the highest income brackets starting at about $190,000 would drive doctors away.

Eby said Friday that an NDP government would also provide incentives for doctors to offer same-day appointments, evening and weekend care, and would add 1,000 training seats for nurses, nurse practitioners, allied health workers and care aides.

He said the NDP would also build 20 additional primary care clinics in the province.

In his pitch to seniors on Friday, Doerkson said there are 7,200 people in British Columbia waiting for long-term care beds and that the NDP “piled so many unnecessary rules on home care design that the proposed beds reached a cost of $1.8 million each.”

The government cancelled contracts earlier this year for five health-related projects, including the Beedie Long-term Care Centre in Delta, as well as long-term care projects in Abbotsford, Chilliwack and Kelowna.

At the time, the government said the contracts were being deferred or rescheduled, noting that estimated budgets were coming in well over projections.

Doerkson said Friday that Conservatives will build long-term care beds and review the design rules, but said seniors in need can’t be asked to wait for that construction.

“So, for those people, we will be making long-term care funding portable. That means the public money follows the senior and not the other way around,” he said.

“If you’re eligible for publicly funded care, you and your family will choose your provider. Any qualified provider, public or non-government that meets strict standards for safety and quality, and we’ll hold them to those standards.”

The Conservative platform also includes promises to expand the HandyDart service for those who can’t take standard transit, and reverse NDP changes to the property-tax deferment program as a way of allowing more seniors to remain in their communities.

The Conservatives say they would also implement the B.C. Seniors Advocate’s recommendation to expand access to home care with “more consumer-directed, publicly funded choices for quality accredited homecare.”

stories.title: Missing wires, cut hoses: P.E.I. farmers face theft and damage at harvest time
stories.summary: Farmer Pat McIver says he’s facing up to $10,000 in repairs after wiring and hoses on his harvester were slashed, effecting the crops that need harvesting.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Newton, P.E.I. - Farmer Pat McIver says he’s facing up to $10,000 in repairs after wiring and hoses on his harvester were slashed, effecting the crops that need harvesting.

P.E.I. RCMP have received a string of similar reports from farmers on the Western part of the Island. The added expense puts more financial pressure on them, as they already grapple with higher prices for fuel and fertilizer.

“It comes right off the bottom line,” McIver said. “Everything has shot up this year.”

McIver also has to find time for repairs during what he calls a “chaotic” stretch.

Six incidents have been reported in recent weeks, with police suspecting copper wire was the target, said Insp. Shaun Coady. Four took place in Prince County and two in Kings County.

“Copper wire is obviously a valuable metal. So there is some scrap metal value,” he said. “But we have seen that the amount of copper that they’re getting from these pieces of equipment is quite low. And so the damage that they’re causing far exceeds the value of the scrap.”

It’s still unclear whether the crimes are connected, but Coady said the reports seem “unusual.” As far as he knows, there have not been similar incidents in previous years.

Back on his farm, McIver is pulling turnips to fill orders, with carrots and parsnips still to come out of the ground.

He estimates he has less than two weeks’ worth of harvesting left, making repairs to the machine one of his priorities.

McIver is putting up a $5,000 reward for information leading to an arrest. Since sharing his story, he says he’s heard from other farmers as well.

“It’s crazy to hear so many people that have been hit,” he said.

The RCMP is encouraging people to report suspicious activity or pass along any information to police in their jurisdiction or Crime Stoppers.

stories.title: Bank of Canada says aging population, low immigration ‘reshaping’ economy
stories.summary: In 2025, Canada’s population growth slowed to 0.5 per cent – the slowest rate of growth in more than a century after 150 years of steady growth.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Canada’s rapidly aging population and declining immigration levels are “reshaping” the country’s economy and consumption patterns, new analysis from the Bank of Canada shows.

The rapid population growth in the first half of this decade, when Canada’s population grew annually by three per cent after 50 years of steady 1.2 per cent growth, added new workers to the economy and “helped ease labour shortages” in the country, the report said.

However, it also added pressure on housing and social services.

In 2025, Canada’s population slowed to 0.5 per cent – the slowest rate of growth in more than a century after 150 years of steady growth. This immediately followed the federal government’s decision in 2024 to reduce immigration levels.

“In the coming years, fewer new immigrants will arrive. Canadians will also continue to get older. This will affect the size of our workforce, what we buy and how much the economy can produce,” the report said.

The housing sector typically responds much more slowly to higher population levels than businesses that can quickly ramp up production by hiring more workers, it said.

Fewer immigrants will mean reduced demand for housing, which could lower pressure on housing costs, however, demand for other goods and services is expected to also decline sharply, leading to a slowdown of Canada’s economic growth.

“Less immigration will mean fewer workers and weaker demand for other goods and services. The economy won’t grow as fast as a result,” the report said.

Canada is also aging, the report said, noting that the median age in Canada has gone from 26 in 1971 to over 40 in 2026.

An older population will mean the goods and services Canada produces and consumes will also change, it said.

With the baby boomer generation largely having reached retirement age, Canada will see an increase in the cost of travel services such as flights and accommodations since retirees tend to travel more.

At the same time, the demand for pharmaceuticals, adaptive living products and supportive home care services will also rise.

“Given Canada’s system of universal health care, it could also change how much governments need to spend on hospitals and long-term care—as well as the level of taxation needed to fund these services,” the report said.

An older, rapidly retiring population also means there will be fewer young workers to replace them in the workforce. This means that some sectors, which could see massive labour shortages, will also see wages rise and businesses try to attract the best workers.

This could also push up prices and contribute to inflation, the report added.

In 2025, Canada’s population slowed to 0.5 per cent – the slowest rate of growth in more than a century after 150 years of steady growth. This immediately followed the federal government’s decision in 2024 to reduce immigration levels.

“In the coming years, fewer new immigrants will arrive. Canadians will also continue to get older. This will affect the size of our workforce, what we buy and how much the economy can produce,” the report said.
The housing sector typically responds much more slowly to higher population levels than businesses that can quickly ramp up production by hiring more workers, it said.

Fewer immigrants will mean reduced demand for housing, which could lower pressure on housing costs, however, demand for other goods and services is expected to also decline sharply, leading to a slowdown of Canada’s economic growth.
“Less immigration will mean fewer workers and weaker demand for other goods and services. The economy won’t grow as fast as a result,” the report said.
Canada is also aging, the report said, noting that the median age in Canada has gone from 26 in 1971 to over 40 in 2026.
An older population will mean the goods and services Canada produces and consumes will also change, it said.

With the baby boomer generation largely having reached retirement age, Canada will see an increase in the cost of travel services such as flights and accommodations since retirees tend to travel more.
At the same time, the demand for pharmaceuticals, adaptive living products and supportive home care services will also rise.

“Given Canada’s system of universal health care, it could also change how much governments need to spend on hospitals and long-term care—as well as the level of taxation needed to fund these services,” the report said.

An older, rapidly retiring population also means there will be fewer young workers to replace them in the workforce. This means that some sectors, which could see massive labour shortages, will also see wages rise and businesses try to attract the best workers.
This could also push up prices and contribute to inflation, the report added.

stories.title: CAQ minister apologizes, is booted from caucus after attending PQ election party
stories.summary: Quebec's former culture minister is apologizing for attending a Parti Québécois election night gathering as his own party suffered a crushing defeat.
stories.author: Vicky Fragasso-Marquis The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Coalition Avenir Québec expelled Mathieu Lacombe from the party after La Presse reported Thursday that he’d attended the PQ gathering in Montreal.

Outgoing Premier Christine Fréchette also removed Lacombe from her cabinet.

While the PQ won Monday’s election, Fréchette and her ministers will remain in office until PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, the premier-designate, appoints his new cabinet.

Article continues below

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

Fréchette’s office says someone will be named to succeed to Lacombe until the new PQ government is sworn in.

The PQ will form a minority government after winning 59 seats in Monday’s election, while the Coalition Avenir Québec failed to win any seats.

Lacombe, who announced last June that he would not seek to be re-elected, wrote on social media that he had attended the rival party’s gathering “to celebrate the victory of people I respect and with whom I have forged bonds over the years.”

He acknowledged he shouldn’t have been there given his role as a minister.

“I would like to offer my sincere apologies to all the party supporters, my colleagues, and my friends whom this decision May have hurt or disappointed,” he wrote.

Lacombe raised eyebrows this spring when he expressed pro-sovereignty views, despite his party’s opposition to a referendum.

“I think that right now, the majority of Quebecers don’t want a referendum, so we’d be on the side of those who don’t want one,” he said. “But if, by any chance, there were to be one, I think it’s clear that I’d be on the ‘Yes’ side, as would some of my colleagues.”

The Parti Québécois has promised to hold a referendum by 2030, but not until U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 9, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Laval, Que., mayor’s 13-hour brain surgery sparks a wave of support
stories.summary: Laval Mayor Stéphane Boyer issued a highly anticipated health update following a thirteen-hour brain surgery to remove a golf ball-sized tumour. An online post on of the 38-year-old’s Instagram and Facebook accounts declared “Success” indicating the operation went well.
stories.author: Genevieve Beauchemin
stories.content:
Laval, Que. – Laval Mayor Stéphane Boyer issued a highly anticipated health update following a 13-hour brain surgery to remove a golf ball-sized tumour. An online post on the 38-year-old’s Instagram and Facebook accounts declared “Success” indicating the operation went well.

The message was accompanied by a photo of Boyer in his hospital bed. Giving a thumbs-up despite a bandage on his head and a heavily swollen face, Boyer wrote, “I look like a boxer who has lost his match. But it is quite the contrary.”

Boyer has served since 2021 as mayor of Quebec’s third-largest city, focusing on public safety, and city finances during his five years in office. On Sept. 7, he went online to reveal that an MRI had uncovered a brain tumour after he experienced months of headaches and vision problems.

A week later, Boyer posted an image of the MRI scan, calling it a shock to see the white mass lodged between his eye and brain. He paired that photo with an image of himself holding a box of doughnuts.

“There’s not just negatives to receiving this diagnosis,” he wrote at the time. “Stress and everyday problems suddenly seem more mundane, less serious. I take things as they come. That’s why I got my favourite doughnuts to share at the office. I urge you to do the same and to treat yourself and others well.”

Days later, Boyer shot a video of himself from his hospital room while wearing a gown, announcing the big day had arrived.

“Doctors will remove the tumour lodged between my brain, my eye, and an important artery,” said Boyer in the video. He went on to describe some of the risks of the operation, including paralysis, hemorrhaging and losing his eyesight, but added that his chances of a full recovery were excellent.

View this post on Instagram

Boyer expressed gratitude for modern medical advances. He noted that while access to health services can be difficult in Quebec, he could see first-hand the competency of health-care workers. Boyer also encouraged people to appreciate the era in which we live.

“There are problems,” Boyer said. “Yes, there is Trump, tariffs, and potholes, but there are also good things. Let’s take time to appreciate the positive things, and the people around us. Let’s take time to love one another.”

He also sent a message offering support to others struggling with health issues, reminding them they are not alone, that he would think of them and wished them well.

Thousands of people across Quebec, including fellow politicians, sent messages of support and shared their own health battles.

In Laval, many were anxious to get news of his surgery.

“We are sorry about his condition, and we hope we will be better fast. We hope the best for him,” said Louise Godin, who has lived in Laval for decades.

“I like him a lot, I voted for him and I pray for him,” added resident Adil Hamdouna. “He is young, it really makes you think about life.”

Ray Khalil, the vice-chair of the city’s executive committee, will fill in as interim mayor while Boyer recovers. His recovery period is expected to take at least two months.

In his post-surgery update, Boyer said he looks forward to being back in office to discuss public finances and water systems.

stories.title: Suspect charged with murder after deadly shooting in Niagara Region: police
stories.summary: Port Colborne - Police in Niagara Region say the suspect in a deadly Port Colborne shooting has been charged with murder.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Port Colborne - Police in Niagara Region say the suspect in a deadly Port Colborne shooting has been charged with murder.

They say officers responded to an address on Fares Street on Thursday evening for a shooting.

Police say the forensic services unit is working to identify the victims and notify next of kin.

stories.title: Couche-Tard buying fuel retail sites from Irving Oil in Quebec and Ontario
stories.summary: Deal includes 50 locations in Quebec already operated by Couche-Tard and two in eastern Ontario
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Alimentation Couche-Tard Inc. ATD-T has announced a deal to buy dozens of retail sites from Irving Oil in Quebec and Ontario.

The acquisition includes 50 locations in Quebec already operated by Couche-Tard under an alliance with New Brunswick-based Irving, as well as two in eastern Ontario.

Laval, Que.-based Couche-Tard is also buying 18 cardlock sites serving commercial customers like truckers. Sixteen of the sites would be on the same site as retail outlets.

In addition, the deal covers fuel supply to 71 retail sites owned and operated by Couche-Tard in Quebec.

“This agreement builds on our long-standing relationship with Irving Oil and our experience operating these locations,” said Stéphane Trudel, senior vice-president of operations at Couche-Tard, in a news release.

“These are markets and customers we know well. The transaction would support our continued investment in the everyday convenience experience we offer our customers.”

Couche-Tard did not say in the news release how much it is paying for the assets.

It said the deal is subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals, including under the Competition Act.

The deal comes weeks after Irving appointed European energy executive Alfred Stern as its next president and chief executive officer.

Stern is to step into the top job on Nov. 1. He replaces Jeff Matthews, who is retiring after a 32-year career.

Stern most recently served as chairman and chief executive of Austrian oil and gas group OMV AG.

The decision to bring in an outsider to fill the Saint John, N.B., company’s leadership role comes after an 18-month strategic review, which wrapped up in January, 2025.

The review of the oil refiner and retailer’s future ended with Irving Oil choosing to keep the family-owned business independent rather than pursue a sale.

stories.title: How close is Canada to a new West Coast oil pipeline? Here's where it stands
stories.summary: Wondering how close Canada actually is to building a new oil pipeline from Alberta to the West Coast? We have you covered.
stories.author: National Post
stories.content:
Ottawa — If you’re wondering how close Canada actually is to building a new oil pipeline from Alberta to the West Coast, this Spelled Out explainer video has you covered.

Prime Minister Mark Carney was in Fort McMurray on Oct. 1 to unveil major developments for the proposed pipeline. Now renamed the Pacific Link, it’s being designated a project of national interest, which will put it on a regulatory fast track.

If all goes to plan, there’s enough money coming out of this pipe to seriously boost Canada’s economy. But it’s far from a sure thing with many kinks still left to straighten.

Both Indigenous groups and environmentalists have voiced opposition to the proposed pipeline, the former for lack of consultation, the latter for its negative effects on climate change and the marine life in the path of oil tankers.

Business groups, ON the other hand, are very supportive of the idea, though not with their own money yet.

In the spring, the Government of Alberta submitted a West Coast pipeline as its biggest contribution to Carney’s major projects initiative. Those are the projects to be nationally promoted under the Building Canada Act.

It’s all part of Carney’s mantra of controlling what you can in spite of unpredictable things, like U.S. trade.

“Our government was elected to change things, to build Canada strong, and we’re doing just that,” Carney said at the announcement.

The proposed route will run 1,200 kilometres from Bruderheim, Alberta, to a proposed port in Roberts Bank, B.C. Heavy oil from Alberta’s oil sands would be shipped ideally to Asia, where it could get better prices than the U.S. pays.

The pipeline is expected to generate more than $20 billion in GDP per year and add $100 billion in government revenue by 2060.

It’s also projected to create 140,000 jobs across the country.

For a deep dive on the issue, check out the video above.

stories.title: Gratitude and support: The story of a mayor’s major 13-hour brain surgery
stories.summary: Laval Mayor Stéphane Boyer issued a highly anticipated health update following a thirteen-hour brain surgery to remove a golf ball-sized tumour. An online post on of the 38-year-old’s Instagram and Facebook accounts declared “Success” indicating the operation went well.
stories.author: Genevieve Beauchemin
stories.content:
Laval, Que. – Laval Mayor Stéphane Boyer issued a highly anticipated health update following a 13-hour brain surgery to remove a golf ball-sized tumour. An online post on the 38-year-old’s Instagram and Facebook accounts declared “Success” indicating the operation went well.

The message was accompanied by a photo of Boyer in his hospital bed. Giving a thumbs-up despite a bandage on his head and a heavily swollen face, Boyer wrote, “I look like a boxer who has lost his match. But it is quite the contrary.”

Boyer has served since 2021 as mayor of Quebec’s third-largest city, focusing on public safety, and city finances during his five years in office. On Sept. 7, he went online to reveal that an MRI had uncovered a brain tumour after he experienced months of headaches and vision problems.

A week later, Boyer posted an image of the MRI scan, calling it a shock to see the white mass lodged between his eye and brain. He paired that photo with an image of himself holding a box of doughnuts.

“There’s not just negatives to receiving this diagnosis,” he wrote at the time. “Stress and everyday problems suddenly seem more mundane, less serious. I take things as they come. That’s why I got my favourite doughnuts to share at the office. I urge you to do the same and to treat yourself and others well.”

Days later, Boyer shot a video of himself from his hospital room while wearing a gown, announcing the big day had arrived.

“Doctors will remove the tumour lodged between my brain, my eye, and an important artery,” said Boyer in the video. He went on to describe some of the risks of the operation, including paralysis, hemorrhaging and losing his eyesight, but added that his chances of a full recovery were excellent.

View this post on Instagram

Boyer expressed gratitude for modern medical advances. He noted that while access to health services can be difficult in Quebec, he could see first-hand the competency of health-care workers. Boyer also encouraged people to appreciate the era in which we live.

“There are problems,” Boyer said. “Yes, there is Trump, tariffs, and potholes, but there are also good things. Let’s take time to appreciate the positive things, and the people around us. Let’s take time to love one another.”

He also sent a message offering support to others struggling with health issues, reminding them they are not alone, that he would think of them and wished them well.

Thousands of people across Quebec, including fellow politicians, sent messages of support and shared their own health battles.

In Laval, many were anxious to get news of his surgery.

“We are sorry about his condition, and we hope we will be better fast. We hope the best for him,” said Louise Godin, who has lived in Laval for decades.

“I like him a lot, I voted for him and I pray for him,” added resident Adil Hamdouna. “He is young, it really makes you think about life.”

Ray Khalil, the vice-chair of the city’s executive committee, will fill in as interim mayor while Boyer recovers. His recovery period is expected to take at least two months.

In his post-surgery update, Boyer said he looks forward to being back in office to discuss public finances and water systems.

stories.title: Plans advance for floating nuclear plant in New Brunswick, a first among G7 countries
stories.summary: Facility would be the first nuclear project majority-owned by First Nations and could serve as ‘commercial blueprint’ for developer Prodigy Clean Energy
stories.author: Matthew McClearn
stories.content:
Plans for a floating nuclear power plant advanced this week with its backers’ selection of a small reactor to power it.

The demonstration facility, dubbed a Transportable Nuclear Power Plant, would mark many firsts. Set for near a small port in Belledune, N.B., it would be the first floating nuclear plant in a G7 country, as well as the developer’s first commercial deployment.

It would also be the first nuclear project majority-owned by First Nations. Belledune is situated in the traditional territories of Pabineau First Nation and Eel River Bar First Nation, which support the project.

And it would be a prototype for the barge’s developer, Prodigy Clean Energy Ltd., which hopes Belledune will serve as a “commercial blueprint” for remote communities and coastal industrial operations in Canada and globally.

The facility would feature two 22-megawatt microreactors known as the Bwxt Advanced Nuclear Reactor (Banr). It’s currently being designed by BWX Technologies Inc. Bwxt-N , a U.S.-based manufacturer of nuclear components with operations in Ontario.

Unlike many upstart reactor developers, Bwxt has actual experience: Its core focus is building naval components and reactors, often in more challenging settings than a moored barge.

“They’re the quickest and most ready,” said Terry Richardson, Chief of Pabineau First Nation, who helped select the Banr. “They have the proven technology with what they’ve been doing in the States, with aircraft carriers and submarines.”

Floating nuclear plants are rare. One, the Akademik Lomonosov, operates in the Russian Arctic. This year, nuclear giant Rosatom said it had manufactured two reactors (variants of the Ritm-200 reactors used in Russian icebreakers) to be incorporated in floating plants that will power a remote copper mine.

“Information regarding this project has been erratic, and construction has apparently started on one barge only,” reported Mycle Schneider Consulting in an assessment of the global nuclear industry’s progress, published last month.

Prodigy has not disclosed a price for the Belledune facility. Mycle Schneider Consulting has concluded that a market for reactors in remote mines and communities is “unlikely to materialize” because the electricity they would generate would be far too expensive.

The partners’ challenge is to find investors who disagree – a task that has defeated most reactor developers. Prodigy says they seek a mix of private and federal funding; Prodigy’s chief executive officer, Mathias Trojer, said Ottawa spends more than $2-billion annually subsidizing electricity costs in the North, so it is motivated to fund alternatives to the region’s aging diesel plants.

The Belledune proposal ticks some of the boxes in a federal nuclear strategy unveiled earlier this year , which sought to “demonstrate a Canadian-controlled Generation IV microreactor by 2035 to support defence facilities and operations and, in the longer term, remote and northern communities.”

The Banr is not Canadian-controlled, however. It’s been under development for several years already as part of the U.S. Department of Energy’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program. John MacQuarrie, Bwxt’s president of commercial operations, said Belledune’s Banr would be a variant of that reactor, containing a mixture of American and Canadian intellectual property.

Bwxt has not pursued commercial certification for the Banr in either country, but Mr. MacQuarrie said it plans to engage with the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission shortly.

Mr. Trojer, said the design should be completed in the next two years or so, and a final investment decision would be made around that time; the facility could be built in roughly 18 months and be operational in the early 2030s.

Politicians regard the Prodigy/Bwxt barge as a potential boon for industry. René Legacy, New Brunswick’s Deputy Premier and Energy Minister, said his province wants to build the barge, an undertaking “directly in line with our strengths, which is lots of machinists, lots of welding, lots of industrial might.” But New Brunswick can’t build reactors: his Ontario counterpart, Energy Minister Stephen Lecce, said his province’s supply chain stands ready to assist.

New Brunswick has signed an agreement signaling its intent to buy power produced by the barge, and announced plans to bring it before the federal Major Projects Office for designation as a project of national importance.

The Banr would be powered by what’s known as tri-structural isotropic (Triso) fuel. Bwxt, which makes nuclear fuel for clients including the U.S. government, says it can already produce Triso in non-commercial quantities. But its crucial ingredient is high-assay low-enriched uranium, which is enriched to contain nearly 20 per cent of the fissile isotope of uranium – much higher than fuel for existing commercial reactors.

Only Russia and China produce Haleu in appreciable quantities, according to the World Nuclear Association. The U.S. is investing heavily to grow its own minuscule domestic capacity, but other reactor vendors have reworked Haleu-fueled designs due to their inability to obtain the fuel.

Mr. MacQuarrie said the Banr’s Triso would likely be produced in the U.S. Mr. Trojer added that the Belledune project would require only modest amounts.

“It’s a long lead item, but if anyone can deliver it, then it’s Bwxt or some combination of their business relationships.”

stories.title: Police investigate small plane crash in field near Fergus, Ont.
stories.summary: Police say emergency crews responded at 10:15 a.m. to the crash near the intersection of Beatty Line and Wellington Road 17, north of Guelph.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Ontario Provincial Police say they are investigating a small plane crash near Fergus.

Police say emergency crews responded at 10:15 a.m. to the crash near the intersection of Beatty Line and Wellington Road 17, north of Guelph.

They say a small aircraft crashed into a field and caught fire.

Police say the extent of injuries is unknown.

Transport Canada has been notified.

Police say the crash is still under investigation and drivers should avoid the area.

stories.title: Supreme Court sets out new sentencing framework for cases involving Indigenous offenders, victims
stories.summary: Court says Indigenous people are disproportionately and excessively imprisoned, while women and girls suffer from unacceptably high levels of violence and abuse
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
The Supreme Court of Canada says in cases where an Indigenous offender commits an offence against an intimate partner who is an Indigenous woman, a judge must apply sentencing principles related to both Indigenous offenders and victims of crime in a harmonious way.

In a 5-4 judgment Friday, the top court provided guidance and set out a new framework for determining an appropriate sentence in such cases.

The court said Indigenous people are disproportionately and excessively imprisoned, while Indigenous women and girls suffer from unacceptably high levels of violence and abuse. “Both of these pressing issues have been shaped by the experiences of colonization, and addressing them together is central to the ongoing process of reconciliation,” Justice Michelle O’Bonsawin wrote on behalf of the majority.

Parliament has tried to address both concerns through the criminal sentencing process, the top court noted.

In light of the phenomenon of Indigenous over-incarceration, a Criminal Code provision that took effect in the 1990s directs judges to consider sanctions other than prison that are reasonable in the circumstances. The court pointed out particular attention is to be paid to the circumstances of Indigenous offenders.

The court also underscored the importance of two provisions added to the Criminal Code more recently. One requires a sentencing judge to squarely consider the objectives of denunciation and deterrence when the offence involves the abuse of a person who is vulnerable because, for example, they are an Indigenous woman or girl.

Another section directs a judge sentencing an offender for abuse of their intimate partner to consider the increased vulnerability of women and girls, and to pay particular attention to those who are Indigenous, the court noted.

Sentencing circles May include participants such as the offender, lawyers, the sentencing judge, Elders, the victim or their proxy and community members with knowledge of the offender. The top court said information gleaned from a circle can help the sentencing judge properly apply the principles specific to Indigenous offenders and victims.

The court said although the sentencing provisions invite engagement with distinct Indigenous perspectives on crime and punishment, they do not create a parallel regime for Indigenous offenders, and the consideration of Indigenous perspectives cannot displace a sentencing judge’s authority and responsibility under the Criminal Code.

The court said the sentencing judge must take three specific steps in such cases.

First, the judge must assess the gravity of the offence and the degree of responsibility of the offender in light of the Indigenous backgrounds of the parties.

Second, the judge must sensitively identify the relevant criminal sentencing objectives, emphasizing denunciation and deterrence, while still considering other relevant sentencing objectives.

Third, the judge must select the proportionate and just sentence in light of the Indigenous context, given that Parliament has expressly directed sentencing judges to consider all available sanctions other than imprisonment.

The top court added that the sentencing circle process can be relevant to understanding the availability of alternative sentencing options in the community, as well as the community’s perspective on the sentence that would best achieve the objectives.

The court said the sentencing methodology in such cases is not a mathematical formula but a guide to help judges take into account the circumstances of Indigenous offenders and the vulnerability of Indigenous women and girls to abuse and violence.

“Proportionality requires due attention to the circumstances of the offender and of the victim in light of relevant sentencing objectives,” O’Bonsawin wrote. “The appropriate balancing will inevitably vary depending on the specific circumstances of the offence.”

The ruling comes in the case of Harry Arthur Cope, a Mi’kmaq man with severe mental health challenges who was sentenced to five years in prison after pleading guilty in 2022 to aggravated assault against his partner, a Mi’kmaq woman.

The Nova Scotia Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to three years. The Supreme Court ruled Friday the three-year sentence should stand.

The top court found the sentencing judge did not recognize that the offender’s mental illness contributed to the commission of the aggravated assault and did not consider the effect of that illness on the relevant sentencing objectives.

The sentencing judge would have settled on a shorter prison term had she properly considered the offender’s significant mental health issues, particularly when viewed in light of a sentencing circle’s recommendations in the case, the Supreme Court said.

The four dissenting Supreme Court judges said the Crown’s appeal should be allowed and the original sentence imposed by the sentencing judge restored.

They said the majority’s sentencing framework fails to reflect Parliament’s direction to sentencing judges to prioritize denunciation and deterrence, and to generally impose harsher sentences for the abuse of vulnerable victims, including Indigenous women and girls.

stories.title: Salah Bachir, film media entrepreneur and philanthropist, dead at 71
stories.summary: Toronto - Salah Bachir, one of Toronto's most fashionable entrepreneurs and philanthropists, has died. He was 71.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A post on Bachir’s Facebook profile says he died Thursday after a prolonged illness and his husband confirmed the news in an email to The Canadian Press.

Bachir, who immigrated to Canada from Lebanon at age 10, started several film industry magazines including Videomania.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

Image 9Image 10

He ran theatre chain Cineplex Inc.‘s media division for 15 years and served as chancellor of OCAD University in Toronto from 2017 to 2021.

The openly gay businessman, known to wear strings of pearls and other fashionable accoutrements, was sometimes nicknamed “Gala Salah” because he fundraised so voraciously for the arts, social justice, health care and the LGBTQ+ community.

The efforts led to five honorary doctorates and Order of Canada and Ontario investitures. He also had a prolific art collection, containing works by the likes of Andy Warhol, that he often lent to galleries and museums.

Bachir is survived by his husband, artist Jacob Yerex. A funeral is planned for Oct. 15 in Toronto.

“I feel as though I have lived several lives and I am profoundly grateful to the friends, family and colleagues whose support has helped me realize my dreams and make my achievements possible,” Bachir said in a pre-written Facebook post announcing his death.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 9, 2026.

stories.author: Shawn Knox
stories.content:
Quebec saw major political upheaval in their 2026 provincial election.

The separatists are back in power, and the governing party was wiped out. And there’s still potential for more shake-ups.

Phil Authier, political correspondent with the Montreal Gazette, joins host Dave Breakenridge to discuss why the voters soured on the CAQ, whether a separatist win means a referendum is imminent, and the prospects on a minority government lasting more than a few months.

stories.title: 'Praise the paragliders': Government-funded journal under review after poem applauds Oct. 7 Hamas attack
stories.summary: The writer describes the events of an October morning, a reference to October 7 — when 1,200 Israelis were murdered by Hamas in 2023.
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
An internal review is underway after the latest issue of a journal funded by the Canada Council for the Arts appeared to support terrorism as a form of resistance and featured a poem by a Toronto writer who praises the events of October 7.

The poem, called Flood, was written by Bahar Orang and is featured in The Ex-Puritan.

In the piece, Orang describes the events of an October morning, a reference to October 7 — the deadliest day for the Jewish community since the Holocaust, when 1,200 Israelis were murdered by Hamas terrorists in 2023.

“Praise the paragliders, their gentle ascension, their unbroken morning, and of course their triumphant descension…,” she writes.

Hamas terrorists fired rockets across the border from Gaza into Israel and then used paragliders to invade and attack civilians. Videos and photos obtained by Reuters and CNN showed how those horrific scenes unfolded.

In the poem, Orang also writes “praise the fighters,” and acknowledges their courage, cunning and patience. She describes “the tanks on fire, the enemy fleeing.”

“Praise the missiles, the recognitions written in blood on each one, the names carved already into your own flesh,” she continues.

In a statement to National Post, the arts council said it has “retained legal counsel to assist with our review of this matter.”

It said that the views expressed in The Ex-Puritan do not reflect the council’s views, although the council “takes concerns regarding the content published in the most recent edition of Ex-Puritan very seriously.”

In 2024, the journal was awarded a four-year grant with annual funding of $22,000 to support its overall operations.

“As an arm’s length funder, the Canada Council supports a diverse range of artistic and literary expression across the country, and funded organizations make their own editorial and artistic decisions,” the council’s statement said. “At the same time, freedom of expression is not without limits, and concerns that published content May contravene Canadian law warrant careful review and consideration.”

Orang was a guest editor for the edition and wrote an editorial note explaining why the issue turns “deliberately toward armed resistance.”

“Among our obligations as Westerners, one is straightforward: to honour that creation of possibility, even when — or especially when — it takes the systematically disavowed form of armed resistance,” she explains. “Taking resistance seriously in all its forms alters what we, as cultural workers, are able to perceive: the violence already structuring ordinary life, and those who fight it as political agents.”

Orang’s biography on the website of Book*hug Press, which published her first book in 2020, describes her as an award-winning author who lives and works as a psychiatrist in Toronto. Her work is expected to be featured in Best Canadian Poetry 2027.

National Post has reached out to Orang’s publisher for comment.

stories.title: Power bills in Nova Scotia May spike as utility looks to refinance $1B in assets
stories.summary: Halifax - Nova Scotia Power Inc. is applying for permission to refinance nearly $1-billion worth of assets, including several coal plants scheduled to close by 2030.
stories.author: Devin Stevens The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Halifax - Nova Scotia Power Inc. wants to refinance nearly $1-billion worth of assets under a plan that could further increase a previously approved electricity price hike coming next year.

The privately owned utility announced Friday that it had asked the Nova Scotia Energy Board to approve a complicated financial scheme known as “securitization.”

If approved, the plan would result in a 2.9 per cent surcharge on residential power bills next year. Including a previously approved rate increase, residential electricity bills could be going up by a total of 6.8 per cent in 2027.

The utility says the average surcharge for all customer groups would be 3.3 per cent.

Ageing coal plants make up the bulk of the assets Nova Scotia Power is trying to refinance, with about $713 million of their value yet to be paid off by utility customers. Environmental legislation requires the plants to be shuttered by 2030.

Securitization would allow Nova Scotia Power to remove those assets from its books and issue bonds to investors. Bonds are essentially loans that investors can provide to companies and governments in order to collect interest before the bond matures.

Nova Scotia Power says this approach would allow it to finance the assets over a longer period of time and at lower interest rates. If approved the plan could also result in a higher credit rating for the utility, which could decrease financing costs.

The utility, a subsidiary of Halifax-based Emera Inc., says in its 430-page application that securitization would save customers $265 million over 30 years, when compared with not using the finance mechanism.

It says customer payments through securitization would amount to $977 million over three decades, compared with $1.24 billion over 13 years without it. The province has been asked to indemnify bond holders against any potential shortfall in their payouts, though it has not yet agreed to do so.

Securitization is relatively common in the United States, but the Nova Scotia Power proposal would be one of the first arrangements of its kind in Canada, if approved.

The utility publicly released its application soon after provincial Energy Department officials held a hastily organized media briefing Friday morning. The officials announced that the provincial cabinet had enacted rule changes allowing the utility’s application.

Premier Tim Houston, an accountant who is also the provincial energy minister, dismissed the securitization plan earlier this year.

“I would find it a little hard to believe that Nova Scotia Power has come up with some way to use accounting to save ratepayers money,” he told CBC in January.

The premier also said he had “major concerns” about Nova Scotia Power’s valuation of the coal plants.

However, Stephen MacDonald, the deputy minister of energy, told reporters Friday that “we haven’t seen anything coming out of the energy board which would necessarily lead us to question the value of those (coal plants) but it is something that we’re paying very, very close attention to.”

Houston did not attend Friday’s briefing and officials repeatedly declined to explain what had changed since the premier first expressed skepticism over the plan.

The premier later issued a statement saying the government was taking politics out of the discussion by allowing regulators to determine if securitization is in the best interest of ratepayers.

Interim Liberal Leader Iain Rankin said in a statement that Houston could have allowed the application 10 months ago, and that the delay will increase consumer costs.

“The premier … should have been there today to explain why he has reversed his position on securitization, an approach he once so aggressively opposed,” said Rankin.

NDP Opposition Leader Claudia Chender called the plan a “bailout” for Nova Scotia Power, noting the Energy Department had previously argued that the company’s shareholders should be paying the costs.

“(Houston) is dumping that extra cost on Nova Scotians who are already seeing their power bills soar,” she said.

MacDonald told reporters that the government’s green light for a securitization application is unrelated to the recent blockbuster merger announcement from Nova Scotia Power’s parent company.

Emera announced Tuesday that it planned to merge with Calgary-based Canadian Utilities to create a new company worth about $72-billion, creating one of North America’s largest utility companies.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 9, 2026.

stories.title: Workers rescued from Montreal highrise after platform malfunction
stories.summary: Two people repairing windows are safely on the ground after hanging multiple storeys in the air when their platform malfunctioned.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Two people repairing windows are safely on the ground after hanging 14 storeys in the air when their platform malfunctioned.

The Montreal fire department said it received the call around 7:45 a.m. Friday, and crews were dispatched to the scene of a highrise building at 1001 Robert Bourassa Blvd. near de la Gauchetière Street.

“The platform was stuck and it derailed about three feet,” a spokesperson for the fire department said.

Rescue crews were lowered down from the roof, secured the workers and brought them to safety.

Montreal police were also on scene to secure the area.

The fire department said no injuries were reported.

The on-site superintendent said the situation was worrisome and he is glad the workers are safe.

The investigation has now been handed over to the province’s workplace safety board to determine what caused the malfunction.

stories.title: Suspected Wwii grenade prompts closure around Stratford police headquarters
stories.summary: A suspected Second World War-era grenade prompted a temporary closure around Stratford Police Service headquarters Thursday evening after it was brought to the station by a resident who discovered it while cleaning out a home.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A suspected Second World War-era grenade prompted a temporary closure around Stratford Police Service headquarters Thursday evening after it was brought to the station by a resident who discovered it while cleaning out a home.

Police said the individual arrived at headquarters shortly before 7 p.m. on Oct. 8 to turn over the device, which had been left inside a vehicle parked in the municipal lot across from the station.

As a precaution, officers closed the area surrounding police headquarters, including George Street West between Downie Street and St. Patrick Street, and restricted public access while the situation was assessed.

The Waterloo Regional Police Service Bomb Disposal Unit arrived at about 8:50 p.m. and safely removed the grenade without incident. The area was reopened by 9 p.m.

Police said explosives of that age can be highly unstable and May pose a serious risk of injury or death if moved.

The Stratford Police Service is reminding the public not to handle suspected explosive devices. Anyone who discovers a potentially dangerous item should leave it where it is and contact police, who can arrange for its safe removal and disposal.

stories.title: Halton police in Ontario uses AI in hiring, training 911 call takers
stories.summary: Halton regional police in Ontario say they are using artificial intelligence in the recruitment and training of 911 call takers and dispatchers.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
They say American AI firm GovWorx provides the technology to create emergency call simulations to help 911 applicants improve their decision-making, communication and crisis management skills.

Halton police say the use of AI in the hiring of 911 communicators reduces candidate evaluation time by 50 per cent.

Article continues below

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

They say the force is the first in Canada to use AI in training for 911 call takers and dispatchers.

Halton police started using another AI technology called Sara AI to take certain types of non-emergency phone calls.

They say the bot has answered 95,367 calls so far this year and sent more than 2,470 text messages to people to report events through alternate means like websites or the collision reporting centre.

stories.title: Charges laid after ‘Code Silver’ at St. Thomas hospital
stories.summary: A 40-year-old London resident is facing multiple charges after an alleged threat against an employee at St. Thomas Elgin General Hospital prompted a lockdown Thursday.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A 40-year-old London resident is facing multiple charges after an alleged threat against an employee at St. Thomas Elgin General Hospital prompted a lockdown Thursday .

St. Thomas police say officers were called to the hospital on Thursday after reports that a suspect had threatened a hospital employee.

As a precaution, the hospital issued a Code Silver, locking down the building while police investigated.

Police said a 40-year-old London resident was arrested and charged with two counts of uttering threats to cause death, possession of a weapon for a dangerous purpose, administering a noxious substance with intent to endanger life, and mischief causing damage to property.

The accused was being held in police custody and was scheduled to appear in court Friday morning.

Police have not released the identity of the accused.

stories.content:
ST. John’s - Shell Canada has agreed to buy a 30 per cent stake in the proposed Bay du Nord oil project off the East Coast of Newfoundland from Norwegian energy giant Equinor, which will continue to lead the $14-billion development.

Equinor is expected to decide early next year whether it will proceed with what would be the first deepwater oil development in Canada.

stories.title: Buying a home with points, where our cities are shrinking and the Home of the Week: Canadian real estate news for the week of Oct. 9
stories.summary: Plus, this week’s lowest fixed and variable mortgage rates in Canada
stories.author: Moira Wyton
stories.content:
This week: A way to buy a home with rewards points, and the parts of our fastest-growing cities that are actually shrinking. Plus, a clash over discipline for a real-estate scandal, and one home worth a look.

Rewards programs can help you travel, get cash back or even enjoy a free birthday treat, but what about buying a home? A new company offers a way for your everyday spending and even paying your rent on time to earn you points towards perhaps the biggest purchase of your life – no credit card required.

Quarters connects to all your bank accounts and credit cards, awarding you 1 per cent on most purchases that you can use to cover a realtor’s broker fee, potentially saving you thousands on closing costs. As Salmaan Farooqui reports, co-founder Romir Joshi says the program helps aspiring homeowners feel their goal is within reach, realtors get referrals for reliable clients, and institutional landlords attract tenants who are further incentivized to pay rent on time. “We just literally need to show them the property, sign a couple pieces of paper, and they [the realtors] can get paid,” Joshi told Salmaan.

But should you use Quarters? It’s gotten a couple of glowing reviews, with one user saying he saved $8,000, largely through purchases on Uber Eats, a partner app. Calgary-based rewards expert Patrick Sojka says the program is worth it because it allows you to stack your rewards on top of existing credit card rewards like Rbc’s Avion or Blue Rewards (formerly Air Miles). However, it’s common for rewards programs to start out strong and then cut back benefits, so read Salmaan’s piece and keep an eye out for diminishing returns down the road.

Has the solution to the housing crisis been right in front of us all along? Toronto and Vancouver’s populations have doubled in the last 50 years, but there are pockets where the population has shrunk since 1970s – sometimes by as much as 40 per cent. One of those neighbourhoods is affluent Kerrisdale, where my weekend bike rides take me by more and more shuttered shops. And as Alex Bozikovic reports with Yang Sun’s data analysis , the west-side Vancouver neighbourhood is far from an anomaly.

Using census data on clusters of a few blocks, the data shows something you can’t see from the street. In the Vancouver region, 21 per cent of these clusters declined in population between 1971 and 2021, losing 76,424 people in total, and many others failed to keep up with growth. The pattern is even more stark in and around Toronto: Almost three-quarters of those established areas had declined, shedding a total of 540,789 people. Statistics Canada advises against such a granular analysis because boundaries change over time, but, as Yang told me, “that is the level urban planners, demographers, cartographers or journalists often want to see how a place has changed.”

So what’s going on in your neighbourhood, and could building more into these shrinking areas help us avoid urban sprawl? Experts say they could absorb more residents and at a lower cost than building new communities, but as Alex writes, it’s not as simple as that. Read the story to see where cities are gaining or losing population , and why some see a solution to the housing crisis in the data.

Things are getting heated in the Prairies. The decision to allow two real estate agents who broke provincial and Saskatchewan Real Estate Commission rules dozens of times to keep their licenses has the Saskatchewan Realtors’ Association riled up over the “wholly inadequate” punishment and calling for an overhaul at the regulator. And as Shane Dingman reports, the disagreement is renewing attention on the scandal and how realtors are disciplined.

Paul Chavady and Jerry Hallgrimson failed to represent the interests of buyers when representing both buyers and sellers on 67 occasions, failed to remove conditions on sales contracts and, in one case, failed to disclose the presence of asbestos in a home they sold in dual agency, according to the commission’s recent disciplinary decision. The two business partners held key roles at Epic Alliance Inc., a real-estate investing and property-management company that collapsed in 2022, after it was found to have broken securities trading rules in raising $211-million from investors across Canada.

Their punishment? Each must pay $100,000 in fines and serve a six-month suspension, staggered so that at least one can continue practising real estate while the other is suspended. The SRA says it’s not harsh enough to uphold the trust consumers place in realtors, and has called for an inquiry and overhaul at the Srec. However the commission defended its decision, saying the evidence didn’t demonstrate the criminality required to permanently revoke their licenses. Read more about the scandal and why the two bodies are at odds over how to regulate realtors.

What’s old is new, and that goes for your home, too. But how can you actually turn good bones into something fit for this millennium? These three heritage home renovations took different approaches to balancing original character and modern comforts, but all got beautiful results. From opening up a vaulted ceiling in a 1920s Tudor in Toronto to preserving a neo-Georgian’s stunning woodwork in Quebec, take a peek inside the transformations to get inspired.

And while these projects weren’t necessarily on a budget, designers told Silvana Longo there are plenty of ways to keep a home’s character without breaking the bank. You might think it’s cheaper to gut everything, but read their tips for preserving your home’s history and your finances before you get out the sledgehammer.

816 248 St., Langley, B.C. – Full gallery here

This historic home offers a lesson in creative vision. Built in Langley’s farm country in 1922, the original one-room schoolhouse was expanded in 1970, shuttered in 1983 and became a private residence in 1987, with many haphazard renovations following. But carpenter Alex Oosthoek and his wife Jill, an artist, saw through the peculiarities to the cozy space it would become for their two daughters to grow up.

After taking it down to the studs, harmonizing the rooflines of the expansion and turning the covered former play area into an in-law suite, the vision started to come to life. The 1970s addition was once the school office, but now houses the kitchen, three bathrooms and lounging and dining areas with a wood stove and exposed beams on the ceiling. There is a modern farmhouse feeling throughout the inside of the four-bedroom, 2,724-square foot home, but vestiges of the former classroom remain, including panelled ceiling and walls painted white in the entry area. Outside, cedar shake siding gives it a distinctly West-Coast feel.

Sitting on an acre whose designation protects against urban sprawl, the property is surrounded by large equestrian estates and, save for the stars, “black, black, black” at night, said Mr. Oosthoek. But while the family enjoyed the quiet, the surrounding community’s connection to the schoolhouse – and, sometimes, their escaped cows – also made living there special. Inspired by the school’s pancake breakfast every Christmas, the Oosthoeks hosted a holiday potluck for neighbours, former students and retired teachers. “The school was a community hub, and it was really nice to do that again,” Ms. Oosthoek said.

content_blocks.html: Rewards programs can help you travel, get cash back or even enjoy a free birthday treat, but what about buying a home? content_blocks.text: Quarters connects to all your bank accounts and credit cards, awarding you 1 per cent on most purchases that you can use to cover a realtor’s broker fee, potentially saving you thousands on closing costs. As Salmaan Farooqui reports, co-founder Romir Joshi says the program helps aspiring homeowners feel their goal is within reach, realtors get referrals for reliable clients, and institutional landlords attract tenants who are further incentivized to pay rent on time. “We just literally need to show them the property, sign a couple pieces of paper, and they [the realtors] can get paid,” Joshi told Salmaan.

content_blocks.text: The population is declining in pockets of Vancouver and Toronto. What if we built more housing there?
content_blocks.html: The population is declining in pockets of Vancouver and Toronto. What if we built more housing there?

content_blocks.text: Has the solution to the housing crisis been right in front of us all along? Toronto and Vancouver’s populations have doubled in the last 50 years, but there are pockets where the population has shrunk since 1970s – sometimes by as much as 40 per cent. One of those neighbourhoods is affluent Kerrisdale, where my weekend bike rides take me by more and more shuttered shops. And as Alex Bozikovic reports with Yang Sun’s data analysis , the west-side Vancouver neighbourhood is far from an anomaly.

Toronto and Vancouver’s populations have doubled in the last 50 years, but there are pockets where the population has shrunk since 1970s – sometimes by as much as 40 per cent. One of those neighbourhoods is affluent Kerrisdale, where my weekend bike rides take me by more and more shuttered shops. And as Alex Bozikovic reports with Yang Sun’s data analysis, the west-side Vancouver neighbourhood is far from an anomaly.

content_blocks.text: Using census data on clusters of a few blocks, the data shows something you can’t see from the street. In the Vancouver region, 21 per cent of these clusters declined in population between 1971 and 2021, losing 76,424 people in total, and many others failed to keep up with growth. The pattern is even more stark in and around Toronto: Almost three-quarters of those established areas had declined, shedding a total of 540,789 people. Statistics Canada advises against such a granular analysis because boundaries change over time, but, as Yang told me, “that is the level urban planners, demographers, cartographers or journalists often want to see how a place has changed.”

content_blocks.text: Things are getting heated in the Prairies. The decision to allow two real estate agents who broke provincial and Saskatchewan Real Estate Commission rules dozens of times to keep their licenses has the Saskatchewan Realtors’ Association riled up over the “wholly inadequate” punishment and calling for an overhaul at the regulator. And as Shane Dingman reports, the disagreement is renewing attention on the scandal and how realtors are disciplined.
content_blocks.html: Things are getting heated in the Prairies. The decision to allow two real estate agents who broke provincial and Saskatchewan Real Estate Commission rules dozens of times to keep their licenses has the Saskatchewan Realtors’ Association riled up over the “wholly inadequate” punishment and calling for an overhaul at the regulator. And as Shane Dingman reports, the disagreement is renewing attention on the scandal and how realtors are disciplined.

content_blocks.text: Paul Chavady and Jerry Hallgrimson failed to represent the interests of buyers when representing both buyers and sellers on 67 occasions, failed to remove conditions on sales contracts and, in one case, failed to disclose the presence of asbestos in a home they sold in dual agency, according to the commission’s recent disciplinary decision. The two business partners held key roles at Epic Alliance Inc., a real-estate investing and property-management company that collapsed in 2022, after it was found to have broken securities trading rules in raising $211-million from investors across Canada.

The two business partners held key roles at Epic Alliance Inc., a real-estate investing and property-management company that collapsed in 2022, after it was found to have broken securities trading rules in raising $211-million from investors across Canada.

content_blocks.text: Their punishment? Each must pay $100,000 in fines and serve a six-month suspension, staggered so that at least one can continue practising real estate while the other is suspended. The SRA says it’s not harsh enough to uphold the trust consumers place in realtors, and has called for an inquiry and overhaul at the Srec. However the commission defended its decision, saying the evidence didn’t demonstrate the criminality required to permanently revoke their licenses. stories.title: Did Canada add jobs in September? StatCan to release data
stories.summary: The Bank of Canada has kept its key lending rate unchanged at 2.25 per cent for about a year, but market expectations have been shifting lately.
stories.author: Craig Lord
stories.content:
Statistics Canada is set to report its latest jobs numbers Friday.

A Reuters poll of economists predicts employers added 9,200 positions in September, a slight bounce back after roughly 42,000 jobs were lost in August.

The consensus among economists is the unemployment rate ticked up to 6.5 per cent from 6.4 per cent.

The August job losses snapped a hot streak for the labour market, but economists weren’t overly concerned and instead pointed to the relatively stable unemployment rate as a sign the labour market wasn’t taking a major step back.

The jobs data will be the Bank of Canada’s last look at the labour market before its next interest rate decision on Oct. 28.

The central bank has kept its key lending rate unchanged at 2.25 per cent for about a year, but market expectations have been shifting lately, with slightly higher odds we’ll see a hike coming sooner rather than later.

stories.title: Permanent resident who left sex assault victim 'choking on blood' gets 12 years, could get deported
stories.summary: Kepra Udup Bang, an Ethiopian immigrant, was convicted of the aggravated sexual assault of a woman in 2019 thanks largely to DNA evidence.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
A man who brutally beat and raped a woman, leaving her unrecognizable and “choking on blood” in the bushes of a Calgary subdivision, was sentenced to 12 years in prison last month.

Alberta Court of Justice Judge Allan Fradsham convicted Kepra Udup Bang, 27, earlier this year of the 2019 aggravated sexual assault of the woman identified as MM in court documents under a publication ban to protect her identity.

“It was a crime of egregious violence which grossly violated the victim’s sexual integrity and left her with significant, life-altering injuries,” Fradsham wrote in his recently published decision.

Although the decision does not mention it, under Canadian law, Udup Bang, a permanent resident who immigrated to Canada from Ethiopia with his family in 2017, could face deportation after serving his time.

Under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act , anyone found guilty of an offence under federal law and sentenced to more than six months is automatically deemed inadmissible to Canada, which can lead to a removal order and deportation. That complex legal process begins with a Canada Border Services Agency (Cbsa) admissibility report, followed by a hearing with the Immigration Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB). If deemed inadmissible, a removal order is issued and can’t be appealed for sentences of six months or more.

As highlighted by a different Alberta judge’s sentencing of another Ethiopian man in Calgary earlier this year for pointing a loaded handgun at someone during a road rage incident, a stay of removal could be granted due to recurring political violence in the African nation.

At present, the nation is not on Canada’s list of countries where administrative deferral of removal measures are in place for situations of humanitarian crisis. Nor is it on Cbsa’s temporary suspension of removal list of countries where “general conditions, such as armed conflict or an environmental disaster, pose a risk to the entire civilian population.” Tsr’s are only in place for Afghanistan, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Iraq, per the Cbsa website.

“Individuals with serious inadmissibility, such as national security and criminality, do not benefit from a stay of removal under these provisions,” the agency writes online. “However, no one is removed from Canada without consideration for their individual needs for protection. When the situation in a country stabilizes, the deferral and suspension of removals can be lifted, and the Cbsa will resume removals for all individuals who have an enforceable removal order.”

Cbsa does not comment on individual cases due to privacy laws. National Post has contacted the agency for more information on current policies regarding removal orders to Ethiopia. Ircc deferred to Cbsa for comment.

During trial last December, the court heard that police were called to a Forest Lawn neighbourhood around 5 a.m. on July 14, 2019, ON reports of someone being attacked and the sound of screaming.

“I could tell he was raping her,” testified one witness who looked out her window to see a man with his pants down holding up a woman from behind.

“After a few minutes of searching, the attending officer heard sounds of someone choking and struggling to breathe” and found MM lying on her back with no clothes below her waist, her legs spread open and her face a mess of blood.

“The officer said that the facial trauma which MM had suffered was so extensive that even if he had found photo identification with the victim… he would not have been able to identify her using it,” Fradsham wrote.

The victim, then a 28-year-old transient with drug addiction issues, was taken to hospital where she remained unconscious for eight days and underwent surgeries to reconstruct her nose, fix her orbital bone and repair a laceration under her chin over the next three months.

As a result of her severe traumatic brain injury, she did not recognize her own mother for several weeks after waking up, lost a month of memory after the attack, and to this day has no recollection of it. Today, she lives at her mother’s house with her husband and 10-year-old child. While now “clean and sober,” she’s unable to work and “does not often leave the residence because she is bothered by noise and collections of people.”

“This aggravated sexual assault has had severe and permanent detrimental effects on MM and her family,” Fradsham noted.

Udup Bang, now a father of two with a common-law partner, wasn’t charged until 2025 after DNA he’d submitted as part of a separate criminal investigation in 2024 — a break-in conviction, according to CBC — matched the samples obtained from MM and a wristband found at the scene of her attack in 2019.

Under questioning by police, he initially alleged that he did not recognize MM when shown a photo of her, but during trial testified that he and MM had met at a child’s birthday party a month before, connected via Snapchat and then engaged in consensual sex on a night in July he was unsure of. The victim maintained all along that she did not know Udup Bang.

“He explained that he lied to police because he had been arrested for aggravated sexual assault resulting in another person being injured, which he understood to be very serious, and was afraid that admitting he knew MM would lead to the police concluding he was guilty,” Fradsham wrote in his March verdict.

That lie and the DNA evidence led Fradsham to dismiss Udup Bang’s version of events and find him guilty. His lack of a criminal record at the time was his only mitigating factor and the judge decided the evidence didn’t support his race as a “significant mitigating weight… on his moral blameworthiness.”

The Crown wanted Udup Bang to spend 10-12 years behind bars, while the defence argued for seven to nine. Fradsham respectfully disagreed, noting the Crown’s “does not adequately address denunciation and deterrence, and gives insufficient weight to the degree of responsibility of the offender.”

As for the defence submission, the judge said he was “mindful of his difficult time growing up” — Udup Bang was born in a refugee camp and “described an unstable upbringing marked by frequent relocations, multiple school changes, and exposure to conflict” — but said none of the evidence allowed him “to conclude that his experiences would materially diminish his moral culpability.’

Udup Bang, in custody since his arrest, was granted credit for 893 days, leaving him with roughly nine years and seven months in prison.

In his pre-sentence report, Udup Bang said “his short-term goal is to become a book publisher within five years,” and long-term goals include “owning an online store… and developing a food-production company within” the next decade.

“He plans to return to school, complete high school, and pursue post-secondary education with the intention of obtaining degrees in business and law,” the report states, per Fradsham.

That lie and the DNA evidence led Fradsham to dismiss Udup Bang’s version of events and find him guilty. content_blocks.text: A man who brutally beat and raped a woman, leaving her unrecognizable and “choking on blood” in the bushes of a Calgary subdivision, was sentenced to 12 years in prison last month.

Alberta Court of Justice Judge Allan Fradsham convicted Kepra Udup Bang, 27, earlier this year of the 2019 aggravated sexual assault of the woman identified as MM in court documents under a publication ban to protect her identity.
“It was a crime of egregious violence which grossly violated the victim’s sexual integrity and left her with significant, life-altering injuries,” Fradsham wrote in his recently published decision.

content_blocks.text: Although the decision does not mention it, under Canadian law, Udup Bang, a permanent resident who immigrated to Canada from Ethiopia with his family in 2017, could face deportation after serving his time.

Under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act , anyone found guilty of an offence under federal law and sentenced to more than six months is automatically deemed inadmissible to Canada, which can lead to a removal order and deportation. That complex legal process begins with a Canada Border Services Agency (Cbsa) admissibility report, followed by a hearing with the Immigration Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB). If deemed inadmissible, a removal order is issued and can’t be appealed for sentences of six months or more.
