stories.title: Montreal mayor says city will offer 3,000 spots in emergency shelters for unhoused
stories.summary: The mayor says homelessness is the biggest humanitarian crisis the city is facing.
stories.author: Erika Morris
stories.content:
Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada says the city is planning to provide 3,000 beds in emergency shelters to address homelessness this winter.

The mayor says homelessness is the biggest humanitarian crisis the city is facing.

The new beds are needed, the mayor says, noting that many people using the emergency shelters have had to sleep in chairs over the last few years.

She adds that she believes the city will get the funding it needs after premier-elect Paul St-Pierre Plamondon promised to make homelessness a top priority.

The announcement comes after a woman died in an encampment in the Montréal-Nord borough early Wednesday following a fire.

Representatives of community organizations say they welcome the additional resources.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Many Quebec voters got false election information from chatbot, MPs hear
stories.summary: Because Quebec news outlets don't allow chatbots to access their content, voters couldn’t obtain the most accurate and up-to-date information, a McGill political scientist said.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
Canadians turning to chatbots for election information don’t always get accurate responses, a Parliamentary committee heard Thursday.

An estimated 40 per cent of Quebec voters asked AI chatbots for election information, said Aengus Bridgman, a McGill political scientist who led a study tracking chatbot activity during the recent Quebec election.

But because most Quebec news outlets don’t allow chatbots to access their content, he said, those voters couldn’t obtain the most accurate and up-to-date information.

“Almost all Quebec newsrooms have blocked AI chatbots from collecting their content. Which means that AI chatbots are going elsewhere for information,” he said.

Taylor Owen, associate professor in the Max Bell School of Public Policy at McGill, said researchers found that in the last three weeks of the election campaign, 39 per cent of voting advice provided by ChatGPT came from an error-filled hobby website built by AI.

“There was nothing nefarious by this person’s actions nor necessarily by the design of the chatbots themselves, nor by the publishers who de-indexed themselves,” he said.

“It was just this confluence of events that led to, likely, a large number of people getting false information about the election.”

“That’s actually a little bit terrifying … If that can happen by accident, imagine what could happen potentially on purpose,” Conservative MP Blaine Calkins responded.

Owen said that’s the question that needs to be asked “quite urgently.”

Thursday’s meeting was the first for a new study on AI and Canada’s democratic institutions launched by the House of Commons procedure and House affairs committee.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Ottawa declassifies new details about Cia’s role in resettling Nazi war criminals in Canada
stories.summary: Government lifts veil on sections of historian’s report kept secret for 40 years
stories.author: Marie Woolf
stories.content:
The government has declassified portions of a report on the resettlement of Nazi war criminals that reveal new details of how dozens of people, including those suspected of collaboration with the Third Reich, were helped to come to Canada after the Second World War through a secret CIA program.

The newly declassified information sheds more light on the role American intelligence agencies played in facilitating the settlement of Nazi collaborators in Canada, in some cases by providing false identity papers. Sections of the report kept secret for decades also reveal new specifics about the number of people thought to have entered the country with U.S. covert help.

The federal government Thursday declassified more of a 40-year-old report written by historian Alti Rodal for the 1985-86 Commission of Inquiry on War Criminals in Canada, headed by former Quebec judge Jules Deschênes. The commission investigated allegations that Canada had become a safe haven for Nazi war criminals.

Last month, a Federal Court judge ordered Ottawa to publish redacted parts of the Rodal report. Canadian Identity Minister Marc Miller decided not to appeal the court ruling, which followed a legal action by Jewish organization B’Nai Brith.

Most of Ms. Rodal’s report had already been made public, with further declassified details released in 2024.

The report found that Nazi collaborators who had aided the United States, including by providing information, were assisted in entering Canada by the Research and Resettlement Branch of the United States Army in Europe (Usareur).

The Rodal report said Usareur was then a cover organization for the Central Intelligence Agency and other such U.S. agencies. The U.S. Army organization admitted that some of its informants had criminal records, including a number arising from cases involving moral turpitude – the category under which Nazi collaborators were listed.

According to the newly unredacted text, the RCMP had reported to Ottawa in 1954 “that some forty persons had been presented for admission to Canada in 1953 by Usareur.”

Another unredacted section says that American intelligence personnel “could well have assisted persons with war criminal background to immigrate to Canada.”

“They were in a position to provide such persons with false documentation and to report to Canadian Visa Control officers in the course of their routine checks that there was nothing adverse about these prospective immigrants,” one declassified section of the report said.

Another newly unredacted section shows that the RCMP pushed back against admitting dozens of suspected war criminals to Canada by rejecting some applicants sponsored by the covert U.S. program.

A 1954 memorandum from the then-RCMP commissioner to a former Canadian undersecretary of state referred to 35 people who had already come to Canada with the assistance from Usareur. It added that there were “52 additional names of applicants sponsored or advanced by Usareur but rejected by the RCMP, mainly on security grounds.”

Another declassified section of the report suggests the RCMP was not aware of the precise number of suspected war criminals who settled in Canada with American help: “The RCMP for its part was convinced in 1954 that larger numbers than those actually detected had been pushed through the Canadian immigration stream with false documentation arranged by Usareur.”

Jared McBride, a history professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, who provided witness testimony during the court hearing, said the declassified information is “more revealing than previously anticipated.”

Most of Ms. Rodal’s report had already been made public, with further declassified details released in 2024.

stories.title: Routine childhood vaccination coverage remains below level needed for population immunity, report finds
stories.summary: Coverage rates fell during the COVID-19 pandemic and have not rebounded
stories.author: Alanna Smith
stories.content:
Routine childhood vaccination coverage in Canada has not bounced back to pre-pandemic levels, opening the door to infectious disease spread, national data on immunization show.

The Public Health Agency of Canada on Wednesday said that parents should be discussing childhood vaccinations now that kids are back in school, pointing to its latest report on vaccination as a warning sign that coverage is lower than the level needed for population immunity.

Natasha Crowcroft, vice-president of infectious diseases and vaccination programs at the national health agency, underscored in an interview on Thursday that Canada cannot stay in the “risk zone” for too long without consequence.

“We need a whole of Canada approach where we’re all pulling in the same direction to get vaccines to kids,” said Dr. Crowcroft. “We cannot be complacent.”

The Standardized Reporting on Vaccination, or STARVAX, report shows that vaccination coverage in two-year-old children has decreased since 2019 with some stabilization after 2022. And, in seven-year-old children, there has been a continuous decrease with “no apparent recovery.”

The report includes routine childhood vaccination data from Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Ontario, Quebec, Saskatchewan and Yukon on coverage rates as of Dec. 31 last year. The other four provinces and territories have not yet submitted data for the STARVAX report.

When vaccination rates decline, forgotten diseases can make a comeback. Take measles for example, which had a resurgence in Canada and has sickened more than 5,000 people since the outbreak began in November, 2024. The country is still trying to regain its measles elimination status as a result.

The report shows that 85.3 per cent of two-year-olds have been vaccinated against measles, mumps and rubella, as of Dec. 31 last year. But because measles is highly contagious, 95 per cent of the population must be fully immunized, meaning they have received two shots, to achieve herd immunity.

Coverage also varies greatly at the community level, dipping below 50 per cent in some pockets of Canada, which helped fuel the outbreak that gripped Ontario and Alberta for months last year. Both provinces have since brought the situation under control but sporadic cases are still popping up elsewhere.

Coverage rates have also dipped since the COVID-19 pandemic for other vaccine-preventable diseases, including meningococcal disease, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis (whooping cough) and polio, according to the report.

Dr. Crowcroft said there are a range of reasons for declining childhood rates, including mistrust in the medical system, vaccine hesitancy and opposition, practical or logistical challenges for families, and health system hurdles.

“Some provinces deliver everything through the public health system and some are really reliant on primary care,” she said. “So, if you haven’t got access to good primary care, then that’s obviously a major barrier, and there are also language barriers and other things like that.”

Underimmunized communities are fertile ground for these diseases to spread.

Saskatchewan, for example, is experiencing an outbreak of invasive meningococcal disease, which helped Canada reached its highest annual level of infections in more than a decade last year. As of last month, eligible infants, six weeks to under 12 months of age, can receive additional doses of meningococcal vaccine to provide earlier protection against the disease.

In 2019, meningococcal coverage for two-year-olds (based on data from five provinces, including Saskatchewan) reached roughly 90 per cent. Coverage dropped to about 82 per cent in 2025. Meningococcal disease can cause severe and life-threatening infections.

Additionally, the report shows diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis coverage at two years of age dropped nearly 20 percentage points to 69 per cent in 2025 from 2019, according to the same data set. For polio, coverage decreased to 80.1 from 88.3 per cent.

Dr. Crowcroft said work is under way to increase immunization across Canada, but it can be time-consuming to get the word out and speak to parents, while also building trust among those who are reluctant to get their children vaccinated.

“The complacency is the thing that makes it hard,” she said. “People think ‘oh, we’re okay’ and ‘Canada’s okay’ ... it just makes it much harder to get the momentum toward getting coverage levels back up to where they need to be.”

stories.title: Doctors who receive gifts or payment from pharmaceuticals prescribe more frequently, review finds
stories.summary: Cochrane review of nearly 100 medical studies finds gifts and payments have a ‘harmful effect on prescribing appropriateness’
stories.author: Tu Thanh Ha
stories.content:
Doctors who receive gifts or payments from pharmaceutical companies end up prescribing more frequently, and choosing less suitable medications, a review of nearly a hundred medical studies has concluded.

The findings were released on Thursday in a Cochrane review, an analysis that aggregates results from previous health care research. “We found high-certainty evidence that gifts and payments have a harmful effect on prescribing appropriateness and are associated with higher volumes of prescribing,” the paper said.

The review looked at studies conducted in the United States and Europe, where researchers have access to databases documenting payments received by health care professionals. There was no data for Canada since pharmaceutical companies here are not required to declare what they give to physicians.

Innovative Medicines Canada, an association that represents about 40 drug makers, said in a statement that its code of ethical practices prohibits members from providing gifts or other personal benefits.

The code, however, permits companies to offer “reasonable meals/refreshments” during promotional activities. It also allows them to compensate health care professionals for participating in activities such as speaking engagements, chairing meetings, advisory boards or market research.

“Canada and the U.S. operate under different regulatory and disclosure frameworks. These differences are important context when comparing practices between the two countries,” the association’s statement said.

However, Joel Lexchin, a professor emeritus at York University’s Faculty of Health and one of the review’s co-authors, said the findings of the Cochrane analysis could apply to Canada. “Based on the 45 years that I’ve been looking at these issues, it’s pretty clear to me the way that the drug companies promote their drugs here in Canada is the same as the way that they promote them in the United States,” he said in an interview.

Prof. Lexchin added that Ottawa should step in and make payment disclosure mandatory. “But the federal government has never shown any interest in doing this,” he said.

Alexandre Bergeron, a spokesperson for federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel, said that regulating physicians is a provincial and territorial jurisdiction.

Ontario is the only province to have passed a law requiring companies to divulge their payments to health care professionals and organizations. The Health Sector Payment Transparency Act was enacted in 2017 under former Liberal premier Kathleen Wynne. However, it never came into force because its regulations hadn’t been finalized by the time Premier Doug Ford’s Conservatives took power in 2018.

Prof. Lexchin said it would be preferable to have a federal disclosure law, rather than provincial legislation. “Much, much more” data for the whole country would be available that way, he said.

The Cochrane review looked at 93 studies – 82 from the U.S. and others from France, the Netherlands, Denmark, Germany, Sweden and the United Kingdom. “The vast majority of the studies, all but one, showed that exposure to the promotional activity of gifts or payments made the prescribing less appropriate,” said the review’s senior author Lisa Bero, a University of Colorado Anschutz medicine professor.

Dr. Bero and another co-author, Barbara Mintzes, a University of Sydney pharmacy professor, spoke to reporters at a technical briefing on Tuesday.

They shared a graph from one study showing that the number of meals that doctors received from opioid manufacturers correlated with the number of doses they prescribed the following year.

The same pattern occurred with other classes of drugs, such medications for diabetes or blood pressure, Dr. Mintzes said. “This isn’t just an individual doctor-patient issue, and it’s certainly not just an issue of a few bad apples. It’s more of a systemic problem.”

Even “very small payments” influenced physicians to prescribe higher doses, beyond national guidelines, Dr. Bero said.

In the U.S., the Physician Payments Sunshine Act requires pharmaceutical companies to declare all payments to physicians. France has a similar public database, Transparence Santé.

The French data, for example, enabled researchers to analyze records for more than 41,000 family doctors , documenting how those who received gifts prescribed more.

Some Canadian companies voluntarily release their payment information. GSK Canada, for instance, made public a breakdown of the $18.9-million it paid in 2025 to health care professionals and corporations. Other manufacturers provide only the total sum they disbursed, with no further details.

stories.title: Michigan Republican faces pressure during heated debate on Trump's Canada tariffs
stories.summary: Grand Rapids - Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers faced pressure over U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada during a heated debate tonight.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Grand Rapids - Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers faced pressure over U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada during a heated debate that could sway voters in a consequential midterm race where neither candidate ruled out future duties.

Trump’s escalating tariffs targeting Canada came up within the first 10 minutes of the debate. Rogers was asked about an advertisement released Wednesday in which he said “Canada is not our enemy,” and how he squares that with longstanding support of the duties.

stories.title: The suspicious texts on day of Toronto airport gold heist between Air Canada workers accused of pulling it off
stories.summary: “We looking good anyways for today,” Simran Preet Panesar, now a wanted fugitive, texted to Parmpal Sidhu, now on trial in an Ontario court.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
On the morning of the Toronto airport gold heist, an Air Canada employee working at the cargo depot where the loot was about to be stolen received a text message from his supervisor’s personal phone: “Gooooood morning it is.”

Minutes later the employee replied saying he was “soo tired.. no sleep.”

“We looking good anyways for today,” came the manager’s replied.

Both men stand accused of being part of the insider conspiracy that pulled off one of the world’s largest gold heists, and their friendly chats prior to the theft — and a sharp falling out afterwards — is revealed in a trove of data extracted from a seized phone.

The Air Canada manager was named in court as Simran Preet Panesar, 34, who is considered a wanted fugitive in the heist case and believed to be in India. The employee was Parmpal Sidhu, a 56-year-old former Air Canada cargo warehouse employee who is on trial for the heist in a Brampton, Ont., court.

Sidhu has pleaded not guilty to theft and conspiracy.

Sidhu’s phone was seized by Peel Regional Police when he was arrested on April 5, 2024, almost a year after the high-profile heist. His home was searched as well.

Det.-Const. Edil Aden told court on Thursday that investigators extracted the phone’s contents using Cellebrite, a digital-forensics software tool.

“So it has text messages, phone calls, logs, images, videos. Their phone is put onto a screen for us,” Aden said. The printed data report was about two inches thick.

Aden said messages found on Sidhu’s phone had been sent and received through various tools, including text, encrypted apps and social media direct messaging.

One chat on Sidhu’s phone from a few months before the heist in April 2023 was with a jeweller about how to accurately test for nearly pure gold that had been melted without contamination.

Most of the messages that court heard about, however, were linked to Panesar, who might have been a co-accused at this same trial if he had returned to Canada. Panesar was the manager with Air Canada at the cargo warehouse at Pearson airport to whom Sidhu reported.

Sidhu and Panesar were friends outside of work. Their messages refer to going to the gym, having haircuts, getting coffee, sharing rides to work and laser hair removal recommendations.

Sidhu had five different means of contacting Panesar saved on his phone, including on encrypted communication apps Signal and WhatsApp.

The profile photos of Panesar saved on Sidhu’s phone look different from the widely circulated photo of Panesar in his police mug shot because he sometimes wears a hairpiece, court was told.

On the day of the heist, the two exchanges dozens of short messages, some highlighted to Judge Gordon Cudjoe as suspicious, or, in the words of Crown prosecutor Tyler Powell, “potentially relevant to this investigation.”

They included Panesar’s enthusiastic greetings for the day and a message from him a few hours after the heist.

“I think I’ll be going to India for days off just to get away few days,” the message from Panesar’s phone says. He said it was his wedding anniversary.

“Happy Anniversary,” Sidhu replies.

A few hours later, a message to Panesar’s number from Sidhu’s phone said: “Hey….gotta a call from my cuz who’s in peel. said he heard about a brings heist at cargo last night… lol. Hear anything?”

“No nothing like that happened,” was the reply.

Court heard little or no context to the messages. Presumably the reference to “brings heist” is a misspelling of Brink’s, the security transit company that was moving the gold from Switzerland to Toronto on an Air Canada flight for their client, TD Bank. It wasn’t until Brink’s guards arrived to collect the crate hours later that anyone realized it was gone.

Aden also testified about a screen recording found on Sidhu’s phone that appears to capture a thoroughly modern falling out between the two men: There is a screen shot of a message reading “Last chance” and then a sequence showing Sidhu’s phone blocking Panesar on Instagram.

Adel said police can’t say the screen recording was made by Sidhu, only that it was on Sidhu’s phone. It is not clear when the recording was made.

gotta a call from my cuz who’s in peel. said he heard about a brings heist at cargo last night… lol

In a series of direct messages on Instagram dated Jan. 30, 2023, there is more evidence of acrimony.

“14” a message from Sidhu’s account says.

“Yes I know” is the reply from Panesar’s.

“Bullshit,” says Sidhu’s.

“And I have news for you. We speak tomorrow. Cool?” says Panesar’s account.

“Talk to your lawyer. I urge you guys to do the right thing. U listen to me when u took the us cash… your full of shit.” In another message in the same string from Sidhu’s account, he mentions someone who was once a suspect in the heist and a misspelled version of Arsalan Chaudhary’s name.

In April, Chaudhary, 43, admitted to being the ringleader of the heist and was sentenced to four years in prison.

Aden was asked by Sidhu’s lawyer, Shale Wagman, if Sidhu’s fingerprints were found on the air waybill that was used to collect and steal the crate of gold and cash, worth more than $22 million. Court heard the waybill was printed from inside the Air Canada warehouse by someone logging in with Sidhu’s credentials.

She said she doesn’t think they were. She also agreed that no gold bars were found in the police search of Sidhu’s home.

Wagman asked her if the text massage saying “We looking good anyways for today” could mean almost anything. “It can mean anything, but the pertinence of it was that that’s the date of the heist,” Aden said. “It could be something work related,” Wagman asked. “It could be. It could be not,” she replied.

The trial continues Tuesday.

Sidhu’s phone was seized by Peel Regional Police when he was arrested on April 5, 2024, almost a year after the high-profile heist. His home was searched as well.
Det.-Const. Edil Aden told court on Thursday that investigators extracted the phone’s contents using Cellebrite, a digital-forensics software tool.
“So it has text messages, phone calls, logs, images, videos. Their phone is put onto a screen for us,” Aden said. The printed data report was about two inches thick.
Aden said messages found on Sidhu’s phone had been sent and received through various tools, including text, encrypted apps and social media direct messaging.
One chat on Sidhu’s phone from a few months before the heist in April 2023 was with a jeweller about how to accurately test for nearly pure gold that had been melted without contamination.

Most of the messages that court heard about, however, were linked to Panesar, who might have been a co-accused at this same trial if he had returned to Canada. Panesar was the manager with Air Canada at the cargo warehouse at Pearson airport to whom Sidhu reported.
Sidhu and Panesar were friends outside of work. Their messages refer to going to the gym, having haircuts, getting coffee, sharing rides to work and laser hair removal recommendations.
Sidhu had five different means of contacting Panesar saved on his phone, including on encrypted communication apps Signal and WhatsApp.
The profile photos of Panesar saved on Sidhu’s phone look different from the widely circulated photo of Panesar in his police mug shot because he sometimes wears a hairpiece, court was told.

On the day of the heist, the two exchanges dozens of short messages, some highlighted to Judge Gordon Cudjoe as suspicious, or, in the words of Crown prosecutor Tyler Powell, “potentially relevant to this investigation.”
They included Panesar’s enthusiastic greetings for the day and a message from him a few hours after the heist.
“I think I’ll be going to India for days off just to get away few days,” the message from Panesar’s phone says. He said it was his wedding anniversary.
“Happy Anniversary,” Sidhu replies.
A few hours later, a message to Panesar’s number from Sidhu’s phone said: “Hey….gotta a call from my cuz who’s in peel. said he heard about a brings heist at cargo last night… lol. Hear anything?”
“No nothing like that happened,” was the reply.

Court heard little or no context to the messages. Presumably the reference to “brings heist” is a misspelling of Brink’s, the security transit company that was moving the gold from Switzerland to Toronto on an Air Canada flight for their client, TD Bank. It wasn’t until Brink’s guards arrived to collect the crate hours later that anyone realized it was gone.

Aden also testified about a screen recording found on Sidhu’s phone that appears to capture a thoroughly modern falling out between the two men: There is a screen shot of a message reading “Last chance” and then a sequence showing Sidhu’s phone blocking Panesar on Instagram.
Adel said police can’t say the screen recording was made by Sidhu, only that it was on Sidhu’s phone. It is not clear when the recording was made.
gotta a call from my cuz who’s in peel. said he heard about a brings heist at cargo last night… lol
In a series of direct messages on Instagram dated Jan. 30, 2023, there is more evidence of acrimony.
“14” a message from Sidhu’s account says.
“Yes I know” is the reply from Panesar’s.
“Bullshit,” says Sidhu’s.
“And I have news for you. We speak tomorrow. Cool?” says Panesar’s account.

“Talk to your lawyer. I urge you guys to do the right thing. U listen to me when u took the us cash… your full of shit.” In another message in the same string from Sidhu’s account, he mentions someone who was once a suspect in the heist and a misspelled version of Arsalan Chaudhary’s name.
In April, Chaudhary, 43, admitted to being the ringleader of the heist and was sentenced to four years in prison.

Aden was asked by Sidhu’s lawyer, Shale Wagman, if Sidhu’s fingerprints were found on the air waybill that was used to collect and steal the crate of gold and cash, worth more than $22 million. Court heard the waybill was printed from inside the Air Canada warehouse by someone logging in with Sidhu’s credentials.
She said she doesn’t think they were. She also agreed that no gold bars were found in the police search of Sidhu’s home.

Wagman asked her if the text massage saying “We looking good anyways for today” could mean almost anything. “It can mean anything, but the pertinence of it was that that’s the date of the heist,” Aden said. “It could be something work related,” Wagman asked. “It could be. It could be not,” she replied.
The trial continues Tuesday.

stories.title: Downtown reconstruction, arena refurbishment celebrated in Goderich
stories.summary: It’s been two summers since anyone could drive around the entirety of Goderich’s Courthouse square, but last week the construction barriers finally came down, and people could cruise downtown Goderich once again.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
It’s been two summers since anyone could drive around the entirety of Goderich’s Courthouse square, but last week the construction barriers finally came down, and people could cruise downtown Goderich once again.

“People are actually celebrating their first ringer, right? We still call it a ringer here, driving around the Square. There were people celebrating, claiming that they were the first person to do a ringer around the new Square. So, that’s how excited people are in the community,” said Goderich’s mayor Trevor Bazinet.

Work to replace 100 year old sewer and water pipes under Goderich’s Courthouse Square started on May 12, 2025. Half the square was closed to traffic at a time, as crews dug up and replaced the aging infrastructure.

While they were at it, downtown sidewalks were widened, intersection signage and bump-outs were added, and for the first time ever, driving lanes were painted on the one-way circular downtown street.

“It’s a legit two lane pathway for people to get around the Square now. It was kind of a free for all before. With the wider sidewalks, it provides more accessibility for our pedestrians, and people with accessibility needs. We’ve added more accessible parking on the spokes of the Square, as well,” said Bazinet.

The Downtown reconstruction project cost about $11 million, and will receive it’s final top coat of asphalt next spring.

Bazinet says the project was on time, and on budget.

“It was a long process, Two years is a long time, but I’ll tell you, everyone was really positive about it, and the support that the businesses received was incredible. So, I can’t thank our business owners enough for their patience,” said Bazinet.

Across town, a project of a different kind is being celebrated this weekend. The grand reopening of the Goderich Memorial Community Centre. The former arena was closed in January 2025, due to required safety and accessibility upgrades.

Late last year, community groups joined forces, and volunteers did the majority of the work to get the 77-year-old building reopened as a multipurpose community centre.

“We’ve got floor hockey in here. We’ve got conversations underway with Minor Baseball. We’ve got wrestling in here next week. We got Comic-Con coming back. We’ve got a Home Show coming in. We’ve got rentals upstairs. Shuffleboard. Pickleball. I’m really looking forward to the next 12 months to see what we can make of this,” said Randy Carroll, and Matt Hoy, Co-Chairs of the Goderich Memorial Community Centre.

A community led board will run the facility, while Goderich retains ownership of the building.

Carroll says Goderich’s service groups have spent $133,000 so far to refurbish the old arena, and have raised $38,000 towards their $750,000 fundraising goal.

“We just do like anyone would do with a building of this age, you just work on it as you can afford to work on it. It’s a good start. We’re in a better place than we thought we’d be, that’s for sure,” said Carroll.

A grand reopening celebration for the Goderich Memorial Community Complex is happening Saturday, Oct. 10 starting at 2 p.m.

stories.title: Canada pulls out of global disinformation conference with panels pointing to U.S. as source of foreign interference
stories.summary: It attracts researchers, people who work in counter-disinformation, journalists, think tanks, academics and government officials.
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
The federal government has withdrawn its sponsorship for a European disinformation conference that includes panel discussions about the U.S. government as a risk for foreign interference.

The conference is an annual event focused on countering disinformation. Organized by EU DisinfoLab, a non-profit based in Brussels, it attracts researchers, people who work in counter-disinformation, journalists, think tanks, academics and government officials. The 2026 edition is taking place in Vilnius, Lithuania this week.

More than one panel slated for Disinfo2026 , discusses the U.S. as a source of foreign-information manipulation and interference (Fimi), which refers to state-backed actors engaging in coordinated efforts to sway public debate aiming to undermining elections and institutions.

Global Affairs Canada says Ottawa isn’t comfortable with how those discussions were framed, so while Canadian officials will still be participating in the conference, they will not be chairing any discussions.

“Following changes to the framing of several panel discussions, Global Affairs decided to revise its participation in those sessions at the EU DisinfoLab 2026 conference,” says Samatha Lafleur, spokesperson for Global Affairs.

The department “carefully assesses participation in, and sponsorship of, external events on a case-by-case basis,” she said in an email to National Post on Thursday. “We respect the right of the organizers to frame discussions as they see fit and recognize the independence of civil society actors and speakers at the conference.”

Despite the sponsorship cancellation, Lafleur added that “Canada remains firmly committed to addressing the challenge of disinformation and misinformation. Global Affairs Canada officials continue to participate in the … conference and look forward to engaging with partners and stakeholders on efforts to counter disinformation.”

The Guardian is reporting that the Trump administration “pressured multiple countries to withdraw their sponsorship” and that Canada, as well as Lithuania and the EU’s diplomatic service agreed. Lafleur did not respond to this allegation.

Feds to restructure fund for combating disinformation, end program for hiring diverse journalists

Paul Deegan: Real journalists matter in an AI worldPaul Deegan: Real journalists matter in an AI world

Just days before the conference was to begin, the logos of the main supporters, including the Lithuanian ministry of foreign affairs, the European External Action Service and Global Affairs Canada, were removed from the conference website, states the Guardian. Both the Guardian and CBC are reporting that photos of the event show white stickers placed over the logos of these organizations on official conference materials.

On Wednesday, a panel that Lithuania took exception to, according to the Guardian, explored how Europe’s disinformation community could rebuild resilience without Washington, the first time the conference appears to have entertained the idea that the U.S. could be a disinformation actor in Europe. It’s called “USA as a Fimi threat: adapt, acknowledge, push back.”

Another session will discuss “growing evidence” that the United States has in some Arctic contexts, operated as a Fimi actor.

The U.S. State Department is neither confirming, nor denying the application of pressure to withdraw conference sponsorship.

In an emailed statement to National Post on Thursday, State Department spokesperson Jennifer Viau said: “While we are unable to comment on the details of diplomatic conversations, it should not be a surprise that countries would disaffiliate from this conference upon learning that it labeled the U.S. a ‘Fimi threat.’ Labeling the United States a Fimi threat – a term normally reserved for describing influence operations of adversaries – undermines shared goals and should alarm those involved.”

An EU spokesperson confirmed to the Guardian that the European External Action Service decided to withdraw its support from the conference because “the organizers chose to frame some of the discussions in a way which does not align with the official positions held by the EU.” Despite withdrawing its sponsorship, the EU continues to fund the conference.

Canada’s move comes at a time when the country is caught in the ongoing tensions of a bitter trade dispute with U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration.

Another session will discuss “growing evidence” that the United States has in some Arctic contexts, operated as a Fimi actor.
The U.S. State Department is neither confirming, nor denying the application of pressure to withdraw conference sponsorship.

In an emailed statement to National Post on Thursday, State Department spokesperson Jennifer Viau said: “While we are unable to comment on the details of diplomatic conversations, it should not be a surprise that countries would disaffiliate from this conference upon learning that it labeled the U.S. a ‘Fimi threat.’ Labeling the United States a Fimi threat – a term normally reserved for describing influence operations of adversaries – undermines shared goals and should alarm those involved.”

An EU spokesperson confirmed to the Guardian that the European External Action Service decided to withdraw its support from the conference because “the organizers chose to frame some of the discussions in a way which does not align with the official positions held by the EU.” Despite withdrawing its sponsorship, the EU continues to fund the conference.
Canada’s move comes at a time when the country is caught in the ongoing tensions of a bitter trade dispute with U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration.

stories.title: B.C. campaign trail: Conservatives promise $1,000 tax cut by boosting exemption level
stories.summary: Taxation is back at the forefront of the British Columbia election campaign.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Taxation is back at the forefront of the British Columbia election campaign.

Here are some of the latest developments from the campaign trail on Thursday.

B.c. Conservatives offer $1,000 tax cut

Interim leader of the B.C. Conservatives Lorne Doerkson says he would cut provincial taxes by $1,000 for nearly every working British Columbian amid a “cost-of-living crisis.”

The Conservatives plan to raise the basic personal income tax exemption level in B.C. from $13,216 to $32,000, making it “the most generous in Canada.”

They say a typical two-income family would benefit by about $2,000 a year, or $167 a month.

Doerkson has already pledged no new taxes under a Conservative government, at a time when the province is facing a projected deficit under the NDP of $13.8 billion.

While campaigning in Surrey, Doerkson said that B.C. will have to “supercharge the economy” to meet funding and revenue challenges.

NDP candidate Spencer Chandra Herbert said the tax-cut vow by the Conservatives would “blow a $2.5 billion hole into the B.C. budget,” and suggested health care spending would have to be cut to meet the shortfall.

Ndp would freeze icbc rates three more years

British Columbia New Democrat Leader David Eby says his government would freeze the province’s vehicle insurance rates for another three years if elected on Oct. 24.

Eby, as the attorney general, moved the Insurance Corporation of B.C. to a no-fault system in 2021, after saying the Crown agency was a financial “dumpster fire.”

Eby said while campaigning in Richmond that his government saved the average B.C. driver about $500 a year and it’s been able to freeze rates for seven years.

A leaked letter sent to trial lawyers and others by Doerkson said if his party wins the election he’ll repeal the no-fault plan for a hybrid model.

While Eby acknowledges the current system is not perfect, he said the Conservative plan would hike car insurance costs and send more money to lawyers and private insurers.

CentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko has called on Doerkson to explain his insurance commitments, saying British Columbians “deserve to know what is being promised in their name.”

Sturko wants Doerkson to publish his proposal in full and describe the potential impact on premiums.

Greens release schools plan

BC Green Party Leader Emily Lowan has announced the party’s plans for schools, including a vow to close what they say is a $317 million funding shortfall for the costs of inclusive education.

The party said it would increase the number of counsellors to achieve a ratio of one counsellor for every 250 students.

It also said it would deliver universal programs for school food and supplies, “so every student gets fed and has what they need to learn.”

Lowan, who is a candidate for Saanich North and the Islands, said “no child should have to try to learn when they’re hungry,” or lack a trusted counsellor.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Investment guru Stephen Jarislowsky was a crusader for ethical business practices
stories.summary: While building one of Canada’s most powerful institutional money management firms, he fought for shareholder rights and became an outspoken critic of inept corporate leadership
stories.author: Jason Kirby
stories.content:
As a young counterintelligence officer with the United States Army stationed in postwar Japan, Stephen Jarislowsky honed his investigative skills hunting black marketeers and rooting out Nazis from among the Germans living in the country.

The posting also gave him his first exposure to the concept of governance. One day his unit picked up rumours that the wife of U.S. General Douglas MacArthur was attempting to influence the outcome of postwar reconstruction contracts. Chasing down that lead resulted in Mr. Jarislowsky’s unit being temporarily suspended.

Years later, according to his 2005 book, The Investment Zoo , Mr. Jarislowsky would draw heavily on those early experiences as he built a small securities research firm into one of Canada’s most powerful institutional money managers.

In the process, the former chairman of Jarislowsky Fraser Ltd. emerged as a crusader for shareholder rights and a sharp-tongued critic of underperforming or inept corporate executives and the board of directors who blindly supported them.

An investor, entrepreneur and philanthropist, Mr. Jarislowsky died on Thursday in Montreal at the age of 101, according to his family.

At its peak, Jarislowsky Fraser was a powerhouse in the world of institutional investing. In 2007, the firm oversaw roughly $60-billion in assets for pension funds, foundations, corporations and high-net-worth individuals from its Montreal head office.

During the prior four decades, Mr. Jarislowsky had repeatedly deployed his growing clout to cross swords with a who’s who of Canadian corporate titans, including the Billes family behind Canadian Tire, Montreal’s powerful Bronfman clan, the former media mogul Conrad Black and auto parts magnate Frank Stronach.

Though the circumstances were different in each case, he took up the fight against transactions and deals he saw as manipulative and abusive toward minority shareholders, doggedly battling his opponents with biting language that earned him a reputation for being quick to temper – and made him a favourite source for multiple generations of business journalists.

When the Billes family in 1986 attempted to sell its voting-class shares to Canadian Tire dealers in a transaction that disadvantaged investors with non-voting shares, he publicly derided the deal as “crap” and “grossly abusive” while successfully convincing regulators and courts to block it. Likewise, he clashed repeatedly with Mr. Black over the latter’s management fees at Southam Inc. and later his attempt to take Hollinger Inc. private, describing his former friend as a “bully” and demanding regulators take action.

Mr. Jarislowsky also frequently used his pulpit to lambaste other targets: boards of directors for being “puppets of management”; lax regulators for allowing white-collar crime in Canada to become “a pretty good bet – almost as good as the house in Las Vegas”; and successive governments that “placed self-perpetuation through massive vote buying policies ahead of long-term economic progress.”

Mr. Jarislowsky was born in Berlin on Sept. 9, 1925, to accomplished parents, both Jews. His father was an industrialist and a merchant banker, his mother, a lawyer. When Mr. Jarislowsky was 4, his father died from scarlet fever, and he and his siblings were sent to live near relatives in Amsterdam.

It was the first of several challenges the family would endure. When the Nazis rose to power, the businesses his father had built were seized (then later nationalized by East Germany’s Communist government in 1947). The family moved to Paris, where Mr. Jarislowsky studied and became fluent in French and English. But when his stepfather’s work helping refugees escape German-occupied France for the U.S. was uncovered by the Gestapo, the family too had to flee, again, arriving in New York in 1941.

After he graduated from Cornell University with a mechanical engineering degree, Mr. Jarislowsky was drafted into the U.S. Army, becoming a U.S. citizen in the process. Upon his return to America from his posting in Asia, he delved back into education, completing a degree in Far Eastern Studies at the University of Chicago before enrolling in the Harvard Business School where he got his first taste of investing.

Harvard led to a stint at Alcan Aluminum Ltd. and to Montreal, the city where he would eventually settle permanently with his first wife, with whom he had two sons.

As a hobby in 1955 he developed an “experimental” statistical service, crunching balance sheets, income statements and valuation ratios on roughly 200 Canadian companies. After teaming up with Scott Fraser, a junior broker at the time, Jarislowsky Fraser was born, selling subscriptions to its statistical review before branching into field research through interviews with company executives. Soon, firms in Chicago, New York and London were turning to the fledgling outfit for investment counselling services. (Mr. Fraser left the firm roughly 20 years later.)

By the 1970s and 80s, Mr. Jarislowsky was regularly at the centre of corporate battles as foreign companies sought to take their publicly-traded Canadian subsidiaries private, often at opportunistic valuations. It was shareholder activism before most people had ever heard the term.

The success Mr. Jarislowky was having for his investor clients translated into a windfall for himself that eventually grew into one of Canada’s largest personal fortunes. Though he made regular appearances on various rich lists – Forbes last estimated his net worth at US$3.9-billion – he lived a relatively modest life with his second wife Gail, who he married in 1968. (The couple had two more children, daughters. One of Mr. Jarislowsky’s sons from his first marriage died in 2014 after an illness.)

Mr. Jarislowsky didn’t own yachts or luxury vehicles, though he was an avid collector of Chinese jade and art, particularly works by Canadian artists and French impressionists. The couple still lived in the same Westmount home they bought in 1972.

That said, he recognized the value of wealth, writing: “Money doesn’t mean reckless spending, but it does mean freedom.”

Similar to his investment strategy, he applied a studied approach to his philanthropic giving. In 1993, he established the Jarislowsky Foundation, which oversees assets worth more than $386-million and donated millions annually to hospitals, universities, nature trusts, cultural institutions and organizations that promote democracy and foster political leadership training.

“Charity should be effective, should achieve measurable goals, should be implemented by people with integrity, should be fully researched so you know that your gifts will not end up in the wrong pockets,” he wrote. “You should not give sentimentally, but insist on regular reviews of stewardship, throughout the process.”

Mr. Jarislowky’s other legacy is a heightened awareness in Canada about the importance of corporate governance. Whereas in the 1980s he guided an informal network of institutional money managers who together accounted for roughly 60 per cent of stock market trades and used that clout to influence recalcitrant boards of directors, he formalized that approach amid accounting scandals in the early 2000s at the likes of Worldcom, Enron and Nortel.

In 2002, he co-founded the Canadian Coalition for Good Governance, made up of powerful institutional investors to press for improved board oversight of public companies, and in 2005 he helped establish the Institute for Governance of Private and Public Organizations, a think tank to research and recommend ways to improve governance.

In 2008, Mr. Jarislowsky was named a companion of the Order of Canada, with the official citation highlighting his advocacy for shareholder rights; he has also received honorary degrees from 20 Canadian universities.

But Mr. Jarislowsky and his firm faced stumbles, too. In the late 1990s, as dot-com mania gripped investors’ psyche and quaint concepts such as value and fundamentals fell out of favour, he faced a drumbeat of complaints from clients unhappy with the lagging returns generated by the Old Economy stocks he kept their money in. His response: “Then take your money and gamble with it if you want,” he told this reporter, while explaining his deep skepticism for tech stocks. “Technology is just about new ways to communicate, nothing else. People still eat. They still drive cars. They still fornicate. What’s new?”

His stubbornness was eventually rewarded. By 2001, the narrative turned after the internet stock frenzy collapsed in spectacular fashion and investors chased the safety of dividend-paying stocks and disciplined portfolio management.

However, other headwinds were building. The emergence of lower cost passive investment products and increased competition from Canada’s big banks and hedge funds for institutional clients put pressure on the company, which saw its assets under management fall 40 per cent between 2007 and 2012 to $37-billion.

At the same time as money was leaving the firm, so too were staff and high-level executives who departed to launch their own money management firms.

The upheaval prompted a leadership shake-up. For more than two decades, questions swirled about Mr. Jarislowsky’s eventual retirement – one 1995 feature in The Globe and Mail on the then-69-year-old began, “As he slips quietly into retirement …” – but this time he stepped back as chief executive officer for real, allowing a management committee to take over.

Even so, when Mr. Jarislowsky struck a deal in 2018 to sell the investment management company to Bank of Nova Scotia for $950-million, he was still handling accounts for 200 personal clients at the age of 92.

Despite having been born to Jewish parents and educated by Calvinists, Jesuits and Episcopalians, Mr. Jarislowsky wrote that he eschewed traditional religious doctrine and considered himself “basically agnostic.”

“I can’t see myself sitting silently and quietly on top of a cloud for the next million years. That would be awfully dull. Those ideas are the inventions of humans,” he wrote. “But that doesn’t mean that ethics and behaving responsibly don’t have a place in the universe. To me, the ethics of Aristotle is religion.”

paragraphs: As a young counterintelligence officer with the United States Army stationed in postwar Japan, Stephen Jarislowsky honed his investigative skills hunting black marketeers and rooting out Nazis from among the Germans living in the country.

The posting also gave him his first exposure to the concept of governance. One day his unit picked up rumours that the wife of U.S. General Douglas MacArthur was attempting to influence the outcome of postwar reconstruction contracts. Chasing down that lead resulted in Mr. Jarislowsky’s unit being temporarily suspended.

Years later, according to his 2005 book, The Investment Zoo , Mr. Jarislowsky would draw heavily on those early experiences as he built a small securities research firm into one of Canada’s most powerful institutional money managers.

In the process, the former chairman of Jarislowsky Fraser Ltd. emerged as a crusader for shareholder rights and a sharp-tongued critic of underperforming or inept corporate executives and the board of directors who blindly supported them.
An investor, entrepreneur and philanthropist, Mr. Jarislowsky died on Thursday in Montreal at the age of 101, according to his family.

At its peak, Jarislowsky Fraser was a powerhouse in the world of institutional investing. In 2007, the firm oversaw roughly $60-billion in assets for pension funds, foundations, corporations and high-net-worth individuals from its Montreal head office.

During the prior four decades, Mr. Jarislowsky had repeatedly deployed his growing clout to cross swords with a who’s who of Canadian corporate titans, including the Billes family behind Canadian Tire, Montreal’s powerful Bronfman clan, the former media mogul Conrad Black and auto parts magnate Frank Stronach.

Though the circumstances were different in each case, he took up the fight against transactions and deals he saw as manipulative and abusive toward minority shareholders, doggedly battling his opponents with biting language that earned him a reputation for being quick to temper – and made him a favourite source for multiple generations of business journalists.

When the Billes family in 1986 attempted to sell its voting-class shares to Canadian Tire dealers in a transaction that disadvantaged investors with non-voting shares, he publicly derided the deal as “crap” and “grossly abusive” while successfully convincing regulators and courts to block it. Likewise, he clashed repeatedly with Mr. Black over the latter’s management fees at Southam Inc. and later his attempt to take Hollinger Inc. private, describing his former friend as a “bully” and demanding regulators take action.

Mr. Jarislowsky also frequently used his pulpit to lambaste other targets: boards of directors for being “puppets of management”; lax regulators for allowing white-collar crime in Canada to become “a pretty good bet – almost as good as the house in Las Vegas”; and successive governments that “placed self-perpetuation through massive vote buying policies ahead of long-term economic progress.”

Mr. Jarislowsky was born in Berlin on Sept. 9, 1925, to accomplished parents, both Jews. His father was an industrialist and a merchant banker, his mother, a lawyer. When Mr. Jarislowsky was 4, his father died from scarlet fever, and he and his siblings were sent to live near relatives in Amsterdam.

It was the first of several challenges the family would endure. When the Nazis rose to power, the businesses his father had built were seized (then later nationalized by East Germany’s Communist government in 1947). The family moved to Paris, where Mr. Jarislowsky studied and became fluent in French and English. But when his stepfather’s work helping refugees escape German-occupied France for the U.S. was uncovered by the Gestapo, the family too had to flee, again, arriving in New York in 1941.

After he graduated from Cornell University with a mechanical engineering degree, Mr. Jarislowsky was drafted into the U.S. Army, becoming a U.S. citizen in the process. Upon his return to America from his posting in Asia, he delved back into education, completing a degree in Far Eastern Studies at the University of Chicago before enrolling in the Harvard Business School where he got his first taste of investing.
Harvard led to a stint at Alcan Aluminum Ltd. and to Montreal, the city where he would eventually settle permanently with his first wife, with whom he had two sons.

As a hobby in 1955 he developed an “experimental” statistical service, crunching balance sheets, income statements and valuation ratios on roughly 200 Canadian companies. After teaming up with Scott Fraser, a junior broker at the time, Jarislowsky Fraser was born, selling subscriptions to its statistical review before branching into field research through interviews with company executives. Soon, firms in Chicago, New York and London were turning to the fledgling outfit for investment counselling services. (Mr. Fraser left the firm roughly 20 years later.)

stories.title: Ontario to begin removing Toronto bike lanes next week
stories.summary: Government to remove bike lanes along stretches of Bloor Street, Yonge Street and University Avenue
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The province says work to remove bike lanes on a stretch of a major Toronto road will begin next week.

It comes after Ontario’s top court overturned in August a ruling that blocked the government’s bid to remove protected bike lanes along stretches of Bloor Street, Yonge Street and University Avenue in Toronto.

Dakota Brasier, a spokesperson for Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria, says work to restore vehicle lanes on Bloor Street West will begin on Tuesday.

A lower court last year stopped the province from replacing the protected bike lanes with car lanes, but the Ontario Court of Appeal found that judgment had effectively created a right to bike lanes where none existed.

The province has since been pressing ahead with its plan to overhaul the cycling network over the city’s objections.

Last month it put out a bid request to study and design options to restore vehicle traffic on bike lane sections of the affected roads, and said the successful bidder will also be expected to look for ways to retain or reconfigure bike lanes, “where they make sense and do not make gridlock worse.”

stories.title: Rideshare insurance fraud in Winnipeg prompts crackdown: MPI
stories.summary: Winnipeg rideshare drivers will face more enforcement to ensure they have the correct auto insurance, after a review found many are operating without the correct coverage.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
Winnipeg rideshare drivers will face greater scrutiny of their auto insurance policies after a Manitoba Public Insurance (MPI) review found many are operating without proper coverage.

Uber and Lyft are among the approved rideshare providers in Winnipeg, which are determined by the city. When they apply to use the platforms, drivers must prove they are insured to operate as a vehicle for hire by MPI. This helps to ensure that they are paying their fair share of premiums and cost claims, Satvir Jatana, president and CEO at MPI, said at a news conference Thursday.

Approximately 3,000 drivers were temporarily halted from operating rideshares in Winnipeg from February to August of this year, due to a lack of proper insurance, she said. Some drivers were said to have opted in to the rideshare coverage to be approved for the apps, then switched back to basic coverage while continuing to offer customers rides.

“Vehicle for hire coverage is designed to account for the additional risk associated with rideshare drivers being on the road more. When the vehicle owners choose to change their required coverage, and continue providing rideshare services, that risk is no longer reflected in the premiums that they should pay,” Janata said.

“That is fraud. Plain and simple. It creates an unfair advantage for those who choose not to follow the rules and shift those costs onto other honest drivers and Manitobans.”

A preliminary assessment by MPI identified 36 claims, worth around $189,000, involving improperly insured rideshare drivers, Janata said, adding that the Crown corporation is working on recovering those funds.

“We will continue to hold those individuals accountable to ensure that they have the appropriate coverage. And they are responsible for paying their fair share,” she said.

Mpi’s legal team is reviewing options to recover those funds. The public insurance president said it “will pursue all options that are afforded to us under the legislation,” when asked if law enforcement is involved with the alleged fraud.

Grant Heather, manager of vehicles for hire at the City of Winnipeg, told reporters that drivers who were actively driving without the appropriate insurance were issued penalty notices under the vehicle for hire bylaw. His department regulates rideshare drivers and collaborates with MPI.

“Ultimately, this joint approach helps protect passengers, drivers and the public while supporting a fair and accountable vehicle for hire industry,” Heather said.

Owners of vehicles that are acting as a rideshare without the appropriate insurance in Winnipeg can face a $1,000 bylaw fine.

A spokesperson for Lyft said it holds all drivers “high standards and requires they maintain the insurance coverage required by Manitoba and the City of Winnipeg,” in an emailed statement.

“We will continue to work collaboratively with MPI and the City of Winnipeg to help ensure drivers meet all applicable insurance and regulatory requirements.”

Uber Canada also said rideshare trips must be properly insured in accordance with government regulations.

“Uber has worked closely with MPI and the City of Winnipeg to strengthen insurance compliance,” an emailed statement from an Uber Canada spokesperson reads.

“In light of Manitoba Public Insurance’s (MPI) recent review, we believe it’s time for Manitoba to adopt the model used across Canada, where rideshare companies like Uber purchase umbrella insurance coverage for trips on their platform, rather than requiring drivers to arrange their own rideshare coverage.”

While speaking at the conference, Mpi’s president said that a program like the one Uber spoke of is in the works.

stories.title: Thamesville resident fined for deer hunting violation
stories.summary: The Ministry of Natural Resources said on Nov. 7, 2025, a conservation officer did a deer hunting compliance check and found the man did not have a valid deer hunting license because his tag was already used. It added that the man was trying to party hunt using the tag of someone not actively hunting.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
The Ministry of Natural Resources said on Nov. 7, 2025, a conservation officer did a deer hunting compliance check and found the man did not have a valid deer hunting license because his tag was already used. It added that the man was trying to party hunt using the tag of someone not actively hunting.

Further investigation found that the man falsely applied for a farmer/landowner controlled hunt validation through another person’s licensing account and didn’t have the necessary approval to partake in the deer hunt.

The deer was seized and the man was fined $5,000.

It comes after Ontario’s top court overturned in August a ruling that blocked the government’s bid to remove protected bike lanes along stretches of Bloor Street, Yonge Street and University Avenue in Toronto.

stories.title: ‘The explosion would have been a huge ball of flame!’: Suspected chainsaw hydro police cutter risked all for little return
stories.summary: Police and London Hydro officials continue their search for information after a high-voltage utility pole was allegedly cut down by a chainsaw, sparking an explosion and widespread power outage.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
Police and London Hydro officials continue their search for information after a high-voltage utility pole was allegedly cut down by a chainsaw, sparking an explosion and widespread power outage. Hydro officials concede the blast could have seriously harmed or killed the perpetrators.

The incident took place shortly after 5 p.m. Tuesday on Exeter Road near Sholto Drive when lines touched, sparking a 27,000-volt blast. “The explosion would have been a huge ball of flame! It was so intense, and the heat was so, so high,” said Allan Van Damme, VP of engineering and construction at London Hydro.

As fire and line crews contained the blaze, Van Damme said officials worked to assess the damage. “It became evident very quickly that this was not a normal failure of a component on our grid.” Hydro later confirmed a chainsaw was used to take the pole down.

Grainy video surveillance images released by police show a suspect, wearing a black hoodie with writing on it and grey sweatpants. Police want the public to help identify him and their assistance in tracking this 2019 Honda CRV.

Meanwhile, Van Damme conceded that the suspect or suspects are fortunate to be uninjured. “They are extremely lucky because they would have been standing right in the line of fire as that explosion came down to the ground.

So, it appears that they left the site through the surveillance footage and that they made it out alive. But that could have ended very differently.” The motivation for the act is being investigated by police. It comes as London Hydro continues to be hit by copper thieves who risk their lives for what Van Damme says is very little return.

Meanwhile, the cost to replace the pole and the transformers has reached $30,000. Which is why Hydro has made it harder to cash in on stolen copper by providing examples of their wiring and parts to local metal recyclers.

But ultimately, ongoing pubic support will be needed to combat theft, confirmed Van Damme. “We have 30,000 poles in this city alone. And to stop a guy with a chainsaw who wants to cut a wood pole down is impossible. So, this is the challenge we face.”

stories.title: Conservatives vote in favour of Liberals’ Bill C-39, but promise amendments to 'protect the rights of workers'
stories.summary: Unions warned on Thursday the bill will lead to more labour unrest
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa – Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre told reporters Thursday that his party intends to bring amendments to the Liberal government’s latest major projects bill, to ensure workers benefit from the government’s build agenda.

“We will be putting forward amendments, to protect workers, their jobs, their rights and the working-class people who build this country,” said Poilievre, during a scrum on Parliament Hill.

Bill C-39, titled Building Canada Strong Act, which makes several changes to Canada’s regulatory and environmental laws, promises a one-year timeline and one review for the approval of major projects.

The bill also makes changes to the Canada Labour Code, including changes to collective bargaining and giving the labour minister “guardrails” on when they can intervene to end a lockout or strike. Those “guardrails” include a special mediator and a national interest test.

The government has argued this gives more transparency to the labour minister’s use of Section 107 of the labour code, although labour unions argue it gives too much discretionary power to a member of cabinet and threatens workers’ fundamental right to strike.

The Liberal government has used Section 107 to end several strikes and lockouts at ports, railways and airlines.

The omnibus bill passed second reading on Thursday, with help from the Conservative Party, and will now go to a special committee for members of Parliament to study. Members of the Bloc Québécois, NDP and Green parties voted against the legislation.

Poilievre did not provide details on what sort of amendments his party will bring forward but has been in contact with labour unions about the bill.

New bill should help prevent strikes in the 'centre of the economy,' think tank report says

Poilievre rips Carney’s omnibus bill as Conservatives agonize over how to vote on it

“I think it’s appalling that after the Carney Liberals have destroyed the paycheques of the working class through high taxes and inflation, they are now blaming those same workers for our economic weakness that he caused,” said Poilievre.

Green Party Leader Elizabeth May warned Thursday, that like its predecessor Bill C-5, which was passed last year, the latest major projects bill gives immense discretionary power to ministers.

“Once Cabinet decides a project or undefined region of national interest has been decreed by Cabinet (then) every future decision will be taken for the furtherance of the project,” said May. “It’s quite extraordinary.”

May said this allows government to bulldoze through existing laws to get things built faster, which does not necessarily mean better outcomes.

“When you move fast, you often end up with projects being 300 to 400 per cent over budget,” said May, citing empirical evidence from a book titled “How Big Things Get Done.”

Liberal MP Patrick Weiler appeared to criticize the bill on Tuesday evening, while debating the bill in the House of Commons, to voice similar concerns outlined by May.

“Given that the powers in this bill would be permanent, it is important that where new flexibility or discretion is created, Parliament instils clear and transparent processes,” said Weiler.

Weiler said he ultimately supports the aim of the bill and voted in support of Bill C-39 with his caucus on Thursday.

Meanwhile, labour unions continued to voice their concerns about the bill on Thursday, urging the Liberal government to remove the provisions related to Section 107, or face the risk of more labour unrest.

“I can tell you that our national executive board has just made a decision that said if locals who are out on strike want to defy, our union will stand with them,” said Candace Rennick, national secretary-treasury at the Canadian Union of Public Employees (Cupe), during a press conference in Ottawa.

“Because it’s Cupe members and Cupe members only that should decide when their picket lines end,” she added.

stories.title: Toronto bookstores celebrate Canadian Anne Carson's Nobel Prize in Literature win
stories.summary: Toronto - In the days before the Nobel Prize in Literature was set to be awarded, Claire Foster was holding out hope this would be Anne Carson's year.
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - In the days before the Nobel Prize in Literature was set to be awarded, Claire Foster was holding out hope this would be Anne Carson’s year.

A manager of Toronto independent bookstore Type Books, Foster has been a longtime enthusiastic fan of the Canadian poet. When she learned that Carson had indeed won the prestigious prize on Thursday, her reaction was one of pure delight.

“I was just so excited and so happy,” she said. “It’s the happiest I could have been for the announcement today, I think.”

Foster said Carson “has been a mainstay of our poetry shelves” for 20 years, so the Queen Street West location she manages was stocked with some of Carson’s books. When Foster arrived at the store in the morning, she built a shrine to the Toronto-born writer, displaying a number of her titles in front of the cash register, knowing that the Nobel win would create buzz and curiosity from customers.

In the coming weeks, Foster said the store plans to order more and display them prominently.

“We want them to be easily findable and recognizable,” she said.

According to Indigo spokesperson Madi Downey, “Autobiography of Red” was the bookseller’s top-selling book online by midday and “Anne Carson” was their top-searched term, up 2,272 per cent from the day before. Her book “Nox,” priced at $83.95, had also sold quite a few units, Downey said.

Meanwhile, at Toronto’s Ben McNally Books, store operator Rupert McNally arrived early this morning to order as many Carson works as he could. He said he knew customers would be clamouring to get their hands on her books. Sure enough, two minutes after the doors opened at 10 a.m. two customers arrived, inquiring about Carson.

A poet, essayist, classical scholar and translator, Carson is renowned for her singular, genre-bending style. With a bibliography of more than 20 books of poetry, essays, plays, libretti and translations of ancient Greek texts, Carson has earned praise from across the literary world, while also defying conventions.

Her well-known works include her verse novel “Autobiography of Red,” which reimagines the Greek myth of Heracles killing the winged monster, Geryon. The book of poems and prose, “Men in the Off Hours,” won the inaugural Griffin Poetry Prize in 2001, while “The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos” was awarded the prestigious T.S. Eliot Prize.

McNally said a Canadian winning the Nobel Prize in Literature is a “huge boon” for the business.

“We see a huge jump in sales of her books and books that she’s worked on,” he said. “Even books onto which she’s done introductions of other people’s works, we’ll see a jump in sale on those as well.”

While McNally said he hasn’t read a lot of her work previously, he knows she is “very thoughtful and very erudite.”

“And I love that for the Nobel,” McNally said. “I love that it’s not necessarily the most in-your-face choice, but someone who I think will be a new find for a lot of readers.”

Meanwhile, when Foster is not working at the bookstore, she said she translates works from French so Carson’s “work as a person who translates has always been so important to me,” she said, adding her favourite Carson book is “Plainwater.”

“But it’s really hard to choose,” she said. “I find her thinking so admirable and ethical and inspiring.”

For Foster, she said she’s excited the Nobel Prize might prompt readers to dig into Carson’s catalogue that includes works published 40 years ago.

“She has such a vast backlist and the Nobel is such a great occasion to think backwards, too, in terms of the work that she has been doing for decades. To be able bring in older titles and obviously for us to be able to celebrate the second Canadian ever to win a Nobel is huge,” Foster said.

“It’s huge for Canadian reading and appreciation, and we feel lucky to hopefully be a beacon that people can come to to find her.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Toronto Zoo sees drop in 2026 visitors due to wildfire smoke, extreme heat
stories.summary: Wildfire smoke along with extreme heat in July is the main culprit, as it depressed visits for the first three weeks of what is a crucial month for the zoo to welcome visitors.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Extreme weather, driven by climate change , has resulted in fewer visits to the Toronto Zoo so far this year, according to zoo staff in a report submitted to the city Thursday.

Wildfire smoke along with extreme heat in July is the main culprit, as it depressed visits for the first three weeks of what is a crucial month for the zoo to welcome visitors, said Jamie Austin, the zoo’s chief transformation officer.

“When there are advisories for people to avoid the amount of time they’re spending outdoors, a trip to the zoo just isn’t on the top of their list,” he said.

In mid-July this year, smoke from fires burning in northern Ontario drifted over Toronto, turning the sky orange and causing the city to be one of the worst places in the world for air quality. As a result, July visitor figures are 14 per cent below the zoo’s targets, according to the facility’s report.

By the end of September, 1,095,286 people had visited the zoo in 2026, which is nine per cent below the predicted target.

The City of Toronto warns on its website that Canada is warming at twice the global rate on average. As a result, Toronto, like many other cities, is experiencing more extreme heat and intense storms with heavy rainfall that increase flooding, power outages and infrastructure damage. These issues also impact the everyday health of residents.

Continued extreme weather through the winter and summer is driving popular attractions like the zoo to engage in substantive preparations for climate change resilience to maintain visits.

And it wasn’t only July that caused a drop in visits, said Austin. The first few months of 2026 featured a cold, long, snowy winter. “We had a couple of closures due to snow accumulation on site; it just wasn’t safe to open. That’s very rare in the zoo’s history,” he said.

What followed winter was a cool, rainy spring that also did not encourage extended time outdoors. But now into the fall, above-target visitor numbers through September are indicating the zoo will have a strong October, said Austin. September saw close to 162,000 guests visit the zoo, which is 13 per cent higher than the facility predicted.

Events at the zoo like the Glow in the Wild lantern festival happening Thursdays through Sundays until January 2027 are drawing visitors. Regardless, Austin said preparations are ongoing to make the zoo more of an attraction that is not so reliant on the summer season.

“We’re looking long-term at how to make the site more resilient to things like climate change and make it more comfortable for guests to be here year-round, no matter the weather and no matter the time of year,” he said. The zoo has many indoor spaces to explore, he adds.

Yet guests remain relatively exposed to the elements within the facility’s Rouge National Urban Park campus that features exposed outdoor trails leading to pavilions and enclosures.

Climate change was also on the zoo’s radar when examining a drop in 2025’s attendance as well. Zoo visits in 2025 reached just over 1.25 million, down from about 1.36 million in 2024. In January, zoo CEO Dolf DeJong said 2025 heat waves and an ice storm in November that year also hurt demand.

The long-term vision for the zoo will increase the site’s resilience for animals and visitors, said Austin. That involves cooling stations, warming stations and more shading and shelter.

For now, Austin said he wants to encourage residents to visit this fall as they welcome new animals, including a baby wombat.

“I’d say it’s my favorite time of year to visit the zoo. The comfortable weather, the beautiful colors as the trees change and active animals…we’re seeing good attendance,” he said.

stories.title: St. Thomas police investigate targeted threat at Stegh
stories.summary: St. Thomas Elgin General Hospital (Stegh) declared a code silver, person with a weapon at about 3:30 p.m.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
St. Thomas Elgin General Hospital (Stegh) declared a code silver, person with a weapon at about 3:30 p.m.

As a precaution, the hospital was placed on active hold and all public entrances were secured.

At about 6 p.m. code silver was declared over.

Stegh says while there is no ongoing threat, the hospital remains in a controlled access situation as an added precaution.

Access to the hospital is currently limited to one designated entrance, the north entrance beside the Emergency Department.

In a social media post, St. Thomas police said it was a threat targeted at an individual staff member at the hospital.
