stories.title: Diplomat Ian Hamilton led operation to save desperate refugees afloat on the South China Sea
stories.summary: The immigration official, who was haunted by what he had witnessed, said the crisis was ‘probably the greatest human tragedy of our time’
stories.author: Alan Freeman
stories.content:
It was an image that caught the world’s attention: A rusty freighter, the Hai Hong, appeared off Port Klang on the coast of Malaysia in early November 1978, its filthy decks teeming with 2,500 refugees from Vietnam.

It had been three years since the fall of Saigon and the collapse of the South Vietnamese regime to the communist forces. There had been an initial outflow of refugees fleeing the country but by 1978 that stream had turned into a torrent, creating what became known as the “boat people” crisis, as tens of thousands of Vietnamese boarded any watercraft, no matter how flimsy, to escape their homeland, heading out across the South China Sea. They were joined by victims of repression in Cambodia and Laos.

Malaysia, already overwhelmed by the influx of refugees, wanted nothing to do with the Hai Hong’s human cargo and threatened to tow the ship and its desperate passengers out to sea. The country’s Malay majority was hostile to the ethnic Chinese people on board. And Malaysian authorities claimed the passengers weren’t real refugees because they had paid for their passage.

As international pressure grew for wealthy countries to do something, the Canadian government decided to act. Immigration minister Bud Cullen announced that Canada would take 600 of the ship’s refugees for resettlement.

The officer in charge of Canada’s tiny immigration office in Singapore was Ian Hamilton, a seasoned 42-year-old official, who was sent to Kuala Lumpur to lead what became a heroic operation that saved thousands over the coming months. Tall, charming and rugged-looking with an infectious sense of humour, Mr. Hamilton, who died in Ottawa on Sept. 15 at the age of 89, was also determined and dedicated to the task at hand.

Malaysian officials wanted the Hai Hong and its passengers to leave their country’s waters, but nonetheless threw roadblocks in front of Mr. Hamilton’s small team. They wouldn’t allow the freighter to dock or permit the Canadians to board it. But, according to the 2017 book Running on Empty: Canada and the Indochinese Refugees, 1975-80 , Mr. Hamilton persuaded the officials to allow him to set up shop on a Malaysian minesweeper, anchored near the Hai Hong, to conduct his screening.

Armed Malaysian police escorted small contingents of the refugees to the deck of the naval ship where the immigration officers, plus a doctor and an interpreter, assembled a rudimentary office consisting of two wooden tables and a few chairs under a tarpaulin to protect them from the scorching tropical sun. The refugees were short of food and traumatized by their days at sea, with the Hai Hong refused entry by neighbouring countries.

“It was an appalling situation, probably the greatest human tragedy of our time,” Mr. Hamilton told a CBC film crew.

“The pressure of saying yes and no just squashes you,” Mr. Hamilton said 10 years later in an interview with The Ottawa Citizen, recalling how frail and terrified the refugees were. “You’re doing the best job that you can and you’re just being eaten up by the decision-making process. You want to say yes, but obviously you can’t.”

He did what he could, sometimes bending the rules to save lives. Dick Martin, who was No. 2 in the Singapore immigration office, remembers an incident where a woman slipped and fell to her death on the Hai Hong. The next day, her son, who was seven or eight and now an orphan, appeared before the Canadian immigration officers with a group of other refugees. Alone.

“I told Ian the story and he was overcome. He already had in front of him a young family, a mother, father and two children,” Mr. Martin recalled in an interview with The Globe. “Ian looks at them and says, ‘are you taking your nephew with you?’” Perplexed, the father initially said he didn’t have a nephew, but Mr. Hamilton insisted, gesturing to the little boy in the queue. The man relented, and his new-found nephew was on his way to life in Canada.

Despite the awful conditions, Mr. Hamilton and his crew interviewed and accepted as many as 356 refugees on a single day in an era when the standard was 12 interviews a day. By the end of November, the first Boeing 707 full of refugees from the Hai Hong arrived in Montreal. Three more flights followed. In all, 604 Vietnamese from the Hai Hong restarted their lives in Canada. The remaining refugees were taken by the U.S., France, Germany, Belgium and Switzerland.

Over the next two years, Canada welcomed 60,000 Southeast Asian refugees, many of them under the pioneering private sponsorship program, where church and other groups got together to support newcomers as they adapted to Canadian life. After the Hai Hong, Mr. Hamilton travelled throughout the region processing thousands of refugees at wretched refugee camps, renting fishing boats and leaning on reluctant bureaucrats to facilitate his work, armed with nothing more than a stack of Maple Leaf pins, which he distributed widely.

“He was a real leader, a mentor, the kind of guy who set an example,” said Scott Mullin, who as a 21-year-old junior immigration officer in Hong Kong, was assigned to work with Mr. Hamilton. “He was a superb guy. I loved working with him,” added Florent Fortin, who represented the Quebec government, which had recently signed an immigration agreement with Ottawa, and was part of the team.

“They were young and they were tough,” said Mike Molloy, a senior Immigration official at the time who worked on co-ordinating the refugee influx from Ottawa and co-wrote Running on Empty .

“Ian was a really compassionate person,” Mr. Molloy told The Globe. “There are people who are really good and Ian was one of those people, in terms of being compassionate and caring about people.”

Ian Stewart Hamilton was born on Sept. 23, 1936 in Ottawa, the eldest of three children of John Hamilton, a vice-president of the E.B. Eddy forest products company, and his wife, the former Shirley Stewart. Ian grew up in Aylmer, Que., and attended boarding school in Ontario, winding up at Valley Forge Military Academy in Pennsylvania, where he completed high school.

He earned a degree in psychology at Curry College, a small liberal-arts institution near Boston and began work as a psychologist for Corrections Canada. After two years, he joined Canada’s foreign service as an immigration officer, posted successively to Cologne, Stockholm, Sydney and Madrid before moving to Singapore in 1977. By that time, he was married and had three sons.

After the Hai Hong, Mr. Hamilton continued his resettlement work in refugee camps along the Malaysian coast, gaining considerable media attention for his work. “Hamilton has waded out to tossing boats carrying dead and dying in his arms,” read one account in The Toronto Sun. “There are lines of fatigue around his eyes where the laugh lines were once etched. It comes from tropical diseases, from endless days of interviewing in the filth and heat of a refugee camp.”

By the summer of 1979, the ceaseless work proved too much. Mr. Hamilton had contracted hepatitis. “It was hard on him physically. It was hard on him emotionally,” his eldest son, Shawn, said. Mr. Hamilton and his family moved back to Canada. Soon after, he and his wife separated.

Mr. Hamilton was honoured with a Public Service Award in 1979 but remained in Ottawa for the rest of his career, working in immigration and consular affairs, never venturing out on another foreign assignment.

“He did not want to travel again. It was a purposeful choice,” Shawn said. “He was done. He just wanted to find peace and tranquillity.” Mr. Hamilton retired in the early 1990s, spending lots of time in nature, ON extended camping trips in Quebec’s La Verendrye Park and salmon fishing on the Miramichi River.

He seldom talked about his time in Southeast Asia, only opening up as he aged. Shawn says he discovered 80 per cent of what he knows about that crucial period of his father’s life in the last two or three years. “The veil lifted.”

Mr. Hamilton’s role wasn’t forgotten by the people most important to him, members of Canada’s Vietnamese community, who would send him greeting cards on his birthday and Christmas. He befriended Can Le, a retired Ottawa economist and a leader of the Vietnamese-Canadian community who has been working for years to erect a Boat People Museum in Ottawa.

Last March, Mr. Le invited Mr. Hamilton to a fundraising event for the project in Ottawa. “He gave a very eloquent and moving speech,” Mr. Le said. Mr. Hamilton recalled how he was haunted by the awful things he had seen in the refugee camps after he returned to Canada decades ago. Distraught, he would walk through Ottawa’s Chinatown neighbourhood and found solace in seeing how the newly arrived refugees were adapting well to their new home.

“I love you all dearly,” Mr. Hamilton told the crowd. “I’m proud of what I did. And you are the ones who are building our country.” The crowd gave him a standing ovation.

Mr. Hamilton leaves his sons, Shawn, Matthew and Nicholas; five grandchildren; and his sister, Susan. Bonnie Boyle, his wife of 41 years, died in 2013. His first marriage ended in divorce.

Mr. Molloy said he recalled that Mr. Hamilton was once asked how he decided on whether a displaced family should be accepted for resettlement or not. “He replied, ‘by the light of their children’s eyes.’”

content_blocks.text: The officer in charge of Canada’s tiny immigration office in Singapore was Ian Hamilton, a seasoned 42-year-old official, who was sent to Kuala Lumpur to lead what became a heroic operation that saved thousands over the coming months. Tall, charming and rugged-looking with an infectious sense of humour, Mr. Hamilton, who died in Ottawa on Sept. 15 at the age of 89, was also determined and dedicated to the task at hand.

content_blocks.text: Malaysian officials wanted the Hai Hong and its passengers to leave their country’s waters, but nonetheless threw roadblocks in front of Mr. Hamilton’s small team. The refugees were short of food and traumatized by their days at sea, with the Hai Hong refused entry by neighbouring countries.

stories.title: B.C. Conservatives drop candidate over ‘racist’ social media posts
stories.summary: Screenshots shared by NDP show Joachim Agou saying car that drove through pro-Palestine protest ‘should have reversed’ over demonstrators
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Interim leader of the British Columbia Conservatives Lorne Doerkson has swiftly dumped a candidate in the provincial election over online posts that the NDP called racist.

Doerkson said Thursday that the posts by Victoria-Beacon Hill candidate Joachim Agou cannot be tolerated and if he is elected, he will not be part of the Conservative caucus.

Agou’s ejection from the Conservative election slate was announced about 90 minutes after Agou’s posts on social media platform X were highlighted by the NDP.

Although Agou’s account has now been deleted, screenshots shared by the NDP show him saying last year that a car that drove through a pro-Palestine protest “should have reversed” over the demonstrators, and he also shared a meme while using an expletive to describe Pakistan.

Agou did not immediately respond to a request for comment sent to his campaign.

The Conservative website describes Agou as a professional engineer and small-business owner with more than 15 years of experience in engineering research and industry.

His biography says he was born in France, studied in the United States and came to Canada in 2011.

He is also the interim vice-president of the Victoria Conservative Association.

Doerkson said in a statement that there is “no excuse” for the posts.

He told reporters at an event earlier in the day that he hadn’t seen the allegations, but he “of course” would never support the comments.

“Trust me when I say this, I’ll be looking into them the second I leave this podium.” he said about an hour before Agou’s removal was made public.

NDP candidate Amna Shah had shared the screenshots and called on Doerkson to fire Agou immediately for what she called “horrific racism.”

Victoria-Beacon Hill is consistently considered a safe NDP riding, with the party winning the seat in every provincial election since 2005.

stories.title: Countering drones is ‘critical’ as warfare evolves, Canada’s military says
stories.summary: The Canadian Armed Forces has been spending on both building its drone warfare capabilities and defending operations from 'unmanned aerial systems.'
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
The increasing availability of sophisticated drone technology has led the Department of National Defence (DND) to move to take “critical” steps to counter “unauthorized drone activity” that could threaten Canadian military installations.

Global News reported last week the department was looking to purchase anti-drone defences for military facilities on Canadian soil, similar to the protection given to Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) personnel deployed in Europe.

The story was based on federal procurement documents, but the records provided no detail on what systems DND is looking to purchase, or what threat the department envisions deploying drones on Canadian soil.

In a statement this week, a DND spokesperson said that as drone technology becomes more widespread and capable, “defence and security organizations (are examining) how best to address the risks.”

“(Counter-drone) capabilities are a critical consideration in modern security and defence planning,” Laura McIntyre-Grills wrote in a statement to Global News.

“DND has procurement activities planned to support the continued evolution and enhancement of its approach to countering (drone) threats, building on existing measures and capabilities. This work forms part of broader efforts to support the Caf’s ability to effectively respond to evolving operational and security requirements and enhance the security of defence establishments.”

2:01 UN condemns Russian attacks on Ukraine civilians after fatal bus strike kills 33

McIntyre-Grills noted that due to operational security reasons, the department would not comment on specifics, and that some aspects of the procurement will be subject to a national security exception and kept from public release.

As part of the Canadian Nato deployment in Latvia aimed at deterring Russian aggression, Canadian military leaders have closely watched the evolution of drone warfare in Ukraine.

Ukrainian forces have deployed low-cost but highly-effective drones in the efforts to push back Russia’s invasion force. Reuters reported earlier this year that drone-related casualties in the conflict have jumped from 10 per cent of the total in 2022 to roughly 80 per cent in 2025.

The skies above Ukraine’s battlefields are now haunted by the unmanned machines, making troop and artillery movement much more dangerous. Both Ukraine and Russia deploy drones to strike at the opposing side’s territory. On Oct. 8, a Russian drone blitz killed four and injured 19 others in Kyiv and led to emergency energy shutdowns, according to the Kyiv Independent.

This year the Canadian military embarked on a multi-year research and procurement project to boost Canada’s drone capabilities, called the Drone Defence Initiative (DDI). Through the project, the Canadian government hopes to “accelerate” research, development, adaptation and production of drones for use by both the CAF and the Canadian Coast Guard.

stories.title: Alberta’s Cold Lake First Nations seek judicial review of Pacific Link pipeline designation
stories.summary: Cold Lake First Nations filed an application for judicial review in Federal Court on Thursday challenging Ottawa’s decision to designate the Pacific Link pipeline as a project in the national interest. Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced last week the pipeline from Alberta to British Columbia would be fast-tracked under t…
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Cold Lake First Nations filed an application for judicial review in Federal Court on Thursday challenging Ottawa’s decision to designate the Pacific Link pipeline as a project in the national interest.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced last week the pipeline from Alberta to British Columbia would be fast-tracked under the Building Canada Act. The goal is to complete the required reviews and consultations over the next year so that construction can begin next September.

Cold Lake First Nations Chief Kelsey Jacko previously told The Canadian Press his community was left out of consultations on the pipeline designation, despite the fact that his community is situated in the oilsands region.

In the application for judicial review, Cold Lake First Nations’ lawyers said the designation breached Canadian law and is inconsistent with the honour of the Crown.

“Increasing oilsands production will have significant adverse effects on the ability of Clfn members to maintain their Luechogh Tue Denesuline way of life as promised by Treaty no. 6,” the application said.

“Canada has made no effort to understand or mitigate the massive cumulative effects of oilsands development on Clfn’s Luechogn Tue Denesuline treaty rights.”

The First Nation is asking the court to quash the national interest designation and to declare that Canada has a duty to consult with the community on the pipeline.

The Assembly of First Nations previously told The Canadian Press it had identified “many red flags” in the pipeline’s national interest designation and says the federal government appears to be predetermining outcomes and approving projects in advance of meaningful consultations.

Prime Minister Carney promised his major projects agenda would not interfere with Canada’s obligations under the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples.

stories.title: Two house explosions shake Hamilton, send three people to hospital
stories.summary: Hamilton - Firefighters in Hamilton say two house explosions shook the city on Thursday, sending three people to the hospital with burns.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Hamilton - Firefighters in Hamilton say two house explosions shook the city on Thursday, sending three people to the hospital with burns.

Hamilton Fire Chief David Cunliffe says the explosions, which took place within hours of each other, were unrelated and investigators are still trying to determine the causes.

Cunliffe says fire crews arrived at the scene of the first explosion at 182 Springside Dr., and found a large debris field and what was believed to be a garage on fire.

A victim believed to have been inside the garage when it exploded was taken to the hospital in serious condition.

Cunliffe says it was a “significant blast” that tore through the building and the explosion was felt at nearby fire stations and a police station.

While the fire was quickly brought under control, Cunliffe says two adjacent homes were significantly damaged.

Cunliffe says the second explosion at 8 Lampton Place sent up a large plume of smoke that was visible to firefighters as they raced to the scene.

The fire chief says two people were inside the home when it exploded and neighbours ran into the burning building to rescue them.

The occupants were both hospitalized, Cunliffe says, one with serious injuries and the other in stable condition.

Cunliffe says gas provider Enbridge is working with authorities as neighbours reported smelling natural gas prior to the blast.

Part of the house collapsed in the approximately 30 minutes it took for firefighters to beat back the blaze, Cunliffe says, causing an estimated $750,000 worth of damage.

Cunliffe says the twin explosions are an anomaly in Hamilton.

“We don’t get a lot of buildings that explode and quite frankly to have two in the same day within hours is really not something that we see a lot,” he told reporters at the scene.

The Ontario Fire Marshal’s office and Hamilton police are investigating the causes of the twin explosions.

Hamilton Mayor Andrea Horwath thanked firefighters, police and first responders for their quick response to the explosions and said her thoughts are with those who were impacted.

“I sincerely hope that everyone that was hurt is going to recover completely; and my heart goes out to those facing uncertainty and distress as a result of these incidents,” she wrote in a social media post.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Arrests and detentions of Canadians spike in the U.S. Travel registrations surge, too
stories.summary: Global Affairs Canada says the number of arrest and detention cases involving Canadians citizens has jumped 60 per cent.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Global Affairs Canada says the number of arrest and detention cases involving Canadians citizens has jumped 60 per cent.

The department’s annual report on consular cases , published today, tracks an increase in arrests between April 2025 and March 2026, despite a 25 per cent decline in visits by Canadians to the U.S.

The report does not explain what caused the increase, though U.S. President Donald Trump has expanded immigration raids and Canadians have reported facing uncomfortable questions from U.S. border officials.

Overall, the report tracks a one-fifth increase in the number of arrests of Canadians around the world, including a threefold increase in the number of arrests in Thailand.

Global Affairs Canada has warned in recent years that the growing frequency of wars and natural disasters is resulting in more consular cases that are more complex and expensive to manage.

The data also shows an increase in the number of Canadians voluntarily registering with the department when they go abroad, which helps Ottawa send safety advice and co-ordinate evacuations.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

By Allison Jones The Canadian Press

Two campuses of Citi College of Canadian Careers are among six schools the province blocked from the Ontario Student Assistance Program in May for the 2026-27 year, alleging “high-risk admissions” practices and other concerns.

They have filed an application in Divisional Court asking for a judicial review of that decision, similar to a court challenge by three Academy of Learning locations affected by the May order.

Image 9Image 10

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn did not base his decision on a “rational chain of analysis” connecting evidence to the ministry’s conclusions, and the order does not refer to any specific instances of alleged non-compliance, Citi College wrote in its court challenge.

“In making the decision, the minister reached findings regarding ‘compromised participation,’ ‘inadequate attendance tracking,’ and ‘inability to reliably determine bona fide studies’ that are not justified, transparent, or intelligible, having regard to the ministry’s own prior approvals ... and the systems and safeguards Citi College had previously implemented,” the school wrote.

Citi College had been approved to administer OSAP in each of the preceding 20 years, they wrote, and two audits by the ministry last year “concluded without adverse findings.” The ministry’s allegations have not been tested or proven in court.

Quinn’s decisions to bar the six schools from receiving OSAP this year come after Career Colleges Ontario had been warning for years about possible “suspicious” OSAP activity at a small number of schools.

The minister announced last week that KPMG started an audit in August of OSAP at career colleges and he referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police based on “serious concerns” uncovered in the audit’s preliminary findings. He did not name the colleges that were the subject of the concerns referred to police.

Citi College is not aware of being subject to any issues raised by KPMG or the OPP referral, its lawyer said.

A January 2025 letter from Career Colleges Ontario to the government highlights what it calls concerning increases in OSAP usage at 10 schools, including one school that saw a nearly 2,700 per cent increase in two years. The letter was filed as part of the Academy of Learning court challenge, and all of the schools listed except for Academy of Learning are redacted, so it is not known if Citi College was included.

Data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request earlier this year shows that Citi College’s two campuses had about 133 people on OSAP in 2021-22, and three years later that rose to 1,754 students, an increase of about 1,200 per cent.

A lawyer for Citi College said in a statement Wednesday to The Canadian Press about the judicial review application that the school “continues to maintain compliance with its regulatory obligations and support its existing students in completing their programs.”

Harris Rosen also wrote in a previous statement about the OSAP increases that a more accurate calculation would use a pre-pandemic figure and rely on a compound annual growth rate, in which case Citi College would have been at about 38 per cent per year.

“The percentage increase you’ve cited appears substantial largely because it is calculated from a relatively low 2021–22 base,” Rosen wrote.

“When that figure is considered alongside the expansion of online education, broader geographic accessibility, and the relatively short duration of my client’s programs, Citi does not believe the growth is as unusual as the percentage alone may suggest.”

In the court application, Citi College argues that the minister unfairly assessed the school based on new “technological and monitoring expectations” that weren’t previously communicated to them.

Those included continuous webcam participation, long-term IP retention, forensic IP analytics, and VPN prohibitions, Citi College wrote.

When Quinn announced last week that he had referred concerns to the OPP, he said many had centred around online-only programs. This fall, the government will introduce legislation to exclude predominantly online programs at private career colleges from OSAP eligibility.

In the meantime, Quinn has also paused OSAP payments at all private post-secondary institutions.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Supreme Court hears challenge of law clearing path for Ontario Place redevelopment
stories.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada plans to hear arguments from a coalition challenging the constitutionality of legislation that smooths the way for major changes at Ontario Place.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
The Supreme Court of Canada plans to hear arguments Thursday from a coalition challenging the constitutionality of legislation that smooths the way for major changes at Ontario Place.

The case unfolding in Canada’s top court could reverberate far beyond the Toronto waterfront park that opened in 1971.

Over the years, the theme park featured a spherical theatre that showed movies on a huge screen, children’s play areas, a revolving concert stage and several pavilions suspended above the water.

The provincial government wants to redevelop Ontario Place to include an elaborate spa operated by a private company, a relocated Ontario Science Centre, revamped play and shoreline areas, a parking facility and a provincial police detachment.

The coalition Ontario Place Protectors challenged the province’s Rebuilding Ontario Place Act on the basis that it insulates state action from scrutiny by the courts and therefore violates the Constitution.

The coalition also argued that exemptions from environmental and heritage laws and municipal noise regulations amount to a breach of public trust.

An Ontario judge dismissed the application in 2024 and a challenge of the ruling in the provincial Court of Appeal was also unsuccessful.

Writing on behalf of a unanimous Court of Appeal, Justice Grant Huscroft said there was no doubt that the provincial government’s decision to redevelop Ontario Place is strongly opposed by a number of concerned citizens and organizations.

Political opposition to the plan has not swayed the government and the coalition has turned to the court in an effort to stop it, Huscroft said.

“But there is no basis for the court to do so. The court is not an alternative forum for resolving political grievances. The only legitimate question for the court is whether the impugned provisions of Ropa violate the law or the Constitution,” he wrote.

“They do not, and the appeal must be dismissed.”

In January, the Supreme Court agreed to hear the Ontario Place Protectors’ case.

The coalition says provincial superior courts have historical and inherent jurisdiction to review laws and government actions protected under section 96 of the Constitution Act, 1867, and to provide effective remedies when governments do not respect the limits on their powers.

The coalition says the Rebuilding Ontario Place Act’s scope is unprecedented and appears to violate section 96 by removing the essential core powers of the courts.

It argues the legislation severely limits or entirely eliminates the ability of courts to hold Crown officials accountable through declaratory actions, damage awards and injunctions when they have acted beyond their powers.

The coalition is also seeking to have the doctrine of public trust acknowledged as an unwritten constitutional principle rooted in English common law and inherited by Canada.

It argues the doctrine of public trust maintains that natural and cultural assets are essential to public welfare and must be safeguarded by the state in its role as trustee.

Margie Zeidler, the daughter of Ontario Place architect Eberhard Zeidler, remembers visiting the park as a child.

“It was extraordinary. It was a public place,” she said in an interview. “You could have a picnic in the forest. You could watch films at Cinesphere. You could watch any musical performance at the forum.”

Zeidler, a member of the Ontario Place Protectors coalition, says the provincial government’s actions have made the fight about more than just the historic theme park. “It became more, not about Ontario Place, but about, wait a minute, what democracy are we living in here?” she said. “I didn’t know governments could do that.”

In their written submission to the Supreme Court, the Crown and the Ontario attorney general say the case should be dismissed.

The immunity provided by the provincial legislation does not go as far as the coalition alleges, the submission says: “(The act) does not make Ontario Place a lawless zone.”

Rather, it immunizes the Crown, its servants and agents from civil causes of action arising from specific circumstances, the submission says.

The Crown and attorney general also urge the court to reject the claim that the legislation is invalid because of the doctrine of public trust.

“The novel doctrine articulated by the Appellant is not an unwritten constitutional principle, and even if such a doctrine existed in law, which is denied, there is no evidence in the record that could warrant applying this far-reaching new doctrine to Ontario Place,” the submission says.

The case has attracted submissions from interveners, including several provinces, First Nations, civil liberties groups and environmental organizations.

The Supreme Court often reserves its decisions until a later date, meaning a ruling in the case might not come until next year.

stories.title: Kenora residents applaud ‘fantastic’ move to permanent daylight time
stories.summary: The provincial government announced Tuesday that northwestern Ontario communities west of the 90th meridian would stop the twice-annual clock changes.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Whether it’s watching NHL games, appointment scheduling or just less confusion, some residents of Kenora, Ont. say permanent daylight saving time is a “fantastic” move.

Scott Green, owner and operator of Lake of the Woods Marina and Service Centre, said Wednesday he loves that the community will stick to the same time zone as Manitoba going forward.

“I love it as long as we’re still matching with Winnipeg and Manitoba,” he said in an interview with Global News.

Green added his marina also has a restaurant and bar that hosts Winnipeg Jets watch parties during the season. He said with the permanent change, watching the game “just times out better.” He added it will also make it easier if travelling to Winnipeg for a Jets game.

The Ontario government announced Tuesday that northwestern Ontario communities west of the 90th meridian would stop the twice-annual clock changes and stay on daylight time year-round.

Kenora, along with communities like Dryden, Sioux Lookout and Pickle Lake, currently observe Central daylight time, the same time zone observed by Manitoba.

That means come Nov. 1, it will be the same time in Manitoba and all of Ontario. But when the clocks tick forward an hour in March for much of Ontario, people in the province’s northwest and Manitoba won’t have to adjust their time.

Tuesday’s announcement from the Ontario government came after what MPP for Kenora-Rainy River Greg Rickford says was “unanimous consensus” across the region.

“Through the collective efforts of communities and First Nations across the northwest, we’ve led a process to build consensus the right way, with detailed and nuanced considerations,” said Rickford in a news release on Tuesday.

Several communities conducted surveys from residents to see if there was support for a change.

In Kenora, about 6,000 of its approximately 16,000 residents responded to the survey and Mayor Andrew Poirier told Global News 93 per cent supported keeping daylight time.

“So we listened to the people of Kenora and we stand by what we did as a council to pass a resolution that we would look at aligning ourselves with Manitoba, and so did lots of our neighbouring communities, which was very important in this whole process,” Poirier said Wednesday.

The mayor said though in Ontario, Kenora is “much more linked” to Winnipeg or Manitoba.

He said whether during much of summer or winter, travel between the Ontario and Manitoba communities is “like the 401” highway that runs through Toronto.

“That’s how much economic activity, tourism, visiting back and forth occurs between the two jurisdictions,” Poirier said.

But it’s not just economic activity, it’s also logistical aspects like medical appointments or tourist bookings.

“So when somebody makes an appointment for a boat taxi or a tour and we are on the same page for a time frame (or) often Zoom meetings if people are calling out of Toronto you have to definitely make sure that you’re on the same time,” said Green. “So this will really make things efficient and a lot easier for bookings and communications.”

Northwestern Ontario is not the only region to observe a different timezone than the majority of the province it is in.

The Kootenay Region in B.C. is on Mountain Time, Nunavik and Lower North Shore in Quebec are on Atlantic Time and parts of Labrador are also on Atlantic Time unlike the rest of Newfoundland and southeastern Labrador.

Golden, B.C., Coun. Wesley Routley said his community last month originally planned to shift to Mountain standard time permanently on Nov. 1, but after hearing from hundreds of residents, council reversed course.

He said people felt they wanted to be aligned with other communities like the Regional District of East Kootenay to the south and other communities on Mountain daylight time.

He added a large share of visitors to Golden are from Alberta, so it could limit confusion for people visiting the community.

British Columbia, Alberta and Manitoba have each announced they will remain on daylight time starting Nov. 1, with Saskatchewan having observed central standard time year-round. The remaining provinces have said in recent months no changes are expected though discussions and analyses are ongoing.

He said whether during much of summer or winter, travel between the Ontario and Manitoba communities is “like the 401” highway that runs through Toronto.

content_blocks.text: “That’s how much economic activity, tourism, visiting back and forth occurs between the two jurisdictions,” Poirier said.
But it’s not just economic activity, it’s also logistical aspects like medical appointments or tourist bookings.

“So when somebody makes an appointment for a boat taxi or a tour and we are on the same page for a time frame (or) often Zoom meetings if people are calling out of Toronto you have to definitely make sure that you’re on the same time,” said Green. “So this will really make things efficient and a lot easier for bookings and communications.”

He said people felt they wanted to be aligned with other communities like the Regional District of East Kootenay to the south and other communities on Mountain daylight time.

stories.title: Doug Ford says Republicans might ‘pull the carpet’ under Trump if midterms are lost
stories.summary: As the mid-term elections draw closer, Ford is dipping a toe into American politics, stating that the Democrats might be able to flip the Senate and House of Representatives.
stories.author: Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford is predicting that Republicans might “pull the carpet out from underneath” U.S. President Donald Trump if the party loses the midterm elections in November, but warns that little would change for Canadians impacted by tariffs.

During a speech and fireside chat at the Empire Club, Ford also appeared to hold back his views on American politics and expressed concerns that Trump might use his comments to retaliate against its northern neighbour.

In recent months, as the trade war between the two countries escalated, Ford and Trump took multiple verbal swipes at one another.

In August, Ford called Trump a “loser,” the “king of bankruptcies,” and told him to “kiss my ass” while Trump called Ford the “less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, (former Toronto Mayor) Rob Ford”.

The war of words ended with the White House renaming Lake Ontario to Lake America, and Ford erecting a $25,000 sign asserting the correct name.

As the mid-term elections draw closer, however, Ford is once again dipping a toe into American politics, offering new hope that the Democrats might be able to flip the Senate and House of Representatives on Nov. 3.

“President Trump is not going to last forever. He has a couple more years,” Ford told the audience.

“I spent 20 years of my life in the U.S. If he loses the Senate and the House, the Republicans are just going to pull the carpet out from underneath him. He has about a 30 per cent base (support), but that’s even being dwindled down as well,” he said.

Ford’s comments come amid a warning from U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra to Canadian politicians to “keep your nose out of American politics”

During an appearance on The Really Big Show podcast, Hoekstra said Ford’s infamous 2025 Ronald Reagan commercial amounted to “election interference” and said the Trump administration is “closely watching Canadian activities.”

“We’re monitoring it, we’re evaluating it, and if some of it becomes election interference then we’ll respond to it.”

When asked during the fireside chat whether Trump could be “weakened by his own party” after the midterms, Ford said: “I got to pick my words here.”

“He’ll change another lake on me if I say anything else.”

stories.title: London researchers explore outcomes for patients with high potassium
stories.summary: Researchers have shown the risk of death was lower among patients who went to the emergency department soon after a high potassium reading.
stories.author: Crystal Mackay
stories.content:
High levels of potassium in the blood, common in people on certain medications or with kidney disease, often come with no symptoms, but can be deadly in severe cases.

Because people with hyperkalemia, or high potassium, often “feel normal,” their treating physicians must determine whether their condition can be safely managed outside the hospital or requires more urgent treatment in the emergency department.

Researchers at Western University and London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute (Lhscri) have shown that the risk of death was significantly lower among patients who were able to get to an emergency department within 24 hours of an abnormally high potassium reading. The study was recently published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal .

“The challenge is patients with hyperkalemia can feel completely fine, even when their potassium is at a dangerously high level. It can be difficult for patients to understand why they need to get to the emergency department right away,” said Dr. Michael Chiu, professor at Western’s Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry and scientist at Lhscri.

What’s the role of potassium?

Potassium is a normal electrolyte found in the body, but for people with certain kidney conditions or on some blood pressure medications, the body’s ability to flush the potassium is impaired, leading to a build-up in the blood. Because potassium is a key player in the electrical activity of the heart, elevated levels can trigger abnormal heart rhythms and potentially fatal cardiac arrest.

Using population health data from the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences , the researchers explored patients who weren’t already admitted to hospital to determine how many went to the emergency department and how that correlated with their risk of dying.

“It was the first study to investigate if patients with diagnosed high potassium were going to the emergency department or not, and for those who went, what their outcomes were,” said Chiu. “When people are admitted to hospital or seen in the emergency department, there are medications we can give that help protect the heart. There are also intravenous medications that can lower potassium levels quickly by moving it into cells or helping remove it from the body. These emergency treatments can only be done in a hospital setting.”

The team hopes to use this as a starting point to develop a clinical decision-making tool for health-care providers to consider patient characteristics like age and other chronic conditions, as well as laboratory values, when managing patients with a high outpatient potassium value and making a determination about whether or not they need in-hospital care.

“One of the reasons we wanted to do this research is that if we get a call in the middle of the night from a lab saying a patient has high potassium, we have to decide whether the patient needs to go to the emergency department and convince the patient why it is important to do so,” he said. “We also need to ensure that patients who May not benefit from in-hospital treatment, aren’t making an unnecessary trip to the emergency department.”

stories.title: Supreme Court will rule on Ottawa's single-use plastics ban
stories.summary: Ottawa - The Supreme Court of Canada says it will hear an appeal of Ottawa's ban on single-use plastics.
stories.author: Nick Murray The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Federal Court of Appeal overturned a lower court decision in January, allowing the federal government to keep the ban in place.

A 2023 Federal Court decision in a case brought by the plastics industry said Ottawa had overstepped by designating all “plastic manufactured items” as toxic.

Article continues below

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

Image 9Image 10Image 11

But in a unanimous decision in January, the three-judge appellate panel ruled the federal government’s decision to list plastic manufactured items as toxic was reasonable.

Ottawa used that designation to issue a ban on the manufacturing and importing of six types of single-use plastics, including straws, grocery bags, stir sticks and the six-pack rings used to hold soda and beer cans.

The government said it chose those items because they were commonly found in litter and had known and accessible alternatives.

This report from The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

stories.title: Fry and Sim face off in Vancouver, but other mayoral candidates reject spoiler label
stories.summary: Vancouver - Vancouver mayoral candidates Ken Sim and Pete Fry view each other as their main rival in the battle for City Hall.
stories.author: Marissa Birnie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VANCOUVER - Vancouver mayoral candidates Ken Sim and Pete Fry view each other as their main rival in the battle for City Hall.

But while recent polling suggests the mayoral race is indeed a faceoff between incumbent Sim and two-term Green Councillor Fry, there are three other big-name candidates who reject the label of spoiler.

Kareem Allam — Sim’s former chief of staff turned litigation adversary — is running with the Vancouver Liberals, which is not affiliated with the federal party.

“The pollsters don’t always get it right. Municipal government is also the hardest level to poll. It’s got its tricks and nuances, especially in an at-large system,” he said in an interview Tuesday.

The Vancouver race culminates Saturday, when municipalities across British Columbia go to the polls.

Interest in the Vancouver race appears high. The City of Vancouver says more than 103,000 people have voted in advance, up 60 per cent from roughly 65,000 voters over five advance days in 2022.

Sim, who is campaigning for a second term as mayor with the right-of-centre ABC Vancouver, said while he would be the first to admit he didn’t get everything right during his tenure, he believes he can lead the city in the right direction.

“We’ve gotten some pretty significant things done, but there’s way more work to do,” he said in an interview Wednesday.

Other candidates include Rebecca Bligh, a two-term councillor who helped get Sim elected with ABC Vancouver in 2022 and is now running with Vote Vancouver, and TEAM candidate Colleen Hardwick, a former councillor.

Allam, Hardwick and Bligh all rejected the notion their candidacies could split the centre or centre-right vote.

“The question is not left or right. The question is about who we are serving at city hall,” Hardwick said Tuesday.

Bligh said she was running to govern for Vancouver’s ignored middle class, and polling did not change how she campaigned.

“It’s anyone’s race,” she said in an interview Wednesday.

Fry, son of longtime Liberal MP Hedy Fry, has acknowledged benefiting from the narrowing of the progressive field, after the withdrawals of William Azaroff from OneCity Vancouver and Stephanie Allen for COPE Vancouver.

After ending his candidacy, Azaroff appeared at City Hall with Fry, who praised him for running a serious campaign that “raised real issues” such as housing, small business and affordability.

“I think folks are excited to be able to talk up a viable alternative to Ken Sim as the mayor of Vancouver and really reset,” Fry said in an interview Tuesday.

He added that Azaroff’s withdrawal was recognition that he was the person best suited to defeat Sim.

Bligh said she’s a progressive candidate with a centrist platform. Meanwhile, Allam said he believed he was taking votes from Sim and Fry equally.

The candidates’ platforms all emphasize quality-of-life issues, including affordability and public safety. Sim’s promises include a zero per cent property tax increase.

The election ballot also includes two plebiscite questions on public safety.

The non-binding questions ask voters if they’re in favour of the city “strengthening its laws to forbid open-air hard drug use in public spaces,” which is already illegal in B.C. The other asks if the city should ask the province to convert portions of the old St. Paul’s hospital into a “secure medical facility” with 100-plus involuntary care beds.

Hardwick called the questions a “populist election tactic,” while other critics said they aren’t realistic.

Sim said strengthening the city health bylaw — regulating conduct such as smoking in common areas — would allow officers to issue tickets or confiscate drugs without arrests. The involuntary care question, he said, is about asking the province to fulfil its accountability to people who pose a risk to their own safety or others.

Fry said he supports managing drug use in public spaces, but differs from Sim in believing that people should be diverted to supervised consumption sites or shelters.

His platform focuses on housing, transportation and the economy. “Folks should be able to have a good life in this city, he said.

Bligh said Sim’s property tax freezes protect wealthy landowners and undercut critical services. She said she would work with the federal government to leverage city-owned land and provide free transit for youth.

Hardwick said the key to livability in Vancouver is effective city planning. She said she wanted to repeal the city’s official development plan and re-establish neighbourhood planning offices

Allam said he wants to bring youth back to Vancouver by improving affordability through jobs and housing, and investing in parks and community centres.

He said his platform cuts across ideologies, and distanced himself from Sim, who filed a lawsuit in May 2025 alleging Allam falsely accused him of drinking and driving.

Sim faces his own defamation lawsuit from councillor Sean Orr, filed after falsely accusing Orr of distributing illegal drugs in comments to Chinese-speaking reporters.

Trials in both cases are far off.

For now, the focus is on the ballot box.

“I think people will be surprised at the results,” Allam said.

The Vancouver race culminates Saturday, when municipalities across British Columbia go to the polls.
Interest in the Vancouver race appears high. The City of Vancouver says more than 103,000 people have voted in advance, up 60 per cent from roughly 65,000 voters over five advance days in 2022.

Sim, who is campaigning for a second term as mayor with the right-of-centre ABC Vancouver, said while he would be the first to admit he didn’t get everything right during his tenure, he believes he can lead the city in the right direction.
“We’ve gotten some pretty significant things done, but there’s way more work to do,” he said in an interview Wednesday.

Other candidates include Rebecca Bligh, a two-term councillor who helped get Sim elected with ABC Vancouver in 2022 and is now running with Vote Vancouver, and TEAM candidate Colleen Hardwick, a former councillor.
Allam, Hardwick and Bligh all rejected the notion their candidacies could split the centre or centre-right vote.
“The question is not left or right. The question is about who we are serving at city hall,” Hardwick said Tuesday.
Bligh said she was running to govern for Vancouver’s ignored middle class, and polling did not change how she campaigned.
“It’s anyone’s race,” she said in an interview Wednesday.

Fry, son of longtime Liberal MP Hedy Fry, has acknowledged benefiting from the narrowing of the progressive field, after the withdrawals of William Azaroff from OneCity Vancouver and Stephanie Allen for COPE Vancouver.
After ending his candidacy, Azaroff appeared at City Hall with Fry, who praised him for running a serious campaign that “raised real issues” such as housing, small business and affordability.
“I think folks are excited to be able to talk up a viable alternative to Ken Sim as the mayor of Vancouver and really reset,” Fry said in an interview Tuesday.
He added that Azaroff’s withdrawal was recognition that he was the person best suited to defeat Sim.
Bligh said she’s a progressive candidate with a centrist platform. Meanwhile, Allam said he believed he was taking votes from Sim and Fry equally.
The candidates’ platforms all emphasize quality-of-life issues, including affordability and public safety. Sim’s promises include a zero per cent property tax increase.
The election ballot also includes two plebiscite questions on public safety.

The non-binding questions ask voters if they’re in favour of the city “strengthening its laws to forbid open-air hard drug use in public spaces,” which is already illegal in B.C. The other asks if the city should ask the province to convert portions of the old St. Paul’s hospital into a “secure medical facility” with 100-plus involuntary care beds.
Hardwick called the questions a “populist election tactic,” while other critics said they aren’t realistic.

Sim said strengthening the city health bylaw — regulating conduct such as smoking in common areas — would allow officers to issue tickets or confiscate drugs without arrests. The involuntary care question, he said, is about asking the province to fulfil its accountability to people who pose a risk to their own safety or others.
Fry said he supports managing drug use in public spaces, but differs from Sim in believing that people should be diverted to supervised consumption sites or shelters.
His platform focuses on housing, transportation and the economy. “Folks should be able to have a good life in this city, he said.

Bligh said Sim’s property tax freezes protect wealthy landowners and undercut critical services. She said she would work with the federal government to leverage city-owned land and provide free transit for youth.
Hardwick said the key to livability in Vancouver is effective city planning. She said she wanted to repeal the city’s official development plan and re-establish neighbourhood planning offices
Allam said he wants to bring youth back to Vancouver by improving affordability through jobs and housing, and investing in parks and community centres.
He said his platform cuts across ideologies, and distanced himself from Sim, who filed a lawsuit in May 2025 alleging Allam falsely accused him of drinking and driving.
Sim faces his own defamation lawsuit from councillor Sean Orr, filed after falsely accusing Orr of distributing illegal drugs in comments to Chinese-speaking reporters.
Trials in both cases are far off.
For now, the focus is on the ballot box.
“I think people will be surprised at the results,” Allam said.

stories.title: Supreme Court hears challenge of law clearing path for Ontario Place redevelopment
stories.summary: Ottawa - The Supreme Court of Canada plans to hear arguments today from a coalition challenging the constitutionality of legislation that smooths the way for major changes at Ontario Place.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - The Supreme Court of Canada plans to hear arguments today from a coalition challenging the constitutionality of legislation that smooths the way for major changes at Ontario Place.

The case unfolding in Canada’s top court could reverberate far beyond the Toronto waterfront park that opened in 1971.

Over the years, the theme park featured a spherical theatre that showed movies on a huge screen, children’s play areas, a revolving concert stage and several pavilions suspended above the water.

The provincial government wants to redevelop Ontario Place to include an elaborate spa operated by a private company, a relocated Ontario Science Centre, revamped play and shoreline areas, a parking facility and a provincial police detachment.

The coalition Ontario Place Protectors challenged the province’s Rebuilding Ontario Place Act on the basis that it insulates state action from scrutiny by the courts and therefore violates the Constitution.

The coalition also argued that exemptions from environmental and heritage laws and municipal noise regulations amount to a breach of public trust.

An Ontario judge dismissed the application in 2024 and a challenge of the ruling in the provincial Court of Appeal was also unsuccessful.

Writing on behalf of a unanimous Court of Appeal, Justice Grant Huscroft said there was no doubt that the provincial government’s decision to redevelop Ontario Place is strongly opposed by a number of concerned citizens and organizations.

Political opposition to the plan has not swayed the government and the coalition has turned to the court in an effort to stop it, Huscroft said.

“But there is no basis for the court to do so. The court is not an alternative forum for resolving political grievances. The only legitimate question for the court is whether the impugned provisions of ROPA violate the law or the Constitution,” he wrote.

“They do not, and the appeal must be dismissed.”

In January, the Supreme Court agreed to hear the Ontario Place Protectors’ case.

The coalition says provincial superior courts have historical and inherent jurisdiction to review laws and government actions protected under section 96 of the Constitution Act, 1867, and to provide effective remedies when governments do not respect the limits on their powers.

The coalition says the Rebuilding Ontario Place Act’s scope is unprecedented and appears to violate section 96 by removing the essential core powers of the courts.

It argues the legislation severely limits or entirely eliminates the ability of courts to hold Crown officials accountable through declaratory actions, damage awards and injunctions when they have acted beyond their powers.

The coalition is also seeking to have the doctrine of public trust acknowledged as an unwritten constitutional principle rooted in English common law and inherited by Canada.

It argues the doctrine of public trust maintains that natural and cultural assets are essential to public welfare and must be safeguarded by the state in its role as trustee.

Margie Zeidler, the daughter of Ontario Place architect Eberhard Zeidler, remembers visiting the park as a child.

“It was extraordinary. It was a public place,” she said in an interview. “You could have a picnic in the forest. You could watch films at Cinesphere. You could watch any musical performance at the forum.”

Zeidler, a member of the Ontario Place Protectors coalition, says the provincial government’s actions have made the fight about more than just the historic theme park. “It became more, not about Ontario Place, but about, wait a minute, what democracy are we living in here?” she said. “I didn’t know governments could do that.”

In their written submission to the Supreme Court, the Crown and the Ontario attorney general say the case should be dismissed.

The immunity provided by the provincial legislation does not go as far as the coalition alleges, the submission says: ”(The act) does not make Ontario Place a lawless zone.”

Rather, it immunizes the Crown, its servants and agents from civil causes of action arising from specific circumstances, the submission says.

The Crown and attorney general also urge the court to reject the claim that the legislation is invalid because of the doctrine of public trust.

“The novel doctrine articulated by the Appellant is not an unwritten constitutional principle, and even if such a doctrine existed in law, which is denied, there is no evidence in the record that could warrant applying this far-reaching new doctrine to Ontario Place,” the submission says.

The case has attracted submissions from interveners, including several provinces, First Nations, civil liberties groups and environmental organizations.

The Supreme Court often reserves its decisions until a later date, meaning a ruling in the case might not come until next year.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

stories.title: Fatal crash on Highway 401 near London
stories.summary: Highway 401 eastbound lanes are closed following a fatal multi-vehicle collision south of London.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Highway 401 eastbound and westbound lanes are closed following two collisions on the eastbound side, one being a fatal multi-vehicle collision south of London.

The first collision was at about 2:15 p.m. near Colonel Talbot Road and involved approximately three vehicles.

Just after 4 p.m. OPP responded to a second collision involving a transport truck and passenger vehicle, further down the highway near Union Road.

The transport truck collided with the rear of a passenger vehicle, that according to OPP was stopped in traffic. The vehicle burst into flames.

OPP says Highway 401 is closed between Colonel Talbot Road and Iona Road.

The number of deceased individuals is unknown at this time.

Motorists are being urged to plan alternate routes.

stories.title: Quebec publishing house stands by author amid AI allegations
stories.summary: Montreal - A Quebec publisher says it will keep Thélyson Orélien’s novel on bookstore shelves despite allegations that it was written using artificial intelligence.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - A Quebec publisher is standing by a novel by author Thélyson Orélien, saying it will remain on bookstore shelves despite allegations that it was written using artificial intelligence.

In a statement released Wednesday, Éditions du Boréal said it received the manuscript on Sept. 12, 2025 and could not verify allegations about the evolution of the book, ‘’C’était ça ou mourir,’’ which translates to “It was either that or dying,” before that date.

The decision to keep the book on sale comes despite lingering questions about the author’s writing process and earlier statements indicating Orélien and his publisher were gathering evidence to support his denial of using AI to write the novel.

The new statement came one day after the publisher released a statement from Orélien, admitting plagiarism in some of his earlier writings in Quebec and French media, while reiterating that he had not used AI for the book.

Orélien said in the statement that he began writing his novel in the fall of 2017, while living in Laval, north of Montreal, completing a first draft of more than 300 pages in 2019, around the time he learned of his mother’s death. He said he spent the following years revising scenes, characters and passages.

The publisher did not confirm this timeline in its new statement. It said it would have liked to provide definitive answers to the allegations, but that it had no evidence beyond Orélien’s word to establish how the novel was written before it was submitted.

Boréal said on Wednesday that the author’s decision not to disclose further details about his writing process was his to make, arguing that publishers should not be expected to monitor authors.

“The publisher’s role is not to demand proof from authors, but to stand by them, and that is what we are doing,” the publishing house said.

The new statement contrasts with what Orélien and his publisher said in September, when Boréal announced it was collaborating with him to compile a detailed record of his work related to his manuscript, before the publisher got involved.

While Orélien told French media outlet Libération the compilation would prove what he was saying about his work, the publisher did not confirm this.

“We would have liked to provide a definitive answer,” the publisher said at the time, adding that it was unable to either confirm or refute the allegations related to AI use.

In his latest statement released on Tuesday through Boréal, Orélien said he had nothing to prove to those making accusations against him.

The publisher’s Wednesday statement did not address the earlier efforts to compile records.

Éditions du Boréal did not immediately respond to questions from The Canadian Press about whether it had revised its efforts or approach.

Orélien also did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The author previously said the novel draws on his experiences of migration and exile, as well as stories he heard from others.

He acknowledged occasionally using tools for research, including to look up foreign expressions, but insisted that no sentence in the novel had been generated by a machine.

“I wrote this novel myself,” he said, describing the allegations as an attack not only on his identity as a writer but also on his humanity.

In its Wednesday statement, Boréal unequivocally condemned the plagiarism in Orélien’s earlier writings, saying the findings violated some of its most deeply held values.

But it also defended the author against personal attacks, arguing that the controversy over artificial intelligence did not justify making him a scapegoat for broader fears about the technology’s growing role in creative work.

Orélien said Tuesday that he had faced threats, racist harassment and what he described as a media lynching over the allegations.

He said that after leaving Haiti following the devastating 2010 earthquake, he became fascinated by the work of numerous authors and sometimes sought to imitate their styles, and admitted making some mistakes.

“Admiration does not give you the right to take, to claim as your own texts that are not yours,” he wrote, apologizing for what he described as unacceptable mistakes.

The allegations have triggered some consequences. Orélien’s novel was removed from the running for France’s prestigious Prix Goncourt earlier this month amid the AI allegations and separate questions about plagiarism in his previous work.

Boréal also suspended promotional activities surrounding the novel in September, citing concerns for Orélien’s well-being.

In its latest statement, the publisher said the novel would continue to be sold in bookstores in the absence of definitive findings about the AI allegations, leaving readers to decide whether to purchase it.

According to the websites of major bookstore chains Renaud-Bray and Indigo, the novel remains available for purchase at most of their locations across Quebec.

’‘It is our job as booksellers to make books accessible to our customers,’’ said Renaud-Bray spokesperson Floriane Claveau.

Claveau said no major variation in the book sales had been observed over the past few weeks.

Boréal acknowledged Wednesday in its statement that the controversy raises questions extending well beyond one novel, particularly about the trust between authors, publishers and readers.

It said it was undertaking a broader reflection on the lessons to be learned from the case and how to continue protecting and promoting human creativity.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Key figure in Pearson gold heist says he’s having trouble testifying due to trauma
stories.summary: A man who admitted his role in the Toronto Pearson airport gold heist is telling the trial for another man accused in the case that recalling his alleged abduction in Pakistan on the stand is leaving him traumatized.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
The testimony of a key player in the Toronto Pearson airport gold heist has been adjourned until next week after he told a Brampton court Wednesday that recalling details of his alleged abduction in Pakistan on the stand has left him traumatized.

Arsalan Chaudhary is serving a four-year prison sentence after pleading guilty to theft over $5,000 in what police have called one of the largest gold heists in Canadian history.

He took the stand Tuesday in the trial of Parmpal Sidhu, who has pleaded not guilty to charges of theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence in the 2023 heist.

Chaudhary testified that he’d planned the heist with Simran Preet Panesar, who is still wanted by authorities, and ended up taking 30 per cent of boxes full of one-ounce gold bars. He said he melted some of the gold and sold it for cash before travelling to Pakistan, where he claimed people in police uniforms kidnapped and abused him.

He said he believed the kidnappers learned he had money from a man who helped him procure his gold-melting machine. He said he was released after giving up the remaining gold he kept in a Greater Toronto Area condo and the cash he had at his cousin’s house in Pakistan.

When Chaudhary returned to the witness stand on Wednesday, he said he couldn’t sleep the previous night after telling the story of his abduction.

“My memory is very vague when I have locked out a lot of stuff from my memory, so that’s why I cannot remember,” he said in response to questions from the Crown.

“If you’ve been through the trauma that I’ve been through, and been shocked and had bruises, you would probably understand where I’m coming from.”

Chaudhary said he has been kept at Maplehurst Correctional Complex for about three weeks, where he didn’t receive his prescribed medications including melatonin and vitamins.

“Last night, I couldn’t sleep. I had terrors, night terrors. I couldn’t eat when I got back, so it does affect me,” he said. “So, that’s why I’m not able to help you, but I would like to.”

He asked the court to send him back to the Collins Bay Institution, a federal prison in Kingston, Ont., where he is serving his sentence.

“I’ve been in Maplehurst, living with three people in a cell by a toilet, and I’ve been not getting no medical attention. I’ve asked for it,” he said.

“I’m not in the right state of mind to remember stuff you’re asking me,” he told the Crown.

After some discussions between prosecutors and defence lawyers, Superior Court Justice Gordon Cudjoe issued an order to return Chaudhary to the Collins Bay Institution and bring him back to the Brampton courthouse on Monday morning to resume his testimony.

Cudjoe also told Chaudhary he will make a recommendation to the prison to have him assessed by a medical professional.

During his testimony on Tuesday, Chaudhary said he didn’t really know Sidhu and that he only called or texted him when he couldn’t get ahold of Panesar.

The Crown asked Chaudhary about text and group chat messages related to the heist, but he repeatedly said he did not remember or recall the content of these conversations, nor who was involved in them.

Prosecutors allege that Sidhu, an Air Canada employee at the time, provided a doctored waybill that allowed another man to pick up more than $22 million in gold and currency from a Pearson airport cargo bay.

Peel regional police have said 6,600 gold bars weighing more than 400 kilograms were stolen from the airport on April 17, 2023, after the shipment arrived from Switzerland.
paragraphs: The testimony of a key player in the Toronto Pearson airport gold heist has been adjourned until next week after he told a Brampton court Wednesday that recalling details of his alleged abduction in Pakistan on the stand has left him traumatized.
Arsalan Chaudhary is serving a four-year prison sentence after pleading guilty to theft over $5,000 in what police have called one of the largest gold heists in Canadian history.
He took the stand Tuesday in the trial of Parmpal Sidhu, who has pleaded not guilty to charges of theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence in the 2023 heist.

Chaudhary testified that he’d planned the heist with Simran Preet Panesar, who is still wanted by authorities, and ended up taking 30 per cent of boxes full of one-ounce gold bars. He said he melted some of the gold and sold it for cash before travelling to Pakistan, where he claimed people in police uniforms kidnapped and abused him.

He said he believed the kidnappers learned he had money from a man who helped him procure his gold-melting machine. He said he was released after giving up the remaining gold he kept in a Greater Toronto Area condo and the cash he had at his cousin’s house in Pakistan.
When Chaudhary returned to the witness stand on Wednesday, he said he couldn’t sleep the previous night after telling the story of his abduction.
“My memory is very vague when I have locked out a lot of stuff from my memory, so that’s why I cannot remember,” he said in response to questions from the Crown.
“If you’ve been through the trauma that I’ve been through, and been shocked and had bruises, you would probably understand where I’m coming from.”
Chaudhary said he has been kept at Maplehurst Correctional Complex for about three weeks, where he didn’t receive his prescribed medications including melatonin and vitamins.
“Last night, I couldn’t sleep. I had terrors, night terrors. I couldn’t eat when I got back, so it does affect me,” he said. “So, that’s why I’m not able to help you, but I would like to.”
He asked the court to send him back to the Collins Bay Institution, a federal prison in Kingston, Ont., where he is serving his sentence.
“I’ve been in Maplehurst, living with three people in a cell by a toilet, and I’ve been not getting no medical attention. I’ve asked for it,” he said.
“I’m not in the right state of mind to remember stuff you’re asking me,” he told the Crown.

After some discussions between prosecutors and defence lawyers, Superior Court Justice Gordon Cudjoe issued an order to return Chaudhary to the Collins Bay Institution and bring him back to the Brampton courthouse on Monday morning to resume his testimony.
Cudjoe also told Chaudhary he will make a recommendation to the prison to have him assessed by a medical professional.
During his testimony on Tuesday, Chaudhary said he didn’t really know Sidhu and that he only called or texted him when he couldn’t get ahold of Panesar.

The Crown asked Chaudhary about text and group chat messages related to the heist, but he repeatedly said he did not remember or recall the content of these conversations, nor who was involved in them.

Prosecutors allege that Sidhu, an Air Canada employee at the time, provided a doctored waybill that allowed another man to pick up more than $22 million in gold and currency from a Pearson airport cargo bay.
Peel regional police have said 6,600 gold bars weighing more than 400 kilograms were stolen from the airport on April 17, 2023, after the shipment arrived from Switzerland.

stories.title: Longtime London MP Irene Mathyssen dies at age 75
stories.summary: Former NDP MP Lindsay Mathyssen announced her mother's passing on Tuesday, saying she always strived to make the world a better place.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Longtime member of Parliament Irene Mathyssen, who served the London, Ont., region both provincially and federally under the NDP banner, has died at the age of 75. She had been battling cancer.

Former NDP MP Lindsay Mathyssen announced her mother’s passing on social media on Tuesday.

“To Londoners and Canadians, she was known for her public service, her dedication to her community, and her commitment to the people and causes she believed in,” she said in a statement on Facebook.

“She believed that our responsibility is to leave this world a better place than we found it. That belief is part of her legacy and I will do my best to honour it throughout my life.”

Mathyssen was first elected provincially in 1990 and served as Ontario’s tourism minister.

She was elected to represent London federally in 2006 and held her seat of London—Fanshawe until her retirement from politics in 2019.

During her time as MP, Mathyssen notably led a successful effort to remove the federal portion of the sales tax from menstrual products.

NDP Leader Avi Lewis said she will be remembered as someone “who fought relentlessly for our movement, and for a Canada that upholds the dignity of every person.”

“In calling for a housing bill of rights, the expansion of EI for workers, and fighting for women’s liberation, Irene pushed to make life better for people on every front,” Lewis said in a statement.

Conservative London-area MP Andrew Lawton said in a media statement that Mathyssen was “a tireless advocate for her values and her constituents and was always generous with her time when I was working in radio.

“My thoughts are with Keith (Irene’s husband) and Lindsay.”

Peter Fragiskatos, Liberal MP for London Centre, called her a “profoundly important” community voice.

“She spoke up for those who had been forgotten and ignored and always approached her work with kindness, humility and dedication. This was a true public servant,” he said in a media statement.

Mathyssen was succeeded in the House of Commons by her daughter Lindsay, who held the seat of London—Fanshawe until 2025.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 14, 2026.
